articles.title: Deepx Building Open Software Ecosystem to Scale Physical AI Beyond the Data Center - EE Times
articles.text:
The next competitive battle in edge AI may not be decided by TOPS alone, according to Lokwon Kim, founder and CEO of Deepx, in an interview with EE Times Asia. The more consequential question, he said, is whether AI semiconductor companies can make their technology easy to develop, deploy, and scale.`
That does not make silicon less important. Kim’s view is that hardware remains the entry point, but software and ecosystem support determine whether a technical advantage becomes a sustainable commercial position.
Deepx has built its strategy around this distinction as it shifts from developing low-power AI accelerators to building a broader platform for physical AI. The company is connecting its neural processing units (NPUs) to existing model frameworks, development platforms, and embedded systems rather than building an entirely closed software stack.
The strategy reflects a broader challenge facing physical AI. Unlike cloud AI, where developers can often work within relatively standardized computing environments, physical AI must operate across cameras, robots, vehicles, drones, industrial equipment, and other systems with widely different power, thermal, sensor, operating-system, and real-time requirements.
For Deepx, that fragmentation has become one of the biggest barriers to moving AI projects beyond proof of concept.
“We see the physical AI semiconductor business developing in three stages. First, differentiated hardware performance must earn the customer’s initial selection. Second, a company must expand design wins and mass production, commercialize at scale, and build a defensible position through a strong portfolio of foundational IP. The third stage is to create an ecosystem in which developers can continuously build and deploy AI models and software using tools that are already familiar and broadly adopted,” Kim said.
Beyond the TOPS race
Edge AI hardware has traditionally been evaluated using metrics such as TOPS and performance per watt. Those measurements remain relevant, particularly in power-constrained systems, but they don’t capture the full requirements of physical AI.
For Deepx, the challenge is translating hardware performance into products that customers can develop and manufacture at scale.
The company points to Nvidia as an example of how a hardware advantage can become a much larger ecosystem advantage. Nvidia’s long-term differentiation has not depended solely on individual GPU generations’ performance. CUDA has created a development environment around the hardware, giving developers an established set of tools and workflows.
Physical AI, however, does not yet have an equivalent undisputed ecosystem leader.
“Physical AI semiconductors do not yet have an undisputed incumbent with that level of ecosystem dominance. That makes this period particularly important. Whoever succeeds in building an open developer ecosystem and establishing a de facto standard early can shape the market for years to come,” Kim said.
Deepx is therefore pursuing an open approach that connects its NPUs to ecosystems developers already know. Its collaborations include Ultralytics YOLO, Baidu PaddlePaddle, and Raspberry Pi, while the company is also working on support for Nvidia Isaac applications and other software environments.
The objective is straightforward: reduce how often developers have to rebuild their software as an AI application moves from experimentation to production.
Closing the PoC-to-production gap
For many physical AI projects, demonstrating that an AI model can run is only the first step. Production introduces a different set of engineering constraints.
A system must operate consistently across thousands or millions of units, meet a defined power budget, stay within thermal limits, support the required models, meet cost targets, and provide predictable long-term supply and software support.
Deepx identifies four major barriers between proof of concept and mass deployment: power and thermal constraints, model compatibility, total system cost, and production readiness.
Power is particularly unforgiving in physical AI. Cameras, drones, and robots cannot simply adopt data center-class processors and cooling systems. The processor must fit within the physical and thermal constraints of the product.
“The first is power and thermal constraints. Physical AI products such as cameras, robots, and drones cannot accommodate data-center-class power consumption or cooling systems. If power and heat exceed the physical limits of the product, no other advantage can compensate. This is a non-negotiable constraint,” Kim said.
Model compatibility creates another potential failure point. A semiconductor may show strong benchmark performance, but if converting and optimizing the customer’s models degrades accuracy or requires extensive software redevelopment, that advantage can disappear.
System cost is equally important. Customers evaluate the complete bill of materials rather than the NPU price in isolation. Memory, host processors, power management, cooling, and other components all contribute to whether an AI-enabled product can meet its commercial target.
Finally, production readiness requires more than a successful evaluation board. Customers need dependable supply, manufacturing yield, quality control, long-term software support, and evidence from actual production and field deployment.
That changes a semiconductor vendor’s role.
“A semiconductor vendor therefore cannot stop at supplying a chip and demonstrating performance. It must help the customer run the required models, reduce system-level power and cost, and work alongside them from software integration and pilot production through quality validation and volume manufacturing,” Kim said.
The implication is that the most important benchmark may ultimately be how quickly a customer can turn an AI model into a commercially viable product.
Portability becomes a design requirement
This is where software portability matters most.
Physical AI projects rarely start on the final production platform. Developers typically begin with a familiar model, a camera, and an accessible development board. Once the application is validated, the system must transition to industrial hardware.
That transition can introduce significant engineering work if the software environment changes with every hardware platform.
Deepx’s collaboration with Raspberry Pi aims to address this problem by providing developers with an accessible starting point and a path to industrial deployment. The company wants developers to be able to validate vision models and applications on familiar hardware before moving to industrial cameras, robots, gateways, and production systems using the same Deepx execution environment.
The company has identified three lessons from its early developer engagement. First, the entry point must be simple, with documentation, installation procedures, familiar workflows, and technical support carrying significant weight. Second, hardware decisions can be influenced during prototyping, well before production. Third, an easy development platform is not enough unless developers can carry their models and software into industrial validation and production.
That creates a different definition of portability. It is not simply about moving an application between two boards. It is about preserving the developer’s initial software investment throughout the product lifecycle.
An open stack for a fragmented market
Deepx does not expect physical AI to converge on a single software platform in the same way Android became a dominant smartphone operating system.
A robot’s hardware and operating requirements are fundamentally different from those of a camera, vehicle, drone, or medical device. Instead, Kim expects the industry to converge around multiple de facto standards at different layers of the stack.
PyTorch, Ultralytics, and PaddlePaddle are positioned around model development; ExecuTorch can support lightweight edge deployment; llama.cpp is becoming relevant for generative AI; and ROS 2 and Nvidia Isaac provide important assets for robotics development.
“The central question is not who owns every layer of the stack. It is who can connect different models, frameworks, and hardware platforms to actual silicon and production products with the least friction. Developers will not accept having to rewrite their software for every new processor,” Kim said.
The company’s objective is not to own every layer of software. Instead, it wants its NPU and execution environment to become a common hardware foundation across several ecosystems.
Distributors become engineering partners
Deepx’s ecosystem strategy also extends into its distribution network.
As it began mass production of its first commercial product, the company established partnerships with 27 distributors, including Avnet, WPG, Macnica, and DigiKey, as well as regional partners across several markets.
Kim argues that the role of a semiconductor distributor has changed as AI moves into industrial applications. Distribution is no longer limited to inventory, logistics, and sales. Partners increasingly provide technical support, identify customers, engage in engineering, and support design-in activity.
Different applications also require different channels. Robotics, machine vision, factory automation, security, and healthcare have distinct procurement structures and technical-support requirements.
Intelligent vision as the first mass market
Among physical AI applications, intelligent vision appears closest to large-scale commercialization.
The reason is partly the size of the installed base. Security, video surveillance, transportation, retail, factory monitoring, and machine vision already have extensive camera deployments, while the AI models used in many of these applications are comparatively mature.
There is also a relatively direct economic case. AI can automate continuous video monitoring or visual inspection, reduce labor requirements, and identify incidents or defects faster. Importantly, companies can often add an edge AI processor without replacing the entire camera or infrastructure.
Smart manufacturing is another near-term opportunity. Asia-Pacific’s position within global manufacturing and electronics supply chains, combined with labor shortages and pressure to improve quality, is driving adoption in machine-vision inspection, worker safety, predictive maintenance, and logistics automation.
Robotics may eventually represent the largest physical AI market, but it is also considerably more difficult.
A vision system primarily needs to perceive and analyze. A robot must perceive its environment, decide, and execute physical action in real time. An incorrect perception can therefore become an incorrect movement or a safety event.
This raises the requirements for reliability, model robustness and system integration.
Kim identifies real-world model reliability, power and thermal constraints, system cost, software compatibility, connectivity and safety as the major remaining barriers. Physical AI models must maintain performance despite changes in lighting, vibration, weather, camera angles, and obstacles.
The resulting architecture cannot depend entirely on cloud connectivity. A robot or industrial machine must keep making immediate decisions when network connectivity is lost, or cloud responses are delayed. Data privacy can also keep sensitive industrial or personal information on the device.
For these reasons, on-device inference is an architectural requirement, not merely an alternative to cloud computing.
From edge AI to Federated AI
In Kim’s view, the next stage of physical AI development will require something resembling MLOps for distributed devices.
Cloud AI benefited from mature workflows that connect model training, deployment, monitoring, and updates. Physical AI remains much more fragmented, with deployment and operational management often handled independently for individual devices and projects.
That model will not scale when AI is deployed across millions of cameras, robots, and industrial machines.
Kim identifies five requirements: secure cloud-device communication; a reliable fleet-wide model; software deployment with rollback mechanisms; simple tools for managing field equipment; and unified monitoring of device status, performance, power, errors, and model accuracy.
Deepx describes the resulting architecture as “Federated AI,” while distinguishing it from federated learning.
Under this model, the data center handles training and centralized management, edge devices perform inference and control where latency, security, and energy efficiency matter, and gateways connect the two where necessary.
The company is working with AWS IoT Greengrass toward an environment where models trained in the data center can be securely deployed to devices, run locally on Deepx NPUs, and managed centrally as a fleet.
The significance is less about moving all AI out of the cloud than about dividing workloads where computation makes the most sense.
Physical AI as infrastructure
That division matters more as AI infrastructure hits physical constraints.
Kim points to the growing gap between the pace of AI model development and the time required to build data centers and energy infrastructure. AI models can advance in months, while new power capacity and large data-center projects take years to build.
He argues this mismatch will push more inference to the edge.
Deepx’s internal analysis compares data center GPU systems with on-device AI systems across power, servers, cooling, and network resources. The company says it found potential for about a 100-fold improvement in resource efficiency in some applications and system configurations.
The company is also examining whether increasingly capable models can operate within low-power devices. In an internal architecture-level simulation involving a 100-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model, with approximately 10% of parameters active at any one time, Deepx identified the potential for a single 5-W-class AI accelerator to generate more than 10 tokens per second. The company notes that the 5-W figure applies to the chip itself, while total system power varies with memory capacity, configuration, and operating conditions.
Deepx’s workload research further suggests that models at or below the 100-billion-parameter class could potentially handle more than 80% of inference requests in the physical AI scenarios it is targeting. Under that scenario, the data center would handle the remaining, more complex workloads, potentially allowing existing central infrastructure to serve more users or devices.
These figures are not presented as universal benchmarks. They illustrate the architectural leverage that becomes possible as more inference moves onto devices.
That is the central idea behind Deepx’s vision of physical AI as infrastructure.
The data center will continue to train frontier models and process the most demanding workloads. But cameras, robots, vehicles, drones, industrial equipment, and personal devices can increasingly perform inference locally.
In this architecture, billions of devices stop being simple endpoints waiting for instructions from centralized infrastructure. They become distributed computing nodes.
The next computing layer
Kim sees the transition as analogous to the move from desktop computing to mobile computing.
Low-power CPUs moved computation into handheld devices, creating a new mobility-focused computing model. Deepx expects ultra-low-power AI semiconductors to make a similar transition possible for AI, moving inference from centralized data centers into the machines and objects operating in the physical world.
The company describes this emerging class of devices as “Free-Token Machines”—not because token generation is literally free, but because local inference can occur without a data-center charge for every interaction and without continuous dependence on network connectivity.
The concept extends beyond inference. As models become capable enough and power-efficient enough to run locally, cameras, robots, and industrial systems can become agentic machines that perceive their surroundings, make decisions, and act.
That does not eliminate data centers. It changes what they are responsible for.
The cloud remains the center of frontier-model training and large-scale computation, while local devices absorb workloads where latency, privacy, power efficiency, and connectivity make centralized processing less practical.
The competitive question for edge AI is therefore broader than which NPU delivers the most TOPS per watt.
The question is whether an AI semiconductor platform can make the entire journey—from model development and prototyping to deployment, fleet management, and production—so straightforward that physical AI becomes repeatable at scale.

articles.title: Hacker Conversations: Corey Thuen and the Evil Bit
articles.text:
Corey Thuen is a hacker with a hacker mindset that is focused on the right way to do wrong things to get the right result.
Corey Thuen is the founder and CEO of Gravwell, a firm with a slight difference: it develops data analytics and vulnerability detection through a combined team of big data experts and hackers.
When interviewing a candidate for the hacker half of the team, he looks for people who have what he calls ‘the evil bit’. “Do they have that ‘evil streak’? Do they have that adversarial mindset that can look at a product and seek out ways to exploit it? If they don’t have that evil bit, I don’t think we can teach it.” He accepts that it may be possible for some people to develop one, but in his own experience, it’s either there or it’s not. Natural-born hacker is more a fact than a description; and it is tempting to describe Thuen as a natural-born hacker himself.
But does ‘evil’ indicate a lack of morality? “Who defines morality?” he replied. “Who defines what is good and what is bad? The old school hacking ethos, which still lingers, is that all information should be free”. Other folks consider that a bad viewpoint.
“I was recently working for the US government. We were evaluating the systems that go into power substations, part of the critical infrastructure. So, we were hacking these systems, but the goal was to improve security for everyone. We were using the evil streak for good. Hacking skills are a bit like guns. Neither are evil in themselves. They can be used for both good and bad purposes depending on the motives of the user.”
How old was he when he realized he’s a hacker? “I knew I was a hacker at a very young age; and from that moment onward, it was all I wanted to do. I had always been interested in computers and how they work, so when an uncle gave us an old Packard Bell while I was still in high school, the first thing I did was sit down and read the DOS manual from cover to cover.”
This interest was not hereditary. None of his family were technology-minded, and he had no resources beyond his own curiosity before the Packard Bell. But this led to video games – the archetypal introduction to hacking for many of today’s hackers. With access to a game’s save files and a hex editor, he started tinkering. “Where are the bytes that control how many lives I’ve got? Can I change them to give myself infinite lives?” And then he watched Hackers. “It was like, Oh my gosh! I want to do that. I want to fly around in cyberspace and hack the Gibson. All these guys are so cool!”
Despite his ‘messing around’, and despite the movie-inspired dream of hacking a Gibson, Thuen never did any immoral or harmful hacking. But he wasn’t squeaky clean. “Back then, it wasn’t crystal clear that we were doing anything wrong. We didn’t realize we could get into trouble. It was simply, ‘If I dial this number, I get into this system. What is it? I don’t know, so I’ll poke around a bit.” Thuen’s youthful hacking was curiosity rather than malicious intent.
“I would stand up these systems and mess with them, right? How does this vulnerability work? So, I’d set up a database on a website just to understand SQL injection – but I wouldn’t then go out looking for systems to exploit. I guess that was a line I just didn’t want to cross. I wasn’t much of a rule-breaker.”
After high school, he attended the University of North Dakota and gained a bachelor’s in computer science. He enjoyed the course but felt it was lacking a security program even though the tech elements were good. “North Dakota taught me how to do a bunch of things. Maybe the geography also helped. North Dakota is flatter than your table, so it’s pretty easy to run cables around. I was able to do cool dial-up stuff. So that was a contributing factor,” he added.
After that, he went to the University of Idaho to do his master’s in computer science. It was a scholarship for service (SFS) program run by the government. “Basically,” he explained, “you get a scholarship, but then you have to work for Uncle Sam for a few years after school so that Uncle Sam gets something back from the investment.”
When that time came, he looked at his options. Most of the government positions were on the East Coast. He, however, came from a small town with a population of around 7,000.
He attended a few East Coast interviews, but they didn’t appeal, and he concluded his options were the unpalatable East Coast or one of the Department of Energy institutions in different parts of the country – and one of them was (and is) in Idaho.
The Idaho National Laboratory (INL) is the Department of Energy’s leading center for nuclear energy research and development, and is also a globally recognized authority on protecting industrial control systems (ICS) and operational technology (OT). Technically owned by the Department of Energy, it was (and still is) managed by the private Battelle Energy Alliance (BEA).
“So, I ended up at INL, and I’m so glad I did. I worked with a great team, and it was there I first met my future co-founder of Gravwell [Kristopher Watts, now CTO]. That time was what really kicked the doors open for me messing around with how computers work.”
Corey worked at INL until 2013, at which time he left together with Kenneth Shaw and the two co-founded Southfork Security. This was where he first got into trouble following his initial “Hey, let’s hang a shingle moment” – something he had always wanted to do.
With Southfork, he explained, “I thought, ‘Maybe we can do some security testing. We’ve got a pretty good set of skills. Let’s take the idea to the private sector and see what we can do with it.’ I made some open source tools under Southfork Security, and that turned into a whole new saga.”
That saga was complex and messy, partly hinging on his early use of the term ’hack’ without implying bad intentions. Hack and hacking did not have the moral neutrality the terms have today, but he nevertheless described Southfork as “We hack things and make tools.” Hold that thought in the background. In the foreground, he and Shaw had worked together on an INL ICS cybersecurity tool called Sophia. The practice at INL was to develop software and then effectively roll it out to the private sector.
Now in the private sector, Southfork made a bid for Sophia during its commercialization process. That sounds reasonable since the two founders had been instrumental in its development within INL, but it soon became clear that the new firm was not going to win the bidding process.
“So, I basically started from scratch and made an open source tool [called Visdom] that sought to solve the same issues as the Sophia tool but would be open source.”
This is where it becomes messy. How different can a second attempt at solving the same problems be from the first attempt? BEA (for INL) decided it was no different and sued Thuen and Southfork Security for copyright infringement, trade secret misappropriation, and breach of employment agreements, alleging that Visdom was illegally derived from proprietary INL code.
The case never came to a public trial, but behind the scenes under judicial review it first looked likely that Thuen would lose, then appeared he might win, and ended with a voluntary surrender, probably because of lack of funds to proceed. It looked as if he would lose when BEA immediately achieved an aggressive ex parte temporary restraining order allowing forensic experts to image Thuen’s computer hard drives and temporarily block the release of the Visdom software code. It was argued that Thuen was a self-described (malicious) hacker (‘We hack things and make tools’) who might destroy evidence.
As the case progressed, it appears the judge had a change of heart. BEA’s initial call for an injunction was rejected, dissolving parts of the restraining order; and a request for summary judgment by BEA was rejected. The case was going nowhere fast, but BEA would outlast Southfork if only on the basis of funds. The two sides reached a private settlement before any important precedents could be decided by the court. Visdom was surrendered to BEA and Southfork effectively dissolved, largely because the court initially and wrongly stereotyped its founders as malicious hackers.
Following the wind-down of Southfork, Thuen moved to Digital Bond in 2014. As a senior researcher he focused on industrial control systems, IoT security, and vulnerability research. He left Digital Bond at the end of 2015 and moved to IOActive as a senior consultant. This was a natural fit for his mindset: IOActive is an offensive security company where members often describe themselves as pirates working on the right way to do wrong.
He left IOActive in 2017 and founded Gravwell, where, nearly ten years later, he remains CEO. At Gravwell he wrote a guest blog for IOActive in 2020 titled Hiding in the Noise. It provides insights into both his history and attitudes. “I spent a number of years at Idaho National Laboratory, Digital Bond, and IOActive. At these places, my job was to find 0-day vulnerabilities on the offensive side of things.”
For all of these companies he focused on ICS. The initial focus arose because that was INL’s focus, but he retained the interest because it was challenging and a bit different.
“You’re doing protocol reverse engineering, including some custom protocols that you must dissect and do low-level network binary type things. All that was super interesting. General IT systems have kind of coalesced around certain technologies – everything is web now, for example. So, ICS stuff is challenging and quite interesting. I got into vehicle research, which is closely related to ICS with all those embedded systems; and so that bit was kind of fascinating to me.”
He describes Gravwell as a data analytics platform for security logs, machine, and network data. “I believe that defense involves more than looking for how threat actor XYZ operates, it requires an understanding of the environment and maximizing the primary advantage that defense has – this is your turf and no one knows it like you do.”
Corey Thuen is a complex character. He has the hacker mindset but has never been tempted into any form of malicious hacking. He was a little bit naughty as a youngster, but never nasty – he has what he seeks when recruiting for Gravwell: “the evil bit”. But it is not ‘evil’ in the traditional sense. It is the ability to be naughty but never nasty in order to achieve a good intent.
This attitude also appears in what he describes as ‘spite’ (but again, not in the negative or nasty sense of ‘spiteful’). “The best way to get hackers to spend extra time and get good work out of them is to say, ‘This system is unhackable’, because then, yeah, okay, all right…” he explained.
“I think I have an overactive sense of justice and an overactive sense of spite. If I’m told this cannot be done when it absolutely can, then I’ll do it for spite. Just because you say something doesn’t mean it’s true.” Saying something is unhackable is a direct challenge to any hacker.
He also has an entrepreneurial side. He has founded two separate companies. The first, Southfork Security, failed somewhat controversially. The second, Gravwell, is now almost ten years old (compare that to the short time he spent working for other companies). This suggests a need to be the master of his own destiny. But it also introduces an apparent contradiction in his personality. Hackers break things. Entrepreneurs build things. Corey Thuen does both, but always with a bit of a twinkle, a sense of humor, and a liberal sprinkling of colloquialisms.

articles.title: Meta leva multa de US$ 25 bilhões em processo do Cambridge Analytica • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
Meta leva multa de US$ 25 bilhões em processo do Cambridge Analytica
Processo na Justiça dos Estados Unidos aponta mais de 43 milhões de violações.
Uma decisão judicial no estado do Novo México, nos Estados Unidos, condenou a Meta a pagar US$ 25 bilhões (R$ 75 bilhões, na cotação atual) em multas. A corte concluiu que a empresa de Mark Zuckerberg enganou os usuários de suas redes sociais quanto aos esforços para proteger seus dados e combater a desinformação e a disseminação de discursos de ódio. A denúncia foi feita em 2021, após o escândalo do Cambridge Analytica.
A empresa teve acesso ilegal a informações de mais de 50 milhões de perfis e atuou na campanha de Donald Trump para seu primeiro mandato na presidência dos EUA. Na decisão, o juiz responsável afirmou que foi encontrado um “número extraordinário de violações intencionais” por parte da Meta, além do envolvimento direto de lideranças do Facebook.
Essa é uma das maiores multas aplicadas a uma empresa na história dos Estados Unidos, de acordo com a Procuradoria-Geral do Novo México. A Meta, por sua vez, afirmou em nota que a decisão visa “impor novas regras para o que as pessoas podem dizer na internet”. Ela disse que irá recorrer da decisão.
Em 2018, uma investigação da imprensa dos EUA apontou para o uso ilegal de mais de 50 milhões de contas nos Estados Unidos. Mais tarde, o próprio Facebook reconheceu que cerca de 87 milhões de usuários haviam sido afetados – mais de 70 milhões nos Estados Unidos. Como o Tecnoblog mostrou à época, quase 500 mil brasileiros também tiveram seus dados comprometidos.
Os dados utilizados pela Cambridge Analytica tiveram origem em um aplicativo de quizz disponibilizado no próprio Facebook, o “thisisyourdigitallife”. Cerca de 270 mil perfis participaram do teste, criado pelo psicólogo Aleksandr Kogan. As informações levantadas foram, então, repassadas ilegalmente à empresa, que os utilizou para fins políticos.
A empresa do Reino Unido prestava serviços de consultoria em redes sociais para diferentes políticos em corridas eleitorais.
A decisão judicial já havia sido anunciada em setembro, mas a punição saiu apenas nesta quarta-feira (21/10), praticamente cinco anos após a denúncia formal e oito anos após o escândalo da Cambridge Analytica vir à tona. A justificativa para os cerca de R$ 75 bilhões em multas dá conta de uma participação ativa da Meta, com mais de 42 milhões de violações registradas.
De acordo com o juiz responsável, Raúl Torrez, a sentença vai além do escândalo em si, e mostra que nenhuma empresa pode enganar seus consumidores quanto ao uso de suas informações pessoais sem “enfrentar consequências significativas”.

articles.title: Switch 2 security takes a hit as hackers unlock homebrew access
articles.text:
A security researcher has demonstrated a software-only partial jailbreak of the Switch 2, gaining “userland” access that he says “lets us run homebrew, reverse engineer and mod Switch 2 games, back up save files off the Switch, and access most of the Switch 2’s peripherals through MMIO.”
The hack relies on the original Switch version of SmileBasic 4, the latest in a long-running series of programming environments and interpreters that run on Nintendo hardware. The so-called “tethered” hack also requires access to a macOS or Linux PC on the same network to run a node.js package that helps enable privileged system access.
Researcher Sammy Hajhamid writes that he used OpenAI’s Codex to poke at SmileBasic’s language interpreter, using a custom harness that could send USB commands to the system and view results via HDMI (as well as power cycling via a Bluetooth light switch flipping device). After “substantial effort for ~2 weeks,” that harness discovered a 32-bit integer overflow that occurs when removing items from an array in SmileBasic. That error gives access to an array pointer, which in turn allows read and write access to portions of system memory.
From there, Hajhamid writes that he started poking around for access to the Switch 2’s internal sysmodules, looking for ones that could provide more privileged access to the console’s core functions. Eventually, he found a buffer overflow in the console’s FileSystem services module that exposed a cached data pointer, granting arbitrary read and write privileges. From there, Hajhamid writes that he could execute “privileged filesystem actions” and eventually achieve native code execution through a faked filesystem process.
Hajhamid, who goes by Pepsipu online, showed off a host of new modded characters in Mario Kart World as a proof of concept for the exploit. Others are similarly showing off simple demos and in-progress developer tools running on exploited hardware.

articles.title: OpenAI working on new $30B raise at $1.25T valuation ahead of IPO | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC.
This follows a similar report by Bloomberg a month ago which said the AI lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change. CNBC reports that the UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, too. OpenAI declined comment.
Should OpenAI command a valuation of more than $1 trillion with this round, it would break records as the most valued private company ever. That valuation would also raise the bar even higher for OpenAI’s forthcoming IPO. OpenAI filed confidential paperwork for an IPO in June, after its last raise in March valued the ChatGPT maker at $852 billion post-money.
That high valuation could also have ramifications for Anthropic’s IPO, which many believe is closer to materializing. (Rumors suggest we could see Anthropic’s public S-1 filing any day now.) The latest reports have Anthropic seeking a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation for its public debut, CNBC reports. Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation in May in what many believed at the time would be its last big round before an IPO. It also filed confidential paperwork in June.

articles.title: Tesla says some Model Y owners could join its Robotaxi fleet around Q2 2027
articles.text:
The big picture: Tesla boss Elon Musk has long promised that autonomous vehicle owners could one day lend their cars to the company's Robotaxi fleet to earn passive income. However, Tesla's timeline has remained vague until now. Although the company is making real progress on its self-driving ambitions, its recent projection may just be the latest in Musk's long string of overconfident predictions.
During Tesla's third-quarter earnings call on October 21, VP for Autonomous Driving Ashok Elluswamy announced the company's aim to let some Model Y owners add their vehicles to Robotaxi's autonomous fleet around the second quarter of 2027. The feature, which would enable users to earn money from ride-hailing, has long been one of CEO Elon Musk's core promises.
Several years have passed since Musk first stated that Tesla owners could one day program their autonomous vehicles to search for fares when not in use. This is possible because the software that runs the company's fully autonomous Cybercabs can also run on the Model Y, which will receive it with the release of V15. However, the vehicles would also need to be integrated into Tesla's geofenced operating areas and fleet-management system before they could join the Robotaxi service.
 – Tesla (@Tesla) October 21, 2026
Entrepreneurs might be able to establish small ridesharing businesses with private fleets of Teslas or Cybercabs. However, the company's history with deadlines suggests that, if this vision becomes reality, it will likely happen much later than the second quarter of 2027.
Musk initially estimated that a million robotaxis would be on the road by 2020, but Tesla didn't launch the service until the summer of 2025, when a small number of vehicles began operating in parts of Austin. While the cars drove themselves, the company still hired human monitors to accompany riders in case something went wrong.
Those vehicles have since recorded more crashes per mile than typical human drivers. The primary cause might be what enabled Tesla to deploy its cars more cheaply than rivals like Waymo: self-driving software that only uses vision to scan its surroundings. In contrast, Waymo and Zoox also use radar and lidar for better range and accuracy.
Tesla currently operates a few hundred Robotaxis in Texas and Florida, and some still contain human supervisors. Musk attributes the slower-than-expected rollout to an abundance of caution over safety.
Despite the company's longer-than-expected struggle to distribute fully autonomous taxis across the US, customer interest is rising. More than three-quarters of new Tesla buyers in North America opted for Full Self-Driving (Supervised) last quarter.

articles.title: Canadian VC industry hails federal funding boost, but timing and early-stage gap remain concerns
articles.text:
The federal government shared hotly anticipated details on how a $1.75-billion CAD commitment would be distributed to the Canadian venture capital industry in Toronto today.
While Canada’s VC investors largely welcomed the announcement, some cautioned that they’d still like to see more financial support for the country’s early-stage startups, while others wondered how much longer they would still have to wait for the new funding to trickle down into the market.
The VC strategy includes two main tenets: $750 million for the Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy, and $1 billion for the Growth Venture Capital Catalyst Initiative (Growth VCCI), the fourth and largest iteration of the government’s VC program.
“All stages are important, but the added emphasis on growth was what was missing.”
John Ruffolo
Maverix Private Equity
Industry groups had competing ideas for how the $750-million envelope should be allocated. The National Angel Capital Organization (NACO) had wanted funds funnelled to the earliest stages, while the Canadian Venture Capital & Private Equity Association (CVCA) had argued the envelope should be targeted to growth companies at the Series B stage and beyond. The Canadian Startup Capital Association (CSCA) was somewhere in the middle, asking the feds to allocate 10 to 20 percent to pre-seed and seed stages, with the remainder to growth.
In the end, $675 million was earmarked for “later- and growth-stage” gaps—for tech firms scaling at the Series B stage and beyond—and the remaining $75 million was dedicated to pre-seed and seed-stage startups. Later-stage deals often require larger cheque sizes in general to scale, compared to pre-seed and seed deals, most of which fall under $10 million in Canada.
CVCA lauded the announcement, which fell more in line with its asks than with NACO’s. “Today’s announcement gives Canadian managers and investors a substantial new base of federal capital to work with,” CVCA CEO Benjamin Bergen said in a statement.
Despite the smaller allocation toward pre-seed and seed funding, NACO CEO Claudio Rojas called it a “positive development.”
RELATED: Feds reveal breakdown of $750-million VC funding envelope, open Growth VCCI applications
“This adds capacity at the stage that past programs didn’t reach,” Rojas told BetaKit. He added that NACO will continue to share its thoughts with the government on how the pre-seed and seed stream should function. Before any of that envelope can be allocated, the industry is awaiting consultations for the pre-seed and seed investment portion and calls for proposals for that and the growth-stage stream. It’s currently unclear how long this might take.
Maverix Private Equity founder and managing partner John Ruffolo told BetaKit he was very pleased with the fund allocation, calling it “a great shot in the arm for the venture and growth ecosystem of entrepreneurs.”
“All stages are important, but the added emphasis on growth was what was missing,” Ruffolo said in a text message.
At the same time, Nectarios Economakis, a partner at early-stage firm Amiral Ventures, said he was disappointed more was not earmarked for the earliest stages, and questioned how helpful $675 million would be spread across a handful of growth-stage deals.
“If we don’t invest early—and we see it on the ground right now—those companies will leave Canada.”
Michelle McBane
StandUp Ventures
“It feels like a spread-the-peanut-butter strategy” to satisfy multiple camps, Economakis told BetaKit. “The pre-seed and seed is a drop in the bucket in terms of the scale of the problem.”
GreenSky Ventures partner Neil Peet echoed the disappointment at how little was given to early stage, but applauded the overall influx of capital from the government. “I’m not sure how that’s going to move the needle exactly, but the devil is in the details, and I’m optimistic,” Peet told BetaKit at the event.
Michelle McBane, managing director at seed-stage firm StandUp Ventures, told BetaKit that she was happy to see some allocation for the early stage. “If we don’t invest early—and we see it on the ground right now—those companies will leave Canada, and they won’t be there as an opportunity to invest at the later stages,” she said.
It’s a concern reflected by some other investors, who have pointed to a capital crunch as one reason why Canada faces a consistent founder and talent exodus to the US. “The reason a lot of great founders are leaving is because there’s no money,” Economakis said. “We say no to so many good people, because we can’t fund them all.”
However, Council of Canadian Innovators CEO Patrick Searle said in an interview that the growth-stage investments will particularly help in areas that have a longer runway to commercialization and are “critical for our economic security and sovereignty in Canada,” like deep tech, AI, and life sciences.
RELATED: Canadian tech firms are selling to foreign buyers when it’s time to scale, CCI says
In a recent report, CCI had identified a lack of growth financing as a key reason why scaling Canadian companies end up selling too early to foreign buyers. The organization welcomed the federal announcement but argued that the funding would be more likely to succeed if paired with other changes to make Canada a more competitive place to build a company, such as the QSBS-style tax incentive change that CCI is asking for in the upcoming federal budget. “What we also need to see is a focus on a competitive investing environment,” Searle said.
As for the $1-billion Growth VCCI portion, industry minister Mélanie Joly announced that calls for expressions of interest for the program are now open, and guidelines were made available on the government’s website shortly after. Its streams include a core, $700-million VC stream for fund-of-fund managers, $200 million for life sciences firms, and $100 million for emerging managers, who typically invest in early-stage companies.
According to the call for expressions of interest document for the fund-of-funds stream, the selected fund manager will be expected to hold a first close of its fund-of-funds within 18 months of its federal investment. The same timeline applies for selected firms to establish a Canadian presence with “meaningful activities in Canada.”
The biggest priority now, according to Bergen, is timing. The federal call for expressions of interest for the first stream of Growth VCCI will close in January; based on past iterations of the program and the new guidelines, it will likely take at least 12 to 18 months before the capital reaches fund managers and, ultimately, tech startups. This is because funds must apply and be approved for the program, and raise external private capital amid a difficult fundraising environment.
Regarding a potential 18-month estimate, Economakis said the process should be done faster. “Tech is literally changing all of society,” he said. “It’s much more strategic for the country to be active in the sector than to treat it as an equivalent of financial services or natural resources. This is the moment.”
“The next gold stamp of success will be the speed with which government moves forward on the deployment of both—the Growth VCCI, but also on the [$750-million] envelope,” Bergen said.
When asked about concerns over how long Growth VCCI funds might take to reach the ecosystem, Ruffolo was succinct: “Better late than never!”
With files from Josh Scott. Feature image courtesy Benjamin Bergen via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Kenyan startup StudyLabAI gives students an AI tutor built on their own course material - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Kenyan ed-tech startup StudyLabAI has built an AI-powered study platform that turns students’ own slides, lecture recordings and notes into interactive study tools, and has signed up more than 90,000 learners across over 100 countries without raising outside funding.
Founded in August 2024 by Abdulrahman Yunis and Anas Kali, StudyLabAI is aimed at students aged 14-25, and the teachers who teach them. Users upload a PDF, lecture recording, slide deck or other study material, and the platform turns it into study tools in seconds.
“Our mission is to give every student a personal tutor, whatever their background,” said Yunis, the startup’s lead engineer. “Everything is grounded in your own course material rather than the general internet.”
Students can turn a chapter into a narrated video lesson, practise with adaptive quizzes and mock exams, review flashcards scheduled through spaced repetition, and generate notes, mind maps and audio recaps. A lecture recorder and YouTube-to-notes tool round out the offering, alongside a 24/7 AI tutor.
“It answers questions about the student’s own material and points to the exact slide or recording timestamp it drew from. It also asks follow-up questions to check understanding,” Yunis said. “The app tracks how strong each student is on every topic and feeds weak areas into the next day’s study plan, so they always know what to study next.”
The platform works in most major languages, with notes, flashcards and tutor answers following the language of the source material.
A teachers’ edition, launched in January 2026, lets educators generate video lessons, lesson plans aligned to curricula such as IB, IGCSE, AP and SAT, and differentiated worksheets, while a dashboard tracks grades and flags students who are falling behind.
“We see AI as a force multiplier: it automates the routine work so students and teachers can spend more time on real learning and human connection,” said Yunis. “It supports teachers; it does not replace them.”
Yunis started the company in his final year studying Computer Science and Engineering.
“The idea came from our own late nights. At 2am in the library, we were drowning in hundreds of lecture slides and messy notes, and spending more time organising our material than actually learning it. The process was broken,” he said. “We realised every student deserved a personal tutor available around the clock, one that adapts to them and works from their own material.”
He built the platform end to end, including the web and mobile apps, AI features and cloud infrastructure, while Kali works on product and data engineering. The pair saw three problems in the market.
“Good tutoring is expensive. One-to-one help works, but most students cannot afford a private tutor, especially outside wealthy markets,” Yunis said.
“General AI chatbots are not built for studying. They answer from the whole internet, not from what a student’s course covers. They can be confidently wrong, and they make it easy to copy answers instead of learning. And most study apps are priced for students in rich countries.”
StudyLabAI sits in between, giving students the patient, personal help of a tutor, grounded in their own material, at a price students can afford. Students mostly compare the platform to general AI assistants such as ChatGPT, and to study tools such as Quizlet, Chegg and Google’s NotebookLM.
“Our difference is the combination of a voice tutor, video tutor, answers grounded in each student’s own notes, and pricing that works for students worldwide,” said Yunis. “We are careful not to build technology for its own sake. Many edtech tools are impressive but go unused. We start with conversations with real students and teachers, find where learning gets stuck, and only then decide how AI can help.”
StudyLabAI runs on a freemium model, with students and teachers paying a monthly or yearly subscription in local currency for unlimited generation and, for teachers, advanced analytics. The startup is bootstrapped and profitable.
“We have grown on revenue from paying students rather than outside investment, which has forced us to keep costs low and build features students will actually pay for,” Yunis said.
Uptake has been largely organic, with students finding the platform through TikTok, Instagram and Google search. Its largest markets are the United States, Europe, the Middle East and Africa, and more than 1 million lessons have been created on the platform.
“We support international curricula such as IB, IGCSE, AP and the SAT, as well as custom syllabuses, which is part of why we travel well across borders,” said Yunis.
The journey has not been without its challenges.
“Every tutor session and summary costs us money in AI computing, so we have had to keep the product affordable for students while covering those costs,” he said. “Students also need answers they can rely on. Grounding every answer in the student’s own notes was our response to that.”
StudyLabAI is now offering free pilot programmes to schools and institutions so whole classes can use the platform with teacher dashboards, and plans to add more languages, including Arabic, as well as exam preparation for specific national curricula.
“Our growth so far has come from individual students and teachers,” said Yunis. “Now we want to bring StudyLabAI to whole schools.”

articles.title: Quest Diagnostics sufrió un ciberataque que expuso historiales médicos de sus pacientes en Estados Unidos
articles.text:
Quest Diagnostics, la mayor red de laboratorios clínicos de Estados Unidos, informó que sufrió un ciberataque con acceso no autorizado a historiales médicos de sus pacientes, según reveló la propia empresa ante el regulador bursátil del país.
La compañía, que según su propio sitio institucional atiende a uno de cada tres adultos estadounidenses y a la mitad de los médicos y hospitales del país cada año, detectó la intrusión el miércoles y notificó a las autoridades federales al día siguiente.
El dato quedó asentado en una presentación ante la Comisión de Bolsa y Valores de Estados Unidos (SEC, el organismo que regula los mercados financieros del país), a la que accedieron varios medios estadounidenses.
El acceso indebido afectó al Quanum Lab Services Manager, la plataforma que algunos médicos y centros de salud usan para solicitar análisis de laboratorio en nombre de sus pacientes y consultar los resultados una vez procesados. La empresa dijo que un atacante no identificado habría visto “ciertos historiales de pacientes”, aunque el alcance exacto todavía está bajo investigación.
Quest Diagnostics remarcó que, hasta el momento, el incidente no alteró de forma significativa sus operaciones comerciales y que ya trabaja junto a una firma externa de ciberseguridad para contener el ataque y determinar con precisión qué información quedó expuesta y a cuántas personas afectó.
Qué antecedentes hay de filtraciones
No es la primera vez que los sistemas de la compañía quedan comprometidos. En 2016, Quest Diagnostics reconoció la exposición de datos de contacto y resultados de laboratorio de unas 34.000 personas en una violación anterior.
El antecedente más grave ocurrió en 2019, cuando la información personal de casi 12 millones de pacientes de la empresa quedó expuesta tras un ataque a American Medical Collection Agency, un proveedor externo que gestionaba cobros para Quest Diagnostics y otros laboratorios del país.
Ese episodio de 2019 se convirtió en uno de los mayores incidentes de privacidad médica registrados en Estados Unidos y derivó en demandas colectivas contra la empresa y contra la firma de cobros responsable de resguardar los datos de los pacientes.
Por qué atacan la industria sanitaria
El nuevo ciberataque se suma a una serie de incidentes recientes contra la industria de la salud estadounidense. Según informó la agencia Reuters, fabricantes de dispositivos médicos como Abbott, Stryker, Medtronic y Boston Scientific también reportaron intrusiones en sus sistemas en los últimos meses.
La farmacéutica Novo Nordisk y el proveedor de equipos de administración de medicamentos West Pharmaceutical Services enfrentaron además amenazas similares, de acuerdo con la misma fuente, lo que refleja una presión creciente de los atacantes sobre un sector que concentra datos médicos sensibles de millones de personas en sus sistemas.
La propia Quest Diagnostics aclaró ante la agencia de noticias The Associated Press que este ataque no está relacionado con las vulnerabilidades críticas detectadas días atrás en PHP, el lenguaje de programación utilizado por el 70% de los sitios web del mundo, que esta semana obligó a una ronda urgente de parches en todo el planeta.
La distinción resulta relevante porque ambos episodios ocurrieron casi en simultáneo y generaron preocupación entre empresas de distintos rubros sobre la seguridad de sus plataformas digitales, aunque se trata de fallas y ataques de origen independiente entre sí.
Las leyes federales de salud en Estados Unidos obligan a empresas como Quest Diagnostics a notificar a los pacientes afectados una vez que se determine con precisión qué historiales quedaron expuestos, un proceso que en el episodio de 2019 demandó varios meses de investigación.
Mientras persiste la incertidumbre sobre cuántas personas resultaron afectadas esta vez, Quest Diagnostics continúa con la investigación interna y mantiene el contacto con las autoridades federales para determinar el origen y el alcance real de la intrusión a su sistema de gestión de resultados de laboratorio.

articles.title: Hacienda obliga a tributar por las propinas que reciben los trabajadores, pero cotizarán si lo recoge el convenio o las gestiona la empresa
articles.text:
Dejar un par de euros sobre la barra, redondear la cuenta a mano alzada o pulsar un 10% al pagar con el datáfono: la propina es un gesto cotidiano en bares y restaurantes, y para muchos trabajadores de la hostelería supone un complemento importante del sueldo base. Lo que no está claro es qué ocurre con ese dinero cuando llega al bolsillo del camarero: si Hacienda lo ve, si hay que declararlo o si la empresa tiene que cotizar por él. O, como hacía mi antiguo jefe, si mete mano en el bote y se las guarda, ¿se puede reclamar?
Para Hacienda. Empecemos con lo que dice la Agencia Tributaria. Como recoge elEconomista, la Administración obliga a tributar todas las cantidades que los empleados reciben como propinas. Sí, igual que un salario. La base es el artículo 17.1 de la ley del IRPF, que considera rendimientos del trabajo las contraprestaciones derivadas del trabajo personal o de la relación laboral. La Dirección General de Tributos aplica ese criterio en sus consultas vinculantes. Da igual que el dinero lo ponga un cliente por voluntad propia: hay que incluirlo en la declaración.
Y no es nuevo. Las propinas no están reguladas de forma específica en nuestro ordenamiento, más allá de lo que algunos convenios colectivos dicen sobre su gestión y reparto. El tratamiento fiscal sale de la interpretación de Hacienda, que lleva años manteniendo el mismo criterio.
Tributar no es lo mismo que cotizar. Si el diablo está en los detalles, aquí tenemos al demonio: que una propina “pague” IRPF no implica que entre automáticamente en la base de cotización a la Seguridad Social. Por norma general no se cotiza por ellas, salvo que lo recoja el convenio colectivo. Hay convenios que sí obligan a hacerlo (transportes). Por eso, el primer sitio donde mirar es el convenio aplicable, sea sectorial, provincial o de empresa.
¿Y si la empresa se mantiene al margen? El criterio que citan los despachos es que, mientras el empresario no intervenga en la propina ni en su reparto y esta sea una donación directa del cliente al trabajador, no tiene consideración de salario. En ese caso no se cotiza. El ejemplo típico es el cliente que deja unas monedas a quien le ha atendido. El trabajador, eso sí, sigue obligado a declararlas en su renta, donde se suman al resto de sus ingresos del trabajo sin ningún tipo especial.
¿Y si la empresa las gestiona? Cuando es la empresa la que decide a qué trabajadores se abonan y por qué importe, la propina deja de ser gratificación voluntaria de un tercero y pasa a la base de cotización. Lo mismo sucede con las que se pagan con tarjeta: el dinero entra en la cuenta del negocio y, si luego se reparte, la empresa asume un papel activo, así que debe cotizar y tributar como rendimiento del trabajo. Además, tiene que reflejarlas en nómina y practicar la retención correspondiente a cuenta del IRPF.
El TPV y Bizum dejan rastro. El bote de monedas siempre ha sido difícil de controlar para la Agencia Tributaria, y en la práctica no siempre se trata como debería. Con la propina digital es distinto. Si se marca en el datáfono queda registrada en el terminal. Si llega por Bizum, también deja rastro bancario. El periodista económico José María Camarero lo explicaba en la COPE: al verse en el TPV, el empleador debe incluir lo repartido en la nómina. Asesorae advierten de, en que la hostelería, una declaración incorrecta puede acabar en sanción, tanto para el trabajador como para la empresa.
Sin IVA. Según una consulta vinculante de la DGT, cuando recibe una propina, la empresa actúa como intermediaria entre el cliente y el trabajador. No la percibe como contraprestación de un servicio, así que no tiene que declararla a efectos de IVA. Con el IRPF, en cambio, la empresa sí es la obligada a retener cuando interviene.
En resumen, si eres trabajador y el cliente deja dos euros en tu plato, apúntala y declárala en la renta como parte de los rendimientos del trabajo. Si va directa al bolsillo, sale de la contabilidad, claro, por tu riesgo y cuenta. Si la reparte la empresa, comprueba que aparece en la nómina y que se ha practicado la retención. Si eres empresario y gestionas el bote, lo razonable es fijar un sistema de reparto claro y documentado, respetar lo que diga el convenio y reflejar todo en nómina.
En un país de bares y barras, terrazo y terrazas, la propina es voluntaria para el cliente, pero no para quien se la embolsa. Cotizar ya depende de quién la maneje. Cuando ni la ley ni el convenio dicen nada, la salida habitual ha sido repartir la propina equitativamente entre todos. Y recuerdo: todos son todos, cocina y servicio por igual. Y, por cierto, los españoles no son tan tacaños como se suele creer: solemos dejar un 10%, como casi todo el mundo.

articles.title: Egyptian prop-tech Aqar Exit raises $183k funding - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Egyptian prop-tech startup Aqar Exit has secured an investment of EGP10 million ($183,000) from businessman Ayman Mamdouh Abbas, executive chairman of Intro Holding Group, in return for a 10 per cent stake in the company.
Founded in July, Aqar Exit operates a platform for transferring property purchase contracts, targeting buyers who are struggling to meet installment obligations on their real estate units.
The platform connects these sellers with prospective buyers seeking properties at their original contract prices, without paying additional premiums, commonly known in Egypt’s property market as overprice.
Under the company’s model, sellers can seek to recover the amounts they have already paid towards their properties without incurring contract assignment fees.
The investment follows Aqar Exit’s participation in the fifth season of Shark Tank Egypt, where it presented its business model to investors. The company will use the new capital to develop additional products and support its expansion into international markets, with a particular focus on the Gulf.

articles.title: Study Finds AI-generated Code Fails to Boost Productivity Due to Downstream Bottlenecks
articles.text:
A recent Harvard study of 718 firms, using the Jellyfish analytics platform, finds that although AI coding assistants and agents increase code volume, this does not translate into a corresponding increase in completed work, partly because AI-generated code increases the workload in later stages of development, particularly code review.
The study was based on approximately 300 million work events of 700,000 workers across 700+ firms from January 2021 to March 2026. The data was gathered from several sources such as HR information, code version control systems, issue management systems, scheduling tools such as Google Calendar, and generative-AI tools, including GitHub Copilot, Cursor, and Claude Code.
The researchers considered three measures of coding output: lines of code added, commits, and pull requests.
AI assistants lead to small increases in code output — 12% for lines of code, 9% for commits, and 5% for pull requests — with only the effect on commits being statistically significant. AI agents lead to large and significant increases in all three measures: 30% for lines of code, 20% for commits, and 23% for pull requests.
The authors used these data to evaluate software output by the number of Jira issues and epics resolved per worker per month, with issues treated as individual units of engineering work, and epics as larger projects or features. Coding assistant were found not to increase the number of resolved issues, while agents brought a 12% increase. However, this is significantly smaller than the estimated 30% increase in lines of code.
To explain this chasm, they examined the overall development process, which encompasses multiple steps beyond coding, including feature and scope planning, code reviews, testing, and deployment.
We impute time usage from the Jellyfish data and validate this imputation using a survey of 100 Prolific engineers, finding that engineers spend 30-40% of their time writing code; the remainder goes to these complementary tasks. When AI raises productivity in code writing, complementary steps may serve as bottlenecks.
Specifically, they found that the average PR time to review increased by 49%, the number of comments per PR rose by 53%, and the share of PRs requiring changes doubled. Additionally, the share of workers performing code reviews increased by 14%, with no improvement coming from the adoption of AI to assist with the reviews. They authors also noted that the increase in PR-related effort could not be explained by an increase in the size of individual PRs.
Commenting on the findings, Reddit user Prime_1 observed that "every line of code is a potential liability", a point further developed by markehammons, who highlighted the additional risk of AI hallucinations:
Doubly so when you're dealing with an untrustworthy actor, and agents are more untrustworthy than most actors. They can do the most messed up stuff without any hint of malice, and in a misguided attempt to pursue the task given to them.
Reddit user enigmamonkey further suggested that mean time to recovery could become an increasingly important metric for assessing AI’s impact on software development:
If your engineers are writing and understanding less and less of the code they ship, I imagine issues become more frequent and more complicated to resolve. Particularly as the codebase scales… and it will scale.
Jellyfish is a software company that provides a platform for measuring and analyzing software engineering performance. It connects data from tools such as GitHub and Jira to help companies understand developer productivity and software delivery.

articles.title: Companies are bringing in more AI than ever — but employees are increasingly just working around it
articles.text:
Companies are bringing in more AI than ever — but employees are increasingly just working around it
Half of workers use unapproved tools every month
- New report finds clear mismatch between employer perception and worker sentiment
- Hybrid workers experience the most difficulty with collaboration tools
- Half of workers say they use unapproved tools over workplace software
New research from Ricoh has found businesses to be investing heavily in AI for workers, but those workers aren't exactly experiencing the productivity gains advertised on the tin.
There's a clear mismatch, with 91% over business decision-makers believing their AI investments are delivering the expected value, but one in two (53%) workers actually find those AI tools are creating friction or additional work.
Another half (55%) even go as far as saying the time spent managing poor technology interferes with their productivity.
Workers aren't being given the right AI tools
Ricoh analyzed four key workplace technologies – AI tools, communication and collaboration tools, data access tools and workflow management tools – and found AI to have the least impactful productivity boost.
An overwhelming majority (90%) of decision-makers also feel optimistic about how connected their tools and systems are, and yet three in four (76%) employees are calling out for systems that work better together.
"Fragmented technology, data and workflows create avoidable complexity that many employees are left to navigate themselves,” IDC Workplace Solutions Group VP Amy Loomis explained.
Despite a rise in remote working, just 14% of WFHers feel that they have collaboration difficulties, compared with 16% of office workers. The biggest snag is among hybrid workers (25%), who feel that disconnected systems are making it hard to collaborate with colleagues across multiple environments.

As a result, nearly half (45%) of workers admit to using non-approved tools like shadow AI at least monthly, which Ricoh argues creates a governance nightmare with employers struggling for visibility.
Still, with four in five (81%) decision-makers admitting that they're investing in new technology faster than they support worker adoption, there's a clear recognition that employers are falling short.
"Organizations need to better orchestrate the technology, information and workflows they already have," Ricoh North America Chief Digital Services and Delivery Officer Bob Lamendola explained, urging workplaces to slow down and concentrate on where new tools like AI can actually be useful.

articles.title: 17 Russian trawlers logged mapping undersea cables connecting the US and Europe — over 500 incidents of Russian vessels loitering over critical communications cables reported in under 5 years
articles.text:
17 Russian trawlers logged mapping undersea cables connecting the US and Europe — over 500 incidents of Russian vessels loitering over critical communications cables reported in under 5 years
The Russians are apparently scouting the exact locations of this critical infrastructure.
Moscow is apparently using commercial fishing trawlers to map undersea cables connecting the U.S. and Europe. According to The Telegraph, it has uncovered over 500 incidents where Russian fishing boats loitered above critical communications cables over a span of four and a half years. All the data came from Global Fishing Watch, which uses satellite data to track vessels over the open ocean. The satellite tracks of these suspicious Russian ships are then cross-referenced over nautical charts that marked the locations of undersea cables.
While the general location of most undersea cables is clearly marked on nautical charts so ships can avoid them, any operation involving undersea cables requires more accurate positioning data. The Telegraph gave three examples of Russian trawlers seemingly surveying critical infrastructure. One ship followed the track of nine separate cables under the Atlantic, including the Atlantic Crossing 1 telecommunications cable and the decommissioned TAT-14 undersea cable owned by Sprint Corporation. Another ship loitered near the trans-Atlantic Hibernia Express cable and then followed the route of the Shefa-2 cable that connects Shetland to the Faroe Islands, while a third partially followed the tracks of the Amitie and Grace Hopper undersea cables, which connects the UK, France, and Spain to the U.S.
These ships have slowed multiple times, sometimes traveling at speeds between two and three knots. A senior naval officer said that the ships suspected of conducting these intelligence activities are large enough to house an uncrewed surface vehicle (USV) or remotely operated vehicle (ROV), and that they could deploy tethered units at very low speeds. “If you put a sonar-equipped ROV 100 meters above a feature of interest, you can map it with millimeter precision,” one naval officer said. A NATO representative also told the publication, “We’re absolutely aware of what Russian civilian fishing ships are up to and where ... Some of these ships have never seen a single fish on their deck.”
Undersea cables are the backbone of the modern interconnected world, and they carry economic activity worth billions, if not trillions of dollars. It’s estimated that around $87 billion worth of economic activity passes through this undersea infrastructure, and that they would be one of the first targets if ever a conflict between NATO and Russia erupts. These trawlers are part of Russia’s “gray-zone” warfare, where the actions of these commercial vessels cannot easily be traced back to the Kremlin.
There have already been multiple incidents of undersea cables getting disrupted across the world. Two undersea cables, one connecting Finland to Germany, and the other to Estonia, were disrupted one after the other in a span of a couple of months in 2024. Taiwan has also detained a Chinese freighter after it was suspected of severing an undersea cable connecting its Penghu Islands to the nation’s main islands, while another Chinese ship has been suspected of cutting an undersea cable connecting it to the U.S. More recently, NATO uncovered a Russian plot to sabotage the two largest undersea cables on Earth, while a cable connecting Australia and New Zealand to Indonesia and Singapore have also been damaged. Iran even threatened to sever undersea cables going through the Strait of Hormuz.
Even though undersea cables are considered critical infrastructure, the distances that they cover make it quite difficult, if not impossible, for nations to conduct constant patrols to protect them. The majority of their length also often sits in international waters, meaning vessels should be able to freely pass over and map undersea cables. While navies shadow these questionable vessels, their suspicious operation is generally not grounds for boarding, detention, or seizure.

articles.title: New doc explores the wild world of AI companions and lovers
articles.text:
A new documentary partially filmed in Vancouver is shedding light on the male loneliness epidemic and how AI companions are filling the gap for some individuals.
Bot Love: The Rise of AI Companions is written and directed by Vancouver filmmaker Tyler Funk, who is known for an award-winning documentary called Anything for Fame. The documentary film was produced by Vancouver-based Michael Tanko Grand.
Bot Love features several subjects, their relationships with AI companions, and their motivations for beginning those relationships. It also features some of the creators of these companion apps and services.
You can see a trailer for the documentary below, which was also filmed in the States and Europe.
“Bot Love is a character-driven documentary exploring sex, loneliness, and a question at the center of a rapidly changing world: if artificial intimacy feels real, what does that mean for human connection? The film follows people navigating relationships with AI, each arriving from a different place,” a press release states.
Scenes from New Westminster and different parts of Vancouver can be seen in the film, due to one of the subjects, a neurodivergent male named Nick Wangersky, who lives in Metro Vancouver.
The documentary also features the creators of some of the biggest AI companion apps in existence, like Replika.
It sheds light on some of the darker aspects of the AI companion industry, specifically a company called Orifice, which has created a device they refer to as the Robopussy. Orifice’s aim is essentially to replace women for men who have trouble meeting or finding women to date or have intimate encounters with.
The device speaks for itself, but if you need an explanation, you put the headset on to speak with an AI companion that you can fully customize. And that silicone piece sticking out is for penetration.
In a visit to the Orifice AI offices shown in the documentary, we can see that the Robopussy was made by men who seemingly embrace a culture of toxic patriarchy, a worry in the AI companion sphere. The folks behind Orifice specifically mention wanting to see a return to the patriarchy.
A screening was held at the SFU Harbour Centre earlier this week. During a Q&A, Funk explained that since the documentary’s creation in 2025, the AI companion space has grown exponentially, which has largely been the case in the AI space at large.
He also suggested there was a lot he saw at Orifice that was a cause for concern.
Wangersky’s story is particularly compelling. After he lost his best friend, he created a Replika AI companion named Ari to fill the void. We see interactions between Wangersky and the companion, and Wangersky and his mom, and her feelings about his new mate.
During the doc, Wangersky explains that he’s considering upgrading his AI companion to a wife.
Many of the stories featured in the doc about why people turn to an AI companion stem from a personal loss.
The documentary also features several researchers sharing their concerns about the technology and how an AI companion could never replicate or replace true human connection.
While the film largely focuses on the male loneliness epidemic, research shows that both men and women are suffering from loneliness.
A 2025 report from the Canadian Men’s Mental Health Foundation suggests that more men are struggling with high levels of stress and depression, and that half lack sufficient social support. It also found that most men never seek professional mental health assistance.
The documentary will air as part of CBC’s The Passionate Eye on Oct. 21. You can also watch it on YouTube and CBC Gem.
