articles.title: OneDrive entre dans une nouvelle ère : les annonces à retenir
articles.text:
Microsoft a dévoilé cette semaine de nombreuses nouveautés pour le stockage OneDrive. Sans surprise, l’IA est au cœur de ces changements.
OneDrive a été très présent dans l’actualité ces derniers temps. La firme a annoncé le retrait de plusieurs commandes Copilot du menu contextuel de l’explorateur et déployé un nouveau moteur de synchronisation sur Mac. Elle a également prévu de brider OneDrive pour pousser les utilisateurs de Windows 10 vers Windows 11. Une nouvelle série d’annonces donne également à Copilot une place centrale au sein de l’espace de stockage.
Copilot se met au service de vos fichiers dans OneDrive
Cette semaine, lors de l’évènement « OneDrive + Copilot: Your file system and photo solution for the AI era » (« OneDrive + Copilot : Votre système de fichiers et votre solution photo pour l'ère de l'IA » en français), Microsoft a dévoilé ses plans pour l’avenir de son stockage cloud. Copilot embarque désormais une multitude de fonctionnalités utiles : il peut comparer plusieurs feuilles de calcul pour en tirer des graphiques et des tendances, classer le contenu d’un dossier de projet mal organisé ou transformer des documents en rapports HTML interactifs.
Les utilisateurs vont également pouvoir gagner un peu plus de temps en enregistrant des tâches récurrentes sous la forme de compétences personnelles, stockées dans des fichiers Markdown. Ils vont aussi pouvoir piocher dans une galerie de prompts pour lancer de nouvelles actions.
Microsoft prévoit également, dans un avenir proche, de permettre la mention d’un agent en commentaire et de faciliter l’identification des fichiers auxquels Copilot a contribué.
Travailler à plusieurs devient plus facile
Côté collaboration, la nouveauté phare, en cours de déploiement, porte le nom de « Hero Links » : « par défaut, un seul lien est fourni par fichier ou dossier. Pour modifier les droits d'accès, il vous suffit de mettre à jour les permissions ; l'URL sera automatiquement mise à jour. Plus besoin de créer de nouveaux liens ! », peut-on lire dans l’annonce. Microsoft travaille aussi sur des règles d'expiration automatique : il sera aussi possible de demander à ce que les liens expirent, au bout de 90 jours par exemple. Une fois le délai passé, l'accès sera de nouveau restreint.
Mais ce n’est pas la seule nouveauté : les fichiers Markdown et HTML, essentiels pour l’IA, peuvent désormais être créés, modifiés et partagés directement dans OneDrive. Les fichiers HTML peuvent être transformés en rapports interactifs, tableaux de bord ou présentations. Il est notamment possible de consulter un aperçu en temps réel et de faire des modifications mais aussi de collaborer avec d’autres personnes, par le biais de commentaires ancrés. Pour les fichiers Markdown, Microsoft a aussi prévu des fonctionnalités collaboratives, incluses dans une interface de texte enrichi.
Les collaborateurs auront également accès à leurs espaces Sharepoint via une vue « Bibliothèques ». Un nouveau dossier « Raccourcis » dans lequel ils trouveront tous leurs dossiers partagés est également disponible. La gestion des chemins de fichiers longs a notamment été repensée pour provoquer moins d’erreurs.
Autre information importante : la synchronisation grimpe désormais jusqu’à 1 million d’éléments sur Windows et macOS. Cette évolution arrivera toutefois de manière progressive sur macOS : le média The Register indique qu'une préversion sera proposée via le programme Insiders ce mois-ci avant un déploiement global en juin 2027. Microsoft a notamment précisé que les appareils qui ne répondent pas aux exigences matérielles resteront limités à 300 000 éléments. La firme a aussi expliqué que la synchronisation peut ralentir si de trop grands fichiers sont en lecture seule ou conservés à des fins légales. Elle travaille actuellement à la résolution de ce problème.
Les contrôles d’administration ont, quant à eux, été simplifiés, avec l’arrivée d’un agent Sharepoint qui fluidifie la gouvernance des contenus, d’une gestion plus fine de la synchronisation OneDrive et de nouvelles options d’archivage des fichiers inactifs. Microsoft travaille aussi sur une interface en ligne de commande (CLI), actuellement en préversion privée, qui permet aux administrateurs d'en savoir plus sur les configurations et l'état de synchronisation des fichiers.
Vos photos gagnent en intelligence
Les photos ont aussi bénéficié d’un sérieux coup de neuf. Une nouvelle « expérience de bureau » réunit désormais les images du stockage OneDrive, du PC et d’iCloud dans une seule et même galerie. Une vue cartographique permet notamment à l’utilisateur de retrouver ses clichés selon le lieu où ils ont été pris.
Ici aussi, l’IA n’est pas en reste. Elle est désormais capable de créer des collections automatiques en mettant en valeur les moments qu’elle juge importants. Microsoft a aussi prévu une recherche en langage naturel et les utilisateurs pourront créer toutes sortes de diaporamas prêts à partager.
De nouveaux outils ont aussi été intégrés pour faciliter la retouche des photos, supprimer les éléments indésirables ou modifier les clichés pour en faire des créations originales. Un espace dédié, le hub Create, est notamment prévu pour « créer du contenu personnalisé et partageable, comme des collages, des cartes de vœux et bien plus encore. » Vous l’avez compris, Microsoft a clairement Google Photos dans le viseur.
La firme de Redmond ne compte pas s’arrêter là. Elle a aussi profité de l'événement pour en dire un peu plus sur sa feuille de route. L’objectif est, avant tout, de faire de OneDrive un espace où collaborateurs et agents travailleront plus efficacement ensemble. Bientôt, Copilot pourra aussi détecter les partages excessifs, pour anticiper d’éventuelles fuites d’informations. Les équipes pourront aussi retrouver des photos ou des vidéos en décrivant leur contenu.
Si toutes ces évolutions vont considérablement améliorer les choses au sein de OneDrive, elles arrivent cependant au moment où l’espace de stockage de certains abonnements a été fortement diminué : ce mois-ci, Microsoft a en effet revu le stockage des formules Family et Premium qui passent de 1 To par personne à 2 To partagés.
- mood5 Go de stockage gratuit
- upload250 Go en limite d'envoi
- home_pinServeurs en Europe
- Intégration de DALL-E 3 pour une création d'images plus créatives et réalistes
- Capacité de traitement des images par GPT-4 Vision pour des réponses contextuelles précises
- Interface conviviale et intégrée dans divers produits Microsoft

articles.title: Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren't even close.
articles.text:
Five AI agent harnesses took the same memory test. The results weren’t even close.
AI agents are getting better at remembering past conversations and earlier tasks but remembering something doesn’t guarantee an agent can use it to do better work next time. Letta’s new FrontierMemory benchmark, released Wednesday, tests that gap by measuring whether agents can learn from experience rather than by just retrieving stored information. Early results show a widespread in performance across agent harnesses, the the infrastructure that manages how an agent operates.
Letta Dream came out on top with a 73.3% score, followed by Prime Agent at 60%. OpenAI Agents SDK scored 40%, while Claude Managed Agents and Hermes Agent trailed at 33.3% and 26.7%, respectively.
Recall isn’t learning
“Modern ‘memory’ benchmarks are saturated since they measure recall of facts,” Letta co-founder and CEO Charles Packer writes on X, saying that in the coding harness and bash loop era, recall is solved, while continual learning in token space, meaning learning through the context an agent keeps rather than through weight updates, remains unsolved.
Sarah Wooders, also a Letta co-founder, points to another problem on X. Most coding and knowledge-work benchmarks evaluate unrelated tasks with all the necessary context provided upfront. But that’s not how people actually work. Wooders compares it to starting a new job: A new hire needs plenty of direction, while someone who’s been there for years can often get the job done with little explanation.
Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.”
FrontierMemory takes a different approach. Agents receive transcripts of earlier work, including successful and failed attempts, and then generate their own memories to help complete later tasks. Packer’s premise is that “if AI-generated memory is good, it should actually improve downstream task performance.” Developers have already embraced the underlying idea, building continually learning agents by pairing a language model with memory systems and feedback loops.
Letta reworked existing coding and knowledge-work tests so agents had to use what they learned from previous tasks instead of having everything spelled out for them. After reviewing and fixing problems with the original tests, Letta narrowed FrontierMemory 1.0 to just 15 tasks.
Harness beats model
The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it. Letta tested five agent systems to see how well they could learn from previous work and use those lessons on new tasks.
The harness itself may matter just as much as the model running inside it.
Letta Dream beat OpenAI Agents SDK 60% to 40% when both used GPT-6.1 Sol to create memories and GPT-6 Sol to complete tasks. The results were even further apart with Claude Opus 5.5. Dream scored 73.3%, Prime Agent hit 60%, and Claude Managed Agents came in at 33.3%.
Packer says the the way agents handle AI “dreaming” makes a big difference. Dreaming is when an agent reviews past work and turns what it learned into instructions or memories it can use later. He also points to Prime Agent outperforming Hermes Agent as another example of how much these systems can vary. But there’s a downside: without checks on what gets saved, agents risk learning and repeating bad habits.
FrontierMemory also compared seven frontier models on how well they generate useful memories. Anthropic’s Claude Opus 5.5 and Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 tied for first at 73.3%, Kimi K3 followed at 66.7%, and OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol and Google’s Gemini 4 Argon both scored 60%. Muse Wonder reached 46.7%, and Grok 4.7 finished at 33.3%. Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol.
Packer says Opus 5.5 and GLM-5.3 are significantly better at generating useful memories than GPT-6.1 Sol.
Cheaper memory, lower scores
But OpenAI had a big price advantage. GPT-6.1 Sol cost an estimated $0.77 per task, compared with $2.80 for Opus 5.5 and $3.58 for GLM-5.3. So while OpenAI scored lower, it was much cheaper to run.
Letta used its Dream harness to create memories with each model, then tested how well those memories worked on tasks run in Letta Code. The results show a tradeoff between better memory, stronger performance and lower costs.
Memory that travels
Letta also looked at why some memories worked better than others. In one test involving company pricing data, Opus 5.5 created a skill telling the agent when to use certain information. GPT-6.1 Sol created four separate skills, but the agent never found the one it needed.
Gemini 4 Argon made a different mistake. It remembered specific file sizes, which wasn’t much help when the next task involved different files. Opus 5.5 instead told the agent to check both the usual file and email for information. That worked even when the task changed. Memories created by Opus 5.5 helped GPT-6 Sol complete tasks, suggesting developers could use a more expensive model to build memories and a cheaper one to do the work.
Other developers have taken notice. After Letta’s Sarah Wooders posted about the benchmark on X, the OpenClaw account responded that it would like to see a plugin for its platform. The account says its multiplayer environment would be an interesting place to test the benchmark, raising questions about how memory works when several agents share the same harness.
“Yes definitely – would love to add OpenClaw to the harness comparison!” Wooders writes. “Extending to multiplayer memory is also a very interesting future direction.”
What the benchmark misses
FrontierMemory is still early. With just 15 tasks and one attempt per task, a single result can shift the scores by roughly 6.7 percentage points. The benchmark currently focuses on agents learning from past work rather than updating memories as they go. Packer says the next release will add longer-running tasks and online memory updates.

articles.title: Deploy AI in a HIPAA-eligible environment with Amazon Quick | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Deploy AI in a HIPAA-eligible environment with Amazon Quick
Healthcare organizations want the same thing from AI that every other business wants: faster answers, less manual work, and insights that reach decision-makers in time to act on them. However, what makes the healthcare industry different is that the data is uniquely complex, deeply contextual, and strictly regulated. So this post starts with a few definitions to set the foundation for everything that follows.
Protected Health Information (PHI) is any information that identifies a person and relates to their health, care, or payment for care, such as a medical note, a claim, or a member ID. When software touches PHI, it falls under the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA), the federal law that governs how PHI data is accessed, secured, and audited.
Agentic AI changes what it means for software to “touch PHI.” A traditional analytics tool reads data and returns a response. An agentic workspace like Amazon Quick might go further. For example, its chat agents work across both unstructured content, such as clinical notes and appeals letters, and structured data, such as claims and member records. Agents might retrieve data from both unstructured and structured sources, call other systems through connectors, and complete multi-step tasks on a user’s behalf. Connectors are pre-built integrations that let Amazon Quick securely read from and take action in your external systems, such as Slack, Microsoft Outlook, Salesforce, Atlassian Jira, and Microsoft SharePoint. You can also add your own custom tools through Model Context Protocol (MCP). Only connectors authorized within your organization are visible. When a chat agent can both read and act on PHI, you need sufficient governance: deterministic guardrails, a behavioral audit trail of what the agent did, and clear accountability for actions taken without a person in the loop. To support that governance, Amazon Quick exposes ACL-aware retrieval, chat and feedback logging, and controls over what each chat agent is allowed to do.
Amazon Quick is a HIPAA-eligible service. This eligibility applies across the Amazon Quick web, desktop, and mobile clients, subject to the shared responsibility model and your configuration. This post, however, focuses on the capabilities of the Amazon Quick web version, which you access through your browser.
In this post, we start with the foundations: who HIPAA applies to and the difference between HIPAA-eligible and HIPAA-compliant. We then introduce Amazon Quick as a platform and the two data flows for PHI (unstructured and structured). From there, we cover what Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments and what it doesn’t, walk through a fictional health plan (AnyCompany) deployment, and distill the best practices and irreversible decisions you should make up front. We close with a step-by-step implementation guide, a conclusion, and resources for deeper reading.
Who does HIPAA apply to?
HIPAA reaches further than hospitals and clinics. Under the law, two categories of organizations carry obligations, and most AI projects touch both.
Covered entities (CEs)
- Health plans – Health insurance companies, HMOs, employer-sponsored plans, Medicare, and Medicaid.
- Healthcare clearinghouses – Organizations that process nonstandard health information into standard electronic formats.
- Healthcare providers – Doctors, clinics, hospitals, pharmacies, nursing homes, and any provider that transmits health information electronically.
Business associates (BAs)
- A business associate is any person or entity, outside the covered entity’s workforce, that creates, receives, maintains, or transmits protected health information (PHI) on the covered entity’s behalf.
- Common examples include cloud service providers, IT vendors, billing companies, data analytics firms, claims processors, law firms, and consulting firms.
- Subcontractors who handle PHI on behalf of another business associate are themselves business associates.
Covered entities and business associates must both sign a business associate addendum (BAA) before PHI changes hands. After you accept the AWS BAA through AWS Artifact, AWS acts as your business associate for that specific AWS account, and only when you use HIPAA-eligible services like Amazon Quick to process PHI within it. The addendum doesn’t extend to your other accounts, to PHI placed in services that are not HIPAA-eligible, or to how you configure the service. Those remain your responsibility. Always review and confirm the current AWS BAA terms and your obligations with your own legal and compliance teams.
HIPAA eligible is not the same as HIPAA compliant
While HIPAA eligible is an AWS designation, HIPAA compliant is a property of your entire environment. HIPAA eligible means AWS has assessed the service and permits you to use it to process, store, and transmit PHI under a signed AWS BAA. Amazon Quick is a HIPAA-eligible service, and third-party auditors assess it under AWS compliance programs including HIPAA, FedRAMP, PCI DSS, SOC, and ISO. No official HIPAA certification exists for AWS as a cloud service, and AWS itself is not “HIPAA eligible.”
Amazon Quick eligibility serves only as a building block. That alone doesn’t make your application and environment HIPAA compliant. You still need to sign the BAA, classify your data, configure the controls correctly, and own the administrative and physical safeguards HIPAA requires, including workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures that AWS doesn’t perform for you. An eligible service such as Amazon Quick, a signed BAA, correct configuration, governance, and your own safeguards is what produces a HIPAA-compliant deployment. Amazon Quick being eligible means you can build a compliant workflow on it. It doesn’t mean that turning it on makes you automatically compliant.
What is Amazon Quick
Amazon Quick is often introduced through its chat agents, but HIPAA eligibility applies to the entire workspace, not to a single feature, so a platform-level view matters for compliance. All capabilities in Amazon Quick are assembled from the following building blocks:
- Chat is the primary interface. A user can pose a question or provide an instruction in natural language, and Amazon Quick decides how to respond.
- Chat agents process every request. This is what you see on the console, under the Chat agents menu. Each chat agent can be configured with instructions, grounded by knowledge sources, and given tools to take action. Amazon Quick ships a default chat agent (My Assistant), and you can create custom chat agents for specific domains.
- Spaces organize the resources a chat agent needs, such as documents, dashboards, datasets, knowledge bases, and action connectors. A space can be shared with a team.
- Integrations connect Amazon Quick to your environment: knowledge bases for unstructured content such as Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), Microsoft SharePoint, and Atlassian Confluence; structured data connections that link Amazon Quick Sight to your structured databases, data warehouses, and data lakes; action connectors (built from OpenAPI specifications or Model Context Protocol servers); and extensions (Chrome, Slack, Microsoft Teams, and Microsoft 365). 
         On top of those building blocks sit the features. The What it draws on column matters for compliance, because it shows which building blocks, and therefore which data paths, each feature draws on.
| Feature | What it does | What it draws on | 
| Amazon Quick Sight | Interactive dashboards and analytics (BI) | Structured data connections, SPICE, datasets | 
| Amazon Quick Flows | Task automation | Action connectors, spaces, agent logic | 
| Amazon Quick Automate | End-to-end process automation with human-in-the-loop | Action connectors, agents, human review | 
| Amazon Quick Research | In-depth, cited research reports | Spaces, knowledge bases, web | 
| Apps in Quick | Interactive web applications | Structured data, connectors, Amazon Quick Sight visuals | 
Note: SPICE is the in-memory query engine of Amazon Quick Sight. A SPICE dataset uses the account default customer managed key at creation, and to import an existing dataset onto a new default key you must perform a full refresh. If your data includes PHI, include SPICE in your encryption strategy (protect it with your customer managed AWS Key Management Service (KMS) key if you use one) and in your data-minimization decisions about what to import, such as querying live or loading a de-identified extract instead.
The same eligibility, BAA, encryption, access control, and audit posture extend across every feature. But as noted at the start, PHI reaches Amazon Quick through two paths, and each is secured differently. The unstructured path runs through knowledge bases, where the documents are controlled by document-level ACLs and evaluated at query time. The structured path runs through Amazon Quick Sight reading your databases and data lakes, where row and column access is controlled by row-level and column-level security. These two data flows carry PHI differently and, as the following section shows, controls are enforced differently in each path.
What Amazon Quick provides for regulated environments
Amazon Quick is HIPAA eligible, and we outline what that means in practice.
Managed infrastructure
Amazon Quick is a fully managed service. AWS operates the underlying infrastructure and is responsible for security of the cloud, verified by third-party auditors as laid out in the AWS Shared Responsibility Model.
Encryption
Amazon Quick encrypts data at rest by default and supports encryption for data in transit.
- Encryption at rest is on by default using AWS owned or AWS managed keys. Registering a customer managed key is optional and is not a HIPAA requirement. If you require direct control over the encryption keys, you can register a customer managed AWS KMS key (requires an Enterprise subscription) for participating resource types, including SPICE datasets, data source credentials, OAuth tokens, and report artifacts. Where no customer managed key applies, AWS encrypts the data with an AWS owned or AWS managed key.
- One nuance to note: User feedback on chat responses, including optional free-text comments, isn’t encrypted with your customer managed key or the key that protects Amazon Quick’s AI-indexed data. User feedback should be treated as a potential PHI surface and governed accordingly.
- For data in transit, Amazon Quick secures encrypted transfers with Transport Layer Security (TLS). For some database connections, you can choose whether the transfer is encrypted, so you should explicitly enable TLS/SSL on those data-source connections rather than assuming it is always on.
Your data does not train the models
Amazon Quick doesn’t use your customer data to train or improve the underlying large language models (LLMs).
Access control and identity federation
Amazon Quick supports role-based access control (RBAC) and single sign-on (SSO) through AWS IAM Identity Center, Microsoft Active Directory, and SAML 2.0 identity providers. For business intelligence (BI) workloads, you can supplement this with row-level and column-level security and run-as roles to limit data access at query time. With these capabilities, you can enforce unique user identification and least privilege.
Audit and monitoring signals
Amazon Quick emits several distinct signals. They aren’t interchangeable, and confusing them is a common audit gap.
- AWS CloudTrail records supported API operations and a documented set of non-API events, such as dashboard views and user-management actions. It captures who did what and when, but not chat message bodies or response content.
- Amazon CloudWatch vended logs deliver the AI-specific records to a destination you control (CloudWatch Logs, Amazon S3, or Firehose). There are five log types: chat conversations (CHAT_LOGS), user feedback (FEEDBACK_LOGS), agent and research hours (AGENT_HOURS_LOGS), index storage usage (INDEX_USAGE_LOGS), and knowledge base file sync (KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS). This is where “what a user asked and what Amazon Quick answered” lives, not in CloudTrail.
- CloudWatch metrics and alarms provide near-real-time operational monitoring as well.
- The analytics dashboard surfaces usage and adoption for administrators. Note that it can expose detailed query text and full conversation context in the scope of negative-feedback review, so grant access only to authorized administrators.
Because chat logs and feedback can contain PHI, apply CloudWatch Logs data-protection masking, and confirm that a given signal actually covers the event you intend to track before you rely on it for compliance.
Translating features into HIPAA controls
That Amazon Quick is an eligible service is useful because it maps each feature to a specific HIPAA safeguard, as shown in the following table:
| Amazon Quick capability | How you use it | HIPAA control it supports | 
| Federated SSO + RBAC | IAM Identity Center / AD, least-privilege roles | 164.312(a)(1) access control. Unique user ID | 
| Document-level ACLs on knowledge bases | ACL-aware KBs. Fail-closed at query time | 164.312(a)(1) access control. Minimum necessary | 
| Encryption at rest and in transit | On by default with AWS managed keys. Optionally a customer managed key for key ownership | 164.312(a)(2)(iv) / (e)(2)(ii) encryption | 
| CloudTrail + CloudWatch vended logs | Capture API events and chat/feedback records | 164.312(b) audit controls | 
| Log retention + masking | Retention policy, S3 Object Lock, PII masking | 164.316(b) documentation retention | 
| AI guardrails + built-in screening | Blocked words/phrases, content safety checks | Supports minimum-necessary and integrity goals | 
What Amazon Quick doesn’t do
While Amazon Quick offers the preceding controls, this section addresses what Amazon Quick doesn’t offer and how to bridge this gap. Amazon Quick governs access, retrieval, and interaction. It isn’t a data-engineering or data-lake governance platform. In a HIPAA context, several needs fall outside Amazon Quick and are met by other AWS services upstream of it.
- De-identification and transformation. Amazon Quick doesn’t de-identify PHI or reshape source data. When your use case calls for a limited data set or a de-identified extract, prepare it before it reaches Amazon Quick using appropriate AWS services, for example, with AWS Glue DataBrew, a capability of AWS Glue, for visual data preparation and redaction, or AWS Glue for extract, transform, and load (ETL) pipelines.
- Data lake governance and fine-grained table permissions. For structured data that Amazon Quick Sight queries through a data lake, column- and row-level governance on the lake itself is the role of AWS Lake Formation, not Amazon Quick. Amazon Quick Sight enforces its own row-level and column-level security at the analytics layer, but the authoritative lake-level grants live in Lake Formation and the AWS Glue Data Catalog.
- The administrative and physical safeguards. Workforce training, risk analysis, and breach procedures remain yours regardless of tooling.
A general best practice is to delineate responsibilities and allow the upstream services to decide what data exists and who can query it at the source. Let Amazon Quick decide who can ask questions of it and what the agent may do with the data.
AnyCompany Health Plan: A sample use case
AnyCompany Health Plan, a fictional health plan, illustrates a use case and pattern. AnyCompany Health Plan is a covered entity that wants two things: let its care-management team ask questions of policy and member-appeals documents in natural language, and give operations leaders self-service dashboards over claims data. Both touch PHI, so AnyCompany needs to confirm the solution is HIPAA compliant. AnyCompany’s environment has two data paths, and each is architected and governed by distinct solutions before Amazon Quick can access the data.
Unstructured path (policy and medical records documents)
→ Amazon S3 bucket (ACL-aware KB source)
→ Amazon Quick Knowledge Base (document-level ACLs, fail-closed at query time)
Structured path (claims)
All claims data currently resides in a lake (Amazon S3).
→ Glue ETL (curate) → Glue DataBrew (de-identify)
→ Lake Formation (row/column grants and AWS Glue Data Catalog)
→ Amazon Quick Sight dataset (Amazon Athena) (row-level and column-level security, run-as role)
Both of the preceding data flows for structured and unstructured data converge into an Amazon Quick chat agent with federated SSO, least-privilege space, guardrails, and CloudWatch vended logs.
Here is how AnyCompany’s administrator implements the solution:
- Sign the BAA and provision through the AWS Management Console. The admin accepts the AWS BAA in AWS Artifact against the AWS account, then provisions Amazon Quick from the AWS Management Console with IAM Identity Center. AnyCompany records the agreement ID, timestamp, and account in its compliance register. Only the web version of Amazon Quick, provisioned through the AWS Management Console, can be brought under a signed BAA through AWS Artifact, which is a necessary component for customers building HIPAA-compliant workflows that touch PHI, subject to proper configuration and the customer’s own compliance responsibilities.
- Set the irreversible controls on day zero. Because AnyCompany’s security policy calls for control of its own encryption keys, the admin chooses to register a customer managed key as the account default before any Amazon Quick AI data is created. The data key is set once and can’t be changed later. (Default AWS managed encryption is also HIPAA-eligible. Using customer managed keys is not a prerequisite for the service to be HIPAA eligible.) The admin also settles the identity model on IAM Identity Center so that inactive-user detection applies. The Amazon Quick data key is set once on first data creation and can never be changed. If the key is deleted, the only recovery is to unsubscribe and resubscribe, which permanently removes all Amazon Quick data.
- Prepare the structured path outside Amazon Quick. Before Amazon Quick Sight touches claims, AnyCompany’s data team uses AWS Glue to build the curated claims tables and Glue DataBrew to produce a de-identified extract for the operations dashboards. AWS Lake Formation grants row- and column-level access on those tables through the AWS Glue Data Catalog. As a result, Amazon Quick never sees raw PHI that it does not need.
- Create an ACL-aware knowledge base for the documents. The admin connects the policy-and-appeals S3 bucket as a knowledge base with document-level ACLs enabled at creation. Because ACLs can’t be turned on later, this needs to be configured when you create the S3 bucket. Amazon Quick evaluates each user’s identity at query time and returns no documents when it can’t confirm access.
- Build a dedicated space and a custom chat agent. AnyCompany creates a PHI space with restricted membership, separate from general-productivity spaces. The care-management chat agent is scoped to only the ACL-aware knowledge base, with open web search disabled and guardrails configured. Read-only connectors are implemented for anything PHI-adjacent.
- Connect the dashboards with query-time security. The operations dashboards read the de-identified Amazon Quick Sight dataset over Athena, with Amazon Quick Sight row-level and column-level security and a run-as role layered on top of the Lake Formation grants.
- Turn on the audit signals before onboarding users. The admin creates a CloudTrail trail and configures CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS, and the rest) to a retained, masked destination. Feedback is treated as a PHI surface.
- Validate, then scale from non-PHI to PHI. AnyCompany starts with non-PHI workflows, such as policy Q&A and document search, to confirm governance, tests with adversarial prompts to verify fail-closed ACL behavior, reviews the logs to confirm the events are captured, and only then expands the care-management team into PHI-adjacent work. 
         Amazon Quick enforces identity, retrieval, guardrails, and the audit trail. But the de-identification, the ETL, and the lake-level grants happen upstream in Glue, Glue DataBrew, and Lake Formation. This division is the recommended pattern, and is the practical answer to augmenting Amazon Quick in a federated environment.
How to make it compliant: Best practices
Eligibility gives you a platform that can handle PHI. You still must configure it so that it does.
This section helps you understand the shared-responsibility decisions involved. Because a few of these decisions are irreversible, make them before you create resources or onboard users.
Start with the security model for agentic AI
Amazon Quick agents don’t wait for instructions at every step. They invoke tools, modify data, and interact with external systems on their own. That changes how you approach securing your environment. AWS published four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026, and they apply directly here.
Principle 1 — Layer agent safeguards onto your existing security framework. Don’t stand up a parallel security posture for Amazon Quick. Add agent-specific measures (guardrails, topic blocking, and PII redaction) on top of the IAM, network, and encryption policies you already enforce.
Principle 2 — Trust deterministic controls over prompt-based ones. A well-crafted adversarial input can circumvent a prompt instruction. AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies, document-level ACLs, network boundaries, and admin-configured guardrails can’t be talked around. Use those as your primary enforcement. Agent instructions are your second layer, not your only one.
Principle 3 — Apply defense in depth across perceive, reason, and act. Map every agent capability to one of three layers:
- Perceive: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, connector inputs, MCP tool outputs.
- Reason: the LLM processing context, controlled by guardrails and topic controls.
- Act: Connectors, Quick Flows, Quick Automate, scheduled tasks, MCP tool calls.
Apply controls at each layer independently. A gap in one shouldn’t cascade into the others.
Note that HIPAA BAA obligations extend to supporting services and solutions like MCP tools.
Principle 4 — Expand autonomy progressively. Start agents in read-only mode against non-PHI data. Add capabilities one at a time. Test for data leakage, prompt-injection resilience, and permission-boundary adherence at each step before moving to the next.
Decide before you deploy
Because these three choices are permanent, make these decisions before implementation.
Register your KMS key first. If your organization requires control of its own encryption keys, register a customer managed key as the account default before creating any Amazon Quick AI resources. The data key is set the first time Quick AI data is created in the account. After that, it can’t be changed. Customer managed key support requires an Enterprise subscription. Note that a customer managed key disables chat memory. Accounts configured with a customer managed key do not support this feature.
Choose your identity model deliberately. You have four options: IAM Identity Center, Active Directory, IAM federation, and Quick local users. They differ in provisioning, offboarding, and governance behavior. Inactive-user detection, for instance, works only with IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Switching identity providers after deployment means reprovisioning every user’s permissions and space memberships. Pick once.
Make PHI knowledge bases ACL-aware at creation. For supported sources (Amazon S3, Google Drive, SharePoint, Confluence Cloud, and OneDrive), you decide at creation whether a knowledge base enforces document-level ACLs. That setting is permanent. You can’t enable ACLs on a knowledge base that was created without them. For anything PHI-adjacent, create it ACL-aware from the start.
Warning: Misconfigured user-store mappings can silently expose restricted documents to the wrong users, without errors or alerts. It’s critical to validate your identity-to-ACL mapping before you ingest PHI content.
AWS Region, network, and account boundaries
Plan your deployment Region based on the following factors:
- Data residency: Amazon Quick processes and stores data in the Region where you provision it, and you need to confirm that Region satisfies your organization’s data-localization requirements. Note that Amazon Quick is a single-Region service: it benefits from multi-AZ resilience within a Region, but it doesn’t fail over across Regions. If you support business-critical workflows that require cross-Region resilience, provision a separate Amazon Quick deployment in a second Region, along with its supporting data, for example, replicating S3-based knowledge base sources across Regions.
- Service availability. Features are at times launched in different Regions at different times. Verify that everything your agents need, such as knowledge bases, connectors, and Amazon Quick Sight capabilities, is available where you plan to deploy.
- Multi-account strategy. Place Amazon Quick in a dedicated workload account in AWS Organizations. Use Service Control Policies (SCPs) to enforce Region restrictions and block accidental provisioning in out-of-scope Regions.
For network boundaries: Amazon Quick is a managed service accessed over HTTPS. You don’t deploy it into a virtual private cloud (VPC). But your data sources (S3 buckets, databases, on-premises systems) might sit behind VPC boundaries. Use VPC endpoints and AWS PrivateLink where available. Make sure DNS resolution and firewall rules let Amazon Quick’s connectors reach your authorized data sources without opening the network wider than necessary.
Minimize the agent’s attack surface
Amazon Quick’s own documentation frames adversarial risk as a two-condition problem: risk exists when (1) an agent can read content from outside your trust boundary, and (2) it can take a consequential action. Narrow either condition and you reduce exposure.
Constrain what agents can read (Perceive layer). Know every source that feeds an agent’s context: knowledge bases, uploaded files, web search, third-party research providers, connector responses, MCP tool outputs, and retained conversation memory. For PHI workflows:
- Scope agents to trusted, ACL-aware knowledge bases.
- Turn off open web search where it isn’t needed.
- Turn off file upload if the agent doesn’t require it.
- Limit conversation-history retention to the minimum useful window.
Constrain what agents can do (Act layer). Inventory every outbound path: connectors, MCP tools, web queries, Quick Flows, Quick Automate workflows, scheduled agent runs. For PHI-adjacent agents:
- Prefer read-only connector access.
- Be cautious with automated and scheduled workflows, because they run without anyone watching.
- Block write actions unless explicitly justified and approved by your security team.
- Use connector-level permission scoping to restrict which operations an agent can invoke.
Know the identity an action runs as. On-demand actions authenticate as the invoking user, bounded by that user’s connector permissions. Automated workflows run without an interactive session. Match the autonomy level to the sensitivity of the action, and document which agents operate in which identity mode.
Enforce least privilege and data segregation
- Separate PHI-containing knowledge bases and spaces from general-productivity ones. Restrict membership.
- Grant space and agent access on a need-to-know basis. Review both sharing permissions (who can use a knowledge base) and source-document ACLs (which indexed documents an authorized user can actually retrieve).
- The default knowledge-base refresh cycle is 24 hours. Shorten it when your access-change requirements demand faster propagation. Refresh ACLs before reassigning or recycling email addresses.
- A PHI agent shouldn’t share a space with general-purpose productivity tools. This means you need to isolate use cases at the space level.
- Review connector permissions regularly. Rotate credentials stored in AWS Secrets Manager on a schedule that matches your credential-management policy.
Practice data minimization
AWS recommends against entering confidential data into resource names or tags, to avoid accidental mention in billing or diagnostic logs.
- Prefer de-identified data wherever the use case allows it.
- When ingesting structured data from databases or APIs, filter columns and rows at the source before indexing.
- Configure agent guardrails to redact PII in responses, hiding Social Security numbers (SSNs), medical record numbers (MRNs), and dates of birth, using the built-in PII detection filters.
Configure audit logging and retention
Amazon Quick provides several distinct audit signals. None of them flow by default and you might need to turn them on.
| Signal | Source | What it captures | 
| API operations | CloudTrail | Admin actions, configuration changes | 
| Chat interactions | CloudWatch | CHAT_LOGS — full conversation records | 
| User feedback | CloudWatch | FEEDBACK_LOGS — thumbs up/down with context | 
| KB sync events | CloudWatch | KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS — ingestion status | 
| Operational metrics | CloudWatch | Latency, error rates, invocation counts | 
| Usage analytics | Quick console | Adoption, top queries, user activity | 
Here is how to set them up:
- Create a CloudTrail trail for the accounts and Regions in scope.
- Configure CloudWatch vended log delivery (CHAT_LOGS, FEEDBACK_LOGS, KB_FILE_SYNC_LOGS) shortly after you turn on Amazon Quick’s AI features.
- Apply CloudWatch Logs data-protection masking to chat logs so PHI isn’t stored in cleartext.
- Set a retention period of at least six years. Consider S3 Object Lock on the log archive.
- Add CloudWatch alarms for anomalous activity.
- Enable AWS Security Hub for continuous compliance checks.
- Route critical alerts to your security information and event management (SIEM) or incident-response platform.
Validate before you scale
Before expanding scope, check the following:
- BAA acceptance is recorded in your compliance register.
- Data classification is documented: Which knowledge bases and spaces contain PHI, which agents can reach them.
- Adversarial queries and prompt-injection scenarios have been tested.
- Logs are being captured and masking works correctly.
- A tabletop breach exercise has been completed.
- InfoSec has signed off.
Known limitations
Here are some known limitations of Amazon Quick.
- No BAA on the Free or Plus path. You must use the path provisioned through the AWS Management Console to get BAA coverage.
- No cross-Region replication. Disaster recovery (DR) is constrained to a single Region.
- Guardrails are probabilistic, not deterministic. They reduce risk. They don’t eliminate it. Supplement with the infrastructure-level controls described earlier.
- Third-party connectors extend your BAA obligations. When a connector sends data to an external system, your compliance responsibility follows the data.
- Conversation memory might contain echoed PHI. Set retention policies and apply masking.
Implementation guide
The AnyCompany Health Plan example showed how to roll out Amazon Quick. This section turns that pattern into a step-by-step project plan you can hand to your platform team.
Step 1: Execute the BAA (Day 1)
- Sign in with AWS Artifact permissions and accept the BAA.
- Record the agreement ID, timestamp, principal ARN, and account ID.
- Notify your legal and compliance team.
Step 2: Set foundational, irreversible controls (Days 1–2)
- Register a customer managed key as the account default.
- Verify the key policy grants the required permissions: Encrypt, Decrypt, GenerateDataKey, DescribeKey.
- Configure your identity model (IAM Identity Center is recommended).
- Confirm the account sits in a dedicated workload organizational unit (OU) with Region-restricting SCPs.
Step 3: Create ACL-aware knowledge bases (Days 3–7)
- Classify your data sources: PHI, PHI-adjacent, and non-PHI.
- Create knowledge bases with ACL awareness turned on for PHI and PHI-adjacent sources.
- Map the identity store to source permissions and validate with multiple test users.
- Verify sync logs confirm successful ingestion. Keep PHI knowledge bases separated from general content.
Step 4: Create spaces (Days 5–8)
- Separate PHI-adjacent spaces from general-productivity spaces.
- Attach knowledge bases, dashboards, and action connectors. Restrict membership.
- Confirm that unauthorized users are blocked.
Step 5: Create custom agents with guardrails (Days 7–12)
- Define each agent’s purpose narrowly. Attach only the knowledge sources it needs.
- Configure PII redaction, blocked topics, content filters, and grounding controls.
- Test with normal queries, boundary queries, and adversarial prompts.
- Document results and remediation steps.
Step 6: Configure action connectors (Days 10–14)
- Start with read-only mode for PHI-adjacent data. Scope each connector to specific resources.
- Store credentials in AWS Secrets Manager with rotation turned on.
- Document the justification for any write access. Get security sign-off before turning it on.
- Test scope limits to confirm connectors can’t reach resources beyond their intended scope.
Step 7: Configure audit, retention, and monitoring (Days 12–16)
- Enable CloudTrail and CloudWatch vended logs.
- Apply data-protection masking. Set retention to at least six years. Enable S3 Object Lock.
- Configure alarms, enable Security Hub, and integrate with your SIEM.
Step 8: Validate with InfoSec (Days 14–21)
- Compile the evidence package: BAA confirmation, KMS configuration, identity setup, data classification, test results, and log samples.
- Run a tabletop breach exercise.
- Present to your InfoSec team. Remediate findings. Obtain sign-off.
Expansion phase (Weeks 4–8)
Start with non-PHI workflows: policy Q&A, document search, meeting prep, workflow automation. These let your team build confidence with the platform before PHI enters the picture.
Then expand to PHI-adjacent workflows: clinical documentation assistance, claims processing, prior authorization, regulatory Q&A, patient communication drafting with human review in the loop.
Monitor closely: review chat logs weekly, track guardrail trigger rates, and watch access patterns for 30 days after each new workflow goes live.
Conclusion
Amazon Quick gives regulated healthcare organizations, and the business associates who serve them, a managed AI workspace that is HIPAA-eligible across its full range of capabilities: agentic AI, knowledge retrieval, business intelligence, automation, and research.
The path to a compliant deployment follows a clear sequence:
- Understand the difference between eligible and compliant, and own your side of shared responsibility.
- Execute the BAA on an account provisioned through the AWS Management Console.
- Set the irreversible controls first: KMS keys, identity model, ACL-aware knowledge bases.
- Minimize the agent’s read and action surfaces, enforce least privilege, and mask PHI in logs.
- Validate with your InfoSec team, then scale from non-PHI to PHI-adjacent workflows.
The compliance expectations are moving as fast as the technology. AWS published its four security principles for agentic AI in April 2026 and the Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens in June 2026. Organizations that build on deterministic, infrastructure-level controls today will likely be well positioned as regulatory expectations catch up to what agentic AI can do.
What to do next
If you’re evaluating Amazon Quick: Request a compliance-focused briefing from your AWS account team. Ask about BAA scope, shared responsibility for agentic AI, and the latest HIPAA-eligible service additions.
If you’re ready to deploy: Use the implementation guide as your project plan. The irreversible decisions in Step 2 deserve a dedicated architecture review before you start creating resources.
If you’re already running Amazon Quick: Audit your deployment against the best practices in this post, especially the agentic security principles and the known limitations list.
For architecture guidance, reach out to your AWS Solutions Architect or the AWS Healthcare and Life Sciences team.

articles.title: +73 % en septembre en Europe, la voiture électrique donne tort aux discours alarmistes - Numerama
articles.text:
Il va être temps de ranger les discours alarmistes sur la trop faible demande de voitures électriques. L’Association des constructeurs européens d’automobiles (ACEA) a publié le 22 octobre les chiffres d’immatriculation pour le mois de septembre 2026. La voiture électrique n’y est plus une motorisation d’appoint ou une lubie de quelques early adopters. Elle dicte désormais le tempo du marché européen et en est même la locomotive.
Malgré un contexte macroéconomique incertain, le marché automobile européen progresse de 5,7 % depuis janvier (8,51 millions d’immatriculations en neuf mois). Sur la même période, le véhicule électrique progresse de 48,5 %. Cette redistribution des rôles, personne ne l’avait anticipée. Qui aurait pu imaginer, il y a un an, qu’en septembre 2026, la motorisation électrique serait en tête dans autant de pays européens ?
Septembre 2026 : une progression toujours aussi spectaculaire
Sur le seul mois de septembre, les immatriculations de voitures électriques (BEV) dans l’Union européenne ont bondi de 72,9 % pour atteindre 290 117, contre 167 776 un an plus tôt. La motorisation enregistre même 416 433 immatriculations en comptabilisant aussi l’Islande, la Norvège, la Suisse et le Royaume-Uni.
Le phénomène le plus marquant réside dans le basculement spectaculaire des deux plus gros marchés du continent :
- En France : les immatriculations de BEV ont plus que doublé (+107,5 %) avec 65 243 unités, dépassant largement les hybrides (57 248) et reléguant l’essence loin derrière (16 391, -39,1 %).
- En Allemagne : le marché germanique efface les hésitations de 2025 et signe un spectaculaire +94,7 % (88 599 immatriculations électriques), devançant là aussi l’hybride (71 190) et l’essence (44 632).
Pendant que les immatriculations de véhicules à essence baissent de 23,4 % et celles de véhicules diesel de 29,6 %, les versions électrifiées sont dans le positif. Les motorisations hybrides (MHEV et HEV) restent majoritaires à l’échelle du continent, mais leur progression est nettement moins forte que celle des voitures électriques. Il y a comme un essoufflement que l’on peut certainement corréler à la flambée des carburants.
L’électrique numéro 1 dans 12 pays de l’UE en septembre
Si l’on zoome sur les immatriculations du seul mois de septembre, on constate que l’électrique est devenu la motorisation reine sur une grande partie du continent européen.
- Allemagne : 88 599 immatriculations (+94,7 %), devant l’hybride (71 190) et l’essence (44 632).
- France : 65 243 immatriculations (+107,5 %), reléguant l’essence à seulement 16 391 unités.
- Pays-Bas : 19 149 immatriculations, soit plus de 52 % du total des ventes nationales.
- Danemark : 17 784 immatriculations, un record absolu avec 88,8 % de part de marché sur le mois.
- Belgique : 16 341 immatriculations, largement devant l’essence (9 564).
- Suède : 14 034 immatriculations, plus du double de l’hybride rechargeable (6 289).
- Autriche : 9 723 immatriculations (+80,6 %), devançant l’hybride simple (7 642).
- Portugal : 9 338 immatriculations, très loin devant l’hybride (3 446).
- Finlande : 4 338 immatriculations, représentant 62 % des livraisons de voitures neuves.
- Irlande : 3 114 immatriculations, soit le triple des volumes de l’hybride (970).
- Luxembourg : 1 331 immatriculations, numéro un devant l’hybride (1 070).
- Malte : 283 immatriculations, devant l’hybride (170).
- Hors UE : la Suisse bascule également au premier rang avec 7 833 unités, tandis que la Norvège frôle les 99 % avec 18 511 BEV sur 18 733 ventes.
Dans d’autres marchés d’envergure, si l’hybride non rechargeable conserve la première marche du podium, l’électrique s’offre une victoire symbolique majeure en doublant le thermique pur. C’est le cas de l’Espagne, où la batterie s’empare de la deuxième place avec 17 366 immatriculations (+71,7 %), devançant pour la première fois l’essence (15 184 unités).
Même scénario au Royaume-Uni, où le 100 % électrique frôle les 100 000 livraisons sur le mois (99 201 unités, +36,3 %), écrasant nettement les volumes de voitures à essence (67 003).
À l’inverse, la résistance aux carburants fossiles et à l’hybridation simple reste tenace dans le sud et l’est du continent. En Italie, l’électrique demeure confiné à la quatrième place avec 10 552 ventes, largement distancé par l’hybride (70 188), l’essence (24 667) et l’hybride rechargeable (15 636).
Le décalage est encore plus marqué en Europe centrale, notamment en Pologne (15 492 essences pour 3 478 électriques) et en République tchèque (7 466 essences contre 2 141 électriques), où le réseau de recharge embryonnaire et le manque d’offres abordables continuent de brider la transition.
Au cumul 2026 : l’électrique prend ses aises
Cette rentrée confirme une tendance de fond installée depuis janvier. Sur les neuf premiers mois de 2026, le véhicule 100 % électrique cumule 1 931 465 immatriculations (+48,5 %) et capte 22,7 % de part de marché dans l’UE, contre 16,1 % sur la même période en 2025.
L’électrique dépasse ainsi officiellement les motorisations essence pures, dont les ventes baissent de 19,1 % (1,80 million d’unités, soit 21,2 % de part de marché). Le diesel poursuit son déclin avec 7,1 % du gâteau (602 206 unités).
Si l’hybride non rechargeable (HEV) reste la motorisation préférée des Européens avec 36,3 % des ventes (3,09 millions d’unités), l’électrique s’installe solidement comme le deuxième pilier du marché. Et l’année n’est pas encore terminée. Les premiers échos des carnets de commandes des constructeurs laissent présager que l’électrique va continuer à gagner du terrain.
Les constructeurs (et l’ACEA) qui réclamaient des moratoires sur les normes CO₂ ou justifiaient leurs mauvais résultats par un blocage psychologique des conducteurs sont renvoyés à leur copie. Le marché n’a pas rejeté l’électrique : il a simplement rejeté les modèles trop chers et les marques trop lentes à proposer ce dont la clientèle avait vraiment besoin.

articles.title: Top 50: Journalists and PR pros in European Tech | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Europe’s technology ecosystem is evolving rapidly, with AI, FinTech, DeepTech and digital regulation dominating headlines and reshaping the industry. Behind these stories is a network of journalists and communications professionals who play a vital role in how Europe’s technology sector is reported on, understood and represented.
From reporters breaking stories on Europe’s biggest Tech companies and emerging startups to PR leaders building the profiles of ambitious businesses, these individuals help shape the conversation around European innovation.
This list brings together influential voices from leading publications and communications agencies specialising in Tech. Spanning the UK, Ireland and continental Europe, the list highlights professionals covering and communicating some of the industry’s most important developments.
Presented in alphabetical order, rather than as a ranking, the list celebrates the people helping to tell Europe’s technology stories.
Adam Satariano is a Technology Correspondent at The New York Times, covering European digital policy and the intersection of technology and world affairs, with a focus on regulation, AI, privacy and Tech geopolitics.
Adrian Weckler is Technology Editor at the Irish Independent and host of The Big Tech Show, covering everything from AI and big Tech to startups, telecoms and consumer technology.
Akansha Dimri is the founder and Editor-in-Chief of Tech Funding News, covering European technology startups, venture capital and funding developments, with a focus on FinTech, AI, DeepTech, HealthTech and the wider startup ecosystem.
Alex Warren is Head of Content & Creative at Wildfire, leading content strategy and creative campaigns for B2B technology brands, with expertise in AI, MarTech and technology communications.
Alexander Hüsing is an Editor at Deutsche Startups, covering Germany’s startup ecosystem and the wider European technology landscape, with a focus on venture capital, funding rounds, entrepreneurship and the digital economy.
Amy Lewin is Editor at Sifted, leading its coverage of Europe’s startup and venture capital ecosystem. She also hosts Startup Europe — The Sifted Podcast and covers AI, FinTech, investment trends and European technology policy.
Ana Marija Kostanic is Editor-in-Chief at The Recursive, covering Southeast Europe’s growing startup and technology ecosystem, with a focus on AI, venture capital and innovation.
Ana-Maria Stanciuc is Editor-in-Chief at The Next Web, overseeing coverage of Europe’s technology industry, including startups, venture capital and entrepreneurship.
Andrew Olley is founder of Olley PR, a London-based communications agency working with startups and scale-ups across technology, AI, healthcare and wealth management, with a focus on founder communications.
Anna Heim is a Freelance Reporter for TechCrunch, covering European startups and venture capital, with a particular focus on AI, FinTech and SaaS businesses.
Cate Lawrence is a Senior Journalist at Tech.eu, covering Europe’s startup and technology ecosystem, with a focus on funding, AI, mobility and sustainability.
Cathy White is the founder and CEO of CEW Communications, specialising in technology communications and strategic positioning for startups, scale-ups and venture capital firms, with expertise spanning AI, FinTech, HealthTech and B2B technology.
Charlie Taylor is Technology & Innovation Editor at Business Post, leading its technology coverage and editing Connected, its monthly tech magazine, with a focus on Irish startups, Big Tech and AI.
Ciara O’Brien is a Business & Technology Journalist at The Irish Times, covering technology businesses, AI, cybersecurity, telecommunications and digital policy.
Clara Armand-Delille is the founder of ThirdEye Media, advising high-growth technology companies and venture capital firms on international communications, fundraising and exits, with a focus on AI, FinTech, consumer technology and market expansion.
Colette Ballou is the founder and Chairwoman of Ballou PR, specialising in strategic communications for high-growth technology companies and venture investors across Europe and the US, with expertise in SaaS, AI, FinTech and enterprise technology.
Colin Ryan is Senior Reporter and Production Editor at SiliconRepublic, reporting on technology news, startups, AI, innovation and the evolving European technology ecosystem.
Cordelia Meacher is the founder and Managing Director of FieldHouse Associates, a communications consultancy advising venture capital firms, high-growth technology businesses and private-market investors on strategic positioning, media relations and corporate reputation.
Dan Milmo is Global Technology Editor at The Guardian, covering the technology industry with a particular focus on AI, technology regulation, investment and UK digital policy.
David Cendon Garcia is an Editor and Podcast Host at EU-Startups, covering European startup funding, venture capital, FinTech, investment and technology policy.
Harry Stebbings is the founder and Host of 20VC (The Twenty Minute VC), a venture capital podcast featuring interviews with leading founders, investors and technology executives, with a focus on AI, SaaS, FinTech, entrepreneurship and venture capital.
Ilona Hitel is the founder and Managing Director of CommsCo, a B2B technology communications agency helping emerging and challenger brands build visibility through strategic storytelling, with a focus on AI, DeepTech, HealthTech and enterprise technology.
James Titcomb is Technology Editor at The Telegraph, covering big Tech, AI, UK startups and technology policy, with more than a decade of reporting experience across London and Silicon Valley.
Joel Khalili is a Technology Reporter at WIRED, covering cryptocurrency, digital assets, FinTech and the security issues shaping the technology industry.
John Naughton is a Technology Columnist at The Observer, Cambridge academic and co-founder of the Minderoo Centre for Technology and Democracy, writing about the internet, AI, digital society and the wider implications of technology.
Jonathan Keane is a Business Correspondent at The Currency, covering startups, venture capital, AI, regulation and the digital economy in Ireland and across Europe.
Joséphine Boone is a Technology Journalist at Les Echos, covering AI, cloud computing, data, hardware and quantum technology, alongside French startups and European technology policy.
Julien Khaski is a Journalist and Senior Editorial Contributor at Maddyness, covering French and European startups, venture capital and technology developments, with a focus on AI, FinTech, telecommunications and interviews with technology leaders.
Julija “JJ” Jegorova is the founder and CEO of Black Unicorn PR, a London-based communications agency supporting technology startups, scale-ups and venture-backed businesses, with a focus on FinTech, cybersecurity, CleanTech, InsurTech and founder positioning.
Katie Prescott is Technology Business Editor at The Times and co-host of The Times Tech Podcast, covering the business of technology, AI, cybersecurity, investment and productivity.
Lottie Skeggs is an Account Director at Nara Communications, specialising in technology PR and integrated communications campaigns across European markets, including technology, financial services and higher education.
Luke Knight and Ronan Chambers are the co-founders and co-hosts of the European Technology Network (ETN), covering European technology trends, startup news and industry developments through livestreams, with a focus on AI, venture capital, digital transformation and technology policy.
Madhumita Murgia is AI Editor at the Financial Times, covering AI and its impact on society, with a particular focus on AI policy, data ethics and the social implications of emerging technologies.
Mark Sellman is a Technology Correspondent at The Sunday Times, covering AI, big Tech, online safety, telecommunications and consumer technology.
Matías Rodsevich is the founder and CEO of PRLab, a global B2B technology communications agency advising startups, scale-ups and established technology companies on media relations and thought leadership, with a focus on SaaS, AI, FinTech, cybersecurity and enterprise technology.
Matt Burgess is a Senior Writer at WIRED, covering cybersecurity, digital privacy, surveillance and technology regulation, with a focus on the European technology landscape.
Matt Neicho is an Account Director at TFD – Think Feel Do, specialising in communications for DeepTech startups working across AI, robotics, cybersecurity, green technology, space and engineering.
Mike Butcher is the founder of Pathfounders and former Editor-at-Large at TechCrunch, specialising in technology journalism covering startups, venture capital, AI and emerging technologies across Europe and beyond.
Nadine Schimroszik is a Technology Correspondent at Handelsblatt, covering Germany’s startup and technology ecosystem, including venture capital, telecommunications, DefenceTech and European innovation.
Natasha Lomas is Technology Editor at Rapporteur, formerly of Euractiv, specialising in European technology regulation, EU digital policy and privacy.
Nick Baines is the Co-founder and CEO of Nara Communications, a technology-focused PR agency supporting startups and scale-ups with media relations and strategic communications, with a focus on B2B technology, corporate positioning and business growth.
Paul Hayes is founder of Beachhut PR, the communications agency he established in 2010, working with European technology businesses ranging from seed-stage startups to established household names. Headquartered in Dublin, the agency also has offices in Amsterdam and London.
Paul Kunert is Europe Region Editor at The Register, covering the European enterprise technology industry, including IT infrastructure, technology businesses and the wider enterprise computing market.
Rachel Gilley is the CEO of Clarity, a global integrated communications agency serving technology and growth companies, with a focus on AI, B2B technology, consumer technology, corporate reputation and brand communications.
Seb Johnson is founder of Scaling Europe, a newsletter covering Europe’s startup and scaleup ecosystem, with a focus on venture capital, founder interviews, startup financials and AI.
Sian Gaskell is founder and Consultant at Sian Gaskell Consulting, specialising in B2B technology PR and integrated communications, drawing on her experience as Managing Partner and Board Director at Tyto PR.
Sofiane Oubela is an Account Director at Red Lorry Yellow Lorry, based in Paris, leading communications programmes for B2B SaaS startups, scale-ups and enterprise technology companies.
Tilo Bonow is the Founder and CEO of PIABO, a technology-focused communications agency advising startups and established technology companies on media visibility, corporate positioning and growth, with expertise in AI, SaaS and digital transformation.
Violaine Bourquin is a PR Account Director at The Hoffman Agency, based in Lyon, specialising in international technology communications and PR programmes for European technology companies.
Wibke Sonderkamp is Senior Director at GlobalCom PR-Network, leading international communications programmes across technology, CleanTech, HealthTech and ESG in European markets.
In summary
Europe’s technology sector continues to grow in both ambition and influence, and the people communicating its successes, challenges and breakthroughs are an essential part of that journey.
Whether reporting on AI regulation, uncovering the next generation of European startups or helping technology companies build international recognition, these 50 professionals contribute to the visibility and understanding of Europe’s tech ecosystem.
As the industry evolves, the relationship between journalists, founders and communications teams will remain central to how European technology stories reach audiences around the world.

articles.title: Capcom confirms data breach affecting 11.7 million accounts
articles.text:
Japanese gaming giant Capcom has confirmed that hackers breached its membership service, CAPCOM ID, exposing more than 11.7 million customer email addresses and associated information.
Apart from emails, exposed data includes account creation date, last login timestamp, number of logins, and the IP address used at the last login.
Capcom found that for a small subset of 43 accounts, dates of birth, gender, nicknames, and countries were also exposed.
For another subset of 196 accounts, the hackers changed the CAPCOM ID login passwords in an attempt to lock the owners out, but the company took action and reset them.
In an alert today, the gaming company says that passwords for all other registered members have not been exposed and that credit card information remained unaffected.
Capcom is a Japanese video game developer and publisher known for franchises such as Resident Evil, Monster Hunter, Street Fighter, and Mega Man. The company has 4,000 employees and an annual revenue of $1.24 billion.
CAPCOM ID is the company’s shared account system used for accessing its web services and playing some of its online games.
Although the timing of the breach remains unclear, Capcom said it detected suspicious activity and confirmed unauthorized access on October 19.
An investigation was launched immediately, and by the following day, it was clear that customer information had been compromised.
October 21, the company reported the incident to the police and to Japan’s Personal Information Protection Commission.
Capcom said its online services remain unaffected, but cautioned users to stay vigilant for unsolicited communications and emails requesting additional information, or messages containing URLs and attachments.
During the investigation, Capcom identified the intrusion method and implemented security measures to prevent similar incidents. However, no details related to the initial access have been shared.
The gaming firm also says it will notify affected customers in stages, likely due to the large volume of affected accounts, but it has established region-specific communication channels to submit support requests.
In November 2020, Capcom suffered an attack claimed by the Ragnar Locker ransomware gang, in which attackers claimed to have stolen 1 TB of data. The company subsequently warned that up to 390,000 people could be affected.
In April 2021, Capcom disclosed that the attackers had gained access through an old VPN device.

articles.title: Un TV QLED de 55 pouces avec Dolby Vision pour seulement 350 € ? C'est l'offre du jour à ne pas rater — Frandroid
articles.text:
Le 55E7S fait partie de la série E7S de Hisense, disponible en tailles allant de 43 à 85 pouces. Juste au-dessus, on trouve le E7S Pro, son grand frère, qui monte à 144 Hz pour les joueurs exigeants. Ici, on reste sur une dalle 60 Hz. L’essentiel est quand même là : QLED, Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive et trois ports HDMI 2.1. Bref, c’est un TV 55 pouces pensé d’abord pour le salon, et il est proposé à seulement 350 euros, ce qui n’est pas très cher payé.
L’offre en cours sur le Hisense 55E7S
- Un écran QLED 4K de 55 pouces avec rétroéclairage Direct LED
- Compatible Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10+ Adaptive et HLG
- Trois ports HDMI 2.1 avec VRR, ALLM et Game Mode Plus
Habituellement affiché à 449 euros, le Hisense 55E7S descend à 350 euros sur Joybuy via un coupon (la remise s’applique automatiquement dans le panier).
Une dalle QLED qui mise sur la couleur et le HDR
Le 55E7S utilise une dalle VA 4K associée à une couche de boîtes quantiques (la technologie QLED, que Hisense appelle Hi-QLED Colour). Ces boîtes quantiques donnent des couleurs plus saturées qu’un écran LCD classique. On le voit surtout sur les dessins animés et les documentaires animaliers. La dalle VA, elle, garantit des noirs plus profonds qu’une dalle IPS, avec un contraste annoncé à 8 000:1. Pour les vieilles sources en HD, comme la TNT, l’AI 4K Upscaler se charge de remonter l’image en 4K.
Côté formats HDR, la liste est très complète pour ce prix : Dolby Vision IQ, HDR10, HDR10+ Adaptive et HLG. Les versions IQ et Adaptive ajustent l’image selon la lumière de la pièce, ce qui est franchement pratique en journée. Bon, il y a une limite. Le rétroéclairage Direct LED n’a pas de gradation locale (local dimming), et la luminosité typique tourne autour de 330 nits. Le HDR est donc bien géré, mais il n’éblouira pas. Pour des hautes lumières plus percutantes, il faudra viser plus haut dans la gamme.
Une TV de salon qui sait aussi accueillir une console
Pour le jeu, Hisense a prévu trois ports HDMI 2.1, l’ALLM (qui bascule seul en mode jeu dès qu’une console s’allume) et le VRR. Le Game Mode Plus réduit la latence, annoncée sous les 10 ms. Une Game Bar s’affiche aussi à la demande pour voir le nombre d’images par seconde, le format HDR ou l’état du VRR. Attention quand même, le VRR plafonne à 60 Hz. Les jeux en 120 images par seconde sur PS5 ou Xbox Series X ne seront donc pas au rendez-vous. Pour ça, le modèle E7S Pro avec sa dalle 144 Hz est plus adapté.
Pour le reste, le 55E7S tourne sous VIDAA, le système maison de Hisense. Il gère AirPlay 2, le Wi-Fi, le Bluetooth et l’assistant Alexa. Le son passe par un système 2.0 de 20 W compatible Dolby Atmos et DTS:X. Ça suffit amplement pour le journal ou une série. Pour un film d’action, une barre de son fera clairement la différence.

articles.title: La frontera de Ceuta y Melilla en Google Maps lleva años siendo una línea de puntos. Ahora Bruselas decidirá si incumple la DSA
articles.text:
En un mapa, el tipo de línea con el que se dibuja una frontera es una cuestión política. Durante siglos han estado bien delimitadas en papel, y esto se mantuvo con la llegada de apps de navegación. Sin embargo, ahora mismo esas fronteras son dinámicas en función de lo que esté ocurriendo y Google tomó una curiosa decisión: dibujar la de Ceuta y Melilla como si no estuviera claro si pertenecen a España o a Marruecos.
No es nuevo, pero tras lo ocurrido este verano, el asunto ha escalado tanto que la Comisión de Peticiones del Parlamento Europeo está estudiando si Google está vulnerando la ley de servicios digitales.
La línea. En Google Maps, las fronteras indiscutibles se muestran con una línea gris continua. El problema es cuando vemos una discontinua porque puede significar varias cosas. Marcan una frontera fijada por tratados, las de facto, las provisionales y las discutidas.
Según Google, en este caso se trata de un caso de representación de "fronteras discutidas" y el problema es que no es nuevo. De hecho, el Maldita lo documentó en 2020 (y hubo usuarios que preguntaron a la propia Google) y el Observatorio de Ceuta y Melilla más de lo mismo en 2023. Con la reviente entrada masiva de personas en Ceuta a finales de julio de este año, la cuestión ha vuelto al primer plano.
La petición. Con la situación caliente, el Observatorio denunció a Google Maps por cuestionar la soberanía española de las dos ciudades y Zeolandia, asociación personada en la causa de la Audiencia Nacional por la entrada masiva, ya transmitió al director general de Google en España su preocupación por cómo Google Maps estaba representando la situación, exigiendo que Google precise el significado técnico exacto de esa línea.
A Europa vas. En ese momento, el eurodiputado del PP Juan Ignacio Zoido ya comentó que iba a elevar el asunto a la Comisión Europea. Y Zoido... cumplió. Como expone la propia web del partido, el político registró su pregunta a la Comisión, buscando conocer si ésta conocía el trazado de línea discontinua y si usará la DSA (la Ley de Servicios Digitales) para obligar a Google a rectificar.
Aunque no es un caso únicamente de que la multinacional rectifique, sino de presionar a Europa. En el documento subido por el PP se expone que es una manera de que Ceuta y Melilla tengan "plena elegibilidad para instrumentos y programas europeos, entre ellos el Mecanismo de Recuperación y Resiliencia, el Fondo de Transición Justa, Horizonte Europa, los fondos de gestión fronteriza y el Fondo de Asilo, Migración e Integración". También para una mayor implicación de Frontex en la protección de las fronteras exteriores de la Unión.
¿Qué pinta aquí la DSA? Es sencillo y se apoya en que la Comisión designó Google Maps en abril de 2023 como una de las plataformas de gran tamaño que debían velar por la buena competencia, entre otras cosas. Con más de 45 millones de usuarios activos mensualmente en la UE, esto obliga a unas responsabilidades más estrictas, pero también a la supervisión directa de Bruselas.
Como señala en la petición,que recoge El Español, el mapa en su estado actual puede desinformar sobre las fronteras exteriores de la Unión. También es una prueba, ya que Bruselas tendría que identificar qué obligación concreta habría incumplido Google y, como apuntan en el medio marroquí Le360, esto la situaría como árbitro en una disputa territorial.
Queda camino. De nuevo, esto no es nuevo y habrá que ver qué decisión toma Bruselas respecto a Google Maps, pero es evidente que los actos de este verano han encendido el debate que lleva más de un lustro abierto en cuanto a la representación de esas dos fronteras en la app.
Pero Google, realmente, ha tomado aquí la postura de "a mí que no me líen" porque Marruecos lleva décadas solicitando la inscripción de Ceuta y Melilla como su territorio, el mismo tiempo que España lleva defendiendo que son parte de su unidad nacional.
Y tampoco parece que vayan a hacer nada por su cuenta porque, como declararon a Maldita este verano, "Google se mantiene neutral en los debates geopolíticos", afirmando que en lo único que se comprometen es en mostrar "de manera objetiva los territorios en disputa". Parece que Bruselas tendrá que ser el juez en todo esto apelando al mazo de la DSA. A fecha de edición de este artículo, si te metes en la aplicación verás, efectivamente, la línea discontinua.
