articles.title: Une page de l'histoire du jeu vidéo se tourne
articles.text:
Fondé en 1995 à Edmonton, le studio légendaire derrière Baldur’s Gate, Neverwinter Nights, Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic, Mass Effect et Dragon Age a officialisé la nouvelle sur les réseaux sociaux. Cette annonce tombe quelques minutes seulement après la publication d’un rapport de Bloomberg détaillant les suppressions de postes, dont 50 touchent directement les équipes de BioWare. Les dirigeants d’EA justifient ces coupes par la nécessité « d’aligner les talents et les investissements là où se trouvent les plus grandes opportunités de croissance ».
La chute d’un pilier du jeu de rôle
Racheté par Electronic Arts en 2007, le studio était autrefois qualifié par l’ancien PDG John Riccitiello de l’une des structures les plus respectées de l’industrie. Mais le rachat d’EA l’an dernier pour 55 milliards de dollars par un consortium comprenant Silver Lake, le fonds souverain saoudien et Affinity Partners a lourdement endetté l’entreprise. Les analystes prévoyaient déjà de telles mesures, la nouvelle direction privilégiant les services en ligne, les jeux de sport annuels et les microtransactions au détriment des studios narratifs.
Les difficultés s’étaient accumulées ces dernières années avec le départ de figures historiques, comme les fondateurs Ray Muzyka et Greg Zeschuk en 2012, ou encore Casey Hudson et Mac Walters. Des titres récents comme Mass Effect Andromeda, Anthem (dont le mode multijoueur et les refontes prévues ont été abandonnés) et Dragon Age: The Veilguard ont également reçu des accueils mitigés de la part de la critique et des joueurs.
Une onde de choc pour toute l’industrie
La fermeture de ce monument du RPG enterre définitivement le développement précoce du prochain volet de la franchise Mass Effect, brisant les espoirs des fans de la première heure. Dans son message d’adieu, l’équipe a tenu à remercier sa communauté pour ces trois décennies d’aventures partagées, de choix cornéliens et de personnages marquants.
À lire : Electronic Arts assume la pub dans ses jeux vidéo, il y en aura même de plus en plus
Cette restructuration menée par la maison mère illustre la transition brutale d’une industrie du jeu vidéo où les créations solos ambitieuses cèdent la place à la rentabilité immédiate des jeux service. Pour les 400 salariés concernés par ces suppressions de postes chez EA, la pilule est amère, marquant la fin d’un savoir-faire historique et tournant une page de l’histoire du jeu vidéo.

articles.title: Indurex Raises $8 Million to Expand Industrial Cybersecurity Platform
articles.text:
Amsterdam-based industrial cybersecurity firm Indurex has raised €7 million (roughly $7.84 million) in a round led by Contrarian Ventures, with Axeleo Capital and Curiosity also participating.
The company said it will use the funding for research and development and to expand its commercial operations in Europe and the Middle East, with the United States and Asia-Pacific markets to follow.
Indurex develops security software for cyber-physical systems used in critical infrastructure and industrial operations. Its SafeGuard AI platform is designed to analyze data from distributed control systems, safety instrumented systems, process historians, alarm management systems and IT security tools. The company says it uses that information to identify anomalies and changes to engineering configurations, protection settings and safety functions that may need operator attention.
The approach targets a gap Indurex sees in conventional OT security tools, which often focus on network-connected assets and activity. The company aims to bring engineering, process, safety and cybersecurity data together so operators can assess security alerts in the context of the physical systems they run.
Indurex emerged from stealth in January 2026 and was founded by Jalal Bouhdada, who serves as the company’s CEO, and Maarten Oosterink, who serves as COO.
Bouhdada previously founded industrial cybersecurity company Applied Risk, which assurance and risk management company DNV acquired in 2021.
Indurex says its early customers include energy and manufacturing operators, from mid-sized companies to multinational enterprises. It is also targeting utilities and data center operators.

articles.title: Elon Musk invirtió USD 1.000 millones en Skydance, la nueva dueña de Paramount y Warner Bros
articles.text:
Elon Musk invirtió aproximadamente USD 1.000 millones en Skydance, la compañía de medios que nació de la fusión entre Paramount y Warner Bros. Discovery, según informó este 22 de octubre de 2026 el medio estadounidense Semafor citando a personas con conocimiento directo de la operación.
El aporte de capital se concretó casi al mismo tiempo que otras inyecciones de accionistas de Skydance, entre ellos Laurene Powell Jobs, viuda del cofundador de Apple Steve Jobs e integrante del directorio de la compañía, según la misma fuente. Ni Musk ni Paramount respondieron a los pedidos de comentarios de la prensa norteamericana.
La operación llega dos semanas y media después de que Paramount cerrara, el 6 de octubre, la adquisición de Warner Bros. Discovery por USD 110.000 millones, un movimiento que unificó bajo un mismo techo corporativo a Paramount+, HBO Max y una cartera de canales que incluye CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central y Food Network.
Los codirectores ejecutivos David Ellison y Ynon Kreiz, llegado desde Mattel en septiembre, deben integrar dos estudios y dos plataformas de streaming mientras ejecutan un recorte de costos de USD 6.000 millones en tres años. Según la prensa económica estadounidense, la compañía combinada arrastra una deuda cercana a los USD 80.000 millones.
Una relación que viene de la compra de Twitter
El vínculo entre Musk y la familia Ellison no es nuevo. Larry Ellison, cofundador de Oracle y padre de David Ellison, invirtió USD 1.000 millones en 2022 para ayudar a Musk a comprar Twitter, hoy rebautizada X, y también integró el directorio de Tesla tras una inversión personal en la automotriz en 2018.
Larry Ellison, además, garantizó personalmente más de USD 40.000 millones del financiamiento accionario que permitió a Paramount quedarse con Warner Bros. Discovery, de acuerdo con lo publicado por el medio citado. Esa cercanía alimentó meses de especulación sobre una eventual entrada de Musk al capital de la nueva Skydance.
El empresario y multimillonario de cable John Malone, fundador de Liberty Media, había anticipado el martes en un encuentro del Paley Center que un acuerdo entre Musk y los Ellison estaba cerca. “Creo que hay un acuerdo en camino”, dijo Malone, quien calculó que la inversión de SpaceX podría llegar a entre USD 8.000 y 10.000 millones.
La acción de Skydance, con un salto y una caída
Las acciones de Skydance llegaron a subir hasta 6% tras conocerse la noticia, pero revirtieron esa ganancia y cerraron con una baja de alrededor de 2% luego de una breve suspensión de la cotización, según datos del mercado citados por agencias financieras.
Más allá del alivio financiero inmediato, la entrada de Musk reavivó las especulaciones sobre una alianza más amplia entre Starlink, la red satelital de SpaceX, y los contenidos de Skydance, que incluyen franquicias como Yellowstone, The Last of Us y NCIS, además de los noticieros de CNN.
David Ellison había dado pistas sobre la dirección tecnológica de la compañía semanas antes del anuncio. “Estamos construyendo un verdadero equipo de producto y tecnología”, dijo en una entrevista con la cadena CNBC a comienzos de octubre, y agregó que la inteligencia artificial debía ser “una herramienta para los artistas, no al revés”.
La inversión de Musk se suma a la lista de apuestas cruzadas entre sus compañías y el resto del sector de medios y tecnología: SpaceX ya había sumado a inversores como Apollo y Nvidia a un programa de asociación vinculado a Grok, el chatbot de xAI, mientras Tesla explora en paralelo una eventual fusión con la propia SpaceX.
Skydance no confirmó de manera oficial el monto ni los términos de la operación, y Semafor precisó que su información surge de fuentes con conocimiento directo de las negociaciones, no de un comunicado de la empresa. Por ahora, el mercado quedó a la espera de una confirmación formal por parte de la compañía o de Musk.

articles.title: Woman spends three nights in jail and faces six years in prison over Cash App account she never opened
articles.text:
WTF?! Digital identity fraud is far from something new, but this case shows just how extreme the repercussions can be. A Cash App account opened in someone else's name and used in scams could lead to an innocent person being sentenced to years in prison. The problem is that the company initially refused to provide information about the account because she couldn't prove that she was the owner.
In April, Amanda Smith was shocked to discover officers at her upstate Pennsylvania home with a warrant for her arrest, writes 404 Media. The alleged crime took place in Arkansas – more than a thousand miles away in a state she'd never visited. Smith was taken to the local jail, where she was locked up for three nights.
Her bail was initially set at $50,000, but Smith says authorities told her there was little point in paying it because they intended to extradite her to Arkansas anyway. After being released, she and her husband drove to Arkansas for a court appearance, where she was fingerprinted and photographed. Another $20,000 bail was imposed before she could return home.
Smith later discovered why she had been arrested: a scammer had tricked someone into sending $1,000 to a Cash App account, one that was in her name but controlled by a criminal.
It turned out that the account had been created using Smith's Social Security number and date of birth. But Smith, who describes herself as not tech-savvy, said she had never used Cash App.
The situation sounds like one that should have been resolved quickly. But Smith says she is still being asked to prove her innocence in an ongoing criminal case. One stumbling block was that Cash App refused to hand over details of the account to Smith because she couldn't prove she was the owner. She eventually received the data through discovery in her case.
Shockingly, Smith is now facing up to six years in prison for a crime she says she didn't commit and knew nothing about. The charges include computer fraud, unlawful use of a communication device, and theft of property. "They're trying to turn it into my problem [...] that I need to prove that I'm innocent," Smith told 404 Media. "That's not what I grew up believing was the way it worked."
Not too surprisingly, the fraud took place on that bastion of honest transactions, Facebook Marketplace. The buyer found items for sale and messaged the seller, who told them to send money to his wife's Cash App account. The name on the account was Amanda Smith.
Unfortunately, the seller's Facebook account had been hacked. There were no items for sale, and the Cash App account had been created just before the scam took place.
Cash App records also revealed what happened to the stolen money. Just hours after the $1,000 arrived, it was divided into smaller amounts and sent to a network of other accounts. Some appeared to be controlled by scammers, while others had changed their usernames, potentially making the money more difficult to trace.
Police obtained Smith's personal details from Cash App through a search warrant. A detective then obtained her driver's license and checked her information using Accurint, a LexisNexis database used by law enforcement. But having someone's details on an account isn't quite the same as proving they operated it.
And there were plenty of discrepancies. According to 404 Media's review, the address on the account was one where neither Smith nor her husband had ever lived. The account had also been accessed through Verizon connections, while Smith says she uses AT&T and has never had a Verizon plan.
There was also a discrepancy involving the phone used to create the account. Cash App's records showed an iPhone running iOS 16.1.1, an operating system dating back to 2022. Smith, however, provided evidence that her iPhone 13 mini was running the much newer iOS 26.5.2.
The phone number associated with the account raised further questions. Although Smith said she might have used it years earlier, 404 Media found it linked to her name in historical data breaches. Tellingly, someone had also used the same number to create a Venmo account under a different name around a week before the fraudulent Cash App account was opened.
Also read: Cash App reaches $45 million settlement over alleged failure to protect users from fraud
A private investigator hired by Smith has questioned whether police established that she actually controlled the account. Her lawyer is trying to have the case dismissed. Neither Cash App nor the prosecutor responded to requests for comment.
Meanwhile, authorities have offered Smith a plea deal including a $1,000 fine, $1,000 in restitution and three years' probation. She has refused, saying she is innocent. A hearing is scheduled for November.
This isn't the first time someone has ended up in jail because of another person's fraud. A grandmother was jailed for six months after facial recognition tech falsely linked her to a bank fraud case. She is now suing the City of Fargo and a Fargo Police Department detective for $10 million over the incident.

articles.title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.text:
EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.
Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber.
Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview.
Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles.
Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving. Today, Rivian offers “Universal Hands-Free” driving software that lets drivers take their hands off the wheel on highways, while still watching the road. The company plans to, by the end of the year, release a version of the software that can handle the entire drive through surface streets and highways without touching the wheel, although the driver will still have to supervise and be ready to take over.
Rivian is also working toward full autonomy, which it will deploy in the robotaxi versions of its R2 SUV that will be available on the Uber app in 2028.
“The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in an interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.”
Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap.
Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.
“For us, it’s about taking real scenarios, but making them simulatable,” Philbin said. “These are not synthetic kind of video game styles, they’re real things that happen in the world, but now we get that extra dial of being able to move the cameras around, shift other agents, have maybe different lighting or weather conditions. So it’s a really powerful tool for us.”
It’s technology that Philbin said the company knew it wanted and had actually “done a pretty extensive kind of evaluation of a lot of different providers.”
Any company developing automated driving technology needs data — and a lot of it. But the quality matters too. Real-world data collected from cameras and other sensors is especially valuable.
Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1T pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day.
Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said.
“Especially when you think about validation, right? So that’s really the piece where you’re saying, ‘is the system good to ship?’” Philbin said. “And there, you really want to have a good sense of this sim-to-real gap, because to do that kind of hand on heart, you really need to trust that answer is in the positive. Otherwise, you’re measuring something that’s not representative of how it will actually perform in the real world.”
This article was updated to include more quotes from Philbin and more details on Rivian’s automated driving strategy.

articles.title: Moderna and Merck say their mRNA cancer vaccine cut death, recurrence by 42%
articles.text:
Personalized mRNA vaccines against melanoma—the deadliest form of skin cancer—reduced the risk of death or recurrence by 42 percent compared to standard treatment in a late-stage trial, pharmaceutical partners Merck and Moderna announced Thursday.
The results are a significant advance in melanoma treatment; Merck and Moderna are already engaging with regulatory authorities to get the vaccine approved. More broadly, the vaccine’s success bolsters hope that mRNA vaccines and individualized cancer-targeting medicines offer a new paradigm for cancer therapies.
“From the beginning, we believed mRNA technology could make it possible to develop cancer treatments uniquely matched to each patient’s tumor,” Moderna CEO Stéphane Bancel said in a statement. The trial results “mark a defining moment for that vision and show what’s possible when we rethink how medicines are made.” They also “reinforce our conviction that mRNA has the potential to fundamentally change how we treat cancer,” he said.
In August, Moderna and Merck reported that the vaccine has succeeded in the trial, but held off reporting details until the data could be presented at an upcoming scientific conference. That conference is the European Society of Medical Oncology, starting now in Madrid, Spain. The data was scheduled for presentation on Saturday, but after an oncology news site reported the results early, breaking the embargo, the companies released the top-line results. The full data has been accepted for publication in the New England Journal of Medicine.
As Ars reported earlier, the Phase 3 trial included 1,137 patients who had stage IIB–IV melanoma that had been surgically removed prior to entering the trial. Patients were randomized 2-1 to receive either a combination treatment including the personalized mRNA vaccine with a standard treatment, or the standard treatment alone. The standard treatment was Merck’s established monoclonal antibody cancer treatment Keytruda.

articles.title: Neo Financial secures $185-million credit facility from credit unions |
articles.text:
Neo Financial has closed a deal to receive $185 million in a credit facility from ATB Financial and a handful of credit unions that it says will support the growth of Neo’s credit card program.
The news: Announced on Thursday, Neo said it had closed a syndicated “warehouse facility at $185 million.” In finance, a warehouse facility is an arrangement where companies can borrow against a pool of assets without giving up equity or taking out a traditional loan. Neo said the lending capital would be used to expand the funding capacity for the FinTech’s credit card receivables.
From the source: “Building a more competitive banking system in Canada is a team sport,” Neo co-founder and chief commercial officer Jeff Adamson wrote on social media. “This funding supports Neo’s credit card receivables as we grow. It also puts a bigger ambition into practice: building a platform where other financial institutions can participate in that growth.”
The context: Terms of the warehouse facility agreement were not explicitly outlined by Neo, but Adamson said under the terms of the arrangement there is room to increase the amount from $185 million up to $250 million. BetaKit reached out to Adamson to ask for details on the deal’s terms, but has not yet received a response.
ATB Financial, an Alberta Crown corporation, is leading the agreement, with additional participation from a handful of Canadian credit unions including Vancity, Beem Credit Union, Alterna Savings and Credit Union, and Innovation Federal Credit Union.
RELATED: Neo Financial lays off roughly 10 percent of its staff
Final thought: Thursday’s announcement comes after significant expansions for Neo’s credit card program in the last year. In June, the company launched four new credit cards, including partnerships with Mastercard and United Airlines. It remains among Canada’s fastest-growing FinTechs, according to The Globe and Mail and Deloitte. However, it has also faced some hurdles, losing two of its largest loyalty card partnerships, with both Tim Hortons and The Hudson’s Bay Company, this year. In September, Neo laid off roughly 10 percent of its staff, citing a desire to streamline operations.
BetaKit’s Prairies reporting is funded in part by YEGAF, a not-for-profit dedicated to amplifying business stories in Alberta.
Image courtesy Neo Financial.

articles.title: Actors for Agents: Patterns for Production AI
articles.text:
Transcript
Manju Rajashekhar: I'm Manju Rajashekhar. I started my career more than a decade ago at Twitter where I helped solve the fail-mail problem. At that time, I worked on distributed caching and I was also a prolific open-source contributor around that time. A lot of the software that I wrote and open sourced around that time is still used today at companies like Uber and Wikipedia to scale your caching systems. GCP and Azure documents it as a reference implementation for designing your caching systems for scale. After Twitter, I ended up founding a company in the deep learning and search space. Our product was search as a service and recommendation as a service. That company was acquired by Etsy, where I spent eight years as a VP of engineering. I ran all of their AI and machine learning functions that included search, ads, recommendation, and personalization engine. Most recently, I started a company called Mad Labs with a couple of really wonderful colleagues of mine. We are an agentic platform company focused on building agents that have reliable execution over long horizons and they're very token efficient and have a strong governance structure around it.
Today, I'm really excited to talk about the topic, which is actors for agents. When I was putting together this talk and I was researching this topic, I realized that surprisingly not much was spoken about this topic, which to me felt crazy because I believe that the actor model or the actor style design fits really well to the runtime of agent existence. My hope with this talk is by the time we get to the end of this talk, I can convince you that the actor model is not like an old concurrency idea, but it really maps well to the agentic system design that you can start using as a tool as you go about in your own day to day working with agents.
From Demoing with Agents, to Prod
Instead of starting with the boring definitions of what an actor is, I thought I could start with a story. The story is something that we all might be familiar with, which is when your demo with agents leaves your beautiful demo environment and makes contact with production. How many of you have built a demo with agents over the past 12 months? What I'm going to share might seem super familiar because when we are designing a demo with agents, our focus is always about modeling the reasoning, like getting the prompts right, figuring out exactly how do we get the guardrails right and all of that. The architecture ends up being pretty obvious. It's a simple architecture. There is some prompt chain over the agentic loop. There's some application glue code. There's perhaps a cue that you put in for the slow work, model calls and a few tool calls and you finally get an answer, and your agentic demo is working.
Then this architecture feels pretty natural. It's good enough to prove that the models can reason, the tools can be called, and the workflow can come back with an answer. It's also good enough to produce a demo that makes the agentic systems feel real. Now your demo gets super popular. Your friends start using it, your colleagues start using it, your relatives start using it, and now the demo makes its first contact with production. The production actually changes the shape of the problem. Because your tool calls are now taking longer than expected. Anthropic decided to tell you that actually we exhausted your token, so I'm going to rate limit you. Users start asking follow-up questions while your agent is still working. Your workers get restarted halfway through the execution. Suddenly the hard part is no longer about the reasoning, the hard part becomes the runtime of the production agents. That's exactly what I want to talk about today is how do we model this runtime of production agents. Really what happens once your demo goes from demo to the production environment, the shape of the problem changes.
Let's now look at what are some of these shapes that change. The first thing that changes is this notion of time. In the demo environment, your tool returns pretty quickly. It feels like a normal request-response cycle that you're familiar with microservices. Everything is happening really quickly. That's no longer true in the production setting because you get rate limited, tool calls can take longer. Sometimes you have to get back to the user for feedback, and the user can only respond back tomorrow because they're not available. A function call ends up being a poor abstraction for work that begins now and results later under uncertain conditions. The second thing that changes is just the interaction. The users do not stop existing while your agent is still working. They ask for follow-up questions. They ask for status. They request for partial results. They change the execution of agent based on new information.
Your agent loop is no longer a single request-response loop. It is a running process that's just receiving information. The third thing that changes is delegation. Unlike everything else that we have seen in the past, agentic systems don't merely execute a series of steps. Actually, they're creating the entire steps on the fly because they're learning more information and coming up with the execution of work. The structure of execution no longer follows a straight line. It ends up becoming a tree, or more precisely, a graph. The fourth thing that changes is just failure. There are different failure models that happen with agents. Tool calls fail, model call fails, your worker processes get restarted, external APIs get rate limited, queues can re-deliver messages, and the list goes on and on. In the demo environment, you're treating exceptions as an afterthought. In the production setting, it's just a part of the normal operating environment.
At this point, because the production changed the shape of the problem, the architecture that you started out with the demo has started to grow sideways. Your chat lives in one place, your workflow state lives somewhere else. The queue knows that the work exists, but doesn't know what the user really intended. The database records progress, but not always the continuation of work. The retry state is scattered across different places. The recovery condition just becomes a second implementation of your workload. The code still works, but the system becomes hard to reason about. The problem is not any of these single components is wrong. It all makes sense. Queues make sense. Databases are useful. You do need workers for parallelism and concurrency. The problem is that the system doesn't have a single execution model. The agent gets treated as a chat in one part of the system, as a workflow or a background job in a different part of the system, as an entire recovery process in yet another.
That is actually the production pain of the runtime of these agents. The conceptual unit of work that agents end up carrying out is actually split across multiple runtime concepts. This happens for one main reason, is that we design these agents as a reasoning problem with LLM and tool calls, which ends up hiding the actual problem, which is the runtime of these production agents. The moment we start looking at production agents as a runtime problem, a familiar system starts showing up, which many of you might be familiar with, that is, the production agents are just distributed systems in disguise. They are stateful. They are concurrent. They are long-running. They communicate with other components, so they're distributed in nature. They can fail in parts, and they can restart independently. They must accept new information while the work is still ongoing.
Actors
Once you see agents as a distributed system, a more fundamental question starts showing up, which is, how do you model the runtime of a system like this? Our answer to that is the actor style reasoning fits really well with the runtime of the production agents. Or at least I would like to convince you that is the case today with this talk. Before we talk about agents, let's just walk through the actor idea from first principles for folks who might not be familiar with. First, the actor idea isn't new. It was actually discovered as part of the AI and concurrency research in the 1970s. It is Erlang and OTP that made the actor style thinking operational in a serious way. In fact, there's this great story about Erlang, which is the story of nine nines, nine nines of availability. Erlang proved it by running a system over 2 million lines of Erlang code that was available for 20 years with nine nines of availability.
That's crazy to think about it. What Erlang showed is that you can build really reliable systems that are extremely concurrent, fault tolerant, and always on. We want to bring the same idea to agents. To understand the actor model from first principles, let's actually take a step back and ask, how do we normally think about computation? Most of us, when we learn to program, we think about software as a single flow of control. A function calls another function, you receive results, you update state, and then you move on. This model is not wrong. It's a great mental model. It's super useful. It quietly assumes a world where control flow is local. Failure is either absent or is handled by the caller. Real systems are not like that. Real systems end up having multiple flows of control. Many things happen at once. Parts need to communicate without sharing all of their internals.
Parts can fail independently. The moment we enter this world, which is the real world, the hard question changes. The hard question is not merely, which function should I call? The hard questions are, who owns the state? How do other parts of the system communicate with it? What happens if one part fails? The actor model is one answer to these questions. In the actor model, the basic unit is actually not a function. It's not a class. It's not a thread. The basic unit is an actor, which is an independent unit of computation. The operative word here being an independent. The actor has a private state that only actor has access to. The actor can receive messages. Because it can receive messages, it must be addressable, which gives it a mailbox. When it receives messages, the actor decides completely based on its local state what to do next.
It can update its state. It can send messages to a different actor. It can create child actors. It can fail. It can stop. It can restart. All of those are options that are available to the actor. The actor ends up starting to behave like this little machine. A machine that has address, which gives it a mailbox. A machine that has a private state. The machine that has an encapsulated behavior of how it should act purely based on its internal state and the messages it receives.
Foundational Design Principles of an Actor
This leads us to the first foundational design principle of an actor, is that the state has an owner. I think we're all familiar with shared memory systems, where many threads end up touching the same piece of memory. We've all dealt with that. The way to achieve consistency in such a system is that you end up having locks, mutexes, transactions, read-only semantics, defensive copying, and a whole lot of discipline. The actor model flips the question. Instead of asking who is allowed to mutate the state, the actor model forces the question that which actor owns the state. That's how you go about designing within the actor model. Only the owning actor can change its state. Other actors cannot reach inside and mutate an actor directly. All they can do is send messages, and the owning actor can receive those messages and decide how to transition. The second foundational principle with the actor model is everything is a message.
I want all of you guys to pause on this principle because this actually shifts the shape of the control flow. Like, instead of code calling code, you now have communicating systems. Like a direct call assumes that the caller and the callee, they live together in the same execution context, now waiting on the same stack. The moment you have messages, now you end up having this loose coupling between two communicating entities. The sender can send a message and move on. The receiver can process the message when it is ready, when the results can come back later, also as another message. That gives us a different way to think about concurrency. Inside one actor, the execution is sequential. Actor receives messages one at a time and goes about executing it. The state is local, so the reasoning is also local. On the outside, across actors, the system is concurrent.
Many actors are working independently, so they can run, they can wait, they can send, they can receive, they can fail. All of that can happen independently. The actor model is not making concurrency disappear. What it is really doing is it's putting boundaries around it, and that gives us a way to reason about things locally while still building concurrent systems. Finally, this loose coupling that is really enabled because everything is a message allows for an actor to operate like an entity. An actor can live over time. It can be created. It can receive multiple messages. It can remember state between messages. It can create child actors. It can crash. It can restart, and it can eventually stop.
Then the final foundational principle with the actor model is that failure has a boundary. In many systems when you're thinking about failure, you have a scattered version of try-catch blocks everywhere, retry loops, maybe a completely different recovery code. Actor model just encourages a different question. Because you have independent operating entities, it just says like where is the boundary, and can we put a boundary around failures that happen around these independent entities? The actor model turns failure into an architectural concern, which is great when we're designing systems. In actor, this idea is called supervision, which we'll see later in this talk, where some actors end up being supervisors and some actors end up being workers. If a worker fails, the supervisor has a policy. The policy is you can restart it, you can stop it, you can escalate the failure to a human, or you can escalate the failure to a system with just partial results.
All of them are policies. There's no single specific policy. The important idea is that the architecture knows where failure happened and what boundary contains it. If you put it all together, an actor is an addressable, isolated, stateful, message-driven unit of computation that lives under a lifecycle and a failure policy. It's addressable because other parts can send it messages. It is isolated because the state is private. It is stateful because it remembers between messages. It's message-driven because communication happens with the mailbox of the actor, and is supervised because failure is contained by the architecture. This ends up giving us a compact model for long-running concurrent failure-prone systems. The runtime for it could either be local and also remote.
Order Actor and Agent Task Actor
This idea then brings us back to agents. Before we talk about agents, let me just make the idea of actor a little bit more concrete. Let's just take an example. This is an example, which is, you're shopping on Amazon or eBay. You add an item to a cart. You put in your payment information, put in your shipping information. The question is, that's an order that you're about to make. How would you model something like that? The first question, when we think about the actor model, it becomes, who owns the truth about the order? The actor-style design, the truth is owned by the owning actor. In this case, we call it the order actor. It owns the items, the payment status, the shipping information, and whatever else defines the order. If the payment happens to complete, how does the payment component communicate with the order actor?
The payment doesn't directly mutate the order. All the payment does is that it sends a message called payment succeeded. Shipping, similarly, doesn't mutate the order actor. When the shipping completes or the shipment is in progress, all it does is sends a message that shipping completed or shipping failed. We looked at both payment and shipment, and they're both examples of the happy path. Even the unhappy path, like cancellations and timeouts, are also messages. This is where the actor model starts paying off, where both the happy path and the unhappy path ends up using the same interface.
Now, take this order actor and replace it with an agent task actor. That's the translation going from an actor to an agent. It's like, ok, Manju, I agree, but tell me how. Let's go through the mapping one by one. The first thing that we need to figure out is like, what is the state of this agent task actor? Obviously, the state must include the goal of the agent, because all agents are autonomous, and the goal gives the task a continuity. A single model call might come and go, but the task continues to make forward progress of what it is trying to accomplish. Encoding it as an agent task actor allows us to do it. The second thing that you would put into the state is context. Context is not just the text in the prompt, it is all of the accumulated state that allows the task to move forward intelligently as new information arrives.
That becomes the context. There's also like the tools in flight. If a tool call can take several minutes, then the task must remember which tool calls are outstanding, know what it is for, what it expects out of the tool call in terms of results, and what kinds of timeouts apply to those tool calls. The task doesn't necessarily own the internals of the tool, but it must remember the fact that there are tools in flight and outstanding. The final thing that is also part of the state is all of the child tasks. We talked about the fact that agents are special because when you're doing agentic execution, the execution changes based on new information. You can create new tasks. You can delegate work to new tools or new child actors. The parent doesn't need to own every single detail of a child task, but it does need to own the relationship.
Like why child was created, what result is expected, what should we do when failure happens, and how the results should be integrated. We have seen that the state of an actor maps really well to the state of an agent task actor. There's also the communication side of the mapping. How does that work? On the communication side, all the events to the agent task actor just ends up being encoded at messages. To make this more concrete, like let's assume you go and tell your agent, I really want you to generate a report looking at different geographies and doing some specific analysis on it. Now, that request to the agent shows up as a user message. When the agent task is running and you're doing a tool call, the tool results also shows up as a tool result message to the agent. If the user, while the agent is still working, says, also include Europe in your analysis, then that also ends up being a follow-up, which also shows up as a message to the agent.
In the non-actor system, you would think of these as three separate pathways. The chat over here, the workflow over there, cancellations over the third place. In the actor system, they all end up being messages with the same running task. All of these messages flow through the mailbox. The mailbox then ends up becoming the single place for the running agent to receive all events of interest. It removes all side channels and allows each agent task to interpret every message it is getting based on just its local state that it has. Once we look at the state side mapping and the communication side mapping, the other mappings from the actor model to the agent task just follows naturally. You have the actor state that maps to the agent task state. You have the actor identity, which maps to a durable handle for the running work. Because a durable handle gives address to an agent, now you can reach to it any time you want because now it is addressable.
Child actors map to delegated subtasks, tool calls, or specialist agents. Supervision maps to failure boundaries. Hopefully at this point, now you can start seeing that there's this one-to-one mapping from actors to agents. Agents are actor shaped because they own state, they receive messages, they can delegate work, they can live over a long period of time, and they can fail independently.
Patterns
Once we start seeing agents as actors, the next practical question is, like what production patterns just follow through once we adopt an actor style design for our agents? The first pattern is that the task becomes the universal execution primitive. What I mean by that is, if you look at many agentic systems, like you have one interface for chat, you have another for tool execution, you have another for workflow, you have another for background jobs, and another for delegation, and they're all separate concepts. Each has its own state model, a lifecycle, cancellation, and recovery path. This fragmentation is exactly what made the original demo architecture move sideways, where we had to fix each problem one at a time. The actor shape alternative is to treat every long-running unit of work as just a task actor. A chat interaction is a task. A workflow is a task.
A tool call is a task. A delegated subproblem is a task. Waiting for the human in the loop input is a task. The point is not that all of these tasks are doing the same thing. The point is that they all end up having the same runtime contract. That contract is the contract given by the actors to the task. The contract of identity, mailbox, state, lifecycle, and supervision. Modeling the problem as task actors gives us a unit of work in the agentic world. The second pattern that follows through is write-through state. Once every meaningful unit of work has state, the next question is what happens when the process that is holding that state crashes or dies? With the write-through state, every meaningful transition to the state can be made durable as it happens. That's easy to see because in an actor-based system, state is local and the only way to modify that state is when you receive messages.
Every time an agent receives a message, if the behavior of the agent dictates a change in state, it can record the changes in a durable store, the state changes would then be applied, and then it can decide what to do next, like emit new messages, create child actors, just based on its behavior. The actor model just brings the durability piece just in the way the problem is modeled. With the write-through state in place, like if the process crashes, the system can just rehydrate the actor from a durable state and resume. This makes recovery the same as normal resumption. There are no two different paths, they're just the same path. The task does not need to discover what it was doing based on the scattered side effects when it crashes. It just wakes up, just like resuming work, and just continues forward. The write-through state gives the unit of work recoverability and it makes it durable.
The third pattern that follows from this is what I call as the indirect continuation. Durability tells you what happens when the process dies, but there's another problem with agentic system, and that's the problem of waiting. We've all seen it. A tool call might take minutes or tens of minutes, a human might respond tomorrow, a child task can create multiple tasks, and so that by the time you get results, might take a long time. The wrong answer when you're building this is to preserve the call stack as all of this happens, because the call stack is just a temporary execution structure. It's not the right place to store the state of the workflow. Instead of waiting on the stack, what you can do is the task delegates work, it records the continuation, and then resumes that continuation only when the message arrives. The continuation is not a blocked thread, it's just another piece of state owned by the task.
It records what this task intended to do while the work is still outstanding. This actually is a subtle, but really important shift, because the system in the previous mode would just preserve the stack frames. Now you're preserving intent. When the tool call arrives or your child has complete back with results, that's just another message, and the task can just continue forward once it receives the message, based on its state. What the continuation does, it gives the unit of work the semantics of waiting without pinning the stack. The fourth pattern that follows through is this thing called the mutable execution graph. Once the work is no longer tied to a stack, now you can start representing work as a graph of tasks. With agents, that graph cannot be fully known upfront. If you recall, like in a traditional workflow, the series of steps that usually need to happen are known in advance.
You can model it as a static, directed acyclical graph. Agents are different because they're discovering steps while you're executing. The agents have a goal, but then they go researching it, they find a gap. They create new subtasks. They can call another tool. They ask for clarification. When the results come back, they can just change the plan. The graph in the context of the agent is not merely executed by the runtime, it is being discovered by the agent as it is executing. Graph ends up being the part of the runtime, which ends up being a very different shift of how you model the problem. The runtime not only has to represent the current step, but has to represent the evolving structure of the work. The mutable graph lets unit of work create more units of work.
By now you've seen this actor style design and it has given us long-running tasks, durable state, continuations, and mutable graph for child tasks, but each of these pieces can fail independently. Failure policy becomes a structural concern, and that's our fifth pattern, which is about supervision boundaries. Supervision is not the same as exception handling. Supervision is about giving failures a boundary and a policy. In an exception handling case, like you think about the way you model it, it's like, what happened wrong here? What should I do here to handle this exception? Supervision says something completely different. It says, a part of this system failed, what policy should I use it for this boundary? Should I restart it? Should I retry it? Should I escalate it to the parent? Should I preserve partial result? Should I ask the user what to do? All of these become architectural concerns.
Once you draw the supervision boundaries of where failure happens, failures stop being a global concern but become local events with policies. Supervision gives the unit tree of work a failure policy. When you put all of these derivations together, now you end up having this coherent architecture for the runtime of agents in production. You have task actors that gives us a unit of work. You have write-through state that makes the unit of work durable and recoverable. You have indirect continuations that let the unit of work wait without pinning the stack. You have mutable graphs that let units of work create more units of work. You have supervision that gives the resulting unit tree a boundary to contain failures and makes failure a local policy.
What Is the Payoff?
We see that we're starting to evolve the design for the runtime of these production agents. A good question to ask here is, what is the payoff of adopting this to model our agents in production? The first thing I want to say is that the actor model is not going to make your agents easy to build. What it does is that it does make the hard parts really explicit and gives them a name. The production AI still continues to be difficult because essentially what you're doing is that you have a non-deterministic LLM model and you're trying to build the correct execution on top of a non-deterministic foundation, and that's really hard. You have things that could fail in production AI. You have external systems that end up being unreliable. You could have models that end up having degraded performance and return different results based on just the non-deterministic nature of it.
The actor model doesn't remove them but it gives us names and boundaries to certain things which allows us to build some reliable systems. The first payoff of using the actor model is the state of your entire system. Instead of the state leaking across a bunch of different places, each meaningful unit of work now ends up having its own state. When a message arrives, there is a single place to look at that state and decide what to do with the incoming message. The second payoff of the actor model is that the unit of work ends up having the address. We've seen this before. A running agent is not just a single request-response loop, but it's constantly being hooked around in order to change its executing direction. That requires you to have an address to get to the unit of work, and the actor model makes the unit of work be an addressable entity.
The system can send it a follow-up question, a cancellation, a timeout, a result from child actors, and they all end up being the same. Users can return to work that is still running, because the work ends up having identity. The third payoff with the actor model is, again, the failure has a boundary. Instead of failures leaking through the entire system, the actor model makes failure a local policy. A tool call can be retried. A child task can be restarted. A branch can be canceled. You can take partial results, and the parent can continue executing. Failure becomes an architectural concern instead of just being a scattering of emergency code. The fourth payoff is that you don't have to think about recovery and resumption in two different ways. They end up just becoming part of the normal path of execution. This happens because the transition of your state is durable so the task can own the continuation and state, and crash recovery can just work the same way as resuming the execution of a task.
Design Checklist
My hope is that you start seeing that the actor model really makes sense for the runtime of agents in production. What I want to ask you is that the next time you're designing an agentic system, it doesn't matter, you can choose whatever framework of your choice. Ask these five questions, which are, what are the actors in my system? What state does each actor own? What messages do they exchange? What can fail independently? Who supervises whom?
Example: Coding Agent in Actor-Style
I realized that all of this is still pretty much theoretical, like there's a framework to think about it. I wanted to make this more concrete with something that we might all be familiar with, which is coding agents. How many people here use Claude Code? How many people use Codex? How many use Kilo Code? The code that I'm going to share here, is just a minimal coding agent. You can connect to a local model like Qwen, or you can connect to an OpenAI model, Anthropic model. It's a coding agent designed in an actor style. It's purposefully super minimal so that you guys can grok the idea of actors. In this coding agent, we have four actors. There is the supervisor actor that lets you grok the idea of supervision and failure boundaries. There's the LLM actor that controls the transport to an OpenAI model, or OpenAI compatible model, or an Anthropic model.
There is the tool registry actor that's responsible for dispatching tool calls. Then there's this agent actor, which is really your tight loop, and it's agentic in nature. What you would see is that at the very top, you have the supervisor actor, and its job is not to do the coding work. Its job is to own the lifecycle and failure policy for all of the work that happens underneath. The coding task itself is done by the agent actor, and it owns the goal, all of the transcripts that you've had during your coding session, the plan, the child task, and the continuation state. You can start seeing the unit of work and how it ends up interacting with other runtime pieces, where not all of the actors need to be agentic, and different actors end up having different roles. For anyone interested, if you wanted to inspect this after the talk, feel free, here's the QR code for getting the repo. It's intentionally kept very simple to serve as a teaching artifact for all of us to think about the actor model.
Greenspun's 10th Rule for Agents
Let me end the talk with a variation of Greenspun's 10th rule. The original version of the rule was that any sufficiently complicated C or Fortran program eventually contains an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden, slow implementation of half of Common Lisp. I think a similar version exists for agents, like any sufficiently complicated agent loop contains an ad hoc, informally specified, bug-ridden implementation of half of an actor system. That really is the point of this talk. If you run your agents over time, they own state, they receive new information, they delegate work, the weight on tools, they recover from failures, and they continue executing, you are building something that is actor-shaped. The choice is you can do it either accidentally or you can do it intentionally.
Questions and Answers
Participant 1: Conceptually, I got it. It's like we can model agents' components as actor models and MVs. Can you share a little bit more about what's in the wild and open? Is there any successful framework or projects following this pattern? For example, you said, there are so many coding agents out there, and there's a toy example. What's the benefit? Why didn't they already fall onto the direction?
Manju Rajashekhar: That's the same question I was asking too, because I was pretty surprised that not much was talked about this concept. This is just a hypothesis, but part of the reasoning is that what coding agents have done today is that the two most popular languages with coding agents ends up being Python and TypeScript. What the actor model does require is it does require a robust runtime to run these actors. What these coding agents and frameworks, they're rediscovering some of the pieces that we talked about in the actor model, and they end up building it, but it ends up being built in a half-baked way. A lot of this talk is really to bring the actor model right, front, and center, and start thinking about all of the runtime of the agents from that perspective. That's one of the key reasons, what's happening today with why the actor model is not super widespread in terms of how we talk about it.
Participant 2: The question here is like agent-to-agent communication. Let us think you are saying the state is owned by the agent. Now in this current world, the context size and the content of the agent which is processing is really large. Now, if I want to send that context to a different agent, in this model, how will it work?
Manju Rajashekhar: The context still gets sent as messages. If you look at what's happening with the agentic system, the main cost with agents is really around how long does an LLM take to process tokens? It ends up being a really small number compared to that cost. You can always send these messages over the wire to a different agent, or you can use some sort of an indirection where you can say, I'll just have a pointer to the same copy of the message that another agent can have access to.
Participant 2: That will defeat the purpose of actor owning the state. If you send a pointer to a different actor, that means now two actors can control that state.
Manju Rajashekhar: No, you're sending a pointer to the copy of the data. If you don't want to use up the network bandwidth, you can just send a copy of the data, but the actor still owns the agent. The context that you're sending is just part of the message. Now, how you encode that message is very different. It's very clear in the actor model, who owns the state. If someone else needs the state in order to update their own local state, you just send that entire data to it.
Participant 3: Do you see ACP as being a natural next step for the proof of concept of being a message bus between not only ACP client and ACP agent, but things like acpx emerging to promote communication between agents themselves. Like a next layer of the actor problem.
Manju Rajashekhar: It seems to be headed that way. It seems like it's heading that way. We haven't formalized the concept. My hope is that as more people start seeing that the actor model can be applied, people start thinking about the problem from the abstraction standpoint, rather than from the protocol standpoint.
Participant 4: Is there a good way of using this right now? The agent frameworks that I'm familiar with are all pretty opinionated about how you register tools with them and how that communication happens. From what I know, which is very little, there's not really a good way of inserting something like this in there. Is there a framework that you're familiar with, or is there a way of like porting this into the existing frameworks that we could use right now?
Manju Rajashekhar: What the previous speaker asked is super interesting. I think that's worth looking at. I'm not familiar with anything where you can put this in, which is also why I'm sharing this code, because it's actually pretty easy to build right from ground up. What's happening today is, because now we have coding agents, a lot of the work that we have to do as developers and architects is really figuring out the mental model of the runtime, and code that in what the coding agents need to be building. Versus asking the coding agents to just solve the work and then they end up solving the work without the right abstractions. We don't need an existing framework, in some way we can just skip that entire step and say, I need to solve a problem that requires using agents. How should I model the runtime? You start from there.
Participant 5: It's just a follow up on that. I love Erlang. Do you think then it's a matter of having the prompt, including as someone who would fix this or would implement this using the Erlang model?
Manju Rajashekhar: Not really. The code snippet is based on Rust. Because you can implement an actor model on Rust really well. It's really like adopting the actor model. The Erlang VM is great. The BEAM VM is great. For some reason, the agentic world and Erlang and the Elixir world haven't really met yet. It would be great for them to do that.

articles.title: Tempête Austen : votre train SNCF est supprimé ou en retard ? Voici les règles pour vous faire rembourser
articles.text:
Ce mercredi 21 octobre 2026, le réseau régional normand Nomad Train a annoncé sur X qu’aucun train ne circulerait vendredi sur les lignes normandes. La reprise doit se faire progressivement samedi après-midi. Les voyageurs normands peuvent échanger ou se faire rembourser leur billet à des conditions assouplies. Par contre, la Bretagne et les Hauts-de-France vont eux aussi perdre des trains, mais n’ont pas annoncé de dispositif similaire. Ce qui signifie qu’à train supprimé égal, un voyageur de Brest et un voyageur de Caen ne sont pas logés à la même enseigne, pour le moment.
Météo-France annonce des rafales de plus de 110 km/h sur une large partie du nord-ouest, et davantage sur les côtes les plus exposées. SNCF Réseau, qui gère les voies, a donc choisi d’arrêter les trains pour qu’aucun ne reste bloqué en pleine voie pendant la tempête.
D’après le plan de transport publié par Nomad, la reprise de samedi dépendra de l’état des voies une fois la tempête passée. Les grandes lignes sont aussi touchées. Selon la SNCF, aucun TER, Intercités ou TGV ne roulera vendredi sur le réseau normand.
Ailleurs, des trains supprimés mais aucun geste sur les billets
En Bretagne, TER BreizhGo a prévenu sur X que le trafic serait coupé vendredi jusqu’à midi sur cinq lignes : Brest-Saint-Brieuc, Lannion-Saint-Brieuc, Quimper-Brest, Guingamp-Carhaix et Guingamp-Paimpol. Le réseau breton ajoute que « des retards et suppressions sont à prévoir sur les autres lignes ». Pourtant, le site de TER BreizhGo n’affiche aucune mesure d’échange ou de remboursement liée à la tempête.
Dans les Hauts-de-France, les premières coupures commencent dès ce jeudi soir. Sur X, TER Hauts-de-France a donné la liste des lignes fermées toute la journée de vendredi : Amiens-Rouen, Creil-Beauvais, Amiens-Compiègne et Beauvais-Le Tréport. Paris-Beauvais, Paris-Laon et l’étoile de Saint-Pol (les lignes qui relient Saint-Pol-sur-Ternoise à Étaples, Béthune et Arras) seront arrêtées de midi à 23 heures. Là non plus, le site de TER Hauts-de-France ne prévoit rien de particulier pour les billets.
Plus au sud, Météo-France attend vendredi des rafales de 70 à 90 km/h dans les Pays de la Loire et pourrait y étendre la vigilance orange « vent ». Le site d’Aleop, le réseau TER de la région, ne présente lui non plus aucun dispositif pour les billets.
Que faire de votre billet de train ?
En Normandie, faites la demande avant l’heure de départ de votre train, à l’endroit où vous avez acheté le billet : site ou application Nomad Train, SNCF Connect, guichet ou borne. Nomad Train détaille ses conditions d’échange et de remboursement sur son site. Si vous avez une question, le compte X de Nomad répond de 6 heures à 22 heures, et des téléconseillers sont joignables par téléphone.
- En Bretagne, dans les Hauts-de-France et dans les Pays de la Loire, vérifiez d’abord si votre train est supprimé. Si c’est le cas, demandez un échange ou un remboursement là où vous avez acheté le billet. S’il roule, les conditions habituelles de votre billet s’appliquent.
- Pour un TGV ou un Intercités, passez par SNCF Connect : un train supprimé s’échange ou se rembourse sans frais.
- Si vous arrivez en retard au travail, téléchargez le justificatif de retard ou de suppression proposé sur les sites TER régionaux.
Attention, ne comptez pas sur une indemnisation pour un retard. Depuis juin 2023, le règlement européen sur les droits des voyageurs ferroviaires autorise les compagnies à ne pas indemniser un retard dû à une météo extrême. Le remboursement d’un train supprimé reste dû. Pour samedi, Nomad Train prévient que son plan de transport est encore en préparation et pas encore entièrement intégré aux outils de recherche d’horaires. Les trains affichés sur SNCF Connect pour samedi peuvent donc encore changer.

articles.title: SA’s Happy Pay launches pay-per-sale ad platform after $6.1m pilot - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
South African buy now, pay later (BNPL) platform Happy Pay has publicly launched Happy Ads, an AI-powered performance media platform that only charges retailers when a campaign results in a sale.
Happy Pay provides zero-cost installment payments through its ad-subsidised payments network. Its platform connects merchants with high-intent shoppers, enabling consumers to split purchases into interest-free installments while helping retailers grow through performance-based customer acquisition, conversion, and basket expansion. The company raised a US$5 million seed round back in March.
Happy Ads lets brands promote products and offers to Happy Pay’s more than 800,000 registered users, as well as two million customers across its partner network. It generated more than ZAR100 million (US$6.1 million) in merchant sales during its pilot phase, delivering more than 268 million impressions and an average 20x return on ad spend. Happy Pay says a further six million users are set to join the network soon.
Unlike traditional digital advertising, where brands pay for impressions or clicks, Happy Ads works on a cost-per-acquisition model. Retailers set the commission they are willing to pay and are only charged when a campaign converts into a completed sale.
“Most digital advertising platforms sell attention and leave retailers hoping that attention eventually turns into revenue,” said Wesley Billett, co-founder and CEO of Happy Pay. “Happy Ads flips that model. If we don’t generate a sale, the merchant doesn’t pay.”
The platform combines product discovery, targeted distribution, payments and transaction-level attribution. An AI recommendation engine ranks products for each shopper based on their browsing, purchase history and interests, with every completed sale feeding back into the model. Shoppers can check out using Happy Pay’s interest-free instalments or any of the retailer’s existing payment methods.
“Buy Now Pay Later should be more than a payment button at checkout,” Billett said. “It creates one of the most powerful customer-acquisition flywheels in retail.”

articles.title: Vercel Labs Open-Sources fx: A Zig Coding Agent Designed to Be Embedded
articles.text:
Vercel Labs has released fx as open source, an experimental coding agent and command-line tool written in Zig and built to be scripted or embedded rather than run as a full-screen terminal application.
Announced in August 2026, fx ships as a 6.3 MiB native binary with a reported single-digit-megabyte memory baseline and a 10-microsecond cold start, figures Vercel states rather than independently verified benchmarks. Instead of taking over the terminal with a persistent interface, fx writes its conversation into ordinary scrollback and exposes the same engine through both a CLI and a library.
The result is aimed at developers building agent infrastructure more than at people looking for another chat window. Structured output is available for automation, so a script or CI job can call a command and parse the response:
fx ask --json "summarise the failing tests"
Editors can attach over the Agent Client Protocol using fx acp, and libfx exposes the engine to JavaScript, including a WebAssembly build.
Early Hacker News feedback also probed the model-agnostic claim. Some first-run reports said setup appeared to route inference through Vercel AI Gateway, and commenters questioned how fx differed from established agents, pointing to OpenCode's more polished terminal experience.
One user noted GLM 5.2 being free:
Just tried and although it’s not that polished or fast imo it’s very cool.
GLM 5.2 totally free even with a free Vercel account.
Make business sense too - fx is the entry point to bring more user to Vercel AI.
Provider choice has since widened: release 0.0.11 added named OpenAI-compatible connections for local servers and alternative gateways, and the README now lists Vercel AI Gateway, ChatGPT and Grok subscriptions, plus endpoints such as Ollama and OpenRouter. Vercel has also slotted fx into its AI SDK harness layer next to Claude Code, Cline, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode and Pi, presenting it as one option behind a shared interface.
A GitHub issue flagged that the name collides with the long-established terminal JSON viewer fx, which already holds the Homebrew fx formula, and a contributor confirmed that packaging and command coexistence were being reviewed.
Vercel is explicit that fx is experimental. The 0.0.13 release on October 4 added an Ultrafast mode on supported OpenAI models with quicker launches and shell calls, but warned that newly written libfx checkpoints cannot be restored by older versions.
CLI users can move up with fx upgrade and should read the changelog first, while embedded users should consult the libfx migration guide, which explains that the earlier createFxAgent() call maps to createFxEngine() in the current documentation.
Its repository documents the CLI, skills, MCP, permissions and SDK, and its browser demo shows the terminal-style experience without an install.
fx is an open-source project from Vercel Labs, the experimental group within Vercel, the company behind the Next.js framework and its platform for building and deploying web applications. Written in Zig and distributed as a single native binary, fx is designed to be run from the command line, scripted in automation, or embedded directly in other applications through its libfx library and WebAssembly build. Still pre-1.0 and changing quickly, it reflects a wider move toward treating coding agents as composable infrastructure rather than standalone tools.

articles.title: Bitchat mesh : pourquoi la messagerie sans Internet de Jack Dorsey cartonne
articles.text:
D’ordinaire, les tops des applications les plus populaires sont accaparés par les gros réseaux sociaux (comme Facebook), les messageries instantanées (Signal, WhatsApp, Telegram), par des apps de discussion (Discord) ou par des outils administratifs (compte Améli, France Identité). Voilà d’ailleurs à quoi ressemble le gros du classement de l’App Store.
Mais voilà, du changement vient d’être observé ces jours-ci. Comme l’a noté un journaliste de BFM TV le 22 octobre 2026, une application a grimpé presque tout en haut de cette hiérarchie. En France, elle s’est même imposée à la première place de la catégorie « réseaux sociaux » et positionnée dans le top 10 général de toutes les applications.
Son nom ? Bitchat Mesh. Curieusement, c’est une application qui n’est pas du tout nouvelle. Ses notes de mise à jour montrent qu’elle existe depuis le 28 juillet 2025. Comment expliquer une telle remontada dans le classement de l’App Store ? Peut-être cela a-t-il à voir à la fois avec le contexte sociopolitique français… et avec la nature de l’application elle-même.
Car Bitchat Mesh, qui est déclinée aussi bien pour iOS que pour Android via Google Play, a une particularité : c’est une application qui permet de discuter avec des gens autour de soi sans compte, sans numéro de téléphone, sans adresse e-mail et sans connexion Internet. Les messages passent par des liaisons locales, avec la technologie Bluetooth. L’application sait aussi utiliser Internet quand il est disponible, via le protocole Nostr, pour des salons à l’échelle d’un quartier ou d’une ville. Mais quand le réseau tombe, c’est le Bluetooth qui prend le relais.
Derrière Bitchat Mesh, il y a un homme bien connu du milieu de la tech : Jack Dorsey, le cofondateur de Twitter. Il en a parlé publiquement sur X le 7 juillet 2025 et dit avoir codé la base un week-end pour s’instruire sur « les réseaux maillés Bluetooth, les relais et les modèles de stockage et de transmission, les modèles de chiffrement des messages, et diverses autres choses ».
Un réseau maillé, comment ça marche ?
Or, tout repose ici sur cette architecture de réseau maillé (ou mesh, en anglais). Dans ce type de réseau, il n’y a pas de nœud ou de serveur central : tout le monde s’interconnecte de manière pair à pair, ce qui donne une structure générale ressemblant à une sorte de filet, avec une multitude de nœuds et de liens.
À l’inverse, WhatsApp ou Messenger reposent sur des serveurs centraux : le message transite par un centre de données avant d’atteindre son destinataire.
Dans le cas de Bitchat Mesh, il n’y a pas cet intermédiaire : chaque téléphone devient client et serveur. Il détecte les appareils proches qui ont l’application et leur envoie les messages en Bluetooth Low Energy (la version basse consommation du Bluetooth). Ces appareils les relaient à leur tour, de proche en proche, jusqu’à arriver à bon port.
Avec le Bluetooth Low Energy, il est possible de faire des « sauts » jusqu’à cent mètres environ, et la chaîne de téléphones permet d’aller plus loin : en effet, plus il y a de monde équipé dans une foule, plus le réseau s’étend et se montre résilient. Lors de l’annonce, Jack Dorsey avançait une portée allant jusqu’à 300 mètres grâce à ces relais, un chiffre théorique qui dépend du nombre de téléphones à proximité.
Jack Dorsey n’a cependant pas inventé le principe. Dès 2014, FireChat exploitait déjà le mesh d’Apple sur iOS, et l’application avait servi aux manifestants de Hong Kong. On commence ainsi à saisir l’intérêt de ce genre d’outil, qui sert surtout quand le réseau télécom tombe ou quand un gouvernement le coupe.
Une application qui décolle quand Internet est coupé
En fait, les téléchargements de Bitchat suivent les coupures de réseau. En septembre 2025, des Népalais l’ont installée en pleine interdiction des réseaux sociaux. Un mois plus tard, elle était top deux des téléchargements en Jamaïque, lors du passage de l’ouragan Melissa. En janvier 2026, elle a aussi décollé en Ouganda et en Iran pendant des coupures d’Internet.
Mais certains gouvernements ne restent pas les bras croisés. Ce printemps, Apple a dû retirer Bitchat de l’App Store chinois à la demande du régulateur local. Cet été, alors que l’Inde a vécu d’importantes protestations, l’app a vu ses téléchargements exploser… avant que New Delhi ne réclame son retrait, sur Google Play comme l’App Store.
L’attention récente autour de Bitchat en France semble liée à la mobilisation nationale contre la vie chère du samedi 17 octobre, émaillée de pillages, et au débat qui a suivi. Invité de RTL ce lundi 19 octobre, Gabriel Attal, ancien Premier ministre et candidat Renaissance à la présidentielle, a plaidé pour un « blocage temporaire » des réseaux sociaux, « ciblé sur les territoires où se déroulent les émeutes ». Le gouvernement n’a annoncé aucun blocage à ce stade.
Bitchat permettrait de contourner un tel scénario, hypothétique. Mais avant de l’installer, il faut avoir conscience de certaines limites : le mesh ne sert à rien si personne autour de vous n’a l’application, et il faut l’avoir installée avant toute coupure, puisque son téléchargement passe, lui, par Internet. Dans le pire des cas, un brouillage des fréquences perturberait aussi le Bluetooth.
Côté avis, l’application obtient 4,8 sur 5 sur l’App Store en France, mais seulement 3,8 sur Google Play. Des utilisateurs se plaignent d’une forte consommation de batterie ou de messages qui ne partent qu’une fois sur deux.
Le code source est public, et le site officiel du projet signale qu’il est versé dans le domaine public. Il faut noter qu’au lancement, Jack Dorsey avait reconnu qu’aucun audit de sécurité externe n’avait été mené. Les notes de la version de janvier 2026 font état de correctifs issus d’un audit tiers. Les plus récentes mises à jour pour Android datent d’octobre et pour iOS de juillet.
Bitchat est gratuite et sans publicité. Elle tourne sur iPhone à partir d’iOS 16 et sur Android à partir de la version 8.0, et les deux versions communiquent entre elles.
