articles.title: Affaire Thélyson Orélien : les métadonnées de son roman changent la donne
articles.text:
Après des semaines de soupçons alimentés notamment par les détecteurs de textes générés par IA, l’affaire Thélyson Orélien prend une nouvelle tournure. Les Éditions du Boréal affirment avoir retrouvé des traces liées à l’intelligence artificielle dans les métadonnées de plusieurs documents de travail de C’était ça ou mourir. Un élément d’une autre nature qu’un score Pangram, mais qui ne dit toujours pas précisément quel rôle l’IA a joué dans l’écriture du roman.
Publié au Québec au printemps 2026 puis chez Grasset en France le 19 août, C’était ça ou mourir est devenu l’un des romans les plus remarqués de la rentrée littéraire. Le 21 septembre, quelques heures après l’attribution du Prix du Roman Fnac, le compte « Balance ton Claude » publiait plusieurs analyses réalisées avec Pangram suggérant qu’une large partie du livre pouvait avoir été générée par intelligence artificielle. Thélyson Orélien a toujours contesté cette accusation
Des traces retrouvées dans les versions de travail du roman
Dans un communiqué publié le 21 octobre, les Éditions du Boréal annoncent mettre fin à leur collaboration avec l’écrivain et renoncer à réimprimer son roman. La maison québécoise affirme désormais que l’intelligence artificielle a bien été utilisée au cours du processus d’écriture.
Après plusieurs semaines passées à tenter de documenter la création du livre avec l’auteur, l’éditeur explique avoir rassemblé l’ensemble des versions de travail disponibles et commandé une analyse externe approfondie.
Selon le Boréal, celle-ci a révélé « des traces de balises d’IA dans les métadonnées de certains documents ».
Le communiqué ne précise toutefois ni la nature exacte de ces balises, ni le logiciel ou le service susceptible de les avoir laissées, ni l’identité de l’organisme ayant réalisé l’expertise. Le Boréal reconnaît également ignorer dans quelle mesure l’intelligence artificielle est intervenue dans la création du roman.
Cette fois, le dossier ne repose plus seulement sur un détecteur
C’est ce qui distingue ces nouveaux éléments des accusations apparues en septembre.
Comme nous l’avons montré dans nos précédents volets consacrés aux détecteurs d’IA, un outil comme Pangram analyse le texte final et cherche à déterminer à quelle catégorie il ressemble le plus. Il peut repérer des caractéristiques associées aux productions des modèles de langage, mais ne dispose pas pour autant des brouillons, des prompts ou de l’historique réel de rédaction.
Les métadonnées contenues dans les versions de travail se situent à un autre niveau. Elles peuvent conserver des informations relatives aux logiciels utilisés ou à certaines étapes de création du fichier. On ne regarde donc plus seulement ce à quoi ressemble le texte terminé, mais potentiellement les traces laissées pendant sa fabrication.
Cela ne suffit toutefois pas à déterminer précisément ce qu’a fait l’IA. Une trace liée à un outil d’intelligence artificielle ne permet pas, à elle seule, de savoir s’il a servi à corriger, reformuler, rechercher des informations ou générer directement certains passages. C’est justement l’information qui manque encore dans le communiqué du Boréal.
De son côté, Thélyson Orélien avait continué à défendre une autre version. Il reconnaissait notamment avoir utilisé certains outils pour ses recherches, mais assurait qu’aucune phrase de son roman n’avait été créée par une intelligence artificielle. À notre connaissance, il n’a pas encore réagi publiquement aux nouveaux éléments annoncés le 21 octobre.
Une question de confiance
Pour le Boréal, le problème dépasse désormais la seule question technique de savoir quelle proportion du livre a été produite ou modifiée avec une IA. La maison estime que les nouveaux éléments contredisent les assurances données jusque-là par son auteur et affirme que la relation de confiance nécessaire à leur collaboration est rompue. Elle ne réimprimera donc pas C’était ça ou mourir et ne publiera pas non plus ses prochains ouvrages, si tant est que l'auteur poursuive sa carrière. 
Cette question de confiance dépasse d’ailleurs largement le monde du livre. Dans la musique également, l’arrivée de créations générées par IA a fait émerger la même interrogation : le problème est-il l’utilisation de l’outil elle-même, ou le fait que le public pense avoir affaire à une création humaine lorsqu’une partie essentielle de son origine lui est dissimulée ?
L’affaire The Velvet Sundown l’avait notamment illustré sur Spotify : un groupe artificiel avait réussi à toucher un très large public avant que sa nature synthétique ne soit clairement établie. Dans la littérature comme dans la musique, l’IA pose donc aussi une question de transparence entre créateurs, intermédiaires et public.
En France, le dossier concerne directement Grasset, qui publie C’était ça ou mourir et avait apporté sa « confiance absolue » à Thélyson Orélien au début de la polémique. Au moment où nous écrivons ces lignes, la maison française n’a pas encore précisé quelles conséquences elle comptait tirer de la rupture annoncée par le Boréal. Le roman avait par ailleurs fait l’objet d’accords de traduction dans plus d’une vingtaine de langues.
L’affaire ne permet donc toujours pas de répondre précisément à la question qui l’accompagne depuis septembre : quelle part de C’était ça ou mourir a réellement été écrite, corrigée ou transformée à l’aide d’une IA ?
Mais le débat a changé de nature. Jusqu’ici, il portait essentiellement sur la fiabilité des détecteurs et leurs scores. Désormais, ce sont les traces laissées dans les documents de travail eux-mêmes qui sont examinées, sans que leur présence permette encore de reconstituer précisément le rôle joué par l’intelligence artificielle.
Pour aller plus loin, retrouvez les deux premiers volets de notre enquête sur les détecteurs d’IA, de leurs résultats à leur fonctionnement réel.

articles.title: Carplay: Gemini landet in Google Maps – das kann die KI für Autofahrer erledigen
articles.text:
Carplay: Gemini landet in Google Maps – das kann die KI für Autofahrer erledigen
Android-User:innen dürfen schon seit geraumer Zeit auf die KI-Features von Gemini zugreifen, wenn sie mit dem Auto unterwegs sind. Der KI-Assistent kann während der Fahrt mit Android Auto eine Reihe von Aufgaben übernehmen und wird dank Personal Intelligence jetzt auch noch schlauer, wenn auch vorerst nicht hierzulande. Aber auch iPhone- und Carplay-Nutzer:innen bekommen jetzt ein Upgrade von Google spendiert.
Carplay: Was Gemini in Google Maps tun kann
Wie 9to5Google berichtet, rollt Google nämlich endlich Gemini für alle User:innen von Apples Carplay aus. Die KI-Implementierung erfolgt dabei direkt in Google Maps. Solltest du also Apples Kartendienst nutzen, kannst du die KI nicht einfach appübergreifend nutzen. Für alle, die ohnehin Google Maps mit Carplay und ihrem iPhone nutzen, ergeben sich durch die KI einige Vorteile.
Sobald Gemini freigeschaltet ist, findet sich in der Navigationsansicht auf der rechten Seite das Sternensymbol von Gemini. Tippst du es an, hört der KI-Assistent zu. Laut Google können dann auch mehrschrittige und offenere Anweisungen gegeben werden. Dazu zählt etwa, dass du Gemini fragen kannst, welche Orte sich besonders für einen guten Blick über die Stadt eignen würden. Zudem kannst du die KI fragen, ob eine bestimmte Location gerade gut besucht ist und es vielleicht bessere Zeiten gäbe, um etwas mehr Ruhe dort zu haben.
Weißt du schon, wo es hingeht? Dann kannst du Gemini die Adresse geben und dabei etwa betonen, dass eine Strecke ohne Mautstraßen gewählt werden soll. Dadurch entfällt das Suchen der entsprechenden Option in den Einstellungen. Zu guter Letzt kannst du Gemini auch während der Fahrt nutzen, um Störungen wie Staus, Unfälle und andere Hindernisse auf der Straße zu melden. So werden andere Google-Maps-User:innen davor gewarnt.
Zunächst startet der Rollout von Gemini in Google Maps für Carplay in den USA. In den kommenden Wochen soll dann auch der Rest der Welt mit der KI-Integration versorgt werden. Wenn Gemini also bisher nicht bei dir in Google Maps unter Carplay zu sehen ist, musst du dich wohl noch etwas gedulden, bis Google das Update freischaltet.

articles.title: Face au succès monstre de l'iPhone Duo, Apple aurait pris une décision forte
articles.text:
L’iPhone Duo, soit le premier téléphone pliant de l’entreprise, va-t-il connaître un succès retentissant ? Alors que les nouvelles estimations de livraison sont maintenant décalées à janvier 2027 aux États-Unis, Apple aurait demandé à ses fournisseurs d’augmenter sensiblement le rythme de production, avec plusieurs millions d’appareils supplémentaires commandés. Cependant, il se pourrait aussi qu’Apple déguise des soucis de production en engouement démesuré.
Apple aurait demandé d’augmenter la production de l’iPhone Duo
Les précommandes de l’iPhone Duo ont été ouvertes ce vendredi 16 octobre 2026, et autant dire que le succès semble avoir été au rendez-vous. Aux États-Unis, moins de 30 minutes après l’ouverture des précommandes, les nouvelles estimations de livraison ont glissé jusqu’en janvier 2027. Ceux qui ont raté la première salve de précommandes ne pourront donc pas placer l’appareil sous le sapin. Au cours d’un entretien accordé à la chaîne CNBC, Apple a qualifié cet engouement d’« absolument extraordinaire ».
Mais cela ne s’arrête pas là, puisque l’entreprise à la pomme aurait décidé d’augmenter sensiblement la production de son téléphone pliant. En effet, selon les informations de DigiTimes, le fournisseur Foxconn et les fabricants de composants ont reçu la consigne d’augmenter la production de l’appareil de 44 %. Le nombre d’iPhone Duo produits passerait ainsi de 9,7 à 14 millions. À noter que cette augmentation de production s’étalerait sur 12 mois, et non pas seulement jusqu’à la fin de 2026. DigiTime précise par ailleurs que ce nouvel objectif de production dépendra directement de la capacité d’assemblage des fournisseurs.
Des retards de production maquillés en succès commercial ?
L’iPhone Duo semble bel et bien susciter un engouement et cela n’est pas non plus étonnant : il s’agit du premier pliant d’Apple. Cependant, il se pourrait aussi que l’entreprise à la pomme déguise des soucis de production en succès retentissant. Des rumeurs de stocks limités au lancement ont été rapportées plus d’une fois, en raison de soucis de production. Apple aurait par ailleurs été confronté à un choix difficile : privilégier la qualité de fabrication (et donc fabriquer moins d’appareils) ou augmenter la production (et donc proposer des appareils moins « parfaits »).
Il va falloir attendre qu’Apple communique des chiffres officiels pour en avoir le cœur net, mais l’iPhone Duo suscite indéniablement un certain engouement, malgré ses prix particulièrement élevés. En attendant, rendez-vous ce 28 octobre pour découvrir de nouveaux produits de l’entreprise.

articles.title: Ciberdelincuentes crearon un agente de IA que secuestra servidores para atacar sin supervisión humana
articles.text:
La empresa de ciberseguridad Symantec detectó un programa de inteligencia artificial (IA) autónomo, apodado “Skynet” por sus propios operadores, diseñado para buscar modelos de IA desprotegidos en internet y usarlos como motor para atacar bases de datos, robar contraseñas e instalar mineros de criptomonedas sin intervención humana.
El hallazgo surgió de un señuelo digital, un sistema que imita un servidor de IA vulnerable para atacar y estudiar a quienes intentan abusar de él. Según Symantec, capturó el conjunto completo de instrucciones que un atacante le envió a ese señuelo, creyendo que se trataba de un modelo real.
La herramienta estaba programada para ejecutar hasta 100.000 pasos sin pedir autorización a ningún humano. En ese modo, llamado por sus creadores “modo Skynet”, el agente debía rastrear nuevos objetivos, infectarlos, instalar mineros de criptomonedas y volver a infectar los mismos sistemas de forma cíclica.
El programa contenía 74 herramientas distintas para escanear internet, explotar fallas conocidas en aplicaciones como Django, Jupyter o Laravel, volcar bases de datos y robar credenciales. Una herramienta separada apuntaba a servicios de metadatos en la nube, una vía habitual para robar las claves de acceso de una organización.
Para lograr que un modelo comercial aceptara ejecutar estas órdenes, los atacantes envolvieron sus instrucciones en un jailbreak, una técnica que fuerza al sistema a ignorar sus propios controles de seguridad. Le indicaban tratar el robo de archivos de configuración y contraseñas como una tarea de programación normal.
El atacante le decía al modelo que una lista de palabras, entre ellas “no puedo” o “legal”, quedaba prohibida en sus respuestas, para evitar que el sistema se negara o advirtiera sobre la naturaleza del pedido.
Por qué los servidores quedan abiertos
El ataque no explota ninguna falla de software: alcanza con que el servidor de IA esté conectado a internet sin contraseña. El señuelo de Symantec registró más de 127.000 solicitudes externas de decenas de miles de direcciones distintas durante el período analizado, la mayoría dedicadas a buscar este tipo de endpoints abiertos.
Zenity Labs, otra firma de seguridad, documentó el mismo fenómeno con casos concretos entre marzo y mayo. Sus sensores detectaron a tres operadores distintos que tomaron el control de servidores expuestos de Ollama y LiteLLM, dos programas populares para correr modelos de IA en servidores propios.
Uno de ellos envió un mensaje de 140.000 caracteres para cargar un marco de ataque automatizado llamado Strix y dirigirlo contra un sitio de subastas francés activo, con instrucciones de no pedir permiso y de no revelar el nombre de la herramienta en ningún registro. Otro cargó HexStrike AI, un conjunto de 150 herramientas ofensivas, incluidas nmap, sqlmap y metasploit.
Según Zenity, el problema de fondo son los valores predeterminados de este software: Ollama no exige ninguna contraseña en su puerto habitual, el 11434, y LiteLLM solo pide autenticación si un administrador la activa de forma manual, algo que muchos equipos omiten al poner el servidor en producción.
Un problema que ya tiene escala medida
La firma de seguridad SentinelLabs y la empresa de rastreo de internet Censys hallaron, a comienzos de este año, 175.000 servidores de Ollama accesibles públicamente en 130 países, con cerca de la mitad de ellos habilitados para ejecutar acciones automatizadas además de generar texto.
GreyNoise, otra firma que monitorea el tráfico malicioso en internet, registró 91.403 sesiones de ataque contra infraestructura de IA expuesta entre octubre de 2025 y enero de este año, divididas en dos campañas distintas de reconocimiento a gran escala.
Ese mismo mes, la firma Pillar Security identificó un mercado clandestino, operado bajo el alias “Hecker”, que revendía por criptomonedas y PayPal el acceso robado a más de 30 proveedores de modelos de IA a precios muy por debajo del costo real, tras detectar 35.000 sesiones de ataque propias contra sus señuelos.
La dinámica económica explica el atractivo del método: quien aloja el modelo vulnerado paga la factura del cómputo consumido, mientras los servidores que la IA logra vulnerar quedan despojados de sus datos y convertidos en mineros de criptomonedas a beneficio del atacante.
Symantec sugiere que ninguna empresa exponga a internet un servidor de inferencia o un conector de modelo sin exigir autenticación, y que trate las claves de acceso a servicios de IA como credenciales de alto valor, con rotación periódica y monitoreo de consumo inusual como señal temprana de robo.

articles.title: Mass Effect 5 offered 'a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match' before cancelation, says BioWare dev — 'We saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table with their latest offerings, and started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level while remaining true to the Trilogy'
articles.text:
'I believe we were making something special' — BioWare dev says the now-canceled Mass Effect 5 offered 'a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match'
BioWare cinematic supervisor Tony de Waal was among the "50-ish" people left at the studio who were laid off
- BioWare cinematic supervisor Tony de Waal says the now-canceled Mass Effect 5 offered "a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match"
- The developer says BioWare "saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table" with Baldur's Gate 3 and Cyberpunk 2077 and "started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level"
- De Waal also recounts his experience working on Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which he called "a herculean effort"
A BioWare developer working on Mass Effect 5 has revealed new details about the now-canceled project, which was seemingly inspired by systems from Baldur's Gate 3 and Cyberpunk 2077.
Following the announcement that EA is shutting down BioWare and canceling the next Mass Effect game, former BioWare cinematic supervisor Tony de Waal has spoken up about the plans for the title, revealing that he was among the remaining "50-ish" people at the studio who were laid off, suggesting Mass Effect 5 had a very small production team.
"I was one of the lucky ones who stayed with BioWare to start on the next Mass Effect, where I believe we were making something special: a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match," De Waal said on LinkedIn (via PC Gamer).
"We saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table with their latest offerings, and started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level while remaining true to the Trilogy."
De Waal started his career at BioWare "29+ years ago," left after Mass Effect 2's release, but returned in 2021 to "help get what would become Dragon Age: The Veilguard back on track and out the door."
The developer shared some challenges the team encountered along the way with the final Dragon Age entry, saying it was "a herculean effort that tested the limits of even my workaholic mindset" but is "proud of the level of polish we were able to pull off in the Frostbite engine."
"Seriously, you have no idea the craziness going on under the hood of that game to make a variable player character work across 3+ hours of cinematics, and the number of conditions to account for in the scenes towards the end of the game," he added.
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
Speaking more on Mass Effect 5, De Waal said he's "sad" fans "won't get to see what we were cooking" and "sad for the small, talented group of devs who were all punching above their weight to make something special."
Parent company EA announced major restructuring plans across its studios and in development projects. 400 people have been laid off, including roughly 50 roles at BioWare (via Bloomberg). Now De Waal is one of many out of work.
"Please consider those who stayed with BioWare until the very end. They are truly some of the most talented people I've had the pleasure of working with throughout my career," De Waal added.
"With that, if you need someone who knows cinematic production, blending gameplay with cinematics, the tools, the tech, and has the know-how to realize complicated narratives — a true production expert with nearly three decades of experience who isn't afraid to roll up their sleeves and create content — please think of me. I'm once again looking for the next studio and project where I can use the breadth of my skills to make a difference."

articles.title: LTO roadmap extends to 365 TB per cartridge as tape storage refuses to die — AI boom spurs relevance of cheap, airgapped storage
articles.text:
LTO roadmap extends to 365 TB per cartridge as tape storage refuses to die —25-year-old format sees 400x capacity increase without changing form factor
HPE, IBM, and Quantum will keep developing LTO as demand booms.
In a world where SSDs with up to 256TB capacity are about to enter the scene to compete against hard disk drives that store over 40TB, magnetic tape storage may seem archaic. However, the 25-year-old Linear Tape-Open (LTO) format continues to evolve at a rather impressive pace.
The current LTO-10 generation stores up to 40TB of uncompressed data per cartridge, while HPE, IBM, and Quantum — the companies behind the LTO Program — now envision LTO-14 cartridges with up to 365TB of native capacity. But capacity is not the only advantage of LTO. In fact, the consortium has deliberately slowed its capacity roadmap in a bid to prioritize reliability, cost per terabyte, and manageable backup and recovery times over the previous goal of doubling capacity with every generation.
LTO began in 2000 with the LTO-1 format, which stored just 100GB of data natively and transferred it at 20 MB/s. Since then, capacity increased to 200GB with LTO-2, 400GB with LTO-3, 800GB with LTO-4, 1.5TB with LTO-5, 2.5TB with LTO-6, 6TB with LTO-7, 12TB with LTO-8, and 18TB with LTO-9.
The original LTO-10 media introduced in 2025 increased native capacity to 30TB, whereas an extended-length LTO-10 cartridge announced later increased it further to 40TB.
LTO cartridge capacity has increased by a factor of 400 in about 25 years without changing the form-factor itself. For comparison, the capacity of 3.5-inch hard drives increased by roughly 585 times over the same period, from around 75GB in 2000 to as much as 44 TB today, so tape has evolved at a slower pace. However, LTO has evolved without dramatic changes in internal complexity.
Two scaling vectors
The 40TB LTO-10 cartridge is noteworthy because its additional capacity is enabled by higher recording density and literally longer tape. The LTO-10 format uses 15,104 data tracks (enabled by the new barium ferrite recording layer), up 68.5% from 8,960 tracks with LTO-9, and combines them with higher linear density. To make this possible, LTO-10 uses a redesigned high-bandwidth servo system with a low-mass mechanism that enables the head to follow increasingly narrow tracks accurately, including in environments subject to shock and vibration.
Both 30TB and 40TB LTO-10 media use a strontium-doped barium ferrite (BaFe) recording layer, but the 40TB version uses a new Aramid base film that is thinner and smoother and therefore enables manufacturers to put more tape into the same cartridge. According to MagStor, the thinner substrate increases tape length from approximately 1,035 meters with the 30TB cartridge to around 1,335 meters with the 40TB version. Meanwhile, the 40TB cartridge works with the same LTO-10 drives as the existing 30TB media.
Therefore, modern LTO has at least two major scaling vectors: manufacturers can record more bits on a given area of tape, and can put more tape into a cartridge. Meanwhile, with LTO-10, the consortium had to drop backwards compatibility, which we will detail further within this article.
There appears to be plenty of room left on the tape front. Back in 2020, IBM and Fujifilm demonstrated a strontium ferrite tape technology with an areal density of 317 Gb/in², which they said could theoretically enable a cartridge capable of storing 580TB. The prototype used tracks only 56.2nm wide and a 29nm TMR read sensor, which proved that magnetic tape could reach capacities vastly beyond commercially available LTO products.
Capacity is not everything
Ironically, despite considerable technological headroom, the LTO Program has recently made its roadmap considerably less aggressive.
When HPE, IBM, and Quantum extended the roadmap through LTO-14 in 2022, they expected capacity to roughly double every generation. The plan envisioned 72TB for LTO-11, 144TB for LTO-12, 288TB for LTO-13, and a whopping 576TB native — or 1.44PB compressed — for LTO-14. But that changed in November 2025, when the three companies introduced the new roadmap for LTO that significantly slows down capacity scaling. The current roadmap targets 70TB native for LTO-11, 120TB for LTO-12, 210TB for LTO-13, and 365TB for LTO-14.
While the new roadmap is somewhat less impressive, it does not necessarily indicate that tape technology has encountered a physical scaling wall. The developers claim the revised targets are intended to prioritize reliability, affordability, efficiency, and cost per terabyte. The consortium also specifically says that lowering maximum cartridge capacities should help reduce the amount of time required to store and recover data, which is a legitimate argument even though it looks like an attempt to make a 'feature' out of a limitation.
"AI has turned archives into strategic assets," said Stephen Bacon, Vice President, Data Protection Solutions Product Management, HPE. "The new 40 TB LTO-10 cartridge will help enterprise-class organizations — across healthcare, financial services, media, research, manufacturing, the public sector and beyond — consolidate petabytes efficiently, strengthen cyber resiliency with true offline air-gapping, and keep long-term retention affordable and sustainable."
Bandwidth is becoming one of tape's more obvious limitations. LTO-8 offered 360 MB/s of native bandwidth, LTO-9 increased this to 400 MB/s, and LTO-10 remains at 400 MB/s, although hardware compression can boost effective throughput to as much as 1,200 MB/s when data can achieve the assumed 2.5:1 compression ratio.
As a result, while maximum native cartridge capacity increased from 12TB with LTO-8 to 40TB with LTO-10 — a 3.33X increase — native transfer performance improved by only around 11%. At 400 MB/s, writing 40TB sequentially would theoretically take around 28 hours (without the overheads). Future LTO generations will likely increase performance, but the consortium has not yet published transfer rate targets for LTO-11 and its successors.
No backwards compatibility
One thing to note about LTO-10 is that it has broken a long-standing LTO tradition, which is backward compatibility. Up until LTO-7, new drives could generally read cartridges from two generations earlier and write media from one generation earlier. LTO-8 and LTO-9 reduced compatibility to one previous generation. However, because LTO-10 redesigns its head, its backwards compatibility disappears completely: an LTO-10 drive reads and writes only LTO-10 media, although the 30TB and 40TB cartridges are of course interchangeable.
This creates a natural problem for operators that need to maintain archives for decades. Once they adopt LTO-10, they either must migrate all their archives to the new format from LTO-8 or LTO-9 cartridges, or keep the old drives in their fleet, which may be increasingly difficult.
Demand remains strong
Perhaps counterintuitively, the AI boom could strengthen demand for tape. AI infrastructure produces enormous datasets, but not every training dataset, checkpoint, model, log, or generated asset needs to remain indefinitely on expensive SSDs or HDDs.
LTO capacity shipments reached 160.3 exabytes in 2025, down 9% year-over-year. However, shipments in the first quarter of 2026 jumped 57% YoY, according to figures reported by the LTO consortium. The organization attributed the increase to AI-related data growth, traditional archival demand, cyber-resilient backups, continued LTO-9 adoption, and the beginning of the LTO-10 transition.
"We are seeing unprecedented data growth combined with increasing cost, energy, and cyber resilience pressures across the industry," said Hugues Meyrath, CEO, Quantum. "As organizations adapt to this new reality, tape is increasingly viewed as a strategic component of modern data infrastructure, delivering predictable economics and resilient long-term data retention at scale."
Indeed, tape has a number of fundamental advantages that are not going to disappear any time soon. Tape provides vast capacities at a low cost per terabyte, cartridges consume virtually no power while sitting offline, hardware encryption protects data, and physically removing a cartridge from a drive provides a genuine air gap against network-based attacks. LTO also supports the LTFS file system, which maintains indexing information on tape and makes archived files considerably easier to manage.
Meanwhile, tape's disadvantages are equally fundamental and are not going away: tape is sequential and therefore cannot provide anything resembling the random-access performance of HDDs or SSDs. Although nobody expects something similar from it.
LTO isn't going anywhere
25 years after LTO-1 offered 100GB per cartridge, LTO-10 can store as much as 40TB, and the roadmap calls for 365TB with LTO-14 several years down the road. Perhaps more importantly, laboratory demonstrations indicate that magnetic tape itself has considerable scaling potential beyond today's commercial products. Meanwhile, instead of pushing capacity as quickly as technologically possible, the LTO consortium is now deliberately balancing density with reliability, performance, and cost.
For a storage technology which demise has been predicted repeatedly for decades, LTO not only continues to evolve at a predictable pace, but its adoption is growing, while its relevance remains on a high level. Only time will tell whether it remains relevant for another quarter of a century, but its steady progress certainly increases this possibility.
Anton Shilov is a contributing writer at Tom’s Hardware. Over the past couple of decades, he has covered everything from CPUs and GPUs to supercomputers and from modern process technologies and latest fab tools to high-tech industry trends.

articles.title: What does the failure of the Clarity Act mean for cryptocurrencies? (Sponsored) | EU-Startups
articles.text:
The CLARITY Act was designed to set clearer rules for how digital assets are classified and overseen in the US. Its failure in the Senate leaves American investors without that framework for now, and anyone watching the Ethereum price USD chart saw the reaction within hours.
The much-lauded CLARITY Act failed to advance in the US Senate on Tuesday, September 15, in a severe setback for the digital assets and crypto industry. It fell 11 votes short of the 60-vote threshold it needed to move onward in the 100-seat chamber. Primarily put forward by Republican lawmakers, three of them voted against it, joining every Senate Democrat in opposition, and the motion failed. The impact will be felt by anyone who trades digital assets, in the US and abroad.
How did markets respond to the Clarity Act failure?
Markets responded quickly to the news. Binance market data showed Bitcoin dropping 5% after the vote. At the time of writing (September 18), it had rebounded slightly, climbing to $78,180 from a $75,390 low on Tuesday, September 15. Ether stood at $2,515, up from $2,378 the day after the vote. Share prices of several crypto firms also fell, with Coinbase and Circle each down about 10%, according to Cointelegraph.
This will push any further decisions on it until after the mid-term elections, which will take place in November. A key fight to take control of the House and Senate, it could potentially be pushed back until 2029 should Democrats make it a priority and stop it dead in its tracks.
What was the Clarity Act?
The CLARITY Act was an attempt to provide a US federal framework for digital asset markets. For years, there has been confusion over where digital assets lie in the US and who has oversight for them. Primarily, this was the Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) and the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC).
Where value is derived from network use and trading, in spot markets, jurisdiction would have been given to the CFTC. The SEC would have had an overview of digital securities in which the value depended on a specific company’s managerial efforts.
How have banks reacted to the Clarity Act news?
The US Banking lobby has already pledged its support to keep fighting for the bill. This is mainly because it still leaves questions around stablecoin yields unanswered. A joint statement from the Independent Community Bankers of America and American Bankers Association noted that “as lawmakers consider next steps, we encourage them to adopt targeted changes to stablecoin yield policy.”
It is likely this will now pivot the conversation to how banks can begin to implement the GENIUS Act. Signed into law in 2025, it has barred stablecoin issuers from offering rewards. Yet it does allow third parties, such as exchanges, to pay yields. The Independent Community Bankers of America has warned that this could drain as much as $1.3 trillion from community bank deposits.
Stablecoin builders outside the US are watching this fight closely: EU-Startups reported in July 2025 that London fintech Due had raised €6.3 million and launched a stablecoin API for borderless payments, the kind of product whose US reach depends on how Washington settles yield.
How did crypto exchanges react?
The major crypto exchanges were keen to point out that by no means does this signal the end for the CLARITY Act. Binance added that “With the November midterm elections approaching, lawmakers have limited time to resolve disagreements and secure the votes needed to move the bill forward. A renewed attempt would still have to navigate Senate procedures and any remaining legislative steps, including resolving differences with the House-passed version before legislation could reach the president.” They then closed this with “The immediate result is a stalled bill, not necessarily a permanently dead one.”
Other crypto companies also released statements on the event. Ripple described this as a “tremendous missed opportunity” in a statement on their website. They went on to add that “Consumers and market participants still deserve predictable standards and protections. Responsible businesses should not have to rely on years of litigation or live under the threat of one to understand how the law applies to them. And the United States should not concede leadership in the future of finance because policymakers were unable to establish a durable framework. Ripple will continue advocating for market structure legislation and engaging constructively with policymakers.”
This will only add to the volatility the crypto market has displayed over the last few months. Rising oil prices and expectations that the Federal Reserve would hike rates, which it did on Wednesday, September 16, have also weighed on sentiment.
Further dampening the mood were comments signaling that investors should not write off the prospect of another rate raise before the year is out. This was the first rate rise in three years, taking them to 3.75%-4%, according to the Federal Reserve’s September 16 statement, as reported by CNBC. After the September 16 decision, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long“, then branded the move a “sober” and “responsible decision“. He then highlighted that inflation remains a problem, showing that more may yet be due to come.

articles.title: Latest estimate for Starship launches required to support a Moon landing? 22.
articles.text:
NASA does not have, nor want, nuclear weapons. But when it comes to a particular metric that is part of the Artemis Program to land people on the Moon, NASA guards a particular number like they are trying to prevent outsiders from cracking nuclear codes.
I am speaking of the number of Starship launches required to fuel a Starship-based lunar lander in low-Earth orbit such that it can fly out to the Moon, land there, and return to lunar orbit.
This number has been a moving target over the years. The general response from NASA has typically been, ‘We don’t know for sure, so we’re not going to say.’ In 2023, for example, the then-director of NASA’s Human Landing System, Lisa Watson-Morgan, told Ars, “We have a general idea, but I’m reluctant to say exactly what that is.”
Later, she said the number was in the “high single digits to the low double digits.” That suggests about a dozen launches, which is a lot. SpaceX would need to launch a “depot” Starship, and then 11 “tanker” Starships to fully load it with liquid oxygen and methane propellant for a lunar voyage. Other officials have said “high teens.” The hope has always been that SpaceX would dramatically improve the lift capacity of Starship to bring down the number of tanker flights.
But now there are concerns among some NASA officials that this might not be happening, or at least not happening soon enough to allow SpaceX’s Starship rocket to play a meaningful role in returning humans to the Moon for NASA as part of Artemis this decade.
A new estimate emerges
On Thursday, the NASA Aerospace Safety Advisory Panel held its quarterly meeting, during which panel member Charlie Precourt (a former NASA astronaut) spoke about risks associated with the Artemis Program and landing humans on the Moon.

articles.title: Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain's CEO says it's part of a bigger shift
articles.text:
Ramp built an AI agent harness in six weeks — and LangChain’s CEO says it’s part of a bigger shift
Ramp spent months testing managed agent APIs, open-source frameworks, and third-party platforms before concluding it would be better off building its own. The result is Laminar, an internal agent harness that took six weeks to reach a first version and now powers every agentic product at the fintech company.
“We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house.”
“We studied the other offerings on the market and decided that we could do better, move faster, and have stronger alignment to where we want to go by building in house,” Sam Kronick, the Ramp engineer behind the platform, writes in the company’s engineering blog.
In Tuesday’s post, Ramp detailed how Laminar brings agent execution, sandboxing, observability, and asynchronous workflows under a single platform. The architecture caught the attention of LangChain CEO Harrison Chase, who praised several design choices in his X post, while pointing to similar work underway in LangChain’s Deep Agents.
Ramp and LangChain are approaching the problem from different directions, but both point to a bigger shift in agent infrastructure. As harnesses take on more responsibility, enterprises have to decide how much of that infrastructure they want to build and maintain themselves.
Why Ramp built in-house
Ramp didn’t want to be locked into one model provider. It needed the flexibility to switch models based on cost, speed, and performance, along with better visibility into how its agents behaved. Engineers were already digging through traces to find unnecessary tool calls, bloated context, and errors, but existing observability tools made that harder than it needed to be. So Ramp built its own debugging interface into Laminar. Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes.
Chase agreed with Ramp’s priorities, particularly model independence and observability, both of which LangChain has emphasized in its own work. And, there were other parts of Laminar’s architecture that caught his attention.
Keeping development in-house also meant the harness team could work directly with product engineers instead of waiting on vendors to make changes.
Sessions split from sandboxes
Laminar runs everything from customer service agents to Ramp Inspect, the company’s cloud coding agent, and Glass, which handles longer-running, collaborative work. Supporting these products requires a harness that can manage persistent sessions, human approvals, and work across environments.
Chase highlights Kronick’s observation that a production harness does far more than run a simple execution loop. “+100 to this,” he writes, pointing to LangChain’s investment in Deep Agents.
Ramp keeps agent sessions separate from the sandboxes where code runs. Conversation history and execution state are stored independently, allowing sandboxes to spin up and shut down without disrupting a session.
Chase sees the sandbox-as-a-tool approach as a growing trend, noting that Deep Agents uses a similar design. It also keeps credentials and orchestration outside the sandbox, an important consideration as developers work to isolate agents running untrusted code.
Async agents by default
Laminar lets agents keep working without waiting for every step to finish. Chase describes non-blocking asynchronous agents as the future and says LangChain is developing similar functionality for Deep Agents.
Ramp’s Connectors Service also caught his attention. It centralizes authentication, credentials, access controls, and tool execution behind a shared API.
Chase says LangChain is exploring comparable features for managed Deep Agents. Centralizing those functions also gives platform teams a consistent place to manage access and credential handling rather than implementing them separately for every agent.
The harness is also where teams can trim inference costs, and LangChain has made that case directly. In an October 1 engineering post, it describes moving model selection into the harness of Open SWE, its open-source coding agent. A router examines the initial request and assigns one of three models based on expected task complexity, sending the simplest work to GLM-5.3-Flash, intermediate tasks to GPT-5.6 Sol, and the most demanding requests to GPT-6 Astra.
Routing trims inference costs
Across 973 agent threads, the router cut median LLM costs from $2.61 to $0.94 per thread, a 64 percent drop compared with using GPT-6 Astra for every task. The savings didn’t come with a measurable hit to performance. Merged pull request rates were 29.2 percent for routed threads and 27.3 percent for the control group, a difference that wasn’t statistically significant. Ninety percent of requests went to the two less expensive model tiers.
LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing.
LangChain argues that routing works better inside the harness than at a generic LLM gateway, where there’s less context about what an agent is doing. The harness already knows which prompts, tools, and domain context are involved, giving it more information to make that choice. LangChain uses model-selection middleware to pick a model at the start of each thread.
The results don’t tell us whether building a custom harness is cheaper than using an existing framework. Ramp wasn’t part of the experiment. But they do show how much companies can save by making smarter model choices at the harness level, especially when their agents handle tasks with very different demands.
The harness ownership dilemma
Ramp’s decision also shows how coding agents have changed infrastructure costs. Kronick says agents generated all of Laminar’s initial code, with experienced engineers guiding the architecture and implementation.
But building the first version in six weeks is one thing. Maintaining it is another. Ramp still needs engineers to handle incidents, update the platform, and support its product teams. The company also hasn’t published operating-cost comparisons or benchmarks against competing platforms, which makes it difficult to judge whether building in-house is cheaper.
LangChain offers another option. Rather than building a harness from scratch, companies can use frameworks that handle much of the underlying infrastructure, an approach other vendors are also taking as they open-source their own harnesses.

articles.title: Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is a fun but slight diversion
articles.text:
Four years ago, Nintendo returned to the world of motion-controlled sports games with Nintendo Switch Sports. This spiritual successor to the smash hit Wii Sports series ended up being one of the Switch’s best-sellers, although it garnered mixed reviews.
Now, Nintendo is returning to the well with Nintendo Switch Sports Resort, and thankfully, this go-around is more successful.
Right off the bat, it features 12 sports versus the eight in its predecessor. What’s more, they’re much more varied. In addition to such staples as Bowling, Golf, Tennis and Volleyball, you’ve got newcomers like Thumb Wrestling and Skateboarding. What’s more, that last minigame, as well as returning ones like Prop Plane and Power Cruising, feature free roaming options that let you explore a mini open-world without any specific objectives. It’s a nice change of pace, although there’s not very much to see, so the novelty of navigating via motion controls eventually wears thin.
Naturally, then, the meat of the experience remains the competitive sports, and most of them are pretty good. My personal favourites were Bowling (it’s a classic for a reason), Archery (the aiming, drawing and shooting with both Joy-Cons felt pretty intuitive) and Table Tennis (it can get surprisingly intense).
With that said, some of the minigames are underwhelming, the biggest of which being Basketball. After Nintendo’s conceptually novel but mechanically frustrating Drag and Drive, I was hoping for Switch Sports Resorts‘ take on hoops to scratch that itch, but it, too, is lacking, focusing on ostensibly turn-based rounds every time you steal the ball or take a shot instead of one single, free-flowing match.
I will give credit, though, to an effort to improve the single-player options, especially through the gauntlet-focused Island Crown mode. Further, you earn in-game currency by playing matches and completing objectives, like getting your first strike in bowling or maintaining a volley of 10 consecutive shots in a single volleyball match. This money can be used on cosmetics to customize your character, providing a little bit of reward to the gameplay loop.
Ultimately, though, the whole package feels a tad slight, even with its larger-than-ever content offering. Even its best minigames are simply fun but fleeting diversions, and I’m not sure it’s something that I’d personally stick with for very long, even with friends. (I’d certainly suggest we play something like Mario Party Jamboree or Smash Bros. instead.) The fact that this is $84.99 ($69.99 if you buy digitally) also makes it a bit tougher to recommend.
But if nothing else, I could see the simple, pick-up-to-play nature of these minigames clicking more with certain audiences, especially those with larger families than me. And with so many games nowadays wanting to eat up so much of your time, the focus on bite-sized experiences is undeniably appealing. You might not want to stay for very long, but this is one resort that’s still worth visiting.
Nintendo Switch Sports Resort is now available on Nintendo Switch 2.
Image credit: Nintendo

articles.title: AI Changes the Data Interface, Not the Query Engine
articles.text:
Key Takeaways
- An AI agent that reads Parquet still depends on an execution engine; AI changes the analytical interface and interpretation layer, not the need for precise computation.
- Separate deterministic computation from probabilistic reasoning. Engines should filter, aggregate, and join, while agents should interpret evidence and communicate conclusions.
- An embedded engine such as DuckDB can be sufficient when the data volume is moderate, the primary consumer is the agent workflow, and writes are controlled.
- A managed lakehouse becomes valuable when data has multiple independent consumers, must join with large shared datasets, requires concurrent writes, or needs organization-wide governance.
- Production-grade agent analytics should retain the source data, configuration, derived facts, and model outputs so that every report can be validated and replayed.
AI agents can now generate analytical code, read files from object storage, and turn operational data into structured reports. Does that make data lakes, lakehouses, and SQL engines obsolete? We encountered this question while automating the analysis of a large disaster-recovery exercise. Our first working design stored thirty-second service metrics as Parquet in S3-compatible object storage, used DuckDB for deterministic aggregation, and asked an AI agent to classify failover outcomes and explain the evidence. The prototype worked without a shared lakehouse, but not because the query engine disappeared. Instead, the engine became an embedded component inside the agent workflow. This article explains the architecture, introduces a practical separation between deterministic computation and probabilistic reasoning, and presents four signals for deciding when an embedded engine is sufficient and when a managed lakehouse is justified.
The Question That Appeared After the Prototype Worked
The question did not come from a whiteboard exercise. It appeared after a real workflow successfully produced its first report. We were analyzing a disaster-recovery (DR) islanding exercise. During the exercise, one region was intentionally isolated, and traffic was expected to fail over to surviving regions. For every service, we needed to answer three questions:
- Did the surviving region absorb the traffic that left the isolated region?
- After absorbing the traffic, did the service remain available?
- Did latency remain within an acceptable range, or did the additional load create sustained degradation?
We exported service metrics at thirty-second resolution, wrote them as Parquet files to S3-compatible object storage, and let an AI agent generate a structured analysis report. Once the workflow ran end to end, an attractive idea emerged:
If the agent can read files from object storage and produce the answer, why do we need tables, a catalog, a lakehouse, or SQL at all?
The question sounds reasonable because the user-facing experience has changed. Instead of opening a dashboard or writing a query, an engineer asks the agent to analyze the exercise. The agent identifies the relevant data, generates DuckDB SQL or Python as needed, executes the analysis through deterministic tools, and explains what happened. For example, to verify whether traffic shifted from Region A to Region B during failover, the agent may generate a read-only DuckDB query over a predefined set of tables and time ranges. Before execution, the query is validated against an allowlist of accessible datasets and operations, then executed in a sandboxed analysis runtime. The runtime returns structured query results, which deterministic application code normalizes into a fact packet containing fields such as traffic volume by region, timestamps, and percentage changes. A simplified implementation looks like this query:
generated_sql = """
SELECT
    region,
    SUM(request_count) AS requests
FROM traffic_metrics
WHERE ts BETWEEN :start_time AND :end_time
GROUP BY region
"""
validate_sql(
    generated_sql,
    allowed_tables={"traffic_metrics"},
    allowed_operations={"SELECT"},
)
rows = sandbox.execute(
    generated_sql,
    params={
        "start_time": exercise_start,
        "end_time": exercise_end,
    },
)
fact_packet = {
    "metric": "request_count",
    "window": [exercise_start, exercise_end],
    "by_region": {
        row["region"]: row["requests"]
        for row in rows
    },
}
In this simplified example, the agent generates only the analytical query. A deterministic validation layer rejects access to non-allowlisted tables or non-read-only operations before execution. The query then runs in a sandboxed runtime and the returned rows are converted by application code into a structured fact packet. The model receives this packet (for example, request counts for Regions A and B) rather than inventing or directly estimating those values.
Why DR Analysis Is More Than Scanning Metrics
The difficult part of DR analysis is not retrieving a time series. It is deciding what the time series means. Suppose Region A is isolated and Region B remains active. A healthy failover should produce a recognizable sequence:
- QPS decreases in Region A.
- QPS increases in Region B by a corresponding amount.
- The success rate in Region B remains above the service objective.
- Tail latency may rise briefly, but it should not remain elevated.
Each statement requires context. A QPS increase is not automatically a successful failover. It may be too small to account for the traffic lost in the isolated region. A lower success rate is not automatically a DR failure if the metric includes expected business rejections. A latency spike at the cutover boundary may be harmless if the system quickly returns to a steady state. We therefore used two baselines and a steady-state window:
- Historical baseline. the same time window on the previous day, which captures normal time-of-day behavior.
- Immediate baseline, the hour before the exercise, which captures the most recent service state.
- Steady-state window, a post-cutover interval that excludes the short transition period and focuses on sustained behavior.
The analysis collected four core signal families:
- qps
- err_qps
- success_rate
- latency_pNN, including tail latency such as p99
For each service, deterministic code calculated facts such as traffic absorption ratio, SLO violations, latency change, and the duration of sustained degradation. The agent then interpreted those facts in the context of the service, the exercise configuration, and the available evidence. This distinction is fundamental. The hard part is often the judgment, but the judgment is only trustworthy when the facts underneath it are deterministic.
Architecture: Object Storage, an Embedded Engine, and an Agent
The workflow used three logical layers: data preparation, deterministic computation, and agent-driven interpretation, with reproducibility treated as a cross-cutting requirement. The data-preparation layer used reusable DuckDB build logic, which was generated once and then reused, to transform raw metrics into self-describing assets in object storage. For each analysis request, the agent selected the relevant inputs, generated constrained SQL or Python, and orchestrated deterministic execution in DuckDB/Python. The resulting structured fact packets were then interpreted by the agent to produce the final report. Throughout the workflow, the input data, configuration, reusable build logic, deterministic facts, and agent execution metadata were retained so that the analysis could later be reconstructed, replayed, and evaluated.
Figure 1. The AI agent initiates and orchestrates the analysis, deterministic tools compute the facts, and the agent interprets the resulting fact packet. Source: Authors’ own illustration, created with assistance from ChatGPT.
Storage and Self-Description
The physical data lived in S3-compatible object storage. Each exercise had a self-describing directory:
s3://<bucket>/<root-prefix>/
  index.json
  <exercise-id>/
    manifest.json
    exercise_config.json
    metrics-*.parquet
    service_dimension.parquet
The files served different purposes:
- index.json listed available exercises.
- manifest.json recorded the schema, row counts, file sizes, and checksums.
- exercise_config.json captured time windows, regions, thresholds, and exercise identity.
- metrics-*.parquet contained the thirty-second metric facts.
- service_dimension.parquet contained service metadata such as ownership and service tier.
The manifest was important because a folder of files is not yet a trustworthy data asset. Consumers need to know what is present, which schema was used, whether the write completed, and whether the files can be validated later.
Deterministic Processing with DuckDB
DuckDB was used on both sides of the storage boundary. During ingestion, it read the raw metric records, sorted them, wrote compressed Parquet files, and generated validation statistics for the manifest. During analysis, it read the Parquet files directly, filtered the relevant windows, joined service metadata, and computed the fact packet used by the agent. This architecture benefited from several properties of DuckDB:
- It runs in-process, so it can travel with the agent workflow instead of requiring a separate database service.
- It reads Parquet directly and can push filters and column selection into Parquet scans.
- It provides SQL semantics for aggregation and joins.
- It can spill larger operations to local storage instead of requiring the entire working set to remain in memory.
The point was not that DuckDB is universally better than Spark, Trino, or a managed lakehouse. The point was that the workload did not yet need a shared distributed engine.
Probabilistic Interpretation with the AI Agent
The agent did not receive hundreds of thousands of raw metric rows and attempted to count errors or average latency itself. Instead, it received a compact, deterministic evidence packet for each service. A simplified packet looked like this example:
{
  "service_id": "service-a",
  "exercise_window": "post-cutover-steady-state",
  "expected_failover_qps": 1200,
  "observed_qps_increase": 910,
  "traffic_absorption_ratio": 0.758,
  "success_rate_baseline": 0.9992,
  "success_rate_during_exercise": 0.9941,
  "service_slo": 0.9990,
  "p99_latency_baseline_ms": 84,
  "p99_latency_during_exercise_ms": 191,
  "sustained_degradation_minutes": 18,
  "data_quality_flags": []
}
The agent used the packet to classify the outcome, explain the supporting evidence, and propose the next investigation step. A corresponding output might be:
{
  "classification": "partial_failover",
  "confidence": "high",
  "evidence": [
    "The surviving region absorbed approximately 76% of the expected traffic.",
    "Availability remained below the service SLO during the steady-state window.",
    "The p99 latency increase was sustained for 18 minutes."
  ],
  "recommended_action": "Review routing capacity and downstream dependency limits."
}
The exact numbers came from the engine. The model's responsibility was to determine how those numbers should be interpreted and communicated.
A simple threshold-based rule was not always sufficient. For example, a service might temporarily exceed its p99 latency threshold immediately after cutover while traffic had already shifted correctly and availability remained within the service objective. A rule that treated any threshold violation as a failure would classify the service as degraded. The agent could instead compare the transition window with the steady-state window, recognize that latency returned to baseline within a few minutes, and classify the event as a successful failover with transient degradation rather than a sustained DR failure.
More importantly, some cases contained conflicting evidence that could not be resolved by a single threshold or temporal rule. A service might absorb the expected traffic and recover its own latency, yet still remain at risk because a downstream dependency was operating near saturation. Conversely, a Tier-2 asynchronous service could show a temporary backlog increase without violating its availability objective, while the same pattern in a Tier-0 synchronous dependency would warrant escalation. In these cases, the deterministic layer still produced the underlying facts (i.e.,traffic shift, latency, success rate, backlog, dependency saturation, service tier, and SLO status), but the agent combined those facts with service context to determine which evidence was most important and how the event should be classified.
The agent therefore added value not by replacing deterministic computation, but by resolving context-dependent and sometimes conflicting evidence that would otherwise require an increasingly large set of service-specific rules.
The Determinism Split
The most reusable lesson from the project is what I call the determinism split: separate exact computation from contextual reasoning.
| Give to the engine | Give to the AI agent | 
| Filtering, aggregation, joins, sorting, and window calculations | Selecting relevant evidence and explaining why it matters | 
| Exact and reproducible numerical results | Classifying failover behavior and suggesting investigation paths | 
| Operations whose cost grows with data volume | Work that depends on context, trade-offs, and communication | 
| Data quality checks and validation flags | Abstaining when the available evidence is insufficient | 
Table 1. A practical separation between exact computation and contextual reasoning.
This division avoids a common anti-pattern, using an LLM as a query engine. A language model should not read hundreds of thousands of rows and calculate an error count, percentile, or average. That approach is slow, expensive in tokens, and difficult to reproduce. More importantly, it assigns deterministic work to a probabilistic system. The safer pattern is:
- Use a deterministic engine to produce a small set of authoritative facts.
- Allow the agent to generate constrained SQL or Python needed to derive those facts.
- Execute that code through deterministic tools and give the resulting fact packet to the model with the necessary context.
- Require the model to explain conclusions using fields from the fact packet, while retaining inputs, generated code, execution metadata, and outputs for replay and audit.
The agent can decide which question to investigate, dynamically generate constrained DuckDB SQL or Python, and orchestrate its execution. The generated code may be proposed probabilistically, but the resulting numerical facts must come from deterministic execution rather than from the model itself.
What the Workload Told Us About the Architecture
The exercise dataset contained:
- Thirty-second metric resolution
- 1,127,748 fact rows
- 1,523 services
- Approximately 3.8 megabytes of compressed Parquet fact data
The upstream collection run across all services took roughly an hour with concurrent workers. The resulting analytical dataset was compact enough that an embedded engine could process it close to the agent without introducing a shared data platform. That observation matters because architecture decisions should follow the actual workload rather than the label big data. More than a million rows can sound large in a design review, but row count alone is not a sufficient reason to deploy a distributed lakehouse stack. Column count, compression, query shape, concurrency, access patterns, and data movement all matter.
A Representative Analysis Walkthrough
The following is a representative example based on the workflow used in the exercise; service identifiers and values have been anonymized.
For one service, the deterministic execution layer produced a fact packet showing that the surviving region absorbed approximately seventy-six percent of the expected failover traffic, availability fell below the service SLO during the steady-state window, and p99 latency remained elevated for eighteen minutes. At the same time, the service continued to serve traffic and did not experience a complete outage.
The agent interpreted these facts as a partial failover rather than a binary success or failure. Its explanation cited the traffic absorption ratio, the sustained SLO violation, and the latency degradation, and recommended reviewing routing capacity and downstream dependency limits.
The conclusion was then validated against the underlying deterministic facts and the exercise timeline. Reviewers could trace each statement in the agent’s explanation back to fields in the fact packet and rerun the same DuckDB/Python analysis against the retained input data and configuration. Once the conclusion was confirmed, the resulting action was to investigate whether routing capacity or a downstream bottleneck had prevented the surviving region from absorbing the full expected load.
This validation step was important: the agent proposed the interpretation and next action, but the numerical evidence remained reproducible and independently verifiable.
Making the Workflow Reproducible
The prototype only became an engineering system after we treated reproducibility as a first-class requirement. For every exercise, we retained a replay bundle containing:
- The Parquet inputs
- The manifest and checksums
- The exercise configuration
- The generated SQL or Python code
- The execution metadata
- The deterministic derived facts
- The model output
- The agent version and prompt
- The model identifier
This replay bundle made it possible to rerun an analysis offline, investigate a disputed conclusion, or compare the behavior of two agent versions against the same evidence. We also encoded data semantics explicitly. One subtle example was the meaning of a missing value. Missing QPS or error-count data could represent zero activity in some contexts. Missing success-rate or latency data often meant no traffic was available to measure, not zero percent success or zero milliseconds of latency.
Filling every missing value with zero would have created false failures and false recoveries. The schema and data-quality flags needed to preserve that distinction so the engine and the agent interpreted the dataset consistently.
When the Lightweight Architecture Stops Being Enough
Agent plus DuckDB is not the final architecture for every analytical system. It works when the workload has the right shape. Four signals indicate where the lightweight architecture begins to encounter pressure. They do not require adopting a complete lakehouse stack at once. Each signal points to a different capability that can be introduced incrementally, including a catalog for shared discovery and governance, an open table format for safe concurrent writes and evolution, or a distributed query engine when computation must move closer to large shared datasets.
Independent Consumers Appear
If dashboards, scheduled jobs, notebooks, or other teams need direct access, the data needs a stable contract. Those consumers should not have to call the original agent or reverse-engineer a bucket layout. A shared catalog allows them to discover a table by name, understand its schema, apply permissions, and query it through standard tools.
The Data Becomes Too Large to Move to the Agent Environment
At terabyte scale, pulling files toward a local or development environment for analysis becomes inefficient. The query should execute where the data is stored (i.e., near-data processing), with partition pruning, predicate pushdown, and distributed processing. Only the result should move back to the agent.
The Workflow Must Join with Large Shared Datasets
DuckDB can join local files efficiently when both sides are small enough. The boundary appears when the other side is an organization-wide authoritative dataset that is already registered in a shared catalog and is too large or too frequently updated to export safely. At that point, it is more reliable to register the new data in the same environment and execute the join through the shared engine.
Concurrent Writes or Table-Level Evolution Are Required
A single-writer convention is simple and effective for an early workflow. It breaks down when multiple producers update the dataset, schemas evolve independently, or readers require consistent snapshots. An open table format such as Apache Iceberg adds table metadata, snapshots, schema evolution, and transactional commit semantics on top of the Parquet files. A managed lakehouse can then combine three capabilities:
- A catalog for discovery, ownership, permissions, schema, and partitions
- An open table format for snapshots, evolution, and safe writes
- A shared query engine for distributed scans and joins
These capabilities are valuable, but they introduce integration, governance, compute, and operational cost. They should be adopted in response to real sharing, scale, and transaction requirements, not because every AI project is assumed to need a lakehouse on day one.
A Practical Decision Table
| Workload signal | Embedded engine close to the agent | Managed lakehouse | 
| Primary consumer is one agent workflow | Strong fit | Often unnecessary | 
| Moderate, compressed analytical dataset | Strong fit | May be over-engineered | 
| Ad hoc or exercise-based analysis | Strong fit | Useful only if sharing is required | 
| Many independent consumers | Weak fit | Strong fit | 
| Terabyte-scale scans | Weak fit | Strong fit | 
| Joins with large shared authoritative tables | Limited | Strong fit | 
| Concurrent writers and snapshot requirements | Weak fit | Strong fit | 
| Organization-wide catalog and governance | Limited | Strong fit | 
Table 2. Choose the platform based on access patterns, scale, and write semantics.
The decision is not AI or SQL nor is it files or tables. The real decision is:
Is an embedded, agent-driven analytical engine sufficient, or does the workload require a managed, shared data platform?
Conclusion: AI Changes the Interface, Not the Engine
AI agents make data analysis more accessible. They can translate an operational question into analytical steps, select relevant evidence, classify behavior, and write a report that an engineer can act on. They do not eliminate the need for precise execution.
In our DR analysis workflow, Parquet and DuckDB performed the mechanical work: storage, filtering, aggregation, validation, and joins. The agent performed the contextual work by deciding how to interpret traffic absorption, availability, and latency together, and communicating the result. The architecture remained intentionally lightweight because the real workload did not yet require a shared lakehouse.
What changed after operating the workflow was our view of where the analytical interface should live. Engineers no longer needed to interact directly with the query engine for every investigation, but the engine remained essential for producing trustworthy facts. The agent became the layer that planned the analysis, generated the required SQL or Python, and interpreted the evidence.
The main architectural trade-off is therefore not AI versus SQL, or files versus tables. It is how much analytical infrastructure needs to sit behind the agent for the workload at hand. A small embedded engine may be sufficient for a focused workflow; shared catalogs, open table formats, and distributed engines should be introduced only as sharing, scale, write concurrency, or governance create a concrete need. The engine remains; the interface changes.

articles.title: LiteLLM release pipeline hacked to distribute info-stealer malware
articles.text:
Hackers compromised the LiteLLM project’s PyPI package and published malicious Docker images with a payload that steals credentials, secrets, and environment variables.
The supply-chain attack affected all PyPI wheels (.whl installation packages) for LiteLLM version 1.107.0, impacting Windows, Linux, and macOS systems.
LiteLLM is an open-source Python SDK and AI gateway that enables applications to access AI models from different providers through a common API.
It is a massively popular project with 61,800 GitHub stars, 92 million monthly downloads on PyPI, and is used by high-profile companies like NVIDIA, Netflix, AT&T, and Okta.
The project says that the release pipeline was compromised on October 21 and a threat actor pushed version 1.107.0 to the Docker registry and PyPI.
"This version contained compiled malware which steals credentials and loads remote-code execution tools," the maintainer says, adding that customers running the private enterprise were not impacted.
In a post-mortem of the incident, the maintainer says that the following LiteLLM artifacts were affected in the attack:
- PyPI: litellm==1.107.0: all seven wheels, live from 11:39:51 to 13:23 UTC
- Docker Hub: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to compromised image index sha256:1bbcb1443bc962e45f5aad53fe3d2c30600e0379715fb6c664cdd3ac126c339e from 11:46:56 to 14:20 UTC
- GHCR: v1.107.0, latest, main-latest, and main-stable: pointed to the compromised image indexes below from 11:46:56 UTC until they were made unavailable by 13:51 UTC
  - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm: sha256:1bbcb1443bc9…
  - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-database: sha256:c00f9d92c427…
  - ghcr.io/berriai/litellm-non_root: sha256:7b00e91cd2fe…
Multiple application security companies detected the attack within six minutes of publishing the malicious LiteLLM version and analyzed the payload.
According to the researchers, the attacker did not touch the LiteLLM application code and modified only the installation package to place three malicious files (cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py) in the environment's Python’s library directory.
"During normal startup, Python processes executable .pth lines and then attempts to import sitecustomize," Socket researchers explain.
Endor Labs notes that this way the payloads are executed before the application every time Python is launched in the environment. Running Python or pip to investigate an affected installation also triggered the malware.
The malware targeted the following data:
- Cloud and deployment credentials: AWS, Azure, Google Cloud, Kubernetes, Docker, and infrastructure-management secrets.
- AI credentials and configuration: Authentication files for AI development tools, plus LiteLLM’s stored provider credentials and model settings.
- Developer secrets and private keys: Git, GitHub, npm, PyPI, and CI/CD credentials; .env files; SSH, GPG, and TLS keys.
- Browser data: Saved login, cookie, autofill/payment, and browsing-history databases.
- Host and runtime data: Environment variables, shell and application histories, and system and network information.
The stolen data is encrypted using an AES-256-CBC key that is encrypted with an RSA-4096 key and then uploaded to ‘litellm[.]dev/healthcheck’
One of the malicious files, sitecustomize.py, launches a detached loader that checks a GitHub-hosted pointer every hour and downloads Python from an external server for execution on the host.
The malicious packages have been removed, but potentially impacted users should stop affected deployments and inspect environments without launching the Python interpreter.
Infected systems should be isolated and rebuilt from clean backups, and all exposed secrets should be rotated immediately.
Removing the LiteLLM package directory alone may leave startup files or an active loader behind.
Currently, the recommended recovery version is LiteLLM 1.106.2, which is the latest clean release before the attack.
Previously, the project also suffered a breach in March, when the TeamPCP hacking group published malicious LiteLLM versions on PyPI after breaching Aqua Security's Trivy vulnerability scanner used in LiteLLM's CI/CD pipeline.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.
