articles.title: How Nigeria’s ECS Network is building a structured e-sports ecosystem for Africa - Disrupt Africa
articles.text:
Nigerian startup ECS Network is looking to bring long-term structure to competitive gaming in Africa, offering a league system with divisions, promotion and relegation, player statistics and team rankings.
Launched just over a year ago, ECS Network started out as competitive Call of Duty: Mobile (CODM) “scrims” – or practice games – before evolving into a broader e-sports organisation covering multiple games.
“A lot of competitive gaming activity was centred around standalone tournaments, where everything essentially started and ended with one event. We wanted to build something with continuity, where teams and players could compete consistently and have their performances tracked over time,” CEO Larry Channel told Disrupt Africa.
That led the startup to develop a structured league system featuring multiple divisions, promotion and relegation, player statistics, team rankings, MVP recognition and competitive integrity systems.
ECS now has more than 50 staff working across its different titles and operational areas, including event management, competitive integrity, verification, rankings, community management and media.
Channel said there were several tournament organisers and esports communities operating across Africa, but most were primarily focused on individual tournaments or events.
“Our main difference is the long-term structure. ECS is built around an ongoing competitive system where teams can progress through divisions, players can build statistics and rankings, and performances continue to matter beyond a single tournament,” he said.
The approach is resonating. ECS has grown to more than 43,000 players and over 5,000 registered teams across 10 titles, while more than 1,600 teams and 15,000 players have competed in CODM alone since launch. Having started with CODM, the platform has expanded to include Free Fire, PUBG Mobile, eFootball, FC Mobile, Blood Strike, Mobile Legends and Valorant, among others.
“The response has been very strong,” said Channel.
Though its core competitive base is in Africa, ECS has also built an audience in Europe, North America and the Middle East. The startup plans to continue expanding across more games and to strengthen its position as a wider African esports ecosystem.
ECS is self-funded by its management team, and has so far awarded more than NGN75 million (US$56,000) in prize money across its events. It generates revenue primarily through sponsorship and commercial partnerships.
“At this stage, revenue is largely reinvested into the operation and development of the league, including events, prize pools, staffing, infrastructure and community development, rather than being taken as profit,” Channel said.
The journey has not been without its challenges, chief among them changing how players view competitive gaming.
“One of the biggest challenges was changing the mindset around competitive gaming from viewing each tournament as a standalone event to seeing it as part of a longer competitive journey. Building that trust and getting teams and players to buy into a structured system took time, but we’ve seen that improve significantly,” he said.
Sponsorship remains a hurdle too.
“African e-sports is still developing commercially, so securing long-term sponsorship support remains something we’re actively working on,” said Channel.

articles.title: A SpaceX no le gusta que China le pise los talones, así que va a hacer lo que nadie ha hecho: recuperar y reutilizar las dos etapas de un cohete
articles.text:
Parece que a Elon Musk no le gusta sentir que alguien le pisa los talones. Hace tiempo que la compañía china Deep Blue Aerospace publicó su interés en recuperar un cohete mediante un sistema de torre con palillos, como Mechazilla. Ahora, además, ha anunciado que las primeras piezas del cohete están saliendo de la cadena de montaje y que todo va viento en popa. Ha sido el momento ideal para que SpaceX anuncie que intentará algo aún más difícil que lo que ya hizo en Mechazilla: recuperar las dos etapas de su cohete Starship mediante ese sistema.
Hasta ahora, ni SpaceX ni ninguna otra compañía espacial ha logrado recuperar y reutilizar un cohete completo. Por lo general, la primera etapa se recupera, se analiza y se prepara para un nuevo lanzamiento, pero la segunda se desecha. Es lo que quiere hacer la compañía china, de hecho. Eso abarata los costes, pero la recuperación total los abarataría aún más. Por eso, SpaceX está lista para comenzar las pruebas de una recuperación de la segunda etapa. Según ha explicado Elon Musk, el primer intento será en el vuelo 15 de Starship, durante el próximo mes de noviembre. Si no lo consiguen a la primera, habrá muchos intentos más.
Una misión complicada. Starship es el cohete más grande del mundo, con 122 metros de altura cuando se encuentra totalmente apilado. También es el más potente. Por eso, construir una segunda etapa cada vez que se quiera reutilizar es demasiado caro incluso para SpaceX. Para solucionarlo, pretenden recuperar la segunda etapa después de los lanzamientos, pero no es fácil, ya que esta viaja más alto, lejos y rápido que la primera. El sistema elegido será el de “palillos chinos” de la torre Mechazilla. De los 14 vuelos de prueba que se han realizado hasta el momento con Starship, se ha recuperado la primera etapa en 3. Llega el momento de ir a por el siguiente paso.
Del vuelo 14 al 15. El vuelo 14 de Starship tuvo lugar el 28 de septiembre y fue todo un éxito, ya que se consiguió por primera vez alcanzar la órbita y depositar su carga útil en ella. En este caso, la carga constaba de 26 satélites de Starlink V3, una nueva constelación en la que se espera colocar alrededor de 100.000 dispositivos. De momento no hay fecha para el vuelo 15, solo sabemos que está planeado que sea en noviembre. A Elon Musk le gustaría seguir con la racha de buenas noticias. De hecho, considera que hay al menos un 50%-60% de probabilidad de lograrlo.
Muchos más vuelos. El CEO de SpaceX ha asegurado que pretenden mantener una buena cadencia de lanzamientos en lo que queda de 2026 y que el ritmo se acelerará aún más en 2027. Siguen con su estrategia de lanzar, lanzar y lanzar, así que lo lógico es que en alguno de esos intentos se consiga la ansiada recuperación de la segunda etapa. Con cada intento fallido aprenderán de los errores, ya que su objetivo es atrapar la nave completa en cada lanzamiento del futuro. Así, sería más fácil lograr hazañas como la colonización de Marte.
Datos económicos. Además de este anuncio, SpaceX ha dado a conocer recientemente sus datos económicos durante el tercer trimestre de 2026. Ha sido una gran etapa financiera para la compañía, con ingresos de 14.600 millones de dólares, un 161% más que hace un año. Además, han obtenido un beneficio neto de 4.400 millones, frente a pérdidas de 1.100 millones en el mismo periodo de 2025. Eso sí, solo 1.800 millones vinieron de los lanzamientos y el resto del segmento espacial. La mayor parte procede de la conectividad de Starlink y los centros de datos de inteligencia artificial.

articles.title: Fatu Ogwuche bets on live video with new African tech show
articles.text:
Big Tech This Week, a media company founded by entrepreneur and former Meta executive Fatu Ogwuche, is launching a weekly live technology show, betting that African tech audiences want to hear directly from the founders and operators behind the products they use.
The show, Tech This Week, will combine a rundown of technology news with interviews spanning business, products and culture. Ogwuche said it will be free to watch and funded through sponsorships, advertising and paid segments.
The launch expands Big Tech This Week’s coverage into live video, building on an earlier Twitter Spaces series that Ogwuche said attracted more than 100,000 cumulative listeners over a year. That programme featured conversations with founders, investors and other technology professionals.
Ogwuche said the show is starting with about four sponsors, whose support has provided enough runway for a year of weekly broadcasts. She declined to disclose the investment or identify the sponsors during an interview with TechCabal.
Her proposition is that a news article or a recorded podcast does not always give audiences enough opportunity to engage with the people building companies that increasingly shape their lives.
“It’s a very important time to hear directly from the people who are essentially in the middle of your life,” Ogwuche said.
She points to TBPN, the live technology show covering Silicon Valley, as a reference for the format. Tech This Week will seek to bring a similar immediacy to African technology coverage, with conversations tied to developments across the industry.
Its intended audience includes founders, investors, operators, regulators and the people who use technology products. Across Big Tech This Week’s existing formats, Ogwuche said its largest audience falls between ages 25 and 44, with viewers and readers in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, South Africa, Ethiopia and diaspora markets including Britain, the United States and Canada.
Beyond the funding announcement
The show arrives as Ogwuche sees a widening range of stories emerging from African technology businesses.
She argues that in the past decade, many businesses have been devoted to solving essential problems like helping people make payments, save money, invest and run businesses. Those businesses remain central to the industry, but she also sees founders pursuing interests in gaming, entertainment, sport and other areas.
For her, that creates an opportunity to cover technology through the people and cultural changes around it, alongside company announcements and fundraising milestones.
“The last decade has been building for survival,” she said. Now, she sees more founders building from “joy” and “curiosity”.
The programme will bring established industry figures into conversation alongside newer founders, engineers and product managers. Ogwuche said her industry relationships will help secure guests who do not regularly give interviews.
That access is central to the pitch. The show’s appeal will depend partly on whether it can bring compelling guests into a regular broadcast and give audiences a reason to follow the conversation live.
Ogwuche also plans to cover companies beyond Nigeria. Speaking from Addis Ababa, where she had been meeting founders, she said the programme would seek stories from across the continent.
“Even now with the show, it’s also going to make me be more disciplined about ensuring that we’re adequately covering milestones from other parts of the continent,” she said.
The ambition presents an editorial challenge: building a recognisably African show while avoiding an overwhelming focus on Nigeria’s founders and companies. Ogwuche said the weekly schedule would require greater discipline in covering developments elsewhere.
Access and scrutiny
A programme built around access to founders must also decide how to use it.
Asked how she would prevent the show from becoming a platform for guests to promote themselves without scrutiny, Ogwuche said her approach would include coverage of both business achievements and regulatory trouble.
“If you’re building and you’re doing something incredible, I’m going to cover it,” she said. “If you land in trouble, I’m also going to cover it.”
She described her approach as avoiding “gotcha” journalism while rejecting the suggestion that access should mean favourable treatment. Still, she made clear that the programme would emphasise innovation and promising developments in the industry.
“What I really want to focus on is the positive things that happen,” she said.
Alongside sponsorships and advertising, Ogwuche said some segments would be paid for, with product reviews among the formats being developed. She did not detail how commercial segments would be distinguished from independent editorial coverage. For viewers, those distinctions will matter as the programme develops its authority.
Building a weekly habit
Ogwuche has invested in equipment and commissioned a set for the programme, choosing to build production capacity for a recurring show. Sponsorship has helped finance those preparations and, she said, secured the runway to broadcast consistently for 12 months.
The live programme will also feed a wider distribution operation. Full interviews and clips will appear on YouTube and social media, including Instagram and LinkedIn, while audio will be distributed through Spotify and Apple Podcasts.
That gives the company several ways to reach people who miss the live broadcast. It also means the show’s reach will extend beyond the audience watching at a scheduled time.
Internet access remains a limit. Ogwuche said the programme would primarily serve a digital audience, although she hopes journalists and broadcasters can draw on its interviews to bring relevant information to people through other channels.
Her larger ambition is to demonstrate that African technology coverage has room for more formats, and that audiences will return for them.
“We need to keep creating things that are fun, enjoyable, but also authoritative,” she said.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Stream low-latency speech from AI agents using Kokoro TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
A customer asks an AI voice agent a question and waits. The agent already has an answer, it’s midway through generating a long, multi-paragraph response, but the customer hears nothing for five seconds. By the time an answer arrives, the customer is frustrated, confused, and no longer paying attention.
Text-to-speech integrations create exactly that gap. A one-sentence response might generate in 600 milliseconds, but the full response takes five seconds, and the integration waits for all of it before synthesis starts.
This post shows how to close that gap. We stream each sentence to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech (TTS) model on Amazon SageMaker AI as soon as an agent produces it, so synthesis begins on sentence one instead of the finished response. Getting that audio back to a browser needs its own solution too, so we also cover both transports for doing it and what each costs in practice.
Solution overview
This solution closes the gap by streaming synthesis alongside generation instead of waiting for it to finish. As the agent produces each sentence, that sentence streams immediately to a hosted Kokoro-82M text-to-speech model, so audio playback can start before the agent finishes speaking its full response. Kokoro-82M holds only 82 million parameters, small enough to run cheaply on a single mid-tier GPU instance. That keeps both latency and inference cost low for a voice agent handling real traffic.
Kokoro-82M runs in a custom container on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance. The container exposes two routes: POST /invocations, which streams a response for one complete input, and WS /invocations-bidirectional-stream, which keeps one connection open across many messages in both directions.
The following diagram shows the request path from client to model:
Prerequisites
Before you begin, you need:
- An AWS account with permissions to create SageMaker AI endpoints; AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore; AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles; and an Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repository, including at minimum the sagemaker:CreateEndpoint, sagemaker:CreateEndpointConfig, sagemaker:CreateModel, sagemaker:InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream, and bedrock:InvokeModelWithResponseStream actions.
- The sample container pins an older PyTorch with a known advisory (PYSEC-2026-2286, fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use.
- AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) v2, installed and bootstrapped in your target account and AWS Region.
- A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint deployed from a container that declares the com.amazonaws.sagemaker.capabilities.bidirectional-streaming=true Docker label.
- Python 3.12 or later, uv, and Docker to build the container image (the underlying HTTP/2 client only ships pre-built wheels for Python 3.12 and newer).
- The AWS SDK for Python (Boto3) with support for invoke_endpoint_with_bidirectional_stream.
- Familiarity with WebSockets and Starlette or a comparable ASGI framework.
- The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post.
Walkthrough
The walkthrough first deploys the endpoint and agent, then works through the client-side changes that make incremental streaming work end to end.
Deploy the endpoint and agent
The Kokoro-82M endpoint and the agent runtime deploy through two CLI tools, each wrapping its own AWS CDK stacks:
speech-infra deploy provisions the Kokoro-82M endpoint. This includes the foundation and model-cache stacks that create the underlying IAM roles and sync the model’s weights into Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3). The endpoint stack then builds the container image and creates the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. agent-infra deploy provisions the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime hosting the Strands agent, which calls the endpoint you just deployed, so deploy the endpoint first.
Step 1: Handle the WebSocket frame type SageMaker AI actually sends
The bidirectional transport SageMaker AI uses delivers every piece of a client’s message to your container as a binary WebSocket frame. A common way to write a Starlette WebSocket handler is calling receive_text(), which reads message["text"] and raises KeyError if that key isn’t present. Because every message this client sends arrives as binary, that handler fails on every request.
The failure is commonly misdiagnosed. A generic exception handler that forwards str(e) to the client turns KeyError('text') into an error frame reading 'text', which looks like a missing field, not a framing issue. The endpoint itself reports InService throughout, since it accepts connections and responds to every message, with an error each time.
Accept either frame type explicitly instead of assuming one will show up:
This decodes bytes as UTF-8 when no text field is present, rather than assuming one frame type. Test it by sending a binary frame, because this failure mode produces a well-formed error frame and a healthy endpoint status, not an obvious crash.
Step 2: Keep the session open between messages
After your container finishes synthesizing one message’s audio, the instinct is to close the session, the way an HTTP cycle ends. That’s wrong here. After sending a message’s audio and a synthesis_complete control frame, the container loop should go back to waiting on receive() for the next message on the same, still-open session. Close the connection only when the client sends an explicit {"type": "close"} message.
The following diagram shows one session carrying two sentences in sequence, closing only at the end:
This way, you can send several sentences, one after another, on one persistent session, with no reconnection cost between them. Closing eagerly after one response would force a new connection per sentence, undoing most of the latency benefit.
Step 3: Stream sentences as the agent produces them
With the session behavior in place, the client-side fix for the latency problem is a class that normalizes text arriving in two shapes: a complete string known up front, or a live token stream. It produces the same output either way: complete sentences, ready to send as soon as each one is complete.
Call feed() once per fragment of text as it arrives. It returns any newly completed sentences, holding back trailing text. Call flush() once, at the end of input, to release whatever partial text remains even without trailing punctuation. This keeps a stream that ends before a period arrives from dropping a final sentence.
This isn’t concurrent synthesis. Every bidirectional handler is a strictly sequential loop: receive a message, synthesize its audio, send that audio, send synthesis_complete, then receive the next message. Sentence two’s audio isn’t generated while sentence one’s still transmits. What incremental sending buys is narrower: synthesis on sentence one begins the instant it exists, rather than waiting for the full response. For a multi-sentence response with real generation time between its first and last sentence, that’s the entire latency win.
We verified this against a live endpoint sending a three-sentence input over one session. All three chunks arrived with audio matching the text sent for each:
| Chunk | Text | Audio bytes | Duration (s) | 
| 1 | “Hello there.” | 73,200 | 1.525 | 
| 2 | “This is a post deployment check.” | 108,000 | 2.250 | 
| 3 | “It has three sentences.” | 98,400 | 2.050 | 
Step 4: Choose a transport for getting audio back to the client
Streaming text into the model incrementally solves half the problem. The other half is getting the resulting audio out to whatever renders it, commonly a browser. Most agent and chat frontends already stream text over Server-Sent Events (SSE): one-directional, and supported natively by most browsers. SSE is a text protocol, not built to carry a raw binary payload. A team adding voice to an existing SSE pipeline naturally reaches for the pattern it already has: base64-encode the audio and wrap it in a JSON event.
We measured the cost of that approach across 24 clips, confirmed with Amazon Transcribe that quality didn’t differ across encodings, and compared MP3 against AAC:
| Candidate | Raw bytes | Base64 bytes | Bitrate | 
| Raw PCM | 2,396,400 | 3,195,200 | 384 kbps | 
| MP3 48k | 308,304 | 411,072 | 49.5 kbps | 
| AAC 32k fMP4 | 258,039 | 344,084 | 41.6 kbps | 
Base64 inflates every payload by close to the expected 33%. The subtler cost is frame alignment. SSE events are delimited by a blank line, but the audio inside is delimited into MP3 frames. The two schemes don’t necessarily align with how the transport chunks the data. In one measured response, four logical MP3 frames arrived as six delivery chunks, two ending mid-frame. A consumer that treats each delivery chunk as one complete unit fails on ordinary, healthy traffic. The fix buffers incoming bytes and acts only once a delimiter is found:
The alternative used today for the model-facing leg skips base64 and SSE framing entirely. It multiplexes raw binary audio and JSON control frames over the same bidirectional session already carrying incremental text input, and tells them apart with one rule.
A chunk that fails to decode as a JSON object is audio, forwarded as received, with no encoding step anywhere in the path. One edge case matters: raw PCM audio can legitimately begin with byte 0x7b, the ASCII character {, the same character that opens a JSON object. This rule avoids misclassifying that audio because it requires the entire chunk to parse as valid JSON, not its first byte alone, something a PCM frame will essentially never do.
        Note: If your frontend already has a working SSE pipeline for text, base64-encoded audio inside an SSE event is the pragmatic choice. It costs roughly 33 percent extra payload and a buffer-and-reassemble step, but reuses infrastructure you already operate. If you’re building the voice path fresh, or latency is the priority, the unified binary and JSON approach avoids both costs and reuses the connection already carrying text.
Step 5: Put it together in a real agent
The fuller, end-to-end case is a live, generative agent composing its response one token at a time, with no way to know sentence four until sentence one exists. This example runs as a Strands agent, backed by Amazon Bedrock, deployed to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime, calling the Kokoro endpoint with the pattern from Step 4. Three communication legs connect in this design: the browser-facing leg carrying Server-Sent Events back to the caller, the agent’s streaming call to Amazon Bedrock for text generation, and the agent’s bidirectional session with the Kokoro endpoint for synthesis.
The following diagram shows those three communication legs, and where the overlap between generation and synthesis happens:
The request payload carries a mode field, either "bidi" or "batch", dispatched to two code paths inside the same entrypoint function. A benchmark between them changes exactly one variable: when synthesis starts. In run_bidi, two tasks run concurrently. One drains the Bedrock text stream and feeds completed sentences into the chunker. The other drains the Kokoro session and emits audio chunks as they arrive. Both push into one shared queue, so a consumer yields events in true arrival order: audio for an early sentence can reach the caller while Bedrock still generates a later one. run_batch is the deliberate opposite: it waits for the full response before one synthesis call, kept as a fair baseline.
Going the other direction, the leg from the agent container back to the caller does use base64, for a different reason than Step 4 describes. BedrockAgentCoreApp’s entrypoint must yield plain, JSON-serializable dictionaries, which its SDK turns into data: {json}\n\n frames automatically. There’s no way to hand it a raw binary frame. That’s a consequence of the JSON-native managed runtime, not the choice Step 4 measured and moved away from. Both run_bidi and run_batch pay that identical cost on this leg, so the measured difference between them is purely timing: when the first audio chunk is emitted.
Testing and validation
We isolated the TTS transport’s own contribution to time to first audio by sending the same 267-character, four-sentence block of text two ways: as one message (batch), and as only its first sentence (incremental). We ran five trials each against the live endpoint.
As measured earlier, sending only the first sentence cut mean time to first audio byte from 329.3 ms to 156.7 ms, a 52.4 percent relative improvement, isolated to the TTS transport itself.
We then measured the fuller, end-to-end case with a real language model producing the text, running the identical prompt through run_bidi and run_batch against the same live Bedrock model and endpoint, so the only variable is when synthesis starts.
Using that same methodology, bidi mode’s time to first audio measured 2.4 times faster than batch mode against a local container, and 3.5 times faster against the deployed AgentCore runtime.
The following chart shows that gap across both environments:
The gap widens, rather than narrows, for the deployed case once a real network hop is added. run_bidi absorbs that hop inside the overlap it’s already exploiting between generation and synthesis. run_batch has no equivalent overlap to hide that cost in, since it does one thing at a time, so every added millisecond of network overhead lands directly on its serial wait.
To reproduce this comparison against your own deployment, run the same bidi-vs-batch test the agent container exposes:
This sends the prompt through both modes and reports the timestamp of the first audio_chunk event against agent_start for each. If you see errors instead, check for the KeyError: 'text' symptom from Step 1. An endpoint reporting InService while every request fails signals that bug, not a deployment issue.
Clean up
To avoid ongoing charges, tear down the resources this walkthrough creates in reverse deployment order, agent first, then endpoint:
agent-infra destroy removes the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime resource. speech-infra destroy removes the SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint. Neither empties the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or deletes the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed.
Conclusion
We showed how to remove one source of avoidable latency from a voice agent, waiting for an agent’s full response before starting speech synthesis, and how to quantify a second, quieter cost: base64-encoded audio inside SSE inflates payload by about a third and can misalign with MP3 frame boundaries if you don’t buffer for it. Streaming each sentence into a SageMaker AI bidirectional endpoint as soon as an agent produces it cut time to first audio by more than half in isolation, and by 2.4 to 3.5 times in a deployed agent. Multiplexing binary audio and JSON control frames over that session, instead of encoding audio as text, removes the size inflation and frame-realignment work a naive SSE relay requires.
If you’re adding voice to an agent that already streams text over SSE, start with the base64 approach in Step 4 and revisit the unified transport once latency becomes the priority. To learn more, see the Amazon SageMaker AI real-time inference documentation and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore documentation. If you’d like help applying this pattern to your own architecture, contact your AWS account team.

articles.title: Google Chrome s'appuie sur Gemini pour détecter les arnaques en ligne
articles.text:
L’explosion des arnaques en ligne alimentées par l’IA pousse Google à renforcer la sécurité de Chrome. Le navigateur Web s’est en effet enrichi de nouvelles mesures de sécurité intégrées dans son mode Protection renforcée. Grâce à Gemini, Chrome peut identifier les tentatives d’arnaque les plus subtiles en s’appuyant notamment sur une analyse textuelle du contenu des pages en temps réel.
Introduit en 2020, le mode protection renforcé de Chrome comptait, en 2025, plus d’un milliard d’utilisateurs à travers le monde d’après Google. La firme de Mountain View l’affirme, les utilisateurs qui l’activent sont dix fois plus en sécurité face « au phishing, à l’ingénierie sociale, aux abus de notifications et d’autres escroqueries par rapport au mode de protection standard » de la Navigation sécurisée de Chrome.
De nouveaux avertissements pour les sites suspects
Jusqu’à présent, dès qu’un site malveillant était détecté, Chrome bloquait automatiquement celui-ci et affichait un écran rouge. Depuis cette année, le navigateur s’appuie désormais sur une double classification pour couvrir un plus grand nombre de risques sans pour autant bloquer inutilement votre navigation. Ainsi, lorsqu’un site Web est fortement suspecté d’être dangereux, Chrome continue d’afficher sa page rouge.
Mais pour les sites considérés comme simplement suspects, notamment les pages adoptant des schémas trompeurs associés à des sites malveillants connus, Chrome affiche de nouveaux avertissements. Plus visuels (ils s’affichent au sein d’un pop-up), ils s’adaptent à la menace en affichant une icône, une couleur et un texte adapté pour vous inciter à faire preuve de prudence.
Gemini, en renfort contre les menaces en ligne
Pour renforcer la sécurité de la protection renforcée de Chrome, Google s’appuie dorénavant sur son assistant intelligent Gemini. Grâce à un modèle Gemini beaucoup plus puissant, déployé côté serveur, Chrome peut détecter plus facilement les menaces pendant la navigation.
Concrètement, Gemini va se charger d’analyser le contenu textuel des pages que vous consultez pour identifier la marque représentée et l’intention du site Web afin d’établir un score de probabilité d’arnaque. Ces données sont ensuite croisées avec la réputation du domaine pour générer un verdict final. À noter que l’analyse de Gemini ne se lance que lorsque des indicateurs suspects sont détectés.
Un bouclier contre Clickfix
Les attaques Clickfix, qui ont fait de nombreux dégâts au cours des derniers mois, sont également dans le viseur de Google. Cette méthode, qui consiste à vous piéger en vous faisant copier-coller une commande dans le terminal de votre ordinateur sous prétexte de résoudre un problème technique, afin de permettre l’installation de logiciels malveillants sur votre PC, peut désormais être repérée par Chrome.
Lorsque la protection renforcée du navigateur est activée, Chrome repère lorsqu’un utilisateur copie une commande suspecte. Les données personnelles qui se trouvent potentiellement dans le texte copié sont automatiquement retirées, et le script est ensuite analysé par la protection renforcée du navigateur qui affiche un avertissement avant que l’utilisateur ne puisse l’exécuter.

articles.title: Welbi acquired by US-based senior care marketing platform Further
articles.text:
Ottawa-based Welbi is looking forward to rapid expansion after being acquired by fellow senior care software platform Further.
The news: US-based Further, an AI sales and marketing platform for senior care communities, announced on Wednesday that it acquired Welbi, a patient engagement software for those same communities. Terms of the deal were not disclosed.
Welbi founder and CEO Elizabeth Audette-Bourdeau told BetaKit over the phone that she will remain in charge of Welbi’s operations and that its team is remaining in place under Further. Welbi plans to double its headcount to roughly two dozen employees by the end of the year, with three hires already made. The two companies positioned the acquisition as a way to connect what a sales team learns about a potential senior resident’s interests through Further, with the team that plans the resident’s day-to-day life in the community using Welbi.
From the source: “We’ve been looking for the right partner to accelerate our growth, and that’s what we found [with] Further,” Audette-Bourdeau said. “Further has over 170 employees; they are international, they have team members all over the world, and they are a dominant player in the senior living space. For us to be able to partner with them and learn from them and grow along their side is something extremely exciting for me.”
The context: Audette-Bourdeau founded Welbi in 2016, after her grandfather suffered a stroke and his health declined after he moved to a retirement home. Welbi raised a $3 million CAD seed round in 2022, backed by Graphite Ventures, MaRS IAF, SoGal Ventures, and Roach Capital, to grow the platform and improve quality of life in senior homes.
Final thought: Audette-Bourdeau told BetaKit that Welbi had doubled its customer base in the past 12 months, serving approximately 1,000 senior care communities before the acquisition. Under Further, the two companies will have a combined reach of more than 8,000 senior communities, making Welbi’s platform directly available to thousands more potential customers.

articles.title: Signal Vulnerability Lets Malicious Callers Block Hang-Ups
articles.text:
Signal has resolved a critical-severity vulnerability that could allow a malicious caller to keep audio and video tracks enabled even after the user hung up.
The security defect is tracked as CVE-2026-113380 (CVSS score of 9.3) and impacts RingRTC, the open source library Signal uses for voice and video calls, which is based on WebRTC.
Due to the issue, a remote peer could flood the call’s Finite State Machine (FSM) event queue with junk, and the call would not terminate.
This happened because the hangup was not treated as a kill switch, but as an event added to the FSM event queue; there was no rate limit on peer-originated events; and the hangup event had no priority.
“Flood the queue with junk and the hang-up waits behind attacker noise forever, so the call (microphone, possibly camera) is never torn down,” a GitHub write-up by a researcher reads.
By exploiting the vulnerability, an attacker could keep the audio and video tracks flowing from a target device while the victim believes they ended the call.
The security defect was resolved in RingRTC version 2.72.0, which was released on September 4.
Details on the flaw, however, were published on Tuesday, along with a conceptual proof-of-concept (PoC). NIST added the CVE to the NVD database on Tuesday.
Signal resolved the issue by ensuring that call termination requests do not remain blocked in FSM’s event queue and are detected independently.
Users should update their Signal applications as soon as possible. Otherwise, they should check the call indicator to make sure the call indeed ended.

articles.title: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia | TechCrunch
articles.text:
The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI.
“Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote.
“Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”
The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser.
On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store.
While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed, with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open source.
But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK) — a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property.
“While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.”
For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.”
Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional.
The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company — which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025 — conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “novelty tax” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.

articles.title: Arista patches new VeloCloud Orchestrator zero-day exploited in attacks
articles.text:
Arista Networks released security updates to patch an actively exploited zero-day vulnerability affecting VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) On-Prem deployments.
VCO is a web-based management portal that helps administrators configure, monitor, and manage VeloCloud SD-WANs (Software-Defined Wide Area Networks) and associated edge devices.
Tracked as CVE-2026-114625, this critical-severity flaw can allow attackers with basic privileges, access to the VCO web interface, and a valid authenticated session to escalate privileges through low-complexity SQL injection attacks that don't require user interaction.
"VeloCloud Orchestrator (VCO) on-prem has a security issue where this issue may allow a remote attacker to access privileged internal functionality and impact the VCO host. Successful exploitation may compromise the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of the orchestrator and data managed by the orchestrator," Arista said.
"On an affected system, any authenticated user can gain operator privileges and masquerade as a local 'superuser operator' user. This includes access to functionality that is intended for internal use only and which is not intended to be remotely accessible."
The company said it has already patched hosted VCO deployments running version 5.2.3.18 or later, 6.1.3.10 or later, and 6.4.2.12 or later.
Until the patches are deployed, Arista advised admins to monitor for connections from known malicious IP addresses, restrict access to the VCO web interface to administrative networks, and review recent administrator activity for unusual changes.
Admins are also recommended to review VCO web access logs for suspicious activity, such as requests with unusual URL-like path components, encoded characters, references to local or internal services, and high request rates.
The company also warned security teams to block the 74[.]82.197.86 and 38[.]54.50.151 IP addresses, which have been observed during ongoing attacks.
"If compromise is suspected, operators should preserve VCO web access logs, backend application logs, system logs, database logs, and relevant file-system timestamps before remediation where operationally feasible," it noted, advising customers to contact the Arista Networks Technical Assistance Center (TAC) for additional assistance.
This year, Arista has patched three other actively exploited zero-day flaws (CVE-2026-7473 in May, CVE-2026-16812in July, and CVE-2026-93952 in September) affecting Extensible Operating System (EOS) and on-premises VeloCloud Orchestrator deployments.
Arista Networks is a Fortune 500 company and one of the largest US corporations by revenue, with over 10,000 customers worldwide.

articles.title: Canadians spent millions on OnlyFans this year, report reveals
articles.text:
Despite consistent complaints about a tough economy, it turns out that Canadians are more than willing to open their wallets for a little exclusive content.
According to the OnlyFans Wrapped 2026 report from OnlyFinder, Canadians spent a whopping $170.2 million on the platform over the past year. That’s a 16.2 per cent increase from the previous year, more than double the global growth rate of 7.6 per cent.
The amount is also enough to be one small Oceania nation’s total gross domestic product (GDP).
OnlyFinder, an independent search tool unaffiliated with OnlyFans, used search and traffic data to model consumer spending across the platform. Its geographic estimates are based on data and anchored to revenue figures reported by OnlyFans’ parent company, the U.K.-based Fenix International.
Many of us are quick to assume the platform only promotes pornography, which is sort of fair.
“On OnlyFans, adult content and adult searches are well over 50 per cent of total platform usage. So the reputation that OnlyFans skews more towards adult content is accurate,” OnlyFinder CEO Max Anderson tells Daily Hive.
Still, the platform also hosts creators in non-adult niches, including fitness and food, alongside celebrities offering fans exclusive access to their lives — all for a few bucks, of course.
According to the report, those customers aren’t just paying for a monthly subscription.
“There is a broad misconception that the primary form of commerce on the platform is monthly subscriptions,” says Anderson.
Tips and pay-per-view purchases accounted for 73 per cent of OnlyFans spending so far this year, up from 67 per cent last year.
In other words, the bulk of the money isn’t necessarily going toward access to a creator’s page. It’s going toward individual interactions and custom content made in response to a fan’s specific request. Flirty feet pics from an Australian model, a 20-minute air fryer recipe from an American soap opera star, you name it.
Anderson says these service-based transactions now account for nearly three-quarters of spending in Canada, suggesting OnlyFans has evolved beyond the traditional subscription model.
He believes loneliness and the desire for personal connection are major drivers behind this astronomical spending, and that feeling of receiving individual attention from someone they admire or follow is worth every penny.
“Fans in Canada will tip $50 just for the creator to chat with them for 15 mins,” Anderson says of the platform, which he believes is better understood as more of a “gig economy platform” than anything else.
Toronto led the Canadian cities in total OnlyFans spending, with an estimated $20.6 million spent on the platform this year.
Vancouver ranked higher globally for spending relative to its adult population, but recorded a total of $5.5 million in the end.
Meanwhile, Montreal saw the fastest year-over-year growth, with spending climbing 37.11 per cent to reach $11.5 million so far in 2026.
Another major Canadian city, Calgary, reportedly spent $7.8 million on OnlyFans in 2026, marking a 22.9 per cent increase from the previous year.
Meanwhile, Vancouver Island recorded the lowest spending amount in the country, at just $993,000.
$170 million is a whole lot of money for Canadians to spend just on OnlyFans. The figure is even more jarring when contrasted with the record number of Canadians turning to food banks this year.
As we recently reported, monthly food bank visits reached 2.35 million in 2026, a 117 per cent increase since 2019.
And that $170 million on OnlyFans only accounts for Canada, which doesn’t even come close to what our neighbours down south are apparently spending.
According to the report, Americans spent a whopping $4.86 billion — yes, billion with a B — on the platform, spending more than the rest of the world combined.

articles.title: OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
articles.text:
OpenAI donates Open Responses, its spec for a common LLM API, to the Agentic AI Foundation
OpenAI on Thursday announced that it is donating the Open Responses API specification to the open source Agentic AI Foundation (AAIF).
In addition to Open Responses, OpenSandbox, Anthropic’s Agent Skills, and HuggingFace’s OpenEv framework for agent environments are also joining the AAIF.
The join other AAIF projects like the MCP and A2A protocols, AGENTS.md (also from OpenAI), the open source AI agent goose, agentgateway, and Agent Router. The foundation, which is part of the Linux Foundation, launched in December 2025, with MCP, goose, and AGENTS.md as its first projects.
As for Open Responses, the core idea here is to provide developers with a set of core API calls that should work across LLM providers. When OpenAI first announced the specification in January, the team behind the project noted that virtually all LLM providers now offer the same building blocks (messages, tool calls, function calling, etc.), but that they also all represent them differently in their APIs.
Open Responses aims to create a spec that standardizes these primitives so that developers don’t have to translate between each vendor’s idiosyncratic API when they switch between models.
“When we co-founded AAIF, we contributed AGENTS.md, a way to give coding agents project-specific instructions,” an OpenAI spokesperson told The New Stack. “Open Responses addresses another part of building agents by giving developers a shared format for working with models across endpoints that support it, so they have fewer provider-specific integrations to maintain. Vercel AI Gateway and Databricks Model Serving already implement it, and AAIF will provide a neutral home for developers and providers to continue developing the specification together.”
Why a neutral home matters
It’s this neutral home that is generally the reason why companies donate projects to a foundation. The AAIF is part of the Linux Foundation, which has become somewhat of the de facto standard for providing vendor-neutral homes for popular open source projects, with a technical steering committee, which will initially be made up of project maintainers, handling the technical discussions.
Who already supports it — and who doesn’t
There is already wide support for the spec, with the likes of AWS (in Bedrock), Databricks, LM Studio, Ollama, Hugging Face, Nvidia, OpenRouter, Red Hat, Vercel, and open source projects like vLLM and OGC (previously Llama Stack) supporting it.
Among the names that are missing from this list is OpenAI’s rival Anthropic, which defines its own Messages API for giving developers access to its models. Anthropic is a member of the AAIF, so maybe we’ll see the company adopt this spec at some point in the future.
With the Interactions API, Google, too, has its default for letting developers work with its models.
Open Responses doesn’t hide its lineage. The project’s own contributor guide notes that its core schema files are copied from OpenAI’s API. And while OpenAI’s earlier Chat Completions API became an early standard that others used to model their offerings after, Anthropic’s Messages API has now also left a clear mark (in large part thanks to the success of Claude Code), with the likes of DeepSeek, Moonshot, Z.ai, MiniMax, and others exposing Anthropic-compatible endpoints, too.
That split is exactly the kind of fragmentation a vendor-neutral spec like this is meant to fix, of course.

articles.title: Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
Stop guessing auto scaling targets for TTS on Amazon SageMaker AI
A traffic spike hits your self-hosted text-to-speech (TTS) endpoint, and requests start queueing. Latency climbs past your service level objective (SLO) right when the most callers are listening. The auto scaling policy behind that endpoint was supposed to prevent this, but the target value it scales on was a guess, and guesses like that fail silently until real traffic proves them wrong.
Get that number wrong, and it’s paid for in one of two ways, and neither shows up as an alarm. Guess too conservative, and the fleet runs GPU instances that sit mostly idle. That cost lands on every invoice but never trips an incident report. Guess too aggressive, and the fleet carries a risk nobody sees. Each instance holds more concurrent requests than it can serve inside its latency promise. Nothing looks wrong until a real traffic spike pushes queueing time past the SLO. That happens right when the most callers are listening. That’s the hidden gap. A policy that looks fine on the console can already be failing the people it’s supposed to serve.
In this post, we deploy Kokoro-82M, an 82-million-parameter TTS model, as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint. AWS Cloud Development Kit (AWS CDK) stacks handle the deployment. We replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint. Q_max is the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total is how long a scale-out takes end to end. We derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Every number in this post comes from an actual deployment and measurement run of the aws-samples repository referenced in this post.
Why default auto scaling metrics don’t work for TTS
Most public guidance on Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling targets short synchronous request/response calls, or large language model (LLM) serving, where the natural metric is tokens generated per second. TTS synthesis fits neither pattern: a single request holds a connection open for several seconds with no token-generation loop to attach a metric to. Kokoro-82M is non-autoregressive, a StyleTTS2 derivative with an ISTFTNet decoder, trained adversarially rather than by autoregressive next-token prediction or iterative denoising. It produces a full utterance from one duration-aligned pass. There’s no generation loop to instrument with a per-token metric in the first place. What determines whether a TTS instance is overloaded is simpler than it sounds: how many requests are queued and executing on it right now.
The deployed policy scales on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel, a native metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes itself rather than one this project’s own container code has to emit. Scaling on a metric Amazon SageMaker AI publishes removes an entire class of failure where a custom metric configuration looks correct on paper but nothing is actually publishing to it.
ConcurrentRequestsPerModel publishes a Maximum statistic over a 10-second window, a different quantity from the mean in-flight count a benchmarking client measures directly. The tooling accounts for this. At every rung of the concurrency ladder it measures both quantities against the same load and records the ratio between them. It then uses that ratio to convert the client-measured threshold into Amazon CloudWatch units before writing it into the deployable configuration. For the Kokoro-82M run in this post, the measured ratio came out to exactly 1.0 at every rung, so the client-measured and Amazon CloudWatch-reported thresholds match directly.
Solution overview
This solution deploys Kokoro-82M in a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, then replaces a guessed auto scaling target with one derived from two measurements taken against that live endpoint: Q_max, the concurrency ceiling one instance serves inside the SLO, and T_total, how long a real scale-out takes. A synthesis request flows through four layers: a client, the Amazon SageMaker AI endpoint, a custom container on a GPU instance behind that endpoint, and the Kokoro-82M model inside the container.
The container supports two wire transports: response streaming (InvokeEndpointWithResponseStream), which streams audio back as it’s synthesized so playback starts before the utterance finishes, and bidirectional streaming (InvokeEndpointWithBidirectionalStream), which holds one long-lived session open for multiple messages.
Running Kokoro-82M in a custom container, rather than behind a managed inference toolkit, is what makes the rest of this post possible. A container you control can enforce its own admission limits and expose the exact concurrency signal Amazon SageMaker AI already publishes, instead of retrofitting a borrowed metric onto a workload it wasn’t built for. The AWS CDK stacks that deploy this endpoint only attach auto scaling resources once a real, measured plan exists for the model, so a guessed configuration can never reach production silently. The rest of this post is that measurement.
Prerequisites
To follow this walkthrough, you need:
- An AWS account with permissions to create AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) roles, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) buckets, Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) repositories, and Amazon SageMaker AI resources. 
         
  - Note: the sample container pins an earlier PyTorch with a known advisory (PYSEC-2026-2286, fixed in torch 2.10.0). Review and upgrade the pin before any non-proof-of-value use.
- AWS CDK v2, installed and bootstrapped in your target account and region.
- Python 3.11 or later, uv, and Docker to build the container image.
- A ml.g5.xlarge service quota with at least one spare slot above your baseline before running the scale-out measurement in this post.
- The deployment code from the GitHub repository referenced in this post.
Walkthrough
By the end of this walkthrough, you will have a live Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling policy for Kokoro-82M, derived entirely from two measurements taken against your own endpoint rather than from a guess.
Deploy the endpoint stacks
The endpoint deploys through three AWS CDK stacks, applied in order: SpeechFoundationStack creates the IAM roles and the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights, SpeechModelCacheStack syncs a model’s Hugging Face weights into that bucket once, and SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.
The gate on the third stack keeps a default, unmeasured scaling configuration from reaching production. scaling_enabled is a static flag, true whenever max_instances is configured greater than min_instances, and it says nothing on its own about whether the numbers behind it were ever measured. The stack adds a second, independent check at synthesis time: does a real, feasible plan artifact exist for this model? Only when both conditions hold does the stack synthesize scaling resources: an EndpointAutoscaling construct that wires the scaling policy and alarms, and an EndpointObservability construct that adds the dashboards and alarms used to monitor it. A model with scaling_enabled=True but no measurement behind it gets the same no scaling resources output as one with scaling_enabled=False.
The project’s CLI wraps the three stacks behind a single command, applying them in dependency order:
SpeechModelCacheStack runs an AWS CodeBuild project that syncs the model’s Hugging Face weights into the cached Amazon S3 bucket once. A cold endpoint start doesn’t need to pull them from the internet. Gated by the preceding scaling_enabled check, SpeechEndpointStack builds the container image, pushes it to Amazon ECR, and creates the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, and endpoint.
The methodology packages as a command-line tool chain, run in a fixed order:
Step 1: Check for drift
drift runs first, every time, before anything that costs money or holds an endpoint under load. It’s a read-only reconciliation between what’s actually deployed (scalable targets, scaling policies, alarm states) and what the config file says should be deployed. An orphaned policy from an earlier model, or a stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run, would otherwise silently move capacity mid-measurement and corrupt the numbers being measured.
A clean result reports no mismatches and exits with a preflight-ok status, clearing the way for qmax. A stopped or canceled qmax or ttotal run is the most common source of a reported mismatch, because it can leave auto scaling frozen on a single instance. uv run tts-bench thaw --endpoint speech-kokoro-82m restores the deployed policy before you proceed, since qmax and ttotal both assume the deployed state matches the config file exactly.
Step 2: Measure Q_max, the concurrency ceiling
Q_max is the largest concurrency, requests queued plus requests executing on one instance, at which a request still reaches first audio byte inside the SLO at the 95th percentile. It’s measured with a closed-loop load ladder: hold a fixed concurrency N exactly, and walk N upward one rung at a time until the SLO breaks. A closed loop avoids coordinated omission, the flaw in fixed-arrival-rate tests where a slowing server makes the client send fewer requests instead of surfacing real queueing delay.
--dry-run prints the schedule and a wall-clock estimate with zero AWS calls, so you can budget the roughly 36-minute cost of a live run first. The live command freezes auto scaling and pins capacity to one instance for the duration, restored automatically on exit, so the number it produces is a genuine per-instance ceiling.
The load ladder recorded the following results:
| Concurrency | p95 TTFAB (ms) | Meets 3,000 ms SLO? | 
| 1 | 65.4 | yes | 
| 5 | 286.2 | yes | 
| 10 | 568.5 | yes | 
| 20 | 1,129.3 | yes | 
| 30 | 1,689.8 | yes | 
| 40 | 2,245.0 | yes | 
| 50 | 2,805.7 | yes ( Q_max) | 
| 60 | 3,374.8 | no (breach) | 
Q_max = 50, and it’s a bracketed result: rung 60 actually crossed the SLO, which makes 50 a real ceiling rather than a lower bound. The same run measured the uncontended service time, the time one request takes with no queueing at all: mean 61.3 ms, p95 66.1 ms. That number drives a second, independent alarm described later in this post.
Step 3: Measure T_total, the real scale-out time
T_total is how long it takes, wall clock, from the moment more capacity is requested to the moment that capacity serves healthy traffic. It’s measured by forcing a scale-out directly, bypassing the deployed policy’s own detection logic, then timestamping every distinguishable stage.
ttotal requires the qmax artifact as input, since its recovery judgment reads off that ladder’s own measured rungs, and refuses to run against a ladder measured on a different wire transport.
The forced scale-out broke down into eight measured stages:
| Stage | Duration | Share of T_total | 
| capacity requested to desired_set | 30.0 s | 9.4% | 
| desired_set to instance visible in logs | 180.8 s | 56.5% (dominant) | 
| instance visible to container started | 3.7 s | 1.2% | 
| container started to framework_init | 0.0 s | 0.0% | 
| framework_init to weights_ready | 6.5 s | 2.0% | 
| weights_ready to warmup_done | 1.0 s | 0.3% | 
| warmup_done to in_service | 20.7 s | 6.5% | 
| in_service to traffic recovered | 47.4 s | 14.8% | 
| measured total (t_total_s) | 260.2 s |  | 
| + policy detection lag, bounded (not measured) | 60.0 s |  | 
| T_total, planned against | 320.2 s |  | 
The dominant stage is Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) instance provisioning plus the container image pull, at 181 seconds, 56 percent of the planned-against total. The highest-impact way to reduce T_total isn’t application code, it’s reducing image size or using warm capacity pools. Everything downstream of “instance visible in logs” is a comparatively small 79 seconds combined.
The 60-second addition on top of the measured 260.2 seconds isn’t measured in this run. It’s bounded from the policy’s own configuration (alarm evaluation period times evaluation periods, plus cooldown), because this run bypassed the policy’s detection logic on purpose to isolate pure provisioning time. plan sizes surge headroom against the full 320.2-second total, because that reaction time is a real part of any production scale-out even though this measurement excluded it.
Step 4: Derive the deployed policy with plan
plan is the only command that never touches AWS. It reads the qmax and ttotal artifacts, combines them with two operator-chosen inputs, an SLO of 3,000 ms p95 TTFAB and a surge ratio of 1.25x (the fleet tolerates traffic growing 25 percent within one scale-out cycle without breaching the SLO), and does the following arithmetic. It then prints a report with a verdict for each finding: ok, warn, or, for a genuinely infeasible plan, stop.
The --peak-rps flag (5,000 requests per second here, alongside an assumed trough of 10) sizes the fleet’s instance count. It doesn’t factor into the threshold arithmetic below.
C_scale_max is the concurrency at which one more instance is added, below Q_max by the surge fraction h, so the fleet still has queue headroom when it asks for more capacity. C_scale_min is the concurrency at or below which one instance is removed, set at (1 - 2h) of Q_max so scale-in triggers only once load has fallen well below where scale-out would trigger again.
The final deployed configuration, exactly as produced by the tooling:
The two cooldowns are asymmetric on purpose. Scaling out is cheap to be wrong about: worst case, you paid for one instance you didn’t need for thirty extra seconds. Scaling in isn’t symmetric in cost, since capacity removed and later needed again costs a full T_total (320 seconds) to replace. The scale-in cooldown is set to roughly three times T_total, so a scale-in decision only fires once load has genuinely, sustainedly dropped.
The container’s own admission control separately enforces queue_max_depth=50, equal to Q_max: past that depth, a request is refused immediately with a 503 queue_saturated response rather than left to queue past the point it could meet the SLO. A FirstChunkLatencyP95 alarm, thresholded at 65 ms (the measured p95 service time at concurrency 1), watches service time on an instance already serving, tighter than the end-to-end SLO, which includes queuing.
Two findings from the Kokoro-82M run are worth including, because they’re the tool correctly surfacing a known, accepted trade-off rather than a defect:
- surge_survival (warn): Holding C_scale_max (37.5) against Q_max (50) puts one instance at 97.4% utilization the moment a scale-out triggers, and a replacement takes a full T_total to arrive. The surge ratio reserves extra queue slots, but surviving a real surge is about flow, how fast the queue drains, and there’s little flow headroom left at 97.4 percent utilization.
- scale_in_safety (warn): Removing one instance from a fleet of N multiplies every remaining instance’s concurrency by N / (N-1). Scale-in stays stable only once that ratio holds under C_scale_max / C_scale_min (1.5 here), which requires N >= 3. With a floor of 1 instance, a scale-in from 2 to 1 lands the survivor at exactly Q_max, right back at the ceiling that triggers another scale-out. The long cooldown damps this flapping without eliminating it. Raising the floor to 3 would remove it structurally, at the cost of standing capacity during low traffic.
Every qmax or ttotal artifact’s file name encodes the configuration it was measured against, instance type and container image digest condensed into a slug (for example, g5xlarge-8b1b96bc). ttotal and plan both refuse to pair artifacts whose fingerprints disagree. That’s downgradable to a warning with --allow-config-mismatch, but refusal is the default.
Step 5: Confirm the deployed policy with validate
validate is the last command in the chain, and the second one, alongside drift, that never mutates anything. It compares the scaling policy actually deployed against the values in the plan artifact, confirming the two match before you treat the configuration as live.
A clean result confirms scaling_target_value, scale_in_threshold, and both cooldowns on the deployed scalable target match what plan derived. Any mismatch means the deployed policy and the measured plan have drifted apart, and should be resolved before relying on the endpoint’s auto scaling behavior.
Testing and validation
Every qmax, ttotal, and plan artifact referenced in this post is a committed file in the repository, not a one-off local output. The preceding worked example, including every number, is independently reproducible by re-running plan against the two committed measurement files, with zero AWS calls and zero new spend:
Clean up
To remove the resources created in this walkthrough, tear down the stacks in reverse order with a single command:
speech-infra destroy removes the Amazon SageMaker AI model, endpoint configuration, endpoint, and any auto scaling or Amazon CloudWatch resources attached to it. It doesn’t empty the Amazon S3 bucket that caches model weights or delete the Amazon ECR repository holding the container image, since both can be shared across models. If you no longer need them, empty and delete the Amazon S3 bucket and remove the Amazon ECR repository manually, since a stored model checkpoint and container image continue to incur small storage charges until removed.
Conclusion
Deploy Kokoro-82M as a custom container on an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint, and replace guesswork with two measurements taken against the live endpoint: Q_max, the highest concurrency one instance sustains before breaching the SLO, and T_total, how long a real scale-out takes. You derive the scale-out threshold, scale-in threshold, and both cooldowns from those two numbers by arithmetic. Scaling on ConcurrentRequestsPerModel, a native, AWS-published metric, and measuring its unit conversion directly rather than assuming it, is what keeps this configuration tied to real concurrency.
The result is an auto scaling policy where every number traces back to a real measurement against your own endpoint, not an assumption carried over from a different workload shape. That distinction is what turns a config-file guess, one that silently overpays or silently breaches its SLO, into a policy you can defend with a specific concurrency ceiling and a specific scale-out time, both measured, not asserted.
Nothing about this four-number model, SLO and surge ratio chosen, Q_max and T_total measured, the rest derived, is specific to TTS. It generalizes to latency-sensitive, concurrency-bound, real-time Amazon SageMaker AI endpoints. For example, a real-time image-embedding endpoint that holds each request open through a GPU forward pass is bound by the same concurrency ceiling, not by a throughput metric. The same qmax/ttotal/plan chain applies unchanged. The real bottleneck there is concurrent in-flight requests rather than a throughput metric borrowed from a different workload shape. The specific numbers here, Q_max=50 and T_total=320s, are true for Kokoro-82M on ml.g5.xlarge. They will differ for a different model or instance type. The methodology and tooling that produce them don’t. The five-command tool chain, drift, qmax, ttotal, plan, and validate, carries over unchanged to the next model you deploy this way.
Clone the sample repository, then run the five-command chain, drift, qmax, ttotal, plan, and validate, against your own endpoint to produce a measured policy. Review the Amazon SageMaker AI auto scaling documentation to adapt the thresholds to your SLO, and open the SageMaker AI console to watch the policy react to live traffic. If you’d like help building a similar measurement-driven deployment, contact your AWS account team.

articles.title: Tesla va livrer son robotaxi Cybercab à des clients qui ne pourront pas le faire rouler où ils veulent
articles.text:
Pendant la conférence de résultats du troisième trimestre qui s’est déroulée ce mercredi 21 octobre 2026, Tesla a dit vouloir en vendre. Jusqu’ici, on ne pouvait que réserver une course en Cybercab dans les rues d’Austin, au Texas. À en croire Lars Moravy, vice-président de l’ingénierie, d’autres personnes pourront expérimenter la voiture sans volant ni pédales puisque Tesla va essayer « de livrer des Cybercab à des clients d’ici la fin de cette année 2026 ». Tesla se donne donc un peu plus de deux mois.
Sauf que dans le même temps, Elon Musk a annoncé que la conduite sans supervision ne sera pas proposée aux clients avant le deuxième trimestre 2027.
Des Tesla Cybercab privés mais pas particuliers
Pour mémoire, Tesla produit le Cybercab au Texas depuis février. Le service a démarré à Austin le 3 septembre avec 45 exemplaires, depuis multipliée par dix selon Elon Musk. Dans son compte-rendu, le constructeur annonce être prêt pour une capacité de plus de 125 000 Cybercab par an, qui doivent tous rejoindre la flotte de la marque.
À la question de la commercialisation du Cybercab, Elon Musk a nuancé l’annonce d’emblée : « La grande majorité des Cybercab appartiendra à Tesla et sera proposée comme un service de transport. » Selon lui, les voitures qu’on achète pour soi restent les Model 3, Model Y et le Roadster. Les « clients » dont parle Tesla devraient donc surtout être des gestionnaires de flottes. En septembre, la marque avait d’ailleurs publié un formulaire pour les acheteurs de robotaxis intéressés, sans dire si elle y donnerait suite.
Le FSD non supervisé sauf pour les propriétaires Tesla
Aujourd’hui, les propriétaires de Tesla ont seulement accès au FSD Supervisé, appelé dorénavant « Tesla Conduite Assistée » en Europe. Cette aide à la conduite exige que le conducteur soit prêt à reprendre la main à tout moment. Or le Cybercab n’a ni volant ni pédales. On pourrait donc en conclure qu’un Cybercab livré fin 2026 resterait inutilisable pendant environ six mois, car personne ne pourrait le conduire, tandis que le logiciel qui lui permet de rouler seul ne serait pas encore disponible.
Ashok Elluswamy, responsable de l’IA chez Tesla, a précisé pendant la conférence que les Cybercab et les Model Y robotaxis utilisent le même logiciel, que la marque compte proposer à ses clients avec la version 15 du FSD.
Si les deux calendriers tiennent, des gestionnaires de flottes pourraient donc profiter de la « vraie » conduite autonome avant les propriétaires de Tesla, à qui la marque promet cette fonctionnalité depuis des années. Le FSD non supervisé reste en fait limité à des zones délimitées. Le responsable de l’IA de Tesla a expliqué que les voitures des clients devront entrer dans ces périmètres et dans le système de gestion de flotte de Tesla pour rouler en totale autonomie.
La NHTSA attend toujours des réponses
Par ailleurs, l’agence fédérale chargée de la sécurité routière (NHTSA) a ouvert une enquête sur le Cybercab début septembre, quelques heures après le lancement du service à Austin.
Le régulateur lui a demandé des preuves sous serment, et la marque a jusqu’au 30 octobre pour répondre. En juin, la NHTSA a bien proposé d’assouplir ces règles pour les véhicules autonomes, mais tant que la réforme n’est pas terminée, les normes actuelles s’appliquent. Au Texas, Tesla a profité d’une nouvelle loi de l’État pour certifier lui-même son service au niveau 4, où la voiture roule sans conducteur dans une zone définie.
Tesla a déjà raté beaucoup de ses échéances. En avril 2019, lors de son « Autonomy Day », Elon Musk annonçait plus d’un million de robotaxis sur les routes dès 2020. Cette fois, Ashok Elluswamy assure que produire en grand nombre « ne serait pas un si grand défi ». Selon lui, tout dépend surtout des autorisations réglementaires. Enfin, il a aussi annoncé que le service Cybercab arriverait à Dallas en novembre.
