articles.title: Chrome : Google corrige cette fois plus de 350 failles de sécurité
articles.text:
Chrome 156 est disponible depuis quelques jours sur Windows, macOS et Linux. Cette version corrige 353 failles de sécurité, dont six jugées critiques, et, une fois encore, plusieurs signalements sont crédités à des outils d’IA.
Google déploie la mise à jour progressivement, sur plusieurs jours ou semaines, avec les versions 156.0.8078.47 (Linux) et 156.0.8078.47 ou .48 (Windows et Mac). L’entreprise n’a mentionné aucune exploitation active de ces failles.
Six failles critiques, dont deux signalées avec des outils d’IA
Les vulnérabilités touchent Skia (la bibliothèque qui dessine les éléments graphiques), Accessibility (les fonctions d’assistance), CSS (la mise en forme des pages), Paint (l’affichage) et WebRTC (les appels audio et vidéo dans le navigateur). Cinq sont classées « corruption de mémoire », lorsqu’un un programme lit ou modifie une zone de mémoire qu’il ne devrait pas toucher. La sixième, dans Accessibility, est un « use-after-free », c’est-à-dire quand le programme réutilise une zone mémoire qu’il avait déjà libérée. Ce type d’erreur crée un risque de sécurité, mais Google ne décrit aucune chaîne d’attaque. Les détails des bugs peuvent d’ailleurs rester inaccessibles tant qu’une majorité d’utilisateurs n’a pas reçu le correctif.
Côté découvertes, Google a remonté lui-même la faille Skia. Xinyang Ge est crédité pour quatre des six failles critiques, mais seul le use-after-free d’Accessibility mentionne Anthropic et l’assistance de Claude. Celle de WebRTC, signalée le 15 octobre, est créditée à OpenAI Codex Security. Sur l’ensemble de la liste, cinq entrées citent l’aide de Claude et quatre sont attribuées à Codex Security.
- Navigation rapide
- Écosystème d'extensions très riche
- Synchronisation multi-appareils fluide
Déjà, avec Chrome 151, Google avait déployé 370 correctifs. Les versions majeures de Chrome ne corrigent pas seulement les failles trouvées juste avant sa sortie. Elles regroupent celles qui s’accumulent au fil des mois, voire sur plusieurs années. Pour Chrome 151, les signalements remontaient surtout à mars-juin 2026. Pour cette dernière mouture, nous retrouvons un schéma assez similaire. La plupart des signalements datent de 2026, mais quelques-uns sont bien plus anciens, jusqu’à 2018.
Les failles particulièrement sensibles touchent notamment ANGLE, le moteur JavaScript V8, GPU, Network et FileSystem. Google verse 10 000 dollars pour un use-after-free dans SiteIsolation (le mécanisme qui cloisonne chaque site dans un processus distinct), signalé par Quyen Son (VinFast).

articles.title: Windows 11 optimiert RAM-Verbrauch: So gut läuft das System jetzt auf einem PC mit 8 Gigabyte
articles.text:
Windows 11 optimiert RAM-Verbrauch: So gut läuft das System jetzt auf einem PC mit 8 Gigabyte
Seit August 2026 arbeitet Microsoft daran, Windows 11 effizienter zu gestalten. Damals hatte das Unternehmen versprochen, dass gerade Geräte mit acht Gigabyte RAM davon stark profitieren sollen. Wie genau diese Speicheroptimierung aussehen sollte, verriet das Unternehmen damals noch nicht. Jetzt zeigen sich aber schon die ersten Auswirkungen. Seit dem Update auf Windows 11 26H2 verbrauchen die besagten Systeme deutlich weniger RAM.
Windows 11 26H2: So gut funktioniert die RAM-Optimierung
Den Test dazu hat Windows Latest zunächst mit zwei Windows-Geräten durchgeführt. Eines davon lief noch mit der „alten“ 25H2-Version von Windows 11, das andere mit 26H2. Die ältere Systemversion benötigte im normalen Gebrauch schon etwas mehr als fünf Gigabyte der vorhandenen acht Gigabyte RAM. Nach dem Update auf Version 26H2 sank der Arbeitsspeicherverbrauch auf 3,3 Gigabyte.
In einem zweiten Test wurde Windows 11 in einer virtuellen Maschine installiert. So, als hätten User:innen das System komplett neu aufgesetzt. In diesem Zustand verbrauchte das Windows-System mit dem Oktober-Update von 25H2 rund 4,1 Gigabyte Arbeitsspeicher während des Normalbetriebs. Nach dem Update für die virtuelle Maschine lief das System mit einem RAM-Verbrauch zwischen 2,8 und 3,2 Gigabyte.
In einem Blog-Post erklärte Navjot Virk, Corporate Vice-President of Windows Experiences, wie diese Optimierung zumindest teilweise zustandekommt: „Windows kann jetzt bis zu zwei Gigabyte mehr von deinen aktiven Daten im Speicher behalten, statt sie an langsameren Speicher weitergeben zu müssen. Das hilft dabei, dass dein PC reaktionsschnell bleibt, während du mehr Apps und Browser-Tabs öffnest.“
Zudem werden Widgets auf Windows-PCs mit acht oder weniger Gigabyte RAM jetzt nur noch geladen, wenn sie wirklich geöffnet werden. Dadurch sollen allein 200 Megabyte Speicher für andere Apps und Aufgaben freigeworden sein. In den Fällen, die Windows Latest gezeigt hat, erklären diese Änderungen nicht die gesamte Verbesserung. Dementsprechend dürfte Microsoft auch noch einige weitere Änderungen am Speicherverbrauch von Windows 11 vorgenommen haben, die es nicht in die offizielle Erklärung geschafft haben.

articles.title: Unicorn NEURA Robotics reveals new robot along with a training facility for European robotics | EU-Startups
articles.text:
NEURA Robotics continues its roll of recent announcements with the launch of a new robot and the opening of a new branch of their Neura Gym in partnership with the Technical University of Munich (TUM).
The two have today opened the TUM RoboGym powered by NEURA at LabCampus near Munich Airport. Spanning more than 2,300 square meters, the new centre brings together research, robot training and industrial application.
It was built in partnership with TUM’s Munich Institute of Robotics and Machine Intelligence (MIRMI). The joint initiative is initially set up for three years. In total, the partners are investing around €17 million, of which NEURA is contributing approximately €11 million.
To mark the opening, NEURA is also launching 4NE1 Gen 4 (“For Anyone”), the new generation of its humanoid robot.
“Our companies hold knowledge that has been built up over generations,” says David Reger, founder and CEO of NEURA Robotics. “People know how to work materials, assemble components and master difficult processes. This knowledge is one of our greatest strengths in the age of Physical AI. With TUM, we are building a powerhouse for physical capabilities, where this knowledge becomes the foundation for new possibilities. The Mittelstand, in particular, should be able to help shape this future.
“With the launch of the humanoid 4NE1 Gen 4, we are showing today which robots are ready for it: designed for series production, built for productive work and powered by Neuron AI, our own foundation model that learns from experience in the NEURA Gyms. Developed, built and trained in Germany, for the world.”
Across Europe, other robotics companies are pursuing similar efforts to bring adaptable machines into industrial environments.
London-based Humanoid raised €133 million in July to advance its humanoid robots, while fellow German companies Sereact and RobCo, itself a TUM spin-out, secured €93 million and €89.2 million respectively to develop physical AI and autonomous industrial systems.
Spain’s THEKER added €73 million for AI-native industrial robots, while Norway- and US-based Trener Robotics raised €26 million to develop adaptable robot skills.
Alongside smaller rounds for Poland’s Nomagic, Hungary’s Allonic and Belgium’s Motion, these 2026 rounds total approximately €430.2 million.
“The TUM RoboGym robotics center is unique in Germany and Europe,” adds Prof. Thomas Hofmann, President of the Technical University of Munich. “By collaborating with a robot manufacturer based in Germany, we are also sending a clear signal for Germany as an industrial location in geopolitically uncertain times.”
Today’s partnerships marks an even closer relationship between one of Germany’s premier Unicorns with what is arguably the country’s foremost tech/innovation university.
Founded in 2019, Neura develops the technologies that enable intelligent machines to learn, adapt and work side by side with humans in the real world. The company develops cognitive robots that can see, hear, feel and learn, as well as the software, AI and data infrastructure required for their large-scale deployment.
On the education side, TUM MIRMI is an integrative research institute of the TUM focused on robotics and AI. MIRMI holds leading expertise in key areas of robotics, including perception and data science. Nearly 80 TUM chairs are networked within TUM MIRMI to develop robotic and AI-supported solutions for the environment, health, mobility, labor, and security and defense.
The TUM RoboGym brings together AI research and industrial application. Companies contribute concrete tasks and their process knowledge. Researchers and development teams investigate how robots can learn these tasks faster and perform them more reliably.
Partners have been training concrete workflows at the TUM RoboGym since September. Companies from more than ten industries are involved, including automotive, pharmaceuticals, medical technology, packaging, logistics, agriculture and care. Demand is high: capacity in Munich is already in strong demand.
Tasks range from handling cardboard boxes and filling bottles to loading and unloading wooden components. Companies can test applications, identify training needs and assess the suitability of different robot systems before expanding use in their own operations.
The RoboGym combines three approaches to generating data:
- Real-world robot data: Different robot systems perform tasks. Their sensors capture movements, contacts and the outcomes of their actions.
- Human demonstrations: People demonstrate workflows. Sensor-equipped data suits, motion-capture systems and teleoperation help translate movements and interactions into usable training data.
- Simulation and Data Amplifier: Virtual training environments expand real-world experience with additional variations and situations, allowing skills to be trained under changed conditions and then validated on real robots.
With 4NE1 Gen 4, NEURA is launching the new generation of its humanoid robot, already in operation at the TUM RoboGym for the opening: slimmer, lighter and powered by Neuron AI as its brain.
Alongside the opening of the TUM RoboGym in Munich, the robot is also appearing at the NVIDIA GTC conference in Berlin and is already in operation at the NEURA Gyms.
“We want companies to carry their experience into the next industrial era,” says David. “To develop capabilities, protect their know-how and decide for themselves, in the future, where and under what conditions they make it available to others. What we are opening today in Munich is meant to have an impact far beyond this location. From Europe, together for the world.”
The TUM RoboGym marks the start of an international network of NEURA Gyms. Further locations are being established in Europe, the United States and China. In Germany, another Gym is being built in cooperation with RWTH Aachen.

articles.title: Meta creció solo 18% en publicidad en Europa tras ofrecer anuncios menos personalizados por orden de la UE
articles.text:
La publicidad de Meta en Europa creció apenas 18% interanual en el tercer trimestre de 2026, muy por debajo del 33% registrado en Estados Unidos y Canadá, después de que la Unión Europea obligó a la empresa a ofrecer una opción de anuncios menos personalizados en todo el bloque.
La compañía reportó el miércoles ingresos publicitarios globales de USD 63.100 millones, un alza de 26% frente al mismo período de 2025, según su comunicado de resultados. Pero el desempeño europeo fue el más débil entre sus grandes mercados: la región aportó USD 14.230 millones, apenas por encima de los USD 12.070 millones del año anterior.
La desaceleración viene de antes. El crecimiento publicitario europeo había caído de alrededor de 40% a 24% en los dos trimestres previos, mientras que en Estados Unidos y Canadá se aceleró de 30% a 31% en el mismo lapso, según datos que la propia Meta presentó a sus inversores.
La caída coincide con la entrada en vigor, en enero de este año, de la opción de “anuncios menos personalizados” que la Comisión Europea exigió a Meta tras encontrarla en infracción de la Ley de Mercados Digitales, la norma que regula a las grandes plataformas tecnológicas en el bloque.
El origen del conflicto con Bruselas
En noviembre de 2023, Meta había lanzado en la Unión Europea un modelo binario: los usuarios de Facebook e Instagram debían elegir entre pagar una suscripción mensual para no ver publicidad o aceptar que la empresa combinara sus datos personales para mostrarles anuncios segmentados.
La Comisión Europea concluyó en abril de 2025 que ese esquema no cumplía con la ley, porque no le daba a los usuarios una alternativa real con menos uso de sus datos pero de calidad equivalente. La multa fue de 200 millones de euros, una de las primeras sanciones aplicadas bajo esa norma.
Para cumplir con la decisión, Meta empezó a ofrecer en enero de 2026 una versión gratuita con publicidad “menos personalizada”: los anuncios se eligen según lo que el usuario ve en esa sesión y datos básicos como edad, ubicación y género, en lugar de su historial completo de actividad.
Meta calcula que ese modelo usa 90% menos datos que la publicidad totalmente personalizada, aunque no revela cuántas personas eligieron esa opción.
Menos datos, anuncios menos efectivos
La propia empresa había advertido que los anuncios menos personalizados son menos eficientes: generan menos transacciones y los usuarios cierran más avisos por considerarlos irrelevantes o repetitivos. Esa ineficiencia se refleja en lo que los anunciantes están dispuestos a pagar por anuncio en Europa, que crece a menor ritmo que en Estados Unidos y Canadá.
“Creemos que la opción de publicidad personalizada gratuita de la Unión Europea está contribuyendo a la desaceleración europea”, dijo Dominic Ball, director de investigación de renta variable de la firma Rothschild & Co Redburn.
La directora financiera de Meta, Susan Li, ya había anticipado el impacto en julio pasado, durante la presentación del segundo trimestre: “estamos viendo el efecto de la oferta de anuncios menos personalizados en Europa ahora que está completamente implementada, y eso podría ser un viento en contra adicional”, dijo entonces.
Durante la presentación del tercer trimestre, Li no atribuyó explícitamente la desaceleración europea a la medida regulatoria, pero aseguró que la empresa tiene “mucho margen” para mejorar la eficiencia y las conversiones de sus anuncios en la región.
Meta apeló la multa de 200 millones de euros en julio de 2025 y, según su propio escrito judicial más reciente, la disputa seguía abierta en julio de este año. La Comisión Europea dijo que evaluaría la adopción de la nueva opción, pero todavía no publicó ninguna cifra sobre cuántos usuarios la eligieron.
Meta presentará sus resultados del cuarto trimestre con una proyección propia de ingresos globales de entre USD 73.000 millones y USD 76.000 millones.

articles.title: Xiaomi 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max : les prix français fuitent, la hausse s'annonce spectaculaire — Frandroid
articles.text:
Xiaomi n’a encore annoncé aucun prix, mais la grille française de ses deux prochains haut de gamme a déjà fuité. Ce jeudi 22 octobre, billbil-kun, spécialiste des fuites de prix chez Dealabs Magazine, a publié les tarifs, les coloris et la fiche technique européenne des Xiaomi 18 Pro et 18 Pro Max. En février, il avait déjà donné les bons prix européens des Xiaomi 17 et 17 Ultra, ce qui rend cette fuite très crédible. Surtout, le 18 Pro démarrerait à 1 399 euros, soit 400 euros de plus que le Xiaomi 17 à son lancement.
Les deux téléphones sont sortis en Chine le 23 septembre. Ils reprennent l’idée des Xiaomi 17 Pro et 17 Pro Max, restés réservés au marché chinois en 2025 : un second écran OLED placé au dos, dans le bloc photo. À l’intérieur, on trouve un Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 (la version Extreme sur le Pro Max), la puce haut de gamme de Qualcomm gravée en 2 nanomètres. Côté photo, Leica signe trois capteurs de 200, 200 et 50 mégapixels, dont un téléobjectif périscopique, qui replie le trajet de la lumière dans le téléphone pour zoomer sans bosse géante. Nous avons d’ailleurs acheté le Xiaomi 18 Pro en Chine pour le tester avant sa sortie française.
En France, les deux modèles arriveraient avec 12 gigaoctets de mémoire vive, en noir, blanc ou bordeaux. Un quatrième coloris, bleu, pourrait rester exclusif à la boutique Mi Store de Xiaomi. Le passage de 256 à 512 gigaoctets de stockage coûterait 200 euros sur les deux modèles.
- Xiaomi 18 Pro, 256 gigaoctets : 1 399 euros
- Xiaomi 18 Pro, 512 gigaoctets : 1 599 euros
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, 256 gigaoctets : 1 599 euros
- Xiaomi 18 Pro Max, 512 gigaoctets : 1 799 euros
Plus cher que le 17 Ultra, à peine moins cher qu’un iPhone
Les modèles ne se remplacent pas un pour un, mais la hausse saute aux yeux. Le Xiaomi 17, un compact dont la grosse autonomie nous avait convaincus, avait été lancé à 999 euros. Le 18 Pro coûterait donc 400 euros de plus en 256 gigaoctets (+40 %). En 512 gigaoctets, version que le Xiaomi 17 proposait à 1 099 euros, l’écart grimperait à 500 euros (+45 %). Plus surprenant encore, le Pro Max en 512 gigaoctets dépasserait de 300 euros le Xiaomi 17 Ultra, lancé à 1 499 euros avec le même stockage et 16 gigaoctets de mémoire vive. Or l’Ultra reste le meilleur photophone de la marque, celui qui nous avait fait oublier notre appareil photo.
Avec ses tarifs français, Xiaomi se calerait juste sous Apple. Sur sa boutique en ligne, Apple vend l’iPhone 18 Pro à partir de 1 479 euros et le 18 Pro Max à partir de 1 629 euros, en 256 gigaoctets. Le Xiaomi 18 Pro resterait donc 80 euros moins cher que l’iPhone 18 Pro. Entre les deux grands modèles, l’écart tombe à 30 euros.
Moins de batterie et de mémoire qu’en Chine
Comme les Xiaomi 17 et 17 Ultra avant eux (6 330 et 6 000 mAh en Europe, contre 7 000 et 6 800 mAh en Chine), les versions européennes perdent de la batterie. Le 18 Pro passe de 7 000 à 6 000 mAh, et le Pro Max de 8 500 à 7 050 mAh, soit 17 % de capacité en moins pour le grand modèle. Pourtant, les deux utilisent une batterie silicium-carbone, une technologie qui stocke plus d’énergie dans le même volume. Les Européens vont donc payer plus cher pour moins de batterie.
Dealabs a aussi consulté les fiches EPREL, la base européenne où les fabricants déclarent l’étiquette énergie de leurs smartphones. Elles mentionnent 5 880 et 6 915 mAh, soit la capacité nominale, c’est-à-dire le minimum garanti. Xiaomi affichera plutôt la capacité typique, une moyenne un peu plus flatteuse. Les fiches estiment l’autonomie à 66 heures pour le Pro et 70 heures pour le Pro Max, mesurées sur le cycle d’usage normalisé de l’étiquette énergie européenne.
Le reste de la fiche technique change aussi. Le 18 Pro descend à 90 watts en charge filaire, contre 100 watts en Chine, alors que le Pro Max garde ses 100 watts. Les deux conservent la charge sans fil à 50 watts. En revanche, l’Europe n’aura droit qu’à 12 gigaoctets de mémoire vive, alors que les versions chinoises montent à 16 gigaoctets et à 1 téraoctet de stockage.
Xiaomi a confirmé l’arrivée des deux modèles en Europe et promis, dès la présentation chinoise du 23 septembre, un lancement international avant la fin de l’année. La marque n’a pas encore communiqué la date de sortie ni les offres de lancement. Selon Dealabs, les précommandes pourraient ouvrir dès novembre 2026, et le Xiaomi 18 Ultra aurait été annulé.

articles.title: AI in African Banking: Are Lenders Seeing the Returns Yet?
articles.text:
According to a 2026 report surveying 277 banking executives across 37 African nations, 83.2% of institutions plan to increase their AI spending over the next 12 months. Yet nearly a third do not formally track the return on investment. More strikingly, among the lenders that do not measure returns at all, 82% still plan to expand their budgets anyway. Between dollar-denominated cloud hosting bills, legacy core banking integration bottlenecks, and an acute regional deficit of machine learning engineers, African lenders are doubling down on an expensive technology whose ultimate fiscal contribution is still an article of faith. In this edition of Delve into AI, EMMANUEL NWOSU examines the uncomfortable disconnect between operational speed and audited balance-sheet yield inside Africa’s multi-million-dollar banking automation race.
Loan documentation has historically been an administrative bottleneck, even within well-capitalised financial institutions. At Standard Bank, a vetting process that previously took roughly an hour now wraps up in about 60 seconds, powered by artificial intelligence.
The metric, disclosed in the South African lender’s Capital Markets Day filing in March 2026, applies to its commercial asset finance division. It serves as a flagship case study for how Africa’s largest bank by assets is operationalising machine intelligence.
Standard Bank reported that its conversational bot handles 65% of all incoming digital customer queries, while over 39,000 employees—approximately 72% of its total workforce—were regular enterprise users of generative AI by August 2026.
These workflows showcase the immediate operational promise of automation: administrative backlogs evaporate into single-minute tasks, customer friction drops, and bank staff are freed to focus on high-touch advisory roles requiring human judgement.
Yet the net financial dividend remains murky. Deploying AI across regulated financial environments requires rigorous data governance protocols, expensive software licencing, complex systems integration, and widespread workforce reskilling. For these outlays to be commercially defensible, banks must prove that bottom-line yield outweighs implementation overhead.
Industry data reveals an uncomfortable divergence between capital expenditure and performance tracking. According to The State of AI in African Banking—a 2026 joint report by banking software provider Backbase and African Banker, surveying 277 executives across 37 African nations—83.2% of institutions plan to increase their AI allocations over the next 12 months. Yet only 67.1% formally track the return on investment (ROI) of those deployments.
More strikingly, among the third of respondents whose banks do not track AI returns at all, 82% still plan to expand their budgets. African banking leaders are aggressively capitalising a technology whose commercial contribution they have yet to quantify.
This absence of measurement does not signify failure. Algorithmic systems can compress turnaround times, sharpen fraud monitoring, and elevate customer experience without immediately shaving costs from the income statement.
But the distinction between operational efficiency and financial return becomes harder to ignore as AI moves beyond isolated experiments and into systems that banks use every day.
However, as AI transitions from experimental sandbox pilots into core banking architecture, the distinction between unmonetised operational speed and audited fiscal return becomes impossible to ignore.
Faster work, uncertain financial returns
Standard Bank has been building its AI capabilities on technology investments made over several years. In its March investor presentation, the bank said conversational AI was handling 65% of digital queries on its personal banking app, reducing the workload associated with customer service.
It also reported that engineering productivity had improved by more than 20% in the previous year, while AI was beginning to accelerate work in lending. Its commercial asset finance example, in which loan documentation processing fell from roughly an hour to a minute, underscores the extent of the improvement possible in some administrative processes.
The bank has also expanded the technology across its workforce. In August, it reported more than 39,000 active users of generative AI, supported by approved enterprise tools.
Consider the loan documentation process. Reducing processing time from an hour to a minute frees up the employees responsible for that work. The bank may then be able to process more applications with the same workforce, reduce overtime, or redirect staff to other responsibilities.
Those benefits become measurable financial savings only when they result in expenses avoided or additional income that can reasonably be attributed to the investment.
Standard Bank said it plans to redirect the time employees save using AI towards customer relationships and work requiring more complex decisions. This suggests that the bank is looking beyond cutting operating costs to extracting more value from its existing workforce. On its own, it does not specify revenue generation or cost savings.
Sticking with Standard Bank’s lending business, AI could help employees process more loan applications without a corresponding increase in staff costs. If used to assess borrowers’ creditworthiness, it could also help the bank make better lending decisions and reduce the risk of defaults. These are two different benefits, and Standard Bank has not established whether its AI investments have delivered either financially.
The bank’s non-performing loan ratio stood at 5.6% at the end of June, down from 6.2% the previous year. Credit impairment charges, which reflect expected losses from loans, also fell by 12% to R7.13 billion ($435.5 million) in the first half of 2026. The lender has not attributed the improvement to AI usage.
At Nedbank, another tier-1 South African lender, the improvements are also measurable.
According to its 2025 integrated report, the bank said it implemented 30 advanced AI use cases during the year. Its broader programme, combining AI, generative AI, analytics, machine learning, and robotic process automation, helped save approximately 312,000 employee-hours across media and content creation, document translation, and personal productivity. Global payment processing times also fell by about 30%.
Nedbank has applied predictive models to identify customers more likely to purchase investment products, alongside analytics that help it target potential credit card and loan customers.
These uses illustrate how banks expect to earn returns from AI in two broad ways: spending less to provide existing services and earning more by serving customers more effectively.
The cost of making AI work
AI does not operate independently of a bank’s existing technology. Models need access to reliable data, secure computing systems, and the applications through which employees and customers use them. Banks also need processes for testing outputs, controlling access to sensitive information, and monitoring decisions made with AI.
Those requirements can make the expense of deploying AI considerably larger than the cost of a software subscription.
At its 2026 Capital Markets Day, Standard Bank reported total technology spending of R23.5 billion ($1.44 billion) in 2025, equivalent to 27.7% of its operating expenses. It said 88% of its legacy servers had been decommissioned and that 71% of computing workloads eligible for migration had moved to the cloud at the time of the presentation.
The bank subsequently reported that cloud migration had reached 78% of eligible computing workloads by the end of June 2026.
Standard Bank said its technology investments helped improve efficiency over several years, contributing to a decline in its group cost-to-income ratio from 59.1% to 50.2%. This means that for every R100 ($6.09) the bank earned in operating income, it spent about R50 ($3.05) on operating expenses, compared with roughly R59 ($3.6) previously.
Standard Bank’s technology spending has continued to rise alongside its expanding AI operations. The bank spent R23.51 billion ($1.43 billion) on technology in 2025, up 4.9% from R22.4 billion ($1.36 billion) in 2024. In the first half of 2026, its software, cloud, and technology-related expenses rose 6% to R7.16 billion ($436.5 million). The bank attributed the increase partly to expanding its AI capabilities, alongside investments in specialised technology expertise, core banking systems and cybersecurity.
Yet, its overall technology spending grew by only 2% to R11.83 billion ($721 million) during the six months, as lower amortisation and other technology costs offset part of the increase. Standard Bank has been following what it calls a save-to-invest strategy, using efficiencies from earlier technology investments to fund newer capabilities, including AI.
The bank’s investment in modernising its technology systems comes amid the backdrop of its AI-readiness ambition; it illustrates the work required to introduce new capabilities into an established banking business.
To prove this point, African banks face AI integration challenges. In the Backbase and African Banker survey, 50.2% of respondents identified integrating AI with existing technology as their biggest internal obstacle to adoption.
Banks may have to connect customer records, transaction histories, and other information stored across systems developed at different times. A lender introducing AI into credit assessment, for example, needs reliable access to the financial information used to evaluate borrowers. Bringing those records together can require upgrades to existing systems, additional computing infrastructure, and specialised employees to maintain them.
These requirements add to the initial and ongoing cost of using AI. Where banks purchase cloud services or software in foreign currencies, exchange-rate movements can also increase their expenses in local currency.
The financial case for AI depends on more than how much time a system saves. Banks must weigh those gains against the full cost of introducing and operating the technology, including the infrastructure needed to support it.
Why the returns remain difficult to measure
The Backbase and African Banker research suggests that some African banks are getting the financial results they expected from AI. Among respondents whose institutions formally measure returns, 85.1% said their investments had met or exceeded their projections.
The banks, however, were measuring performance against their own targets. The survey does not establish how much they invested, the financial value generated, or whether returns were calculated consistently across institutions.
Consider AI-powered lending. If a bank approves more applications after introducing AI, the additional loans could increase its interest income. But the financial benefit would depend on funding costs, the performance of those loans, and whether the technology improved lending decisions. Similarly, an AI fraud detection system’s value lies in the losses it prevents, not simply the number of suspicious transactions it flags.
The survey also found that 71.7% of respondents working with third-party AI providers measure returns, compared with 31% of those developing AI entirely in-house, underscoring how banks differ considerably in their ability to deploy proprietary AI—another cost centre.
In June 2026, Evident’s inaugural AI Index for Banks in the Middle East and Africa assessed 25 major banks on AI talent, innovation, leadership, and transparency. Standard Bank ranked second and Nedbank fourth, making them the only two South African banks among the four regional leaders. Other South African lenders, FirstRand, Capitec, and Absa, rounded off the top ten list.
Evident attributed their comparatively strong performance partly to larger pools of AI talent, proximity to research universities, and engagement with emerging central bank regulation.
The concentration suggests that South African banks have built stronger AI capabilities than many of their regional peers. Across the 25 institutions assessed, Evident found that specialist AI development talent, relative to workforce size, was only half the level recorded among its benchmark of major global banks.
This shortage has financial implications. Banks without sufficient internal expertise must either invest in building their own AI capabilities or rely on external providers, while still paying to integrate and maintain the technology.
Some banks outside Africa have begun providing a clearer account of the financial value they derive from AI. Singapore’s DBS Bank reported approximately S$1 billion ($783 million) in economic value from data analytics and AI in 2025, up from S$750 million ($587 million) in 2024. By the end of 2025, it had deployed more than 2,000 models across over 430 use cases.
DBS has gone beyond reporting how many tasks AI completes or how much time employees save. It has placed a monetary value on the technology’s contribution to its business, although it is unclear whether the Singaporean lender is now profitable on its AI usage.
The comparison brings the financial question facing African banks into clearer focus. Standard Bank and Nedbank have demonstrated improvements in productivity, while many institutions surveyed by Backbase report meeting their AI investment targets. But they provide little indication of how much individual AI programmes cost or what they return financially.
Productivity is a key use case for AI in banking, and across other non-financial organisations. But the opportunity here is establishing what that productivity is worth.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Madrid encara el reto más complicado de la A-5 con el corte total del tráfico para alcanzar "el punto de no retorno"
articles.text:
No pasará ningún coche por la A-5. Es el planteamiento que se ha puesto encima de la mesa ante uno de los momentos más importantes en las obras que se están llevando a cabo para enterrar la carretera en su entrada a Madrid. Llega uno de los momentos clave. Por el paso que se dará y por las molestias que se pueden causar.
El entronque. Es el nombre técnico. Para bajarlo al lenguaje de la calle, podemos hablar de la unión entre el túnel que se ha estado excavando desde que dieron inicio las obras de enterrado de la A-5 y la actual salida del túnel de la M-30. La gran obra de Madrid enfrenta un momento crucial.
Esta intervención es crucial porque el objetivo es que, una vez el nuevo túnel se una con el anterior, los coches ya circulen bajo tierra. En ese momento es cuando se empezará a excavar un segundo túnel. Cuando éste se termine será cuando cada uno de ellos pueda ser utilizado para cada sentido de la circulación.
¿Qué se va a hacer? La actuación principal para poder enlazar los dos túneles, el viejo y el nuevo, pasa por derribar las rampas de entrada y salida del túnel anterior. De esta manera, ambos túneles quedarán unidos a una misma altura y el conductor no tendrá que enfrentar una subida y bajada repentina como sucede, por ejemplo, en Madrid Río a la altura del antiguo estado Vicente Calderón.
De momento, en lo que se está trabajando en el paso subterráneo es en terminar las instalaciones necesarias para poder circular con seguridad bajo tierra. Realmente, la primera excavación ya está terminada pero se siguen dando pasos en la instalación del sistema eléctrico y los elementos de seguridad.
¿Para cuándo? Es la gran pregunta. No hay una fecha concreta en el calendario pero sí una estimada: final de año. El objetivo, aseguran desde el Ayuntamiento de Madrid, es acometer esta obra cuando el tráfico sea reduzca por las vacaciones de Navidad. En ese momento, se hará un corte total del tráfico como ya se vivió el pasado verano en otra intervención clave para el enlazado de ambos túneles.
El problema es que, al menos de momento, no hay un plazo estimado para la ejecución de las obras. Es decir, sabemos cuándo se cortará el túnel pero el Ayuntamiento no ha señalado en qué momento se podrá reabrir. Este paso no se dará hasta que se pueda hacer "con total credibilidad", en palabras de Borja Caravante, responsable de movilidad del Ayuntamiento de Madrid que han recogido en Europa Press.
¿Y el plan? De nuevo, es algo que todavía no se ha confirmado. El Ayuntamiento de Madrid, en este enlace, hace un repaso cronológico con todas las afecciones de tráfico que está sufriendo la ciudad en esta zona. Una vez llegado el momento del corte, se informará de las mismas pero puedes ver qué se hizo en anteriores ocasiones.
De momento, lo que se han señalado son generalidades. Se ha especificado que la idea es intentar desviar el tráfico en el entorno de la M-40 y Carabante ha anunciado que se pondrá en contacto con los responsables de Renfe para aumentar la circulación de trenes en la línea C-5.
Hay que recordar que los primeros días de obra con cortes de tráfico, en enero de 2025, fueron algo caóticos. Desde entonces, la situación ha mejorado pero los conductores lidiaron los primeros días con una estación de autobuses improvisada en la estación de Cuatro Vientos y la instalación de un carril bus que no existía hasta ahora.
"No retorno". Lo que el responsable de movilidad en Madrid ha querido dejar claro es que estamos ante un punto de "no retorno". Una vez que la unión entre túneles esté lista y el tráfico se reinicie, éste lo hará ya bajo la superficie y no volveremos a ver coches en lo que hasta ahora ha sido una autopista urbana.
En ese momento empezarán los trabajos de excavación del túnel paralelo. Finalmente, una vez que ambos ya estén terminados, se podrá empezar a construir un parque que promete cambiar por completo la fisonomía de los barrios de Aluche, Batán y Lucero. Hasta ahora estaban separados por una autopista de cuatro carriles por sentido, una vez finalizado, un gran parque permitirá su unión con la Casa de Campo.

articles.title: Tech and Security Companies Respond to PHP2Shell Vulnerabilities
articles.text:
Tech vendors, cybersecurity companies and government agencies have published advisories, detections and mitigations for the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities, while many software makers are still checking whether their own products are exposed.
The two critical bugs, CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, can let unauthenticated attackers execute code remotely. Wiz, OpenAI and Calif identified them in August, and PHP addressed them on October 21 with versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
PHP pushed out the release one day ahead of the planned disclosure, after the CVE identifiers started circulating online on October 20.
Amazon says the first exploitation attempt came on October 17, before the embargo lifted. Hadrian, Patchstack and Cloudflare all detected attack attempts in the hours leading up to the patches. WatchTowr saw mass exploitation soon after the fixes were published, although the PoC exploits in circulation did not achieve code execution.
With PHP built into a wide range of commercial software, appliances and cloud services, companies across the industry have had to check their exposure.
Tech vendors check products, update PHP runtimes
Cisco’s advisory names over 30 products and cloud services under review. Among them are Identity Services Engine, Catalyst Center, Catalyst SD-WAN Manager, Expressway, Umbrella, Webex and the AppDynamics PHP Agent. “Currently, no products are known to be affected,” Cisco says.
Cisco Talos has outlined the Snort coverage for PHP2Shell, including Community Ruleset rules. Based on open source data, the threat intelligence unit estimates that about half of PHP systems won’t get a patch, and it urges anyone on PHP 8.1 or earlier to move to version 8.2 or newer right away.
Red Hat’s assessment is less severe than NVD’s: it scores both bugs 8.1, compared with 9.8, and doesn’t rate them critical. Regarding CVE-2026-109618, it says that “reliable exploitation requires precise heap manipulation and timing” and notes that “remote code execution is difficult in practice and typically requires non-default behavior”.
On October 21, Ubuntu shipped fixes for all its supported releases, and Debian addressed the flaws in its bookworm and trixie releases.
AWS is addressing the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities in Elastic Beanstalk, WorkMail, Amazon Linux, and Amazon Lightsail.
Google Cloud itself is not vulnerable, but supported PHP runtimes in the App Engine standard environment were updated automatically, and new base images are being rolled out for the company’s serverless PHP services.
Among hosting control panels, cPanel, Plesk and DirectAdmin shipped patches. cPanel and Plesk also released fixed builds for the end-of-life PHP 7.4, 8.0 and 8.1 branches.
SolarWinds says it has reviewed its products and internet-facing assets. “Pingdom uses PHP, but we have implemented compensating controls to protect the product,” the company says. It has taken the same approach for its PHP-based external website and says customers don’t need to do anything.
Security firms roll out detections and mitigations
Palo Alto Networks says upcoming PAN-OS releases will address the issue, and it has shared workarounds and mitigations for customers to apply in the meantime. The company considers the impact on its products high severity, with a CVSS score of 8.7, and says it has no knowledge of attacks against them.
Fortinet has confirmed that two dozen of its products, including FortiOS, FortiManager, FortiAnalyzer and FortiWeb, are not impacted. It is still investigating several others.
Sophos found that its MyUTM portal, a legacy licensing service it hosts for the end-of-life SG UTM product, was running a vulnerable PHP version. The company took the portal offline on October 21 and is updating it before bringing it back.
Broadcom says it has not confirmed any of its Enterprise Security Group products as affected. Its Symantec and Carbon Black offerings provide behavior-based signatures, a file-based detection for related hacking tools, and four application control rules for spotting activity potentially tied to PHP2Shell attacks.
CrowdStrike says it confirmed through testing that one unauthenticated POST request is enough to make an Apache mod_php worker start a shell and execute a command chosen by the attacker, with no vulnerable application code required. It has added PHP2Shell detection content to Falcon Next-Gen SIEM.
Cyber insurer Coalition says it notified some policyholders it knew were running vulnerable PHP versions on October 20, ahead of public disclosure. Between October 20 and 21, its honeypots logged requests matching the patterns used to exploit the flaws.
Corelight, one of the organizations involved in the coordinated response, created Zeek and Suricata detections ahead of disclosure and made them available as open source.
Qualys rolled out a mitigation that switches off PHP’s session upload-progress feature on affected hosts, and JFrog cautioned that fake PoCs appeared around the time of disclosure.
Datadog, Endor Labs, Huntress, Patchstack, Recorded Future, Sansec, SOCRadar and Tenable have also published technical analyses and remediation advice.
Governments warn of hidden PHP, take sites offline
CISA called on organizations to patch right away, starting with internet-facing systems, and cautioned that PHP is frequently embedded in other software, so its presence may not be obvious.
The UK’s NCSC says discovery efforts should cover every PHP installation, not just outdated ones, and that organizations should keep an eye out for updates from vendors of appliances and services that may ship with PHP. It also recommends hunting for backdoors that attackers may have planted before patches or mitigations were applied.
The Dutch NCSC is tracking potentially affected software that depends on PHP in a public GitHub repository.
CERT-EU urges organizations to update without delay and to isolate internet-facing applications until the fix has been applied and verified. In a joint statement with the European Commission, ENISA, Europol and the EU’s network of national incident response teams, it warned that products may be vulnerable even when PHP runs behind the scenes and isn’t obviously in use.
Canada’s Cyber Centre and Germany’s BSI have also issued alerts, both urging organizations to install the updates without delay.
Some organizations chose to go offline rather than stay exposed. According to Reuters, several government, school and hospital websites in Europe were taken down on October 21.
Related: ‘Context Bombs’ Cut AI Attack Success by Misleading Agents With Fake Targets
Related: High-Severity Flaws Exploited in Three Days as Ransomware Dominates Q3: Rapid7

articles.title: Harbor Adds Docker Sandboxes to Run Reproducible AI Agent Evals in Isolated MicroVMs
articles.text:
Docker announced that Harbor, the open-source agent evaluation framework, now works with Docker Sandboxes. This change allows each evaluation task to run in its own microVM. So, instead of sharing a container, tasks are isolated for better performance. The same tasks run locally or in Docker Cloud Sandboxes, and Docker says it has tested Harbor with 64 concurrent tasks in the cloud.
Evaluating a coding agent means letting it install packages, edit files, and run commands, and a benchmark repeats this thousands of times. Docker's engineers describe this as running untrusted, AI-written code at scale. They also flag reward hacking, where an agent earns a passing score by tampering with tests or overwriting the file that records its score instead of solving the task. Harbor manages orchestration. It runs tasks, collects scores, and logs. It also supports benchmarks like Terminal-Bench. It needs an execution environment that is both isolated and consistent.
Each task runs in a Docker Sandbox, a microVM with its own kernel, so agent activity stays inside the VM and cannot reach the host, other tasks, or anything outside the environment. In Docker Cloud Sandboxes, configurable network policies let a task pull dependencies during setup, then restrict internet access while the agent works. Every agent is then evaluated under the same network conditions, which addresses a common source of non-reproducible results. Docker Compose is supported, so Harbor can run multi-container tasks inside a single cloud sandbox, with services and sidecars sharing the same microVM.
The announcement does not include benchmark data on startup overhead, per-task cost, or eval score variance. The one concrete scale figure is the 64 concurrent tasks Docker tested on Cloud Sandboxes. Higher limits are available on request through Docker's contact channel. Teams sensitive to per-task latency or cost will need to measure those themselves.
The integration is available now in the nightly release of Docker Sandboxes, and Docker says it will reach the stable release on October 23. Harbor is installed with the sbx extra, and the nightly build is pinned to version 0.24.1.dev202610150414. Cloud runs require a Docker account with Cloud access enabled. You also need a personal access token that has the Cloud Sandboxes permission. Harbor reads this from the SBX_DOCKER_USERNAME and SBX_DOCKER_PAT environment variables. A run selects the sandbox environment with the -e sbx flag, for example, harbor run -t hello-world/hello-world -a oracle -e sbx. The post presents the local option as free, while cloud scaling depends on Docker's Cloud Sandboxes offering.
The teams already using Harbor can try the integration today on the nightly build or wait for the stable release on October 23. Local runs go through the Docker Sandboxes CLI after sbx login, with --ek target=local added to the Harbor command. The local integration currently supports only public and no-network modes, subject to the machine's existing sandbox policy. The finer-grained network policy described for fair comparisons is tied to Cloud Sandboxes, so teams that need that control should plan for the cloud path. Network restriction removes one avenue for cheating, but the post does not claim to prevent reward hacking within the sandbox, such as an agent modifying test files it can write to. Harbor and Docker Sandboxes documentation covers the pre-integrated sandbox setup.
Docker's Harbor integration adds to the growing list of sandbox backends for the framework. It also expands the range of agent-runtime integrations with Docker Sandboxes.
On the Harbor side, the framework shows horizontal-scaling integrations with cloud sandbox providers. These include Daytona, Modal, E2B, Runloop, Tensorlake, LangSmith, Blaxel, Novita Sandbox, EC2, and Beam. You can find more details in its GitHub repository. The latest addition before Docker is LangSmith. By installing the langsmith extra, you can run evals in LangSmith production sandboxes. This works through the same interface used for Daytona, E2B, or Modal. For more details, see Towards AI. Harbor's cloud deployment docs suggest Daytona as the best choice. Daytona allows multi-container deployments using a docker-compose.yaml file. In contrast, Modal, E2B, and Runloop do not support this feature.
Beyond Harbor, Docker has been placing Sandboxes under other agent platforms. NanoCo and Docker have teamed up. Now, you can deploy NanoClaw, a claw-based agent platform, in Docker's MicroVM sandbox with just one command. This info comes from DevOps Digest. In July 2026, GitHub Agentic Workflows added Docker Sandboxes as a supported agent runtime, shipped in gh-aw version 0.82.9. Docker's walkthrough says the sandbox has its own Docker daemon. This setup allows an agent to run Testcontainers-based integration tests without needing to mount the host Docker socket. The Harbor integration builds on the Cloud Sandboxes launch from September 24. This launch extends local sandbox isolation to Docker-managed cloud infrastructure. Now, agent workflows can continue even if a laptop shuts down. Third-party coverage of the launch reports a one-hour default session with a 24-hour maximum, and that paused sandboxes carry no compute charge. The same launch introduced Kits, packaged as OCI images, and Docker has committed to submitting the Kits specification to the CNCF. NanoClaw Integrates with Docker Sandboxes +4

articles.title: Comcast loses more customers, claims other ISPs' cheap prices are "irrational"
articles.text:
Comcast reportedly plans significant job cuts in its cable division as the firm continues to lose residential broadband and TV customers. Comcast lost 144,000 residential broadband customers in Q3 2026, up from a 91,000-customer loss in the same quarter a year ago, the company said in its earnings report today.
Comcast historically capitalized on a lack of competition for high-speed wired broadband. But now it faces stronger competition from fixed wireless providers and from fiber providers in parts of its cable territory.
“Fixed wireless remains aggressive and continues to take share, while fiber construction remains elevated, with pockets of irrational pricing and promotional activity,” Comcast co-CEO Mike Cavanagh said today in an earnings call.
Comcast CFO Jason Armstrong said “irrational pricing” from fiber operators includes $30 to $40 monthly broadband offers “in specific markets in the third quarter.” He said $30 to $40 pricing is irrational because deploying fiber costs $1,500 or more per home, and is “getting more expensive with construction costs up as you get into more suburban and rural areas.”
“As we look at the return profile of that, to us, that is irrational competition,” Armstrong said. While he didn’t name any specific competitors, Verizon has been pitching FiOS fiber plans that start at $30 a month. Comcast’s network is a mix of fiber and cable, and it offers fiber-to-the-home in only small portions of its cable territory.
Armstrong said more Comcast customers are leaving when they face “pricing transitions,” apparently referring to the price hikes customers get when promotional offers expire. “We’ve been refining our offers and retention strategies to better manage these transitions and strengthen customer retention,” he said.
Cavanagh said that “satellite is not yet a material factor” in the competition Comcast faces, but that Comcast is focused on “anticipating emerging forms of competition and positioning our business to respond as the market evolves.”
Fewer jobs, more AI agents
After the latest quarterly drop, Comcast has 28.3 million residential broadband customers in the US. Comcast said it has a plan to turn things around.
“We’ve embarked on the most significant operating and cost transformation in our company’s history, with an opportunity we believe will ultimately amount to billions of dollars over time,” Cavanagh said. The organizational changes will result in a “significant charge” of over $1 billion to be applied in the fourth quarter earnings report, Armstrong said.

articles.title: Artemis 2: comandante relata momento de medo durante viagem à Lua
articles.text:
O comandante da Artemis 2, Reid Wiseman, viveu alguns minutos de medo real durante a histórica viagem tripulada ao redor da Lua. No sexto dia da missão, o astronauta percebeu que a cápsula Orion continuava se afastando da Terra, mesmo depois de atingir a distância máxima prevista. Por um momento, ele pensou que a tripulação talvez nunca conseguisse voltar para casa.
Wiseman contou o episódio durante o festival Starmus VIII, realizado nesta semana em Tenerife (Espanha). Segundo o astronauta, a equipe havia sido informada de que a distância máxima em relação à Terra seria de 219.667 milhas náuticas, o equivalente a aproximadamente 406.823 quilômetros.
O comandante acompanhava o indicador de distância da espaçonave, chamada Integrity. Quando o número chegou ao limite previsto, ele esperava que o valor começasse a diminuir, sinalizando o retorno. Mas o contador subiu novamente. “Eu estava olhando para esse número e vi chegar a 219.667. Pensei: ‘Ótimo, esta será a maior distância que ficaremos da Terra, e o próximo número que vou ver será 219.666 — estaremos voltando para casa’”, relatou Wiseman.
Cerca de três minutos depois, porém, o indicador mostrou 219.668 milhas náuticas. O astronauta achou a situação estranha, mas o número continuou aumentando. “Mais ou menos três minutos depois, chegou a 219.669. Foi naquele momento que senti medo de verdade, porque pensei que tínhamos ido longe demais — nunca vamos voltar para casa. Fiquei muito assustado”, contou.
O alívio quando a cápsula começou a voltar
O medo durou pouco, mas foi intenso. Finalmente, Wiseman percebeu que o contador começava a diminuir. Quando o indicador voltou a marcar 219.668 milhas náuticas, ele anunciou aos colegas: “Estamos voltando para casa”.
A tripulação comemorou a mudança. “Eu sabia que havia uma boa chance de conseguirmos”, acrescentou o comandante.
Enquanto Wiseman acompanhava o indicador, os outros astronautas estavam concentrados em suas próprias tarefas. Victor Glover e Christina Koch observavam a Lua pela janela da cápsula, enquanto o canadense Jeremy Hansen enviava informações à equipe de controle da missão. Por isso, o momento de apreensão do comandante passou despercebido pelos colegas.
Leia mais:
- Japão lança sonda que tentará trazer pedaços de uma lua de Marte
- O que existe no ponto mais distante da Terra já alcançado por uma nave?
- SpaceX tentará capturar Starship e seu propulsor em pleno voo pela primeira vez
- NASA revela próximos passos da SpaceX e da Blue Origin rumo à Lua
Missão histórica ao redor da Lua
- A Artemis 2 foi lançada em 1º de abril a partir do Centro Espacial Kennedy, na Flórida (EUA). A missão durou quase dez dias e levou quatro astronautas ao redor do lado distante da Lua antes de retornar à Terra;
- Foi o primeiro voo tripulado da cápsula Orion e a primeira missão com astronautas a viajar até a Lua desde a Apollo 17, em 1972. Durante a viagem, a tripulação também superou o recorde de distância da Terra alcançado por seres humanos;
- Ao comentar o retorno seguro, Wiseman fez questão de destacar o trabalho das equipes em solo. Para ele, o sucesso da missão foi resultado do rigor da engenharia e da atuação dos profissionais responsáveis pelo controle do voo;
- “Voltar para casa em segurança é um testemunho do rigor da engenharia e das equipes de controle de voo aqui no planeta Terra, que construíram esse foguete e depois o controlaram enquanto fomos até a Lua e voltamos. Esses são os verdadeiros heróis desta missão. Eles têm coragem de verdade”, afirmou;
- Os quatro integrantes da Artemis 2 receberam a Medalha Stephen Hawking de Comunicação Científica durante o festival Starmus VIII.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Feds reveal breakdown of $750-million VC funding envelope, open Growth VCCI applications
articles.text:
The Government of Canada has shared how it plans to deploy its previously announced “early growth-stage” funding envelope, alongside a call for expressions of interest in the latest version of its longstanding fund-of-funds program. These measures aim to stimulate investment in Canadian venture capital (VC) and technology by attracting private funding.
The breakdown of the former had been eagerly awaited by Canada’s VC sector, with leading investor advocacy organizations having presented competing visions for how the funds should be distributed in recent months.
Both developments were announced this afternoon in Toronto at local autonomous driving unicorn Waabi’s headquarters. The two programs, which will be managed by the Business Development Bank of Canada, total $1.75 billion CAD; together, they encompass the Government of Canada’s Venture and Growth Capital Plan. The feds hope the funds will help to attract at least $3.8 billion CAD in private capital to invest in Canadian tech companies across stages.
“The hardest cheque isn’t the first one,” Waabi founder and CEO Raquel Urtasun said, while introducing Minister of Industry Melanie Joly at Thursday’s announcement. “The pre-revenue growth rounds are really where too many promising companies are lost along the way. That’s the gap that today’s announcement seeks to address, with the idea that many more founders will be building many more Waabis in Canada.”
Applications for the first stream of Growth VCCI are expected to open today.
With the $750-million Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy, first promised in Budget 2025, the federal government has confirmed that it aims to address financing gaps for nascent and scaling domestic tech companies alike, though the bulk of the funding has been allocated towards the latter group.
Of that fund, $675 million will go to addressing “later- and growth-stage” gaps and ensuring that more tech firms at the Series B stage and beyond have the capital they need to scale and remain anchored in Canada. The remaining $75 million has been dedicated to bolstering the country’s pre-seed and seed-stage startup investment landscape in sectors like advanced manufacturing, cleantech, life sciences, quantum, and other strategic industries.
“Historically, Canada has been very good at starting companies … but too often, when our most promising companies scale up, there are too few Canadian investors willing to back this critical phase of growth, and it’s time to change that,” Joly said at the podium. “We want our startups to grow up. We want them to do so right here at home, and we want more Canadian global champions.”
The feds have not yet made clear how much of this $750 million will go directly towards other funds versus startups. Given that the government is seeking feedback to inform the design of the later stream before Nov. 23, those plans appear to still be under development.
“We’re betting that Canadian companies can start, can scale, and can stay here,” Joly added.
RELATED: CVCA and NACO offer competing visions for feds’ $750-million venture envelope
A spokesperson for Innovation, Science, and Economic Development Canada (ISED) told BetaKit over email that consultations for the pre-seed and seed investment portion, as well as calls for proposals for both that and the growth-stage stream, would follow at a later date, while Joly said the feds would have more to share on this later this month regarding how that $75 million will be delivered.
The other key part of the Government of Canada’s Venture and Growth Capital Plan is its $1-billion Growth Venture Capital Catalyst Initiative (Growth VCCI), initially announced in late 2024 by the previous Liberal government. Through that initiative, the feds aim to attract an additional $2.1 billion in private dollars to invest in Canadian firms by co-investing in other fund-of-fund managers.
The country’s current Liberal government revealed earlier this year that Growth VCCI would include a core, $700-million VC stream for other fund-of-fund managers, $200 million for firms that invest directly in life sciences startups, and $100 million for emerging managers, who typically back early-stage companies, including VCs focused on strategic sectors and located outside traditional hubs like Vancouver, Toronto, and Montréal.
RELATED: Canadian VC dollar deployment sees first early-year increase since 2021
The call for expressions of interest for the first, fund-of-funds stream of Growth VCCI opened today and is due to close on Jan. 21.
Growth VCCI is the fourth and largest iteration of the government’s VC fund-of-funds program to date. The matching ratio for Growth VCCI will be at least 3:1 private to public capital. The call indicates that applicants must either have or establish a principal office in Canada, commit to ensuring at least 60 percent of their fund investments are in Canadian VC firms, and that 90 percent of their direct investments (to which these funds are permitted to put up to a maximum of 30 percent of their overall capital) are in domestic startups.
Participating funds-of-funds are expected to raise funds of at least $150 million and secure a first close of either that amount or half their ultimate target within 18 months of being confirmed as a Growth VCCI recipient. Fundraising targets will be negotiated with BDC and other limited partners, and federal funding will be deployed as those milestones are met. Should those funds fail to meet these targets, any promised capital could be redeployed elsewhere.
Canada’s VC sector has been waiting for this news since 2025 and 2024, respectively. While industry leaders whom BetaKit spoke with expressed excitement that the process is finally moving, based on historical precedent and the current stage, it could still take at least 12 to 18 months before this capital actually reaches the country’s fund managers and, ultimately, tech startups, if the government does not take steps to expedite the process.
On the Growth VCCI side of the equation, feds must now gather submissions and choose recipients, and then those firms will need to secure a certain amount of private capital in order to unlock any government funding. The ultimate size of fund managers’ Growth VCCI allocations will be dependent on how much they are able to raise elsewhere. Given the state of the VC fundraising market, which has seen steep declines in dollars raised and funds closed in recent years, that last step could take longer than usual.
The same will likely hold true for the Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy, which has yet to release a call for expressions of interest at this time.
RELATED: “A perfect storm”: 2025 was the worst year for Canadian VC fundraising since 2016
Multiple industry leaders whom BetaKit spoke with expressed optimism that funding through the Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy will start to flow faster than Growth VCCI.
Through Growth VCCI, the federal government hopes to encourage greater domestic investment by the country’s large pension funds.
“My message today to our pension funds and major investors is simple: be bold about Canada,” Joly said. “Look at the ideas being developed right here. Look at the entrepreneurs building right here. Look at the strength in AI, in quantum, in life sciences, in advanced manufacturing, and put your capital behind them.”
During a media scrum following the announcement, Joly said she has also already had “many conversations” with key Canadian pension funds about potentially coinvesting alongside the federal government via the Early and Growth Stage Investment Strategy, expressing optimism that the feds and those funds could co-create new funds at “a ratio of 1:2 or 1:3.”
Competing visions
This year, industry organizations representing Canadian investors, including the National Angel Capital Organization (NACO), the Canadian Venture Capital & Private Equity Association (CVCA), and the Canadian Startup Capital Association (CSCA), had each put forth differing assessments on where the ecosystem’s biggest challenges lay alongside competing visions for how that $750-million envelope ought to be spent.
NACO had pitched for the envelope to go to supporting early-stage funds and infrastructure programs, while the CVCA had argued the money should be targeted to growth at the Series B stage and beyond. CSCA had proposed a bit of both, asking the feds to allocate 10 to 20 percent to pre-seed and seed, and the remainder to growth.
While its ultimate breakdown aligns much more closely with what the CVCA had been calling for, rather than NACO’s wishlist, it still includes some funding for the early-stage ecosystem, and the $75 million for pre-seed and seed falls within the range that the CSCA had requested.
“CVCA has been making the case for a strong capital base that can follow Canadian companies as they grow, and the announcement today really is a continuation of that,” CVCA CEO Benjamin Bergen told BetaKit in an interview.
Bergen said this response illustrates understanding on the part of government “that they have done a tremendous amount of work” since the plan for the VCCI program was first developed 13 years ago in order to get seed, pre-seed, Series A, and Series B funds created and structured. Now, Bergen argued, “we’ve got to close that gap in Series B and beyond.”
CVCA had previously shared data on this growth funding gap, illustrating the outsized role that US investors play in scaling Canadian tech firms. The next marker of success, Bergen added, will be the pace at which the feds deploy capital through both programs.
Feds need to move with “agility and speed”
Previous versions of the VCCI program have moved slowly, frustrating industry leaders. For his part, NACO CEO Claudio Rojas hopes to see the feds move with “the agility and speed” that today’s “hyper-competitive global environment” requires.
The government could do that by speeding up its consultation and decision-making processes and lowering the minimum amount raised necessary to access Growth VCCI funding.
Though this is a far cry from what NACO had initially sought, Rojas hailed today’s announcement as a positive development for early-stage Canadian tech. “For the first time, Canada’s VC strategy starts at pre-seed … This adds capacity at the stage that past programs didn’t reach,” he told BetaKit in an interview.
Rojas noted that this new $75-million commitment, coupled with the $100 million for emerging managers through Growth VCCI, will help entrepreneurs building at that level.
As to how far these amounts move the needle in terms of filling the early-stage financing gap NACO has previously identified, he argued that “it’s the start of a journey” that “makes [Canada’s] whole strategy stronger.”
BetaKit has also reached out to the CSCA for reaction to today’s announcement, but the organization had not responded by publication time.
In the future, Bergen said the CVCA would like to see the federal government turn VCCI into an evergreen fund that is not beholden to federal budget structures and timelines.
With files from Madison McLauchlan and Sarah Rieger.
Feature image courtesy Melanie Joly via LinkedIn.

articles.title: How Goodram Validates DRAM and SSD Reliability in Europe - EE Times
articles.text:
From burn-in testing at 80°C and more than 400 diagnostic platforms to advanced environmental validation, we examine how quality control procedures at Goodram’s Polish manufacturing facility contribute to the reliability of embedded and Industrial IoT (IIoT) systems.
In industrial systems, memory and storage reliability directly influence Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) and the Total Cost of Ownership (TCO). A DRAM module or SSD failure in an industrial computer controlling a production line can generate costs far exceeding the price of the component itself, ranging from production downtime and on-site maintenance to the potential loss of critical data.
For OEM system integrators, predictable memory performance under extreme operating conditions and consistent parameters across production batches are essential. Standard electrical testing performed by contract manufacturers may prove insufficient to detect latent defects that only emerge under prolonged stress.
To address these challenges, Goodram, a Polish manufacturer of DRAM modules and SSDs, has implemented a comprehensive, multi-stage functional, thermal, and environmental validation system at its manufacturing facility in Łaziska Górne, Poland.
Eliminating Early-Life Failures: Technology-Specific Testing Approaches
One of the key challenges in reliability engineering is identifying and eliminating early-life failures, commonly referred to as infant mortality, which correspond to the initial phase of the bathtub curve.
However, extending the testing duration of every product on the assembly line is economically inefficient. In the case of flash memory, excessive testing can also lead to unnecessary NAND cell wear before the product even reaches the customer.
Goodram therefore applies different testing methodologies to DRAM and SSD products, tailored to the underlying physical failure mechanisms of each technology.
Thermal Acceleration and Proprietary Low-Level Algorithms for DRAM
For DRAM modules, thermal acceleration through burn-in testing is a primary diagnostic method. Elevated temperatures increase charge leakage in memory cells, enabling the rapid identification of data retention anomalies and marginal timing characteristics.
At Goodram’s Polish facility, DRAM modules undergo full-load testing at 80°C, with temperatures measured directly on the component surfaces. Depending on the test procedure, this process lasts between 30 and 180 minutes.
Testing is conducted using dedicated infrastructure comprising more than 400 computer platforms based on Intel and AMD architectures. This enables compatibility and functional verification with real-world memory controllers across different DRAM generations, including ECC and Registered DIMM configurations.
Test workloads are generated by proprietary software developed by Goodram’s in-house R&D team. Low-level algorithms written in assembly language and utilizing SSE/MMX instructions generate complex read/write patterns, including intensive random and sequential memory access operations.
The system also supports mapping logical memory addresses to physical silicon structures. This capability enables engineers to identify the specific DRAM die responsible for a failure, facilitating root-cause analysis and providing valuable feedback to the manufacturing process.
Precise SSD Diagnostics Without Excessive NAND Wear
Goodram applies a different validation methodology to SSDs, specifically designed to minimize unnecessary consumption of the drive’s Total Bytes Written (TBW) endurance budget.
Following controller initialization and firmware integrity verification, each SSD undergoes two complete write-and-read cycles covering the entire Logical Block Addressing (LBA) space. For a 1 TB drive, this corresponds to approximately 2 TB of data written during validation.
Testing stations operate under a customized Linux environment that continuously monitors Self-Monitoring, Analysis and Reporting Technology (SMART) parameters and the accumulation of Developed Bad Blocks (DBB).
This configuration enables the simultaneous detection of data transfer errors, communication protocol anomalies, and potential stability issues affecting PCIe and SATA interfaces.
By combining full-address-space verification with real-time diagnostic monitoring, Goodram aims to identify potentially defective drives while limiting unnecessary NAND flash wear during production testing.
Environmental Qualification and Bill of Materials Stability (BOM Freeze)
Production-level testing is complemented by advanced environmental validation conducted using a Binder MKTF 240 climatic test chamber, offering a temperature range from −70°C to +180°C with humidity control.
This equipment enables engineers to assess the resistance of solder joints, printed circuit boards (PCBs), and electronic components to temperature cycling and humidity exposure.
Testing procedures reference established environmental standards, including the IEC 60068 series (such as IEC 60068-2-14 and IEC 60068-2-30) and MIL-STD-810.
For embedded system manufacturers, another important capability is the option to perform validation directly on customer-supplied hardware platforms. This allows memory compatibility and stability to be assessed under conditions that more closely reflect the intended application.
For industrial system designers, long-term component consistency is just as important as operational reliability.
An uncontrolled change in controller revision or memory die process technology can introduce compatibility issues, particularly in real-time systems where deterministic behavior and predictable response times are critical.
To address these requirements, Goodram Industrial Solutions offers a fixed Bill of Materials (BOM freeze), ensuring component consistency across production batches.
The company also provides firmware optimization capabilities tailored to application-specific workloads. For example, SSD firmware parameters can be adjusted to prioritize lower write latency over maximum sequential throughput, depending on the requirements of the target system.
European Manufacturing as a Foundation for Supply Chain Resilience
As electronica 2026 in Munich approaches, supply chain resilience and European technological sovereignty are becoming increasingly important considerations for industrial electronics manufacturers.
Goodram’s integration of R&D, testing laboratories, and manufacturing operations within a single facility in Łaziska Górne, Poland, enables the company to adapt memory and storage parameters to specific OEM application requirements.
This vertically integrated approach also facilitates direct communication between engineering, quality assurance, and production teams, accelerating technical issue resolution and supporting consistent manufacturing processes.
For European OEMs and industrial system integrators, access to local engineering expertise, controlled component configurations, and manufacturing capabilities within the European Union can help reduce the complexity and risks associated with geographically dispersed supply chains.
By combining in-house engineering, production-level testing, environmental qualification, and long-term component consistency, Goodram demonstrates how European memory manufacturing can contribute to more reliable and predictable industrial computing systems.
About Goodram
Goodram is a brand of Goodram S.A., a Polish company and the only manufacturer of DRAM memory modules and SSDs in the European Union. Founded in 1991 and based in Łaziska Górne, the company designs and manufactures memory and storage solutions for over 40 markets worldwide.
With its own production facilities, R&D capabilities, and advanced testing laboratories, Goodram represents a vital link in the European semiconductor value chain, contributing to technological sovereignty and supply chain resilience. Its Goodram Industrial and Goodram Enterprise portfolios serve industrial, embedded, server, data center, and AI applications.
Goodram is a member of the Polish Technology Platform for Photonics (PPTF) and the Polish Chamber of Commerce for Electronics and Telecommunications (KIGEiT), actively participating in the European technology ecosystem and supporting cooperation between industry, research institutions and technology partners.
