articles.title: Pour s'excuser de la panne, Orange annonce un cadeau à ses abonnés
articles.text:
La panne qui a touché le réseau mobile d’Orange et de Sosh le 21 octobre 2026 est désormais terminée, mais les abonnés en ont largement subi les conséquences. Dès la fin de matinée, les signalements se sont multipliés sur Downdetector, dans plusieurs villes de France.
Dans la soirée, Orange a confirmé le rétablissement de ses services, évoquant la défaillance d’un équipement de son cœur de réseau mobile.
Contacté par Numerama, Orange confirme ce 22 octobre 2026 que l’incident est survenu sur un équipement de son nouveau cœur de réseau mobile. L’opérateur exclut toute cyberattaque et lien avec l’affaire PHP.
Selon nos informations, la panne serait liée à une migration vers ce nouveau cœur de réseau, qui aurait perturbé la gestion des connexions de millions d’abonnés. Orange a mis plusieurs heures à trouver une solution provisoire avec l’aide de Nokia, avant de resynchroniser progressivement les lignes concernées. Selon l’opérateur, la situation a commencé à revenir à la normale vers 19h, avant un rétablissement complet annoncé à 21h.
Reste désormais une question pour les abonnés touchés : Orange prévoit-il un dédommagement après cette panne, et sous quelle forme ?
Quel dédommagement pour les abonnés Orange et Sosh ?
Face à l’ampleur de la panne, Orange a décidé de proposer un geste commercial aux abonnés concernés. L’opérateur annonce qu’il va doubler l’enveloppe de données mobiles incluse dans leur forfait pendant un mois, à compter de leur prochain renouvellement.
Concrètement, un abonné disposant habituellement de 100 Go de données mobiles pourra donc en utiliser 200 Go pendant un mois. Orange ne prévoit pas, dans sa réponse, de réduction sur les factures. L’opérateur ne précise pas non plus, à ce stade, les modalités exactes permettant d’identifier les clients éligibles à cette compensation.
En juillet 2012, après une importante panne nationale de son réseau mobile, l’opérateur avait déjà proposé plusieurs compensations : une journée d’appels et de SMS gratuits pour certains abonnés, 1 Go de données mobiles supplémentaires pour d’autres. Un geste commercial qui avait toutefois été critiqué par l’UFC-Que Choisir, qui aurait préféré une réduction sur les factures. Il y a fort à parier que, là aussi, de nombreux abonnés auraient préféré une réduction sur leur facture. Selon nos informations, en interne, la décision d’Orange divise. Des cadres de l’entreprise plaidaient pour un vrai dédommagement.
Les abonnés 4G Box et 5G Box pas dédommagés ?
Le doublement de la data est intéressant pour les abonnés mobiles… mais oublie totalement les abonnés 4G Box et 5G Box, qui ont déjà de l’Internet illimité. Eux aussi ont pourtant été déconnectés, parfois même avec de gros impacts sur le télétravail ou des commerces.
Que font habituellement les opérateurs ?
Plus récemment, en juin 2025, SFR avait offert 100 Go de données mobiles supplémentaires à ses abonnés, y compris ceux de RED, après une panne nationale. Cette compensation avait été accordée automatiquement, sans aucune démarche nécessaire.
En dehors de ces gestes commerciaux exceptionnels, les conditions générales d’abonnement prévoient déjà des possibilités d’indemnisation individuelle. Chez Orange, les clients peuvent demander un remboursement au prorata de la durée d’interruption totale du service, sous certaines conditions. Ils doivent notamment avoir signalé l’incident et pouvoir justifier leur présence dans la zone touchée. Le remboursement, s’il est accordé, prend la forme d’une réduction sur une prochaine facture.
Chez Sosh, les conditions prévoient une indemnisation si le service mobile n’est pas rétabli dans les deux jours ouvrés suivant le signalement. Une durée supérieure à celle de la panne du 21 octobre, donc. Dans les deux cas, les demandes sont donc soumises à des conditions précises, sans garantie de compensation automatique.

articles.title: Rouleau autonettoyant et station d’entretien : le robot Ecovacs Deebot T90S Pro Omni est à 649 €
articles.text:
Le robot aspirateur laveur Ecovacs Deebot T90S Pro Omni est à 649 € (-19 %)
Le robot aspirateur laveur Ecovacs Deebot T90S Pro Omni associe un rouleau rincé en continu, une navigation avec détection d’obstacles et une station d’entretien.
Amazon propose le robot aspirateur laveur Ecovacs Deebot T90S Pro Omni noir à 649 €, contre un prix conseillé de 799 €. L’économie atteint 150 €, soit environ 19 %. Par rapport au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, de 699 €, la baisse représente 50 €, soit 7 %. L’ensemble comprenant le robot et sa station est vendu par ECOVACS et expédié par Amazon, avec la livraison gratuite proposée.
Un rouleau rincé pendant le lavage des sols
Le robot aspirateur laveur Ecovacs Deebot T90S Pro Omni utilise le système OZMO Roller 3.0, composé d’un rouleau en microfibre de 27 cm. Celui-ci frotte le sol tout en étant rincé à l’eau propre pendant le nettoyage. Le dispositif vise à évacuer les saletés recueillies et à limiter leur redistribution sur la surface.
Le rouleau peut se déporter pour longer les bordures et se relever sur les tapis. Côté aspiration, Ecovacs annonce une dépression maximale de 40 000 Pa. La brosse principale ZeroTangle 4.0 est conçue pour limiter l’enroulement des cheveux et des poils, sans supprimer les vérifications et le nettoyage réguliers.
Une station pour entretenir le rouleau et recharger le robot
La station Omni automatise le lavage du rouleau et la collecte des poussières. Elle prend également en charge le séchage à l’air chaud. Ces fonctions réduisent les manipulations après les passages, mais il reste nécessaire de gérer l’eau propre, vider les eaux usées et entretenir les éléments de la station.
La navigation AIVI 3D 4.0 aide le robot à identifier les obstacles et à adapter sa trajectoire. Le système de recharge PowerBoost permet, selon Ecovacs, de récupérer 10 % de batterie en trois minutes pendant les retours à la station pour laver le rouleau. Le temps nécessaire pour terminer une session dépend toutefois du logement, des réglages et des surfaces à nettoyer.

articles.title: Una firma de inversión aseguró que la IA de Anthropic diseñó un antídoto contra el veneno de escorpión, pero no es así
articles.text:
La firma de inversión Citrini Research difundió un relato viral en el que aseguraba haber usado el chatbot Claude, de Anthropic, para diseñar un antídoto contra el veneno de escorpión. Especialistas consultados por el medio The Verge afirmaron que el resultado está lejos de ser un tratamiento real.
Citrini, una firma de investigación para inversores sin científicos en su equipo, se propuso demostrar que la inteligencia artificial podía revolucionar el desarrollo de fármacos. Según su propio relato, ninguno de sus integrantes tenía conocimientos previos sobre el cruce entre IA y biología.
Para el experimento, la firma se asoció con Anthropic y una versión interna, aún no publicada, de Claude. Eligieron como objetivo el antídoto contra el veneno de escorpión, un tratamiento costoso y difícil de producir que suele fabricarse inyectando veneno a caballos.
Las picaduras de escorpión afectan a 1,2 millones de personas por año en el mundo y provocan más de 3.250 muertes, sobre todo entre niños, según el informe técnico que Anthropic publicó el 20 de octubre.
320 mil diseños y apenas 17 funcionaron en el laboratorio
El objetivo era que Claude diseñara proteínas capaces de unirse a las toxinas del veneno. Según el informe de Anthropic, el modelo generó 318.484 diseños de proteínas y evaluó computacionalmente 553.052 combinaciones posibles contra cinco toxinas de escorpiones de México, Brasil, el norte de África y Medio Oriente.
De ese total, el sistema seleccionó 180 diseños y, con ayuda del equipo, sumó otros 31 hasta llegar a 211 candidatos. Todo el proceso de diseño insumió 64 horas de trabajo autónomo, de acuerdo con el documento de Anthropic.
Citrini envió esos 211 diseños a dos laboratorios externos, la biotecnológica suiza Adaptyv Bio y la estadounidense Twist Bioscience, para comprobar si las proteínas se unían realmente a sus objetivos. Diecisiete de ellas cumplieron los criterios de unión fijados por los investigadores, repartidas entre cuatro de las cinco toxinas buscadas. Ninguna logró unirse a más de una toxina a la vez.
La proteína con mejor desempeño, llamada Cn2-B1, mostró una afinidad muy alta contra una toxina mexicana y compitió en los ensayos con un anticuerpo ya conocido por neutralizar ese veneno en ratones, según precisó Anthropic en su informe.
Unirse a una toxina no es lo mismo que neutralizarla
El propio informe de Anthropic reconoce que ningún diseño fue sometido a pruebas que confirmaran si efectivamente neutraliza el veneno, ni en células ni en animales. Tampoco se evaluaron aspectos como la seguridad, la estabilidad o el comportamiento de las proteínas dentro de un organismo.
“Es relativamente fácil descubrir un buen compuesto que se une a toxinas de serpientes y escorpiones. La parte difícil es traducir eso en un medicamento”, dijo Andreas Hougaard Laustsen-Kiel, profesor de tecnología de anticuerpos en la Universidad Técnica de Dinamarca, a The Verge.
Melisa Benard Valle y Anne Ljungars, investigadoras de la misma universidad, coincidieron en que los resultados son “técnicamente prometedores” pero describieron el entusiasmo generado como “prematuro” y “lejos de ser un medicamento”. Según explicaron, todavía se desconoce si las proteínas diseñadas por Claude son seguras, estables o viables para convertirse en un tratamiento.
Pese a estas limitaciones, Citrini calificó el experimento como un éxito, aunque reconoció en su propia publicación que “ningún experimento probó todavía si los compuestos realmente detuvieron el funcionamiento de la toxina”.
La firma sostuvo que buscaba mostrar oportunidades de inversión en el desarrollo de fármacos asistido por IA, no fabricar un medicamento. Citrini y Anthropic no respondieron a los pedidos de comentarios de The Verge.
Anthropic planteó como próximos pasos comprobar si las proteínas también se unen a toxinas extraídas directamente del veneno, probar si bloquean su efecto en células y, eventualmente, evaluar si protegen a animales de laboratorio, los pasos que todavía separan a estos diseños de un antídoto real.

articles.title: Panne Orange/Sosh : voici pourquoi des millions d'abonnés ont été privés de réseau mobile
articles.text:
[Mise à jour le 22 octobre à 11h52 : interrogé par 01net.com, Orange indique que l’« incident technique a eu lieu sur un équipement de [son] nouveau cœur de réseau » et qu’il « a impacté une partie de [ses] abonnés sur le territoire ». L’opérateur écarte toute cyberattaque et tout lien avec la faille PHP. Orange a aussi annoncé un geste commercial pour ses clients touchés.]
Article original
Hier, vers 11h20, des signalements ont rapidement afflué sur les sites comme Downdetector, ou bien sur les réseaux sociaux : des abonnés Orange et Sosh se plaignent de ne plus avoir aucun service. Après cette panne massive, c’est l’heure du bilan. Et une première piste sur la cause se dessine : la panne proviendrait d’un nouveau cœur de réseau mobile.
Une panne massive sur le réseau mobile d’Orange
Pour les abonnés, impossible de passer des appels, d’envoyer des SMS et d’utiliser les données mobiles. Un incident rapidement reconnu par Orange sur ses réseaux sociaux, qui annonçait tenter de rétablir le réseau dans les plus brefs délais. Et on peut penser que c’est ce qu’il s’est passé, puisque l’incident a concerné tout le réseau mobile d’Orange sur l’ensemble du territoire français. Sosh, la marque low cost du groupe, utilise la même infrastructure : l’opérateur était également touché.
Difficultés à joindre des proches, messageries indisponibles, impossibilité de contacter les services d’urgence… les conséquences ont été particulièrement gênantes pour les quelque 21 millions d’abonnés mobiles d’Orange et de Sosh en France. Le tout durant près de 10 heures, de la fin de matinée jusqu’en début de soirée. Une astuce permettait cependant de retrouver du réseau : il suffisait de forcer son smartphone à utiliser la 3G plutôt que la 4G ou la 5G. A priori cependant, les opérateurs virtuels utilisant le réseau Orange comme Prixtel, Cdiscount Mobile ou encore NRJ Mobile n’ont pas été impactés. Pour BFM Tech, il faut remonter à juillet 2012 pour trouver une panne d’une ampleur comparable chez Orange.
D’où vient cet incident ?
Après la fin de la panne, la question de sa cause se pose. Selon les informations de Clément Domingo, alias SaxX, il s’agirait d’un nouveau cœur de réseau mobile qui est tombé en panne. Cela aurait entraîné une mauvaise gestion des sessions clients, qui leur aurait fait perdre l’accès à la 4G et à la 5G. En fait, Orange aurait tenté de migrer une partie de ses abonnés vers ce nouveau cœur de réseau 5G SA (appelé 5G+ par Orange). Une bascule qui aurait mal fonctionné : des lignes migrées se seraient retrouvées incapables de s’authentifier.
 Infos exclusives panne géante Orange en France… "Ce n'est pas un hack"
Il ne s'agit pas d'un piratage on me dit en interne ! 
Orange introduit un nouveau coeur de reseau mobile (5G). Les lignes qui sont migrées dessus sont a priori Hs. 
Pour rappel, depuis 11h ce matin plus… https://t.co/IWyaEbZT66 pic.twitter.com/A8vkUGHjpl
— SaxX ¯_(ツ)_/¯ (@_SaxX_) October 21, 2026
Orange aurait peiné durant plusieurs heures avant d’identifier la panne. Les lignes auraient été resynchronisées une à une, puis par vagues. Pour le moment, Orange n’a fait aucune déclaration sur l’origine de cette panne. On sait que l’opérateur peut faire des gestes commerciaux à ses clients suite à de tels incidents, mais là aussi, aucune annonce pour le moment.
Contrairement à ce qu’on aurait pu penser, cela ne provient pas des failles dans PHP découvertes tout récemment. Orange a bel et bien suspendu l’accès à certains sites et applications afin d’y déployer les correctifs nécessaires. On a même pu penser que Free et ses Freebox étaient touchées, avant que l’information ne soit démentie.

Es el momento de decidir qué candidatos deben pasar a la final en las categorías de mejor ordenador portátil, mejor portátil gaming, mejor portátil convertible, mejor componente y mejor monitor.
Vuestros votos decidirán qué candidatos pasan a la final en cada categoría. Después votará el jurado y ambos resultados se combinarán para elegir a los ganadores.
La gala de los Premios Xataka Verisure 2026 tendrá lugar el 17 de noviembre, cuando conoceremos a los ganadores. Antes, tienes hasta el 29 de octubre a las 23:59 para votar en estas categorías.

Mejor ordenador portátil

Para elegir a los ganadores de los Premios Xataka Verisure 2026 seguimos la mecánica de ediciones anteriores, dividida en tres fases:

articles.title: Pourquoi le successeur de l'iPhone Duo pourrait rendre le premier modèle très vite obsolète
articles.text:
L’iPhone Duo d’Apple sort ce vendredi 23 octobre, à partir de 2 339 euros en 256 Go. Nous avons déjà pu le prendre en main et vous donner nos impressions, sans omettre les sacrifices que le premier pliable d’Apple a dû faire. Parmi eux, l’absence de Face ID, le système de reconnaissance faciale d’Apple.
Pour atteindre une épaisseur de 5,2 mm une fois ouvert, il a fallu amputer l’appareil du module TrueDepth nécessaire au fonctionnement de Face ID. Les utilisateurs devront se contenter de Touch ID dans le bouton latéral du smartphone.
Il est logique de penser qu’Apple cherchera à corriger le tir dans les prochaines versions de l’appareil, mais à partir de laquelle ? Dès l’iPhone Duo 2 ? Selon Mark Gurman, journaliste de Bloomberg, qui s’exprimait ce jeudi 22 octobre, Apple y travaille déjà, avec en prime une nouveauté technique ; rien n’est toutefois arrêté.
Apple testerait un Face ID sous l’écran pour l’iPhone Duo 2
Dans son podcast Power On diffusé ce jeudi 22 octobre, Mark Gurman avance qu’Apple travaille à l’intégration de Face ID sous l’écran de son prochain iPhone pliable. Une innovation que l’on attend également pour l’iPhone qui fêtera les 20 ans de la gamme, attendu l’an prochain.
    À lire aussi : 
Premier pliable d’Apple, l’iPhone Duo résiste-t-il à un usage intensif ? 10 000 pliages plus tard, voici le verdict
L’iPhone Duo dispose déjà d’une caméra sous sa dalle interne, une première chez Apple (Samsung l’avait inaugurée sur le Galaxy Z Fold3 en 2021, avant de l’abandonner sur ses derniers Fold). Apple pourrait s’appuyer sur ce savoir-faire pour glisser Face ID sous l’écran du successeur.
Apple a déjà fait un pas dans cette direction en septembre : sur les iPhone 18 Pro, la caméra infrarouge de Face ID est passée sous la dalle, dans le coin supérieur gauche, ce qui a permis de rétrécir la Dynamic Island. Le projecteur de points reste en revanche dans la découpe, avec la caméra frontale ; l’ensemble du système TrueDepth n’est donc pas encore caché sous l’écran.
Pour l’iPhone Duo 2, Mark Gurman évoque toutefois une petite différence avec la caméra. Là où l’iPhone Duo possède deux caméras selfie (une sous l’écran interne, une autre de 12 mégapixels logée dans un poinçon sur l’écran externe), le capteur Face ID ne serait présent que sous l’écran externe.
D’après Gurman, des prototypes de l’iPhone Duo 2 équipés de ce Face ID sous l’écran externe existeraient déjà chez Apple, mais la marque n’a pas encore tranché pour le modèle commercial, attendu à l’automne 2027. En septembre, le journaliste tablait encore sur un retour de Face ID avec la troisième génération ; il évoque désormais une correction « à la première ou à la deuxième mise à jour », soit d’ici deux à trois ans.
Gurman ajoute que des équipes d’Apple ont étudié l’ajout du bouton Action, également absent de la première mouture du pliable, une piste qu’il juge moins avancée que Face ID.

articles.title: How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC | Amazon Web Services
articles.text:
Artificial Intelligence
How Rescale built an AI triage agent with Strands Agents and AI-DLC
Every engineering team knows the ritual, and Rescale was no exception. A nightly test suite fails. An on-call engineer pulls the logs, classifies the root cause, and routes it to the right team, only to repeat the process the next morning. At scale, across distributed services and dozens of repositories, this ritual becomes a full-time job hiding inside an on-call rotation.
Rescale is the digital engineering platform built for the AI era. R&D and engineering teams across aerospace, automotive, energy, life sciences, semiconductor, and manufacturing use the Rescale platform to accelerate innovation, bringing intelligent HPC, advanced modeling and simulation, agentic digital engineering, and AI physics together on a single platform.
Beyond coding, Rescale uses AI across the engineering lifecycle, from planning and design through implementation, testing, review, and operations, while keeping engineers accountable for the result. AI can propose and execute, but people define scope, validate the work, and approve production changes. Engineers can then focus on architecture, product judgment, and the context required to operate complex distributed systems.
In this post, we show how Rescale used the AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) framework on AWS to build an intelligent triage agent. They went from problem definition to staging deployment in five days, and to production within weeks. The post also covers how Rescale is extending AI-DLC across their engineering organization.
The challenge
As Rescale’s platform grew, so did the operational overhead of keeping it running. Engineers were spending significant time on a repetitive but critical task: classifying automated end-to-end test failures. Hundreds of test cases run in the suite, and when failures appeared, every alert, bug report, and escalation needed to be classified, prioritized, and routed to the right team. After routing, engineers would need to gather evidence from multiple logging and monitoring systems, along with several source repositories before debugging could even begin. Passing end-to-end tests were required to deploy services to production and thus debugging these system failures was in the critical path to getting new changes to production.
In the manual workflow, engineers moved from the test report to logs, historical patterns, and source code to classify failures and identify the likely owning team. Because these integration tests gate weekly production releases, unresolved failures could pull several teams into hours of coordination before a deployment was allowed to proceed.
The team had a clear idea of what a solution looked like: an intelligent agent that could classify and route issues automatically. What they were looking for was a structured way to go from that understanding to a working system in production, with enough structure to extend the approach to other use cases afterward.
Why Rescale chose AI-DLC
Rescale’s triage agent was a well-scoped problem with a tight timeline. The team needed a development approach that could move at that pace without skipping the architectural decisions that would determine whether the system worked in production.
The AI-Driven Development Lifecycle (AI-DLC) is an open source, AI-centric methodology for software development built around two ideas:
- AI executes, humans decide: AI generates work plans, writes code, and proposes architecture, but it surfaces decision points and asks clarifying questions rather than guessing. Humans validate and steer at each step.
- Team sessions replace async handoffs: Instead of one person building alone and requesting review later, AI-DLC uses focused group sessions: Mob Elaboration (defining requirements together) and Mob Construction (building together while AI handles implementation). Decisions happen in real time.
AI-DLC fit because the hard part wasn’t writing code. It was making sure the AI understood what the team wanted to build. In mob sessions, Rescale engineers answered the AI’s questions together and approved each plan before the AI moved on, so nothing was left to assumptions.
Solution overview
Rescale’s triage agent automates the classification and routing of nightly end-to-end test failures. It runs as a step within Rescale’s existing Argo Workflows continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipeline on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS). When a nightly Playwright suite of hundreds of test cases produces failures, the pipeline triggers the triage agent pod.
The agent performs the following steps:
- Invokes Claude Opus 4.8 on Amazon Bedrock to classify each failure into a root cause category: infrastructure issue, code bug, flaky test, or environment problem.
- Retrieves relevant historical failure patterns from a knowledge base for additional context.
- Queries pod logs through Model Context Protocol (MCP) for runtime evidence supporting the classification.
- Generates a structured remediation report with specific file references, function names, and recommended fixes for engineer review before any action is taken.
The agent completes this workflow in seconds and outputs directly into the team’s existing reporting pipeline. The following diagram shows how these components fit together:
The AI-DLC workshop experience
The engagement was structured as a five-day, in-person workshop. AWS architects guided the build while Rescale engineers worked hands-on-keyboard, co-building in real time.
Inception phase (days 1–2): From vision to validated requirements
The team started by scoping requirements, capturing the intent in a vision document and a technical environment document that grounded the work before any building began. That intent began as a single statement, “We want AI-powered test triage that classifies failures and recommends remediation”. Working collaboratively in mob format, the team answered 20+ clarification questions generated by AI. This produced a scoped requirements document with Phase 1 boundaries explicitly defined and Phase 2 items deferred. Five user stories were consolidated into four units of work:
- Knowledge base for historical failure patterns.
- AI triage agent as the core classification and remediation engine.
- Argo Workflow Integration for trigger, infrastructure, and deployment.
- Evaluation Harness for accuracy measurement and regression gating.
Human decisions drove the critical boundaries: what belongs in Phase 1 versus Phase 2, priority ordering, and deferred features like automated pull request (PR) generation.
Construction phase (days 2–4): Architecture to running code
The team defined interface contracts and data schemas, completed functional and non-functional design questions, and signed off on the architecture. Two architecture pivots emerged during the build, and the team validated each one before changing course.
First, the team planned to host the agent on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, then moved it to Amazon EKS, where Rescale already runs its Argo Workflows CI/CD pipeline. Keeping the agent in the existing cluster meant no new runtime to operate and a direct trigger path from Argo. Second, in the early build the agent pulled log evidence from a third-party logging service through MCP. The team moved log retrieval to Amazon CloudWatch, which simplified the dependency chain. The MCP pattern stayed the same. Only the source behind it changed. Because AI-DLC keeps requirements and design decisions in shared documents, the team updated them in place and kept building without losing context.
The agent was built using the Strands SDK, supporting concurrent failure analysis with structured output in JSON and HTML, containerized on Amazon EKS.
By Day 4, the full pipeline was running in staging: Argo workflow trigger, triage agent pod, MCP log query, knowledge base retrieval, and structured triage output.
Operations phase (day 5): Evaluation and handoff
The team built a PyTest-based evaluation framework with live and stubbed test modes, establishing an initial classification-agreement baseline to measure the agent against and improve from. The agent was demoed live to Rescale’s CTO and VP of Engineering, correctly classifying both an infrastructure failure and a real code bug with specific file-level fix recommendations.
How AI-DLC scaled rigor to complexity
Not every unit of work gets the same treatment. The knowledge base needed minimal design and deployed using Terraform in hours. The Triage Agent got full rigor: architecture review, interface contracts, 12 design questions, and iterative code review. Argo Integration focused on infrastructure contracts and IAM. The Evaluation Harness used lightweight design but heavy implementation. AI-DLC matched depth to complexity automatically.
By the end of Day 5, the agent was live in staging, processing real test failures with a measured accuracy baseline and a clear path to production.
Production outcomes
The triage agent has been running in production since the workshop. It automatically classifies nightly end-to-end test failures, replacing manual first-pass triage with an automated first pass that engineers validate. For each failure, the agent generates a structured remediation report with actionable next steps rather than raw logs. The agent’s classification agreement with human triage has risen from 44% at initial deployment to 68% today. It continues to improve as the team iterates on the golden dataset and prompt engineering.
Since the triage agent entered production, the team has measured a 20% decrease in time blocking production deployment while test failures are analyzed. Because these tests gate Rescale’s weekly production releases, that reduction shows up directly in how quickly changes reach production. Engineers also spend less of the on-call rotation on repetitive classification.
Life after the workshop: From one agent to an AI-first practice
The workshop delivered one production agent, but its larger effect was on how Rescale approaches engineering work. The triage agent is part of a broader push at Rescale to deliver digital engineering capabilities for the AI era. Internally, Rescale is applying these same benefits realized from AI across its own engineering organization. AI-DLC gave Rescale’s engineers a structured, repeatable way to put that direction into practice.
Scaling AI-DLC across the organization
Rescale is evaluating an internal AI-DLC Center of Excellence, a small group that codifies best practices and helps other teams adopt the methodology independently.
The engineers who participated are already applying what they learned. One of the engineers noted that the process “will be part of my workflow going forward,” not only for building agents, but for any complex development work where AI can contribute.
Broader AI-native development
Rescale is now incorporating AI-DLC into the standard software development lifecycle for new engineering simulation products. The framework brings simulation-domain expertise, product requirements, platform architecture, validation, and operations into one structured design process. Teams resolve key questions early, capture reviewed decisions in executable specifications, and give coding agents focused work with clear acceptance criteria. This shortens the path from product concept to validated implementation while engineers remain accountable for product correctness.
The same approach is already being used in product-enabling platform work and agent systems:
- HPC simulation application catalog management.
- Container vulnerability tracking and remediation for government compliance requirements.
- Workflow-based cloud coding agents.
Conclusion
For the triage agent, the most useful output of AI-DLC was not the code itself. It was the structured path from an initial idea to a reviewed system design: clarifying questions, scoped requirements, and evaluation criteria.
That specification gave coding agents a narrower, better-defined problem to solve. Instead of asking an agent to infer the architecture while implementing it, the team could use agents for focused construction against decisions that humans had already reviewed. The result was more focused, reviewable output that was easier to integrate and improve. For Rescale, that is the repeatable pattern: use AI-DLC to structure the design conversation, turn the decisions into a specification, and then use coding agents to accelerate implementation.
Key takeaways
- Start with a real problem. Rescale’s triage agent succeeded because it solved an engineering challenge. The problem drove the solution, not the other way around.
- Human oversight accelerates, not decelerates. Every architecture pivot that improved the system came from human validation of AI proposals. The mob format, where AI generates and humans validate, is faster than working alone.
- The AWS stack provided each layer the agent needed. Amazon Bedrock supplied foundation-model access for classification in an environment Rescale was already using, so the team could build the triage workflow without taking on additional model-infrastructure overhead. The Strands SDK provided the agent framework, and Amazon EKS hosted the containerized agent within Rescale’s existing pipeline.

articles.title: BGH zum Schufa-Score: Wann Verbraucher Auskunft verlangen können
articles.text:
BGH-Urteil zum Schufa-Score: Wann Verbraucher Einblick verlangen können
Die Schufa wirbt seit einiger Zeit mit Transparenz: Ihr im März eingeführter neuer Score bewertet die Bonität von Verbrauchern auf einer Punkteskala von 100 bis 999 Punkten anhand von 12 klar definierten Kriterien. Doch das war nicht immer so.
Lange galt die Schufa als “Blackbox”. Wie ihr Score zustande kam und welche Kriterien sie dafür nutzte, war ein gut gehütetes Geschäftsgeheimnis. Daher gab es immer wieder Klagen gegen den alten Schufa-Score, mit denen Kunden mehr Einblick in das Zustandekommen der Bewertung ihrer Kreditwürdigkeit erstreiten wollten.
Schließlich nutzen Banken, Vermieter oder Telekommunikationsunternehmen solche Bonitätsscores regelmäßig, um die Kreditwürdigkeit von Verbrauchern zu bewerten. Die Schufa besitzt nach eigenen Angaben Daten über rund 68 Millionen Menschen in Deutschland.
BGH verwirft Urteile zu Schufa-Score
Der Bundesgerichtshof (BGH) hat am Mittwoch in vier Verfahren entschieden, in denen Kunden Auskunft über ihre Daten bei der Schufa verlangten, nachdem ihnen Verbraucherkredite verweigert wurden. Die von der Schufa bereitgestellten Datenkopien hielten sie aber für unzureichend. In den Verfahren ging es auch um die grundlegende Frage, wie transparent algorithmische Entscheidungen sein müssen.
Das BGH-Urteil ist erstmal ein Gewinn für die Schufa: Denn das Gericht hob die Entscheidungen des Oberlandesgerichts (OLG) Dresden auf, die zugunsten der Verbraucher ausgefallen waren.
Das OLG hatte die Schufa verpflichtet, offenzulegen, wie sie in konkreten Fällen zu ihrem Score gekommen ist. Nach den europäischen Datenschutzregeln zur „automatisierten Entscheidungsfindung“ hätte die Auskunftei dabei zwar keinen Einblick in ihren Algorithmus geben, aber die Verfahren und Grundsätze des Scores sehr konkret beschreiben müssen.
Der BGH hat die Urteile aber nun mit der Begründung aufgehoben, Verbraucher hätten nur dann ein solches Auskunftsrecht, wenn sie nachweisen können, dass ihnen durch den Scorewert tatsächlich “maßgebliche” Nachteile entstanden sind. Nun muss das OLG Dresden die Fälle erneut prüfen.
Die Hürde für so einen Nachweis darf das Gericht laut dem BGH-Urteil aber nicht zu hoch ansetzen. Schon der zeitliche Zusammenhang zwischen den Nachteilen für den Kunden und der Score-Übermittlung an das Unternehmen sollen demnach ausreichen, um eine „tatsächliche Vermutung“ zu begründen, dass die Entscheidung maßgeblich auf den Schufa-Score zurückzuführen ist. Das bedeutet in der Praxis: Solange die Schufa nicht das Gegenteil beweisen kann, muss sie Auskunft über den Score geben.
Neues Gesetz für mehr Transparenz
Die Schufa selbst sieht laut Pressemitteilung ihre Auskunftspraxis “in zentralen Punkten bestätigt“, zumal es in den Klagen noch um den alten Schufa-Score ging. Sie verweist darauf, dass der neue Score Kriterien und Gewichtungen bereits vollständig offenlegt.
Aus Sicht von Datenschützern ist das BGH-Urteil trotzdem auch für den neuen Score relevant. Denn der BGH hat damit klargestellt, unter welchen Umständen ein Recht auf Auskunft zu den Schufa-Daten besteht.
Recherchen von NDR und Süddeutscher Zeitung hatten außerdem zuletzt gezeigt, dass die Schufa Daten aus dem alten Score immer noch nutzt. Die Datenschutzorganisation NOYB bereitet daher eine Sammelklage gegen die Schufa und ihre „Schattendatenbank“ vor. Die Schufa begründete die Nutzung der historischen Daten unter anderem damit, gesetzliche Anforderungen erfüllen zu müssen.
In der Praxis wird es für Verbraucher ab dem 20. November aber ohnehin leichter, Einblick in ihre Bonitätsdaten zu nehmen. Dann sind Auskunfteien durch einen neuen Paragraphen im Bundesdatenschutzgesetz verpflichtet, bei maßgeblichen Scores die einflussreichsten Kriterien zu erläutern und zwar “in präziser, transparenter, verständlicher und leicht zugänglicher Form“.
Die Schufa gibt an, schon heute über die zukünftig geltenden gesetzlichen Anforderungen hinauszugehen, weil sie alle Kriterien ihres neuen Scores offenlegt und nicht nur, wie vom Gesetz gefordert, die wichtigsten.

articles.title: Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
articles.text:
Google and AWS open new paths for PyTorch beyond Nvidia
At PyTorch Conference North America 2026 this week, Google open-sourced TorchTPU, a native PyTorch stack for Google TPUs, now available on GitHub. AWS also launched TorchNeuron in public beta, its open-source native PyTorch backend for AWS Trainium, also available on GitHub.
Both releases seem aimed at making it easier for developers to move beyond Nvidia GPUs, whose CUDA software ecosystem has long dominated AI development. But while Google and AWS’s new offerings do ease some of the challenges of switching hardware, getting top-tier performance still isn’t straightforward.
For developers eager for more computing options, it’s promising but somewhat disappointing.
Google wants to make TPUs more PyTorch-friendly
Google put TorchTPU in preview with select customers in April (PyTorch says Google’s been working on the project since mid-2025), teasing a simpler way to run PyTorch workloads on Google’s AI chips. PyTorch support has long been an awkward dance, so the new backend could make it easier to run existing models on TPUs.
Google says it wants to make its TPU software ecosystem more open and developer-friendly for the PyTorch community, as it works to make the chips a more practical option for developers already using PyTorch.
Developed in collaboration with the PyTorch team at Meta, TorchTPU allows developers to run existing PyTorch workloads without JAX dependencies in the runtime. This way, rather than requiring extensive code changes, developers can migrate existing workloads with only “trivial code changes,” according to PyTorch.
Specifically, developers can use eager execution to debug models and torch.compile to optimize TPU utilization and reduce memory overhead. 
The new PyTorch stack from Google and Meta comes alongside a slew of other products and integrations announced at the conference, which Google says are “designed to help you run PyTorch effectively on Google Cloud or in your own infrastructure.” Google also announced integrations involving Hugging Face, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, TorchTitan, Ray and TorchRec, while contributing LiteRT to the PyTorch ecosystem.
AWS wants in, too
AWS’s release extends the same PyTorch-native approach to its own AI chips.
Like TorchTPU, TorchNeuron gives developers a way to natively experiment and build models with PyTorch — this time for Trainium, AWS’s portfolio of AI chips designed for deep learning training and inference workloads. The public beta supports Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances.
AWS says moving a model to Trainium can be as simple as switching to .to(‘neuron’) for eager execution. Compiled models also need the Neuron backend selected, either as the default or in a torch.compile call.
TorchNeuron also integrates with Neuron Kernel Interface (NKI) — a bare-metal language and compiler for programming AWS Trainium and Inferentia NeuronDevices — so developers can create custom operators and optimize performance on Trainium. AWS and PyTorch have published more detailed guidance on the backend’s execution modes and performance tradeoffs.
Both are getting closer, but not there yet
While TorchTPU and TorchNeuron are notable steps forward in opening up more hardware choices for PyTorch developers, neither is a silver bullet.
PyTorch says a simple code change can get models running on TPUs, but peak performance can require TPU-specific optimization.
For distributed workloads, PyTorch says TorchTPU’s default Skinny Collectives approach can incur an end-to-end performance penalty of roughly 30–40% compared with an optimized approach because it prevents the XLA compiler from overlapping computation and communication.
For workloads seeking peak performance, PyTorch recommends additional tuning and production-grade stacks:
“Of course, for production workloads seeking peak performance we would absolutely recommend pursuing an optimal approach based on Pallas kernels and production-grade stacks such as vLLM-TorchTPU, SGLang-TorchTPU, or TorchTitan-TorchTPU, as examples.”
TorchNeuron is in public beta. In a separate blog post, AWS says teams can try Trainium with a configuration change instead of a code or model rewrite “in most cases,” leaving open which workloads need more changes.
In a case study, AWS describes how its Generative AI Innovation Center worked with AI research and technology company i14 to adapt its Laplace 3B model for Trainium2. The implementation required three changes: 1) using native PyTorch for the GLA attention kernel; 2) redesigning how Muon communicates; 3) compiling the sequential backward pass.
The releases give PyTorch developers more options beyond Nvidia GPUs. For now, moving existing code is easier than getting peak performance on unfamiliar chips.

articles.title: Flutterwave offers employees share-backed loans in rare move
articles.text:
Flutterwave employees can now borrow money against their vested shares without selling them, through a programme with Techdollar, a US private-credit startup. The loans give staff access to cash before a company sale or stock-market listing while allowing them to retain any future gains on their equity.
“I always say that our people are our secret sauce and the driving force behind our success at Flutterwave, and we believe they should share in the value they create without having to wait for a major liquidity event,” Olugbenga “GB” Agboola, Flutterwave’s founder and CEO, said in a statement.
The deal offers an alternative to selling shares during a funding round or waiting years for an exit—two of the few ways startup employees in Africa have historically been able to turn equity into cash. Flutterwave, valued at $3.25 billion, said in April that it was not close to an initial public offering (IPO).
Techdollar will lend against employees’ vested shares for six to 12 months, typically advancing less than half their value. If a borrower defaults, the lender can seize and sell the pledged shares. Employees keep their equity if they repay the loan but risk losing it if they don’t.
The loans will be paid into accounts that employees open with Nuvion, a Miami-based digital bank for businesses that already powers Flutterwave’s stablecoin products.
For African startup employees, equity can represent a significant part of their compensation without providing a way to meet immediate expenses. Companies rarely sell or list, leaving staff waiting for a liquidity event that may take years or never happen.
In 2025, Moniepoint and Arnergy allowed employees to sell part of their equity while the companies were raising money. In both cases, employees sold shares at a discount to the price new investors paid.
A Stears and Ventures Platform report found that a recent rise in African exits came as much from a 33% fall in funding as from a 36% rise in exits, and that fund managers held their stakes for an average of 6.2 years before exiting.
The same report counted 181 verified VC-backed exits across the continent between 2011 and 2026, showing how rare exits remain.
How the loans work
Techdollar lends to employees, founders, and investors at private companies, using their shares as collateral. The company says it prices loans using live secondary market data, though few African startups have shares that trade often enough to produce it. It verifies ownership through audits and pays out within 24 to 48 hours.
Loans run for a fixed six to 12 months and are secured by vested shares. Techdollar typically lends less than half the value of the pledged equity. Interest runs from 0.80% to 1.5% a month, which is 9.6% to 18% a year in simple terms, with an average starting rate of 16%.
Employees keep any gain if Flutterwave’s valuation rises, and they could lose the pledged shares if it falls. If the shares lose value during the loan, borrowers get a window to add cash.
According to Techdollar’s terms of service, pledged shares can face margin calls, forced sale, or seizure on default, and borrowers “may lose some or all of their pledged equity.” Shares change hands only after a qualifying default.
“Traditional lenders have historically catered to founders and executives with substantial equity holdings, while employees with millions of dollars in private-company shares are often left with limited options,” said David Tollemache, Techdollar’s co-founder.
Founded in 2016, Flutterwave lets businesses collect and send payments across 34 African countries. In June, it raised a Series E at a $3.25 billion valuation, with an undisclosed investment from Ripple, the US blockchain payments company. The valuation was slightly above the $3 billion it reached in February 2022 after a $250 million Series D led by B Capital.
In June, Flutterwave promoted more than 100 employees, about 25% of its global workforce. It made a one-time economic relief payment to all staff and added tax support and cost-of-living adjustments for employees in Nigeria.
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. articles.title: Splunk, SolarWinds Release Fresh Security Updates
articles.text:
Splunk and SolarWinds this week released patches for multiple vulnerabilities, including flaws leading to code execution, privilege escalation, denial-of-service (DoS), and information disclosure.
On Wednesday, Splunk rolled out security updates for Splunk Enterprise and SOAR to resolve dozens of security defects, including multiple flaws in third-party packages.
Splunk Enterprise versions 9.4.16, 10.0.11, 10.2.8, and 10.4.4 were rolled out with fixes for 16 CVEs in the product’s code, including CVE-2026-76299 and CVE-2026-76302, critical-severity improper access control and improper neutralization issues.
High-severity remote code execution (RCE), DoS, authorization bypasses, and improper resource control weaknesses were also addressed.
Splunk SOAR version 8.7.0 was released with patches for 15 vulnerabilities in its code and over a dozen in third-party libraries. The most severe are CVE-2026-76531 and CVE-2026-76407, critical-severity data exposure and improper access control issues.
The update also resolves high-severity information disclosure, improper neutralization, improper resource control, and protection defects.
SolarWinds released fixes for a high-severity bug in Observability that could allow low-privileged users to access restricted information. Tracked as CVE-2026-28328, the flaw is described as a broken authorization schema issue.
Additionally, the company released security updates that address medium-severity XSS and SSRF vulnerabilities in Observability, and a medium-severity information disclosure bug in Patch Manager.
Observability Self-Hosted version 2026.4 and Patch Manager version 2026.4 contain patches for these security defects.

articles.title: Spanish VC Seaya closes new fund at €600 million in just six months | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Seaya, a Spanish investment platform, has announced the launch of Seaya Nova, its new growth fund, following a first close of €600 million in just six months – tickets will range from €20-50 million per company.
The fund is backed by the European Investment Fund (EIF) under the European Tech Champions Initiative (ETCI); the EIB Group programme created to help close the funding gap facing Europe’s growth-stage technology companies, alongside other institutional investors, corporates and family offices.
Beatriz González, founder of Seaya and Managing Partner of Seaya Nova, says: “Seaya Nova is the natural evolution of what we have built over thirteen years. We started backing Public founders at the earliest stage, we added a sustainability strategy with Seaya Andromeda, and now we can stay with the best European companies all the way to global leadership. We are delighted to welcome Vinoth to lead this next chapter with us.”
Seaya Nova’s launch follows a series of European VC fundraising announcements in 2026 targeting growth-stage technology companies.
In Spain, Barcelona-based Kembara secured a €750 million first close for its EIF-backed DeepTech growth fund, while Samaipata reached €70 million towards a €110 million early-stage AI-focused vehicle.
Elsewhere, UK-based Molten Ventures raised €203 million for a Series B+ growth fund, London’s Mouro Capital secured approximately €343.7 million, 2150 closed a €210 million climate-focused fund, and Paris-based SlateVC reached a €132 million first close.
Together with Seaya Nova, these announcements represent approximately €2.31 billion in reported fund closes and capital raised. The launch also builds on Seaya’s previous fundraising activity, including the €300 million final close of Seaya Andromeda in 2024.
Vinoth Jayakumar, Managing Partner of Seaya Nova, adds: “Europe now produces companies capable of leading their categories globally. The question is no longer whether they can be built here, but whether they can be scaled from here. AI is compressing the path from product-market fit to category leadership, and the capital that decides the winner is needed earlier and in larger amounts. Seaya Nova is built for that reality, and I could not be more excited to join Seaya to build it”.
Seaya is a European multi-stage technology investment platform founded in Madrid in 2013. The firm operates through three complementary investment strategies: Seaya Ventures at the early stage, Seaya Andromeda in sustainability, and Seaya Nova in growth.
Seaya Nova will invest €20 million to €50 million per company, leading or co-leading Series B to D rounds in European technology companies with proven models, durable economics and global ambition.
Seaya Nova is led by Beatriz González, Founder and Managing Partner of Seaya, and Vinoth Jayakumar, who joins Seaya as Managing Partner of Seaya Nova after more than a decade of European growth investing, including backing Revolut, Wise, Thought Machine and ICEYE et al.
His appointment coincides with the opening of a new Seaya office in London, complementing its Madrid headquarters – aiming to strengthen the firm’s presence across European technology markets.

articles.title: E-commerce platforms Cymax and CommerceBear reportedly shut down
articles.text:
Two Canadian e-commerce brands, Cymax Group Technologies and CommerceBear, appear to have shut down this year amidst tough market conditions.
This week, Vancouver Tech Journal noted that multiple employees from Burnaby, BC-based Cymax were looking for work and discussing the company’s shutdown on LinkedIn. This included a post from senior leader David Tse, who noted he was “helping the company with the wind-down.”
Bijan Vaez, the founder and CEO of Vancouver e-commerce company Merchkit, also posted about Cymax’s shutdown and said he would help connect affected employees to other players in the industry. Cymax did not respond to BetaKit’s attempts to confirm its shutdown, but did share Vaez’s post with the comment “Sharing for reach!” on its LinkedIn page
The number of employees affected by the shutdown remains unclear, but Cymax’s LinkedIn profile lists 145 associated members.
Cymax was founded in 2004 as a furniture marketplace and grew to include multichannel e-commerce platform Channel Gate and shipping management platform Freight Club. Channel Gate helped furniture vendors with e-commerce sales management, while Freight Club helped vendors and manufacturers with shipment quoting, booking, and tracking.
In 2024, Plenty of Fish founder and Cymax majority owner Markus Frind took over as CEO, saying at the time he was “stepping into this subsidiary to provide direction, vision and focus” shortly after former CEO Rizwan Somji left to spend time with his family.
RELATED: Majority owner Markus Frind named permanent CEO of Cymax Group
In his post, Vaez said he’s aware of many similar retail brands from furniture to consumer-packaged goods “having a hell of time” trying to manage their supply chains amidst the tariff dispute between Canada and the United States.
“Missing parts or ingredients needed for production. Not enough inventory to sell,” Vaez wrote. “There’s not much optimization to be had when the product keeps going out of stock and the marketplaces penalize you … all that effort gets wasted!”
Vaez’s post has since been edited to remove a mention of the similar recent closure of Toronto-based CommerceBear, referenced by Vancouver Tech Journal. BetaKit reached out to CommerceBear founder Sam Vlessing for comment, but did not hear back by press time. However, a source familiar with the company confirmed CommerceBear has shut down, and its website now delivers a 404 error.
CommerceBear was launched by Vlessing in 2019 to provide furniture manufacturers with an end-to-end e-commerce solution to sell their products on markets like Wayfair, Amazon, and Walmart. By 2022, the company had raised a total of $10.5 million USD from the likes of Garage Capital and Inovia to help it win more of the market and make e-commerce accessible to the entire furniture and home goods industry. Vlessing’s LinkedIn indicates he now works on the Labs team at Ottawa-based wellness platform Fullscript.
As Vaez noted, retail-associated businesses have faced economic headwinds and rising costs amidst the Canada-US trade war. However, the furniture market that both CommerceBear and Cymax specialized in has been particularly rocked by slowed growth after a consumer spending boom during the COVID-19 pandemic.
Feature image courtesy Cymax Group Technologies via LinkedIn.

articles.title: Audeze and Audiokinetic announce collab that 'advances native spatial audio content creation possibilities for game developers' by adding head-tracking support to the Maxwell 2 ANC gaming headset into the Wwise audio creation suite
articles.text:
'We’re removing the friction between creator vision and spatial execution' — Audeze and Audiokinetic are introducing native head-tracking support for the Maxwell 2 ANC headset directly inside Wwise
"This collaboration is set to transform how game audio is created and experienced"
- Audeze and Audiokinetic are collaborating to add native head-tracking support to Wwise with the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC headset
- The Maxwell 2 ANC integration into Wwise will "advance spatial audio content creation possibilities for game developers"
- Audiokinetic CTO Martin Dufour says the collaboration will unlock "new creative possibilities for developers, making it easier to implement vivid spatial audio that elevates player immersion"
Audeze has announced a new partnership with cross-platform audio solution provider Audiokinetic to introduce native head-tracking support for the Audeze Maxwell 2 ANC headset directly inside Wwise.
The collaboration will "advance spatial audio content creation possibilities for game developers" by integrating Audeze’s next-generation Maxwell 2 ANC gaming headset with Audiokinetic’s Wwise audio creation suite, leveraging both companies' tech and expertise to push its "commitment to driving innovation across gaming audio and delivering world-class tools to creators."
This will support sound designers and game developers alike, who can use Wwise and tap into Audeze’s Maxwell 2 ANC headset, which is equipped with real-time, self-calibrating head-tracking technology.
The tech will help creatives achieve highly accurate 3D sound placement and enhanced spatial audio authoring with a plug-and-play setup, with zero external software required.
"Simply connect the Maxwell 2 ANC via USB-C or its ultra-low-latency wireless USB-C dongle to begin monitoring directly in Wwise," Audeze said. "This collaboration is set to transform how game audio is created and experienced—from VR emulation and Tempest 3D AudioTech binauralization to non-standard speaker layouts for Location-Based Entertainment (LBE) using the AK Custom Panner."
Sankar Thiagasamudram, CEO of Audeze, shared a statement, saying, "By natively integrating Maxwell 2 ANC’s self-calibrating head tracking directly into Wwise, we’re removing the friction between creator vision and spatial execution."
"Game developers now have a portable, studio-grade reference system that lets them place, audition, and mix 3D audio effortlessly in any environment. Together with Audiokinetic, we’re establishing a new benchmark for spatial audio creation across the interactive media industry."

The Maxwell 2 ANC integration will also allow developers to take full advantage of the headset’s hardware-based, low-latency head tracking, "providing unparalleled spatial accuracy for creating immersive soundscapes in video games," as well as 90 mm planar magnetic drivers with Uniforce, Fluxor, Fazor, SLAM acoustic technologies, and Active Noise Cancellation (ANC), which is designed to maintain a consistent frequency response.
"We’re unlocking new creative possibilities for developers, making it easier to implement vivid spatial audio that elevates player immersion," added Martin Dufour, CTO of Audiokinetic.

articles.title: Disgraced eMudhra drops out of TLS business after using cert private key of 4
articles.text:
eMudhra, the certificate authority that issued eight intermediate TLS credentials so weak that anyone could mint certificates for any website or mail server—one had a private encryption key of just 4—said it’s getting out of the business.
V. Srinivasan, chairman of India-based eMudhra Limited, cited increasing costs and complexities of compliance requirements—paired with the business generating just 1 percent of its revenue. He also said that the emergence of organizations providing TLS certificates free of charge further reduced returns on investment when compared to other products and services the company offers.
Don’t let the door hit you on the butt
“However, the level of social media amplification around this incident has brought scrutiny that is out of proportion to SSL/TLS’s place in our business,” the company continued in a Thursday post. “In view of this, after detailed deliberations our board has concluded that withdrawing from global SSL/TLS is the right decision for eMudhra and its shareholders.”
The announcement came two days after researchers revealed eMudhra had issued eight certificates with private keys so defective they were trivial to discover. Anyone who took the time—which was measured in milliseconds—could crack them and then use them to generate TLS certificates that would be trusted by all major browsers, as well as an untold number of email servers, IoT devices, Docker containers, forgotten Linux machines, and unmaintained CLI tools that ship their own copy of the roots.
Whereas NIST P-384 elliptic curve cryptography private keys—used in the type of certificates eMudhra issued—are supposed to contain roughly 384 bits of entropy, the eight compromised certificates had key sizes ranging from 3 to 8 bits. Stated differently, whereas there are supposed to be 2384—a number with 116 digits—different key possibilities, the strongest of the defective keys had a maximum of just 256. The private keys were 4, 56, 66, 115, 155, 156, 230, 237.

Start building a 4K-capable gaming PC with parts for just over $1,000

articles.title: Canva releases its first image generation model | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Design platform Canva released its first image generation model, called Canva Craft, developed by its research team to compete with same-category models from Google, OpenAI, ByteDance, and Meta.
The company said its model works in two stages. In the first stage, it interprets users’ prompts and creates a plan with details like spatial relationships of elements, relative scale, visual hierarchy, and information for text generation. In the second stage, its model generates an image of up to 2K resolution in a possible 30 different aspect ratios for various platforms.
Canva said that this approach allows it to create images with accurate details of objects and legible text. Plus, users would be able to make precise edits without changing other parts of the image.
The company noted that rather than using photographs, it used designs to train this model using human-designed templates from Canva’s library, including posters, social posts, presentations, infographics, menus, and typography-rich layouts.
That means images generated with Canva Craft could be converted into layered designs using Canva Magic, the company’s image-to-design transformer. Last year, the platform released its own model that understands designs and layers.
Canva Craft is available on the company’s platform to all users, who can access the model from the Dream Lab tab. The model will also be available through the Canva API. Plus, the company plans to support image generation in third-party chatbots like ChatGPT and Gemini through Canva’s MCP.
Canva has used a bunch of image models for generation in its platform, so it’s likely that the new models will help save API costs for the company. It said that besides costs, the new model also allows the platform to have better quality and speed control.
In 2024, Canva acquired media generation platform Leonardo.ai. It said that the researchers from Leonardo contributed to the new image model.
Canva said that it is developing two cost-efficient versions of the model, called Craftfast and Craft-ultrafast, which will be released soon.
The company was on track for $4 billion in revenue last year. However, it cut its growth forecast for 2026, causing its valuation to reportedly plummet from $42 billion to $35 billion, according to external analysts.

articles.title: Tom Skerritt, estrella de 'Alien' y 'Top Gun', ha muerto a los 93 años
articles.text:
Tom Skerritt, uno de los actores más prolíficos y reconocibles de Hollywood, dueño de una carrera que se extendió por más de 60 años, ha fallecido a los 93 años. El actor es especialmente recordado por sus roles en películas como M*A*S*H (1970), Alien (1979), Top Gun (1986), The Rookie (1990) y El río de la vida (1992), por solo citar algunos títulos de su extensa filmografía.
Según reporta Variety, Tom Skerritt falleció por causas naturales. Su deceso se produjo ayer, 21 de octubre, pero recién en la jornada de hoy se hizo público. El intérprete tuvo cinco hijos producto de tres matrimonios diferentes.
La carrera de Tom Skerritt no solo incluyó un gran número de películas, sino que sus trabajos en televisión fueron también muy destacados. En los años sesenta y setenta interpretó a múltiples personajes en títulos como Combat!, The Virginian, Death Valley Days, 12 O'Clock High, Gunsmoke y The FBI.
Sin embargo, su rol televisivo más conocido y recordado fue el del Sheriff Jimmy Brock en Picket Fences (1992 a 1996). Su trabajo en dicha serie le valió un Premio Emmy y dos nominaciones a los Globos de Oro.
Muere Tom Skerritt, un ícono del cine y la TV
Claro que los roles que lo hicieron mundialmente famoso estuvieron en el cine. Alien fue el primer gran papel que le dio reconocimiento internacional a Tom Skerritt, interpretando a Arthur Dallas, capitán del Nostromo. Otro papel icónico le llegó en 1986, de la mano de Top Gun, cuando dio vida al comandante Mike Metcalf, alias Viper.
En los años 90 y 2000 continuó trabajando en cine y TV con gran asiduidad, apareciendo en títulos como The Rookie, El río de la vida, Contacto, The West Wing, La ley y el orden: UVE, Brothers & Sisters, y muchos más.
Tom Skerritt se mantuvo activo como actor a pesar de su edad avanzada. Su último crédito en televisión fue en 2022 con Going Home, una serie emitida en la plataforma cristiana Pureflix. En tanto que su última aparición en una película fue en 2025 con el western Broke, protagonizado por Wyatt Russell y Dennis Quaid. No obstante, dicho título no se lanzó en cines, sino debutó directamente en Netflix.
Más allá de su vasta filmografía en películas y series, Tom Skerritt también tuvo un par de participaciones en el mundo de los videojuegos. En 2005 prestó su voz a Gun, un western de acción que desarrolló Neversoft y publicó Activision. En tanto que en 2014 volvió a interpretar al capitán Dallas en Alien: Isolation, de SEGA.

articles.title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
articles.text:
Sponsored
Designing an AI serving harness built to last
The engineering system surrounding an AI model increasingly determines whether its intelligence can be delivered reliably, economically, and at scale.
Provided byEXL
The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it.
That’s an important shift. For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores. Those advances have been extraordinary. But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?”
Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management, scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability.
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it.
Start with the workload, not the model
There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture. There is only the right solution for the business problem.
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight. An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures.
The workload defines the constraints. The constraints should determine the architecture.
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments. During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion. Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic.
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application's latency requirements. Not every workload needs a Ferrari. Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn't.
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload. That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern. It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn't worth the cost.
Engineer the system, not the model
Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another. Serving architecture influences memory utilization. Memory management affects concurrency. Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency.
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value. This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance.
GPU memory is a good example. During inference, the model's weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length. As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available. Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive.
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize. Identify the dominant constraint. Address it. Measure the result. Then determine if another bottleneck emerged. Repeat.
Don't think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn't to collect them all. The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application's business requirements.
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question. Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value.
Build for change, not today's benchmark
Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today's leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s. Models will improve. Hardware will evolve. New optimization techniques will emerge. The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances.
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy.
Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs. A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset.
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series. It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable.
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models. Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes.
The model provides the intelligence. The harness determines whether the enterprise can deliver outcomes reliably, economically, and at scale.
