articles.title: Ink droplets in motion snag top prize in Nikon Small World contest
articles.text:
A 25-year-old German experimental photographer has won the 2026 Nikon Small World photomicrography competition with a striking image of droplets of ink being deposited on paper by an inkjet printer. Ole Bielfeldt beat out 1,802 other entries hailing from 69 different countries.
Bielfeldt became interested in photomicrography during the COVID-19 lockdown after discovering an old microscope in his parents’ attic. He figured out how to build an adaptor out of a tube and some wood to connect the microscope to his father’s camera and taught himself the art through trial and error, building custom tools as needed. He documents how he captures transformative images of everyday objects with behind-the-scenes videos posted to macrofying, his photography and videography brand.
It was Bielfeldt’s curiosity about the inner workings of inkjet printers that inspired his winning entry, but capturing the action of ink drops being deposited on paper was a challenge, given that the process happens so quickly. The droplets, for instance, moved faster than the camera’s shutter speed. Bielfeldt’s solution was to deconstruct the printer so that the paper moved under a stationary (rather than moving) printhead, and then take the image in a dark room, using a flash to serve as the shutter, thereby freezing the ink drops mid-air. There was no need for pricey equipment. Bielfeldt does not use AI in his images, preferring to rely on traditional techniques.

articles.title: Calor extremo matou mais de 50 mil pessoas em cidades europeias no verão de 2026
articles.text:
As ondas de calor que atingiram a Europa no verão de 2026 podem ter causado 50.391 mortes em áreas urbanas do continente, segundo estimativas científicas revisadas por pares. Desse total, aproximadamente 32.619 óbitos — cerca de dois terços — são atribuídos ao aquecimento provocado pela atividade humana, principalmente pela queima de combustíveis fósseis.
Os números foram calculados por pesquisadores do Imperial College London e da Escola de Higiene e Medicina Tropical de Londres, ambos na Inglaterra. O estudo analisou 854 cidades e áreas urbanas de 30 países europeus, considerando dados meteorológicos, características da população e a relação entre temperaturas e mortalidade. Os resultados indicam que o verão de 2026 foi o mais mortal por calor desde o início da série analisada, em 2000.
A estimativa representa aumento de aproximadamente 71% em relação a 2022, quando o calor provocou cerca de 29.480 mortes nas mesmas áreas. O verão de 2003, marcado por ondas de calor devastadoras, registrou estimativa de 28.462 óbitos.
Como os pesquisadores calcularam as mortes
- Os números não correspondem a uma contagem oficial de pessoas cujas certidões de óbito apontaram o calor como causa da morte. As temperaturas elevadas também podem agravar problemas cardiovasculares e respiratórios, por exemplo, sem que o calor seja identificado diretamente nos registros médicos;
- Para estimar esse impacto, os pesquisadores combinaram dados de temperatura, informações demográficas e modelos que relacionam as condições climáticas ao risco de morte. Em seguida, simularam um cenário hipotético no qual o planeta não teria sido aquecido pelas emissões humanas de gases de efeito estufa. A diferença entre os resultados dos dois cenários permitiu calcular a parcela das mortes associada ao aquecimento provocado pela atividade humana;
- O levantamento, porém, tem limitações. As 854 áreas analisadas representam aproximadamente 40% da população dos países considerados, e os resultados não necessariamente refletem a situação de toda a Europa. Além disso, os cálculos não incluem uma onda de calor registrada em maio, o que pode fazer com que o total estimado para o verão fique abaixo do impacto real.
Leia mais:
- Tempestades de calor se multiplicaram e já atingem quase todo o planeta
- Eleições 2026: o que Lula e Flávio Bolsonaro propõem para clima e energia
- Temporais avançam pelo Brasil e podem atingir várias regiões
Uma onda de calor concentrou parte das mortes
Segundo os pesquisadores, cerca de um terço das mortes estimadas ocorreu entre 17 de junho e 1º de julho, durante um episódio particularmente intenso. Nesse período, as temperaturas ficaram, em média, 5,3 °C acima do normal.
Em algumas cidades europeias, a diferença em relação às temperaturas habituais chegou a 12 °C. O calor extremo também expôs trabalhadores ao ar livre a condições perigosas e contribuiu para incêndios florestais de grandes proporções na França e na Espanha. Os incêndios deslocaram cerca de 300 mil pessoas.
O verão de 2026 foi o mais quente já registrado na Europa Ocidental e o terceiro mais quente no continente como um todo.
Idosos foram os mais afetados
As pessoas com 85 anos ou mais concentraram mais da metade das mortes estimadas relacionadas ao calor. Ainda assim, os efeitos não ficaram restritos à população idosa: mais de 800 mortes foram estimadas entre pessoas de 20 a 44 anos, segundo Garyfallos Konstantinoudis, pesquisador do Imperial College London que participou do estudo.
A vulnerabilidade ao calor varia de acordo com fatores, como idade, condições socioeconômicas, características das cidades e acesso aos serviços de saúde. Clair Barnes, cientista climática do Imperial College London e principal autora dos estudos, afirmou que o aquecimento provocado pela atividade humana elevou ainda mais o risco de morte durante episódios de calor que já seriam perigosos.
A Europa também vem ampliando o monitoramento dos impactos das altas temperaturas. Agências de saúde de países, como Reino Unido, França, Alemanha e Espanha, passaram a divulgar estimativas de mortes relacionadas ao calor enquanto o verão ainda está em andamento, segundo Barnes.
Os pesquisadores defendem que a preparação para temperaturas extremas inclua sistemas de alerta, acesso a formas de resfriamento e medidas para proteger as populações mais vulneráveis. A redução das emissões de gases de efeito estufa também é apontada como necessária para limitar o agravamento dos riscos à saúde.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: OpenAI makes its Jev competitor widely available as decision model competition heats up | TechCrunch
articles.text:
OpenAI made its Decisions API model widely available to users for the first time, entering the market for fast, cheap intelligence that recently made TypeSafe, a startup founded by a former researcher at the frontier lab, a $7.6 billion company.
TypeSafe’s Jev model created a category for deep learning models that act as super classifiers: Given a set of options, they can quickly make choices and offer a confidence rating in their decision. Software developers quickly found that these decision or System One models could replace LLMs in a variety of workflows, operating more quickly and a at dramatically lower cost.
Nikunj Handa, the product lead for OpenAI’s APIs, told TechCrunch that his colleagues saw Jev and said “wow, we we have like a million use cases for this.” Handa’s team sprinted to offer their own version: Rather than building a specifically calibrated decision model, the team took ChatGPT Luna and reconfigured it to speed up the inference and lower the cost.
“The big unlock with Decisions API has been the speed, shrinking things from one to three seconds to 100, 120, 180 milliseconds,” Handa said. “In the future, we may sort of like have specific training to make our models like even better in these ways. But right now, it’s just plain old Luna that gets the job done.”
Announced at the company’s developer day on September 29, the Decisions API became available to all customers on Thursday. OpenAI added new voice and visual modalities to the public version, and worked to ensure lower latency in regions around the world by targeting its inference resources geographically.
In initial trials with customers like Box, Datadog, Ramp, and Speak, engineers used the API to replace OpenAI’s LLMs with higher throughput. Andrew Hsu, the CTO at Speak, which builds AI language tutors, said the Decisions API allowed the company to cut the time between actions from 1.4 seconds to .13 seconds. OpenAI also used the product to improve their Dots voice assistant’s responsiveness.
Still, it’s not clear exactly what makes a good decision model, other than “it works for you” — optimization across intelligence, cost, calibration, and speed seems to differ by workload. TypeSafe CEO Diogo Almeida distrusts benchmarks and urges people to trial the models in their own work, but even TypeSafe released its own rankings last week alongside the release of its latest Jev model, which includes new features including support for images and smart-if statements.
Public benchmarks like the AIM System One Index and the Artificial Analysis Decision Index tend to favor D1 Ultra, a new decision model that Liquid released last week, and Base Lab’s Elephant-1. The latest Jev model remains competitive on both indices, in seventh and third, with OpenAI’s Decision Model falling eighth and fourteenth, respectively. However, TypeSafe’s offerings are, for now, the most widely-queried on OpenRouter.
The most fun Jev benchmark, however, is JevMan, a benchmark where decision models play PacMan; the latest Jev model tops that ranking. Felix Wunderlich, the chief growth officer at Opper AI, which built the benchmark, said the classic game “is an interesting test because of its nonstop stream of quick, high-stakes decisions. At every junction the model must decide where to go in a few hundred milliseconds.”
Where OpenAI’s arguably more capable model may have an advantage is in multi-modality—for image classification, “Luna is extremely powerful and has been showing better calibrations,” Handa told TechCrunch, adding that OpenAI customers want the Decisions API to be more flexible about using images as outputs as well.
Handa also saw further increases in speed enabling new use cases: “Can we get this to something like you know 60 milliseconds, and then you could imagine like an API like call like for every single frame in like a video?”
As these offerings get faster and cheaper, we can expect them to live up to Jev’s namesake, an economist who explained how using a resource more efficiently makes it more ubiquitous. Or, as Handa sees it, there will be an expanding “crazy set of use cases” that were hiding in plain sight until the decision models revealed them.

articles.title: Es oficial: 'Carrie' tendrá segunda temporada en Prime Video
articles.text:
Era solo cuestión de tiempo hasta que se anunciara, y ya es oficial: Carrie regresará a Prime Video con una segunda temporada. La aclamada serie de Mike Flanagan, basada en la obra homónima de Stephen King, expandirá su adaptación televisiva con más episodios que irán más allá de los eventos contemplados dentro del libro original.
Amazon MGM Studios lo hizo oficial a través de su blog oficial, apenas un par de semanas después de que la primera temporada de Carrie cosechara excelentes críticas tanto del público como la prensa especializada, convirtiéndose además en uno de los títulos originales más exitosos de Prime Video.
Carrie debutó en la plataforma de streaming de Amazon el pasado 7 de octubre y se convirtió en un hit inmediato. De acuerdo con la compañía, la miniserie de Flanagan alcanzó de inmediato el primer puesto del ranking de títulos más vistos en 105 países.
Si bien la nueva serie de Carrie cubre los eventos del libro de Stephen King al completo, su conclusión dejaba abierta la puerta a una posible continuación. Es posible que su concreción o no estuviese vinculada con la recepción que lograra tanto en críticas como en cantidad de espectadores, por lo que no sorprende esta renovación para una segunda temporada.
Además de ser N°1 en los rankings de Prime Video en más de un centenar de mercados, Carrie ha gozado de muy buenas reacciones de parte del público y la prensa. En Rotten Tomatoes, por ejemplo, tiene un 85 % de calificaciones positivas de los críticos y un 82 % de comentarios favorables del público.
Carrie tendrá temporada 2 en Prime Video
Uno de los puntos fuertes de Carrie, de Mike Flanagan, fue que logró adaptar una historia escrita hace más de 50 años a los tiempos modernos. En la serie, Carrie White se ve envuelta en una campaña de bullying y acoso escolar a través de redes sociales, lo que también deriva en el escándalo del baile de graduación.
Sin entrar en demasiados spoilers, la serie de Carrie también aborda la mítica escena del baño con sangre de cerdo y las consecuencias del despliegue total de los poderes de la protagonista. Flanagan ha mantenido varios de los puntos cruciales del libro de Stephen King que en su momento también vimos en el clásico cinematográfico de Brian de Palma. Sin embargo, la conclusión de los primeros 8 capítulos hace un par de cambios drásticos respecto del libro original y de la película de 1976.
Todavía no se sabe qué historias presentará temporada 2 de Carrie, ni tampoco qué integrantes del elenco original regresarán. Es un hecho que Summer H. Howell repetirá su aclamada interpretación como Carrie White, pero lo demás es todavía un misterio. Tampoco hay detalles sobre cuándo podría estrenarse, pero tiene sentido pensar que la próxima entrega se hará esperar un par de años como mínimo.
Prueba Amazon Prime Video totalmente gratis durante 30 días y disfruta del catálogo completo de la plataforma sin límites. Solo con darte de alta tendrás acceso instantáneo a las mejores películas y series, además de envíos gratis en Amazon y otras ventajas.
Por lo pronto, Stephen King le ha dado el visto bueno al trabajo de Flanagan y a lo que traerá Carrie en el futuro. "Me muero de ganas de que el público vea lo que le espera a Carrie White. Mike Flanagan y yo estamos entusiasmados con lo que viene a continuación. Sin duda, será algo apasionante", comentó el autor.

articles.title: Spotify says yes, it is busting people for using Family Plan sharing too widely
articles.text:
Spotify co-CEO Alex Norström confirmed on this week’s earnings call that the company is trying to catch Spotify Family plan users who don’t actually live together with a new QR code verification method that requires scanning the plan manager’s phone. TechCrunch reports that in response to a question about the “crackdown,” he called it a “routine improvement” instead:
Spotify says yes, it is busting people for using Family Plan sharing too widely
Spotify’s co-CEO said it will keep tweaking verification as people ‘find holes around’ methods like its new QR codes over time.
This is not as much a crackdown as it is actually a routine improvement of our verification methods for our Family Plan. Family Plan has existed for a long while. It has been around for, I think it is now close to 12, 13 years in Spotify history, and it makes up a pretty significant proportion of our subscriber base.
As such, it is important for us to just make sure over time that we improve the verification methods that we have. There are certainly ways, over time, to find holes around it. As that happens, we figure out how to improve it over time. This is not something that has an end date. This is not an implementation that is going to complete. This is just ongoing routine.
This isn’t the first time Spotify has tried to limit sharing Family plans, which it says are only for people living in the same household. The new QR code verification method has forced some users to get creative to stay on their shared Premium subscriptions — the code refreshes every few seconds and anyone who misses the seven-day window to scan it gets banned from joining a different Family or Duo plan for 12 months.

articles.title: Chip Scaling Moves Beyond The Transistor
articles.text:
SEMICON West 2026: Advanced packaging, photonics, test, and AI are increasingly intertwined; very different conversations ahead.
Key Takeaways:
When SEMICON West gathered in San Francisco in 2023, the semiconductor industry was forecasting a path to $1 trillion in annual revenue by 2030. Three years later, the industry has already blown past that number. SEMICON West 2026 returned to San Francisco with a sold-out exhibit floor, more than 30,000 attendees, and an industry confronting a different question: How does it keep up with the growth it once aimed for?
SEMI’s own projections show how steep that curve has become. In his opening keynote, SEMI President and CEO Ajit Manocha forecast a market of more than $2 trillion by 2030, and potentially $3 trillion by 2035. At the SEMI Market Symposium, the association projected 300mm fab equipment spending of $149 billion this year, rising to $227 billion by 2029, with construction beginning on 20 new 300mm fabs or production lines in 2026 alone.
AI infrastructure is driving much of that growth, but electrification, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and industrial automation are adding semiconductor content, as well. What makes the current expansion unusual is the growing complexity of the systems those chips will enable, not the almost insatiable demand for chips.
“We’ve started talking about how to re-engineer engineering because you need to co-design and optimize across multiple intersections,” said Sassine Ghazi, president and CEO of Synopsys. “That’s at the physics level, material, process technology, architecture, design, along with the software and the model itself, because the model itself is what’s defining the workload, and how do you optimize along that stack?”
Across presentations, panels, and discussions on the show floor, several issues kept converging around that problem. Advanced packaging is becoming part of system architecture. Photonics is moving closer to compute, while bringing new manufacturing and test challenges with it. Test, inspection and metrology have to follow more complicated assemblies and manufacturing histories. And AI is moving from something the industry builds to something it uses to design and manufacture. None of these technologies is new, but each is becoming harder to optimize independently, and that may be the clearest indication of what the industry will be working on in the coming years.
Scaling becomes a system-level challenge 
The shift was apparent in conversations ranging from transistor scaling and HBM to advanced packaging, optical interconnects, and cooling, where improving any one of those can move a bottleneck elsewhere. More compute increases pressure on memory bandwidth and power delivery. Moving memory closer reduces data movement but concentrates heat. Disaggregating a large die can improve yield and allow functions to use different process nodes, but it creates more interfaces that have to be connected, powered, cooled, and tested.
“Packaging is no longer simply the place where semiconductor innovation ends,” said Lalitha Immaneni, vice president of semiconductor R&D at Intel Foundry. “Increasingly, it’s the place where system innovation begins.”
That makes memory, data movement, power delivery, and thermal management part of the architecture rather than downstream considerations.
“The challenge is not to co-optimize one component,” Immaneni said. “It is to co-optimize across the system from end to end between silicon, packaging, and platform.”
Nitin Deshpande, Marvell’s vice president of advanced packaging, made a similar point during imec’s pre-show ITF USA program. “The package is really becoming a system where the compute, the memory, the interconnects, the power, the cooling, all of these things come together.”
Making those pieces work together is only part of the challenge. Larger, more heterogeneous packages still have to become high-volume products with acceptable yield, reliability, and cost.
“We can have very cool concepts, but if we cannot scale these into high volumes, if we cannot have a high-yielding, reliable process with a supply chain that can provide the parts in time, everything that we do cannot be converted into a business,” Deshpande said.
Patrick Vandenameele, CEO of imec, noted that AI infrastructure can keep growing by adding accelerators and racks, but adding hardware isn’t scaling in the traditional semiconductor sense. “These data centers are true engineering marvels,” he said. “But at the same time, this is not what we semiconductor people call scaling. It looks a little bit more like multiplication.”
That distinction helps explain why so many separate topics at SEMICON West kept leading back to the same place. The industry isn’t abandoning transistor scaling. It’s adding another level above it, where performance depends on how effectively different technologies can be combined into a functional system.
Fig. 2: Redefining a system. Source: SEMI
AI moves from assistant to operator 
AI was nearly impossible to avoid at SEMICON West, but the conversation is shifting. Machine learning has been part of design, process control, and defect classification for years, and generative AI added natural-language access to complicated tools and data. Agentic AI goes further, allowing engineers to hand an agent an objective and let it invoke other tools, models, or agents to reach it.
“We started from an assistant copilot to generative capability to now what we’re describing as long-horizon autonomous agents, where instead of giving a prompt, you give an outcome,” said Synopsys’ Ghazi.
The appeal of agentic AI becomes clearer when looking at the size of the spaces engineers are being asked to optimize. “The space that we’re optimizing in has exploded,” said David Fried, chief AI officer and corporate vice president of Semiverse Solutions at Lam Research. “We’ve now gotten to a place where the parameter set is intractable.”
A current Lam etcher, for example, can have a potential recipe space on the order of 1023 possibilities, which is well beyond what any engineer can explore manually. “That’s really where AI is coming to the rescue,” Fried said. “It’s the ability to get through massive multi-parameter dimensional spaces, massive sets of intertwined sensitivities between a much larger parameter space, and a much larger spec space.”
Acting on what AI finds is where the discussion gets more complicated. Flagging an unusual process signature is different from letting an AI system alter a recipe, and predicting equipment degradation is different from stopping production. Ghazi said Synopsys already has engagements where autonomous agents can take a customer specification through verified RTL. This is work that traditionally required multiple engineers and months. Human judgment is still needed to define the architecture and sign off before manufacturing, but the boundary is moving.
On the manufacturing side, that raises questions likely to become more prominent over the next year. What decisions can an agent make without approval? How much of its constraint comes from physics-based models rather than statistical inference? What evidence is required before an autonomous decision can affect production?
The question coming out of SEMICON West isn’t whether AI will be used to design and manufacture semiconductors. That’s already happening. The new question is how much authority engineers are prepared to give it.
Fig. 3: What comes next is an evolving topic of great interest to a lot of people. Source: SEMI
Packaging has to become manufacturable 
Advanced packaging showed up almost everywhere, but the emphasis has moved beyond proving that heterogeneous integration works. The harder problem is doing it repeatedly, economically, and at volume while protecting the value accumulated during assembly. That is changing the meaning of “known good.”
Known-good die has been an objective for years, because attaching a bad die to a good package wastes everything around it. As substrates, bridges, and intermediate assemblies grow more complicated and expensive, the same logic is moving outward.
“Even though the bridge is a passive component with just metal lines, we sort it,” said Ravi Mahajan, Intel fellow and director of substrate and advanced packaging pathfinding at Intel Foundry. “We make sure we have known-good bridges going into a package, and what comes out should be a known-good package.”
Mahajan was careful to treat “known good” as an aspiration rather than an absolute.
“You bring into your assembly process a known-good substrate, and the word ‘known-good’ has to be understood,” Mahajan said. “It’s not always known-good, but you know as much of this as you can. And to do that, you put in the right kind of features to test so that you have as much coverage as possible.”
ASE is approaching the problem in much the same way. In some fan-out flows, the interconnect structure can be fully tested before any active silicon is attached.
“The known-good methodology is what we’re striving for,” said Yin Chang, executive vice president of ASE. “Everything we do, every layer, we have the ability to confirm that it is good before we put on the most expensive part.”
Some silicon and HBM combinations can represent as much as $30,000 in value, and ASE uses AOI and X-ray extensively, with AI helping distinguish subtle differences across assemblies that can contain as many as half a million joints.
“The goal for our industry is trying to take out as much unknown as we can in the overall processes,” Chang said. “It is too expensive already today. We just can’t scrap anything.”
Assembly complicates that goal. Bonding creates interfaces that didn’t exist when the individual components were inspected, and heat, pressure, and materials interactions can alter the state of the assembly, so some defects can’t be detected until another process step has occurred. The objective progressively becomes how to reduce uncertainty as value is added, and the sampling calculation shifts from how much inspection maintains yield to how much uncertainty a manufacturer can afford to carry into the next step.
Test follows the system 
That same pressure is reshaping test, particularly as photonics enters the package. Digital manufacturing test compares a response with an expected result, but optical devices can produce a range of acceptable responses that still have to be correlated with possible defects. Co-packaged optics adds a physical problem, as well.
“What our customers are demanding from OSATs is to be able to do dual-sided electrical/optical probe and expect efficiencies,” said Vineet Pancholi, senior director, manufacturing test technologist at Amkor. “Even if the ASPs are that high, they are still looking for manufacturing tests to be way more efficient.”
“The mechanical structure is different,” Pancholi said. “The package, physical x,y,z, weight of the package, the density of the package — that’s all changing. All of it is changing.” Asked whether those changes were increasing test-cell time, the number of insertions, or both, he added. “The high-level test workflow with probe, burn-in, final test, and system-level-test insertions remains the same. However, since the optical test content is newly being architected, test times are expected to be higher in the short term. They are expected to lower once defects based on fabrication and assembly process maturity are attained.”
Knowing where a problem occurred also depends increasingly on retaining information from earlier process steps.
“Even if you don’t know exactly which level it is, you can bracket the issue from historical images,” said Reiner Fenske, CEO of Microtronic.
Microtronic is approaching inspection partly as a historical record, retaining wafer images that can be compared across process steps when a defect appears later. That becomes increasingly valuable as additional layers make earlier defects difficult or impossible to see.
“The information that we gather is so valuable to them that throughput is a secondary issue, but having the history, that’s key,” Fenske said. “So six months from now, you can retrieve the entire lot run from archive which retains all of the data and images.”
Determining whether something is good increasingly requires context. Wafer test results, inspection data, assembly history and earlier insertions can be fed forward to alter later testing or fed backward to identify process drift. At the same time, following a die from its original wafer coordinates through reconstituted wafers, panels and multi-die assemblies makes traceability much harder.
Test is becoming less a final pass/fail gate than a continuous evidence trail, and that brings it into the AI discussion as well. AI can find patterns across that history, but only if the data can be tied to the right device, process step, and physical context.
Photonics faces manufacturing challenges 
The motivation for photonics is well established. Electrical interconnects struggle with power and signal integrity as bandwidth and distance rise, pushing optics from pluggable modules toward near-package and co-packaged designs. The closer optics gets to compute, however, the more the problem moves into semiconductor manufacturing.
“For precision bonding, it needs to not only control in all six degrees of freedom,” said Huan Ma, senior technologist at Intel Foundry. “It also needs to deliver throughput at a semiconductor manufacturing scale with automation and standardized material handling.”
The same requirement extends to materials, which have to preserve alignment through assembly, reflow and reliability stresses, and to metrology.
“For metrology and inspection, how do we measure the variables that actually predict optical yield?” Ma said. “We need to measure the geometry, the angles, the positions of optical features, and what really matters to the insertion loss and to the coupling efficiency. Co-packaged optics will not scale just because the optics work. It will only scale when we industrialize the optics through advanced packaging.”
The same issues surfaced across the show floor. EV Group pointed to the metrology and throughput burden of measuring multiple alignment points across hundreds of dies in die-to-wafer integration. Lam Research discussed waveguide fabrication, new modulator materials, and fiber coupling. Advantest described high-volume test as one of the remaining bottlenecks, with electro-optical probing and optical connectors adding requirements that don’t exist in electrical test.
Assembly complicates known-good here, too, because alignment, bonding, thermal processing and fiber attachment can alter an optical path that met specification before integration.
“Coming through the door, you have an understanding of what is known good on the PIC and the EIC,” Intel’s Mahajan said. “The biggest question is how do you ensure you have alignment? These processes in photonics are not recoverable and not reworkable, so we have spent a lot of time figuring out the yield limiters in assembly.”
Mahajan doesn’t see an intrinsic barrier, pointing to fiber attachment as a step considered particularly difficult less than a decade ago, but which has improved substantially through repeated process learning.
“I cannot think of any intrinsic showstoppers in any of these processes,” he said. “It’s now a matter of practice to do it right.”
The question surrounding co-packaged optics is becoming less about whether the technology can work and more about how quickly it can be aligned, inspected, tested, and manufactured at semiconductor volumes.
Engineering boundaries are blurring 
What stood out at SEMICON West was how often discussions in one area crossed into another. A package decision becomes a thermal decision. Memory placement becomes a power decision. Photonics becomes a packaging and test problem, inspection becomes a data problem, and manufacturing data becomes an AI problem. The old engineering boundaries still exist organizationally, but they increasingly don’t describe the physical system.
In her keynote, Intel’s Immaneni described the response as moving beyond design-technology co-optimization toward system-technology co-optimization, where silicon, packaging, and platform are considered together.
“A beautiful technology can be a good choice, but if I cannot manufacture it repeatedly, quickly, and with high quality, then it is not a customer technology,” she said.
Digital twins fit into the same transition, but their value depends on connecting electrical, thermal, mechanical, and manufacturing models closely enough that a decision in one domain can be evaluated against its consequences in the others. During his discussion with Semiconductor Engineering Editor-in-Chief Ed Sperling, Synopsys’ Ghazi added the workload to that list, since model behavior can drive power and thermal conditions in the hardware underneath it. As AI expands into robots, vehicles and other physical systems, sensors, safety requirements and real-time constraints compound the problem further.
Conclusion: Five months to Phoenix 
SEMICON West won’t have a full year to see how those conversations develop. This was the show’s last scheduled run in San Francisco. SEMI has signed a three-year agreement with Phoenix, and the next event moves to the Phoenix Convention Center March 30 through April 1, 2027, beginning a new spring schedule. That leaves about five months between shows, and some useful markers should be visible by then.
Fig. 4: View from the show floor. Source: SEMI
Agentic AI will be judged by which engineering and manufacturing decisions companies are willing to let agents make, and the constraints they apply. Heterogeneous integration will put more pressure on inspection, metrology, and test to establish confidence before more value is committed to assembly. Co-packaged optics will have to move from demonstrations toward repeatable manufacturing. Alongside those, high-NA EUV is moving toward production, power delivery is moving deeper into packages, and materials suppliers are being asked to understand interface and process interactions that aren’t part of traditional specifications.
Three years ago, SEMICON West was talking about how the industry could reach $1 trillion by 2030. Having reached that milestone years early, the conversation has changed. The challenge is no longer just increasing density or manufacturing more chips. It’s building increasingly complex semiconductor systems fast enough, reliably enough, and economically enough to keep pace.

articles.title: Bruxelles ouvre une enquête sur les pratiques de Booking.com
articles.text:
La Commission européenne soupçonne Booking.com de ne pas avoir évalué avec sérieux, ni réduit efficacement, les risques d’annonces frauduleuses et de phishing. Les autorités européennes vérifient aussi que les logements mis en avant contre paiement sont bien présentés comme des publicités.
La Commission européenne a ouvert hier une procédure formelle contre Booking.com au titre du règlement sur les services numériques (DSA). Trois sujets sont passés au crible : les fausses annonces, les arnaques qui exploitent les données de réservation et les annonces« boostées ».
Fausses annonces, messagerie détournée, publicités floues : ce que Bruxelles veut vérifier
Booking.com est classée VLOP (Very Large Online Platform) depuis le 25 avril 2023, un statut réservé aux plateformes de plus de 45 millions d’utilisateurs dans l’UE. Les articles 34 et 35 du DSA lui imposent d’identifier régulièrement les risques que son service peut créer, de les évaluer, puis de les réduire. Il y a tout d'abord les fausses inscriptions (logements inexistants, usurpation d’identité, hébergements non conformes). Selon The Register, la Commission vise notamment des personnes qui se font passer pour le propriétaire d’un bien qu’elles ne possèdent pas.
Le deuxième sujet concerne le phishing. La Commission regarde comment les données de réservation et d’invité sont partagées avec les hébergeurs, comment la messagerie de Booking.com est conçue, et si des garde-fous empêchent leur détournement. Elle soupçonne aussi une protection insuffisante des données des consommateurs et des professionnels. Dans le scénario décrit par ses porte-paroles, des escrocs prennent le contrôle du compte d’un propriétaire, récupèrent ses coordonnées et réclament des paiements supplémentaires aux voyageurs. Nous rapportions déjà le cas d'un voyageur qui, quelques minutes après sa réservation, recevait un message reprenant ses vraies informations, par WhatsApp, SMS, email ou via la messagerie de Booking.com. La plateforme affirmait alors que ses systèmes n’avaient pas été piratés.
Le troisième sujet concerne la publicité. Un hébergeur peut payer une commission plus élevée pour que son annonce remonte dans les résultats. Cette visibilité accentuée doit alors être identifiée comme une publicité. L’article 26, paragraphe 1, du DSA demande aussi que l’utilisateur sache qui est derrière l’annonce, qui l’a payée, pourquoi elle s’affiche et comment modifier les réglages qui la déterminent. Sans ces informations, difficile de savoir si un logement arrive en tête parce qu’il correspond à la recherche ou parce que l’hébergeur a payé.
Pour justifier la procédure, des responsables de la Commission rappellent que Booking.com a reconnu en juin 2024 une hausse de 500 à 900 % des arnaques au voyage sur 18 mois. Aux Pays-Bas, plus de 1 000 signalements ont été déposés début 2026, pour 82 000 euros de préjudice, soit dix fois plus qu’un an plus tôt. Booking.com prend déjà des mesures, mais la Commission juge l’évaluation des risques insuffisante. Elle attend un retrait rapide des annonces signalées, un contrôle des licences et une révision de l’accueil des propriétaires. La plateforme dit coopérer pleinement. Bruxelles va poursuivre l’enquête avec de nouvelles demandes d’informations, des entretiens ou des inspections. Elle peut aussi imposer des mesures provisoires, rendre une décision de non-conformité ou accepter des engagements de Booking.com.

articles.title: Laut einer Studie hält ein Drittel der Führungskräfte KI für schlauer als sich selbst: Was bedeutet das für Unternehmen?
articles.text:
Cognitive Offloading: Wie KI das Urteilsvermögen von Führungskräften untergräbt
Rund ein Drittel der Führungskräfte gibt an, KI mehr zu vertrauen als dem eigenen Urteilsvermögen. Bei Angestellten auf niedrigeren Positionen ist das nur etwa halb so häufig der Fall. Das geht aus einer Umfrage des Forschungs- und Medienunternehmens Charter hervor. Im August wurden dafür über 5.000 Personen in den USA befragt, die angaben, KI bei der Arbeit zu nutzen. Für Unternehmen entsteht aus dieser Begeisterung ein großes Problem: Sie stellen Führungskräfte wegen ihrer Erfahrung und ihres Wissens ein – nicht, um Entscheidungen an KI zu übergeben.
Führungskräfte lagern Denkprozesse aus
Immer mehr Menschen nutzen KI, um E-Mails vorzuformulieren, Präsentationen zu erstellen oder die Entscheidungsfindung zu beschleunigen. Dafür gibt es sogar einen eigenen Begriff: „Cognitive Offloading“. Er bezeichnet die Tendenz, Denkarbeit an ein KI-System auszulagern, um die eigene geistige Belastung zu verringern. Wer beispielsweise einen Text zusammenfassen lässt, statt ihn komplett selbst zu lesen, spart Zeit und kognitive Kapazität. Ähnliches gilt für die Auswertung von Lebensläufen oder aktuellen Geschäftszahlen.
Die Charter-Umfrage zeigt allerdings, dass die Erfahrungen von Führungs- und Fachkräften auseinandergehen. So fühlen sich rund 60 Prozent der Manager:innen im Umgang mit KI sehr kompetent. Bei den Beschäftigten sagen das nur knapp 37 Prozent. Ein ähnliches Bild zeigt sich bei der Frage, wer aktuell tatsächlich vom KI-Einsatz profitiert: 55 Prozent der Führungskräfte geben an, dass die Technologie sowohl ihre Arbeit als auch ihr persönliches Leben verbessere. Bei den Mitarbeiter:innen sagen das nur etwa halb so viele.
Rückgang kognitiver Fähigkeiten befürchtet
Die Charter-Forscher:innen erkennen in den Antworten der Befragten einen Teufelskreis. Von den Personen, die KI mehr als einmal täglich nutzen, sehen über 62 Prozent einen positiven Effekt auf ihre Arbeit und ihr Leben im Allgemeinen. Bei den Personen, die KI weniger als einmal pro Woche nutzen, sagen das nur neun Prozent. Besonders positiv äußern sich Führungskräfte, die über die meiste Erfahrung und Verantwortung verfügen. Laut den Autor:innen der Studie könnte das am hohen Druck liegen, unter dem viele von ihnen stehen. Sie müssen sehr schnell Antworten auf viele Fragen finden, wobei KI zumindest kurzfristig helfen könne.
Aber was passiert, wenn Menschen ihr Denken zunehmend an KI-Tools auslagern? Eine Studie des Center for Universal Education hat dieses Phänomen schon an Schüler:innen untersucht. Die Forscher:innen kamen zu dem Ergebnis, dass KI-Modelle Bildungsprozesse untergraben können, wenn Kinder ihr Denken zunehmend an KI abgeben. 65 Prozent der befragten Schüler:innen äußerten sogar selbst die Sorge, dass ihre kognitiven Fähigkeiten dadurch langfristig nachlassen könnten. „Es ist einfach. Man muss sein Gehirn nicht benutzen“, sagte ein Schüler den Forscher:innen gegenüber.
KI-Systeme haben kein echtes Urteilsvermögen
Dieses Phänomen erinnert an das sogenannte „Deskilling“: So wie beispielsweise Taschenrechner die mathematischen Fähigkeiten schwächen können, hat auch die Nutzung von KI Auswirkungen auf das Urteilsvermögen. Das zeigt auch eine Studie des MIT Media Lab: Proband:innen, die sich einen Monat lang bei der Faktenprüfung auf KI-Systeme verließen, waren danach schlechter darin, Falschinformationen zu erkennen, wenn der Chatbot nicht mehr zur Verfügung stand.
Anku Rani, Doktorandin und eine der Hauptautor:innen der Studie, warnt in einem Beitrag des MIT vor einer unkritischen KI‑Begeisterung. Nutzer:innen würden häufig vergessen, dass KI-Modelle lediglich statistische Vorhersagen treffen. Wenn Führungskräfte Datenauswertungen und Entscheidungen zunehmend an KI-Tools delegieren, steigt deshalb das Risiko von Halluzinationen, irreführenden Schlussfolgerungen oder Voreingenommenheiten – mit potenziellen Folgen für Mitarbeiter:innen und das gesamte Unternehmen.

articles.title: Pillages du 17 octobre : la police nationale fait polémique avec une photo de saisie retouchée par IA
articles.text:
Ces 17 et 18 octobre, environ 3 000 commerces ont été touchés et beaucoup ont été pillés. Vinted et Leboncoin sont inondés d’annonces de produits volés et de fausses cagnottes de soutien aux commerçant apparaissent. Parmi tout ce bazar, la police traque et arrête les pilleurs et receleurs. Dans le Val d’Oise, la Police Nationale en a attrapé 12 et a présenté les produits mis à la revente. Sauf que l’image des produits publiée a été générée par intelligence artificielle, bien que les produits existent.
La Police nationale publie une image générée par IA : les internautes le remarquent et font monter la polémique
C’est sur X ce 20 octobre que le compte de la Police Nationale du Val d’Oise a publié une image. On y voit des vêtements et des jeux vidéo exposés, résultats de l’interpellation de 12 receleurs dans le département. Cependant, des détails clochent : les logos des marques sont pleins de défauts, et les écritures sur la jaquette d’Elden Ring Nightreign sont assez étranges.
 #ValDOise | Présents. Mobilisés. Engagés. Ce week-end, @PoliceNat95 aux côtés de @prefpolice après les pillages à #Paris :
👉 1️⃣2️⃣ receleurs interpellés dans le 95
📦 Saisies :⌚ de grande valeur, 🧢 de marque, 👓 #LouisVuitton et autres produits de luxe encore munis d’antivols https://t.co/BODLxxVPoT
— Police Nationale 95 (@PoliceNat95) October 20, 2026
En passant l’image dans l’outil de vérification d’OpenAI ou de Google DeepMind, on remarque qu’elle a été générée avec les outils d’OpenAI. C’est même OpenAI qui le dit. En effet, il apparaît sur cette photo un filigrane SyntID provenant d’OpenAI : la photo a bel et bien été retouchée ou générée avec ChatGPT. Depuis quelques jours, il est possible d’utiliser ces outils SynthID gratuitement. Pour rappel, SynthID est une technologie développée par Google DeepMind qui ajoute des filigranes numériques invisibles sur les contenus générés par IA. Cela permet de les détecter plus tard, notamment pour démonter des fake news. SynthID fonctionne sur l’audio, la vidéo et les images, comme c’est le cas ici.
La police dément et donne la véritable explication
Il n’en fallait pas moins pour que des centaines d’internautes soient scandalisés sur X. Le tout dans un contexte de défiance d’une partie de la population envers la police, accusée de violences et de corporatisme. Beaucoup sous le premier tweet dénoncent en effet une manipulation de la part de la police, qui fabriquerait de fausses preuves pour justifier des interpellations de manifestants et de casseurs ou pilleurs.
Le lendemain, le compte officiel de la Police Nationale a publié un démenti : « Cette photo n’est pas une création 100% IA. » Le compte explique que sa section du Val d’Oise a modifié une image à l’aide d’une application d’IA « afin d’être recadrée et d’en retirer les éléments superflus (chaises et climatiseur). » Le tout sans publier de réponse en dessous du premier tweet. Mais le mal est fait : la publication originale a dépassé le million de vues en moins de 24 heures, quand la publication du démenti en compte près de quatre fois moins.
 👉🏻 Suivez l’actualité tech en temps réel : ajoutez 01net à vos sources sur Google, et abonnez-vous à notre canal WhatsApp.

articles.title: GitLab warns of new max severity code execution vulnerability
articles.text:
GitLab has released security patches for a maximum-severity Regular Expression Compiler flaw that can let remote attackers run arbitrary code on vulnerable servers.
This security issue is tracked as CVE-2026-110264 and was reported by a security researcher using the 'joaxcar' handle through GitLab's HackerOne bug bounty program.
CVE-2026-110264 stems from an integer overflow weakness in GitLab's Regular Expression Compiler, a background engine that parses and validates regular expressions in configuration files.
GitLab has fixed the vulnerability in GitLab Community Edition (CE) and Enterprise Edition (EE) versions 19.5.1, 19.4.3, 19.3.6, 19.2.9, 19.1.9, 19.0.10, and 18.11.13, and warned users to patch their instances immediately.
"GitLab has remediated an issue that, under certain conditions, could have allowed an unauthenticated user to execute arbitrary code on the GitLab server due to integer overflow when compiling a specially crafted regular expression," the company said.
"We strongly recommend that all installations running a version affected by the issues described below are upgraded to the latest version as soon as possible. [..] GitLab.com is already running the patched version. GitLab Dedicated tenants running 19.3.5-internal0 and 19.4.2-internal0 or later already include these fixes and do not need to take action."
Internet threat watchdog Shadowserver now tracks over 2,700 GitLab Community Edition instances exposed online, but it doesn't provide any information about how many of them are honeypots or have already been secured against attacks.
GitLab warned customers ten days ago about another critical remote code execution vulnerability (CVE-2026-97229) with a 10/10 CVSS base score in the CI/CD Regular Expression Compiler, reported by the same security researcher.
Last month, it fixed another maximum-severity GitLab CE/EE flaw (CVE-2026-85706) that lets unauthenticated attackers read sensitive data (e.g., credentials and other secrets) from vulnerable servers.
One day later, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added CVE-2026-85706 to its list of actively exploited flaws and ordered federal agencies to secure their systems within three days.
Since November 2021, CISA has flagged five GitLab flaws used in the wild, including one exploited in ransomware attacks.
GitLab's DevSecOps platform has over 30 million registered users worldwide and is used by over 50% of Fortune 100 companies, including Nvidia, T-Mobile, Lockheed Martin, Airbus, and Goldman Sachs.
Once attackers have valid credentials, only 37% of their actions are blocked
Overall prevention scores can hide what happens after initial access. Once attackers are using valid credentials, prevention drops sharply.

articles.title: Cette batterie externe EcoFlow 20 000 mAh, avec son câble USB-C rétractable, perd 44 % de son prix — Frandroid
articles.text:
On connaît surtout EcoFlow pour ses stations d’alimentation haut de gamme. Le fabricant décline aussi son savoir-faire en format nomade, avec tout un tas de solutions pour ne plus tomber en rade de batterie. La Rapid 20 000 mAh reprend d’ailleurs la protection X-Guard de ces grosses stations et vise clairement les possesseurs de Samsung Galaxy, avec la charge rapide officielle de la marque. Aujourd’hui, elle profite en plus d’une remise de 44 % sur Amazon.
Les atouts de l’EcoFlow Rapid 20 000 mAh
- Charge rapide PPS 45 W, compatible Super Fast Charging 2.0 de Samsung
- Un câble USB-C de 25 cm fixé au boîtier, qui sert aussi de dragonne
- Trois appareils rechargés en même temps, via le câble intégré, un port USB-C et un port USB-A, avec 45 watts au total
Sur Amazon, l’EcoFlow Rapid 20 000 mAh est proposée à 27,99 euros au lieu de 49,99 euros, le prix de référence affiché par Amazon.
Un câble intégré pour ne plus fouiller le sac
Cette batterie mise d’abord sur son câble USB-C de 25 cm, fixé directement au boîtier. On branche le téléphone et c’est parti, sans câble à chercher. Attention, il ne se rembobine pas : il reste dehors une fois la recharge terminée. Pas de câble à transporter à part (ni à oublier sur la table de nuit d’un hôtel), pas de connecteur qui finit tordu au fond d’une poche. Ce même câble fait office de dragonne pour la porter à la main.
Pendant la recharge, le smartphone reste collé à la batterie, ce qui oblige à garder les deux dans la main ou posés côte à côte. Pour brancher une tablette ou des écouteurs en parallèle, il faudra passer par le port USB-C ou le port USB-A, avec vos propres câbles. Les trois sorties se partagent 45 W au total : avec plusieurs appareils branchés, le Galaxy n’a plus droit à sa charge rapide maximale.
45 W pour les Galaxy, 20 000 mAh pour tenir le week-end
La Rapid s’appuie sur la norme PPS à 45 W, celle qu’utilise Samsung pour son Super Fast Charging 2.0. Selon EcoFlow, un Galaxy S25 Ultra passe ainsi de 0 à 50 % en 30 minutes. Les autres smartphones USB-C se rechargent aussi, mais ce chiffre annoncé concerne bien les Galaxy compatibles. Gardez en tête qu’il s’agit des données du fabricant : nous n’avons pas mesuré ces temps de charge nous-mêmes.
Avec ses 20 000 mAh, la batterie promet jusqu’à trois recharges complètes d’iPhone, un peu plus de trois pour un Galaxy S25 et jusqu’à 1,5 recharge de MacBook Air. Honnêtement, c’est le genre de réserve qui tient un week-end entier sans chercher de prise. Pour l’ordinateur portable, voyez-la plutôt comme une roue de secours. La protection X-Guard surveille en temps réel la surchauffe, la surcharge, la décharge profonde et les courts-circuits. EcoFlow assure qu’on peut ainsi la laisser branchée sur un téléphone toute la nuit.
Si vous souhaitez la comparer à des modèles plus compacts ou plus puissants, jetez un œil à notre guide des meilleures batteries externes.

articles.title: Why Yango doesn't see Africa's fragmentation as a flaw
articles.text:
Ask any founder who has built a business across different African markets, and they would agree the continent’s digital market is fragmented. The fragmentation shows up in how people pay, how businesses are regulated, consumer behaviour, and how digital services are delivered.
Companies also face different licencing requirements, tax regimes, data rules, infrastructure availability, and consumer behaviours as they move from one country to the next. Even within a single country, the rules can sometimes change from one city to another.
Norebase’s State of Expansion in Africa 2026 report offers a glimpse into just how different those markets can be. Based on data from more than 40,000 companies that have expanded through its platform, the report found differences in how long it takes to establish a business across African countries, as well as the rules and requirements companies have to navigate.
Yango Group, a Dubai-headquartered company that provides digital services, including mobility, delivery, foodtech, and entertainment across over 30 countries, has had to contend with many of those differences as it expands across African markets.
However, Adeniyi Adebayo, the company’s Chief Business Officer, sees the fragmentation differently. In an interview with TechCabal in October, he argued that while Africa is undoubtedly fragmented, the differences are more nuanced than they are often made out to be.
The smartest people in African tech are TC Insiders.
Join other readers from across the continent.

articles.title: Panne réseau mobile Orange : l'opérateur annonce un geste commercial en guise de dédommagement
articles.text:
Panne réseau mobile Orange : l'opérateur annonce un geste commercial en guise de dédommagement
Après sa panne nationale le 21 octobre 2026, Orange a annoncé quelle forme prendrait le dédommagement pour les millions de clients affectés. Si vous espériez un remboursement, c'est raté.
Si vous êtes client mobile Orange ou Sosh, nul doute que vous aurez remarqué qu'hier, mercredi 21 octobre 2026, le réseau mobile de l'opérateur était en panne une bonne partie de la journée. Après 9 h de crise, le service a été restauré dans la soirée, permettant aux utilisateurs de passer à nouveau des appels, d'envoyer des messages et de naviguer sur Internet. Au lendemain de l'incident, et alors que bien des utilisateurs se demandent déjà comment Orange va se faire pardonner, ce dernier a annoncé sa décision.
Une compensation d'Orange qui ne servira pas à grand monde
Si certains espéraient une ristourne sur leur prochaine facture, il va falloir revoir leurs espoirs à la baisse. En effet, Orange a annoncé : "Afin de compenser ces désagréments […], Orange a décidé de doubler l’enveloppe de data incluse dans le forfait de ses clients concernés pendant un mois, à compter du prochain renouvellement de leur forfait."
Ainsi, si vous disposez d'un forfait avec 100 Go d'enveloppe de données, au prochain renouvellement vous pourrez profiter de 200 Go. Bien des clients risquent de ne pas avoir l'utilité de cette quantité doublée, comme ceux disposant déjà d'une grosse enveloppe, ceux ne consommant que peu de data, ou encore les clients 4G et 5G Box, qui ont déjà data illimitée.
Le réseau mobile Orange est rétabli.
Les appels, SMS et services mobiles sont de nouveau opérationnels pour l’ensemble de nos clients, particuliers comme entreprises.
Nos équipes techniques restent mobilisées et continuent de surveiller le réseau pour garantir la stabilité des…
— Orange France (@Orange_France) October 21, 2026
Orange n'indique pas comment il compte identifier les clients concernés par la panne, ni si une action sera à réaliser côté client pour pouvoir en profiter. En juin 2025, SFR offrait 100 Go automatiquement à ses abonnés après une panne.
En 2012, après une panne nationale similaire, Orange proposait alors deux compensations, à savoir une journée d’appels et de SMS gratuits ou 1 Go de données mobiles. Pas question là encore d'une réduction sur la facture.
Pour obtenir un geste plus concret, il faudra contacter directement le service client d'Orange et de Sosh, en respectant des conditions souvent complexes. Chez Orange, pour espérer une poignée d'euros de réduction sur sa prochaine facture, les clients peuvent demander un remboursement au prorata de la durée d’interruption totale du service, après avoir signalé l'incident et en justifiant leur présence dans la zone concernée. Chez Sosh, c'est encore plus compliqué, car les pannes qui durent moins de 2 jours ouvrés ne sont pas éligibles.
La cause de la panne se dessine
Concernant les raisons de la panne du 21 octobre, Orange évoque vaguement qu'un "incident technique a eu lieu sur un équipement de notre nouveau cœur de réseau qui a impacté une partie de nos abonnés sur le territoire". D'après les bruits de couloirs, un problème lié à l’introduction et à la migration vers un nouveau cœur de réseau mobile 5G serait plus spécifiquement en cause.

articles.title: Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
articles.text:
Who on-calls an AI? This is the unresolved crisis of agent ownership
At 2:07 a.m., an AI agent starts failing.
The application is still running, but requests are timing out because a downstream API is returning errors. The agent has already retried twice, using more tokens than usual, and its response time has roughly doubled.
The first question should not be:
	“Which model should we use?”
It should be:
	“Who owns this system right now?”
That question is easy to overlook when building AI agents. Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.
“Teams often pour effort into prompts, retrieval, tools, and model selection, but production ownership determines whether an agent becomes a dependable service or another source of operational risk.”
A production agent needs an owner, boundaries, telemetry, failure policies, escalation paths, and a clear distinction between what the system may automate and what requires human intervention.
A production agent should not have a direct path from reasoning to action. Each tool invocation should pass through explicit controls, remain observable, and have a defined path to human intervention.
Here’s a practical way to build those controls.
Step 1: Treat the agent as a production service
An agent should have the same operational identity as any other production service.
Start by defining its ownership metadata.
Python
from pydantic import BaseModel
class AgentService(BaseModel):
    name: str
    owner_team: str
    service_tier: str
    escalation_channel: str
agent_service = AgentService(
    name="incident-command-agent",
    owner_team="platform-engineering",
    service_tier="critical",
    escalation_channel="#platform-oncall",
)
This may look simple, but it changes the conversation.
The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.
“The agent is no longer an experiment running somewhere in a Python process. It is a service with an accountable team and an escalation path.”
You can later attach the same metadata to logs, traces, dashboards, alerts, and deployment records.
Step 2: Define what the agent is allowed to do
Ownership also means being clear about what an agent is allowed to do.
An agent that can only read telemetry carries far less risk than one that can restart production services, change infrastructure, or deploy code.
That’s why I prefer an explicit tool allowlist, which limits the agent to the actions you’ve deliberately granted it.
Python
ALLOWED_TOOLS = {
    "get_service_health",
    "get_recent_deployments",
    "search_runbooks",
    "summarize_incident",
}
class ToolAuthorizationError(Exception):
    """Raised when an agent attempts to use an unapproved tool."""
def authorize_tool(tool_name: str) -> None:
    if tool_name not in ALLOWED_TOOLS:
        raise ToolAuthorizationError(
            f"Tool '{tool_name}' is not authorized."
        )
The guiding principle is deny by default.
Adding a new capability should be an intentional engineering decision, not something that happens because a tool became available to the agent.
For destructive operations, authorisation should be even stricter. A production restart or deployment should require authenticated human approval, not the agent’s own judgment.
Step 3: Put budgets around agent execution
An agent that can reason indefinitely is difficult to operate.
Every production workflow should have limits around execution time, model calls, tool calls, and ideally token consumption.
Python
import os
class ExecutionBudget:
    def __init__(
        self,
        max_steps: int | None = None,
        max_tools: int | None = None,
    ):
        self.steps = 0
        self.tool_calls = 0
        self.max_steps = (
            max_steps
            if max_steps is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_AGENT_STEPS", "5"))
        )
        self.max_tools = (
            max_tools
            if max_tools is not None
            else int(os.getenv("MAX_TOOL_CALLS", "8"))
        )
        if self.max_steps <= 0 or self.max_tools <= 0:
            raise ValueError(
                "Execution budget limits must be positive."
            )
    def check_step(self) -> None:
        if self.steps >= self.max_steps:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent step budget exceeded."
            )
        self.steps += 1
    def check_tool_call(self) -> None:
        if self.tool_calls >= self.max_tools:
            raise RuntimeError(
                "Agent tool-call budget exceeded."
            )
        self.tool_calls += 1
Execution limits should be configurable rather than buried in application code. By passing these limits through the constructor, engineers can assign different budgets to different agents without changing global settings. A diagnostic agent might need only three steps, while a more complex research workflow may require considerably more. When no limits are supplied, the class falls back to environment variables. What matters is that every workflow has a defined ceiling, and that the same budget is enforced throughout its execution.
Step 4: Make model calls observable
An owner cannot operate what they cannot see.
At minimum, record:
- request latency;
- model used;
- success/failure;
- tool calls;
- token usage where available;
- correlation or request ID;
- escalation events.
A simple wrapper provides a useful boundary.
Python
import logging
import time
import uuid
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
def invoke_model(model, messages):
    request_id = str(uuid.uuid4())
    started = time.perf_counter()
    # Extract the model name across different provider libraries.
    model_name = (
        getattr(model, "model_name", None)
        or getattr(model, "model", None)
        or "unknown_model"
    )
    try:
        response = model.invoke(messages)
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        logger.info(
            "agent_model_call_success",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )
        return response
    except Exception:
        elapsed = time.perf_counter() - started
        logger.exception(
            "agent_model_call_failed",
            extra={
                "request_id": request_id,
                "model": model_name,
                "latency_seconds": round(elapsed, 3),
            },
        )
        raise
The request ID becomes especially valuable when an incident involves several services.
An engineer should be able to move from an alert to the agent request and then to the underlying model and tool calls.
In production, supplement this logging layer with distributed tracing and metrics for a more complete view of system behaviour and performance.
Step 5: Separate failure from escalation
A failed model call does not necessarily mean the entire service should fail.
Likewise, a successful model call does not mean the agent’s recommendation should execute automatically.
These are different decisions.
Python
def handle_agent_failure(error: Exception) -> dict:
    logger.error(
        "Agent execution failed; escalating to human.",
        exc_info=(
            type(error),
            error,
            error.__traceback__,
        ),
    )
    return {
        "status": "escalated",
        "message": (
            "The AI agent could not complete the operation. "
            "Human intervention is required."
        ),
        "error_type": type(error).__name__,
    }
This distinction matters during a real incident.
The agent might go down, but the engineering team should still be able to respond using the underlying workflows and runbooks. That is what graceful degradation looks like in practice.
Step 6: Make high-risk actions human-gated
One of the most useful patterns for enterprise agents is separating recommendation from execution.
For example:
Telemetry
    ↓
AI Agent
    ↓
Diagnosis
    ↓
Recommended Action
    ↓
Risk Check
    ↓
Human Approval
    ↓
Production Change
The agent might recommend:
	“Increase the database connection pool.”
But it shouldn’t push that change to production just because the model generated the recommendation.
Here’s what a simple approval boundary looks like:
Python
def execute_action(
    action: str,
    approved_by: str | None,
) -> dict:
    if not approved_by:
        return {
            "status": "awaiting_approval",
            "action": action,
        }
    return {
        "status": "approved",
        "action": action,
        "approved_by": approved_by,
    }
A real system needs a more sophisticated implementation, but the architectural boundary is what matters.
“The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.”
The agent can own reasoning without owning authorisation.
Step 7: Give the agent a health check
A production agent needs a health endpoint just like any other service.
With FastAPI:
`Python
import os
import httpx
from fastapi import FastAPI, Response, status
app = FastAPI()
SERVICE_NAME = "incident-command-agent"
@app.get("/health/live")
async def liveness():
    """Check whether the application process is responsive."""
    return {
        "status": "alive",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }
async def check_provider() -> bool:
    """Check a configured provider health endpoint."""
    health_url = os.getenv("MODEL_PROVIDER_HEALTH_URL")
    if not health_url:
        return False
    try:
        async with httpx.AsyncClient(timeout=2.0) as client:
            result = await client.get(health_url)
            return result.status_code == 200
    except httpx.RequestError:
        return False
@app.get("/health/ready")
async def readiness(response: Response):
    """Check whether required dependencies are available."""
    if not await check_provider():
        response.status_code = (
            status.HTTP_503_SERVICE_UNAVAILABLE
        )
        return {
            "status": "unhealthy",
            "reason": "Model provider unavailable",
        }
    return {
        "status": "ready",
        "service": SERVICE_NAME,
    }
Liveness and readiness serve different purposes. The liveness endpoint confirms that the application process is responsive, while readiness checks whether the service can handle requests based on the availability of its required dependencies.
In this example, the readiness endpoint checks a configured model-provider health URL and returns HTTP 503 when the check fails. The check is deliberately lightweight and time-limited to avoid introducing unnecessary delays or costs. In production, teams should adapt it to their provider’s supported health-check mechanism and other critical dependencies, such as a vector database or configuration service.
Keeping these checks separate lets orchestration platforms such as Kubernetes distinguish between an application that needs restarting and one that can’t serve traffic temporarily.
Step 8: Fail closed when safety controls break
One of the worst failure modes is letting an agent keep running after its safety mechanisms go down.
For example:
Python
def run_controlled_agent(
    tool_name: str,
    model,
    messages,
    budget: ExecutionBudget,
):
    try:
        authorize_tool(tool_name)
        # Reuse the budget across agent steps and tool calls.
        budget.check_step()
        budget.check_tool_call()
        return invoke_model(
            model,
            messages,
        )
    except ToolAuthorizationError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent authorisation check failed."
        )
        return {
            "status": "blocked",
            "message": (
                "The requested operation is not authorised."
            ),
        }
    except RuntimeError:
        logger.exception(
            "Agent execution budget exceeded."
        )
        return {
            "status": "escalated",
            "message": (
                "The agent exceeded its execution budget. "
                "Human investigation is required."
            ),
        }
    except Exception as exc:
        return handle_agent_failure(exc)
Notice that different failures produce different outcomes. An authorisation failure should block the requested operation, while an exhausted execution budget should trigger escalation rather than another retry. A temporary model failure, meanwhile, should follow the system’s defined failure-handling policy.
Another important detail: the execution budget must persist throughout the agent’s workflow. Creating a new budget for every invocation would reset its counters, allowing repeated calls to bypass the intended limits. Instead, create the budget once and pass it into each successive invocation, as shown below.
Python
# Create one budget for the entire agent workflow.
budget = ExecutionBudget(
    max_steps=5,
    max_tools=8,
)
# Reuse the same budget across successive invocations.
for tool_name in planned_tools:
    result = run_controlled_agent(
        tool_name=tool_name,
        model=model,
        messages=messages,
        budget=budget,
    )
    if isinstance(result, dict) and result.get(
        "status"
    ) in {"blocked", "escalated"}:
        break
With the same budget shared across invocations, each counted step and tool call contributes to the workflow’s overall limit. Once that limit is reached, the agent stops rather than continuing with a fresh budget. These controls only work if they remain effective throughout execution, especially when an agent encounters repeated failures.
Step 9: Define the 2 a.m. runbook
This is where operational ownership becomes real.
Suppose the agent starts failing at 2 a.m.
The on-call engineer should be able to answer five questions quickly:
- Is the agent itself healthy?
- Is the model provider healthy?
- Are retrieval or tool dependencies failing?
- Has the agent exceeded its normal cost or latency envelope?
- What happens if we disable it?
The last question matters most.
Every production AI system should have a clear degradation path.
For an incident-response agent, that might mean:
AI Agent unavailable
        ↓
Incident still created
        ↓
Telemetry remains available
        ↓
Standard runbook activated
        ↓
Human engineer continues investigation
The AI system should speed up operations, not become something the organisation can’t operate without.
So, who owns the agent?
The answer should never simply be:
	“The AI Team.”
Production ownership needs to be explicit.
Someone owns:
- deployment;
- infrastructure;
- model configuration;
- tool permissions;
- monitoring;
- incident response;
- cost;
- security;
- rollback;
- the decision to disable the agent.
That doesn’t mean one person has to handle everything. It means everyone knows their role well enough that, when an incident hits, the team isn’t wasting time figuring out who should take charge.
The real test of an AI agent
The easiest time to operate an AI agent is during business hours when everything is working.
The real test comes at 2 a.m.
A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget that prevents runaway behaviour, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries that constrain what it can do, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.
The goal isn’t to take humans out of the loop.
“A production-ready agent should have an owner who can be paged, an execution budget, observability that explains what happened, authorisation boundaries, and a fallback that allows engineers to continue without it.”
It’s to make it clear where the agent’s responsibility ends and where a human needs to step in.
Because when something goes wrong at 2 a.m., the question isn’t whether the model was smart enough.
It’s whether the system was designed well enough that the person on call knows what happened, what the agent did, and what to do next.

articles.title: The EU-Startups Podcast | How European BioTech is changing cancer care - Roundtable special | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Key points:
- Bridging the gap between scientific breakthroughs and real-world cancer care remains one of Europe’s biggest challenges
- Sustainable, microalgae-based biomanufacturing could become a serious alternative for producing antibodies and other biologics
- Moving cell therapy from highly personalised treatments to scalable, “off-the-shelf” solutions is key to reaching far more patients
- AI and generative chemistry open up RNA as a drug target that traditional discovery has struggled to reach
- Europe excels at world-class research, but scaling BioTech companies still faces friction in funding, infrastructure, and ecosystem support
- Practical lessons from founders on turning research into a company – and how Women TechEU creates impact well beyond the grant itself
In this Women TechEU Roundtable episode, three founders building DeepTech cancer companies in France sit down together for a candid conversation about science, scaling, and what it really takes to move a breakthrough from the lab to the patients who need it.
Muriel Bardor (Alga Biologics), Inna Menkova (Allogenica), and Emily Fang (InFocus Therapeutics) each tackle cancer from a different angle: sustainable microalgae-based manufacturing for antibodies, allogeneic “off-the-shelf” T-cell therapies, and AI-driven generative chemistry to design small molecules that directly target RNA.
Together, they represent a new generation of European innovators working across advanced therapies, regenerative medicine, and next-generation drug discovery.
Beyond the technology, this roundtable digs into the harder questions every founder faces. Where is the biggest gap between great science and real-world cancer care in Europe today? What happens when the science looks promising, but building a company around it proves far more difficult than expected?
The founders share their most difficult moments, what Europe’s ecosystem does particularly well, where it still slows companies down, and what they wish someone had told them before turning their research into a business.
Looking five to ten years ahead, the discussion explores which change could most transform outcomes for cancer patients and reflects on how the Women TechEU programme shaped their journeys as founders beyond the grant itself, from confidence and visibility to networks and access to the next stage of growth.

As part of the consortium team implementing the programme, our mission is to foster inclusive innovation by supporting women-led startups, including under-represented deep tech sectors and European regions. We believe that diversity drives innovation, and we are here to provide women in deep tech with more opportunities, resources, and support in order to build market-shaping companies at global level.
