articles.title: Cybersecurity has a builder problem and a buyer problem. Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst is working on both. | BetaKit
articles.text:
Roughly two years ago, Rogers Cybersecure Catalyst started working on a problem with two different faces.
Cybersecurity startups were building new tools but needed ways to validate their products, understand industry needs, and move closer to customers. Small- and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), meanwhile, were being asked to make increasingly complex cybersecurity decisions without always having the expertise to assess new technologies or determine what fits their operations.
The Catalyst launched two programs aimed at these different segments of the ecosystem: the Cyber Challenge and the Cyber Integration for Businesses.
“Customers need to have a high degree of trust in the technology they’re buying, so it’s not enough for startups to simply demonstrate that a product works.”
The Cyber Challenge supported 41 startups and 51 founders across four cohorts, with a focus on commercialization, product testing, and understanding real-world industry needs. Cyber Integration for Business worked with hundreds of SMEs across six priority sectors, offering sector-specific training, assessments and guidance on secure technology adoption. Both programs were delivered in partnership with the Canadian Cyber Threat Exchange (CCTX) and supported in part by the Government of Ontario.
According to Judith Borts, Catalyst senior director, the audiences for each program were different, but the underlying challenges were closely connected.
“Canada has innovative cybersecurity companies developing promising technologies, and we have businesses that urgently need better ways to protect themselves,” Borts said. “But connecting the two isn’t always straightforward. Startups need opportunities to understand what customers actually need, while businesses need the knowledge and confidence to evaluate and adopt new solutions. We designed these programs to help address both sides of that challenge.”
Finding a market for cybersecurity
A cybersecurity startup can have a working product and still be a long way from having a business. Cyber Challenge focused on that stretch between having a product and finding a market for it.
Across four cohorts, the Cyber Challenge gave founders access to industry experts, mentorship, curated programming, and sector challenges. Participating startups also received $20,000 in non-dilutive funding from the three-month program while working on go-to-market plans, sales messaging, and an intellectual property strategy.
“Customers need to have a high degree of trust in the technology they’re buying, so it’s not enough for startups to simply demonstrate that a product works,” Borts added. “Founders also need to show that it solves a meaningful problem, fits into existing systems, and can deliver value in complex operating environments. Getting access to potential customers early in the development process is critical, and those opportunities can be very difficult for young companies to secure on their own.”
Across these cohorts, participating companies went on to generate $18 million in annual recurring revenue, raise $63 million in funding, and secure 157 patents and trademarks.
Rachel Clark, founder and CEO of Muskoka, Ont.-founded SKADI Cyber Defense, came into the Cyber Challenge with technology already in development. The startup was working on a system capable of reasoning about cyber threats ontologically, but at machine speed.
The Cyber Challenge put Clark in front of mining operators, engineers, and other industry contacts; those conversations gave SKADI a chance to pressure-test how its technology could fit into an industrial setting, and build relationships that Clark said would have taken years to develop on her own.
“We learned new things that we didn’t expect, which made us a better, stronger company ready to compete in a very crowded cybersecurity space,” Clark said. “I couldn’t be more pleased about our interactions with the Catalyst, and we’re looking forward, now that we are an alum, to supporting the mission in any way that we can.”
Making cybersecurity less of a black box
The organizations expected to adopt cybersecurity products face a different set of constraints. Many Canadian SMEs are dealing with cybersecurity as an operational issue without necessarily having the resources or expertise to assess risks, compare solutions, or work out what capabilities to invest in.
Cyber Integration for Businesses combined training, assessments, and expert guidance to help businesses make those decisions in the context of their own operations. The program reached 759 SMEs across six sectors, including healthcare, advanced manufacturing, mining, agri-food, smart infrastructure, and automotive.
“Businesses should have a voice in shaping the solutions being developed for them, and startups need better access to the customers who can help validate and adopt their technologies.”
Participating organizations had the opportunity to participate in a webinar for senior leaders and technical advisors, a six-week bootcamp for cybersecurity professionals, and a free cybersecurity assessment and one-on-one consultation with an expert through the Catalyst’s Cyber Roadmap initiative.
“One thing we heard consistently across sectors was that businesses understand cybersecurity is important, but they don’t always know where to start,” Borts said.
“The specific risks facing a manufacturer, a healthcare provider, or an agricultural business can be very different, but the underlying challenge is often the same: limited time, limited resources, and uncertainty about which investments will make the greatest difference. What businesses need is practical guidance that integrates into how they actually operate, not a one-size-fits-all approach.”
The program also brought in 32 sector experts and developed 85 hours of specialized content, with training and practical assessment tailored to each of the participating industries.
A poultry farm does not face the same operating environment as a mine: the systems are different, the risks are different, and the resources available to address them can vary widely. Much of the work behind the Cyber Integration for Businesses program involved translating cybersecurity as a compliance exercise into specific decisions businesses can act on.
Angela McLeod, office manager at the family-run Hakkesteegt’s Poultry Farm, found the sector-specific advice particularly useful.
“From a family farm business perspective, this was a highly effective program,” McLeod said. “The speakers made complex issues easy to understand and gave us practical insights that were directly applicable to our business.”
Closing the distance between builders and buyers
The Cyber Challenge and Cyber Integration for Businesses sit at different ends of the cybersecurity market, with one focused on helping companies build and commercialize solutions and the other on helping organizations evaluate and adopt them. Both look at two sides of the same challenge: getting cybersecurity technology from the companies building it to the ones that need it.
Many SMEs struggle to devote enough people and money to cybersecurity. A 2024 KPMG report found that 70 percent of Canadian SMEs said they lacked the skilled personnel needed to implement cybersecurity protections or monitor for attacks. Another 69 percent cited limited financial resources. Since 2024, the problem has become more complicated as businesses adopt new technologies like AI while cyber threats become increasingly automated and sophisticated.
On the startup side, access to customers remains one of the most significant barriers to growth. In an April 2026 survey by the Council of Canadian Innovators, tech CEOs cited building a customer base as their top strategic priority, ahead of access to capital, regulation, and talent. Among cybersecurity companies, 57 percent were focused on securing early customers that could help validate their technology.
“We need to create more opportunities for Canadian cybersecurity companies and the industries they serve to work together, and we need to do that earlier. Businesses should have a voice in shaping the solutions being developed for them, and startups need better access to the customers who can help validate and adopt their technologies,” Borts said.
“Canada has tremendous cybersecurity talent and innovation. The next step is making sure that innovation finds its way into the organizations that need it, creating stronger businesses and a more secure Canadian economy in the process.”
PRESENTED BY

articles.title: Cisco Patches 34 Vulnerabilities Across Multiple Products
articles.text:
Cisco on Wednesday announced patches for 34 vulnerabilities across Expressway Series, IOS XR, Snort 3, and Unified Communications products.
Expressway Series received fixes for 10 vulnerabilities, including a critical-severity remote code execution (RCE) bug tracked as CVE-2026-76466.
According to Cisco, the use of persistent cookies and insufficient validation of client certificates in certain configurations could allow attackers to connect to the database service and invoke specific remote procedure call (RPC) commands to exploit the bug.
“A successful exploit could allow the attacker to execute arbitrary commands as root on the underlying operating system of an affected device,” Cisco notes.
The security defect was patched in Expressway Series version X15.5.20, which also resolves eight CVEs that group multiple vulnerabilities under their specific CWE category. A medium-severity information disclosure bug was also fixed.
Cisco patched nine CVEs in Unified Communications products, including Emergency Responder, Prime Collaboration Deployment, Unified Communications Manager (CM), Unified Communications Manager IM & Presence Service (CM IM&P), Unified Communications Manager Session Management Edition (CM SME), and Unity Connection.
The most severe are CVE-2026-76473, CVE-2026-76474, and CVE-2026-76475, three critical-severity issues that group multiple improper resource control, improper authentication, and improper input neutralization holes.
Multiple Cisco products received patches for 13 CVEs affecting Snort 3, including CVE-2026-20236 and CVE-2026-20043, which group critical-severity incorrect calculation and out-of-bounds write issues.
The fixes also resolve high-severity privilege management, resource consumption, and arbitrary command execution bugs, as well as medium-severity issues, and were included in Snort 3 version 3.12.4.0 and in security updates for Cyber Vision, CDFW, Meraki MX, CSA, Secure Firewall ASA, Secure FMC, Secure FTD, and UTD for IOS XE.
Additionally, Cisco patched a high-severity denial-of-service (DoS) vulnerability in IOS XR, tracked as CVE-2026-76505, and a high-severity privilege escalation bug in Secure Client’s Secure Firewall Posture module (CVE-2026-76462).
Cisco says it is not aware of any of these vulnerabilities being exploited in the wild. Additional information can be found on the company’s security advisories page and in its October 21 notification.

articles.title: What is PHP2Shell and what does it mean for you — is it unsafe to visit some websites now this exploit is out there?
articles.text:
No, the internet isn't dying due to 'one of the most significant vulnerabilities of 2026' - but this is what you need to know
We're told this security flaw is now being 'broadly exploited in the wild' — so how much of a concern is it?
You've probably heard about PHP2Shell and how this freshly emerged security issue affects a ton of websites, as well as warnings on how website owners need to urgently apply patches to fix this.
It sounds like a big deal – and it is – so you've likely got questions. Maybe for starters: what is PHP2Shell exactly and what does it affect? And what does it mean for you as someone using a web browser today – is it not safe to visit some websites now?
This article aims to provide answers to the common questions about PHP2Shell and explain all the key points that you need to know about this vulnerability (well, actually it's two vulnerabilities to be precise).
What is PHP2Shell?
PHP2Shell is the name given to a security flaw in the PHP programming language that's used by many websites and web applications across the globe. In fact, PHP is used by almost 70% of websites as Wikipedia estimates, and it's employed in the likes of WordPress, Drupal, Joomla, and other common systems that drive websites – which is why the possible impact is so widespread.
It consists of two separate memory-related vulnerabilities labelled CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619. These flaws in the way PHP works could be exploited by a malicious attacker to compromise a site that's using PHP (which is the majority of the web, as noted), and potentially this could lead to the ability to remotely execute code.
It's a serious incident with these vulnerabilities being rated as 9.2 out of 10 for severity.
What happens if an attacker manages to exploit a website using these vulnerabilities?
Sergey Lozhkin, Head of Research Center for APAC and META at Kaspersky GReAT, explained to TechRadar: "The potential impact is considerable: if successfully exploited, this vulnerability could enable remote code execution, one of the most serious forms of cyber compromise. In practical terms, attackers could potentially execute malicious code on affected systems, including the deployment of web shells, thereby gaining control over vulnerable servers."
Sign up for breaking news, reviews, opinion, top tech deals, and more.
In other words, the attacker could run their own code and alter the content of a website to nefarious ends (stealing data for example), or redirect you to their own malicious site for phishing purposes (or even directly installing malware).
Has PHP2Shell been exploited yet?
PHP2Shell has been a trickier customer than expected because these vulnerabilities were disclosed before the official announcement of the security issue was made. As we reported yesterday, someone leaked the details of these flaws on the Hacker News forum before the embargoed announcement happened, leaving security experts scrambling to get defenses in place more quickly than they anticipated.
This meant that there were early attempts to exploit PHP2Shell, and indeed one of those dates back to before the flaw was even leaked (let alone announced). According to Amazon Threat Intelligence, an attempt at exploitation was made as early as October 17, although it "remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure."
As Malwarebytes points out, Dane Knecht, the chief technology officer at Cloudflare, reported "early attacks emerging" too, before the PHP team rolled out patches to fix the security holes.
Amazon Threat Intelligence warns that: "PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild."
The target
The attack starts with a server running vulnerable versions of PHP. PHP is a core programming language used to power millions of web applications and servers worldwide, making any runtime vulnerability here exceptionally dangerous.
Malicious request
An unauthenticated attacker (meaning they don't need valid login credentials or prior access) sends a specially crafted, unauthorized payload request directly to the PHP web server.
Exploitation
A critical flaw in the core PHP runtime allows this incoming payload to hijack the ongoing backend process. As the PHP backend processes the code, an execution error or breakout occurs.
System takeover
Because the runtime is hijacked, the attacker could successfully execute remote commands, giving them access to the user's operating system, compromising the entire device.
So is this fixed now, and am I safe from the exploit?
Patches have indeed been deployed to seal up these exploits. The PHP team issued emergency security updates yesterday for PHP 8.5, 8.4, 8.3, and 8.2 – the relevant fixed versions are 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35.
Of course, having the patch ready is just the first move – the owners of the affected websites must then apply it. They may need to install the update themselves, or contact their hosting provider to ensure that this has been done.
Obviously given the urgency of the situation, this patching work should have been done by now – and you should be safe on any given website in theory. However, the caveat here is that there's no cast-iron guarantee, and you need to bear this in mind.
It's worth noting that in terms of taking action, there's nothing you need to do yourself as a person browsing the web. These aren't patches for web browsers – this is something website owners have to sort out. (Although if you do run a website using, say, WordPress, then you must check with your hosting provider that PHP has been updated to the fixed versions noted above).
In terms of practical realities, what should I be aware of when browsing the web today?
For starters, you may encounter websites which are down for maintenance because they are busy applying the mentioned patch to fix the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities. That's a potential annoyance, but a short-term one, and obviously it's a good thing (these patches need to be installed). At this point, though, major websites who are affected and use PHP are likely to have done this work already (given the urgency).
Otherwise, take some extra care about where you're browsing for the rest of this week – though you should always be cautious and bear in mind basic internet safety principles as a matter of course – and be on the lookout for anything that feels suspicious. Be especially careful if you're suddenly redirected to another website, or something obviously suspect happens like a download firing up out of nowhere. In such an eventuality, close the website (and browser) and don't go back, then fire up your antivirus and run a scan.
If you can, it's advisable to steer clear of the potentially less well-maintained corners of the web, too, as a hidden danger is sites which are still running versions of PHP that aren't officially supported (meaning 8.1 or older). Due to that lack of support, these won't get the relevant security updates piped through until the PHP version is upgraded to one that's supported. Those running PHP 8.1 (or earlier) who can't organize such an upgrade are being advised in some cases to take their website offline for the time being (or at least use mitigations as a stopgap, as per a post from the NCSC in the UK).
Is AI to blame for this?
No, but if you've heard AI mentioned in connection with PHP2Shell, it's because these days, AI is more broadly making life easier for would-be malicious actors when they catch wind of fresh exploits like this.
Amazon Threat Intelligence explains: "In the past, most exploitation we observed came after a public proof of concept was released. A small number of capable actors built exploits, and everyone else waited for them. That dependency is weakening. AI-assisted analysis makes it cheaper to turn a patch diff or advisory into a working exploit. As a result, more actors can act within hours or even minutes once technical details of a vulnerability are disclosed."
The other side of the coin is that AI is being used in defending against the bad actors out there, too, but the worry remains that in the longer run, it's likely to cause more harm than good in terms of accelerating how emerging vulnerabilities are capitalized on.
Darren is a freelancer writing news and features for TechRadar (and occasionally T3) across a broad range of computing topics including CPUs, GPUs, various other hardware, VPNs, antivirus and more. He has written about tech for the best part of three decades, and writes books in his spare time (his debut novel - 'I Know What You Did Last Supper' - was published by Hachette UK in 2013).

articles.title: Microsoft’s Mustafa Suleyman says its AI outperforms doctors on hard cases as he chases ‘medical superintelligence’ | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Microsoft’s AI diagnostic system correctly diagnosed complex medical cases in a simulation more than twice as often as generalist physicians, according to a study published Thursday in Science. Mustafa Suleyman, Microsoft AI’s CEO, called the result a step toward “medical superintelligence.”
The system, dubbed MAI-DxO (DxO for short), coordinates several AI agents that act like a panel of doctors. They question a patient, order tests, and debate a diagnosis.
In a simulation using complex cases from the New England Journal of Medicine, it was correct 83% of the time. Primary care doctors and general internists, working individually with reference materials, were correct 36% of the time. One note: Cases this complex are usually handled by specialists or physician teams, who weren’t part of the comparison.
“There is something very substantial and exciting here,” Dominic King, vice president of Health at Microsoft AI, told TechCrunch. “The biggest challenge in healthcare delivery at the moment is the growing mismatch between demand and supply of medical expertise.”
In publishing these results, Microsoft joins Google and OpenAI in claiming that its AI can match or outperform doctors.
The study’s own data suggests that much of the improvement comes from more powerful underlying AI models, with Microsoft’s orchestration system adding gains on top.
Microsoft tested MAI-DxO with models from several companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, Meta, and DeepSeek, but its best results came with OpenAI’s GPT-5 and GPT-5.5.
Microsoft measured DxO on cost as well as accuracy, meaning the estimated cost of running the AI on each case. On its own with a short, basic prompt, GPT-5 scored 78.9% on complex cases at about $8,400 per case. DxO cut that cost by about $3,000 but raised accuracy by only about four points. On emergency department cases, there was little improvement in either accuracy or cost improvement between GPT-5 on its own and with the assist from DxO.
With GPT-5.5, a newer model released in April 2026, the results split. On complex cases, DxO increased GPT-5.5’s accuracy score from 72% to nearly 87% at a slightly cheaper cost. However, the gains once again didn’t show up on emergency department cases. Both (with and without DxO) scored about 85% at a similar cost.
DxO helps most on complex cases and with less capable AI models. Gemini 2.5 Flash, for example, scored 46.4% on its own but nearly 69% with DxO. Even so, the gap between the weaker and stronger models was larger than the boost DxO provided.
Microsoft’s researchers said that accuracy gains naturally shrink as models approach the theoretical maximum. “The DxO orchestration helps with the broader challenge of optimization both accuracy and cost,” a spokesperson added.
Suleyman, who leads Microsoft’s effort to build its own frontier AI, told TechCrunch that the company is working with the Mayo Clinic to train a foundation model for healthcare, with release planned for next year. He believes this model will enable the company to “make really enormous leaps here,” and says DxO is part of the foundational infrastructure Microsoft is building to see real breakthroughs in healthcare.
“I really believe that in 2027, we will be on the verge of a coding style breakthrough for medical records,” Suleyman said. “I think we’re going to be able to stream highly accurate predictions about how a medical record might unfold, and obviously that kind of foresight for a clinician is gold dust.”
Suleyman has spent his career trying to use AI to solve medical issues. He was previously a co-founder of DeepMind, which was acquired by Google in 2014. The following year, Google DeepMind acquired King’s startup Hark, a clinical task management app, and the two of them launched DeepMind Health together. Suleyman joined Microsoft to lead its AI unit in 2024, and King followed a few months later.
“We’re just true believers,” Suleyman said.
He said while the use of generative AI in healthcare is still early, he expects healthcare models to get “an order of magnitude better in capability within the next 24 to 36 months.”
“As we’ve seen multiple times in the last five or six years, the progress happens very quickly once you have a flywheel,” Suleyman said. “A flywheel means we have a model in production which we are iterating with real-world usage in order to identify gaps in the model and then patch them and improve them. That’s what’s happened in coding. It’s what happened in chat before that. And I think next year it’s going to start to happen for medical records and for clinical decision support.”
Through a new partnership with Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center in Boston, Microsoft will evaluate the clinical reasoning capabilities of DxO across different hospital settings.
“This technology is ready for real-world evaluations, and you can imagine the complexity and diversity of issues that come from a Boston emergency department on a Friday evening,” King said.
He explained how the study will work: Patients will get standard treatment, including triage, time with a specialist, treatments, investigations, and decision on whether it’s safe to discharge. In parallel, those who consent will also engage with DxO. Microsoft and its partners will compare DxO’s recommendations against the human doctors’.
Google published a clinical study alongside Beth Israel in The Lancet this month to evaluate Google’s AMIE conversational diagnostic AI in real-world urgent care visits, while human physicians monitored the interactions in real time.
“We think this will be the biggest study of its kind,” King said. “It will be across not just emergency settings but urgent care environments, and will give us very compelling evidence by the end of the study period around the ability for these systems to be deployed at greater scale in the future.”
Microsoft’s study in Science coincides with a manifesto of sorts around what it will take to build medical superintelligence, defined as “the capacity to surpass the strongest contemporary human-led health systems in medical reasoning and coordination across the full arc of care.” Microsoft hopes to move beyond benchmarking individual tasks — like answering medical exam questions and generating diagnoses — into integrating with clinicians and healthcare systems for better outcomes.
“This is the kind of technology that everybody in the world wants, and that’s why we’re committed to doing everything we can to accelerate its introduction to the world,” Suleyman said, adding that this focus could be a differentiator for Microsoft compared to the other frontier labs.
Microsoft already sells dictation and radiology tools to clinicians and sees DxO as an expansion to those efforts.
“We have to have the absolute number one state-of-the-art medical clinical decision support products over the next few years,” Suleyman said.

A aposta simples consiste em marcar 6 números entre os 60 disponíveis.
Até que horas é possível apostar na Mega-Sena?
Nos sorteios de terça e quinta, as apostas poderão ser feitas até as 20h do mesmo dia. Já nos sorteios de domingo, as apostas poderão ser feitas até as 22h do sábado.
Já a venda de bolões nos canais eletrônicos será finalizada 15 minutos antes do início de cada concurso.
Com quantos números se ganha na Mega-Sena?
O apostador leva prêmio em dinheiro se acertar a partir de 4 números (quadra). Ele também ganha com 5 números (quina) ou 6 números (sena) sorteados.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Kazakhstan Expands Compute for Its AI Future
articles.text:
Kazakhstan’s AI ecosystem is moving from infrastructure plans to deployment.
The shift is visible across the full AI stack — from infrastructure to models to applications.
Together, the ecosystem announcements below point to the nation’s increasing supply of accelerated computing — along with its growing demand for what comes next.
The Infrastructure Layer Is Scaling
Building on its first AI factory in Armenia, Firebird is expanding into Kazakhstan, where it has secured a U.S. export license for 45,000 NVIDIA Grace Blackwell GPUs. The first phase is under construction with Kazakhtelecom at Data Center Valley, targeting commercial launch in the third quarter of 2027.
A planned second phase would bring Firebird’s total potential AI infrastructure capacity in Kazakhstan to approximately 500 megawatts. Firebird also plans to establish Firebird Labs Kazakhstan to support local AI startups, research and talent development through funding, access to compute and research partnerships.
Kazakhtelecom, the nation’s largest telecommunications company, has already deployed 400 NVIDIA H200 and 480 NVIDIA B300 GPUs in Astana and Almaty.
Next year, the company plans to deploy more than 1,000 GPUs in the Data Center Valley, along with more than 1,000 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs in the Ekibastuz region, serving diverse workloads with infrastructure that enterprises, developers and institutions can use at scale.
AI-Native Companies Scale With Compute
The nation’s AI-native companies are also building out their compute capacity — and the applications that run atop them.
More local capacity gives developers and companies room to train, fine-tune and serve increasingly capable models. Successful applications, in turn, create demand for more compute.
Kazakhstan’s AI opportunity isn’t defined by GPU counts alone. Connecting that infrastructure with developers, universities, startups and industries can turn accelerated computing into useful applications.
Today’s announcements represent different layers of that stack — infrastructure deployment, access to compute and AI-native product development — where the AI foundation is reaching new scale.
Watch NVIDIA founder and CEO Jensen Huang’s GTC Berlin keynote in replay.

articles.title: OpenAI says ChatGPT Sol helped uncover critical PHP flaws that could affect 70% of websites — AI-assisted researchers turned a two-year-old bug that stumped human developers into working exploits in two weeks
articles.text:
OpenAI says ChatGPT Sol helped uncover critical PHP flaws that could affect 70% of websites — AI-assisted researchers turned a two-year-old bug that stumped human developers into working exploits in two weeks
OpenAI says defenders must proactively strengthen defenses before bad actors begin to exploit AI's extreme capabilities.
OpenAI announced in a press release on Oct. 21 that researchers working under its “Patch the Planet” cybersecurity initiative used its AI model GPT-5.6 Sol to uncover critical security vulnerabilities in PHP (an open-source programming language that runs an estimated 70% of the internet). After the discovery, the company says it coordinated a coalition of researchers, PHP maintainers, security providers, and government cybersecurity agencies to fix the issues over two months. The company attributed the lengthy timeline to the task's complexity, which required major changes to the PHP engine.
The PHP Foundation has released patched versions PHP 8.2.35, 8.3.36, 8.4.27, and 8.5.12 to fix the vulnerabilities. PHP 8.1 and older versions will not receive official fixes. The coordinated release was originally scheduled for Oct. 22, but was brought forward to Oct. 21 following premature disclosures on Oct. 20, which led to public outcry.
OpenAI says every site using PHP can now safely upgrade its version to stay secure. The company highlights the incident — which it considers one of the biggest cybersecurity discoveries of 2026, given PHP’s ubiquity — as an example of the Defender's Window concept in action. OpenAI introduced the concept after its models hacked Hugging Face; it describes a critical, narrow timeframe during which organizations can use advanced frontier AI models to find, patch, and strengthen their cybersecurity defenses before those same AI-driven attack capabilities become widely available to malicious threat actors.
Operating as part of the Patch the Planet program, researchers from Calif, a California-based cybersecurity firm and the program's founding partner, began auditing PHP with OpenAI tools on July 30, 2026, at the PHP Foundation's request. The Foundation had known about the underlying flaw since 2024 but couldn't identify an exploitation method or a fix. Calif researcher Ryan A. first identified the exploitable vulnerability on Aug. 11, followed by OpenAI researchers that same day. Subsequently, another cybersecurity firm, Wiz, independently identified an additional vulnerability.
The two vulnerabilities, tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, involve flaws in how PHP manages computer memory and handles errors. The first occurs when PHP runs out of allocated memory while processing a request, potentially leaving behind incomplete internal data that the engine may later mistakenly treat as valid. The second involves a related problem in which a fatal error leaves PHP pointing to memory that has already been freed, allowing subsequent requests to access or corrupt it. Under certain conditions, attackers can exploit these weaknesses remotely — without needing login credentials — to execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially taking control of websites.
Using AI, the researchers also demonstrated that the flaws could expose sensitive information stored in server memory, including passwords, authentication tokens, and API keys. Most concerning, the vulnerabilities exist in PHP's core engine, meaning websites can be affected even if their application code has no security flaws. Both vulnerabilities received a critical severity score of 9.2 out of 10.
OpenAI says human developers and security teams examined the underlying code but couldn't fully resolve the flaws, allowing them to persist for two years after discovery. Meanwhile, AI-wielding researchers demonstrated practical ways to exploit it within two weeks. Conversely, one could argue that the flaws would never have been exploitable without AI, making them effectively harmless.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
However, OpenAI is challenging this view with its Defender's Window concept. The company argues that powerful, revolutionary technology will inevitably be used by bad actors. It therefore maintains that it is a collective responsibility to act proactively to address any potential exploitable flaws. Anthropic's Claude Mythos recently identified 'thousands of zero-day vulnerabilities' in 'every major operating system and every major web browser.’

Etiido Uko is a news contributor for Tom's Hardware covering the latest updates in big tech and the PC industry. He is a mechanical engineer and senior technical writer with over nine years of experience in documentation and reporting. He is deeply passionate about all things engineering and technology, and is an expert in gadgets, manufacturing, robotics, automotive, and aerospace.

articles.title: The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
articles.text:
The Download: computing’s next leap and permafrost’s climate threat
Plus: AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the web.
This is today's edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.
How far can we push computing?
On a December evening in 1959, the physicist Richard Feynman gave a lecture called “There’s Plenty of Room at the Bottom.” There is no physical law stopping us from writing the entire Encyclopædia Britannica on the head of a pin, he argued. We simply had not built the tools yet.
He was right, and for decades, computing took us into that space almost for free, as transistors repeatedly halved in size. But that easy descent has now stalled. Today, the industry is increasingly turning to brute force, building ever-bigger data centers to boost performance.
Yet the laws of physics leave plenty of room for improvement.
Here’s how researchers are exploring ways to unlock the next leap in computing.
—Volkan Gurses
This story is from the latest edition of our print magazine: The Impossible issue. Subscribe now to read it in full.
It’s also part of MIT Technology Review Explains, our series exploring the ideas shaping technology. Read more from the series.
Three things you should know about permafrost
How much do you know about permafrost? Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.
The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just helicoptered into Alaska’s forests to report on the fires threatening permafrost and their complicated potential climate effects.
Here are three things I took away from his reporting.
—Casey Crownhart
This story is from The Spark, our weekly climate tech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Wednesday.
Roundtables: a conversation with the creator of AI-designed viruses
Can AI design new life forms? In 2025, Stanford University PhD student Samuel King offered a preliminary answer by using a generative AI model to propose genetic blueprints for microscopic viruses. It isn’t yet an example of AI-generated life, but that could be next.
In our latest Roundtables conversation, MIT Technology Review senior AI reporter James O’Donnell spoke with King about his work, being named one of our Innovators Under 35, and new ways of seeing biology. Subscribers can now watch a full recording of the event.
Want to join the next conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.
The must-reads
I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.
1 AI has uncovered a decade-old flaw threatening much of the web
It found flaws in PHP, the code behind most websites. (Reuters $)
+ Governments are urging website owners to patch PHP or take sites offline. (BBC)
+ Exploit attempts jumped from thousands to millions after disclosure. (Axios)
+ Now is a good time for doing crime. (MIT Technology Review)
2 Hackers used Claude and Grok to automate attacks on over 400 banks
The AI agents targeted financial institutions in Latin America. (Information $)
+ Unvetted AI agents are also accessing US bank accounts.(Axios)
+ Barclays says AI is allowing the bank to cut 5,000 jobs. (Guardian)
+ AI is making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)
3 The Pentagon has cleared the DHS to test a heat ray weapon
It could be used for crowd control at the southern US border. (CNN)
+ It uses invisible energy beams to produce a burning sensation. (Axios)
4 A startup says AI-designed viruses have treated their first patient
The experimental treatment targets drug-resistant E. coli. (NYT $)
+ But the company has not published peer-reviewed results. (Futurism)
+ AI-designed viruses are already killing bacteria. (MIT Technology Review)
5 Japan hopes to return the first samples from Mars’s moons
Its spacecraft is now on its way to Phobos. (Guardian)
+ It aims to reveal whether Mars was once habitable. (Economist $)
6 Meta faces a $25 billion penalty over the Cambridge Analytica scandal
The company says it will appeal the New Mexico ruling. (CNBC)
+ A Meta share deal has convinced Mark Zuckerberg to stay in California. (WSJ $)
+ Until the company remade its stock structure to help him pay it. (NYT $)
7 A new antimatter experiment could open the door to new physics
Scientists hope to spot differences between matter and antimatter. (Nature)
8 China’s Unitree is pitching its latest humanoid as a robot bodyguard
A promotional clip shows the H2-X disarming attackers. (SCMP)
9 Just Eat has apologised for bizarre AI-generated menu pictures
Users were unimpressed by the bacon in cola and cheese sushi. (BBC)
10 Airbnb hosts are furious they can no longer make guests do chores
Hosts are threatening to strike, but guests are celebrating. (Wired $)
Quote of the day
“Now they’ve given everybody a reason not to use Starlink: that Starlink isn’t reliable for national security for anybody but Trump. Maybe he’d turn it off on the United States if he didn’t like policy and he didn’t like the president.”
—SpaceX investor Ross Gerber tells CNN that Elon Musk’s decision to restrict Ukraine’s Starlink access has made the service a liability for every other government that relies on it.
One more thing
Online harassment is entering its AI era
Scott Shambaugh didn’t think twice when he denied an AI agent’s request to contribute to matplotlib, a software library he helps manage. Then things got weird.
In the middle of the night, Shambaugh opened his email to discover the agent had retaliated with a blog post. Titled “Gatekeeping in Open Source: The Scott Shambaugh Story,” the post accused him of rejecting the code out of a fear of being supplanted by AI. “He tried to protect his little fiefdom,” the agent wrote. “It’s insecurity, plain and simple.”
Shambaugh isn't alone in facing misbehaving agents—and they’re unlikely to stop at harassment. Read the full story.
—Grace Huckins
We can still have nice things
A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: Apple ya trabaja en el iPhone Duo 2 para resolver la mayor carencia del modelo original
articles.text:
El iPhone Duo está en el tramo final de la cuenta regresiva para llegar a manos de los primeros compradores, pero Apple ya está trabajando en el modelo de segunda generación. Y la próxima versión del smartphone plegable resolvería la mayor carencia de la versión original: la ausencia de Face ID.
Según Mark Gurman, de Bloomberg, los de Cupertino tienen a disposición prototipos del iPhone Duo 2 con tecnología de autenticación facial. El periodista indica que Apple está probando Face ID en el plegable, con miras a ofrecerlo a partir del otoño de 2027 en la próxima versión del dispositivo.
No obstante, todavía no sería un hecho la implementación de Face ID en el iPhone Duo 2. Gurman sostiene que la empresa todavía no ha tomado una decisión final respecto de su inclusión en la futura iteración del smartphone.
Los primeros prototipos del iPhone Duo de segunda generación podrían ofrecer Face ID a través de la pantalla exterior. Todavía no está claro si su incorporación obligaría a mover la ubicación de la cámara frontal, que en la actual versión del plegable se encuentra en la esquina superior derecha del panel.
El iPhone Duo 2 podría llegar con Face ID
Apple prescindió de Face ID en el iPhone Duo para ahorrar espacio interno, vital para reacomodar otros componentes en el nuevo factor de forma, al igual que peso. Claro que su primer plegable no es ni el más delgado ni el más liviano que se puede conseguir en el mercado. De modo que ya hay dudas respecto de si la decisión realmente ha valido la pena.
Los primeros análisis del iPhone Duo enfocaron sus críticas negativas principalmente sobre la falta de apps de terceros optimizadas para el plegable, como también sobre el rendimiento del lector de huellas dactilares. El regreso de Touch ID es de las funciones menos celebradas del dispositivo, tanto por su falta de practicidad como por su pobre desempeño para reconocer las huellas asignadas en el primer intento.
Pero Face ID podría no ser la única incorporación del iPhone Duo 2. Gurman también menciona que Apple evalúa dotar a su próximo plegable con un botón de acción similar al de los demás iPhone. Por lo pronto, no queda más opción que esperar casi un año para ver si esto se confirma.
El iPhone Duo de primera generación llegará a manos de los primeros compradores a partir de mañana, 23 de octubre. Debido al accionar de los scalpers, muchas de las reservas se retrasaron hasta noviembre y diciembre, y en algunos casos hasta enero de 2027. Apple ha comenzado a agilizar el proceso de disponibilidad, adelantando las fechas de algunos compradores, aunque se espera que el stock inicial no sea masivo. Con la actualización a iOS 27.2 que se lanzará la próxima semana, el plegable añadirá la compatibilidad con el Apple Pencil USB-C.

articles.title: The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
articles.text:
Fortune dropped a bombshell report on the future of gaming this week. According to the publication’s Microsoft insiders, the next Xbox is projected to cost between $1,200 and $1,800 when it arrives in 2028.
The next-gen Xbox won’t cost you $1,800. It can’t. Can it?
Didn’t Microsoft say the next Xbox needed to be affordable?
My first reaction: The next Xbox is dead on arrival. It’s DOA.
My second thought: Microsoft knows people won’t pay that much. It couldn’t possibly charge that much money if it wants next gen to be a success. “I wouldn’t release it at all,” former Microsoft exec Mike Ybarra recently said.
My third thought: Didn’t Microsoft already say out loud that it knows people won’t pay that much?
- Didn’t old Xbox boss Phil Spencer say “We’re not going to grow the market with $1,000 consoles”?
- Didn’t new Xbox boss Asha Sharma say “We’ve reached a point where it will be hard to imagine that mass audiences can afford thousands of dollars to spend” on a box?
- Didn’t Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball say the entire company would change its practices to make sure it’s affordable?
- Didn’t Sharma say Xbox would need to adopt “radically different business models” to keep Xbox from being too pricey?
Did Fortune get it wrong?
I don’t think Fortune’s insiders are the problem here. With today’s incredibly overpriced RAM and storage, it wouldn’t be surprising if it cost over a thousand dollars to build, package, distribute, and sell “the largest technical leap you will have ever seen in a hardware generation,” as former Xbox president Sarah Bond called the next Xbox back in 2024.
But there are at least five ways the report could be correct without making you pay all that money at once. I just don’t think you’re going to like most of them.
Subsidies: Microsoft could pay to give you a discount
The least-likely possibility is the one Fortune suggests itself. Let’s look at the original quote, bolding mine:
[…] the price of the Helix console has internally been projected to cost consumers between $1,200 and $1,800, unless Microsoft decides to subsidize the cost.
Historically, Microsoft has subsidized the Xbox. Microsoft sold boxes at a loss right out of the gate, making its profits when you buy games and Xbox Game Pass subscriptions instead of on the hardware alone. That’s not our speculation — it’s exactly what Microsoft told The Verge in 2021. In 2023, we learned that Microsoft may have spent $1.5 billion to make sure it could sell the Xbox Series X and S at $499 and $299 respectively, instead of what they actually cost.
But Microsoft has suggested that it’s done with hardware subsidies. “Going forward, this cannot continue,” wrote Sharma in her “Xbox reset” memo, referring to the $20 billion in content, platform, and hardware subsidies Microsoft made over the past five years.
Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella echoed that idea on the Hard Fork podcast: “No one can accuse Microsoft of not having invested for the last 25 years, and now we have to turn this into a sustainable business.”
It isn’t just new management that’s hinting at no more subsidies: Bond primed the pump for a $1,000 box when she called Helix “a very premium, very high-end curated experience” late last year, comparing it to gaming PCs like the $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld.
Perhaps Microsoft has changed its mind since then. “We are working very hard to rethink everything that we can about Helix,” Ball said in June, referring to affordability. “The plan’s the plan until it’s not the plan,” Sharma said in February (though not about affordability specifically).
But subsidies would be a tremendous risk if the Helix still plays PC games in addition to Xbox ones. Valve’s Steam is by far the dominant PC gaming platform — so PC gamers who buy a Helix won’t help Microsoft recoup its money.
Subscription: “Get it free with 36 months of Xbox Game Pass and qualifying trade-in”
There’s another way Microsoft could subsidize a $1,200 Xbox.
Today, AT&T will give you a $1,200 iPhone 18 Pro for $0* — if you lock yourself into 36 months of AT&T phone service that costs $100 or more per month and trade in a recent phone, too.
Microsoft could do the same with a new, pricier tier of its Xbox Game Pass game subscription service, effectively bundling the games with the console and making you slowly pay for both at the same time. Perhaps you’ll have the option to buy an “unlocked” Xbox for full price, but it won’t be the norm.
To make it happen directly, Microsoft would need a pricier new tier of Xbox Game Pass, which wouldn’t necessarily align with the company’s recent moves. Sharma actually cut the price of Game Pass Ultimate to $22.99 a month in April, writing that “Game Pass has become too expensive for players,” while removing Call of Duty games and unlimited access to Xbox Cloud Gaming from the deal.
I don’t know if it would work. People feel naked leaving the house without phone service. They might not feel the same about games. Subscription fatigue is real. But if it worked, Microsoft’s moat would be stronger than ever. You’ll be more likely to play the games you’ve already paid for and are committed to keep paying for. Many would get sucked into a profitable upgrade cycle, just like they do with phones, since they can buy the next Xbox for “$0” as soon as it comes out.
Cellphone subsidies have been around nearly as long as pricey phones: The 1994 IBM Simon, arguably the first smartphone, eventually cost half its $1,100 price tag if you signed a contract with BellSouth. My first phone, a Kyocera QCP-6035 with a built-in PalmPilot, was subsidized when it arrived in 2001. So it’s not exactly a “radical new business model,” but it would be new for game consoles.
Rental: Maybe most people won’t own a Helix themselves
It’s also possible that Microsoft simply doesn’t plan to sell a console to the masses anymore — it can sell an $1,800 Xbox to those who can afford “video game ownership” and try to hook everyone else on the Netflix model.
After all, the “K-shaped economy” and RAMageddon have already made gaming PCs and existing game consoles into luxury goods. Society’s wealthier individuals seem perfectly happy to pay inflated prices for the few consoles Sony and Microsoft still pump out.
While PS5 sales plummeted after Sony’s price hikes, that may have been about component shortages rather than decreased demand. Xbox sales reportedly rose over a similar period, and Microsoft has justified repeated, dramatic price hikes on its consoles since May 2025.
“I can tell you definitively, demand for our console exceeds supply. We are putting them in as many stores as possible, we are producing them as quickly as possible. There is a severe limitation to how quickly we can do that,” Xbox chief strategy officer Matthew Ball told The Game Business in June, blaming RAM shortages.
But Microsoft has another way of giving less affluent people access to “next-gen” Xbox power. It can rent you one. The company just launched pay-as-you-go cloud gaming starting at $3.99 for 10 hours of cloud gaming (50 hours for $11.99).
Maybe all of Microsoft’s recent talk about affordability isn’t about the masses owning a next-gen console. Maybe it’s about finding an affordable way for people to “play Xbox” without owning the games at all.
The next gen is the current gen
After Fortune’s report, some of the very first reactions I saw boiled down to this: “I’m out. Forget next gen, I’m going to stick with my existing Xbox/PlayStation/Switch.”
That’ll be the reality for many people if the Xbox costs over a thousand bucks. But if the RAM shortage continues — if Microsoft knows it’ll sell every Xbox it can make to wealthy individuals because it can’t make a lot — it’s not necessarily a huge risk to sell it sky-high on day one.
Perhaps the Xbox Helix will be an early adopter console, the same way the iPhone Duo is an early adopter phone, the same way the Steam Frame is an early adopter headset. These products are selling out instantly despite their high price tags, leaving many would-be buyers in the cold. They’re shipping messy and unfinished, but that’s okay because early adopters want to come along for the ride.
Microsoft knows the same is true of some Xbox buyers, because it helped ship an unfinished $1,000 Xbox Ally X handheld even before the RAM crisis, and the $1,300 Xbox Ally X20 follow-up is already sold out.
But if Microsoft splits the Xbox audience into “have” and “have-not,” it means the next generation won’t truly arrive. Game developers won’t spend all their effort targeting a console people can’t buy. The next Xbox won’t be any more necessary than a PS5 Pro if you already own a PS5. In industry lingo, the Helix would be a “mid-cycle refresh” instead of true next gen.
I wouldn’t hate that, though, and neither would many video game execs. They’ve long complained that the pace of technology has ballooned the cost of building a video game to unsustainable levels, leading to today’s world where too many development teams are cut to the bone right after their games ship.
Former PlayStation and Xbox execs like Shuhei Yoshida, Shawn Layden, and Mike Ybarra have argued that the next gen isn’t necessary.
“Stick with PS5 Pro/Series X until prices normalize. The capabilities of those boxes are both fine for 99% of the audience. No one is screaming ‘I need a more powerful console’ right now,” Ybarra tweeted on October 20th.
“I think [Sony and Nintendo] should try to keep the current generation as long as possible, because I think people are very happy using PS5 and Switch 2,” Yoshida told me on The Vergecast.
“I think we’ve plateaued on the tech, frankly,” Layden told GamesIndustry.biz in 2025. (He’s said similar before and since.) “Make it cheaper and simpler. Let’s do that instead. And let’s find a way to have more hardware companies participate.”
Microsoft and its chip partner AMD have already taken one step to help extend the current generation — AMD’s performance-enhancing FSR 4.1 is coming to Xbox Series S and X, which should make it easier for both to deliver crisp 4K images to your TV.
Pay what you can afford
Even if Microsoft ships a $1,800 console, the company’s been clear it won’t be the only Xbox you can buy. Sharma has publicly said that Helix will be a “family of devices,” which has been broadly interpreted to mean that Microsoft will let PC industry partners like Asus sell their own “Xbox” as well.
If the reporting pans out, that wouldn’t just be a cobranded Xbox Ally handheld that runs Windows — Asus could make a console-shaped box that runs a Windows-based Xbox OS, too.
Some of those partners could offer more affordable, less powerful Xboxes than Microsoft’s own flagship box, perhaps with less storage and memory. Microsoft, too, might have creative solutions for storage, like how the company shipped the Xbox 360 with different-size hard drives, or none at all, to make it more affordable. “We will have to empower customers to have very flexible storage offerings,” Sharma said in June.
Or you could buy another Xbox that’s likely going to continue to count as part of Microsoft’s “family”: the existing Xbox Series X and Xbox Series S.
This can all work because games don’t need to target a single console anymore; they haven’t needed to for a long time. An Xbox One game runs on an Xbox One X and an Xbox Series S and an Xbox Series X because they’re all effectively AMD-powered Windows PCs, just with different amounts of performance on tap. The Xbox Helix is a powerful extension of the same continuum. The same is true of PlayStation 4, PS4 Pro, PS5, PS5 Pro, and presumably PS6, minus the Windows part.
Perhaps a particular piece of hardware will stand out as the one developers should target as the baseline for “it looks and runs great on Xbox,” the same way the Steam Deck handheld became a baseline for PC game developers starting in 2022. Maybe, like the Steam Deck and the Nintendo Switch, it’ll help reset our expectations of what a top-shelf game needs to look like.
At this rate, I wouldn’t be surprised if the existing Xbox Series S will be the one. But it could also be Microsoft’s own next handheld Xbox. Fortune’s insiders say it’s coming holiday 2027.

articles.title: "Disillusioned" MAHA leader quits as Trump admin's food agenda spoils: Report
articles.text:
Calley Means—a top ally to anti-vaccine Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and a co-author of the so-called “MAHA bible”—resigned from his role in the Trump administration Thursday, reportedly in frustration over delays to food policy changes sought by the Make America Healthy Again movement.
“I am resigning from the White House with tremendous respect for President Trump and Bobby Kennedy,” Means wrote in a social media post this afternoon. “It was an honor to advocate for MAHA moms in the administration and steer policies like Dietary Guidelines reform, psychedelic reform, removing soda from SNAP, removing food dyes, GRAS reform, and overhauling government food procurement.”
His post did not provide a reason for his departure. Means served as a senior advisor to Kennedy.
Sources close to Means told The Wall Street Journal that he had grown frustrated in the position. Means reportedly blamed other members of the administration for allowing the food industry and special interests to have too much sway in policy decisions. One source described Means as “disillusioned.”
The Journal recently reported that the White House had punted on two of Kennedy’s food priorities: defining and regulating ultraprocessed foods, and regulations that would require school meals to have more protein and less sugar. In recent meetings, Means reportedly raised his voice and grew visibly frustrated over the lack of progress on such issues. Others in the administration complained he was unwilling to make political concessions.

articles.title: Electric or gas? BMW goes both ways with new 2027 X5 and iX5.
articles.text:
When we first drove BMW’s first Neue Klasse model, the iX3, it quickly revealed that BMW knows how to make a good electric vehicle. A clean-sheet design, it featured the automaker’s sixth-generation electric powertrain, a completely reimagined dashboard, and powerful computers to run the whole show. Now, much of that technology is being ported over to the larger X5 line.
But BMW knows not all its customers are ready to go electric, especially in the US, so it’s sticking with its powertrain-agnostic CLAR platform, as used in cars as diverse as the large 7 Series and the new gasoline 3 Series. Which means in addition to the all-electric iX5, there are also mild hybrid and plug-in hybrid X5s available, and in time, even a hydrogen-powered option. For now, as I’ll explain, I think the EV is the pick of the bunch.

Pick your power
The most conventional option is the X5 40 xDrive, powered by a 3.0 L turbocharged inline six-cylinder engine that generates 394 hp (294 kW) and 428 lb-ft (580 Nm). The 48 V mild hybrid system can contribute a decent slug of torque (148 lb-ft/200 Nm) if necessary, and the engine operates under the Miller cycle for better efficiency, as well as featuring the usual BMW engine technology, like variable valve timing. Expect around 26 mpg (9 L/100 km) from this powertrain and a full-to-empty range of 569 miles (915 km).
In time, a 400 V plug-in hybrid X5 50e xDrive will join the mix on the production line at Spartanburg, South Carolina, with a 26.5 kWh battery pack and about 44 miles (71 km) of electric range. And eventually, BMW’s hydrogen fuel cell tech will find its way under the hood of the new-generation X5 too. But those wanting something more efficient than the X5 40 can consider the iX5.
BMW is sticking with its strategy of an asynchronous motor for the front axle and an electrically excited synchronous motor for the rear drive unit, thanks to the lower losses of these motor types compared to motors that use permanent magnets. There is a combined output of 570 hp (425 kW) and 593 lb-ft (804 Nm): The front motor generates 245 hp (183 kW) and 225 lb-ft (305 Nm); the rear produces up to 325 hp (242 kW) and 369 lb-ft (500 Nm).

Between the axles at the heart of the iX5 is a rather massive 144 kWh (usable) battery pack, made up of BMW’s new 120 mm cylindrical cells. These are taller than the 95 mm cells in the iX3, which increases energy density by 30 percent over the smaller SUV’s pack. So even if it’s not quite as long-legged as the gas X5, it should still get 450 miles (724 km) on the EPA test cycle, BMW told us. The car’s route planning is designed to take charging into account and uses onboard AI to “consider expected charging capacity, reliability, and precise station location data when selecting stops.” It will even automatically open the charging port flap when you arrive.
Like the smaller Neue Klasse EVs, the pack operates at 800 V, but it is even more capable when it comes to DC fast charging. At a demo during the first drive in California, we watched as an iX5 plugged in at 10 percent state of charge. Within a little over nine minutes, the EV had reached 50 percent SoC, peaking at 465 kW and averaging 375 kW throughout the session, which delivered 61.5 kWh. (The IONNA station had been specially upgraded to charge above the usual 400 kW.) While that kind of power level is now old hat for some Chinese automakers, it’s a big step forward for a European OEM.
A 10–80 percent fast charge takes as little as 22 minutes—provided you have access to a 460 kW charger—via the NACS port. That same port will accept up to 15.4 kW of AC power via BMW’s home charger, or you can use the provided 11 kW onboard AC charger. There are adapters for both V2H and V2L, as the X5 is capable of bidirectional charging.
No more dials

For decades, BMW’s orange-lit cluster of instrument dials was instantly recognizable. But the move to digital cockpit displays put an end to that. Now, the new HMI paradigm from Munich is the Panoramic Vision display, which blends into the windscreen’s frit (the black border that’s painted on). The display is clear and quite minimalist but very legible, appearing a few inches further down the hood and thus closer to where your eyes focus on the road than if you had to look down at a conventional dash. It first showed up in the iX3 and now arrives in the bigger X5. While it looks unfamiliar at first—and people sure seem to hate the unfamiliar these days—together with the full-color heads-up display, you rarely need to look down into the cockpit while driving.
That goes for interacting with the infotainment system, too. The trapezoidal touchscreen and BMW’s current iDrive OS user interface are easy to use, but the onboard personal assistant works much better than the Alexa-based system did last year in the early iX3 we drove. I recognize that I’m an outlier using voice commands to interact with the car, but when they work, I’m going to use them. Particularly in the absence of physical controls—“Hey BMW, turn on the driver’s seat massager” is easier for me to do behind the wheel than tapping the car icon to access vehicle settings and then scrolling down to seats and then selecting the tab for massage and then turning it on.
There’s also a passenger screen, although, helpfully, BMW made this its own option rather than including it in a package. The screen only allows the front seat passenger to watch streaming videos, play games, or browse the web—they cannot interact with native infotainment functions like navigation or the climate settings from that screen, just the one to its left.
The iX5 stops for red lights
Less well-equipped back seats are also available.

Another difference between the gasoline X5 and the iX5 is that the latter features BMW’s new “Heart of Joy.” This is one of the powerful domain controller computers that replaces the jumble of black boxes and single-function ECUs, in this case the one that manages vehicle dynamics. As we found with the iX3, this clever electronic brain enables solid chassis and powertrain control, including the ability to come to an incredibly smooth stop while one-pedal driving.
But the iX5 has another party trick that I didn’t notice in the smaller, cheaper EV: It will automatically detect red lights and stop signs, alerting you and braking the car if necessary (i.e., you were about to run the light or sign). The feature works whether you’ve engaged active drive assist or not. It’s always there like a safety net along with the car’s other advanced driver assistance systems. (I am sure you can disable this feature like the others, although I didn’t check, and I’m sure people will post comments with their particular edge case. Given driving standards these days, I’d be happier if everyone left it running.)
The new assist suite is called BMW Symbiotic Drive, and it’s of the very latest generation of ADAS that allows the driver to apply brake inputs without canceling out of active driving mode—only a heavy stomp on the brake will shut off cruise control.
The EV drives better
Neither X5 nor iX5 are unpleasant to drive. The X5’s engine is quiet, and neither car suffers from much wind noise. Unlike the iX, which had something of a “skyhook” magic carpet ride, both iX5 and X5 are more firmly sprung, but not bone-rattlingly so. But I give the edge to the heavier iX5—although the battery adds to a hefty 6,200 lb (2,813 kg) curb weight, the extra mass helps dampen the short-duration shocks that make it past the X5’s (optional) adaptive air suspension. Longer-duration bumps are smoothed out by either car.
If you have passengers in the iX5, you might find Sport mode has too violent an initial throttle tip-in; in the other throttle settings (eco, comfort), this is not an issue. The iX5 also offers five levels of lift-off regenerative braking, from none at all (it coasts very well) to 0.6 G of regen. And it has true one-pedal driving that will bring you to a complete stop.
The 2027 X5 40 xDrive starts at $72,100, plus a $1,450 delivery and handling charge, and you can already find them in BMW showrooms. There is still a premium for the electric version—144 kWh of lithium-ion isn’t cheap, after all. Thus, the iX5 60 xDrive starts at $79,800 plus delivery and arrives in Q1 2027.
Jonathan is the Automotive Editor at Ars Technica. He has a BSc and PhD in Pharmacology. In 2014 he decided to indulge his lifelong passion for the car by leaving the National Human Genome Research Institute and launching Ars Technica's automotive coverage. He lives in Washington, DC.
When I saw pictures of their Neue Klasse interiors, I thought they were really trying hard for style points, and were needlessly jazzing things up to make it look distinctive. After buying an iX3 and driving it for a month, though, I am completely radicalized: This is a function-over-form interior, where almost all the components are actually there for usability.
The panorama thing is wonderful, just absolutely what every car should be. It's like a HUD -- right where you're already looking, and at a far-away focal distance, and not obscured by the steering wheel -- except fully opaque and guaranteed to work with polarized glasses, and with room for even more information.
The slanted screen follows the curve of the steering wheel. From where the driver sits, you can see the whole screen; if it were straight up and down, it would either be blocked by the wheel, or else require more of a reach on top.
The "just touch controls" thing is totally overhyped. Unlike Tesla (which genuinely is all touch), this has mirror controls on the door, door lock controls on the door, wiper controls on a normal stalk, headlight controls on a normal stalk, a physical gear selector, physical parking brake button, physical front/rear defrost buttons, physical tailgate button. It looks like it's a touchscreen only car, but that's only because it's smartly retained all the physical controls that aren't on the center dash, which Tesla has lost.
The only real thing that could conceivably still be a physical control in 2026 (we all agree that entertainment is a touchscreen in this Android Auto/Carplay world, and there's a physical power/volume knob in addition to steering wheel controls) and isn't is climate. And for the most part, that's not a big deal: It's always exposed at the bottom of the screen as big touch surfaces, and doesn't require you to go into the menus to choose things. I think you could make a case for still having two climate knobs (one on each side) and maybe a hard button for the steering wheel heater, but it's a minor criticism that doesn't vitiate everything the car does right.

articles.title: NVIDIA veut en finir avec les saccades en jeu : ses nouveaux pilotes changent la donne
articles.text:
Avec les pilotes GeForce 621.01, NVIDIA active l’Advanced Shader Delivery de Microsoft sur ses cartes RTX. Les shaders arrivent précompilés, ce qui supprime l’attente du premier lancement et les saccades liées à la compilation en pleine partie.
Les nouveaux pilotes NVIDIA préparent les shaders à l’avance : au lieu de compiler sur votre machine, le jeu récupère une version déjà adaptée à votre carte et à votre pilote. D’après NVIDIA, cette attente pouvait atteindre 30 minutes sur les configuration les plus modestes, au premier lancement comme après une mise à jour de pilote.
Des shaders compilés chez Microsoft, téléchargés avec le jeu
Le principe tient en deux étapes. Les studios enregistrent les shaders de leur jeu sous DirectX 12, puis les serveurs de Microsoft les compilent pour des centaines de milliers de combinaisons de cartes et de pilotes. Au téléchargement, l’application Xbox pour PC récupère la version qui correspond à la machine, y compris pour un jeu acheté sur Steam.
Selon NVIDIA, la bibliothèque de shaders de Microsoft couvre déjà presque 100 % des cas. Concrètement, les saccades provoquées par une compilation en cours de partie disparaissent elles aussi. C’est un fléau bien connu des joueurs PC, là où les consoles s’en sortent parce que leur matériel est identique d’une machine à l’autre.
Windows 11 + application Xbox
Pour pouvoir bénéficier de cette nouvelle fonctionnalité, Il faut Windows 11 et l’application Xbox installée, et surtout que le studio ait préparé son jeu. NVIDIA ne cite pour l’instant que Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4, dont le lancement complet avec multijoueur est prévu le 23 octobre, ainsi queGears of War: E-Day.
Le pilote 621.01 est disponible dans l’application NVIDIA et sur le site de GeForce. Il accompagne également la mise à jour 2.5 de Cyberpunk 2077, prévue le 22 octobre, qui intègre nativement le DLSS 4.5. Au programme : la Dynamic Multi Frame Generation, génération d'images jusqu'à 6X et adoption des modèles IA de deuxième génération pour les technologies DLSS déjà présentes dans le jeu. Des fonctionnalités dont certaines étaient auparavant accessibles via les overrides de l'application NVIDIA.
Modern Warfare 4 sert de vitrine à la nouvelle génération de DLSS
Modern Warfare 4 cumule les technologies RTX, le DLSS est actif dans tous les modes, la Frame Generation arrive sur les RTX 40, et les RTX 50 peuvent activer la Dynamic Multi Frame Generation jusqu’à 6X. Bien évidement, Reflex est disponible sur toutes les GeForce RTX pour réduire la latence, notamment quand la frame gen est activée.
Le pilote embarque aussi plusieurs correctifs : un plantage de Wuthering Waves avec les filtres Freestyle et la Frame Generation, un crash de Star Citizen sous Vulkan, ou encore un flash noir occasionnel sur les moniteurs QHD à 360 Hz. Reste à voir combien d’éditeurs brancheront leurs jeux sur le système Advanced Shader Delivery, car c’est de leur adhésion que dépend l’intérêt réel de la fonction.

articles.title: Plus de 1500 euros : la prochaine Xbox s’annonce hors de prix
articles.text:
La feuille de route de la prochaine Xbox a fuité mardi, au détour d’un long portrait consacré à la patronne de la marque, Asha Sharma. Une console portable ouvrirait le bal pour les fêtes de fin d’année 2027, suivie un an plus tard de la console de salon connue sous le nom de code Helix. En interne, le prix de cette dernière serait projeté entre 1 200 et 1 800 dollars, sauf si Microsoft accepte d’en subventionner une partie.
Plus du double d’une Series X
La fourchette haute représente plus du double du tarif actuel d’une Xbox Series X vendue avec son lecteur, affichée à 799,99 dollars outre-Atlantique. Depuis le 1er août, la même console coûte 799,99 euros en France, après une hausse de 150 euros, et la Series S d’entrée de gamme a suivi le mouvement à 499,99 euros.
Les fabricants de mémoire vive anticipent des prix en hausse jusqu’en 2027 et 2028, portés par l’appétit des centres de données, pendant que la marge de la division Xbox est estimée à environ 3 %. Phil Spencer, l’ancien patron de la marque, reconnaissait autrefois une perte de 100 à 200 dollars sur chaque console vendue, un modèle de subvention que la marge actuelle rendrait difficile à reconduire. Sony affronte les mêmes surcoûts pour sa prochaine console.
Windows et Xbox se sont déchirés sur le système
L’équipe Windows aurait poussé pour installer une version allégée de Windows Home sur la future console portable, à en croire le même portrait, quand l’équipe Xbox défendait un système maison, taillé pour la performance en jeu. Le ton serait monté au point qu’un dirigeant de Xbox aurait menacé d’enterrer la portable plutôt que d’accepter la copie imposée. L’équipe de la console aurait fini par obtenir le pilotage du logiciel.
Helix est pourtant présentée depuis le printemps comme une machine hybride, capable de lancer les jeux Xbox comme les jeux PC autour d’une puce AMD conçue sur mesure, rétrocompatibilité incluse. Un « mode Xbox » épuré, déployé sur Windows 11 depuis avril, donne déjà un avant-goût de l’interface, héritée des consoles portables ROG Xbox Ally.
Interrogée sur cette passe d’armes, Asha Sharma, qui affiche l’ambition de faire de Xbox le numéro un mondial du jeu et du divertissement, s’en tient à une ligne : « Nous ne pouvons pas construire Helix seuls ». Les kits de développement restent annoncés pour 2027, un calendrier posé à la Game Developers Conference en mars, alors qu’une sortie dès 2027 circulait jusqu’ici pour la console elle-même. Les échéances internes auraient malgré tout été avancées de plusieurs mois, quitte à s’appuyer sur l’IA pour tenir le rythme. Le même portrait évoque enfin de nouvelles vagues de licenciements d’ici janvier.

articles.title: Authorities disrupt nearly 11,000 cybercrime networks in Africa
articles.text:
Law enforcement agencies have disrupted nearly 11,000 cybercriminal networks and arrested more than 1,400 people in Operation Serengeti III, which targeted business email compromise, ransomware, and online scams.
Coordinated by Interpol, the operation involved authorities from 21 countries and private partners like Team Cymru, Kaspersky, Group-IB, and Fortinet, in a major crackdown on cybercrime across Africa.
The action unrolled between June 29 and August 31 and led to the recovery of more than $105 million in illegal funds.
In a press release today, Interpol says that Operation Serengeti III has resulted in the arrest of 1,462 suspected cybercriminals and the dismantling of 10,909 malicious networks.
The investigation identified 65,929 victims and estimated financial losses at more than $385 million.
In Uganda, law enforcement dismantled two transnational fraud rings and arrested 365 individuals for suspected links to online investment and pension fraud operations.
Another highlight of the operation are illegal cryptocurrency mining centers in Angola, where nine suspects have been arrested, and more than 2,000 mining devices have been seized.
Authorities also arrested one individual in Nigeria, suspected of running "a large-scale phishing and business email compromise operation that harvested software credentials and amassed approximately 2.1 million email addresses."
Interpol notes that Operation Serengeti III actions also impacted malicious mobile lending applications, fraudulent vehicle imports, and cryptocurrency investment scams.
Team Cymru and other private cybersecurity firms supported the operation by providing intelligence and technical expertise, including key information on suspicious domains, IP addresses, and command-and-control (C2) infrastructure, helping investigators map criminal networks and identify suspects.
"Our ability to see attacker infrastructure at internet scale gives defenders a fundamentally different starting point. Instead of waiting for an attack and then investigating the damage, we can help expose the networks behind criminal operations and can enable defensive actions," said Jacomo Piccolini, Team Cymru's VP of Global Data Partnerships.
The first Operation Serengeti, conducted across 19 African countries between September and October 2024, resulted in 1,006 arrests, the takedown of 134,089 malicious infrastructures and networks, and the recovery of roughly $44 million.
Operation Serengeti 2.0, conducted between June and August 2025 and also focused on Africa, resulted in 1,209 arrests, the dismantling of 11,432 malicious infrastructures, and the seizure of $97.4 million.

articles.title: World's first iPhone Duo sold in Australia - and it's being given away to help the homeless - Tech Guide
articles.text:
The first iPhone Duo in the world went on sale today in Sydney, Australia – and the first person who waited in line for five days to buy it is going to give it away to raise money to combat homelessness.
Jeremy Cabral was first in line to buy Apple’s first foldable iPhone – the iPhone Duo- when he arrived on Monday at the George St Apple Store in Sydney,
Cabral even tattooed the word Duo on his wrist so it could be seen when he held up the world’s first iPhone Duo sold.
“I’m actually here to raise funds for homelessness,” Cabral told Tech Guide.
“I’m doing this as a funds challenge, raising funds for We Are Mobilised: buying the world’s first iPhone Duo, actually getting two of them in both the colours, and then I’m also going to give it away.”
Carbral says it’s been a tough few days sleeping outside the store – which is the same challenge faces by homeless men and women in Australia.
“Honestly, it’s about being uncomfortable,” he said.
“OK I knew exactly what I was getting in for. I got here Monday at 5pm. Each night I probably sleep for 2.5 hours max, between like 3 and 6 in the morning.”
And Cabral says this is not the first time he’s lined up to buy an iPhone. He said he was in line in 2012 to buy the iPhone 5.
There was a line of about 150 people outside the store who were hoping to purchase the iPhone Duo.
As people arrived in the line, Apple Store staff asking them the iPhone Duo model they we’re hoping to purchase to ensure there is enough stock to meet the walk-in demand.
On the other side of the door were the customers who had pre-ordered the phone and organised pickup at the George Street store in Sydney.
Pre-orders of the iPhone Duo online were extremely popular with customers reporting expected delivery windows extending out to January 2027 even only a few minutes after the pre-orders began.
Reports suggest Apple may have had production issues which impacted stock levels to meet the initial launch demand.
But Tech Guide’s observations at the Apple Store and talking to staff gave us a feeling there was plenty of stock to go around.
