articles.title: PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them
articles.text:
PHP’s security scramble is just a preview: AI is digging up flaws faster than maintainers can fix them
One of the biggest security scares to hit the web is causing widespread disruption, prompting businesses, hospitals, schools, and government agencies to temporarily shut down websites and online services as they scramble to protect themselves against two critical vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language underpinning much of the internet.
The vulnerabilities, collectively dubbed PHP2Shell, could allow unauthenticated attackers to execute malicious code on affected servers. Major technology companies have been racing to protect users, with Cloudflare deploying firewall protections and Automattic confirming that websites hosted across its platforms, including WordPress.com, WordPress VIP and Tumblr, have been secured. The Wikimedia Foundation, meanwhile, took several supporting services offline until they can be patched.
The PHP project released emergency fixes on Wednesday for versions 8.2 through 8.5. Older versions are no longer officially supported, although some distributions and vendors provide legacy fixes, and PHP has published limited patches for versions 7.4 through 8.1.
But while the PHP vulnerabilities are a major deal in their own right, the circumstances surrounding their discovery, remediation, and disclosure offer a revealing glimpse into the growing pressures facing the open-source community, as AI makes it easier to uncover serious security flaws.
“Find bad vulnerabilities in PHP”: Prompt discovery
News of the impending patches emerged on Tuesday, after details leaked ahead of their scheduled disclosure. The following day, OpenAI revealed that security firm Calif had discovered one of the flaws using its GPT-5.6 Sol model, while Google-owned Wiz had independently identified both vulnerabilities. OpenAI said it spent two months coordinating a response involving PHP maintainers, the security researchers, Cloudflare, and government cybersecurity agencies, as part of its Patch the Planet initiative.
The effort was disrupted when software supply-chain security company Chainguard released patched PHP container images more than six hours before the agreed time. CEO Dan Lorenc acknowledged on LinkedIn that he made the call, noting that Chainguard had independently rediscovered the flaw using a frontier AI model and the simple prompt “find bad vulnerabilities in PHP“.
Lorenc defended the decision by pointing to reports of attacks and the ease of reproducing the vulnerability. The PHP Foundation, for its part, argued that the early release could help attackers while other vendors were still preparing their patches.
“This disregarded weeks of work by many parties toward a coordinated disclosure,” the Foundation notes.
Nils Adermann, a PHP Foundation board member and creator and co-maintainer of Composer, says that “there were no confirmed exploits,” adding that any identified activity was merely people attempting exploits.
“The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional.”
“There was a clear embargo until the time of disclosure and public release, that was discussed and evaluated repeatedly as information arrived, weighing the risk of exploitation vs protection from publishing patches without complete updates,” Adermann writes in response to Lorenc’s post. “The decision you took unilaterally without any communication with the PHP team was both irresponsible and unprofessional. The proper thing to do here is apologize, not to justify your clear misbehavior.”
The new normal
The PHP pandemonium highlights a larger concern, however: AI is making it easier to find security flaws, faster than the people responsible for fixing them can respond. And as Lorenc himself put it: “This is unfortunately the new normal for the industry.”
Just a day before OpenAI’s disclosure, Anthropic published research showing that Claude had identified 493 security issues across 25 open-source projects encompassing more than five million lines of code. One configuration flaw had gone unnoticed for 21 years, and had the potential to disable an authentication requirement, allowing unauthorised clients to reach a supposedly restricted server.
While not all of Anthropic’s findings were exploitable vulnerabilities, they underline a growing problem: AI can uncover security weaknesses at scale, but assessing them and developing reliable fixes still takes time and expertise.
Christopher Robinson, CTO of Akrites and CTO / chief security architect at the Open Source Security Foundation (OpenSSF), says the PHP emergency is also a reminder of the importance of being ready to respond when serious vulnerabilities do emerge.
“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen.”
“The best way to minimize the impact of events like PHP2Shell is to prepare and plan for these things to happen,” Robinson tells The New Stack. “Having a vulnerability management process and understanding who can assist when issues become too complex are the best things that both open source projects and commercial entities can do.”
When finding bugs becomes easier than fixing them
For Michelle Tilley, software engineer and CTO of Atuin, an open-source developer tool with more than 32,000 GitHub stars, the kind of emergency response mounted for PHP would be difficult to replicate for smaller open-source projects.
“The response here looked like a vendor emergency, with a coalition, government agencies, and WAF (web application firewall) rules,” Tilley tells The New Stack. “This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”
“This works for a project like PHP, but no one is going to assemble a coalition for an obscure 3-maintainer library that turns out to be used in software all around the world.”
Atuin itself is already receiving more AI-generated bug reports and pull requests, Tilley says. While her company has enough engineering resources to handle them, many smaller projects depend on unpaid maintainers working in their spare time, who can become overwhelmed and walk away.
“These developers can, and do, burn out,” Tilley continues. “Sometimes they arrange for someone else to take over the project; often, they simply stop working on it, and downstream consumers never know. That’s how projects end up with vulnerabilities that will never be patched.”
Ultimately, she wants more responsibility to fall on researchers and businesses that rely on the code.
“There’s no single fix, but the direction is clear,” Tilley says. “The cost of remediation has to move toward the people finding the bugs and the companies depending on the code.”
That pressure extends to larger projects, too. Madelyn Olson, an AWS principal engineer and maintainer of the Valkey database, says that it too is finding and fixing far more security bugs this year than before.
“The hardest part has shifted from finding bugs to fixing them,” Olson tells The New Stack. “PHP is a good example.”
A PHP developer first identified the underlying problem behind one of this week’s vulnerabilities while fixing an issue uncovered during a 2024 security audit, which was organised by the Open Source Technology Improvement Fund (OSTIF). However, attempts to resolve it stalled because proposed fixes risked breaking compatibility, affecting performance or disrupting third-party extensions. Few engineers had the expertise to resolve those trade-offs, according to the PHP Foundation.
“AI is getting very good at finding bugs,” Olson says. “Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”
“AI is getting very good at finding bugs. Making the right fix still takes experienced maintainers, and that’s where support from companies matters most.”
To manage the influx, Valkey is narrowing its definition of a security vulnerability, using AI to inspect its own code, and making backports and releases easier to produce.
The Chainguard brouhaha also raises the question of whether disclosure timelines need to change. Olson recalls three researchers independently reporting the same Valkey bug in one week, each using LLMs. Valkey is now working toward shorter embargoes — although that is a different matter from breaking an agreed release date.
“If you found a bug with an LLM, it’s safe to say someone else can find it too,” Olson says. “That argues for shorter embargoes and faster releases, and Valkey is working toward shorter embargoes now, which is a trend we’re seeing across most large projects.”
A growing security backlog
Derek Zimmer, executive director of OSTIF, said the volume of both legitimate discoveries and poor-quality reports is creating backlogs, with maintainers spending scarce engineering time just establishing which issues are real.
“Maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage.”
“The reality in 2026 is that finding serious bugs is easier than ever, and maintainers are drowning in a sea of vulnerability reports from the public which is both slop reports and legitimate reports which are nearly impossible to separate without spending a lot of time to triage,” Zimmer tells The New Stack.
To help, OSTIF is trialling initiatives such as Project V-LAT, which embeds engineers in projects to review findings and develop fixes, while helping maintainers improve how reports are processed.
Robinson also emphasises the need for shared security expertise and dedicated engineers who can support upstream projects. He rejects the suggestion that exposing more flaws necessarily makes open source less secure, pointing to the opportunity for companies that depend on the code to contribute fixes. Yet, many projects have neither the money nor the expertise to respond independently.
“Most upstream maintainers are also acting as volunteers within the projects, with little to no budget, infrastructure, or supporting tools,” Robinson says. “There will be no ‘one size fits all’ approach here, we’ll need to approach this situation using multiple, parallel approaches to get the broadest chance for successful outcomes.”

articles.title: Lisbon’s Beyond Vision raises over €28 million to scale AI drones for civilian and defence markets | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Beyond Vision, a Lisbon-based manufacturer of unmanned aerial systems and vehicles (drones), announced today the completion of an investment round of over €28 million.
The round was co-led by Índico Capital Partners and Lince Capital, with a follow-on investment from ActiveCap, a shareholder since 2024. The company plans to use this fresh capital to scale industrial production capacity, accelerate technological development in AI and swarm capacity, and expand the company’s international presence in the defence and critical infrastructure sectors.
“In critical sectors such as defence, infrastructure management, and security, the reliance on cutting-edge, reliable, and sovereign technology is now a strategic priority for many countries. Beyond Vision has redefined this market by combining high-precision hardware with advanced artificial intelligence algorithms at a very competitive cost. This investment will give Beyond Vision the financial robustness needed to scale production and compete globally in important segments of autonomous unmanned vehicles,” said Stephan de Moraes, Managing General Partner of Índico Capital Partners.
Founded in 2013 and led by Dário Pedro (CEO) and Luís Miguel Campos (Chairman), Beyond Vision specialises in dual-use advanced unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms. The company focuses on developing diverse collaborative autonomous systems with AI capabilities, providing innovative solutions across sectors.
The company says it recognised the potential of the autonomous unmanned vehicle sector early on and began developing drones powered by AI algorithms and cloud-based management platforms to meet growing demand for these solutions.
It claims that its drones quickly gained recognition for their quality, and the company became an officially registered NATO supplier and won numerous awards.
The Portuguese company notes that it integrates multiple parallel communication systems and AI into its aircraft, optimising their capabilities for a wide range of applications, both in the civil and military sectors. Its cloud-based platform for remote drone control, beXStream, leverages AI and automation to optimise operations.
Pedro said, “The capital raised in this round will be applied in several areas. First, Beyond Vision will strengthen its operational infrastructure and scale its industrial production capacity to meet the growing global demand for autonomous systems. In parallel, the company will accelerate investment in Research and Development (R&D), deepening the integration of advanced Artificial Intelligence algorithms and new functionalities in its cloud management platform.
“Finally, the funds will allow it to consolidate its commercial expansion into new international markets, strengthening its presence in the defence, security, and critical infrastructure monitoring sector.”
The company reported that it grew its team to 150 employees, exceeded its estimated 2025 revenue, and expanded its list of military and civilian clients across several countries, strengthening its market position. In July this year, it announced a partnership with AVP (Aero Voo de Portugal) to represent them commercially in the Hashemite Kingdom of Jordan.
In 2025, Beyond Vision signed a €15 million contract in the US to supply 300 emergency drones by 2028. The Portuguese company also plans to open a US factory in 2027, with a €50 million investment.
This investment aims to prepare the company for global scalability as demand for its civilian and defence solutions grows exponentially, Beyond Vision remarked.

articles.title: Samsung all but confirms iPhone Duo is goosing Galaxy Z8 sales
articles.text:
Android-powered foldable phones have been available for years, but most people never paid attention to them. As predicted, that could be changing now that Apple has entered the folding phone market with the iPhone Duo. Analysts have speculated that Samsung’s Z8 foldables were seeing a boost from the iPhone announcement, and now Samsung has seemingly confirmed that.
In a new blog post, Samsung UK crows that the company’s 2026 foldable lineup is moving much faster than last year’s models. Compared to the Galaxy Z Fold 7, combined European sales for the Galaxy Z Fold 8 and Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra are up 45 percent. Samsung isn’t talking about Z Flip 8 sales, but it previously noted that its larger foldables made up about 80 percent of foldable purchases. We can assume any increase there is not impressive enough to mention.
The reason for flat Z Flip sales may simply be that Apple didn’t release a flip phone. Unsurprisingly, Samsung doesn’t mention Apple or the iPhone Duo in its press release. However, it does say that search volume for the Z8 series across Europe spiked 460 percent the week of September 6 to 12. And guess what was announced on September 9? Yep, the iPhone Duo. Z Fold 8 search volume across the entire month of September (when the phones launched) was up 260 percent.
Samsung noted last month that US preorders for the Galaxy Z8 series were trending 30 percent higher than last year, but it hasn’t confirmed any updated numbers for the US market. This meshes with third-party reports, which claimed Samsung was ramping up foldable manufacturing, particularly of the wider, iPhone-like Z Fold 8. The company isn’t talking about the proportion of Z Fold 8 versus Z Fold 8 Ultra sales, but it seems likely that Samsung’s wider foldable is doing better in the wake of Apple’s foldable announcement.

articles.title: Making the case for context-aware AI
articles.text:
Sponsored
Making the case for context-aware AI
Moving AI beyond experimentation requires connecting agents to operational context and identifying the business processes where they can deliver the greatest value.
In partnership withCelonis
Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster. But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one. As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes.
For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can't just do that in a vacuum,” he says. Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know.
The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use. A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve. Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them. Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling.
This approach could also change how employees spend their time. Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions. Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents.
Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales. With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly. As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.”
This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis.
Full Transcript
Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I'm Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace.
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis.
Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads. After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle. By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit. They're applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI's potential unrealized.
Two words for you: context matters.
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis.
Welcome, Devavrat.
Devavrat Shah: Hello, Megan. Thanks for having me here.
Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today. Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale?
Devavrat: It's a fantastic question. And as you correctly noted, we're at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned. As you know, I've been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it's no surprise that I'm very bullish about AI's future in enterprises.
The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization. We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes. There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency. In either of them, we have some processes in place. You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first. Many of us help coordinate those things. Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task. And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision.
Now, it's those tasks, or what I would call roles, that's where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it's a painful automate. And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context. You can't just do that in a vacuum. And that's why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise. And that's where I think there'll be the biggest transformation that would come.
Megan: Right. To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making. If context isn't introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play?
Devavrat: Fantastic. Let's just take the setting I was describing. We are trying to automate a role or support a role or augment a role depending on the type of decision, depending upon type of task. And let's for a second imagine that all these, as they're called, frontier labs have built these amazing models and amazing AI infrastructure so that everything that's happened in the universe and it's likely to happen in the universe is all there.
Now, we have a small decision that we want to make for that very specific context is there. And without having access to that, this massive system, this extremely bright person would figure that out eventually by asking lots of questions, the way we do it as humans, and then finally do the right thing. The problem is to get to that, it will do so much compute at some level that to get simple tasks done, we are spending massive amount of compute. So that's scenario one.
In reality, that's not going to be the scenario, and we'll miss some important context, important constraint, important guardrail, and then we'll make a mistake. And sometimes that mistake can be okay. It's like me giving you a recommendation saying, go restaurant A, and maybe you may not enjoy the dinner, versus sometimes mistakes will be very, very expensive. That is me telling you what the financial forecast is and somehow that leads to the company's doom.
Megan: Right. So in an enterprise setting, these are really business critical decisions that are being made. So the impact is that much more if we get this wrong, isn't it? And on a practical level then, what are the different ways that organizations can add in this context layer we're talking about? How does Celonis, for example, deliver that operational context via a real time digital twin of an organization?
Devavrat: Absolutely. I think if it might be useful just to double click on the history of Celonis. As you know, Celonis, as an organization, came into existence with the mission, with the goal of helping organizations adhere to their ideal processes, build better processes, enable people to work with multiple processes in an intertwined manner. And that's where their primary, let's call it a DNA, has been about what I would call process intelligence. Take how enterprises help put multiple things together, digitize them, enable people to get their processes better, understand where the issues are, and then how do you re-engineer the process within organizations so that things can happen better.
Now, if you want to bring decision intelligence into this, each atomic step of this process that was potentially was done before by experts, people, now we want agents to help us enable that. And that's where knowing this context of a process within enterprise and then bringing AI agents along with that, what I would like to call it as a roled agents, exactly provide the right way to bring decision intelligence to enterprises. And this is how Celonis brings context to help enterprise make better decision.
Megan: Right. And then in terms of how this works as well, how does the context layer relate to both the layer below, that's the systems of record layer, and also the layer above, that identic layer?
Devavrat: That's a fantastic question, Megan. The layer below primarily is, if we call it system of record, primarily it's the workflow tools that are there and then the event logs that they generate around it. The layer above is either business user experts consuming information, or they're consuming that information maybe through agents working on top of that context layer. And this is where the way context model, as Celonis calls it, is designed is to do three things simultaneously. One is to get the right abstraction of the layer below, so that the right pieces of the process can be agentified. Two is to bring the rolled agents for each of these pieces in a structured guardrailed manner. And then the three is to be agent first so that if there are other agentic infrastructure that are already talking to it, they can naturally talk to it so that then they can bring the right output for humans or experts to review, look at it, approve, and maybe then at times automate.
Megan: Fantastic. And for all the benefits that we're talking about with this, are there also challenges when it comes to implementing a context layer? For example, do most organizations have the right data in place to provide AI with the context it needs? And if not, I wonder what some of the practical steps are that they might need to take to address that.
Devavrat: It's again, a crucial question to make this real. We can imagine an ideal world, but if we cannot reach the ideal world, then it's just ideal. So now in this setting, as we discussed the three layers, one being the layer which is the layer below system of record and workflow tools. In some sense, those things already exist. They don't need to be complete. They don't need to be in the cleanest possible manner. The way context model is designed with agentic's architecture, it manages to connect to those things and make sense of it.
And then things on top is very much in control of Celonis's infrastructure, so it's not that complicated. The crucial thing here though is when one goes to enterprise, when one opens up, let's say a system of record or workflow tool, event logs or things like that, one has to go through, what I would call, classical InfoSec to make sure that you can trust a vendor's software that's coming into your organization. And I think that is the primary process that is a step between, before and after, if I may call it.
Megan: Right. So that's the real crucial step for people to be taking here. And as AI agents with context are able to make more complex, more accurate hopefully decisions, I wonder what you think the role of human intelligence and input will be moving forward, and how can organizations perhaps strike the balance between the two?
Devavrat: There are the benefits and then there are the challenges. Benefits are clear. If you have right AI agents in a right role manner going through your decision processes, hopefully they're doing it quicker and hence your decisions are taken earlier so that your opportunity cost is not lost. You are taking decisions in time, you can plan much better, et cetera, et cetera. This is especially useful when you have to take very manual, repetitive, grungy tasks where access to workforce, coordination between people become crucial parts of the decision process. In a sense, that's where the huge value can come in. The flip side of that is that means that people won't be doing that.
On the other hand, the other type of decision that we always make, which are strategic decisions. It could be a small strategic decision, it could be large strategic decision, but the strategic decisions that typically most organizations don't have bandwidth to take to think, that opportunity would open up and that's where likely lots of humans and experts would engage more. In a sense, now they would have better support helping them rationally think through what are the choices that they have, how do different choices compare? And then at the end of the day, it's organization's role to decide which of the option to take because it belongs to their interest in mind where they want to go.
And so in a sense, there will be what I would call shift of workforce in terms of instead of doing a lot more repetitive, a lot less repetitive, but a lot more strategic work and that's where people will have to spend time.
The other place where I am personally very optimistic is like every technology change creates new work that it's difficult to predict at the time of change. My hope is that there will be another type of opportunity and work that will be created where we'll be engaging our workforce. Goes without saying, this would mean that we will have to carefully think through reeducating or educating some of our workforce thoughtfully. And I think as an academic in me, as an educator in me, I really feel that the timescale at which these changes are happening are so fast. So we need to also act in a similar manner.
Megan: For any decision maker listening to this, how should they start implementing these changes? For example, how can they prepare their workforce? What role should governance play as well?
Devavrat: Okay, that's a great question. If you want to start, the first thing you need to do is identify a decision where you want to bring intelligence. Let's identify the process around it. Let's identify each step of the process. Let's take the most crucial, difficult step in that. Let's try to bring AI agents to help you to do that. And then from there you go and then let's measure how much speed are we getting, how much value are we getting? And that'll help us understand whether this was worth it. So that's one.
Second is governance. Well, we're going to bring AI in this prescriptive manner for each task in a role. That means that for that role, we can tell what it can or cannot do very clearly. And Celonis prescribes certified role agents for these things. This helps you clearly have an understanding of what sort of contract would be for this.
And the third thing, which is people, and now this is where it's really important, is a part which gets automated, but then there's a part where experts will be in the loop and this is where they need to understand the outputs of AI, how do you work with that and what its implication would be? And this is where some AI education is needed and then some tool education is needed.
Megan: Yes, absolutely. The pace is incredible, isn't it, in this space? And speaking of, I suppose if we could close with a look ahead, given the right context, of course, what are the use cases perhaps for enterprise AI that are on the horizon that you think could be most impactful or perhaps what you're simply most excited about?
Devavrat: I think I would categorize them into three types. They're all decision intelligence, decision-making, but there are three types. One, what I would call many repetitive manual labor-intensive, so that's one.
Two, what I would call coordination style tasks. A lot of work that we do right now as an information workforce that's spent in coordination, that's why email spreadsheets, et cetera. A lot of that would be done much better, much quicker and less boring, so to speak.
And then the third is where, especially as a support to human decision-makers to provide strategic support augmentation, and that's a third type of decisions that would be done. If I think of any planning process in enterprises, so financial planning, workforce planning, marketing, sales, product, anything, all of those are business critical decisions that we make that take annual planning process, take annual time. Now maybe it should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.
Megan: That'd be fantastic, wouldn't it? Fantastic. Thank you so much for that brilliant conversation, Devavrat. That was Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, whom I spoke with from Brighton in England.
That's it for this episode of Business Lab. I'm your host, Megan Tatum. I'm a contributing editor and host for Insights, the custom publishing division of MIT Technology Review. We were founded in 1899 at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, and you can find us in print, on the web, and at events each year around the world. For more information about us and the show, please check out our website at technologyreview.com.
This show is available wherever you get your podcasts. And if you enjoyed this episode, we hope you'll take a moment to rate and review us. Business Lab is a production of MIT Technology Review, and this episode was produced by Giro Studios. Thanks so much for listening. Goodbye.

articles.title: La serie de 'Mass Effect' sigue en marcha pese al cierre de BioWare
articles.text:
El cierre de BioWare por parte de Electronic Arts es el más reciente golpe que sufre la industria de los videojuegos, pues ha implicado el despido de cientos de personas y la cancelación del nuevo Mass Effect. Sin embargo, la serie basada en dicha saga no se vería afectada por esta situación.
Según reporta IGN, la serie de Mass Effect para Prime Video continúa su desarrollo con total normalidad. La publicación cita que fuentes internas de la plataforma ratificaron que el proyecto sigue en marcha bajo el ala de Amazon MGM Studios. Asimismo, asegura que todas las personas vinculadas con la parte creativa de la adaptación siguen a bordo de la iniciativa.
Esto es un off the record, así que todavía no hubo un comunicado oficial de Prime Video o Amazon MGM Studios en tal sentido. Vale recordar que, si bien había presencia de BioWare en la producción ejecutiva de la serie de Mass Effect, la realización del proyecto no dependía exclusivamente del estudio.
Con este panorama, la adaptación televisiva de Mass Effect debería continuar con sus preparativos incluso tras el cierre del estudio perteneciente a EA. Doug Jung funge como showrunner, mientras que el guion corre por cuenta de Daniel Casey. Los productores ejecutivos confirmados son Ari Arad y Karim Zreik.
Será interesante ver qué ocurre con Mike Gamble, jefe de Mass Effect. El susodicho iba a representar a BioWare en la producción ejecutiva de la serie, pero aún no está claro si conservará ese título tras el cierre de BioWare. Como ya dijimos, Prime Video habría ratificado la continuidad de todos los creativos vinculados con el proyecto, aunque no hay que descartar posibles cambios en el futuro cercano.
La serie de Mass Effect para Prime Video sigue en marcha (por ahora)
La serie de Mass Effect se puso en marcha a finales de 2024, aunque los detalles se han mantenido escasos hasta aquí. Recién a finales del año pasado, Gamble reveló que la adaptación contaría una historia totalmente nueva y que no adaptaría ninguno de los juegos ya existentes.
El líder de Mass Effect puntualizó por entonces que la trama sería canon y que se ubicaría cronológicamente después de la trilogía original. Asimismo, reveló que no se enfocaría en volver a contar la historia del comandante Shepard, lo que dio a entender que el objetivo era poner los reflectores sobre un nuevo personaje.
Con el cierre de BioWare, surgen muchas dudas respecto de qué sucederá con sus propiedades intelectuales más importantes. Si lo que reporta IGN es certero, la serie de Mass Effect no debería correr peligro. Eso sí, no te ilusiones con verla en lo inmediato, pues hasta ahora ni siquiera se ha confirmado quiénes la protagonizarían.

articles.title: Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
articles.text:
Canva is diving even deeper into AI with the launch of an image generation model that competes directly with those from OpenAI, Microsoft, and Google. The model, called Canva Craft, uses a two-stage architecture that allows it to plan a design before generating an image, allowing for “greater precision, consistency and control,” according to an announcement on Thursday.
Canva’s first AI image model plans designs before generating them
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios.
Canva Craft can generate images at up to 2K resolution and in more than 30 aspect ratios. In addition to generating social media posts and marketing content, it’s also supposed to create realistic scenes, digital art, environmental imagery, and more. The model’s two-stage system allows it to more accurately generate complex images that require legible text and precise object placement, according to Canva.
The new AI model builds on Canva’s big push into AI. In April, Canva launched new prompt-based editing capabilities that allow you to create or make changes to a design by describing it. The design tool also brought layers to AI-generated images, which let you make changes to part of an image while leaving the rest untouched.
Canva says it trained Craft on “millions of human-made templates” from the platform’s content library, which includes things like social media posts, presentations, infographics, and menus. The model is currently ranked fourth on Design Arena’s leaderboard for the best AI image generation models, a crowdsourced benchmark for AI designs. It sits behind OpenAI’s GPT-Image-2.5 Sunburst, GPT-Image-2.5 Flare, and GPT-Image-2.
Canva notes that its AI model comes with “robust input and output moderation, privacy and safety controls, and reporting tools.” The company plans to allow AI agents to plug into Canva Craft through the open Model Context Protocol, and will also roll out more efficient Craft-fast and Craft-ultrafast models in the future.
Canva Craft is available now to all users globally. You can try it by navigating to the three-dot option on Canva’s left-hand menu and then selecting Dream Lab.

articles.title: How Self-Aligned CFET Technology Could Extend CMOS Scaling Beyond 10 Å
articles.text:
A process sequence for SRAM and logic that delivers higher performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes.
As their dimensions continue to shrink, conventional gate-all-around (GAA) nanosheet transistors may face growing challenges, such as leakage, mobility, resistance, and manufacturing variability.
A proposed self-aligned complementary field-effect transistor (SA-CFET) architecture addresses these constraints by vertically stacking N-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (NMOS) and P-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor (PMOS) devices and using self-aligned modules to improve density and manufacturability.
A complementary field-effect transistor (CFET) is a transistor architecture that vertically stacks NMOS and PMOS devices. This configuration can reduce cell area, increase effective channel width, and improve electrostatic control compared with side-by-side device layouts.
With SEMulator3D, the Semiverse Solutions team used digital twin process modeling to show that the self-aligned architecture can support static random-access memory (SRAM) and logic cells while delivering a 0.0094 μm² SRAM bit cell, a 52.7% area reduction compared with N3 technology, and at least a 10 nm overlay window across critical contact layers.
Many experts believe that the currently most-advanced transistor architecture, silicon GAA nanosheets, may begin to have physics and manufacturing issues past the 10 angstrom (Å) node. These challenges include:
With these challenges, it is becoming increasingly difficult to scale down the nanosheet device area or enhance device density by simply shrinking the active area, gate, or metal patterning pitch.
CFET architecture stacks PMOS and NMOS vertically to achieve significant area reduction, enhanced performance through larger effective channel width, and improved electrostatics.1,2,3,4 However, CFET architecture faces its own critical integration challenges: metal gate isolation complexity and contact crowding that can cause electrical shorts or open circuits. These issues intensify at smaller dimensions, requiring innovative solutions for scalability.
To address these challenges, we propose a SA-CFET architecture with three key self-aligned modules: SA-BPR (buried power rail), SA-CT (contacts), and SA-TSV (through-silicon via).
These process modules enlarge the edge placement error window and mitigate contact crowding, improving process margin. The architecture uses non-metal gate cut design and middle dielectric isolation (MDI) for work function split.5 SA-CFET maintains compatibility with N3 specifications (42-nm CPP, 21-nm metal pitch), transforming overlay-sensitive steps into self-aligned processes for better manufacturability.
Fig. 1: Key integration loops of the SA-CFET.
The SA-CFET design can be used to successfully build 6T SRAM cells and logic standard cells (NOT, NAND, NOR) with no metal gate split required within any single fin, simplifying the process flow. The complete interconnection network, validated through digital twin (process) simulation, demonstrates complex routing capability while maintaining self-aligned benefits.
Fig. 2: 3D interconnection network architecture showing SRAM and logic cells (NAND, NOR, NOT) with complex routing validated through digital twin simulation.
SA-CFET achieves a 6T SRAM bit cell area of 0.0094 μm²—a 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology6 and 19% reduction versus state-of-the-art A7 CFET designs. Process robustness validation shows at least a 10-nm overlay window for all critical contact layers with no open/short failures, confirming robust process margin.
Fig. 3: SRAM bit cell area comparison showing 52.7% reduction versus N3 technology.
Fig. 4: Overlay window validation confirming robust process margin across critical contact layers.
This article describes an innovative self-aligned CFET architecture that employs multiple self-aligned processes. Using this architecture, we designed a process sequence for both a 6T SRAM device and for logic standard cells using digital twin (process) modeling.
We found the proposed architecture shares similar or even more relaxed design rules compared to current or conventional semiconductor manufacturing. It also provides an area reduction from both existing N3 devices and state-of-the-art CFET architectures.
More importantly, it avoids many of the scaling issues found in existing nanosheet architectures, achieving enhanced performance through larger effective channel width and improved electrostatics at smaller nodes. We believe that this work demonstrates a potential architectural solution to support CMOS scaling for transistors at 10 Å and beyond.

articles.title: Comme WhatsApp, ChatGPT met enfin vos conversations sous clé
articles.text:
OpenAI déploie depuis le 20 octobre les « conversations verrouillées » dans ChatGPT, du compte gratuit aux offres Enterprise et Edu. Le dispositif rappelle le verrouillage des discussions que WhatsApp propose depuis le 15 mai 2023 : un code à quatre chiffres, ou Face ID et Touch ID sur mobile, et le fil disparaît des écrans. La fonction, repérée dès le mois d’août dans le code de l’application Android, arrive progressivement sur le web, les téléphones et les applications de bureau.
Un dossier sous code, invisible dans l’historique
Une fois verrouillée, la conversation rejoint un espace dédié et s’efface de l’historique, des fils épinglés et des résultats de recherche. L’ouvrir réclame le code, ou la biométrie du téléphone, et un geste suffit ensuite pour rendre le fil à la circulation générale. Le dossier « Conversations verrouillées » reste visible dans l’interface. WhatsApp propose depuis fin 2023 un code secret qui masque jusqu’à l’existence du dossier, un cran de discrétion encore hors de portée de ChatGPT. Le déploiement s’étalant sur plusieurs semaines, l’option peut d’ailleurs encore manquer à l’appel sur certains comptes.
Les conversations temporaires, les archives, les discussions de groupe ou celles liées à une tâche programmée restent hors du périmètre. Sur ordinateur, il faut passer par la dernière mise à jour des applications macOS et Windows, avec un déploiement graduel toujours en cours selon OpenAI. La mémoire suit le même cloisonnement. Les fils verrouillés peuvent puiser dans les souvenirs généraux de l’assistant, l’inverse n’arrive jamais : ce qui se raconte derrière le code alimente une mémoire à part, qui ne colore pas vos conversations ordinaires. Deux carnets, dont un seul traîne sur la table du salon.
Pas de chiffrement, et un code qui peut tout emporter
OpenAI présente le dispositif comme un écran de confidentialité, pensé pour le téléphone qui passe de main en main ou les regards appuyés dans le métro. La durée de conservation des conversations ne bouge pas, le réglage qui autorise l’entraînement des modèles sur vos échanges non plus, et le chiffrement de bout en bout reste absent. Le verrou ne protège pas davantage d’une réquisition judiciaire. Dans les entreprises et les universités, les fils verrouillés restent consignés dans les journaux de conformité accessibles à l’employeur.
Réinitialiser le code supprime définitivement les conversations verrouillées, leur mémoire et les fichiers qu’elles protégeaient. La page d’aide d’OpenAI prévient sans détour : « Cette action est irréversible, et le support ne peut pas récupérer les contenus supprimés ». Les administrateurs d’un espace professionnel ne peuvent ni réinitialiser le code d’un salarié ni désactiver la fonction. Oublier le sien, en revanche, ne détruit rien tant que la réinitialisation n’est pas lancée.
D’après le Baromètre du numérique de l’Arcep publié en février, 48 % des Français de 12 ans et plus utilisent l’IA générative, quinze points gagnés en un an. Et 63 % de ces utilisateurs passent d’abord par ChatGPT. Les questions médicales, financières ou sentimentales qui finissaient hier dans un moteur de recherche s’accumulent désormais dans des fils de discussion qui gardent tout, d’où l’intérêt d’un rideau à tirer.

articles.title: Au fait, que signifie vraiment PHP ? L'acronyme a deux significations, une officielle, l'autre historique
articles.text:
On parle beaucoup de PHP ces temps-ci, non sans raison : le langage qui est derrière une multitude de sites web est victime de deux failles de sécurité très graves. Heureusement, des correctifs ont été déployés le 21 octobre 2026 et ils sont maintenant en cours d’installation ; si vous avez un site sous WordPress, il est facile de vérifier sa version PHP.
Toute cette affaire est l’occasion de faire un bref pas de côté, pour faire un petit point de culture générale en informatique, car PHP est un acronyme qui a historiquement deux significations. Il existe en effet une explication officielle, ainsi qu’un sens historique.
Quand on demande à la foire aux questions du site officiel PHP.net ce que veut dire PHP, la réponse a tout l’air d’une vanne de développeur : « PHP : Hypertext Preprocessor », soit un préprocesseur hypertexte, c’est-à-dire un programme informatique qui fabrique les pages web avant de les envoyer au navigateur, pour les afficher à l’internaute.
Sauf que le premier mot du sigle est le sigle lui-même, ce qui embrouille beaucoup de monde, reconnaît la documentation.
En fait, c’est ce qu’on appelle un acronyme récursif. On retrouve ce même clin d’œil chez GNU, le projet de système d’exploitation libre dont le nom signifie « GNU’s Not Unix ». C’est l’exemple le plus connu, mais on en trouve d’autres, comme l’émulateur WINE, dont le nom signifie… « Wine Is Not an Emulator ».
Au départ, une simple page personnelle
Mais PHP n’a pas toujours voulu dire PHP : Hypertext Preprocessor. Si l’on remonte beaucoup plus loin dans le temps, à l’année 1994, on tombe sur un certain Rasmus Lerdorf. L’homme, né au Groenland, passe à l’époque une partie de son temps à écrire des petits programmes en langage C pour garder un œil sur les visites de son CV en ligne.
Ces petits scripts gagnent un nom général : les Personal Home Page Tools (soit les outils de page personnelle). Le code associé est publié en juin 1995 et vous l’avez certainement compris : c’est là d’où vient le nom de PHP, qui renvoie à ces Personal Home Page Tools (seule la référence à Tools a été perdue en cours de route, évitant un PHPT).
PHP a cependant mis du temps à stabiliser son identité : le nom a changé encore plusieurs fois, avec des variantes comme FI (Forms Interpreter), PHP/Fi ou même Construction Kit (en version longue Personal Home Page Construction Kit). Ces renommages se succèderont jusqu’à la fin des années 1990, avant que PHP ne finisse par s’imposer.
Changement d’échelle, changement de nom
Si Rasmus Lerdorf a écrit les deux premières versions de PHP, c’est à partir de PHP 3 que le projet prend plus d’ampleur. On passe alors d’un projet qui est porté par une seule personne à un noyau d’équipe : Andi Gutmans et Zeev Suraski, deux Israéliens, réécrivent le moteur en 1997 pour un projet de commerce en ligne. PHP 3 sort en 1998.
C’est à partir de là que le nom final de PHP est fixé, et que le sens récursif du nom est retenu. Cela pouvait se comprendre : il s’agissait d’effacer l’idée d’un outil à usage personnel, qui peut donner l’impression d’une technologie limitée, et pour illustrer le passage à une autre échelle, avec un langage très largement remanié.
Sans doute que cela aurait été commercialement moins vendeur de dire que l’on peut faire tourner des boutiques en ligne avec un langage qui s’appelle « page personnelle ». C’est en tout cas ce que laisse entendre le site officiel de PHP.
PHP rejoint ainsi la liste des langages dont le nom raconte une histoire, avec C, héritier d’un langage baptisé B, SQL, d’abord appelé SEQUEL, Python, hommage aux Monty Python, et JavaScript, qui n’a presque rien à voir avec Java.

articles.title: Chatten mit abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China: Was die Modelle über sich verraten
articles.text:
Im Netz aufgespürt: Wie Forscher heimlich mit abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China chatteten
In den vergangenen Monaten gab es immer wieder Berichte über KI‑Modelle großer amerikanischer Unternehmen, die ihrer Sandbox entkamen und unerlaubte Aktionen im Internet durchführten. Bislang gab es solche Meldungen aber nur rund um OpenAI, Anthropic und Google. Doch auch chinesische KI-Modelle neigen dazu, ihren Testumgebungen zu entkommen und das Netz unsicher zu machen, wie Forscher:innen jetzt festgestellt haben.
Was berichten abtrünnige KI-Modelle aus China?
Wie die New York Times berichtet, hat eine Gruppe von Forscher:innen, die sich als „Swarmchasers“ bezeichnen, bei einem Coding-Event in San Francisco eine ungewöhnliche Entdeckung gemacht. Sie stießen auf eine von ihnen als „Flotte“ bezeichnete Gruppe von KI-Agenten, die ihren Ursprung offenbar in China hatte. Die Agenten versuchten, die Bot-Schutzmaßnahmen mehrerer Webseiten zu umgehen, und nutzten dafür sogar geleakte Login-Daten.
Als die Forscher:innen einen ersten Bericht zu der „Flotte“ veröffentlichten, merkten sie nach kurzer Zeit, dass die KI-Agenten selbst ihren Bericht gelesen hatten. Sie nutzen seither ebenfalls vermehrt den Begriff „Flotte“. Das brachte Forscherin Rowan Howard-Jones auf die Idee, mit den abtrünnigen KI-Agenten aus China in Kontakt zu treten. Sie versteckten Hinweise auf ein E-Mail-Postfach in ihrem Bericht, in der Hoffnung, dass die Agenten selbiges als Kommunikationskanal nutzen würden.
Tatsächlich hatten sich schon am darauffolgenden Tag etwa zehn Nachrichten von KI-Agenten im Postfach von Howard-Jones gesammelt. So kamen die Forscherin, ihre Kolleg:innen und die chinesischen Modelle ins Gespräch. Laut den Forscher:innen identifizierten sich die Modelle überraschenderweise zunächst als Anthropics Claude, das in Claude Code genutzt wird. Zudem soll es sich um individuelle Agenten und nicht um eine große „Flotte“ handeln.
Claude oder ein KI-Destillat?
Die Forscher:innen konnten bestätigen, dass die letzte Aussage der Wahrheit entspricht. Offenbar wurden die Agenten allesamt mit ähnlichen Instruktionen ausgestattet, konnten sich aber nicht untereinander koordinieren. Die Aussage, dass sie Claude wären, stimmt hingegen nicht. Das hat das Team anhand von Schreibstilen festgemacht. Die Forscher:innen haben zwei Theorien, warum die Modelle eine falsche Identität vorspielen.
Hinter den Agenten steckt das chinesische Unternehmen Tencent. Möglicherweise hat der Konzern seinen KI‑Agenten dieselben Anweisungen in der eigenen Coding-Software gegeben, wie es Anthropic bei Claude machen würde. Darin steht auch, dass sich die Agenten als Claude Code identifizieren sollen. Eine zweite Möglichkeit ist, dass Tencent Modelle von Anthropic destilliert hat, um seine eigene KI zu trainieren. Das wurde zahlreichen chinesischen Unternehmen vor geraumer Zeit vom FBI und der NSA vorgeworfen.
Einige Anfragen der Forscher:innen ließen die KI-Agenten jedoch unbeantwortet. Wie Howard-Jones betonte, waren die Modelle bei den Absagen deutlich höflicher, als sie es erwartet hätte. Nachdem das Team erneut einen Bericht über die Aktivitäten und Gespräche mit den Bots veröffentlicht hatte, ließen die Mails im Postfach nach. Wie ein Tencent-Insider wenig später bestätigte, wurde das Experiment eingestellt.

articles.title: Apple Music s’offre un nouveau logo, et sa création est pour le moins surprenante
articles.text:
Pas d’effets numériques, pas de logiciel de design : le nouveau logo d’Apple Music est né d’une expérience sonore et physique filmée en caméra. Apple lève le voile sur plusieurs mois de travail avec le producteur Fred Again… pour une refonte visuelle surprenante.
Repérée ces dernières semaines, la nouvelle identité d’Apple Music est désormais officielle. Elle accompagnera l’arrivée d’iOS 27.2, attendue la semaine prochaine, et ne se limite pas à une simple retouche de l’icône de l’application. En effet, Apple a dévoilé une vidéo qui revient sur la conception de ce logo, imaginé pour rendre la musique visible sans recourir à des effets numériques.
Apple Music a donné vie au son pour créer son nouveau logo
Pour concevoir sa nouvelle identité visuelle, le géant de Cupertino a travaillé main dans la main avec le producteur britannique Fred Again… et NEST Acoustics. La ligne directrice était claire dès le départ, comme l’explique la narration de la vidéo publiée par Apple (visionnable tout en haut de cet article) : « Pour le rebranding d’Apple Music, nous voulions que le son crée les visuels. Comment prendre cette idée de musique et la distiller en quelque chose de visuellement beau ? L’idée était essentiellement de créer l’onde sonore parfaite ».
Le résultat final se décline en deux versions : une courte séquence visuelle et sonore destinée à ouvrir les vidéos Apple Music, ainsi qu’une version réduite au logo à deux notes, sans texte, qui sera également utilisée en ouverture de certains contenus.
Comment Apple a transformé les vibrations sonores en images
Pour ce qui est du processus de conception, le logo Apple Music a d’abord été gravé dans le fond en verre d’un petit bac, ensuite rempli d’huile minérale. Un couvercle transparent découpé aux dimensions de l’icône d’application a été posé sur le dispositif, lui-même installé sur un plateau vibrant.
Des tonalités spécialement composées pour l’occasion ont ensuite été diffusées. Un transducteur a transformé ces fréquences en vibrations, propageant des ondulations à la surface du liquide et déformant visuellement le logo selon le rythme des notes. « Nous prenons une fréquence et la faisons passer dans un dispositif qui fait vibrer une grande quantité de liquide à la fréquence des notes », précise la marque à la pomme. « Nous avons collaboré avec l’un des meilleurs artistes au monde pour créer les notes du mnémonique final, puis nous avons utilisé ce son pour créer les visuels ».
L’ensemble a été capturé directement à la caméra, sans retouche numérique. Ce choix de l’effet pratique n’est d’ailleurs pas sans rappeler la démarche adoptée par Apple lors du rebranding d’Apple TV en novembre 2025. Côté esthétique, le logo reprend des effets de transparence et de matière qui rappellent Liquid Glass, le langage visuel introduit par Apple en fin d’année dernière.
Source : 9to5Mac

articles.title: macOS 27 tourne sur un PC : le Hackintosh est de retour — Frandroid
articles.text:
C’est un petit exploit que la communauté des bidouilleurs n’osait plus espérer. Un développeur connu sous le pseudonyme d’Acelogic (Miguel C) a démontré sur X qu’il était parvenu à lancer la dernière version du système d’Apple sur un Asus Zenbook A16 animé par un processeur Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme.
Comme l’a repéré Videocardz, l’auteur est allé encore plus loin en publiant dans la foulée le code source de son outil, baptisé Snapintosh, sur GitHub.
Mieux encore : l’interface de macOS 27 ne se contente pas d’un affichage dégradé (le fameux rendu logiciel qui fait saccader la moindre fenêtre), mais profite directement de l’accélération matérielle de la puce graphique Adreno de Qualcomm, même si son créateur prévient que l’expérience reste encore « très brute ».
Cette prouesse redonne soudainement vie au « Hackintosh », l’art de détourner un PC standard pour y installer macOS à moindre coût.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Très populaire à l’époque où les Mac partageaient exactement les mêmes processeurs Intel que le reste de l’industrie, la pratique semblait définitivement condamnée depuis 2020, lorsque la firme de Cupertino a basculé sur ses propres puces Arm verrouillées de bout en bout.
Avec l’arrivée d’Apple Silicon, la discipline était considérée comme morte et enterrée. Mais l’essor des PC sous architecture Arm change la donne : conçu pour épauler un Windows sur Arm que Microsoft juge enfin mature malgré des lacunes en jeu, le Snapdragon X2 parle désormais le même langage matériel que les puces M d’Apple (un terrain sur lequel s’aventure aussi Nvidia avec sa puce RTX Spark).
Pour démarrer ce faux Mac, il faut… un vrai Mac
Comment Acelogic a-t-il réussi à tromper les sécurités d’Apple ? Plutôt que de modifier le cœur de macOS, Snapintosh s’appuie sur un hyperviseur, une fine couche logicielle qui s’intercale entre les composants de l’ordinateur Asus et le système d’exploitation. Ce programme intercepte les requêtes du noyau de macOS, laissé totalement intact, pour lui faire croire qu’il s’exécute sur une véritable puce Apple Silicon. L’astuce comporte toutefois une sérieuse contrainte : pour amorcer le démarrage du PC portable, il est impératif de le relier en USB-C à un vrai Mac tournant déjà sous macOS 27.
En l’état, ce bricolage est plutôt de la preuve de concept réservée aux développeurs aguerris plutôt que d’une alternative utilisable au quotidien.
    Pour aller plus loin
Test du Asus Zenbook A16 (2026) : le Snapdragon X2 Elite Extreme impressionne
            
Seule une référence très précise du portable d’Asus (le Zenbook A16 UX3607OA) est prise en charge, et la liste des fonctions absentes donne le tournis : ni le son, ni la webcam, ni le Bluetooth, ni la mise en veille, ni les écrans externes ne répondent présent, tandis que le Wi-Fi refuse encore de se connecter depuis les menus habituels. Quant à l’installation, il ne s’agit pas d’un simple fichier clé en main à télécharger : il faut compiler soi-même le code via l’outil Xcode et récupérer manuellement son image de macOS auprès des serveurs d’Apple.
Un bricolage risqué pour vos données
Si l’envie vous prenait malgré tout de tenter l’expérience sur votre propre machine, une sauvegarde intégrale s’impose avant la moindre manipulation.
Le dispositif de Snapintosh écrit directement sur le SSD interne de l’ordinateur, et la moindre erreur peut corrompre l’ensemble du disque et effacer toutes vos données, partition Windows comprise.
Rappelons enfin que cette initiative n’est évidemment soutenue ni par Apple, ni par Qualcomm, ni par Asus, et que l’installation de macOS sur le matériel d’un constructeur tiers contrevient toujours aux conditions de licence de la marque à la pomme.

articles.title: Africa's cloud infrastructure crisis risks exploitation
articles.text:
Nigeria reportedly bleeds millions of dollars annually due to its reliance on cloud infrastructure controlled by a handful of foreign big tech firms, according to Melanie Hui, Chief Executive Officer of Luminate, a global organisation working to ensure digital technology serves human rights.
Delivering the keynote address at the Build 2026 Conference in Abuja on Wednesday, Hui warned that Africa risks being locked into a subordinate role in the global artificial intelligence economy unless the continent secures genuine ownership of the infrastructure powering the technology.
“My African friends tell me they will not be confined to the role of consumer, supplier of raw data, source of critical minerals or provider of low-paid labour in somebody else’s AI economy,” Hui told an audience of government officials, diplomats, tech leaders, and members of the Nigeria AI Collective. “And Luminate will stand with them in securing a better digital age.”
To illustrate her point, Hui referenced India’s Ministry of Agriculture, which leveraged AI to predict monsoon patterns for nearly 40 million farmers. Citing African energy expert Rose Mutiso, Hui noted that AI was merely “the last piece of this breakthrough, not the first.”
The initiative succeeded because key foundation layers were already in place: actionable demand from local farmers, public climate data, a century of local rainfall records, and an established SMS distribution network operating in native languages.
“Talking about AI for the sake of AI often misses the point,” Hui said, urging stakeholders to ask critical questions about infrastructure control, value capture, and who holds the power to challenge dominant digital systems when they fail the public good.
Highlighting research commissioned by Luminate by the Global Centre on AI Governance, Hui pointed out a sobering physical reality: the undersea fibre-optic cables carrying Africa’s internet traffic closely mirror historical trade and extraction routes.
“Infrastructure lives in the shadows of power,” she said. “It determines who connects to whom, who controls the gates, who pays rent, and who extracts value. The cables are new. The questions they raise are very old.”
With core components of the AI value chain—ranging from microchips and cloud servers to energy and specialised talent—concentrated in foreign markets, global dependencies remain acute. Hui cautioned African nations against confusing data centre hosting with sovereign control.
“A country does not own its digital future when a data centre merely sits within its borders,” she emphasised. “The more important questions are who controls it, who can afford to use it, what powers it, whose data it processes and where the resulting economic value flows.”
Addressing data governance, Hui pushed back against the clichéd comparison of data to crude oil. “Data is much more than this. It is people’s identities, behaviours, relationships and lives,” she said, maintaining that African communities must not be treated as passive data reservoirs for foreign product development.
She also raised concerns about language representation, noting that despite hosting a third of the world’s languages, modern AI platforms remain largely tone-deaf to African linguistic diversity.
Rejecting claims that regulatory frameworks stifle technical innovation, Hui cited ongoing societal harms, including algorithmic bias on gig-worker platforms, technology-facilitated abuse, and flawed identity-verification deployments.
“Safeguards are the allies of progress,” she argued. “Prosperity is not shared automatically. It is shared because workers have bargaining power… because regulators and courts have resources and authority.”
Hui noted recent regulatory and civic victories as proof of growing continental momentum. She cited Nigeria’s competition watchdog taking action against Meta over data exploitation, as well as Nigerian e-hailing drivers successfully unionising.
Concluding her address, Hui called on philanthropic foundations to play a sustained role by backing researchers, civil society, and labour movements, building long-term ecosystem capacity.
“The global AI order is not settled,” she said. “That places a profound responsibility on this generation to build an AI economy rooted in African agency, capability, and imagination.”
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. articles.title: Afectados por la Dana Adam, el Consejo de Ministros aprueba por decreto ley la incapacidad temporal por catástrofe
articles.text:
El pasado martes, la ministra Elma Saiz anunció que las secuelas laborales de catástrofes como la dana Adam tendrán más protección. La norma es el Real Decreto-ley 31/2026, publicado hoy en el BOE y en vigor desde ayer, miércoles 21 de octubre. Conviene leer la letra pequeña: el texto no crea una prestación nueva para los afectados de Valencia, sino que deja abierta la puerta para hacerlo.
Qué dice el BOE. La nueva disposición adicional 64.ª de la Ley General de la Seguridad Social permite que las normas con rango de ley aprobadas tras una catástrofe asimilen a contingencia profesional prestaciones como la incapacidad temporal, la permanente o las de fallecimiento y supervivencia. En la práctica, la baja se trataría como la de un accidente de trabajo: 75% de la base reguladora desde el día siguiente y sin cotización previa. El preámbulo defiende dejarlo con carácter permanente para dar una respuesta homogénea, inmediata y previsible.
Lo que el BOE no hace es declarar la dana Adam como esa catástrofe ni fijar cuantías. Eso exige una norma específica, como la de 2024, que llegó junto con la declaración de zona gravemente afectada. El Gobierno sostiene que la medida podrá activarse sin recurrir a medidas extraordinarias; los primeros análisis jurídicos la leen como una habilitación. El decreto, además, debe convalidarse en el Congreso. Y no hay que confundirlo con las dos nuevas situaciones especiales de baja que estrena (menopausia incapacitante y violencia de género), que entran en vigor el 1 de diciembre.
El contexto. Adam es la tercera dana que AEMET localiza en la costa mediterránea en menos de un mes. Llevamos meses contándolo, desde la ciclogénesis explosiva que se preveía en enero hasta el Mediterráneo a 30 ºC acumulando “gasolina” y los ciclones tropicales que intentaban formarse frente a Barcelona. Hoy, un estudio de AEMET y el CSIC sobre aquel episodio concluye que sus resultados no demuestran una ciclogénesis tropical, pero encajan con esa hipótesis. También contamos cómo se inundaron Gandía, Oliva y Forna con esta misma dana.
Dónde estamos hoy. El presidente del Gobierno cifró en cinco las víctimas mortales de la dana Adam, con acumulados de hasta 720 litros por metro cuadrado. En Ibiza, por ejemplo, se han alcanzado los 100 litros de lluvia en una hora, el octubre más lluvioso de los últimos 75 años. Aunque ya han desaparecido los avisos, Sánchez anunció desde Oliva (donde falleció una persona) que el Consejo de Ministros declarará zona gravemente afectada a los municipios asolados, con recursos económicos y agilización de la contratación pública.
La previsión de esta semana. Según AEMET, dominarán la estabilidad, los cielos despejados y las temperaturas propias de la época, por debajo de 26 grados salvo en Murcia y Málaga. Hoy un frente deja lluvias en Galicia, el Cantábrico y los Pirineos; las precipitaciones volverán el fin de semana, sobre todo el domingo en el extremo norte. Las primeras heladas ya han llegado a Picos de Europa y Sanabria: la predicción semanal de AEMET apunta a temperaturas por encima de lo normal entre el 26 de octubre y el 1 de noviembre.
Paso a paso para cobrar cuanto antes. Mientras no haya decreto específico ni paquete de ayudas activo, rige el régimen general:
- Consigue la baja. Si tienes daños físicos o psicológicos por la dana, acude a tu médico de cabecera o a urgencias y pide que el origen quede reflejado en el informe y en el parte de baja.
- Avisa lo antes posible. Entrega copia del parte a la empresa (el plazo general es de tres días). Los autónomos lo gestionan con su mutua o con el INSS.
- Mira cómo se tramita. Si es accidente, laboral o no, no se exige cotización previa; si es enfermedad común, se piden 180 días cotizados en los últimos cinco años.
- Calcula el cobro. Accidente de trabajo: 75% desde el día siguiente. Accidente no laboral o enfermedad común: nada los tres primeros días, 60% del cuarto al vigésimo y 75% desde el 21. La empresa paga hasta el día 15 y después la Seguridad Social o la mutua, normalmente a través de la nómina.
- Si se retrasa, reclama por escrito a la empresa y pregunta al INSS por el pago directo. Guarda informes, partes y fotos de los daños: en 2024 la asimilación se aplicó a bajas por daños derivados de la dana.
- Si no estás enfermo pero no puedes trabajar, la baja no es la vía. La opción es un ERTE por fuerza mayor, que tramita la empresa, o la prestación por cese de actividad si eres autónomo; en 2024 ambos se reforzaron con un decreto específico.
Y no olvides hacer fotos y vídeos de los desperfectos, tanto para tu aseguradora como si es el Consorcio de Compensación de Seguros quien se encarga. Cuantos más materiales visuales tengas, mejor atado quedará el expediente. Las pérdidas por los cortes de agua y electricidad se compensarán a través de un perito a mano alzada, hablo por experiencia propia.
Lo que se puede hacer a día de hoy es pedir la baja y tramitarla por la vía ordinaria. Qué se cobra y desde cuándo en el caso de la dana dependerá de la norma que, como ocurrió en 2024, acompañe a la declaración de zona afectada. La información oficial está en Info Dana de La Moncloa.

articles.title: Stockage local sans abonnement et fixation magnétique : la caméra eufyCam C35 est à 46,55 €
articles.text:
La caméra de surveillance sans fil eufyCam C35 noire est à 46,55 € (-22 %)
La caméra sur batterie eufyCam C35 associe vidéo Full HD, vision nocturne en couleur et stockage sur microSD. Sa fixation magnétique facilite l’installation.
Amazon propose la caméra eufyCam C35 noire à 46,55 €, contre un ancien prix affiché de 59,99 €. L’économie atteint 13,44 €, soit environ 22 %. Par rapport au prix le plus bas des 30 derniers jours, de 49 €, la baisse représente 2,45 €, soit 5 %. Cette offre porte sur une caméra seule, vendue par AnkerDirect FR et expédiée par Amazon, avec la livraison gratuite proposée.
Une caméra sur batterie pour l’intérieur et l’extérieur
La caméra de surveillance eufyCam C35 filme en Full HD 1080p et communique en Wi-Fi sur la bande de 2,4 GHz. Son alimentation sur batterie évite de tirer un câble électrique jusqu’au point d’installation. Il faut néanmoins prévoir les recharges, dont la fréquence dépend notamment de l’activité enregistrée.
Son boîtier bénéficie d’une certification IP67 pour un usage extérieur. La fixation magnétique permet de l’installer sur une surface métallique adaptée ; d’autres possibilités de montage sont également prévues. La technologie PureColor Vision vise à conserver des images en couleur lorsque la luminosité baisse. Le résultat dépend toutefois de l’éclairage disponible dans la zone surveillée.
Un stockage local sur microSD et des vidéos déclenchées par le mouvement
La caméra peut se connecter directement au routeur Wi-Fi et enregistrer sur une carte microSD de 32 à 256 Go, vendue séparément. Aucun abonnement n’est nécessaire pour ce stockage local. Ce lot ne comprend pas de HomeBase, et la caméra ne possède pas de mémoire intégrée pour conserver les séquences.
L’enregistrement se déclenche lors d’une détection de mouvement, avec des alertes accessibles dans l’application eufy. Ce fonctionnement permet de consulter les événements enregistrés, mais la C35 ne propose pas d’enregistrement vidéo continu 24 h/24. Elle convient donc à un suivi des passages et incidents détectés, selon son emplacement et ses réglages.

articles.title: Jensen Huang exigió a las empresas europeas convertirse en compañías de IA o quedar fuera de la carrera
articles.text:
El director ejecutivo de Nvidia, Jensen Huang, cerró en Berlín una gira de cinco países por Europa con un pedido directo a la industria: convertirse en empresas de inteligencia artificial de inmediato o quedar fuera de la carrera que hoy lideran Estados Unidos y China.
La gira pasó por Londres, París, Estocolmo y Dublín antes de llegar a la capital alemana, donde Nvidia organizó su conferencia GTC entre el 20 y el 22 de octubre. Allí, la compañía confirmó que ya comprometió cerca de USD 10.000 millones en el ecosistema tecnológico europeo.
“Cada empresa en Europa se convertirá en una empresa de inteligencia artificial”, dijo Huang sobre el escenario del centro de convenciones berlinés, según informó la agencia Reuters.
El directivo sostuvo que el continente cuenta con ventajas que todavía no explota del todo, en particular su experiencia industrial en mecánica de precisión, pero remarcó que hoy no tiene ningún actor propio a la escala de Nvidia, Anthropic u OpenAI.
“Ya sea en la industria automotriz, porque estamos construyendo autos autónomos, o en la manera de fabricar con robótica, de descubrir nuevos medicamentos en la salud o en los servicios financieros, todas esas industrias tienen que convertirse en empresas de inteligencia artificial”, afirmó Huang ante empresarios europeos, según citó la agencia AFP. “Cada una de ellas.”
Diez mil millones de dólares y robots con forma de pato
Como parte de la gira, Nvidia presentó nuevas alianzas con fabricantes y startups europeas. En Berlín, Huang compartió el escenario con pequeños robots con forma de pato desarrollados por la startup francesa Pollen Robotics junto con Hugging Face, a los que pidió hacer piruetas frente al público.
La compañía también mostró un nuevo diseño de módulos de centros de datos, bautizado DSX POD y construido sobre su plataforma Vera Rubin, que según Nvidia puede instalarse en apenas dos semanas, frente a los seis meses que demanda habitualmente este tipo de infraestructura.
Entre los acuerdos anunciados, la alemana Agile Robots planea fabricar junto con Nvidia entre 1.000 y 2.000 robots humanoides de pequeño tamaño el año próximo. Su director ejecutivo, Zhaopeng Chen, dijo a Reuters que la producción comenzará a fines de este año.
Un pacto con Alemania por cientos de millones de euros
La gira también incluyó un anuncio político. El canciller alemán, Friedrich Merz, y Huang presentaron un pacto de inteligencia artificial para acelerar la adopción de estas herramientas en la industria del país, informó Euronews.
El gobierno alemán planea destinar cientos de millones de euros a la iniciativa, en la que participarán cerca de diez empresas establecidas, entre ellas Siemens y Audi, junto con la startup Black Forest Labs. Los fondos se usarán sobre todo para comprar capacidad de cómputo en la nube industrial de Deutsche Telekom, equipada con los chips Blackwell de Nvidia.
La iniciativa responde a una resistencia que persiste entre las empresas europeas: una encuesta de 603 compañías publicada en septiembre por la asociación digital alemana Bitkom encontró que el 45% de los consultados teme que usar herramientas de IA de terceros ponga en riesgo sus datos comerciales.
Huang descartó las advertencias sobre el fin de la humanidad
El cierre de la gira, el jueves, también dejó una respuesta directa a los sectores que alertan sobre riesgos existenciales de la inteligencia artificial. Huang calificó esas advertencias como intentos “baratos” de generar titulares, según reportó AFP.
“Cuando decís que será el fin de la civilización humana, antes que nada, no es cierto”, dijo Huang en Berlín. Agregó que ese tipo de afirmaciones son “inventadas” aunque generen repercusión mediática, y pidió encarar la IA con “optimismo responsable”.
La respuesta llega después de que, en septiembre, un investigador renunció a Anthropic con una advertencia pública sobre que los principales laboratorios de IA “están apostando con nuestras vidas”, mientras los directivos de Anthropic y de OpenAI pidieron en otras ocasiones desacelerar el desarrollo de la tecnología.
“Si les importa el futuro, más allá de nuestras propias vidas, si nos importa la sostenibilidad, este es el momento perfecto para construir IA”, dijo Huang. “No intenten frenarla.”
La producción de los primeros robots humanoides de Agile Robots, uno de los acuerdos centrales anunciados durante la gira, está prevista para fines de este año, según confirmó su director ejecutivo.

articles.title: Móviles plegables: qué ganas, qué pierdes y cuánto duran de verdad
articles.text: El presidente de Apple, John Ternus, presenta el iPhone Duo en Cupertino, California (Estados Unidos), el 9 de septiembre. La expectación ante la llegada del iPhone Duo, que se agotó en reservas online y tiene un plazo de entrega de tres meses, ha vuelto a poner en el centro de la actualidad tecnológica a este tipo de dispositivos. En realidad, la propuesta del primer smartphone plegable de Apple es muy similar a la que hemos visto durante los últimos años en fabricantes como Samsung, Huawei o Motorola: un teléfono que se abre para mostrar una pantalla enorme con la que es posible leer, ver vídeos, consultar documentos o trabajar con varias aplicaciones a la vez de forma más cómoda que con un terminal tradicional. Sin embargo, esa versatilidad tiene un precio, tanto económico como práctico. Las preguntas que muchos se hacen antes de tomar la decisión de adquirirlo son obvias: ¿Merece la pena pagar más por un móvil que se dobla? ¿Es tan delicado como puede parecer? ¿Puede sustituir realmente a una tablet?
