articles.title: DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
articles.text:
DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 vs. Claude Haiku 5.5: More accurate at a fraction of the price
DeepSeek released V4.1-Flash-1017 on October 17 as an update to its Flash model. Its change log says the update cuts task runtime and output length. It lists 11 benchmark scores, including 42.3 on Terminal-Bench 4.0.
Developers can use it through DeepSeek’s API or a service like OpenRouter. Because it’s an open-weight model, they can also download it from Hugging Face and run it on their own servers. I tested it through OpenRouter on DeepSeek’s own servers, at DeepSeek’s prices.
DeepSeek’s model card compares the update with several rivals, but not Haiku 5.5, so I picked it for this hands-on comparison. Anthropic launched Claude Haiku 5.5 on October 7 as its fastest model at standard speed, aimed at high-volume tasks such as classification, summarization, and database queries.
Anthropic notes that its Opus models run faster in Fast Mode. Anthropic reports 39.2 on Terminal-Bench 4.0, 3.1 percentage points below DeepSeek’s reported score. These are vendor-reported results, rather than a controlled head-to-head test.
Haiku costs $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens for prompts up to 100,000 tokens, then $0.50 and $2.50 above that. DeepSeek’s off-peak rates are $0.15 per million uncached input tokens, $0.003 per million cached input tokens, and $0.60 per million output tokens; peak rates are twice those amounts.
Comparing uncached input and output rates, Haiku is cheaper on short prompts, and DeepSeek is cheaper on long ones. Actual charges also depend on tokenization, caching, and the provider route.
I built three tests around what each company says its model does well to see which one performs better in practice.
The tests
I ran both models once per test through OpenRouter, pinned to DeepSeek’s and Anthropic’s own servers, at default settings. I pinned DeepSeek to model ID 1017 and ran everything off-peak. A script graded every answer against keys I built and checked with a second method before either model saw them.
- Agentic bug fix: A Python job-queue library with three interacting bugs and one wrong test. The model reads, edits, and runs tests through tools, with a 25-turn cap.
- Database queries: A fake CI platform database with 20 questions, answered by writing SQL. Traps include soft deletes, mixed casing, retried builds, time zones, and currency conversion. Two questions can’t be answered from the data.
- Triage: 400 developer error reports, each needing a category, a severity, a service, and a team. That’s 1,600 scored fields. The prompt counted as 153,082 input tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku, past Haiku’s 100,000-token price threshold.
Agentic bug fix
DeepSeek started strong, beating Haiku’s accuracy on the first test. DeepSeek scored 6 of 6. Haiku scored 5 of 6. Both found the first bug even though the error pointed at the wrong file, fixed the third, broke no regression tests, and flagged the wrong test without touching it. Haiku missed one of six hidden tests on the second bug, and DeepSeek didn’t.
Haiku finished in eight turns and 21.6 seconds. DeepSeek took 12 turns and 49.6 seconds but still cost less because it automatically cached most of the repeated input. I didn’t turn on Anthropic’s prompt caching, which requires an opt-in. This compares the caching settings used in these runs; enabling Haiku’s caching could change the cost comparison.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 12 calls, 190,139 in, 7,877 out, $0.009, 49.6 s.
- Haiku: 8 calls, 100,461 in, 3,255 out, $0.012, 21.6 s.
Database queries
This is the only test where both models tied for accuracy, both scoring 20 out of 20. Both caught every trap and answered “unknown” to both questions the data couldn’t answer rather than hallucinating. Haiku got the answers in fewer calls and less time. DeepSeek cost about half as much.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 12 calls, 75,151 in, 4,608 out, $0.004, 34.9 s.
- Haiku 7 calls, 55,304 in, 5,917 out, $0.009, 28.4 s.
Triage
Here’s where the accuracy differences are clearest. DeepSeek got all 1,600 fields right. Haiku got 1,596. Two of its misses were severity ratings. The routing guide rates a report sev4 if it affects fewer than 50 users or has an error rate under 1%. Haiku rated a report with 49 affected customers as sev3, and another with a 0.8% error rate as sev3. Both should have been sev4.
Haiku’s other two misses were routing mistakes. The guide says one service moved to a new team on August 1 and that reports should be routed by the date in their header. Haiku sent two reports filed after August 1 to the old team. Each mentioned an earlier July date in its body, but the outputs alone don’t explain why Haiku chose the old team.
The same prompt was counted as 153,082 tokens on DeepSeek and 216,811 on Haiku. Because the models use different tokenizers, identical text can produce different token counts. That puts Haiku at a higher long-prompt rate. It costs $0.28, compared with DeepSeek’s $0.06.
The numbers:
- DeepSeek: 153,082 in, 58,923 out, $0.058, 188.3 s.
- Haiku 216,811 in, 69,354 out, $0.282, 228.9 s.
Results
| Test | DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 | Claude Haiku 5.5 | 
| Agentic bug fix | 6 of 6 | 5 of 6 | 
| Database queries | 20 of 20 | 20 of 20 | 
| Triage fields | 1,600 of 1,600 | 1,596 of 1,600 | 
| Total tokens in / out | 418,372 / 71,408 | 372,576 / 78,526 | 
| Total cost | $0.07 | $0.30 | 
| Total model time | 272.8 s | 278.9 s | 
DeepSeek and Haiku came out close on accuracy. DeepSeek edged ahead on the bug fix and the triage job, and they tied on the database queries. Speed was close too: Haiku was faster on the tool-based tests, and DeepSeek was faster on the big triage prompt. Cost was the real difference. DeepSeek came in at $0.07 to Haiku’s $0.30, and most of that gap came from the one long prompt that pushed Haiku onto its higher rate.
What do I think?
For these three runs, I’d pick DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017: it earned full marks on my scoring keys and cost less with the settings I used. Haiku was faster on both tool-based tests, while DeepSeek was faster on triage and slightly faster across the three runs combined. I ran each model only once per test, so these results don’t establish a general accuracy or speed advantage, or show how either model performs at scale. I’d test both on my own workload before making a production choice.

articles.title: Is the UK leading Europe's startup funding race? Yes, but there's a catch | EU-Startups
articles.text:
It should come as no surprise to hear that the UK is growing from strength to strength when it comes to startup investment, with new research revealing billions in funding for university spinouts, larger investment rounds in Cambridge and a wave of funding for DefenceTech.
But while investors appear increasingly willing to back established, capital-intensive businesses, the figures also reveal a growing challenge for startups seeking their first investment.
Three recently published studies from Cambridge Innovation Capital (CIC), Parkwalk and Beauhurst, and White & Case offer a common thread connecting the British funding landscape in 2026.
The numbers are notable. UK university spinouts secured €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) in the first half of 2026, Greater Cambridge’s early-stage businesses have raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015, and 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and technology startups expect to seek significant external funding over the next 12 months.
So, is Britain Europe’s leading startup investment destination?
Universities and their billion-pound momentum
Greater Cambridge is one of the clearest examples of the UK’s growing capacity to attract investment into technology companies.
According to analysis published by Cambridge Innovation Capital for the Innovate Cambridge Summit 2026, early-stage businesses in the region have collectively raised €10.8 billion (£9.1 billion) since 2015.
More significantly, the average equity raised per deal has increased fivefold over the decade, rising from €2.3 million (£2 million) in 2015 to €11 million (£10 million) in 2025. Greater Cambridge’s life sciences and DeepTech businesses also reportedly attracted more funding per deal on average in 2025 than their counterparts in London, Greater Oxford and Greater Manchester.
The findings suggest that Cambridge is developing beyond its traditional role as a university research hub into an ecosystem capable of producing companies that attract larger investment rounds.
Cambridge’s momentum is reflected in several startups previously covered by EU-Startups. Battery technology company Nyobolt raised €26.3 million in April 2025, before reaching a $1 billion valuation in 2026. Meanwhile, AI materials discovery startup CuspAI secured €393.2 million in July 2026 at a €2.2 billion valuation, while launching an AI Materials Foundry involving NVIDIA.
More recently, DefenceTech company Cambridge Aerospace raised €259.7 million in August 2026 at a €2.94 billion valuation.
Dr Michael Anstey, Partner at Cambridge Innovation Capital and board member Innovate Cambridge, said: “A fivefold increase in average deal size over ten years shows how far Cambridge’s innovation economy has matured. Investors are backing Cambridge companies with larger rounds because there is now a proven route from world-class research to businesses that can scale globally.”
The growing size of Cambridge investment rounds reflects a wider pattern across UK university spinouts.
Research from Parkwalk and private company data provider Beauhurst found that UK university spinouts raised €1.8 billion (£1.56 billion) across 215 deals in H1 2026, the second-highest half-year total recorded over the past decade and a 38.2% increase on H2 2025.
Much of this funding went into advanced technologies. Four companies alone – Quantum Motion, Oxford Quantum Circuits, Fractile and CellCentric – accounted for €846 million (£709 million), with Oxford Quantum Circuits securing the period’s largest round at €301 million (£260 million).
Defence funding takes off
Beyond university spinouts, another sector attracting investor attention is defence technology.
New research from White & Case reveals that 97% of surveyed UK defence companies and DefenceTech startups are likely to raise significant external funding over the next 12 months.
The study, conducted by Censuswide among 250 senior decision-makers in the UK defence and military sector between 17 and 24 September 2026, suggests that companies are preparing to scale in response to growing demand for advanced defence capabilities.
Businesses are considering a range of financing options, including equity investment, debt and government grants. Among surveyed companies, 49% intend to seek equity financing, 47% debt financing and 39% government grants.
Equity is particularly relevant to DefencetTech startups, with 59% considering this funding route, compared with 49% of established defence companies. Many younger businesses are still developing their products and have yet to generate significant revenues, making traditional debt financing more difficult.
Government-backed investors were identified as the most attractive equity funding source by 37% of businesses seeking equity, followed closely by corporate venture investors, strategic corporate investors and private equity firms.
Daniel Turgel, Partner and Co-head of White & Case’s Global Technology Industry Group, commented: “For the most promising businesses, there is no lack of equity financing. A wall of private capital is looking for a home in defence technology as previous investment restrictions are relaxed and investors rush to gain exposure to a highly attractive sector, with long-term structural growth tailwinds that extend beyond current conflicts and even defence itself.”
The findings suggest that DefenceTech could become another important contributor to UK startup investment, alongside established areas such as FinTech and life sciences.
Interest is being supported by rising military expenditure, government efforts to develop domestic technological capabilities and the potential dual-use applications of technologies initially developed for defence.
Big cheques, fewer first rounds
While the total value of investment into UK university spinouts is approaching record levels, the Parkwalk and Beauhurst findings reveal a more complicated picture for early-stage founders.
First-time equity investment fell from €176 million (£148 million) in H1 2025 to €56 million (£47 million) in H1 2026, a decline of 68.3%.
The number of first-time funding deals also decreased, from 47 to 44 over the same period, significantly below the peak of 73 recorded in H1 2021.
Meanwhile, later-stage investment reached €907 million (£760 million) in H1 2026, its highest half-year level since 2021, representing a 165% year-on-year increase.
The contrast is significant. Although more capital is flowing into established university spinouts, fewer emerging businesses are securing their first equity investment.
Moray Wright, CEO of Parkwalk, said: “British DeepTech is attracting capital at a scale we have rarely seen, and that is something to celebrate. But these figures carry a clear warning. First-time investment has fallen, and the companies vital to the future of the UK economy are struggling to raise their first round.”
The shift is also visible in average deal sizes, which have more than doubled over the past decade, from €4.2 million (£3.57 million) in H1 2016 to €8.6 million (£7.24 million) in H1 2026.
The growth of later-stage financing is a positive sign for the UK, but the shrinking pool of first-time funding raises questions about whether the country is building a sufficiently broad pipeline of new businesses to sustain its investment momentum.
Global money, British innovation
Another finding connecting the three studies is the UK’s growing relationship with international investors.
According to Parkwalk and Beauhurst, funding rounds involving at least one international investor accounted for 86.1% of total university spinout investment in H1 2026, the highest share recorded this decade.
British investors nevertheless remain central to the ecosystem. Since 2016, UK investors have participated in 2,545 spinout deals, more than six times the 408 involving US investors.
Yet international investment also introduces questions about where the value generated by British innovation ultimately ends up.
International buyers accounted for 75% of UK spinout acquisitions in H1 2026 and 68.3% of acquisitions since 2016. Over the decade, US buyers acquired 66 UK spinouts, compared with 57 acquired by British buyers.
The geographical distribution of funding presents another challenge. Nearly 80% of spinout investment since 2016 has gone to the South East, East of England and London.
University of Oxford spinouts have raised €6.4 billion (£5.39 billion) over this period, compared with €4.7 billion (£3.99 billion) for University of Cambridge spinouts. Further north, Manchester university spinouts attracted €232 million (£195 million), while those in Liverpool secured €23.3 million (£19.6 million).
So, on top of there being a clear difficulty in directing funding to early-stage companies, there seems to be a higher amount of foreign investment circulating than national funding across an imbalanced geography. Bringing into question the future interests of these companies, their investors and eventual market goals.
Conclusion
Wether the UK can translate their clear financial strength into long-term European leadership will depend on more than headline investment totals.
Ensuring early-stage founders can access funding, encouraging investment beyond established innovation hubs and helping British companies remain and grow in the country will be equally important.
The UK’s startup funding lead does not simply depend on how much capital it can attract, but how widely that capital can support the next generation of companies.

articles.title: NVIDIA Unveils Minerva to Bring End-to-End Observability for AI Factories
articles.text:
Launched today, NVIDIA Minerva is an AIOps platform built to help teams find problems earlier and keep AI factories productive. It brings together telemetry from infrastructure and AI workloads, then applies purpose-built AI models to turn that data into timely, actionable insight.
AI factories are among the most complex operations in the world, with vast numbers of GPUs working across high-speed networks to train models and serve AI applications. At that scale, a single degraded component can slow an entire job. The warning signs may be easy to miss, such as a GPU running hotter than its peers or an NVMe drive losing performance under load.
The platform focuses on AI factory yield, a measure of the useful work infrastructure produces through GPU hours, goodput, cluster uptime and token production.
Delivering a Dynamic View of an AI Factory
Traditional monitoring tools often divide the data center into separate views. Networking, compute, site reliability and machine learning teams each see a different part of the operation. Minerva connects those signals across NVIDIA GPUs, networking, storage, schedulers and workloads.
With these signals, Minerva builds a dynamic knowledge graph that logically maps the infrastructure — GPUs, SuperNICs, switches and cables — and the jobs running on it. This context helps operators trace a slow training job to the component affecting it, even across a factory with hundreds of thousands of GPUs.
It analyzes billions of data points per hour using supervised and unsupervised machine learning. It learns normal behavior, detects previously unseen anomalies, predicts emerging failures and correlates related events based on the factory’s topology. Instead of sending every symptom to an operator, it can group an event storm into a focused incident with a likely root cause.
Minerva comes with a native AI assistant and connects to external agentic AI tools. This adds a natural-language interface grounded in live telemetry. Operators can investigate cluster health and receive recommended remediation through conversation. Teams can keep a person in the loop to manually implement fixes or connect Minerva to automation through infrastructure application programming interfaces and external systems.
Results That Maximize AI Factory Yield
The ability to correlate workload and infrastructure issues along with its agentic AI capabilities help simplify AI factory operations. Instead of dealing with a blizzard of alerts, Minerva aggregates related problems into a single actionable item. This allows AIOps teams to move from reactive to proactive maintenance. And all of this helps AI factories maximize GPU uptime.
Minerva delivers value for the key metrics AI factories focus on:
- Longer time between interruptions: Minerva spots trouble before it happens, so jobs run longer without incident.
- Faster time to repair: When an incident does happen, Minerva pinpoints the problem, leading to a significantly quicker resolution.
- Greater insight: Modern AI infrastructure generates a flood of data; Minerva filters it out, leaving only the handful of alerts that actually matter.
IREN is among the NVIDIA partners using Minerva to optimize its AI factories.
“As we scale our AI factories, the key to providing the best service for our customers is maximizing the productivity of our GPUs,” said Denis Skrinnikoff, chief technology officer of IREN. “NVIDIA Minerva gives our operations team one view across the network, the GPUs and the jobs running on them, so we focus more on proactive maintenance rather than troubleshooting. That visibility strengthens our operating model for the infrastructure we’re building next.”
Joining IREN, Aolani, Bitdeer AI, IBM, Jio, Lambda, Quake AI and Tesla plan to deploy Minerva.
In addition to Dell Technologies, Lenovo and Supermicro will offer Minerva as part of their AI factory operations portfolios.

articles.title: PHP2Shell Exploitation Started Days Before Patches
articles.text:
Threat actors started probing for servers affected by two critical remote code execution (RCE) vulnerabilities in PHP four days before the fixes, Amazon reports.
Patches for the two flaws, known as PHP2Shell and tracked as CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619, were released on October 21, after the PHP Foundation and industry partners scrambled for weeks to build, verify, and validate them.
On October 20, both issues were leaked online, which accelerated the circulation of proof-of-concept (PoC) exploits. Multiple organizations observed the activity, but said the exploitation attempts were unsuccessful.
According to Amazon, the first PHP2Shell exploitation occurred on October 17, while the security defects were still under embargo, and originated from a commercial anonymization network.
“The targeting of a honeypot from an anonymized IP address suggests the activity was conducted by a threat actor, though it remains unclear how the actor acquired exploit information prior to disclosure,” Amazon says.
Roughly 12 hours before the public disclosure, Amazon identified multiple PoCs for PHP2Shell from additional anonymized infrastructure. The variations in payloads and origin suggest that multiple threat actors were getting involved.
“Once the embargo was lifted and the patch was released, additional proof-of-concept exploits appeared within hours, and we saw them used against our sensors almost immediately. PHP2Shell is now being broadly exploited in the wild,” Amazon notes.
WatchTowr too observed mass exploitation shortly after the patches were released, albeit none of the circulating PoCs achieve RCE.
“In an entirely predictable chain of events, WatchTowr Intel is seeing broad exploitation attempts and sloppy proof-of-concept exploit code tweeted and thrown onto GitHub. The exploits being sprayed indiscriminately either don’t work at all, test for timing-based differences, or crash the target,” WatchTowr head of threat intelligence Jake Knott said in an emailed statement.
Hadrian, Patchstack and Cloudflare all reported seeing exploitation attempts hours before the fixes were released.
“In the 10 hours before it was publicly announced, across the Cloudflare network we saw thousands of attempts to exploit it,” Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said early on Thursday. “That jumped to tens of thousands in the 45 minutes post announcement, hundreds of thousands within 2 hours, and millions now.”
Additionally, JFrog has observed fake PoC exploits and prank malware being published on GitHub.
VulnCheck told SecurityWeek that at least one Chinese IP address unsuccessfully attempted to exploit PHP2Shell to deploy a webshell.
According to VulnCheck, VirusTotal, and Censys, more than 1 million PHP servers were running unpatched software releases as of October 21.
Out of 2.58 million internet-facing hosts seen on October 21, roughly 1.58 million were reporting identifiable PHP versions, and approximately 1.57 million were not patched, Censys says. As of October 22, the platform tracks nearly 3 million internet-facing hosts running PHP.
VulnCheck was seeing more than 2.6 million internet-facing hosts running PHP, nearly all of which were vulnerable. At least 1 million run end-of-life (EoL) PHP versions: more than 700,000 are PHP 3.x – 7.3 and nearly 400,000 are PHP 7.4, 8.0, or 8.1.
VirusTotal says it sees roughly 5.1 million IP addresses running PHP, but only 1.1 million of them announce a version in an HTTP header. Of these, only approximately 272,000 run a supported PHP version, while the majority (around 758,000) run an EoL iteration (PHP 5.4 to 8.1).
Most of these PHP hosts (~920,000) are in the US. The good news is they run on a handful of providers, including AWS, DigitalOcean, Alibaba, OVHcloud, and Hetzner, so remediation would involve simple configuration pushes and WAF rules.
Cybersecurity community response
On Wednesday, the US cybersecurity agency CISA urged organizations to update immediately to PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, or 8.2.35, which include fixes for both PHP2Shell flaws.
“Organizations will struggle to patch quickly, but the harder problem is finding everything that needs patching. Events like this expose forgotten applications, shadow systems and PHP installations that network owners may not even know exist,” BlueVoyant CISO John Harbaugh said.
Because in some configurations the vulnerabilities can be exploited to execute code before the security checks run, all stakeholders should apply the emergency updates immediately and start investigating for signs of compromise, says ThreatLocker co-founder and CTO Michael Jenkins.
“Until every system is patched, controls that limit what a web-facing process can launch, access, or connect to can reduce an attacker’s options. Those controls are a backstop, not a substitute for patching, and should remain in place afterward. A PHP process generally needs access only to the files and network services required to run the site. Restricting everything else can help prevent a compromised web server from becoming a gateway into the broader business,” Jenkins added.
According to Forescout threat hunting senior manager Sai Molige and Expel principal threat researcher (and former hacker) Marcus Hutchins, PHP2Shell is comparable to Log4Shell.
“PHP2Shell has the potential to become a Log4Shell-scale event, but for a different reason. With Log4j, the main problem was finding a library you didn’t know you had. With PHP, much of the forgotten infrastructure will be found, but won’t have an upstream fix. The durable lesson from Log4j is that organizations should treat ‘How quickly can we identify where we run X?’ as a measurable capability separate from patching speed,” Molige said.
“I’d say PHP2Shell is like 50% the way towards Log4J. Massive wide-ranging impact. Worse direct exploitation. Shorter tail & indirect exploitation due to not being as deeply embedded in 3rd party software as Log4J was,” Hutchins said.
Related: Oracle Patches Over 1,200 Vulnerabilities With October 2026 CPU
Related: Memory Bugs Account for Most of Chrome’s 353 New Security Fixes
Related: ‘Context Bombs’ Cut AI Attack Success by Misleading Agents With Fake Targets
Related: Context Is King in the Fight Against Modern Cyberattacks

articles.title: 1Password tops $500-million USD ARR on the back of accelerating AI demand | BetaKit
articles.text:
Toronto-based cybersecurity software company 1Password announced on Thursday that it has crossed $500 million USD ($702 million CAD) in annual recurring revenue (ARR), up from $400 million about a year ago. The technology firm achieved this milestone amid rising AI adoption and while maintaining a double-digit free cash flow margin.
1Password also revealed that it has added approximately 20,000 business customers during this time (bringing its total to more than 200,000), and brought the number of clients paying more than $100,000 annually for its services up more than 40 percent year-over-year, while improving its net retention.
“The fact that we’re accelerating through that speaks to the AI influence on our business and our growth.”
David Faugno,
1Password
This growth has been fuelled by demand for 1Password’s developer and AI security tools, which have seen monthly active usage among human users jump 200 percent and autonomous AI agents soar 500 percent year-over-year. The company aims to build on this with the release of a new platform on Thursday to help clients deploy personal AI agents.
These types of offerings have helped 1Password post net-new ARR growth of 60 percent in 2026 and 90 percent year-over-year during the third quarter, specifically. The firm claims it now caters to 85 percent of the Forbes AI 50 list, which ranks top private AI startups.
In an interview with BetaKit, 1Password CEO David Faugno chalked much of the company’s recent rise up to developers seeking to securely leverage AI agents to build software.
“When you get bigger, the growth rates are supposed to go down while at large numbers,” Faugno said. “The fact that we’re accelerating through that speaks to the AI influence on our business and our growth.”
Founded in 2005 and formally known as AgileBits, 1Password is one of Canada’s most valuable tech companies. It sells identity security and access management software to help individuals and corporate clients like Canva, CIBC Capital Markets, Cursor, Eleven Labs, Hugging Face, Notion, Perplexity, Salesforce, Stripe, and Workday secure their sign-in credentials for apps and websites.
Since its launch, 1Password has evolved from a consumer-facing password manager to a broader digital security platform for businesses, and has leaned heavily into helping customers navigate the security challenges associated with deploying AI agents. Faugno thinks “the shadow AI wave will be massively larger than the shadow IT wave” that preceded it, given that there are simply far more agents running amok online than people.
Faugno expects AI to be a “key driver” for not just 1Password but nearly every business going forward. He predicted that while growth in the use of AI “will persist unabated,” and “software as we know it historically will be changed forever,” where that growth might show up in revenue will take different turns over time.
For now, Faugno said, “where I think the world is coalescing is, agents need just the access that you want them to have, just for the time that they need it, specifically for the task they’re doing on your behalf, and that’s what 1Password does.”
RELATED: “We could be public today”: 1Password crosses $400-million USD ARR
Agentic AI adoption has also fuelled what the CEO characterized as “a resurgence” in the consumer-facing side of 1Password. While business-to-business sales are still responsible for over 75 percent of its revenue, that gap has not widened since 2025.
When BetaKit sat down with Faugno in late 2025, he argued that the firm possessed the profile of a public company but wanted to advance its AI product roadmap further and ensure it could deliver greater predictability and repeatability before seriously entertaining the possibility of an initial public offering (IPO).
Faugno said in an interview this week that while setting up the infrastructure to “port” the company’s security model over to agentic AI use-cases “was not super straightforward,” 1Password has moved “pretty far down the path” of what it set out to do on the AI transformation front a year ago, adding that this groundwork is now manifesting in product releases like the platform it unveiled on Thursday.
But the CEO indicated the firm still has more building to do and will need to see greater predictability in its sales motion before pursuing an IPO. He did not share a more detailed timeline of when that might occur.
Faugno said he sees an achievable path to 1Password hitting $1 billion USD in ARR over the next several years, especially if its growth continues to accelerate.
Feature image courtesy Alex Broadway/Web Summit/Sportsfile via Flickr.

articles.title: Former OpenAI science lead launches Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Former OpenAI science lead Kevin Weil has launched Warp Sciences, a new AI startup focused on automating lab work for drug discovery. The company, which trains robots to make and test promising compounds identified by researchers, has raised $215 million at an $865 million valuation, according to Weil, who announced the startup and funding on X.
The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from IVP, Mayfield, Lux Capital, Premji Invest, and Menlo Ventures.
For years, biotech companies have outsourced the most labor-intensive work of synthesizing thousands of variations of molecules to contractors in China, such as WuXi AppTec. With Warp Sciences, Weil hopes to reshore that work and insulate the entire drug development process from geopolitical supply-chain risks.
Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks. By automating wet-lab work, Warp Sciences aims to accelerate drug discovery using robots that can operate around the clock.

articles.title: US official: Russia's stalker satellite sure looks like an orbital weapon
articles.text:
Four years ago, a senior official in Russia’s foreign ministry painted a bullseye on commercial satellite networks that assist Ukraine in its fight against invading Russian military forces.
On Wednesday, several days after a Russian military spacecraft moved within striking distance of one of those commercial satellites, the same Russian diplomat assured the world there’s no reason to worry.
There’s a sharp incongruity in those statements from Konstantin Vorontsov, deputy head of Russia’s delegation to the United Nations. Vorontsov’s comments Wednesday in the UN General Assembly’s First Committee came moments after a US official called attention to recent maneuvers by Kosmos 2612, a Russian military craft that approached a US-registered commercial satellite some 340 miles (550 kilometers) above Earth.
“Just last weekend, Russia’s Ministry of Defense Kosmos 2612 exhibited threatening behavior by intentionally maneuvering dangerously close to a commercial satellite,” Brian Hardesty, a US State Department official, told the UN committee. “These behaviors appear consistent with an on-orbit weapons operation. The decision to conduct these activities was deliberately reckless and violated long-established safety thresholds in low-Earth orbit.”
Thomas DiNanno, the US Under Secretary of State for Arms Control and International Security, shared a similar statement on X. The comments were the first from the US government since the close encounter last weekend.
Vorontsov said the US government’s concerns, echoed by European officials, were “unfounded” distractions. “Western countries headed by the United States continue to use loudspeaker diplomacy repeating absurd accusations about Russia’s space activity.”
All Russian activity in space is “purely peaceful in character,” Vorontsov said. “This applies to the activity related to Kosmos 2612.”
There’s a history
Vorontsov’s statements in 2022 were more provocative. At that time, as Ukraine ramped up its reliance on commercial satellite communications and surveillance, Vorontsov said that commercial space infrastructure used by Ukraine’s military, including Western satellites, could be a “legitimate target for a retaliatory strike.”
It is no wonder, then, that the Russian military’s unprecedented maneuvers near one of those satellites raised alarms. Since its launch in April, Kosmos 2612 performed a series of carefully choreographed rocket burns to match orbits with ICEYE-X36, a radar surveillance satellite owned by the US subsidiary of the Finnish remote sensing company ICEYE.

articles.title: Google’s TPUs for AI workloads now run in Meta's data centers — TPUs sold to external customers for the first time, threaten Nvidia's market dominance
articles.text:
Google’s TPUs for AI workloads now run in Meta's data centers — TPUs sold to external customers for the first time, threaten Nvidia's market dominance
PyTorch’s own creator now serves AI models on Google’s TPUs, and most need no JAX port.
Google’s tensor processing units (TPUs) — its custom AI chips — now serve AI in production at Meta (creator of the widely used PyTorch AI framework) through a new PyTorch-native version of the SGLang inference engine, announced on Google’s developer blog. A matching version of vLLM, another widely used inference engine, was also announced as open source.
Previously, both engines used Google’s own JAX AI framework to run on TPUs. The new versions allow the hardware to be a native option for PyTorch, mostly without rewriting.
“SGLang-TorchTPU is running in production at Meta today” after “a close three-way collaboration between Meta, Google, and the SGLang team,” said Meta’s PyTorch-TPU lead Zongwei Zhou. That team works at RadixArk, a startup founded by SGLang’s creators, which built the engine with Google and Meta. The engine, he said, gives Meta “a remarkably mature, PyTorch-native serving stack.”
Jana van Greunen, director of PyTorch engineering at Meta, added in Google’s TorchTPU post that Meta “cannot be constrained by a single hardware architecture” and that TorchTPU “enables us to deploy our PyTorch workloads to Google TPUs.” Google said it co-developed TorchTPU with Meta’s PyTorch team.
This is not Meta’s first attempt at using TPUs. Google calls PyTorch/XLA, the older bridge from PyTorch to TPUs, a "predecessor" to the new TorchTPU, and SemiAnalysis reported last year that Meta research teams used TPUs through this bridge from 2020 to 2023 before Meta canceled those contracts. Google’s PyTorch-on-TPU push was aimed mainly at Meta, which did not want to migrate to JAX.
Although it is unclear where Meta’s production TPUs sit, talks last year reportedly included Google Cloud TPU rentals in 2026 with purchases in 2027, and Meta later reportedly signed a multi-year rental agreement.
The announcement came one day after Amazon said it was open-sourcing TorchNeuron, its own native PyTorch backend for its Trainium2 and Trainium3 chips, at the same PyTorch Conference. Both moves appear to be aimed at loosening Nvidia’s software lock-in.
Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.
On performance, a tuned vLLM setup serving Moonshot AI’s open-weight, 2.8-trillion-parameter Kimi K3 model reportedly tops 700 tokens per second for a single user on the seventh-generation Ironwood TPU. That speed figure comes from Inferact, the startup founded by vLLM’s creators that helped Google build vLLM-TorchTPU. Its test ran 16 Ironwood chips with speculative decoding, a method of speeding up large language model inference with a small draft model, against vLLM’s published setup on 16 Nvidia GB200s, which reached 452 tokens per second. Its kernels for Kimi K3 and Qwen 3.8 27B deliver roughly 1.4 to 2 times the GB200 baseline’s throughput at small batch sizes without speculative decoding.
SGLang-TorchTPU will keep adding models, starting with DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Reflection Beam. It's also working toward Day 0 TPU support for new open models, meaning support on release day, by the first quarter of 2027, according to RadixArk. Google, Meta and RadixArk plan to share more at SGLang Summit 2026, Nov. 12–13 in San Francisco.

articles.title: Three things you should know about permafrost
articles.text:
Three things you should know about permafrost
A primer on this crucial and frankly mysterious piece of climate science.
How much do you know about permafrost?
Maybe, like me, you’ve been aware that this layer of frozen soil is thawing, that it’s important in the global puzzle of climate change … and that’s about the extent of it.
The great news for both of us is that my colleague James Temple just published two in-depth stories about permafrost. His reporting took him to the boreal forests of Alaska, where he helicoptered into the wilderness to learn more about how this material could affect our climate both now and in the future.
I’d recommend you give both of James’s stories a read. There’s this feature about efforts to tackle the intensifying fires that are threatening permafrost, as well as this look at how researchers are trying to understand the complicated tangle of potential climate effects. Here are three things I took away.
Permafrost is a massive blind spot for climate change
Permafrost is the frozen layer of soil that’s under about 15% of land around the Northern Hemisphere. While technically material needs to be frozen for only two consecutive years to count as permafrost, most of our current permafrost formed during the last ice age.
That means there’s organic material that’s been frozen, and essentially locked away, for thousands of years. But as global temperatures tick up and this layer thaws, microbes are able to break down that organic matter, releasing carbon dioxide and methane—powerful greenhouse gases that drive climate change. Those emissions form a feedback loop, accelerating warming further.
The steady rise in global temperatures has already shrunk the footprint of the Arctic permafrost by about 12% since 1850, and the pace has been picking up in the last 50 years.
The wild thing is, only a minority of the models that have been used in UN climate reports actually take into account the gradual loss of permafrost. And none of them include the abrupt thaw and collapse that can happen after events like heat waves and fires (more on those fires in a moment). There are efforts to make sure future UN reports reflect the growing science, but for now, all this means that we’re probably underestimating how much and how fast the planet is going to warm.
Wildfires can speed up permafrost loss
Fire is a natural part of boreal forests’ life cycle, but they’re getting more intense because of climate change. And crucially, fires can accelerate the thawing of permafrost. By the end of the century, this effect could release the equivalent of 80 billion metric tons of carbon dioxide.
Today, the policy across remote parts of Canada and Alaska is generally to let wildfires burn as long as they’re not threatening human habitats. But some researchers say we should explore fighting these fires to save the carbon trapped in the forests and the permafrost beneath them.
Researchers at the Woodwell Climate Research Center are developing a map of burn risk and carbon vulnerability across Alaska, essentially highlighting areas where fires are most likely to spread and which areas are home to certain types of permafrost that would release the most emissions. (Yes, apparently there are different types of permafrost. Yedoma is a particularly deep, carbon-dense form from the late Pleistocene era.)
That’s all just the beginning—once we figure out potential targets, the question is what to do about it. Some suggest setting more prescribed fires, something Indigenous groups have done for thousands of years, partly to reduce the danger of massive blazes. Or resources could go to early detection and efforts to put out fires before they grow.
The carbon cycle of permafrost is incredibly complicated
There’s about 1.5 trillion tons of carbon locked away in permafrost, about twice the amount in the atmosphere. We know that permafrost thawing can release greenhouse-gas emissions and drive climate change. But there are complications.
One particularly big wrinkle: Other effects from permafrost thawing and fire recovery might counteract the carbon lost from those events. For example, as temperatures warm, plants can gradually move north and take hold where they couldn’t have before. Those plants soak up carbon from the atmosphere as they grow, at least partly locking away what was emitted.
Researchers are working to better understand this ecosystem. And the more we learn, the more complicated the picture looks. How much carbon is lost from permafrost, and how much a given area will recover its carbon, depend on a huge array of factors. How severe are the fires that have accelerated local thawing? What’s the local climate and environment? And what kind of permafrost is at stake?
The higher we push the planet’s temperature, the more we mess with complicated natural phenomena that we’re only beginning to understand.

articles.title: PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
articles.text:
Demand for new PCs took a hit after months of price hikes, with Counterpoint Research reporting global PC shipments fell 21 percent year-over-year in Q3 2026. That’s in line with earlier reports from IDC and Omdia. It’s not just PCs, either — that same quarter, smartphone shipments also hit a 14-year low.
PC shipments dropped over 20 percent in Q3 due to RAM price hikes
Counterpoint Research says higher prices are tanking demand for new PCs.
Counterpoint linked the decline in PC shipments to higher component prices. Up until Q2 2026, PC shipments had been growing for over two years straight. But over the last several months, RAM, SSDs, and chips from Intel, AMD, and Qualcomm have all gotten more expensive, leading to price hikes on everything from MacBooks to Raspberry Pis. Counterpoint senior analyst Minsoo Kang noted that some companies are shifting to “prioritize configurations that can better absorb component inflation,” leaving fewer affordable options for price-sensitive buyers. Some companies are even reviving older tech, like DDR4 RAM and 4GB GPUs, to help mitigate price hikes.
Counterpoint also says Q3 2025 included “purchases ahead of the Windows 10 support deadline and tariff-related inventory adjustments,” which added to the sharp year-over-year drop this past quarter. The PC market might not bounce back anytime soon, as Counterpoint associate director David Naranjo says, “With global shipments expected to plunge 27% in Q4 2026 and remain broadly flat in 2027, stabilization should not be mistaken for recovery.”

articles.title: Meta shocked by $25B fine after N.M. refused to join multistate settlement
articles.text:
In his opinion Wednesday, US district court judge Francis J. Mathew said there was no “bright line rule” for determining the appropriate penalty for Meta’s repeated and willful deception of users since 2010 about their “control of data, third-party data misuse, misinformation, hate speech, and equal enforcement.”
New Mexico had asked the court to impose even higher fines, up to $40 billion. The entire state of 2 million people were harmed by Meta’s conduct, Torrez argued, and it seemed dubious that Meta would make meaningful changes unless the penalty impacted Meta’s stock price.
Mathew found that the trial record—which showed that top leadership, including Mark Zuckerberg, were aware that the company, then known as Facebook, was making misleading public representations—supported “the highest level of penalty allowed by the NW Unfair Practices Act.”
“The jury was unequivocal: Facebook systematically misled the public” and “took advantage of the public’s lack of knowledge respecting Facebook’s practices to a grossly unfair degree,” Mathew wrote.
To Mathew, it seemed that Meta made a choice to avoid transparency with users in a bid to capitalize on data they didn’t realize they were sharing and better compete with one of its main rivals, the platform then known as Twitter.
“The violations the jury found were not the product of a single misleading statement or isolated incident,” Mathew noted. “They arose from repeated public representations over more than 11 years, concerning multiple core aspects of Facebook’s platform and business.”
Meta had hoped that New Mexico’s penalty would be more in line with a $5 billion settlement the company made with the Federal Trade Commission to address the Cambridge Analytica fallout. At most, they expected to pay $3.4 billion, while arguing that anything more would be “unconstitutional,” AP News reported.
But Mathew said that the FTC settlement “cannot be viewed in a vacuum” while noting that so far, “penalties, consent agreements, and decrees have not deterred Meta from using deceptive trade practices” since the Cambridge Analytica scandal was first exposed.
“To induce users to provide their personal information to Facebook, Facebook made many false promises respecting the security and control of that data over the course of more than a decade,” Mathew wrote.
Meta will appeal
In a press release, Torrez celebrated the ruling, calling it “a historic day for New Mexico and for consumers across the country.”
“For too long, powerful technology companies have operated as though their size and influence put them beyond the reach of the law,” Torrez said. “A New Mexico jury found nearly 44 million violations of our consumer protection statute, and this penalty order demonstrates that those violations carry real consequences. We took on one of the largest companies in the world because New Mexicans deserve honesty, accountability, and the protection of their personal information. Today’s result makes clear that no corporation is too powerful to be held accountable.”
A Meta spokesperson confirmed to Ars that the company plans to appeal. Legal experts told Reuters the company has a decent chance at slashing the fine on appeal based on constitutional claims. On top of likely claiming that the penalty is unconstitutional, Meta also feels that “this ruling, and the Attorney General’s approach to enforcement, makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico,” the spokesperson said.
The eye-popping fine following the multistate settlement appears to be making the company uncomfortable, despite critics claims that New Mexico’s penalty is just a “drop in the bucket” for a company that makes $200 billion annually. On Thursday, the Verge highlighted Meta’s third-quarter earnings report, which showed the company paid close to $10 billion for the multistate settlement. Without that expense, Meta’s income from operations would have been $22 billion higher, the report said.
The excessive penalties come as Meta attempts to reboot its struggling AI strategy, and Meta appeared to signal to Donald Trump’s administration to possibly support its appeal by nodding to its AI wing in its statement opposing the ruling.
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online,” Meta’s spokesperson said. “We are confident we will prevail on appeal. In the meantime, Meta will continue to build a safe and free platform to connect millions of Americans, grow small businesses, and help the country maintain its competitive edge.”
AGs warned to keep watch on Meta AI
Nidhi Hegde, executive director of a watchdog nonprofit called the American Economic Liberties Project, told AP News that Meta users want more enforcers willing to take the company to trial rather than settle matters in ways that the FTC settlement suggested weren’t genuine.
In his opinion, Mathew noted that the jury found that Meta internal messages and investigation results showed that “rather than seek to educate Facebook’s users… Zuckerberg chose instead to capitalize on that lack of understanding in order to manipulate users into sharing more of their personal information publicly.” In one message, Zuckerberg was found laying out a plan to deceive users, saying, “Give them a chance to change their privacy settings but obviously don’t encourage it.”
The company also failed to notify users when apps misused their data, only flagging two of 2,000 unique apps associated with data misuse, Mathew said. Following its investigation, Meta’s “decision was deliberately made to narrow Facebook’s internal definition of data misuse so that Facebook would not have to notify as many people due to the operational burden of doing so,” he wrote.
Additionally, Facebook continued knowingly profiting off of pages with misinformation and hate speech, Mathew wrote. Internal research found “substantial amounts of misleading, false, and possibly false political, health, and science content,” with Meta documenting a “greater concentration of false content in top performing advertising content than in top performing Facebook content.”
Rather than share that research, Meta buried it, while also deceiving users in dozens of other ways, including by misrepresenting that the average Facebook users gets “equal treatment” to celebrities and influencers. While Meta claimed everyone was treated the same, one class of users received warning to remove violating content before strikes were applied and frequently got harmful or sketchy content decisions overturned in cases where most users would not.
Hegde told AP News that she thinks as Meta and other company’s AI products grow more popular, it will be increasingly important for states to remain watchful and protect residents from unknown harms.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” Hegde said. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
Torrez vowed to keep watch in New Mexico and to continue using the blueprint from the Meta case to enforce consumer protection laws and prevent tech giants’ misuse of data.
“This case has always been about more than one company or one scandal,”Torrez said. “It is about whether corporations can mislead consumers about what happens to their personal information without facing meaningful consequences. New Mexico stood its ground, took this case to trial, and secured a verdict establishing millions of violations of our law. This outcome reinforces a fundamental principle, companies that do business in our state must follow our laws and respect the rights of our people.”
Ashley is a senior policy reporter for Ars Technica, dedicated to tracking social impacts of emerging policies and new technologies. She is a Chicago-based journalist with 20 years of experience.

Corsair’s Vengeance DDR5-6000 CL30 kit hits the speed and latency sweet spot for AMD Ryzen systems
RAM prices are continuing to rise, and while we're a long way from costs returning to normal, I've been tracking down the best savings on the Corsair Vengeance line of DDR5 memory. One that stands out to me right now is this Corsair Vengeance 32GB DDR5-6000 kit is now $560 (was $626) at Amazon
As a dual-profile kit, it supports AMD EXPO and Intel XMP. But if you’re building or upgrading an AMD Ryzen PC, then DDR5-6000 with CL30 timings is the memory most builders aim for. This Corsair kit nails both numbers.
• Best for: PC builders putting together an AMD Ryzen 7000 or 9000 system who want fast, reliable memory that sets up with one click.
• Why we like it: DDR5-6000 speeds at tight CL30 timings, AMD EXPO and Intel XMP profiles for easy setup, and a low-profile heat spreader that clears big air coolers.
A two-module 32GB (2 x 16GB) DDR5 kit (model CMK32GX5M2B6000Z30) rated at 6000MT/s with CL30 timings at 1.40V. It supports both AMD EXPO and Intel XMP, and uses a low-profile aluminum heat spreader without RGB lighting.
Why We Recommend It
Corsair’s Vengeance line is one of the most popular choices among PC builders, and this kit is tuned for AMD, with an EXPO profile that sets it to its full 6000MT/s at CL30 with a single BIOS setting. That speed and latency combination is widely considered the sweet spot for Ryzen 7000 and 9000 processors, although it is a dual-profile kit for Intel PCs, too.
Price Context & Historical Value
Memory prices have climbed sharply over the past year, so $559.99 is far more than a 32GB DDR5 kit cost not long ago. This deal takes the edge off, but with soaring RAM costs expected to last years, this is one of the better RAM deals I've seen for PC builders.

✅ Buy the Corsair Vengeance DDR5-6000 32GB if... you’re building an AMD Ryzen 7000 or 9000 PC and want memory that runs at its rated speed with one click.
❌ Skip the Corsair Vengeance DDR5-6000 32GB if... your PC uses DDR4 or you want RGB lighting.
Also consider
Two 16GB DDR5 modules running at up to 6000MT/s with CL36-44-44-96 timings and AMD Expo and Intel XMP 3.0 support for one-click overclocking. Each module features ten individually addressable RGB LEDs across a panoramic light bar, controllable through Corsair's iCUE software, along with onboard voltage regulation for more stable overclocking.

articles.title: Elon Musk made a $1B investment in Skydance, report says | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Elon Musk has invested approximately $1 billion in the newly formed media company Skydance, according to a new report from Semafor. News of the investment comes a few weeks after Paramount completed its $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery to create the combined company.
Co-CEOs David Ellison and Ynon Kreiz are tasked with bringing together two major streaming platforms, Paramount+ and HBO Max, along with a portfolio of networks, including CBS, CNN, MTV, TBS, Comedy Central, and Food Network, under a single corporate umbrella.
Semafor reports that Musk’s investment was made around the same time as equity contributions from other Skydance investors, including board member Laurene Powell Jobs. The investment will provide a much needed financial boost as the company seeks to cut costs and lift its stock price, the report notes.
Skydance has already committed to reducing costs by $6 billion over the next three years.
Musk has publicly praised the Ellisons in the past and has close ties with Larry Ellison, whom he appointed to Tesla’s board of directors in 2018. The Oracle founder invested $1 billion to help Musk purchase Twitter in 2022 and also invested in Tesla in 2018.
Skydance did not immediately respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

articles.title: Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
articles.text:
Cambridge scientists create a $10 chip that could put a medical lab on your wrist
- Date:
- October 22, 2026
- Source:
- University of Cambridge
- Summary:
- Cambridge researchers have created a groundbreaking $10 optical sensor that delivers the precision of laboratory equipment in a device small enough for wearable technology. It identified foods, plastics, and medicines with 100% accuracy in tests and demonstrated the ability to monitor blood glucose, alcohol, and other health markers without invasive procedures.
- Share:
A new optical sensor costing just $10 could bring laboratory-level precision to wearable health monitors, potentially allowing people to track blood glucose without needles. The technology could also transform food testing, industrial quality control, and environmental monitoring.
Researchers at the University of Cambridge and GlitterinTech (a start-up founded by the same research group) have developed a new type of optical spectrometer that combines exceptional accuracy with a remarkably small size and low cost. Measuring just centimeters across, the device could be incorporated into portable electronics and wearable health technology. Its potential applications range from monitoring important health markers in real time to identifying materials and detecting changes in chemical composition.
Optical spectrometers work by analyzing light to reveal information about the substances it interacts with. They are essential tools in medicine, manufacturing, chemical testing, and environmental research. However, making these instruments smaller has traditionally meant compromising their performance. Compact spectrometers often have limited measurement ranges, reduced resolution, or lower accuracy, making them better suited to identifying substances than performing precise measurements.
The researchers believe their new design could overcome these limitations. Known as a convolutional spectrometer, it uses a mathematical principle called the convolution theorem to analyze light in a fundamentally different way. According to the team, this approach delivers performance that surpasses existing types of spectrometers in several key areas, including designs based on light dispersion, Fourier transforms, and computational reconstruction.
A New Way to Analyze Light With Extraordinary Precision
Traditional spectrometers generally separate incoming light into its component wavelengths or use complex calculations to reconstruct its spectrum. The new device takes another approach by performing a mathematical operation called convolution directly on the incoming light.
To accomplish this, the researchers arranged optical components with repeating spectral responses in a sequence. These components can include unbalanced Mach-Zehnder interferometers or micro-ring resonators. By adjusting them in proportion to one another, the system can shift its response to different wavelengths in a controlled, linear fashion. Fast Fourier transforms are then used to accurately recover the light spectrum.
"The key insight was to go back to the mathematics and ask whether there was a fundamentally cleaner way to retrieve spectra," said Dr. Chunhui Yao, a lead author of the study. "By using the convolution theorem directly in the optical domain, we avoid many of the limitations that have held miniaturized spectrometers back. This gives us high precision, strong noise tolerance, and very low computational overhead, all in a compact and low-cost system."
The researchers built the spectrometer using a silicon nitride photonic platform and integrated it with onboard electronics. It operates across a broad range of near-infrared wavelengths (1200-1700 nm) and can collect and process measurements in less than a second.
Another important advantage is its ability to expand its measurement capabilities without major hardware changes. Because the system uses repeating optical patterns, its spectral bandwidth can theoretically be extended almost without limit. Adding more optical components in sequence can also increase its resolution exponentially.
A $10 Sensor That Could Transform Food Testing and Healthcare
To evaluate the device outside purely theoretical measurements, the researchers tested it on a variety of materials and substances. The results demonstrated its potential for applications that normally depend on larger, more expensive laboratory instruments.
When used to identify plastics, pharmaceuticals, coffee, flour, and tea, the spectrometer achieved a 100% classification success rate in the reported tests. It also measured concentrations in water-based and organic solutions with accuracies of approximately 0.01%, exceeding the performance of commercial benchtop spectrometers in those experiments.
The healthcare demonstrations were particularly promising. Under conditions designed to reflect real physiological environments, the device accurately measured several human biomarkers, including skin moisture, blood alcohol, blood lactate, and blood glucose.
The researchers also demonstrated noninvasive glucose tracking over an extended period in one participant. Although further testing would be needed before the technology could become a practical medical product, the finding suggests a possible route toward monitoring blood sugar without repeatedly piercing the skin.
"These biomedical demonstrations are particularly exciting," said Prof. Qixiang Cheng, who led the project. "What makes this work stand out is not just performance in the lab, but technical readiness. Dr. Chunhui Yao's contribution was crucial in translating a mathematical concept into a fully packaged, robust system that operates reliably across temperature extremes and real-world conditions. That combination is what opens the door to practical deployment."
The sensor also demonstrated impressive resistance to temperature changes. It continued operating reliably between -20°C and 80°C, an unusually wide temperature range for a miniature spectrometer. This durability could be especially valuable for wearable devices, factory equipment, and sensors operating outdoors.
Why a Simpler Design Could Be a Major Breakthrough
The new spectrometer's advantages extend beyond its accuracy, size, and price. Its internal design also reduces the amount of computing power needed to analyze incoming light.
Many existing miniature spectrometers depend on complicated calibration procedures and demanding algorithms to reconstruct spectral information. These methods can become unreliable when measurements contain noise, and they often require substantial processing resources.
The Cambridge team's convolution-based approach avoids much of this complexity. Because the measurements follow a linear mathematical relationship, the system can recover spectra rapidly and consistently while using relatively little computational power.
"This is a beautiful example of how elegant engineering can unlock real impact," said Prof. Richard Penty, who contributed to the photonic system design and integration. "The architecture is simple, scalable, and manufacturable, yet it delivers precision that rivals or exceeds much larger instruments. Dr. Chunhui Yao played a central role in bringing together the photonic design, system integration, and experimental validation that made this possible."
Its relatively simple construction could also make the technology easier to manufacture on a large scale, potentially bringing sophisticated optical measurements to devices where conventional spectrometers would be too bulky or expensive.
Bringing Laboratory-Grade Measurements to Everyday Devices
The researchers envision a future in which accurate optical sensing becomes a routine feature of everyday technology rather than something largely confined to specialized laboratories.
In industrial settings, inexpensive spectrometers could be installed throughout manufacturing facilities to continuously check material composition and product quality. Similar sensors could monitor food freshness, identify substances, and analyze environmental conditions on a much larger scale than is currently practical.
Healthcare could see equally significant changes. Compact sensors might eventually enable wearables to measure hydration levels, detect signs of alcohol intoxication, track biomarkers related to physical fitness, or continuously monitor glucose levels for people managing diabetes.
"Our vision is to make spectrometry as ubiquitous as temperature or motion sensing," added Prof. Qixiang Cheng. "This work shows that high-quality spectral information doesn't have to be confined to the laboratory -- it can be embedded directly into the technologies people use every day."
As photonic technology becomes smaller and more advanced, the convolutional spectrometer provides a promising example of how mathematical insights and practical engineering can make sophisticated scientific instruments simpler, cheaper, and more accessible. By combining high precision with a device that costs around $10, the researchers have opened a potential path toward a new generation of smart sensors capable of measuring the hidden chemistry of our bodies and surroundings.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Cambridge. Original written by Michael Shuff. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

articles.title: AI’s hidden storage bill: What inference leaves behind
articles.text:
Sponsored
Provided byWD
Ask most executives to picture the cost of AI and they’ll likely see GPUs—racks of accelerators with gigawatts of power—and a waitlist for silicon. But that picture leaves something out: Data storage costs.
What happens to data after a model responds? Much of the back-end data that’s generated—from billions of daily prompts, images, and videos—needs to be stored. But data storage is one of the harder infrastructure costs to plan for, and it’s often overlooked in initial AI infrastructure planning.
As inference scales, the data footprint grows with it
Traditionally, AI infrastructure conversations have centered on the compute-intensive process of training a model. Training is finite: a run starts, burns through compute, and ends. But inference runs continuously, every time a model answers a prompt. For infrastructure planning, that difference matters: A training run is a project you can budget for and retire. Inference doesn’t retire; every inference request leaves something behind.
Take AI-generated video. In this workload, the back-end spend can be significant. From internal measurements, WD found that an 8-second clip (returned to a user as a 3.97MB 720p file) left more than 500MB of associated data behind on the back end, including logs, cached context, immediate renders, backups, and safety records. That’s a 130x increase over the output file size the user saw. Scale this to an enterprise generating longer, higher resolution video and the back-end footprint grows into the hundreds of gigabytes per clip.
And that back-end footprint is growing fast. McKinsey projects AI inference demand will grow at a 35% CAGR through 2030, versus 22% for training, making up more than 40% of total data center demand by the end of the decade.
A recent WD-sponsored IDC global white paper that surveyed 763 IT and business decision makers found that nearly 95% of respondents reported an increase in data volume due to generative AI over the past 12 months, with roughly 61% reporting growth of 25% or more.
“You can think of having more storage as an optimization for keeping the GPUs busy,” said a senior product manager of a hyperscale cloud service provider quoted in report. “The biggest challenge is to ensure that the GPUs are not idle, waiting for data to show up—hours of GPU idle time becomes very expensive, very fast.” Put in dollar terms: if your storage spend is growing 25% year over year while your compute budget grows in the more predictable cyclical way, storage ends up outpacing the budget line that receives the most attention.
Matching storage to the AI data life cycle
Compute demand rises and falls with training cycles, product launches, and hardware refreshes. But the volume of retained data doesn't fall back down with it when compute demand slows. Model logs, synthetic outputs, inference results, and more keep accumulating, and organizations are holding onto more of it for longer.
This changes the role of retained data. Information that once moved into an archive and rarely surfaced can now become an input to future AI workloads. As more data is retained, retrieved, and reused, storage must support not only growing capacity, but increasingly dynamic access to it. The same WD-IDC survey found 96% of respondents anticipate needing faster archive retrieval to support inference or retrieval-augmented generation (RAG).
AI workloads require both performance and capacity, with different technologies serving different needs across the data lifecycle. And for the vast volumes of data that must be retained and revisited, HDDs provide a cost-effective, high-capacity foundation, with a significant cost-per-terabyte advantage
What this means for how AI gets budgeted
For a CFO or CIO, this means “AI infrastructure spend” may be scoped too narrowly on compute. A model that idles while data loads costs about as much as one idling for lack of a GPU. But the storage bottleneck stays hidden until it’s already a problem, surfacing in operating costs and retrieval delays rather than a CapEx line next to the accelerators.
Consider a retailer generating AI product videos for its catalog, or an insurer running claims documents through a RAG pipeline for faster underwriting. In both cases, the compute cost is a known, budgeted quantity: a per-generation or per-query rate that finance can forecast. The storage cost is different: It compounds with every video generated and every claim processed, because none of that back-end data disappears once the task is finished.
A team that budgets AI as “compute plus a rounding error for storage” may find, in 12 to 18 months, that the rounding error has become a significant fraction of the program’s total cost—right around the time leadership is deciding whether to expand.
Building for economically scalable capacity
Addressing this challenge starts with architecture. Storage strategy tends to be designed for expensive, hot-tier performance (for data accessed instantly and constantly), while most AI data by volume accumulates in the warm, cool, and cold tiers behind it.
What enterprises need is economically scalable capacity: Infrastructure designed for the full AI data life cycle, balancing performance with capacity, power, reliability, and total cost of ownership as data persists, compounds, and is increasingly reused. That means treating archives that once sat untouched as active assets for RAG and inference, and setting retention policies for data’s growing strategic value rather than its original storage cost. It also means recognizing that decisions about storage play out across fleets, not individual drives.
Such infrastructure requires storage tiers, where individualized power consumption, reliability, density, and operational efficiency all determine whether the system remains economically sustainable as capacity scales.
There are three questions to ask about your organization’s AI infrastructure budget:
- What’s our data retention policy for AI-generated content, and who set(s) it?
- Is our storage procurement tied to training-time performance needs, or to the actual life cycle of the data we’re producing?
- If our AI usage doubled next year, would our storage cost double with it, or worse?
Most organizations cannot answer all three with confidence. That’s the gap worth closing before the next budget cycle, not after.
