articles.title: US-backed vaccine trial on babies canceled after international outcry
articles.text:
Government officials in Guinea-Bissau have formally rejected a clinical trial that would be run by Danish researchers and funded by the US to look for alleged nonspecific harms from the newborn dose of the hepatitis B vaccine. The vaccine dose is currently recommended globally for all newborns and has been used safely and effectively for decades.
In an email to Ars Technica, one of the trial’s lead researchers, Christine Stabell Benn of Bandim Health Project and the University of Southern Denmark, said that Guinea-Bissau’s Council of Ministers “formally reaffirmed its non-acceptance of the study on 16 October.”
The revelation that the study was formally rejected last week comes after news on Monday that judicial police in Guinea-Bissau raided Bandim Health’s offices and seized vaccines. Stabell Benn highlighted that the police search came after the trial was rejected.
Of the trial’s rejection, Stabell Benn wrote: “We regret the decision because we considered the study scientifically and ethically justified, but we respect the government’s authority to decide whether research may proceed in the country.”
Trial ethics
The World Health Organization and many outside experts have sharply disagreed with Stabell Benn and her colleagues on the trial’s justifications and design. It has been widely decried as “unethical” because it would withhold the newborn dose of hepatitis B vaccine from half of the participants.
With the country’s high rates of chronic hepatitis B infections, this would put thousands of babies at risk of developing a lifelong infection that can lead to liver cirrhosis, cancer, and premature death. Experts have further said that there is no scientific justification for the study, given the vaccine’s long use and strong safety record. The WHO wrote in February that the trial “posits hypothetical safety outcomes without sufficient credible evidence” to justify putting newborns at risk.

articles.title: Stacked-Die Multi-Chip Architectures: The Tradeoff Between Scaling And Power Delivery
articles.text:
Integrated voltage regulators reduce current density, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks.
By Kaladhar Radhakrishnan, Nicolas Butzen, and Vishal Javvaji
The semiconductor industry has embraced multi-chip and stacked-die architectures as the primary path for continued performance scaling. As monolithic designs become more difficult and costly to advance, chiplets, advanced packaging, and 3D integration enable higher levels of performance, bandwidth, and functional integration for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) systems.
Yet the success of stacked-die, multi-chip architectures has exposed a growing power delivery challenge. As more compute resources are integrated into a package, there is a sharp uptick in current density and the number of independent voltage domains, placing unprecedented demands on shared power delivery resources.
To address these challenges, we discussed in our recent power delivery white paper how Intel Foundry is moving voltage regulation closer to the load. By enabling higher-voltage power distribution, integrated voltage regulators (IVRs) reduce current density in the package, provide higher regulation bandwidth, and reduce reliance on large decoupling capacitor networks. Intel Foundry’s portfolio spans package-integrated magnetic inductors, fully capacitive IVR chiplets, and advanced package integration technologies, providing multiple paths to improve power integrity, efficiency, and scalability.
Advanced packaging delivers significant gains in performance, bandwidth, and integration density. However, consistently distributing power through increasingly complex packaging and interconnect structures introduces new challenges in maintaining power integrity across the package.
One consequence is voltage droop. As AI workloads generate rapid swings in current demand, the power delivery network must respond instantly. When it cannot, voltage can briefly fall below target levels, potentially impacting performance. To maintain reliability, designers often add voltage guard bands and operating margins. While effective, these safeguards can limit silicon from reaching its optimal efficiency and performance.
Multi-chip and stacked-die architectures also intensify the tradeoff between signal density and power delivery. As more compute tiles, memory interfaces, and die-to-die links are added, routing congestion increases, creating additional resistance, tighter voltage margins, and growing power delivery constraints.
As current density continues to increase, the industry is moving toward architectures that bring voltage conversion closer to the point of consumption, reducing power delivery losses while improving responsiveness to rapidly changing workloads. Intel Foundry is advancing several complementary technologies designed around this principle.
FIVR with CoaxMIL: Intel was an early pioneer of fully integrated voltage regulators (FIVRs), which moves the last voltage conversion stage onto the processor. By shortening the distance between the regulator and the load, FIVR helps reduce distribution losses and improve transient response.
To support rising current densities, Intel developed CoaxMIL, a magnetic inductor technology that delivers significantly higher current density than earlier approaches while requiring less area (see Figure 1). For customers building next-generation AI and HPC devices, this translates into improved power conversion efficiency, faster response to workload changes, and more efficient use of valuable package real estate. The result is greater performance potential without proportional increases in power delivery complexity.
Fig. 1: CoaxMIL magnetic inductor technology.
C2VR: Intel Foundry’s continuous capacitive voltage regulator (C2VR) takes voltage conversion in a different direction. Rather than relying on traditional inductors, C2VR uses high-density capacitor technology to achieve efficient voltage conversion in an extremely compact form factor.
Because capacitors are integrated directly onto the voltage regulator chiplet, C2VR can deliver both high efficiency and exceptionally high current density. It can also respond rapidly to sudden current demands, helping minimize voltage droop during the bursty workload transitions common in AI accelerators. For customers, the benefit is improved power integrity, tighter voltage control, and a scalable solution capable of supporting future multi-kiloamp workloads.
IVR chiplet architectures: These dedicated power management chiplets allow voltage conversion to be positioned closer to the compute die than traditional motherboard-based regulators. The primary advantage of IVR chiplet architectures is flexibility. Architects can position voltage regulation where it delivers the greatest benefit, whether on the landside, embedded within package layers, or beneath compute dies. This flexibility allows architects to optimize power delivery for specific applications while reducing distribution losses and improving overall efficiency. In advanced stacked-die systems, these architectures also open the door to vertical power delivery schemes that reduce distribution distance and improve power integrity.
As AI systems continue their rapid evolution, power delivery is becoming as critical to performance scaling as transistor and packaging innovation. The next generation of data center architectures will require a portfolio of solutions that move power conversion closer to the load, improve efficiency at extreme current densities, and maintain stable operation under increasingly dynamic workloads. Intel Foundry technologies are important building blocks, helping ensure that future compute platforms can continue scaling performance without being constrained by the power delivery network.
This blog is the second in a two-part series on power delivery innovation. Part 1 explores how data center energy trends are affecting chip power delivery.
Nicolas Butzen is a principal engineer at Intel.
Vishal Javvaji is a process integration manager at Intel Foundry.

articles.title: Cambridge Analytica : Meta condamnée à 25 milliards de dollars pour avoir trompé ses utilisateurs
articles.text:
Huit ans après, le scandale Cambridge Analytica colle encore à la peau de Meta. L’entreprise se voit infliger l’une des amendes les plus lourdes de l’histoire des États-Unis.
Ce mercredi 21 octobre, un juge de l’État du Nouveau-Mexique a condamné le géant des réseaux sociaux à verser 25 milliards de dollars. Une décision choc qui conclut une enquête lancée en 2021, à la suite de l’un des plus importants scandales de l’histoire numérique. La société de Mark Zuckerberg est accusée d’avoir délibérément trompé les utilisateurs de Facebook sur la protection de leurs données personnelles.
Une affaire qui colle à la peau de Meta
« L’ampleur du préjudice causé dans cette affaire est difficile à surestimer et touche au cœur même du modèle économique de Facebook », estimé le juge. Le « nombre extraordinaire de violations délibérées », qui se sont répétées pendant des années, « justifie l’application de la sanction la plus sévère », a-t-il poursuivi.
Souvenez-vous : en 2018, plusieurs médias ont révélé que la société britannique Cambridge Analytica a mis la main sur les données personnelles de jusqu’à 87 millions d’utilisateurs de Facebook via une application tierce. Elle s’en est ensuite servi pour établir le profil d’électeurs américains, c’est-à-dire cerner leurs goûts et leurs opinions afin de leur adresser des messages sur mesure. L’équipe de campagne de Donald Trump en 2016 a exploité ces informations pour cibler les électeurs.
De quoi susciter une véritable onde de choc. Facebook est alors accusée d’avoir laissé des tiers piocher dans les informations de ses utilisateurs, forçant Mark Zuckerberg à s’expliquer devant le Congrès américain. En 2019, la Federal Trade Commission, le gendarme américain de la consommation, inflige au groupe une amende de 5 milliards de dollars. Cambridge Analytica, elle, a depuis disparu.
Meta a tout fait pour tourner la page. En 2021, l’entreprise a abandonné le nom de Facebook en partie pour laisser derrière elle une réputation bien entachée. Et cette année, au mois d’août, elle a établi un accord à l’amiable avec la grande majorité des États américains ; celui-ci inclut aussi leurs plaintes liées à Cambridge Analytica. Mais le Nouveau-Mexique a refusé de transiger, et est allé jusqu’au procès. Il faut dire que l’État est devenu un redoutable adversaire de Meta. Il lui a déjà arraché 942 millions de dollars cette année, dans deux affaires liées à la sécurité des mineurs.
Déclarations trompeuses
Au fil des années, les dirigeants de Meta ont multiplié les déclarations publiques sur la confidentialité des données, mais aussi sur la lutte contre la haine et la désinformation. Sur 29 déclarations publiques de l’entreprise et de ses dirigeants, le jury a estimé que 26 étaient trompeuses. Le juge a d’ailleurs cité l’un des e-mails de Zuckerberg pour affirmer que Facebook savait que ses utilisateurs ne comprenaient pas ses paramètres de confidentialité, et en a profité.
Multipliées par le nombre de personnes touchées, elles représentent plus de 43 millions d’infractions à la loi sur la protection des consommateurs. Le tarif maximal a été appliqué à chacune d’entre elles, soit 5 000 dollars par infraction. Si le total dépassait les 219 milliards de dollars, le juge s’est finalement arrêté sur la somme de 25 milliards de dollars pour sanctionner un « schéma systématique de tromperie ».
Un verdict fermement contesté par Meta. Son directeur juridique, C.J. Mahoney, y voit une manière d’imposer « une taxe sur la parole » et promet de se battre : « Nous sommes confiants dans le fait de l’emporter en appel ». Pour rappel, le groupe, valorisé à environ 1 800 milliards de dollars, a dégagé 52,5 milliards de bénéfices sur les neuf premiers mois de l’année.
Sources : The New York Times, The Verge

articles.title: Is this the best camera phone of the year? These are my favorite shots from the triple-200MP Oppo Find X10 Pro Max
articles.text:
The Oppo Find X10 Pro Max is one of the year's top cameraphones — these photos prove it
Three versatile 200MP cameras are just a taste...
- First phone with three 200MP cameras
- A 50MP selfie camera completes the ultra-wide (0.6x), wide (1x) and telephoto (3x) array
- A photographer's kit includes a 300mm teleconverter lens
There's yet another Pro Max phone in our midst, and this time it's the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max that rivals the iPhone 18 Pro Max, following the Vivo X500 Pro Max and Xiaomi 18 Pro Max. For photographers, Oppo's new handset could top the lot as one of the best camera phones for 2026.
I had a good week with the Oppo Find X10 Pro Max ahead of its launch on October 21, including several days in Lisbon, Portugal, where I had the chance to really put the phones camera through its paces. Our full review by Luker Baker is already live, too.
It packs a slightly simpler camera array to last year's Oppo Find X9 Ultra — the company's flagship cameraphone — with an improved ultra-wide f/2.2 (0.6x), a wide f/1.5 (1x) and a telephoto f/2.1 (3x) camera.
Each of those cameras offers the option for 200MP images — that's right, it's the first phone with triple 200MP cameras. Of course, there's a f/2 selfie camera too, with up to 50MP stills.

For me, there's an appealing natural look to most of the photos I've snapped with the Find X10 Pro Max, certainly when compared to the likes of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra. I've included some of my favorite shots so far, below, with notes explaining the camera features.

articles.title: Traquer les tricheurs sur Counter-Strike 2 : Valve recrute les joueurs pour renforcer son anticheat
articles.text:
Depuis plusieurs années, chaque mise à jour de Counter-Strike 2 s’accompagne des mêmes commentaires sur son antitriche. Trois ans après la sortie du jeu, une partie des joueurs juge toujours l’antitriche de Valve trop peu efficace et reproche à l’éditeur de ne rien en dire.
Certains regrettent même Counter-Strike: Global Offensive, qui leur permettait au moins de participer à la lutte contre les tricheurs grâce à Overwatch (rien à voir avec le jeu de Blizzard). Ce système permettait à des joueurs expérimentés d’examiner les enregistrements de parties de joueurs suspects. Valve les choisissait notamment selon leurs victoires en compétition, leur rang, leurs heures de jeu, l’ancienneté de leur compte et le faible nombre de signalements reçus. À eux de déterminer si les comportements observés relevaient de la triche, avec des sanctions possibles lorsque leurs verdicts concordaient.
Valve a recommencé à faire appel aux joueurs le 11 août 2026 avec son portail VACNet, réservé au départ à quelques invités. Ce jeudi 22 octobre, l’éditeur ouvre le portail à davantage de participants.
Valve recrute des joueurs pour améliorer son antitriche
Dans un message publié sur X dans la nuit du 21 au 22 octobre, Valve annonce une nouvelle vague d’invitations à son portail VACNet. Si vous avez été sélectionné, une icône VACNet apparaît déjà dans le jeu et vous permet de rejoindre le portail pour commencer à examiner des séquences de parties.
Pour les autres, il suffit d’en faire la demande au compte officiel Counter-Strike sur X. « Si vous n’avez pas reçu d’invitation, envoyez-nous un message privé depuis notre profil et nous vous en procurerons une », précise Valve en réponse à son annonce. Pas besoin, donc, d’attendre la prochaine vague pour participer à la lutte contre la triche dans le jeu.
Qu’est-ce qui change par rapport à l’Overwatch de CS:GO ?
Une fois connecté au portail, vous pouvez visionner des extraits de parties et repérer les comportements suspects, comme avec l’Overwatch de Counter-Strike: Global Offensive. Le joueur observé, dont le pseudonyme est remplacé par « The Subject » (le sujet), utilise-t-il une aide à la visée (aim assist) ? Semble-t-il connaître la position de ses adversaires à travers les murs (wallhack) ? À vous de déterminer si les images montrent une tricherie.
Vous pouvez aussi indiquer que les images ne permettent pas de trancher. Valve demande d’ailleurs aux participants de ne se prononcer que lorsqu’ils sont certains de leur jugement.
Sur CS:GO, les verdicts concordants de plusieurs enquêteurs pouvaient entraîner le bannissement du suspect. Avec le portail VACNet de Counter-Strike 2, votre jugement n’affecte pas directement le joueur observé. Valve précise que les annotations servent à entraîner de futurs modèles de son antitriche, qui s’appuie sur l’intelligence artificielle pour repérer les comportements suspects.
L’objectif est donc de fournir au système des exemples de comportements évalués par des humains, pour l’aider à mieux reconnaître la triche par la suite. Les habitués d’Overwatch retrouveront le travail d’observation qu’ils connaissaient, au service de la détection automatique. Valve affirme dans son annonce que les récentes améliorations de la qualité des parties sont « le résultat direct » du travail des annotateurs, sans publier le moindre chiffre pour le prouver.

articles.title: Hände am Lenker, Befehl per Zuruf: Was der neue Garmin-Fahrradcomputer kann
articles.text:
Garmin hat mit dem Edge 1060 einen neuen Fahrradcomputer vorgestellt, der ab sofort für 799,99 Euro erhältlich ist. Anders als der Vorgänger Edge 1050 hat das Gerät ein eingebautes Mikrofon. Damit können Radfahrende das Gerät per Sprache bedienen, ohne die Hände vom Lenker zu nehmen.
Was die Sprachsteuerung des Edge 1060 kann
Der Edge 1060 reagiert auf den Befehl „OK Garmin“. Auf Zuruf lassen sich Nachrichten verschicken – allerdings nur über Garmins eigene Messenger-App auf dem Smartphone. Auch die im Radcomputer integrierte Klingel lässt sich per Sprachbefehl auslösen.
Neu ist außerdem, dass das Gerät mehrere Strecken zu einem Ziel berechnet und dabei persönliche Vorlieben berücksichtigt. Zur Wahl stehen etwa die schnellste Strecke, eine besonders beliebte Route, eine Verbindung mit wenigen Höhenmetern oder eine Strecke mit möglichst wenigen Stopps und Kreuzungen.
Fahrrad-Apps im Vergleich: Welche ist die beste für deine nächste Radtour?
Garmin Edge 1060: Training und Auswertung
Zu jedem Vorschlag zeigt der 142 Gramm schwere Computer Entfernung und voraussichtliche Fahrzeit an. Dazu kommen Hinweise auf Straßensperrungen und Gefahrenstellen, die andere Nutzerinnen und Nutzer gemeldet haben. Wie frühere Edge-Modelle informiert das Gerät über die Funktion „Up Ahead“ über Punkte entlang der Route – etwa Cafés, Rastplätze, Toiletten oder Tankstellen.
Der Edge 1060 unterstützt mehrere Trainingsfunktionen, darunter die Anzeige der verbleibenden Ausdauer in Echtzeit („Stamina“) und die Leistungssteuerung „Power Guide“. Erweiterte GroupRide-Funktionen sollen die Vernetzung mit anderen Radfahrenden verbessern. Dazu kommt der kostenlose Garmin Coach: Er erstellt laut Hersteller personalisierte Trainingspläne, die sich an Leistung, Erholung und die Anforderungen einer Strecke anpassen.
Bezahlen und Powerbank-Funktion
Über Garmin Pay lässt sich unterwegs kontaktlos bezahlen. Der Computer kann zudem andere Geräte aufladen – allerdings nur in der Pause und per Kabel über USB-C. Die Laufzeit gibt Garmin mit bis zu 20 Stunden bei intensiver Nutzung an. Im Batteriesparmodus, der Funktionen reduziert, sollen es bis zu 60 Stunden sein.
Das 3,5 Zoll große LC-Display löst mit 480 × 800 Pixeln auf und ist damit genauso groß wie beim Vorgänger. Dafür hat der neue Computer sieben statt bisher drei Knöpfe. Zum Lieferumfang gehören eine Standard- und eine Aerohalterung, ein Befestigungsband, ein Lade- und Datenkabel sowie eine Schnellstartanleitung. Zusätzlich zum Topmodell hat Garmin zwei weitere Radcomputer vorgestellt: Der Edge Explore 3 und der Edge Explore 3 Plus richten sich an Freizeit- und Tourenfahrer und besitzen jeweils ein 3-Zoll-LC-Touchdisplay.

articles.title: La fin d'une ère : Sony met fin à son dernier lecteur UHD Blu-ray au Japon — Frandroid
articles.text:
Sony Japan a mis fin aux ventes de l’UBP-X700/K, son dernier lecteur UHD Blu-ray autonome. L’information a d’abord été révélée par Kunkoku, un blog japonais qui est également revendeur Sony. D’après ce site, l’arrêt des ventes est effectif au Japon depuis ce jeudi 22 octobre.
La boutique en ligne de Sony Japon confirme cette situation. Elle affiche le produit en rupture de stock, avec la mention précisant qu’aucun réapprovisionnement n’aura lieu. En revanche, aucun communiqué ni aucune confirmation mondiale n’ont été publiés à ce stade, et aucun successeur n’a été annoncé.
Cela va à l’encontre de l’arrivée de la marque Krovatar qui propose une gamme complète de lecteurs Blu-ray.
Commercialisé en mai 2025, le modèle avait remplacé l’UBP-X800M2, retiré du catalogue depuis plus d’un an, qui avait lui même suppléé le UBP-X800. Il reprenait largement la plateforme de l’UBP-X700 lancé en 2018, avec la compatibilité HDR10 et Dolby Vision, mais abandonnait le Wi-Fi et les applications de streaming (seul un port Ethernet subsiste, pour les mises à jour). Le Dolby Atmos et le DTS:X restent pris en charge. Sony retire donc un lecteur dont la base technique date de 2018.
La PlayStation 5, seule alternative chez Sony
Avec cet arrêt, la PlayStation 5 devient le seul produit Sony capable de lire des disques UHD Blu-ray, à condition d’être équipée d’un lecteur (la PS5 Digital Edition et la PS5 Pro, livrées sans, demandent le lecteur amovible vendu à part). Toutefois, il s’agit avant tout d’une console de jeu, et elle ne prend pas en charge le Dolby Vision, contrairement à l’UBP-X700/K. Les cinéphiles qui souhaitent ce format HDR doivent donc se tourner vers d’autres marques.
Sony a aussi annoncé, le 1er juillet dernier, l’arrêt de la production de disques pour tous les nouveaux jeux PlayStation à partir de janvier 2028. Le groupe justifie ce choix par le poids du numérique, qui représentait 78 % des ventes de jeux sur PS4 et PS5 lors de son dernier exercice fiscal. De quoi alimenter l’hypothèse d’une PlayStation 6 sans lecteur optique, que Sony n’a pas confirmée à ce stade.
    Pour aller plus loin
Vers une PS6 à plus de 1000 € ? La RAM et le stockage coûteraient désormais plus que la PS5
            
Sony avait déjà quitté le marché des lecteurs CD et SACD autonomes. En février dernier, le groupe a aussi annoncé la fin de ses enregistreurs Blu-ray. Il continue néanmoins de vendre un lecteur Blu-ray standard, le BDP-S1700/K au Japon, ainsi qu’un lecteur DVD.
Un marché désormais tenu par Panasonic
Après ce départ, Panasonic reste la seule grande marque d’électronique grand public à proposer des lecteurs UHD Blu-ray. Son DP-UB9000, modèle de référence compatible Dolby Vision et HDR10+, occupe un segment nettement plus onéreux que le modèle Sony : il se négocie autour de 1 300 euros en France, contre 349 euros indicatifs pour le lecteur Sony.
    Pour aller plus loin
Dolby Vision, FLAC et multizone : Laser dévoile son premier lecteur 4K UHD, presque parfait sur le papier
            
Samsung et LG ont quitté ce marché avant Sony, LG ayant arrêté la production de ses lecteurs Blu-ray en 2024.
Par ailleurs, plusieurs marques, surtout chinoises, lancent leurs propres lecteurs. Le site spécialisé FlatpanelsHD estime toutefois que ces nouveaux venus ne pèseront pas lourd. Il rappelle que Sony a participé au développement du Blu-ray et soutenu l’UHD Blu-ray, et voit dans son retrait un coup dur pour l’ensemble du disque optique.
Le recul du disque profite au streaming, même si sa qualité d’image et de son reste généralement inférieure à celle d’un UHD Blu-ray. Pour les amateurs de supports physiques, l’offre se résume désormais aux lecteurs Panasonic et à ceux des nouveaux fabricants.
Disponibilité et prix
Au Japon, le lecteur était vendu 58 300 yens TTC (environ 330 euros) sur le Sony Store, où il est désormais affiché en rupture de stock définitive.
En Europe et aux États-Unis, l’arrêt n’est pas encore officiellement annoncé, et des stocks semblent encore disponibles. En France, le lecteur reste référencé sur le site de Sony France à un tarif indicatif de 349 euros, même s’il est signalé en rupture de stock sur la boutique en ligne de la marque. Des revendeurs le proposent encore en France, autour de 300 euros sur Amazon ou à la Fnac. Sony n’ayant annoncé aucun successeur, ces stocks pourraient ne pas être renouvelés une fois écoulés.

articles.title: Barcelona’s Masia closes €18 million debut fund and opens a physical hub for frontier tech founders and investors | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Masia, a Barcelona-based venture capital platform, today announced it has closed its €18 million debut fund to invest in early-stage AI and frontier tech companies with a Barcelona connection.
The fund attracted backing from more than 70 limited partners, including successful technology founders, executives and experienced investors, alongside two institutional investors.
“We launched Masia’s first fund last year because we saw Barcelona’s tech ecosystem was nearing a tipping point, and we wanted to connect successful LPs and international VCs in the city with talent choosing to build and scale global frontier tech businesses from here,” said Carlos Trenchs, co-founder and Chairman at Masia.
Alongside closing its debut fund, the firm also announced the opening of Masia House, a 1,000 m² physical community space in the city’s Gràcia neighbourhood, designed to bring founders, international investors, and operators together under one roof. Spanning four floors, Masia House will serve as a physical gathering point for the firm’s community through workspaces, meeting rooms, accommodation for visiting investors, and terrace events.
“Masia House is the next step in that mission, providing a physical space because we know capital alone doesn’t create innovation. It happens when ambitious people repeatedly encounter other ambitious people,” added Trenchs.
Founded by Trenchs and Pepe Borrell in 2025, Masia operates as a super angel fund investing at the pre-Seed and Seed stages, writing cheques of between €125k and €250k. In May 2025, it announced its launch and its intention to deploy €20 million across sixty pre-Seed and Seed investments, specifically in local and international founders building global technology companies in Barcelona.
The firm says it does not lead rounds or take board seats, instead positioning itself as a founder-first, collaborative platform that connects its portfolio with a broad network of experienced operators and capital.
Since launching last year, Masia says it has deployed capital across 46 companies representing 60 founders, co-investing alongside 60 international and special VC firms, including Common Magic, Nina Capital, Point Nine, and Lunar Ventures. Its portfolio companies have subsequently attracted follow-on investments from major names including a16z, DST Global, Norrsken VC, Y Combinator, and Initialized Capital.
The standout in Masia’s portfolio is Biorce, which applies AI to optimise clinical trials and closed a €43.8 million ($52 million) Series A earlier this year; Prosper, an AI-driven patient journey management platform that raised €26.67 million ($30 million) in a round led by a16z; and Didit, a Y Combinator-backed AI-native identity verification platform.
“We’re already seeing companies we backed last year raise Series A rounds and expand into the US. Our focus is on founders using AI and frontier technology to address significant market opportunities, with international ambition from the outset. We want to support that growth through both investment and access to people who can help them scale,” said Pepe Borrell, Founding Partner at Masia Fund.
The debut fund from Masia comes on the back of startups in Barcelona attracting €1.175 billion in investment in the first nine months of 2026, a 14% increase year-on-year, according to Fundación Bankinter. The city also ranks as the sixth-largest hub for DeepTech startup funding in Europe, having raised €610 million between 2020 and 2024, per data from Accio.
With the fund closing and Masia House opening, the firm has grown to seven, with Gemma Torruella joining to lead operations, bringing over 20 years of experience across Spain’s financial and entrepreneurial sectors. Cathy White, a veteran of the European tech and venture ecosystem with more than 15 years of experience and prior roles at Seedcamp, has joined as a Fractional CMO.

articles.title: AI agent security is a lifecycle — not a gatekeeper
articles.text:
AI agent security is a lifecycle — not a gatekeeper
Enterprise security has traditionally operated on a relatively straightforward premise: establish identity, authenticate the requester, determine what that identity can access, and enforce those permissions.
AI agents introduce a fundamental complication. They don’t simply access systems. They interpret objectives, select tools, create sub-agents, make decisions, and execute actions, often using credentials and permissions inherited from humans.
The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform. And unlike conventional software, agents can change their execution paths dynamically in pursuit of an objective.
“The problem isn’t necessarily that an agent lacks proper credentials. It’s that those credentials may authorize actions the human never intended the agent to perform.”
This creates a new operational requirement: security must evaluate not only who or what is acting, but what an agent is attempting to do, on whose authority, and under which policy. Meeting that requirement takes more than a security checkpoint. It requires a continuous agent security lifecycle.
Defense-in-depth needs action-level authorization
Every passing day further shows that agent security is a defense-in-depth problem. Network security controls how agents communicate. Endpoint and runtime protections constrain where and how code executes. Infrastructure and silicon-based protections establish a foundation for trusted execution. Model guardrails help shape behavior. These layers complement each other, and enterprises need them to work together.
But consider an agent that attempts to delete a production database using a developer’s legitimate credentials. Network controls may see authorized traffic. The runtime may see an approved process. An identity provider may confirm that the credentials are valid. All three could be working as designed.
The missing question is whether this particular agent should be allowed to perform this particular action, even if the human whose credentials it inherited could legitimately do so.
That requires identity context and authorization at the point of action.
In practical terms, an authorization decision should consider the agent’s identity, the human or service that delegated its authority, the requested operation, the target resource, and applicable policy. Enforce that decision before the operation executes.
The agent harness (the execution layer that connects an AI model to tools, application programming interfaces (APIs), files, and external systems) is an important place to apply that control. Other trusted enforcement points, including tool services and resource APIs, provide additional protection.
The goal isn’t to replace existing defenses. It’s to make authorization integral to agent execution. But even that is only a partial answer because what is needed is a new framework — an agent security lifecycle.
Four disciplines, one continuous security lifecycle
A practical agent security architecture needs four interconnected disciplines:
Observe. Enforce. Build. Deploy.
These aren’t sequential gates every organization must pass through. They form a continuous lifecycle, and organizations can enter at whichever point reflects their existing infrastructure and maturity.
A company with agents already running in production may begin by observing their behavior. A development team creating a new agent may start by building authorization directly into its architecture. An enterprise expanding an existing deployment may discover new activity that requires revisiting its policies.
Each stage informs the others. The cycle never really ends.
Observe: Understand what agents actually do
Most enterprises have some form of application inventory. Increasingly, they’re extending that inventory to AI agents.
That’s a useful starting point, but knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does.
Security teams need visibility into the actions agents actually attempt:
- Which tools and APIs are being invoked?
- What commands are being executed?
- Which systems and sensitive resources are being accessed?
- What credentials and delegated permissions are being used?
- What sub-agents are being created, and what authority do they inherit?
- Which actions would violate a proposed security policy?
Architectural diagrams or agent configuration files alone can’t reliably answer these questions. The important evidence exists in execution, which is why agent observability must extend beyond conventional logs and application monitoring. Security teams need to connect observed actions with identity, delegation, and authorization context.
“Knowing an agent exists isn’t the same as understanding what it does. You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed.”
Equally important, observation should support evaluating potential policies without immediately disrupting production activity. There are useful precedents here. When intrusion prevention systems and web application firewalls became widely adopted, organizations learned that immediately enabling aggressive blocking rules could interrupt legitimate applications. Monitoring first, establishing behavioral baselines, and progressively enforcing policies proved more practical.
AI agents require similar discipline, although their behavior can be substantially more dynamic.
For organizations already deploying agents, the priority may not be to block more activity. It may be to understand what activity is actually occurring.
You can’t intelligently govern behavior you haven’t observed.
Enforce: Put deterministic boundaries around probabilistic behavior
Once organizations understand how agents behave, they can begin defining and enforcing boundaries.
The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. An agent might interpret instructions differently across executions. It may choose different tools, sequence operations differently, or discover alternative ways to accomplish an objective.
A security policy cannot depend on the model consistently choosing the safest option. Consider a coding agent with permission to work in a source repository. Reading a file might be permitted. Modifying a protected branch might require human approval. Deleting the repository might be prohibited. All three actions could originate from the same authenticated agent operating in the same environment. But they require different authorization decisions.
“The distinction between probabilistic AI behavior and deterministic security enforcement is critical. The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting. It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent.”
Effective enforcement means evaluating the attempted action against policy before execution. A simplified authorization request might contain:
- Actor: Coding agent 42
- Delegated authority: Developer account 17
- Requested action: Delete repository
- Target: Production source repository
- Policy decision: Deny
The important architectural distinction is that the permission check occurs at a trusted enforcement point, not merely within a prompt instructing the model to behave. For high-risk operations, the system may deny execution or require explicit human approval. Lower-risk operations may proceed automatically.
Enforcement also needs to account for agents attempting alternative execution paths. A harness-level check only protects actions routed through that harness. Robust designs therefore combine action-level authorization with independently enforced permissions at APIs, tool servers, and underlying resources.
The objective is not to make agents incapable of acting.
It’s to make the boundaries of their authority explicit, enforceable, and consistent.
Build: Make identity and authorization part of the agent architecture
Observation and enforcement help organizations secure existing agents. But the greatest long-term benefit comes when those lessons influence how agents are built.
Today, developers may implement AI agents using different models, frameworks, tool protocols, and execution environments. If every team must independently design identity propagation, delegated permissions, authorization policies, and audit logging, security becomes inconsistent and difficult to maintain.
Instead, these capabilities should be available as reusable infrastructure. Software development kits (SDKs), APIs, and shared authorization services can make it easier to incorporate controls directly into agent applications. That means establishing several architectural expectations from the beginning.
An agent should have an identifiable execution context. Its authority should be explicitly delegated and constrained. Sensitive tool invocations should require authorization. Security decisions and consequential actions should be auditable.
Importantly, an agent shouldn’t automatically inherit every permission available to the human initiating it. Consider an employee using an AI assistant to reconcile invoices. The employee may have permission to review invoices, approve payments, and update vendor records. The agent’s assigned task requires only invoice retrieval and reconciliation. The correct architecture delegates the permissions required for that task, not the employee’s entire authority.
That distinction matters even more when an agent creates sub-agents or invokes tools under different service identities. Developers need mechanisms to preserve and constrain delegated authority throughout those interactions.
Security should also be portable across implementations. Organizations shouldn’t have to reconstruct their authorization architecture every time a development team adopts a new framework or model. This is why identity and authorization should be infrastructure, not application-specific features.
Done correctly, security becomes something developers build with, rather than something security teams attempt to bolt on after an application is complete.
Deploy: Make consistent security possible at machine scale
Building a secure agent is one challenge. Operating thousands of agents across applications, departments, cloud environments, and business processes is another. At that scale, manually reviewing permissions or trusting individual development teams to implement controls consistently becomes unsustainable.
Agents may invoke new tools, coordinate with other agents, and participate in workflows that span multiple authorization domains. Security controls need to follow them. That requires a deployment architecture that consistently applies identity context, delegated authority, authorization policy, and audit requirements across supported environments.
The underlying model or framework shouldn’t determine whether security controls exist. Nor should adopting a new tool require rebuilding the entire security architecture. This is where framework-independent interfaces and centrally managed policy become especially valuable. Organizations can maintain consistent security expectations while allowing development teams to use the technologies best suited to their applications.
Deployment also changes the meaning of scale. With traditional applications, scale generally means handling more users, transactions, or workloads. With agents, scale can also mean more independent actors making more decisions, invoking more tools, and creating additional agents. The number of consequential actions can increase much faster than the number of deployed applications. Security architectures must therefore operate automatically and consistently at the pace of machine-generated activity.
Deployment creates something else: new evidence. Production activity reveals unexpected workflows, new dependencies, authorization gaps, and opportunities to refine policy. That information feeds directly back into observation and enforcement and informs how the next generation of agents is built.
The lifecycle continues.
The shift from security as a checkpoint to security as infrastructure
The underlying security principles aren’t new. Least privilege, zero trust, separation of duties, identity federation, and defense in depth remain foundational.
What’s changing is how consistently those principles must be applied throughout an agent’s lifecycle, and how close enforcement must be to the actions agents take. Traditional security architectures often assume that controlling system access is enough to govern what happens afterward.
AI agents challenge that assumption because they can make consequential decisions independently within the access they’ve already been granted. As a result, the security model needs to evolve in three important ways.
First, visibility must be based on actual agent behavior rather than configuration alone.
Second, authorization must evaluate individual actions in the context of identity, delegation, and policy.
Third, these capabilities must become reusable infrastructure that accompanies agents from development through production and back into continuous improvement.
This is why treating agent security as a lifecycle, rather than a collection of isolated controls, matters. Observation supplies evidence. Enforcement establishes boundaries. Development incorporates those boundaries into applications. Deployment extends them consistently across environments and feeds new evidence into the cycle.
Each stage makes the others more effective.
Securing the agentic era without slowing it down
Organizations face two tempting extremes. One is to trust agents too broadly, assuming that legitimate credentials and well-written instructions provide sufficient protection. The other is to constrain agents so aggressively that the productivity gains motivating their adoption disappear. Neither is a sustainable long-term strategy.
“Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable.”
A better approach is to establish the visibility, accountability, and controls that make greater autonomy possible. That means knowing what agents actually do, enforcing what they’re permitted to do, building those controls into the development process, and deploying them consistently at scale. It also means recognizing that the work is never finished. New models, frameworks, tools, and workflows will continuously introduce new behaviors and risks.
Agent security cannot be a one-time approval at the beginning of a deployment. It must be a continuous discipline that evolves with the agents themselves. Success isn’t measured by how many agent actions an organization can block. It’s how many valuable actions it can confidently (and safely) enable.
It takes a continuous lifecycle, not a gatekeeper.

articles.title: Volkswagen prépare une citadine électrique de segment A pour 2027
articles.text:
Volkswagen est sur une bonne lancée
Alors que la situation économique de Volkswagen semblait délicate, avec le besoin de revoir son organisation salariale en réduisant le nombre d’employés, le bon démarrage de sa citadine électrique ID. Polo donne une bouffée d’air à Volkswagen. En effet, le constructeur a déjà enregistré plus de 12 000 commandes en France, soit plus du double des meilleures projections de Volkswagen. Évidemment, les délais de livraison s’allongent et constituent le nouveau défi de Volkswagen pour la fin de l’année 2026 et le début de 2027.
Mais alors que Volkswagen pourrait se contenter de ce succès, qui est amplifié par la réussite commerciale des cousines Cupra Raval, Skoda Epiq et Volkswagen ID. Cross, la marque allemande travaille sur une autre citadine électrique plus compacte, qui pourrait concurrencer la Renault Twingo électrique.
Une citadine électrique de segment A prochainement chez Volkswagen
Pour l’année 2027, Volkswagen va lancer une citadine de segment A s’appuyant sur le concept ID.Every 1 déjà présenté. Il s’agira d’une citadine électrique d’environ 3,70 m, au style proche de celui de l’ID. Polo. On ne connaît pas encore son nom, mais il serait logique que Volkswagen utilise la nouvelle nomenclature de ses modèles électriques. On peut alors imaginer une ID. Fox, ID. Lupo ou ID. Up, faisant référence aux anciennes citadines de segment A de Volkswagen.
Concernant la plateforme technique, elle pourrait reprendre celle de l’ID. Polo, la plateforme MEB+, avec un empattement raccourci. Ce qui est techniquement rendu possible par l’aspect modulaire de cette nouvelle plateforme, qui sert aussi des modèles bien plus grands, comme le Volkswagen ID. Tiguan ou le Skoda Peaq. Dans le cas de la citadine de segment A, la batterie pourrait être la LFP de 37 kWh utilisée dans les versions de l’ID. Polo de 116 ou 135 chevaux, soit les versions d’entrée de gamme, qui offrent déjà environ 313 km d’autonomie. Dans le cas d’une citadine électrique de 3,70 m, l’autonomie pourrait être légèrement plus généreuse, avec, imaginons, 350 km en cycle mixte WLTP, ce qui représenterait 80 km d’autonomie de plus que la Renault Twingo, qui sera sa plus grande rivale.
Bien évidemment, il est encore très tôt pour parler de prix. Mais si la Volkswagen ID. Polo, sur le segment B, débute à moins de 25 000 euros, cette citadine de segment A pourrait débuter à moins de 20 000 euros.

articles.title: Amazon lanza gafas inteligentes para conductores
articles.text:
Las gafas inteligentes de Amazon ayudarán a sus repartidores a encontrar los paquetes y llevarlos hasta la puerta del cliente. Además, podrán tomar miles de fotografías de personas y propiedades durante una jornada laboral. La segunda función está llamando la atención, ya que se basa en unas declaraciones de Viraj Chatterjee, el responsable de Amazon del proyecto.
El anuncio inicial sobre los dispositivos se produjo el 22 de octubre de 2025. La expansión prevista sí corresponde a 2026: Amazon anuncia 5.000 dispositivos adicionales, con el objetivo de superar los 20.000 para finales de 2027. Se trata de planes futuros, así que esas cifras no representan a repartidores que ya hayan recibido las gafas.
Las capturas descritas por la información que ha vuelto a llamar la atención se producirían mientras el repartidor camina. Se habla de fotografías probablemente cada pocos segundos, para que personas las revisen y después se incorporen a Wellspring, el sistema de inteligencia artificial (IA) de Amazon para sus mapas de navegación de reparto. La empresa “se encamina sin darse cuenta hacia otra polémica por invasión de la privacidad”, afirmó el columnista de tecnología Dave Lee.
Amazon se ha defendido de este coro de críticas. “La idea de que Amazon utilice gafas inteligentes de reparto como una forma de vigilancia distorsiona la tecnología y su propósito”, declaró la portavoz Leigh Anne Gullett. La empresa afirma que busca reducir los errores y agilizar las entregas con instrucciones que puedan seguirse con las manos libres. Incluso afirma que el programa es voluntario para las empresas asociadas y sus trabajadores.
Las protecciones que anuncia la propia Amazon incluyen difuminar información identificativa, limitar el acceso y disponer de un interruptor físico de privacidad. Amazon ha dicho que los rostros y las matrículas de los vehículos serían difuminados antes de su revisión por un ser humano.
Otros problemas residen en cómo Amazon podría añadir la toma de fotografías de la ruta a pie al seguimiento que ya existe dentro del vehículo. Según se dice, los repartidores afirman que la empresa prefiere destinar el dinero a sus sistemas automatizados en lugar de aumentar los salarios o conceder pausas para ir al baño.
Qué cambia durante una entrega
La descripción general del dispositivo explica cómo se supone que las gafas ayudarán al repartidor mientras está en el sitio de entrega.
Cuando el conductor ha aparcado de forma segura, el dispositivo le indicará dónde está el paquete dentro del vehículo y proporcionará instrucciones para caminar hasta la puerta. Las gafas permiten registrar la entrega y mostrarán un aviso si se ha dejado el paquete en la puerta incorrecta.
Si los datos de entrega indican que podría haber una mascota, se emitirá una alerta sonora y se mostrará un icono de huella. Amazon afirma que más de 500 repartidores han probado las gafas durante 18 meses, con más de 275.000 entregas realizadas.
El repartidor llevará un controlador en el chaleco con batería intercambiable y un botón de emergencia. Las gafas admiten lentes graduadas y fotocromáticas, que se ajustan a la luz. Estas son pruebas operativas, aunque la empresa no muestra en esa página una medición del tiempo ahorrado por entrega ni ofrece una comparación que permita cuantificar la mejora de seguridad.
Wellspring ya incluía datos del entorno en su proceso previo. Amazon describe un sistema que combina imágenes de satélite y de la calle, instrucciones de clientes y datos de entregas anteriores para mejorar la ubicación del reparto. El software ya asocia cada apartamento con el edificio que lo contiene, localiza los lugares de entrada o la sala de paquetes e identifica áreas donde el repartidor puede dejar los paquetes. Además, usa fotos tomadas en entregas anteriores para identificar dónde está la entrada o la sala de paquetes.
Las pruebas fotográficas pueden utilizarse para otra cosa además de justificar las entregas: preparar las futuras visitas al mismo lugar. En la actualización de su programa, la empresa afirma que desde 2024 ha identificado 202 millones de ubicaciones de aparcamiento y cartografiado 2,8 millones de entradas de edificios. Son cifras que Amazon atribuye a Wellspring en conjunto y que no demuestran por sí solas una mejora de eficiencia.
El debate laboral ya estaba presente cuando las gafas se anunciaron por primera vez en octubre de 2025. En ese momento, Xataka se ocupó de las gafas y de las posibilidades de supervisión de los trabajadores. El aumento de la escala de despliegue amplía el debate, mientras siguen sin concretarse los plazos de conservación de las fotos. La información oficial consultada tampoco establece una fecha para su implementación en España.
Europa pide que la captura sea perceptible
Según una declaración del Comité Europeo de Protección de Datos, adoptada el 13 de octubre de 2026, los dispositivos que capturan imágenes o audio deberían proporcionar avisos que las personas cercanas puedan percibir y que no sean fáciles de desactivar. En segundo lugar, el documento recomienda limitar la captura continua y el período durante el cual se almacenan los datos, y difuminar o evitar tratar la identidad de terceros, preferiblemente en el propio dispositivo cuando sea posible.
El tratamiento de datos personales exige que exista una base jurídica válida. El Reglamento General de Protección de Datos (RGPD) recoge en su artículo 6 las condiciones que pueden permitir ese tratamiento. Sin embargo, el tratamiento realizado por una persona física exclusivamente con fines personales o domésticos está excluido de su ámbito de aplicación, según el artículo 2.2.c.
Cuando se recurre al interés legítimo del artículo 6.1.f, debe evaluarse cada caso y comprobarse que no prevalecen los intereses o los derechos y libertades fundamentales de las personas afectadas. Además, el Comité advierte de dificultades para justificar usos posteriores que estas personas no esperarían.
Esas son recomendaciones generales incluidas en el documento; no determinan si el uso de las gafas de Amazon es ilegal ni prohíben su uso. Lo que establece es que los fabricantes y proveedores que sean responsables del tratamiento deben cumplir sus propias obligaciones, sin trasladarlas a quien lleva las gafas. Anu Talus, la presidenta del Comité, explica en su comunicación pública sobre las gafas que la captura debe ser perceptible incluso en lugares públicos. Quienes aparezcan en las imágenes deben poder reconocer que se están captando y conocer para qué se utilizan sus datos.

South Africa is rethinking its proposed cross-border crypto rules
South Africa wanted to bring cross-border crypto transfers under the same controls it uses to monitor money leaving the country. The draft rules would have required people moving crypto offshore to use authorised crypto service providers, stay within existing foreign exchange (FX) allowances, and have those transactions reported to the South African Reserve Bank (SARB). Companies would not initially have been allowed to move crypto offshore.
But the government is rethinking it. On Wednesday, Finance Minister Enoch Godongwana said the National Treasury had received “thousands of comments” on the proposals and would take a different approach. Instead of relying on pre-approvals, the government now wants to focus on whether transactions are legitimate and comply with tax rules. A revised draft will be published for another round of public input.
Between the lines: The rethink follows months of organised pushback from South Africa’s crypto industry. In September, VALR, Luno, AltCoinTrader, and EasyEquities formed a coalition called ‘Catastrophe’ to oppose rules they said treated crypto payments more harshly than equivalent bank transfers. Their biggest objection was that it would shut out exchanges from using crypto, including stablecoins, for cross-border payments that would otherwise be legal through the banking system. GoTyme Bank, part of Tyme Group, which was valued at $1.5 billion in 2024, joined the coalition later that month. The industry argued that regulation should govern the transaction and its risks, rather than discriminate according to the technology used to move the money.
Explain like I’m new here: South Africa already limits how much money individuals and companies can move out of the country. For individuals, the limit is R2 million ($122,280) per calendar year under the single discretionary allowance, with another R10 million ($611,360) available under the foreign capital allowance if they obtain tax approval. Larger transfers require additional approvals.
The government wanted to bring crypto transfers under its FX control system, partly because stablecoins and other digital assets can move across borders without passing through the traditional banking system. The draft rules would have brought crypto providers into that control system and barred businesses from using them for certain cross-border payments.
What will happen next? Godongwana said the government wants to move away from pre-approvals and instead assess transactions for legitimacy and tax compliance, while taking guidance from the Financial Stability Board. Treasury and SARB have not yet published the revised approach, so the details are still to come. Consultations on a revised draft are expected, giving crypto companies another chance to weigh in before the rules return.

Kenyan investors buy KCB as foreigners cash out
Foreign investors are cutting their stakes in KCB Group, one of East Africa’s largest banking groups. Kenyan investors are buying almost exactly what they are leaving behind.
What happened? Foreign shareholders sold 23.6 million KCB Group shares in the three months to September, cutting their stake in Kenya’s largest bank by assets from about 8.8% to 8.02%. At Wednesday’s opening price, the shares were worth about KES 2.1 billion ($16.2 million). Local investors added nearly the same number.
Most of the buying came from Kenyan institutions, whose ownership rose to 47.33%. Individual investors also increased their holdings slightly to 24.87%. The Kenyan government separately owns 19.76% of KCB.
Explain like I’m new here: This does not necessarily mean foreign investors have suddenly lost faith in KCB. Its share price has risen more than 30% over the past six months and traded as high as KES 99.25 ($0.76), allowing early investors to cash in. KCB has produced strong numbers: profit before tax rose 20.8% in the first half of 2026, while its interim dividend jumped 50% to KES 3 ($0.023) per share.
Between the lines: The more interesting part is who could absorb the selling. Kenyan pension funds, institutions, and retail investors bought KES 2.1 billion ($16.2 million) worth of shares, so foreigners no longer had to be the marginal buyer. After years of worrying about foreign capital leaving, domestic money is becoming capable of owning more of its biggest companies.
KCB makes the longer trend particularly clear. Foreign investors owned 29.25% of the bank at the end of 2017. Their stake was 8.88% at the end of March.
Zoom out: Foreigners have also been taking profits across other large Nairobi-listed companies this year. The question for the Nairobi Securities Exchange (NSE) is no longer whether foreign money returns. It is how much of the market local capital can carry if foreign participation declines.
Ten years of telling African tech stories.
Class of 2016, stand up! Meet the storytellers behind a decade of storytelling for African tech. 230+ startups, VCs, and more. From first cheques to unicorns. Have a story to tell? Let’s make it count. #TheWimbarts
ride-hailing
Bolt takes its EV push to Johannesburg
Electric vehicles (EVs) are having a busy week in Africa. Yesterday, Spiro, Africa’s most-funded e-mobility company, launched its first 100 bikes in Accra, Ghana. Now, Bolt is giving South Africa’s EV market another push from the commercial transport sector.
What happened? Bolt, the ride-hailing giant operating in over 50 countries, has launched its Electric Vehicle category in Johannesburg. The category is for electric cars available for rides through the Bolt app. For the Johannesburg rollout, Bolt is working with the South African Meter Taxi and E-Hailing Association (SAMTEA), an affiliate of the South African National Taxi Council (SANTACO), and Chinese EV maker BYD. SAMTEA will own and manage the EV fleet operating on Bolt’s platform. Bolt targets 500 EVs across South Africa by December 2026.
Explain like I’m new here: Bolt first launched the EV category in Cape Town, South Africa, in May, partnering with fleet manager YugoRide to deploy electric cars. South Africa isn’t Bolt’s first electric experiment either. In Kenya, Bolt said in February that 5,808 EVs were operating on its platform—about 23% of the country’s estimated EV fleet—at the time. In Nigeria, it has also experimented with electric mobility, including a three-wheeler pilot in Lagos in 2025.
What does this mean for ride-hailing? The immediate question for riders is whether choosing an electric car will cost more. Bolt has not said that its EV category will carry a premium over its other ride categories, so there is no basis yet to say that an electric Bolt will be cheaper or more expensive for passengers. For drivers, an EV could cost less to run because it does not need petrol and generally has fewer components that require regular maintenance.
Bolt is entering a growing South African EV market; the country recorded 16,716 new-energy vehicle sales in 2025. With SAMTEA managing the fleet and BYD supplying EV expertise, Bolt believes electric cars can move beyond a niche option and become a practical part of South Africa’s everyday ride-hailing market.
Don’t miss Moonshot 2026 for anything in the world!
True scale demands moving beyond surface-level integrations to robust execution. We’ve filtered the noise out of Moonshot 2026, optimising the conference strictly for high-calibre connections between startup founders, global financial operators, enterprise leaders and individuals rewiring Africa’s technical frameworks. Join us on October 28 & 29, 2026. Get your ticket.
streaming
Disney is using Netflix to sell Disney+ originals
Disney, the media giant, spent years pulling its films and shows off rival platforms to make Disney+, its owned streaming platform, more valuable. Now, it is reversing that exclusive strategy and putting some of those titles back on Netflix.
What happened? Disney has started licencing selected titles to Netflix in South Africa and other markets. All five Ice Age films and the first two seasons of Percy Jackson and the Olympians went live on Netflix on October 4, each with a three-month promotional window. The timing is deliberate:Percy Jackson season three premieres on Disney+ on November 20, while a new Ice Age film lands in cinemas in February 2027. The company said more titles are coming, including Will Trent, Tracker, Soul, Elio, and Raya and the Last Dragon.
Explain like I’m new here: When Disney launched Disney+ in 2019, it pulled much of its content away from Netflix and other platforms because exclusivity was part of the sales pitch. If viewers wanted Disney shows, they had to subscribe to Disney. But older films and earlier seasons eventually become less useful at attracting new subscribers.
Licencing them changes the maths. Disney can earn money from Netflix for content it has already paid to produce, while using Netflix’s much larger audience to introduce people to franchises whose newest instalments still sit on Disney+ or in cinemas. Disney+ currently has about 131.6 million global subscribers, according to Statista, compared to Netflix’s 325 million. In South Africa, the gap is wider; Netflix has 1.3 million subscribers, while Disney+ records just over 118,000.
Between the lines: Disney is not giving Netflix the crown jewels. The newer releases stay on its own platforms. Netflix gets enough of the back catalogue to create interest, while Disney keeps the part most likely to convert that interest into subscriptions or cinema tickets.
South Africa makes the strategy especially interesting. In May, Disney+ raised its Premium price from R159 ($1.22) to R179 ($1.38) monthly, while Showmax shut down in April. Disney has fewer local streaming rivals, but it still has to convince people that another monthly subscription is worth paying for.
Zoom out: The streaming wars are becoming less about locking every title behind one wall. A library only creates value if people watch it. Disney has realised that, sometimes, the best place to advertise Disney+ is Netflix.

articles.title: iPhone Duo : nous avons mesuré ses reflets, et Samsung comme Xiaomi ont de quoi trembler
articles.text:
iPhone Duo : nous avons mesuré ses reflets, et Samsung comme Xiaomi ont de quoi trembler
Test labo // Apple promet un écran pliant moins réfléchissant, avec une pliure presque invisible. Nous l’avons confronté à ses principaux rivaux, ainsi qu’à un invité surprise.
Un grand écran qui se déplie comme un passeport, c’est pratique pour lire ou regarder une vidéo. Sauf quand il reflète davantage votre environnement que le contenu affiché. Avec l’iPhone Duo, Apple entend corriger ce défaut tout en dissimulant la fameuse pliure centrale. Nous avons voulu vérifier ses promesses en labo.
Apple iPhone Duo
Trois angles, quatre smartphones et un résultat qui décoiffe
Pour départager les concurrents, nous avons sorti notre glossmeter. Cet appareil éclaire les écrans et mesure la lumière qu’ils réfléchissent sous trois angles (20°, 60° et 85°). Nous calculons ensuite une moyenne, avec un miroir comme référence à 100 %. Plus le pourcentage est faible, moins les reflets directs sont importants.
Et les résultats parlent d’eux-mêmes. L'écran interne du nouvel iPhone Duo affiche seulement 6,34 % de réflectance, contre 20,77 % pour le Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 et 27,96 % pour le Xiaomi 18 Fold. Malgré leurs propres traitements antireflets, les deux modèles Android sont largement distancés. L’écran du premier pliant d’Apple renvoie ainsi plus de trois fois moins de lumière que celui de Samsung dans les conditions de notre test.
Plus surprenant encore, le nouveau venu détrône notre précédent champion, le TCL P80 Ultra, dont l’écran Amoled NxtPaper avait atteint l’excellent score de 8,29 %. Une performance remarquable face à un smartphone spécialement conçu pour limiter les reflets.
Apple a trouvé une astuce pour faire oublier la pliure
Le secret se cache dans la finition nanotexturée de l’écran Oled de 7,6 pouces de l’iPhone Duo. Sa surface mate comporte de minuscules reliefs qui dispersent la lumière plutôt que de produire des reflets bien nets. Ce traitement présente un second avantage : il atténue considérablement la visibilité de la pliure centrale.
Apple accompagne cette technologie d'un assemblage de plus de dix couches ultrafines, d'adhésifs flexibles et d'un renfort en titane. L'objectif est de mieux répartir les contraintes lors du pliage. Face aux écrans de 7,6 pouces du Galaxy Z Fold 8 et de 7,58 pouces du Xiaomi 18 Fold, le résultat nous a particulièrement impressionnés à l'œil nu.
TCL utilise une approche différente, avec une nanogravure sous son verre Nano Crystal Shield. Sa technologie NxtPaper, désormais associée à l'Amoled, ajoute des modes de lecture Papier et Max Ink ainsi qu'une réduction matérielle de la lumière bleue, tout en conservant les noirs profonds de l'Oled.
Attention toutefois à ne pas tirer de conclusions trop hâtives. Notre appareil ne mesure ni la profondeur réelle de la pliure ni la lisibilité complète en plein soleil, qui dépend également de la luminosité. Et l'usage répété pourrait accentuer la marque centrale avec le temps. Reste qu'avec ses reflets remarquablement contenus et sa pliure visuellement discrète, Apple réussit un véritable coup de maître pour son premier modèle pliant.

articles.title: Investigan a un grupo vinculado con México que usó Claude y Grok para atacar bancos de América Latina
articles.text:
Una investigación de la firma Straiker identificó a CyberCartel, un grupo que habría utilizado modelos de IA como Claude y Grok para coordinar ataques contra más de 400 objetivos financieros en Latinoamérica, con indicios de operaciones vinculadas a México.
El reporte, publicado el 21 de octubre de 2026, describe un sistema denominado CARLIY0S, que habría integrado distintos modelos de inteligencia artificial como parte de una infraestructura de ciberdelincuencia.
La investigación también identifica a Kimi, desarrollado por la empresa china Moonshot AI, entre los modelos que presuntamente formaron parte de esta estructura. Straiker también sostiene que la operación estaba relacionada con un grupo conocido como Tr4nsHack Team y una presunta fachada denominada Hexagon Security Labs Mexico.
CyberCartel y los presuntos ataques contra bancos latinoamericanos
Según Straiker, el grupo CyberCartel habría dirigido sus actividades contra organizaciones financieras de distintos países de América Latina. Entre los objetivos mencionados figuran bancos, proveedores de servicios de pago y otras empresas del sector.
La investigación sostiene que la operación buscaba acceder a información financiera y credenciales sensibles.
Una base de datos contenía miles de registros financieros
Uno de los principales hallazgos descritos por Straiker fue una base de datos denominada FinancialSoft, que los investigadores habrían localizado el 24 de septiembre de 2026.
Según el informe, el repositorio contenía 4.493 registros con información que incluía credenciales, contraseñas, claves de acceso y otros datos sensibles. Entre los elementos contabilizados figuraban 2.911 direcciones de correo electrónico y 903 números de cuenta.
El reporte también menciona información relacionada con SPEI, el Sistema de Pagos Electrónicos Interbancarios de México, utilizado para realizar transferencias entre instituciones financieras. La posible exposición de estos datos representa un riesgo, ya que las credenciales comprometidas pueden facilitar accesos no autorizados y fraudes.
Straiker no publicó los nombres de los bancos involucrados, por lo que no es posible determinar qué instituciones mexicanas o de otros países de la región habrían resultado afectadas.
Qué modelos de inteligencia artificial aparecen en el informe
El reporte identifica tres modelos de IA que habrían formado parte de la infraestructura atribuida al grupo: Claude, desarrollado por Anthropic; Grok, de xAI; y Kimi, de Moonshot AI.
La investigación describe CARLIY0S como un sistema que integraba distintos modelos en una estructura coordinada. El caso plantea interrogantes sobre los riesgos de que herramientas de inteligencia artificial comercial sean utilizadas en actividades delictivas.
Straiker afirma que notificó a los proveedores involucrados. Según la compañía, Anthropic revocó una credencial comprometida relacionada con el acceso a Claude, mientras que xAI fue informada y examinaba la actividad reportada.
Una alerta para la seguridad financiera de la región
El caso pone de relieve los desafíos que afrontan los bancos latinoamericanos frente a amenazas que incorporan herramientas de inteligencia artificial. La posible exposición de credenciales y datos financieros puede comprometer tanto a las instituciones como a sus clientes.
Sin embargo, las acusaciones contra los responsables y la magnitud de los daños requieren corroboración independiente. El informe de Straiker aporta indicios sobre una presunta operación, pero no permite confirmar públicamente la responsabilidad de cada involucrado ni el impacto concreto en las entidades señaladas.
La investigación refuerza la importancia de proteger las credenciales, supervisar accesos sospechosos y responder rápidamente ante incidentes de ciberseguridad.

articles.title: iPhone 17 (512 GB) de última geração entra em promoção na Amazon • Tecnoblog
articles.text:
iPhone 17 (512 GB) de última geração entra em promoção na Amazon
iPhone 17 (512 GB) traz chip A19 de ponta, câmeras de 48 MP e tela OLED de 120 Hz; celular da Apple sai 36% mais em conta em oferta no Pix
O iPhone 17 de 512 GB sai por R$ 6.282 no Pix na Amazon. O smartphone da Apple com chip A19, tela OLED e câmeras de 48 MP recebe desconto de 36% sobre o preço base de R$ 9.799. Apesar do reajuste recente nos valores (deixando o iPhone 17 mais caro), esta oferta ainda compete facilmente com os menores preços anteriores.
O iPhone 17 é uma interessante opção de custo-benefício, em parte devido ao chip Apple A19 e aos 8 GB de RAM, que dão conta de apps em multitarefa, games e soluções do Apple Intelligence localmente. Para quem adora fotografar e filmar, os 512 GB de armazenamento disponibilizam espaço interno de sobra.
Falando nisso, o kit principal de câmeras conta com uma wide com OIS e uma ultrawide com ângulo de 120º, que captam belas cenas em ambientes abertos, ambas de 48 MP. A frontal de 18 MP tira ótimas selfies na horizontal, mesmo segurando o celular em pé. Todas filmam em 4K a 60 fps.
Sua tela OLED de 6,3″ tem ProMotion de 120 Hz e brilho máximo de 3.000 nits, combinação que a permite reproduzir imagens com cores excelentes e alta fluidez nas transições em apps e games, além de garantir a visibilidade em qualquer lugar.
O corpo de alumínio do iPhone 17 é revestido de ambos os lados pelo vidro Ceramic Shield 2, resistente a arranhões e pancadas. A certificação IP68 adiciona proteção em cenários como ambientes empoeirados e mergulhos acidentais.
Sua bateria de 3.692 mAh tem autonomia de até 30 horas de vídeo, segundo a fabricante. O suporte a MagSafe e carregamento rápido de 40 W o permitem receber uma carga de 50% em apenas 20 minutos, ideal para quem não tem tempo a perder com tomadas.
O iPhone 17 de 512 GB (R$ 6.282 no Pix) foi atualizado para o iOS 27 e receberá pelo menos mais cinco updates do sistema operacional. O celular da Apple possui conectividade 5G, Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6.0, Ultra Wideband (UWB), NFC e comporta eSIM.
Aviso de ética: ao clicar em um link de afiliado, o preço não muda para você e recebemos uma comissão.

articles.title: Cloud Deployment Incoming: ‘Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4’ Arrives on GeForce NOW
articles.text:
Lock in and load out this GFN Thursday. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 arrives on GeForce NOW at launch, bringing a new campaign, multiplayer action and DMZ, high-stakes extraction mode to supported devices. The campaign also gets an enhanced look: GeForce RTX 5080-class performance arrives for Ultimate members, bringing support for ray-tracing features in the cloud.
There’s a new way to join the cloud, too: Existing supported Fire TV Stick users can now purchase one-month Performance or Ultimate memberships directly through Amazon, making it easier to sign up and start streaming on the big screen.
Plus, Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE brings cinematic pixel art and strategic battles to the cloud, and The Elder Scrolls Online’s Echoes of Skyrim Season adds the entire Greymoor Chapter free for all ESO Standard Edition owners.
It’s all part of six games joining the GeForce NOW library this week.
Deployment Without the Downloads
Squad up and answer the call on the cloud.
Activision and Infinity Ward’s Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 launches today on GeForce NOW. Members can drop into the trenches in Korea, close-quarter combat in New York, high-octane chases through Paris, night raids in Mumbai and city-wide engagements to reclaim occupied territory.
Fight as Private Park, a young South Korean soldier facing live combat for the first time alongside his squad as a routine patrol turns into a desperate fight for survival. Beyond the front lines, operator-turned-outlaw Captain Price is operating outside the system he once served, pursuing revenge through covert missions as the conflict spreads.
Multiplayer pairs precise combat with fluid movement, a dozen core 6v6 maps from around the world and battlegrounds that are shaped by the campaign’s global conflict. The DMZ extraction mode sends players into contested territory to recover valuable technology, weigh objectives and decide when to get out. Loot, fight, negotiate, betray and extract — it’s all fair in the cloud and battleground.
Ultimate members can now experience the campaign with ray tracing, powered by newly added GeForce RTX 5080-class performance across PCs, Macs, handhelds, mobile devices, browsers, supported TVs and more. With game downloads and installs handled by GeForce NOW, members can spend less time preparing a local rig and more time preparing the next loadout.
A New Way to Play
GeForce NOW in-app purchase is rolling out to existing supported Fire TV Stick users, making it possible to purchase a membership directly through Amazon using an existing account. Transactions are processed through Amazon’s billing system, creating a more seamless path from setup to gameplay.
GeForce NOW transforms Fire TV into a powerful PC gaming rig in the cloud. Members can stream supported PC games they already own or purchase new titles from digital stores including Steam, Epic Games Store, Ubisoft Connect, Xbox PC Game Pass, GOG and EA.
The library includes thousands of ready-to-play games, including many of the world’s most-played titles and more than 100 free-to-play games. No downloads, installs, patches or updates stand between a new game and playtime. An Amazon Fire TV Stick, the GeForce NOW app and an Ultimate membership are all it takes to level up the living room with GeForce RTX 5080-powered gaming.
A Pixel-Perfect Fantasy
Classic roots. A new adventure.
Square Enix’s FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE launches today on GeForce NOW, bringing the series’ classic roots into a cinematic pixel-art world.
Travel with companions bound by fate and uncover the truth behind a force threatening to bring everything to ruin. Strengthen the party with Visions of beloved FINAL FANTASY characters, each bringing unique skills and abilities to battle. Dynamic camera angles and pixelized 3D models give familiar fantasy a fresh perspective.
Exploit enemy weaknesses to stagger foes, break their defenses and seize extra turns before finishing the bonus phase with powerful Resonance attacks. Airships, crystals, espers and moogles bring familiar series favorites to a world filled with secrets to discover.
GeForce NOW handles the game’s downloads and storage in the cloud, leaving more space on supported devices for everyday essentials. Save the inventory management for potions and Phoenix Downs.
Step Into a New Season in Tamriel
Familiar lands. Fresh reasons to return.
The Elder Scrolls Online’s second season, Echoes of Skyrim, launched Wednesday, Oct. 21, free for all ESO players and ready to stream through GeForce NOW.
Season Two gives everyone who owns ESO Standard Edition access to its Skyrim content and the Antiquities treasure-hunting system. The Markarth downloadable content follows Monday, Nov. 9, rounding out the additions with two classic zones to explore.
The Season also introduces Solo Dungeons, reimagining challenges previously designed for groups. Moon Hunter Keep and March of Sacrifices have been redesigned and rebalanced for players ready to tackle their dangers alone. Earn new rewards and take on new challenges at your own pace without needing to find a group.
A new Tamriel Tome also launched Oct. 21, offering both free and premium battle pass reward tracks.
In addition, members can look for the following titles joining the GeForce NOW library this week:
- We Were Here Tomorrow (New release on Steam, Oct. 20)
- FINAL FANTASY RESONANCE (New release on Steam, Oct. 22)
- Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 (New release on Oct 23, available in the Call of Duty app)
- CONTROL Resonant (Epic Game Store)
- Crimson Desert (Epic Games Store)
- Planet Zoo 2 (Xbox app, supports XBOX Play Anywhere)
Dates listed above reflect when games are released on their respective stores. GeForce NOW availability may vary, as games are onboarded after release and added throughout the week. Keep an eye on GeForce NOW channels and GFN Thursdays for availability updates on announced titles.
Gamers who want to test out high-performance GeForce NOW cloud gaming can start with a day pass to try premium cloud gaming before committing to a membership. Better yet, the cost of the day pass can be applied toward a first monthly membership — making it easy to try GeForce RTX-powered cloud gaming with the latest releases, then level up for more.
