articles.title: Ameli et la CAF sont en panne, il est impossible de se connecter à son compte, la catastrophe continue
articles.text:
Depuis mercredi soir, la connexion au compte Ameli est très compliquée, voire impossible pour de nombreux assurés, sur le site comme sur l’application. L’Assurance maladie fait état d'une maintenance programmée, sans doute liée aux correctifs des failles PHP. La CAF est aussi touchée.
La connexion au compte Ameli fait de la résistance depuis mercredi soir, et la panne, le problème n'est toujours pas réglé ce jeudi matin, bien au contraire, tout comme du côté de la Caisse nationale des allocations familiales, la CAF. Des centaines de signalements font encore état partout en France d'un accès impossible à l'espace personnel, et donc aux remboursements ou aux droits de chacun, que ce soit sur le site de l'Assurance maladie ou sur son application mobile. Le calendrier nous rappelle en tout cas la journée plus qu'agitée qu'a vécue le Web mercredi, sans parler de l'interminable panne ayant frappé Orange.
Compte Ameli, la connexion est bloquée depuis mercredi soir
Les premiers signalements évoquant l'impossibilité d'accéder à son espace santé sur le site de l'Assurance maladie ou à son compte CAF sont apparus mercredi vers 21 heures sur Downdetector pour le premier cité, avant d'atteindre leur maximum aux alentours de 22 h 30, sans jamais retomber à zéro pendant la nuit. Le phénomène a repris de plus belle ce jeudi matin, puisque le site TotalBug a recensé plus de 500 signalements en 24 heures, avec une courbe grimpant jusqu'à environ 125 par heure vers 8 heures.
Côté utilisateurs, on est assez unanime, comme nous avons pu le constater. Sur l'application, certains tombent dès l'ouverture sur le message « Une erreur est survenue lors de la récupération des données ». Dans un navigateur, d'autres voient la page de connexion refuser de s'afficher, ou apprennent que assure.ameli.fr, l'adresse de l'espace personnel, met trop de temps à répondre. Attention, le site de l'Assurance maladie est consultable, la partie vitrine. C'est bien l'accès au compte personnel, et à Mon espace santé, qui coinçait. La partie la plus sécurisée, donc.
Failles PHP, une piste éventuelle, à prendre avec des pincettes donc
L'Assurance maladie indique, ce matin, qu'« une maintenance programmée est effectivement en cours sur le compte ameli web et appli ». Nous avons essayé de contacter l'organisme pour en savoir plus. On peut évidemment avancer l'hypothèse d'une maintenance préventive liée aux deux failles critiques de PHP, le langage qui fait tourner une large partie des sites web, corrigées mercredi. On rappelle que ces brèches permettent à un pirate d'exécuter des commandes sur un serveur à distance, sans le moindre mot de passe.
Hier, Météo France a aussi fermé tous ses sites par précaution le même jour, et ce pendant plusieurs heures. Et dans la nuit, la CAF a annoncé à son tour une « opération de maintenance » rendant caf.fr temporairement indisponible, en assurant que la sécurité de ses services et des données est sa priorité. Ses allocataires gardent leur délai habituel, jusqu'au début du mois suivant, pour faire leur déclaration. Mais la CAF ne cite pas PHP, même si le scénario semble être le même de son côté, comme du côté de l'Assurance maladie. Sur X, plusieurs lecteurs nous confirment ne pas parvenir à accéder aux deux plateformes, et ce depuis hier soir.
D'autant que des internautes signalaient déjà des difficultés de connexion les jours précédents, pour certains. En attendant un retour à la normale ou une prise de parole de l'Assurance maladie, le plus simple reste le téléphone, au 36 46. Pour le reste, il faudra patienter et retenter la connexion un peu plus tard.

articles.title: Il soulève une voiture et désarme un agresseur, mais il ne faut surtout pas l'approcher : le nouveau robot « garde du corps » d'Unitree — Frandroid
articles.text:
Cabosser des carrosseries à coups de genou, sauter d’une plateforme de quatre mètres de haut ou encore s’interposer face à un agresseur armé d’un couteau avant de soulever l’avant d’une voiture pour dégager une victime coincée dessous : le programme est musclé.
Dans une vidéo d’une minute publiée sur YouTube ce mercredi 21 octobre et décortiquée par Clubic, le fabricant chinois Unitree met en scène son tout nouveau H2-X, surnommé pour l’occasion « Kung Fu Legend Guardian ».
Habituée aux démonstrations virales de robots qui dansent ou enchaînent les mouvements d’arts martiaux, la marque tente cette fois de vendre l’image d’un véritable protecteur mécanique.
Pourtant, derrière le montage spectaculaire, le flou demeure total sur les capacités réelles de la machine. Unitree se garde bien de préciser si son humanoïde agissait de manière totalement autonome, s’il exécutait une chorégraphie préprogrammée au millimètre ou s’il était simplement piloté à distance par un opérateur.
Un colosse de 70 kg aux caractéristiques encore floues
Sur le plan matériel, ce H2-X dérive directement du H2, l’humanoïde à visage bionique présenté par la marque il y a un an. Pour rappel, cette version standard mesure 1,82 mètre pour environ 70 kg batterie comprise, et s’articule autour de 31 degrés de liberté (soit autant d’axes de rotation indépendants pour ses membres).
Côté cerveau, la fiche technique du H2 classique promet jusqu’à 2 070 TOPS, une unité qui mesure en milliers de milliards le nombre d’opérations de calcul IA réalisées chaque seconde. Sur le papier, c’est presque trois fois les 700 TOPS des puces spécialisées qu’Intel prépare pour 2028.
Unitree n’a toutefois pas confirmé que cette déclinaison « garde du corps » embarque exactement les mêmes composants, se contentant d’annoncer une autonomie d’environ huit heures… mesurée uniquement en position debout statique, bien loin de la débauche d’énergie réclamée par de telles cascades.
Un garde du corps qu’il vaut mieux tenir à distance
Un détail glissé à la toute fin de la vidéo prête d’ailleurs à sourire : dans ses mentions d’avertissement, Unitree recommande formellement de rester à deux ou trois mètres du robot lorsqu’il est en marche, tout en déconseillant toute modification dangereuse de la machine. Une consigne pour le moins paradoxale lorsqu’on présente un garde du corps censé escorter au plus près la personne qu’il protège.
En creux, le constructeur admet surtout une réalité physique implacable : un automate de 70 kg doté de moteurs assez puissants pour plier une portière en tôle représente un danger immédiat pour les humains qui l’entourent en cas de faux mouvement.
Ce n’est pas la première fois que les démonstrations martiales de l’entreprise soulèvent des doutes techniques. Le 7 septembre dernier, Unitree avait déjà dévoilé UnifoLM-X2-1.0, un modèle d’intelligence artificielle censé permettre à ses machines de frapper, bloquer et esquiver de façon autonome.
La vidéo mettait alors en scène le G1, un humanoïde plus compact du catalogue, lors d’un combat d’entraînement face à un humain. Or, en analysant les images de près, Interesting Engineering avait repéré à l’écran des journaux de commandes suggérant que l’IA ne tournait pas dans le robot, mais sur un serveur externe chargé de lui dicter ses mouvements à distance. Là encore, impossible de savoir si le H2-X repose sur ce même dispositif.
Un casse-tête réglementaire face à des rivaux tournés vers l’usine
Sans prix ni date de commercialisation, le H2-X ressemble avant tout à une vitrine technologique. À titre de repère, le modèle H2 de base s’affiche déjà à 29 900 dollars (environ 26 600 euros hors taxes).
Mais au-delà du coût, c’est le mur réglementaire qui paraît infranchissable : faire homologuer pour le grand public une machine programmée pour neutraliser physiquement un individu relève aujourd’hui de la mission impossible. Aucun cadre légal spécifique ne prévoit l’intervention d’un robot dans une rixe, et en Europe, le nouveau règlement Machines, qui modernise la directive de 2006 sur la sécurité des équipements, n’entrera en vigueur que le 20 janvier 2027.
Cette posture très spectaculaire isole d’ailleurs Unitree face aux autres géants chinois, qui concentrent leurs efforts sur un terrain beaucoup plus pragmatique : les chaînes de montage.
Pendant que le H2-X joue les cascadeurs sur YouTube, Xpeng a déjà lancé la production en grande série de son robot Iron, Xiaomi fait assembler des voitures électriques par ses propres humanoïdes et BYD finalise son premier modèle industriel. Même l’américain Tesla doit s’appuyer sur les fournisseurs chinois pour produire Optimus en masse, confirmant que la guerre des robots humanoïdes se joue d’abord dans l’industrie automobile.

articles.title: Gemini se vuelve "personal" en el coche: tendrá acceso a tu Gmail, Calendar y Maps mientras conduces
articles.text:
Google se está poniendo las pilas con Gemini en el coche, permitiendo que el asistentede IA pueda ahora inspeccionartus datosen servicios comoGmail, Calendar, Fotos, Maps, YouTube y Search para respondertodo tipo depreguntas mientras conduces.Tal y como explica la compañía en una publicación, la funciónya ha comenzado a implementarseen Android Auto y llegará a los coches con Google integrado en los próximos meses.
Más contexto. Hasta ahora, Gemini tenía la capacidad de responder preguntas generales, abrir ciertas aplicaciones o programarte rutas en Maps, pero tenía poco contexto sobre el conductor. La idea con esta actualización es que su funcionamiento se parezca más a cuando conversamos con Gemini a través de su app o a partir de los servicios de Google, pues es ahí donde hasta el momento contábamos con integraciones en servicios como Calendar, Gmail, etc.
En el blog han puesto de ejemplo que podrías pedirle a Gemini cosas como la puerta de embarque de tu vuelo para dirigirte a ella con Maps o la ruta hacia tu cita médica sin darle más detalles (siempre que los detalles de esa cita los tengas guardados en Calendar o Gmail, claro). Esta medida, lógicamente, también busca vincular a los usuarios más estrechamente al ecosistema de Google, ya que el asistente se vuelve más útil cuantas más aplicaciones de Google conectes.
Qué hace. Google afirma que la función tiene dos puntos fuertes principales: extraer detalles específicos de un correo electrónico, foto o lugar guardado, y razonar a la vez entre varias de esas fuentes.
Entre otros ejemplos que Google cita, la compañía nos anima a indicarle a Gemini cosas como que “encuentre el túnel de lavado de la foto que hice la semana pasada y navegue hasta allí", solicitarle que te lleve a un restaurante que coincida con tus gustos habituales, pedirle que te lleve a una cafetería de la que hablaste con Gemini anteriormente, etc.
Si ya la has habilitado en la aplicación de Gemini la inteligencia personal, Google dice que la configuración se traslada automáticamente al coche.
Y qué pasa con la privacidad. Evidentemente, darle a un asistente acceso a tu bandeja de entrada, fotos e historial de búsquedas es el punto delicado. Google dice que nada está conectado a menos que des tu consentimiento y que puedes desactivarlo en cualquier momento en los ajustes de Gemini. Los usuarios también pueden elegir qué aplicaciones vincular. En los coches con Google integrado, Google afirma que las respuestas personalizadas solo se comparten cuando tu teléfono está conectado.
Sin la Inteligencia Personal, Google dice que la navegación, la música, las llamadas y las preguntas generales siguen funcionando, solo que sin respuestas personalizadas. Vamos, que cuanto más sepa de ti el asistente, más respuestas útiles te podrá ofrecer. Sin embargo, esto conlleva a que inspeccione cualquier información que tengas en las aplicaciones que hayas conectado. Ya está en tu mano escoger si merece la pena.
Mientras tanto, en el iPhone. Gemini también está llegando a los conductores que usan CarPlay de Apple. Google Maps en CarPlay permite ahora a los usuarios de iPhone hacer preguntas conversacionales a Gemini, como el nombre de un lugar emblemático o si un destino estará abarrotado, con la función ya activa en EEUU y un despliegue más amplio planeado en el resto de países. Es una función independiente de la Inteligencia Personal, y se hizo posible después de que Apple permitiera que las aplicaciones de voz de terceros funcionaran con CarPlay en iOS 26.4.

articles.title: Kelly Clarkson dice “Me encanta la IA”, pero los artistas de IA no deberían estar en las mismas listas de música que los humanos
articles.text:
“Me encanta la IA”. Así se expresó Kelly Clarkson en un episodio del podcast “Las Culturistas”, presentado por Matt Rogers y Bowen Yang, al hablar sobre los artistas generados por IA. La actriz y cantante vio en ella la oportunidad de que personas que antes no podían hacer ciertas cosas pudieran realizarlas y afirmó que surgirán creaciones musicales interesantes, pero se opone a que los artistas de IA compitan con humanos en las mismas listas.
El ejemplo que da Clarkson en la entrevista para ilustrar el problema es el de los Juegos Olímpicos: comparó la situación con una prueba en la que compitieran un robot y un humano y se preguntó quién lanzaría más lejos. “No creo que deban competir con humanos”, afirmó. Para resolverlo, propone que los artistas de IA compitan en una lista diferente de la de los humanos, y añade: “No va a desaparecer”. También alude a sus aplicaciones fuera de la música y a los avances científicos que le interesan.
Spotify distingue las identidades de los artistas
Su opinión sobre el futuro es que puede haber demanda para ambos tipos de creación, pero el público necesita la capacidad de distinguir entre ellos.
No propuso prohibir la creación y el consumo de canciones generadas por IA. El 11 de agosto de 2026, Spotify anunció una etiqueta para identificar perfiles de artistas cuya identidad pudiera haberse generado con IA.
La función, denominada “AI Persona”, tenía un despliegue previsto desde mediados de septiembre y, según el comunicado de Spotify, estos perfiles quedarían fuera de sus recomendaciones editoriales y algorítmicas por defecto. Su música puede aparecer en recomendaciones personalizadas si el usuario muestra interés en ella, por ejemplo, siguiendo esos perfiles.
Según Spotify, la etiqueta es una indicación de la identidad pública del artista, no de cómo se creó su música. Un autor o compositor humano que utilice software de inteligencia artificial no pasa automáticamente a ser una “AI Persona”, y la compañía permite recurrir a la asignación de esa etiqueta.
La plataforma utiliza herramientas diferentes para informar sobre cómo se crearon las canciones, denominadas “AI Credits” y “SongDNA”.
Las propuestas para las listas musicales
El 29 de julio de 2026, Sony Music Entertainment, Universal Music Group y Warner Music Group, junto con otras compañías, propusieron criterios para las listas, incluidas las exigencias de servicios de IA autorizados y legales, el requisito de que las grabaciones sean sustancialmente humanas, así como la ausencia de indicios de manipulación de las reproducciones.
La propuesta también excluiría las canciones clasificadas como generadas por IA. Son criterios propuestos a los responsables de las listas, cuya adopción depende de ellos. Billboard anunció el 25 de agosto de 2026 su compromiso de identificar el uso de IA en sus listas y su cobertura editorial, así como de probar herramientas de identificación. El comunicado no anuncia una clasificación de canciones en dos listas separadas ni la adopción universal de la propuesta de las discográficas.
Luminate presentó un sistema de clasificación de canciones y artistas en “CONNECT”, según informó el 25 de agosto de 2026 en su propio anuncio. Las etiquetas se preveían mostrar a sus clientes durante el resto del año; según explicó entonces, aún no había analizado toda su base de datos y advirtió contra la suposición de que la ausencia de una etiqueta de inteligencia artificial implicara que la canción era de origen humano. Para separar listas, sería necesario identificar qué canciones están generadas con IA y qué cobertura tiene esa identificación.

articles.title: Meta Ordered to Pay New Mexico $25 Billion for Deceiving Users About Privacy on Facebook
articles.text:
A judge on Wednesday ordered Meta to pay New Mexico $25 billion after a jury found the company liable for deceiving users about privacy on Facebook, marking the biggest fine ever against the tech giant.
Facebook’s deception was intentional and executives consistently misled users about how the platform worked, state District Court Judge Francis J. Mathew wrote in his ruling.
“Facebook promised users that they (the users) controlled their data. This was false,” he said.
Jurors in September found Meta liable for over 43 million violations of New Mexico consumer protection laws for making misleading public statements about how it handled users’ personal data. The case was brought after political consulting firm Cambridge Analytica harvested Facebook data to generate targeted political ads during the 2016 election season.
The award will serve as a warning to tech companies that New Mexico will hold them accountable, state Attorney General Raúl Torrez said at a news conference.
“This judgment should be a signal, an unambiguous message, to Silicon Valley,” he said.
Meta said the ruling and Torrez’s office’s approach to enforcement “makes it all but impossible to do business in the state of New Mexico.”
“At its core, this lawsuit seeks to impose a tax on speech to enforce new rules for what people can say online. We are confident we will prevail on appeal,” C.J. Mahoney, the company’s chief legal officer, said in a statement.
The Menlo Park, California, company has a market value of $1.8 trillion and brought in more than $200 billion in revenue last year. Company shares traded 2% higher after Wednesday’s announcement, and it was scheduled to report its quarterly earnings later in the day.
New Mexico goes it alone
In August, Meta reached a settlement with nearly all states and territories — except New Mexico and Florida — to pay $18 billion and add stronger child-safety measures to its Facebook and Instagram platforms.
The settlement ended a trial over teen social media addiction and resolved a pivotal case years in the making that sought to hold the tech giant accountable for the role its platforms played in undermining children’s mental health. The effort targeted features designed to grab young people’s attention.
New Mexico didn’t join the multistate settlement, choosing to go after the company on its own.
The director of a nonprofit that supports stronger policies toward corporations said $25 billion is “a drop in the bucket for Meta,” but demonstrates people want accountability.
“Right now, they are rolling out Muse, an AI assistant encouraging people to trust it with everything from their bank accounts to their medical information,” added Nidhi Hegde, executive director of the American Economic Liberties Project. “Which is why we need more enforcers with courage and laws with actual teeth to rein them in.”
At the trial, attorneys for the state cited a 2010 Washington Post op-ed in which Facebook CEO Mark Zuckerberg wrote that the company didn’t sell user data.
“You have control over how your information is shared,” Zuckerberg said. “We do not and never will sell any of your information to anyone.”
New Mexico officials sought fines of $35 billion to $40 billion, arguing the company would only change if its stock price were impacted.
Meta’s lawyers, meanwhile, asserted that the state failed to prove the company made misleading statements and that content moderation actually harmed people in New Mexico. They wanted the company to pay $3.4 billion at most and said an award many times larger would be unconstitutional.
Although interest would accrue on the penalty during the appeal process, Meta could succeed in reducing the number of violations for which it is found liable.
The $25 billion award far exceeds a $5 billion fine the Federal Trade Commission levied against Facebook in 2019.
Peter Ormerod, an associate law professor at Villanova University, was surprised by the size of the New Mexico judgment because previous legal settlements over Cambridge Analytica were much lower.
“It comes out to about $12,000 per person in New Mexico,” he said. “It’s quite unlike anything else we’ve seen.”
Under the New Mexico Constitution, fines for violating consumer protection laws go toward education spending. It could take years for the state to get the money while the company appeals.
Company argues that the state failed to prove harm
The trial focused on accusations Facebook deceived users about a breach stemming from a third-party personality quiz that harvested data from roughly 87 million profiles and sold it to Cambridge Analytica. The now-defunct firm’s clients included Donald Trump’s 2016 presidential campaign.
Attorneys for New Mexico argued that the state’s entire population was deceived, and that Facebook allowed misinformation or violent content to proliferate.
Meta’s lawyers argued the state failed to prove people were harmed by deceptive statements. Zuckerberg in a video deposition denied that Facebook profited off harmful content and said the company had to balance free speech with content moderation.
In a partial win for the company, jurors rejected assertions that Facebook made false claims about removing harmful content, including misinformation about the COVID-19 pandemic.
Meta lawyers said it has changed policies since the lawsuit was filed in 2021 and catches and removes an estimated 99% of content violating its standards.
Related: Meta Says Hackers Took Code, Personal Data of 1,500 in GitHub Breach
Related: Meta Launches Personal AI Agent, Muse, Emphasizes Safety and Privacy
Related: Google Hit With $463 Million Fine for EU Location Data Rule Breach

articles.title: How to Read Data into GPU Memory in Python with NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
GPU applications are processing ever-growing datasets with increasingly powerful accelerators. According to the 2025 Stanford AI Index, compute for notable AI models has been doubling approximately every five months, while the size of datasets used to train LLMs has been doubling approximately every eight months. As computation and data scale together, moving data efficiently from storage becomes a necessity for keeping accelerators supplied.
NVIDIA Magnum IO GPUDirect Storage (GDS) addresses this challenge by enabling a direct data path between supported storage and GPU memory. This avoids unnecessary staging through CPU memory and reduces overall CPU utilization in the system. GDS is supported by a growing ecosystem that includes many major storage vendors.
At the application layer, Python plays a central role in modern AI development. As of August 2025, nearly half of all new AI projects on GitHub were built primarily in Python while the main application interface to GDS is the cuFile C API.
NVIDIA KvikIO, a Python and C++ library for high-performance file I/O, bridges this gap. It provides high-level, idiomatic Python and C++ interfaces, along with additional controls over how I/O requests are performed.
The tutorial in this post demonstrates how to use the NVIDIA KvikIO Python API to configure storage I/O, read data into GPU memory, and confirm that the accelerated path within GDS was activated. It also shows how to inspect the KvikIO and cuFile settings that influence the path each operation takes.
How does NVIDIA KvikIO leverage GDS?
GDS is the broader technology that enables accelerated data movement between supported storage and GPU memory. For file system-based storage, cuFile provides the C library and API through which applications and frameworks access GDS. KvikIO sits above cuFile, providing higher-level Python and C++ interfaces along with its own controls over how I/O requests are executed. Figure 1 shows these layers and their two separate path-selection points. Initialization failures, unsupported configurations, and error-handling paths are omitted for clarity.
The application supplies a file system path and GPU buffer, and KvikIO determines whether to send the request through cuFile or use its POSIX compatibility path, which stages the data through host memory. When cuFile is selected, KvikIO registers the file and issues the I/O using the target GPU buffer.
cuFile then determines the actual transfer path based on system support, the file system, and its configuration. It may use the accelerated GDS path or its CPU-staged compatibility path. Therefore, reaching the cuFile API confirms that KvikIO selected cuFile, but does not by itself confirm that the accelerated GDS path was activated.
The following sections walk through how to configure the system, perform a KvikIO read, and verify the resulting path.
Prerequisites
Before beginning this tutorial, you will need:
- A Linux system with an NVIDIA GPU and GPUDirect Storage installed.
- A GDS-supported storage and file system configuration.
- Permission to create, read, and write files at the storage endpoint, along with access to GDS tools such as gdscheck and gds_stats.
For complete installation and platform requirements, refer to the NVIDIA GPUDirect Storage documentation.
Tutorial system
This tutorial was tested with the following configuration:
- An x86_64 system with an NVIDIA H100 GPU, CUDA 13.3, and cuFile 1.18.
- A local NVMe device formatted with ext4.
- A PIX connection between the selected GPU and NVMe device, meaning the path traverses at most one PCIe bridge.
- IOMMU and ACS disabled to preserve PCIe peer-to-peer transfers.
- The nvidia-fs kernel module is loaded to provide the accelerated path.
You can inspect the GPU-to-storage topology with the following command:
$ nvidia-smi topo -nvme
Step 1: Set up NVIDIA KvikIO
First, create a Python environment and install the CUDA 13 build of KvikIO. CuPy will be installed as a dependency.
$ python3 -m venv kvikio-env
$ source kvikio-env/bin/activate
$ python -m pip install kvikio-cu13
You can verify the installation with the following:
$ python -m pip show kvikio-cu13 cupy-cuda13x
Step 2: Inspect the configuration
Before performing any I/O, inspect the active KvikIO settings and confirm that the system recognizes the GDS components. In the KvikIO defaults API, the compatibility-mode setting is named compat_mode, and its name attribute reports the active mode as AUTO, ON, or OFF. The following commands report the loaded KvikIO and cuFile versions, the active compatibility mode, and the minimum request size KvikIO sends to cuFile:
import kvikio
import kvikio.cufile_driver as cufile_driver
import kvikio.defaults as defaults
kvikio.__version__
cufile_driver.libcufile_version()
defaults.get("compat_mode").name
defaults.get("gds_threshold")
On the tutorial system, KvikIO reports compatibility mode as AUTO and a GDS threshold of 16 KiB. AUTO instructs KvikIO to try cuFile and fall back to its POSIX backend if cuFile is unavailable. Reads smaller than the threshold use the KvikIO POSIX path directly. These settings can also be controlled through KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE and KVIKIO_GDS_THRESHOLD. For the complete list, refer to the KvikIO runtime settings.
Next, inspect the GDS platform and cuFile configuration:
$ /usr/local/cuda-13.3/gds/tools/gdscheck.py -p 2>&1 | less -R
The output lists the installed GDS components, supported file systems, detected GPUs, and active cuFile configuration. Figure 2 shows how to inspect the KvikIO and GDS configuration used in this tutorial.
KvikIO settings can also be changed in Python. For example, defaults.set accepts a dictionary to change several settings at once, or a name and value to change one setting:
defaults.set({"task_size": 1024**3, "num_threads": 8})
defaults.set("compat_mode", kvikio.CompatMode.OFF)
Step 3: Read a file into GPU memory
Next, create the input file once before running the Python example. The following command writes a 1 GiB file with random data using direct I/O and flushes it to storage:
$ dd if=/dev/urandom \
    of=/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin \
    bs=1M count=1024 \
    oflag=direct conv=fsync \
    status=progress
The following program allocates a 1 GiB CuPy array in GPU memory and supplies it to KvikIO as the destination buffer:
from pathlib import Path
import cupy as cp
import kvikio
file_path = Path(
    "/mnt/nvme1/kvikio-tutorial/kvikio-example.bin"
)
# Allocate a GPU buffer large enough to hold the file.
gpu_buffer = cp.empty(
    file_path.stat().st_size,
    dtype=cp.uint8,
)
# Read the file into the GPU buffer.
with kvikio.CuFile(file_path, "r") as file:
    bytes_read = file.read(gpu_buffer)
# Validate that 1 GiB was read.
assert bytes_read == gpu_buffer.nbytes
The context manager opens the file and completes the read into GPU memory. Although the return value confirms that the complete file was read, it does not identify the underlying data path.
Step 4: Determine the data path
One way to validate the data path used by any cuFile-based application is to observe the cuFile runtime per-process statistics. These statistics can be enabled by setting CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 and then inspected with gds_stats while the process remains active.
For this KvikIO example, the environment variable keeps the setting scoped to a single run, although it can also be configured in cufile.json.
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
Running Python interactively keeps the process alive after the read, allowing gds_stats to inspect its accumulated counters.
Figure 3 demonstrates this workflow. In the per-GPU output, nvfs counts operations representing the path taken through the nvidia-fs kernel module, while posix counts operations handled by the cuFile compatibility path.
The KvikIO default 4 MiB task size divides the 1 GiB request into 256 read operations. The per-GPU statistics report n=256, nvfs=256, and posix=0, showing that all 256 operations used the nvidia-fs path.
Step 5: Compare the available paths
The same read can be repeated with different settings to demonstrate the two control layers. First, require KvikIO to use cuFile:
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 \
    KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=off \
    python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
On the tutorial system, gds_stats reports nvfs operations, confirming that cuFile selected the accelerated path. Next, force cuFile to use its compatibility path:
$ CUFILE_STATS_LEVEL=3 \
    KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=off \
    CUFILE_FORCE_COMPAT_MODE=true \
    python3 -i read_with_kvikio.py
KvikIO still calls cuFile, but the operations now appear under posix rather than nvfs. Finally, the KvikIO compatibility mode bypasses cuFile entirely:
$ KVIKIO_COMPAT_MODE=on \
    python3 read_with_kvikio.py
In this case, KvikIO performs the read through its CPU-staged POSIX backend, so cuFile does not record the operation. The next section examines the cuFile settings that control request execution.
Step 6: cuFile configuration for a KvikIO read
After KvikIO selects its cuFile path, cuFile applies another set of controls that determine how the request is executed. These controls are defined in cufile.json and operate independently of KvikIO runtime settings.
Request decomposition and parallel execution
KvikIO and cuFile can both divide a large operation into smaller pieces. KvikIO applies KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE first, with KVIKIO_NTHREADS controlling how those tasks are scheduled. Each task on the cuFile path becomes a separate cuFile request. Once cuFile receives one of those requests, its execution settings determine whether it can be divided again and processed using the cuFile internal thread pool. The following cuFile settings control this behavior:
| Setting | Purpose | 
|---|---|
| execution.parallel_io | Enables cuFile internal parallel processing. | 
| execution.max_io_threads | Limits the number of cuFile worker threads available per GPU queue. | 
| execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb | Sets a target minimum size for internally scheduled pieces; a final remainder may be smaller. | 
| execution.max_request_parallelism | Limits how much parallelism cuFile prepares for one request. | 
| execution.max_io_queue_depth | Limits the number of pending work items in the internal queue. | 
A 1 GiB read, step by step
The configuration used here has four cuFile worker threads, max_request_parallelism set to four, and min_io_threshold_size_kb set to 8192 (8 MiB). With the KvikIO default 4 MiB task size, a 1 GiB read becomes 256 cuFile requests. Each 4 MiB request is handled as one piece by cuFile. This is the run that produced nvfs=256 in the earlier statistics.
If KVIKIO_TASK_SIZE is set to 1 GiB, KvikIO instead sends one large read request to cuFile. The CuPy destination has not been explicitly registered with cuFile, so cuFile uses its unregistered buffer scheduling path. It limits the request to min (4 worker threads, 4 maximum request parallelism) = 4 pieces.
Dividing 1 GiB four ways gives 256 MiB per piece, already larger than min_io_threshold_size_kb which is 8 MiB. With room in its queue, cuFile assigns three pieces to workers, processes the fourth on the calling thread, and waits for them to finish.
Those 256 MiB pieces are units of scheduled work, not individual storage transfers. Because the destination buffer is not registered for storage DMA, cuFile reads into a registered GPU bounce buffer and copies the data into the destination. Since GDS 1.17, these bounce buffers can be configured as slabs. The nvidia-fs path in this configuration uses slabs no larger than 16 MiB, so each 256 MiB piece is processed through smaller transfers. The 8 MiB scheduling target does not set their transfer size.
When the 8 MiB split target matters
In this configuration, execution.min_io_threshold_size_kb is set to 8192 (8 MiB). That target does not change the 1 GiB split, but it would affect a 16 MiB cuFile request. Four equal pieces would be 4 MiB each, so cuFile schedules two 8 MiB pieces instead. KvikIO must use a task size of at least 16 MiB for cuFile to receive that request intact.
KvikIO in NVIDIA CUDA-X for data science
KvikIO is part of the NVIDIA CUDA-X libraries for data science (formerly RAPIDS). Its development is closely connected to the GDS integration originally built for NVIDIA cuDF GPU DataFrame library, where parallel cuFile reads accelerated Parquet and ORC ingestion. This design was later incorporated into KvikIO, building on the cuDF original GDS data-ingest work.
KvikIO has since been used with GDS in cuCIM digital pathology workflows and in the cuPhoton xDataReader for scientific-image analysis, while related GPU-accelerated Presto work shows benefits of GDS in data analytics workloads. Together, these examples show the broader role of KvikIO as an application-facing I/O layer over the storage acceleration GDS provides.
Get started with NVIDIA KvikIO
This tutorial has demonstrated how to read data into GPU memory and use level-three GDS cuFile statistics to distinguish the accelerated nvidia-fs path from CPU-staged compatibility paths. These path decisions matter significantly for popular libraries such as cuDF that use KvikIO for many I/O operations.
The key takeaway is that KvikIO and cuFile make separate decisions. KvikIO selects whether to call cuFile, while cuFile determines the final transfer path and execution strategy. Understanding these layers enables applications to understand the path the I/O is taking and tune the settings that matter for their workload.
Ready to get started? Run the KvikIO Python example featured in this post on your GDS-enabled system. For more examples, explore the C++ and Python KvikIO code in the MagnumIO GDS samples directory. Use gds_stats to check whether reads appear under nvfs or posix, then apply the same verification to your own KvikIO workloads.

articles.title: Google turns the infrastructure behind Gemini’s agents into a cloud service
articles.text:
Google turns the infrastructure behind Gemini’s agents into a cloud service
Google will soon make the infrastructure that powers its Gemini agents available to Google Cloud users in preview.
Announced on Thursday at the Linux Foundation’s AGNTCon+MCPCon in San Jose, Agent Compute Engine will become available in preview to Google Cloud users later this year. It will provide every AI agent with a hardware-isolated microVM that combines the speed of containers with the security of a sandbox.
Who else offers agent sandboxes?
The idea of agent sandboxes is anything but new, of course. Startups like E2B and Daytona offer them to developers (and support them on any cloud), as does AWS with Bedrock AgentCore.
E2B runs each sandbox in a Firecracker microVM, the open source virtualization technology AWS originally built for Lambda. It can pause a sandbox with its memory and filesystem intact and resume it in about a second. Daytona started out with containers but added microVM sandboxes in July. Those can pause a full machine or fork a running one into identical copies.
AgentCore also gives every agent session its own microVM. AWS doesn’t charge for CPU while an agent waits on a model or tool call, though memory keeps billing until the runtime reclaims it. Those sessions top out at eight hours. In August, AWS added EC2-based runtime instances that can keep shared sessions alive for up to 14 days.
It’s worth noting that Google itself isn’t new to this either. GKE already offers a managed version of Agent Sandbox, the open source Kubernetes project Google launched last November. The company also sells code-execution and computer-use sandboxes through its Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform.
Agent Compute Engine, on the other hand, started out as internal infrastructure for Gemini, Antigravity, and Google’s own model training pipelines.
Google’s take
Few companies — if any — run as many agentic workloads as Google, be that for its own internal use or its customers. According to the company, agentic workloads have quickly become one of the fastest-growing consumers of compute and storage across its fleet.
At this scale, the infrastructure services that power all of these autonomous agents don’t just need to be efficient and able to scale, but maybe more than anything, they need to be secure. Google, like some of its competitors, quickly realized that it needed to build a new purpose-built compute service to power all of these agents, similar to how it needed to build Borg, which later inspired Kubernetes, to manage compute in its early data centers.
As Rohit Jnagal and Ramanathan Venkatapathy, both distinguished engineers at Google, note in a technical deep dive, traditional VMs provide developers with a lot of control and flexibility, but at the cost of speed when it comes to booting, suspending, and resuming a machine. Given how fast agents start and shut down, that’s not an option.
Containers solve some of this, they note, “but there are multiple examples like coding agents and developer assistants that need complete isolation as well as kernel- and root-level control of the agentic environment.”
With Agent Compute Engine, Jnagal and Venkatapathy write, the team went back to first principles to build “a unified, agent compute platform for Google” (and now its customers).
A persistent computer for every agent
At its core, it basically gives every agent a persistent, sandboxed computer to work with. That allows the agents to work with shell scripts, use a headless browser, and write code (with root permissions to that machine) in agent loops that could run for weeks.
But the team also built it for large-scale use cases like the eval loops that frontier labs use to test their models, AI benchmarking, and reinforcement learning.
In addition, the team also designed Agent Compute Engine to run sandboxed backends for Google’s own services.
Jnagal and Venkatapathy also note that agents spend most of their time waiting on the model or the user. So once an agent finishes a tool call, the host checkpoints its microVM, which then uses no active resources until the next call comes in.
Nothing to steal inside the sandbox
The key feature here, besides speed, is to be able to trust that the agents can’t break out of their sandboxes. We’ve seen what happens when they do, after all.
Each agent session runs inside a single-tenant, memory-safe microVM. Those environments hold no secrets in memory or on the disk, and their only identity is a short-lived, session-scoped one delivered through a single per-VM local listener. All traffic is end-to-end encrypted in transit, and snapshots and disks are encrypted at rest.
The microVMs don’t get a standard network interface, either. All traffic runs through a proxy outside the sandbox, and when an agent needs to reach a service like Google Drive, Google’s Agent Gateway checks the user’s delegation and the sandbox’s identity before adding the actual credential, outside the sandbox.
The underlying host is basically a stateless appliance with a read-only filesystem, with the hardware and firmware cryptographically verified at each boot.
All of this is backed by Google’s own Titan and Titanium IPU security platform. The microVMs themselves run on Cloud Hypervisor, an open source virtual machine monitor, and each gets its own guest kernel and root access.
Jnagal and Venkatapathy use the example of an enterprise agent that manages a user’s inbox and reads an email with hidden instructions to find any API keys on the machine and send them to an outside address. Most of the time, they note, the model will ignore that, but not always.
“We started from one rule: Assume an attacker controls everything inside the sandbox, and make sure they find nothing there to use,” the team writes.
Agent Substrate brings the same idea to Kubernetes
But not every team will want to have its agents run in a managed Google service. For them, Google also offers Agent Substrate, an open source runtime for the Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) that it first announced in May.
Substrate builds on Agent Sandbox, Google’s Kubernetes project, and adds a lightweight control plane that Google says can handle millions of short-lived tool calls that would swamp Kubernetes.
Similar to Agent Compute Engine, Substrate snapshots an idle agent’s memory and returns the machine to the pool until the agent gets more work.
Google says that means up to 10 times the density of traditional compute. In a 200,000-agent benchmark, Substrate handled 500 activations per second, with agents suspending and resuming in under half a second, the company says.
Teams can isolate each sandbox with a microVM or gVisor, and every agent gets its own cryptographic identity. As with Agent Compute Engine, egress proxies attach credentials outside the sandbox. Substrate runs on any Kubernetes cluster, and Google says it works with any harness, including Claude Code, OpenClaw, and Nous Research’s Hermes.
“We built Hermes Enterprise to enable customers to deploy into their existing infrastructure, while handling per-agent isolation and extensible access control,” Hervé Bizira, Nous Research’s chief business officer, notes in the announcement. “Agent Substrate addresses both at the platform layer in a way that also preserves valuable compute resources.”

articles.text: El logo de la compañía Meta. Nuevo México ha tomado la delantera como un Estado pionero a la hora de poner freno a los abusos de las compañías tecnológicas. articles.title: Backed by Yann LeCun and Arthur Mensch, Swiss Physical AI startup Enact Intelligence exits stealth with €26.68 million | EU-Startups
articles.text:
Enact Intelligence, a physical AI startup headquartered in Zurich, has come out of stealth today with a €26.68 million ($30 million) pre-Seed funding round, one of the largest pre-Seed raises in Europe to date.
The round saw participation from institutional investors redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital, alongside a notable slate of angel investors, including Arthur Mensch, founder of Mistral; Yann LeCun, founder of AMI Labs and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta; and Andrew Lonsberry, founder of Path Robotics.
“Dexterity is the next frontier in robotics, and Enact is tackling it with a new data modality: starting with high precision force data from bespoke actuators they are rethinking the entire stack from the hardware up. We are very excited about Enact’s approach of leveraging orthogonal data to improve existing models and build a data moat,” said Dr. Harald Nieder, General Partner of redalpine.
Founded in March 2026 by Manuel Yves Galliker, Enact is building robots that can not only see their environment but physically sense what is happening when they interact with it. Before founding Enact, Galliker led the software team for the humanoid robot NEO at 1X, helped build 1X’s AI team in Silicon Valley, and went on to work at the robotics lab Physical Intelligence.
The central argument of Enact is that most robots today depend almost entirely on vision to perceive their surroundings, limiting their ability to manipulate objects reliably or learn efficiently from experience. Existing haptic sensing solutions, which extend robots with force and touch, are either too costly or fragile for meaningful industrial deployment.
To solve this physical AI challenge, Enact rethinks the entire stack, from model architectures and data pipelines through to the actuators and sensors that feed the model. As a departure from traditional robots relying on point-based force sensors, Enact’s robots capture force data directly from the actuators themselves, similar to how humans sense tension through their muscles rather than solely through their fingertips.
Manuel Yves Galliker, CEO and founder of Enact Intelligence, said, “Unlike the early days of LLMs, physical AI has the advantage of starting from strong reasoning, language, and vision capabilities already in place. Instead of trying to collect every piece of data needed to teach a robot common sense about the world, we can build on top of existing models, like video models, and adapt them to output robot actions for interacting with the real world. So what we are addressing is the ability to efficiently learn from experience and perform tasks reliably, both of which require the model to understand the physics of the robot and the task at hand.”
This approach, Galliker argues, will lead to the development of “a proprioceptive nerve system and the cortex that makes sense of it,” solving dexterity through whole-body force-awareness at a cost and reality-level suitable for industrial scale.
Enact’s twelve-person team draws its engineering talent from DeepMind, 1X, Amazon Robotics, Helsing, Physical Intelligence and ETH Zurich. Alongside the funding, the company announced bringing Philip Kneis, a former DeepTech investor at redalpine, to lead growth.
“Silicon Valley has traditionally been very strong in software and AI, but it’s lacking in robotics and hardware engineering talent, and with the current excitement around robotics a lot of money is chasing a few people. What we will do is bring the AI experience with us from Silicon Valley and combine it with Zürich’s local talent pool. That’s the winning formula,” added Galliker.
The fresh capital will be used to grow its team fivefold by the end of 2027, accelerate its hardware and R&D pipelines, and roll out its robots with multiple industrial partners across manufacturing, infrastructure, retail, and food processing.

articles.title: Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
articles.text:
Scientists recreate a bizarre quantum effect that stops a particle cold
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of Oxford
- Summary:
- Oxford physicists have recreated a bizarre quantum effect in which a particle responds to a magnetic field without ever traveling through it. Using a hybrid quantum computer, they demonstrated how introducing a simulated magnetic flux could completely halt a particle's movement through quantum interference. The experiment brings a decades-old prediction into a new setting where matter and quantum fields influence one another.
- Share:
A particle does not have to pass through a magnetic field to be influenced by it. That surprising feature of quantum physics has now been recreated by researchers at the University of Oxford, who used a hybrid quantum computer to demonstrate how an invisible magnetic influence can bring a simulated particle's movement to a complete stop.
The experiment reproduced a phenomenon known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect, in which a charged particle traveling around a region containing magnetic flux experiences a measurable change in its quantum state, even though its path never takes it through the magnetic field itself.
The Oxford team achieved this using a quantum system that combines qubits, the basic units of quantum information, with quantum oscillators, which represent vibrating motion. Their findings, published in Nature Physics, demonstrate how this combination could help scientists investigate fundamental interactions between matter and fields that are increasingly difficult to simulate using conventional computers.
A Strange Quantum Effect Predicted in 1959
In everyday physics, a charged particle responds to the electric and magnetic fields it encounters. Quantum mechanics, however, reveals that particles can behave in ways that have no straightforward counterpart in our ordinary experience.
In 1959, physicists Yakir Aharonov and David Bohm predicted that a charged particle could be affected by magnetic flux even if it traveled entirely outside the region containing the magnetic field. Rather than experiencing a conventional magnetic force along its path, the particle would undergo a change in its quantum phase.
Quantum phase describes an aspect of a particle's wave behavior that influences how different possible paths interfere with one another. Although the phase itself is not directly visible, differences in phase can produce measurable effects.
The prediction became known as the Aharonov-Bohm effect and was eventually verified in experiments involving real electrons. It remains one of the clearest demonstrations that the quantum world operates according to rules that go beyond the familiar laws of classical physics.
Researchers are now exploring how this phenomenon behaves in more complex theoretical systems known as lattice gauge theories.
These theories describe how matter interacts with fields associated with fundamental forces. They represent space as a grid, with matter located at individual points and fields associated with the connections between them. Such models are particularly important in particle physics and high-energy physics, where scientists study the basic particles and interactions that make up the universe.
The challenge is that the mathematics becomes extraordinarily demanding as these systems grow more complicated. Even powerful conventional computers can struggle to calculate how all the interacting components evolve.
Quantum computers offer a different approach. Instead of attempting to calculate every aspect of a quantum system using classical computing methods, scientists can construct another quantum system that follows the same underlying rules. They can then observe its behavior directly, an approach known as quantum simulation.
How Scientists Built the Quantum Experiment
The Oxford project began in 2022, when lead author Dr. Sebastian Saner, Dr. Oana Bazavan, and their colleagues started developing a way to simulate lattice gauge theories using a hybrid quantum system. They collaborated with Dr. Alejandro Bermudez of the Instituto de Física Teórica in Madrid.
Their experimental design relied on two different quantum components that performed separate functions.
The first consisted of qubits encoded in the internal states of trapped ions, which are electrically charged atoms held in place using electromagnetic fields. These qubits represented the gauge fields in the theoretical model.
The second component used quantum oscillators, created by the vibrations of those same trapped ions. These oscillators represented matter.
By combining the two, the researchers constructed a simple loop that served as a basic building block of a lattice gauge theory. Two oscillators represented matter at two different locations, while two qubits represented the fields connecting those locations.
Although the arrangement was small, it was sufficient to reproduce an important interaction between matter and magnetic flux.
Quantum Entanglement Creates a Surprising Solution
The researchers next placed the two qubits into an entangled quantum state. Entanglement is a phenomenon in which quantum systems become linked in ways that cannot be fully explained by classical physics.
Within the team's simulated lattice gauge theory, this entangled state represented magnetic flux passing through the center of the loop.
Initially, the researchers had planned to introduce the magnetic flux as a fixed background condition. However, creating the necessary interaction would have required capabilities that their quantum hardware did not possess.
Encoding the flux directly into the qubits provided a practical alternative. More importantly, it allowed the magnetic flux to become part of the evolving quantum system rather than remaining an unchanging external influence.
"For us, the exciting step was to encode the magnetic flux in a gauge field that was itself dynamical," says Dr. Saner. "Rather than having matter evolve in a fixed background, the matter and gauge field become part of the same quantum dynamics."
What began as a technical workaround ultimately enabled the researchers to explore a more interesting version of the phenomenon, one in which matter and the field could participate together in the quantum dynamics.
A Quantum Effect That Stops Particle Motion
With their simulated loop in place, the scientists examined how a matter particle moved between locations through a process known as quantum tunneling.
Quantum tunneling allows particles to move between states in ways that would not be possible under ordinary classical rules.
When the researchers ran their simulation without magnetic flux, the particle could tunnel freely around the loop.
Introducing the simulated flux produced a strikingly different result.
The particle had two possible paths around the loop, but the magnetic flux changed their relative quantum phases. As a result, the two paths interfered destructively, meaning their quantum contributions canceled each other out.
This interference completely suppressed the tunneling, leaving the simulated particle frozen in its original state.
The outcome demonstrated the Aharonov-Bohm effect within a lattice gauge theory containing a dynamical field. Rather than simply reproducing the familiar behavior of a particle moving around a fixed magnetic influence, the experiment showed how the phenomenon can emerge when matter and the field are both represented by interacting quantum components.
A New Tool for Exploring Fundamental Physics
The Oxford findings were published alongside a related study by researchers at the University of Maryland, led by Professor Norbert Linke.
The Maryland team also used a hybrid quantum system, but their experiment focused on simulating the Yukawa potential, a mathematical description of an interaction relevant to nuclear and particle physics.
Although the two research groups developed their methods independently, they later coordinated the submission of their studies to Nature Physics.
Together, the experiments demonstrate how hybrid quantum computers could become valuable tools for investigating fundamental interactions that are difficult to reproduce using classical simulations.
By combining different types of quantum components, researchers can build systems in which matter and fields are represented in ways that more closely reflect the physics they want to study.
The Oxford experiment provides an example of that potential. A phenomenon first predicted in 1959 and later observed with electrons has now been recreated in a quantum simulator where the field itself participates in the dynamics, offering scientists another way to explore the unusual rules governing the quantum world.

articles.title: Meta: parlamentares dos EUA cobram Zuckerberg por atuação nas eleições do Brasil
articles.text:
Um grupo de 13 parlamentares dos Estados Unidos enviou uma carta ao presidente-executivo da Meta, Mark Zuckerberg, cobrando explicações sobre denúncias de tratamento desigual às campanhas de Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva (PT) e Flávio Bolsonaro (PL) nas plataformas da empresa durante as eleições brasileiras de 2026.
O documento foi enviado nesta quinta-feira (22), três dias antes do segundo turno da disputa presidencial, marcado para domingo (25). Os congressistas querem saber se mecanismos de moderação, recomendação de conteúdo e inteligência artificial (IA) da Meta prejudicaram publicações relacionadas à campanha de Lula ou favoreceram conteúdos ligados ao adversário.
A iniciativa ocorre após uma sequência de denúncias sobre restrições a perfis e anúncios políticos, diferenças no comportamento da IA da empresa e possíveis falhas na distribuição de publicações. A Meta nega favorecer qualquer candidato e atribui os episódios relatados a problemas técnicos e erros não intencionais.
Os parlamentares solicitaram reunião com representantes da companhia para sexta-feira (23) e estabeleceram 4 de novembro como prazo para o envio de respostas por escrito.
O que os congressistas querem saber?
- A carta questiona quais regras orientam a moderação de conteúdo político durante eleições realizadas fora dos Estados Unidos e se houve comunicação entre a Meta e integrantes do governo de Donald Trump sobre o Judiciário brasileiro, a regulação das plataformas ou as eleições de 2026;
- Os parlamentares também querem explicações sobre quando a empresa identificou possíveis diferenças de tratamento entre as candidaturas e quais medidas adotou para corrigir os problemas;
- Outro ponto é o acesso de auditores independentes aos dados internos da companhia. O grupo quer saber se especialistas externos poderão examinar informações sobre moderação, recomendação e distribuição de conteúdo político para verificar se as regras foram aplicadas de maneira equivalente às duas campanhas;
- A carta ainda questiona o funcionamento do sistema de revisão humana anunciado pela Meta. Pelo mecanismo apresentado ao Tribunal Superior Eleitoral (TSE), restrições automatizadas aplicadas às contas de anúncios das campanhas presidenciais devem passar por análise humana em até duas horas;
- Os congressistas argumentam que empresas de tecnologia têm responsabilidade na preservação de condições equilibradas para a participação política, especialmente quando seus sistemas influenciam a circulação de informações durante eleições.
Restrições atingiram anúncios da campanha de Lula
Entre os episódios mencionados está a desativação da conta de anúncios de Lula no Facebook em 23 de setembro, 11 dias antes do primeiro turno. A campanha também enfrentou limitações que impediram o impulsionamento de publicações no Instagram por quase 24 horas, entre 9 e 10 de outubro.
Segundo a campanha petista, o bloqueio no Instagram comprometeu o alcance potencial de aproximadamente 1,3 milhão de pessoas.
Reportagens da Folha de S.Paulo também revelaram mensagens internas da Meta nas quais funcionários reconheceram que restrições haviam prejudicado contas de Lula. Os registros mencionados pelo jornal apontaram ainda recomendações do perfil de Flávio Bolsonaro e de um canal de WhatsApp associado à candidatura.
A empresa contestou a interpretação de que os episódios representariam favorecimento político deliberado. A Meta afirma que os problemas tiveram causas técnicas distintas e que seus sistemas não são projetados para distribuir conteúdo com base em ideologia política.
A ferramenta de IA da empresa também entrou na discussão. Testes e relatos de usuários apontaram diferenças na geração de imagens eleitorais: a Meta AI teria recusado alguns pedidos relacionados a Lula, enquanto atendia solicitações semelhantes envolvendo Flávio.
A empresa informou ter adotado medidas para corrigir o problema e garantir tratamento igual às duas candidaturas.
TSE elevou multa e exigiu tratamento igualitário
A controvérsia também chegou à Justiça Eleitoral brasileira. Após reclamações da campanha de Lula, o TSE determinou que a Meta assegurasse tratamento isonômico às duas candidaturas na distribuição e recomendação de conteúdos políticos.
Na semana anterior, o tribunal havia aplicado uma multa à empresa e estabelecido medidas para impedir restrições discriminatórias. Quatro dias depois, a penalidade foi elevada diante da cobrança por comprovação do cumprimento da decisão.
Em resposta enviada à Corte em 20 de outubro, a Meta afirmou ter concluído a implementação de 17 medidas para atender às determinações. Entre elas está a revisão humana de restrições aplicadas automaticamente às contas de anúncios das campanhas.
A companhia também declarou que conteúdos relacionados às duas candidaturas são tratados de forma igualitária e não discriminatória.
A decisão judicial estabelece que a empresa não pode reduzir a distribuição, excluir da recomendação ou restringir a busca de conteúdos eleitorais de uma candidatura em relação à outra, salvo nas exceções previstas na própria decisão, como regras previamente divulgadas e aplicadas de forma idêntica.
Leia mais:
- Meta descumpre ordens do TSE sobre IA e pode ser multada no Brasil
- Meta é processada na Austrália por suposto vício de crianças em redes sociais
- Meta derruba e depois restaura vídeo de MC Cabelinho sobre Flávio Bolsonaro
Conselho de Supervisão também apontou falhas
A pressão sobre a Meta não vem apenas dos parlamentares estadunidenses. Em 20 de outubro, o Conselho de Supervisão da empresa apontou falhas recorrentes na aplicação das regras de integridade eleitoral no Brasil.
O órgão criticou tanto o excesso de rigor, que pode suprimir manifestações políticas legítimas, quanto a aplicação insuficiente das regras, que pode comprometer a integridade do processo eleitoral.
Um dos exemplos citados foi a aplicação excessivamente rigorosa de políticas antifraude às contas de anúncios de Lula. Para o conselho, o episódio deveria ter sido encaminhado a uma equipe interna de especialistas responsável por analisar casos dessa natureza.
O colegiado também cobrou indicadores públicos que permitam avaliar de maneira transparente a eficácia das medidas de proteção eleitoral e identificar suas principais deficiências.
Em paralelo, especialistas independentes vinculados a mecanismos da Organização das Nações Unidas (ONU) questionaram se os sistemas de moderação, recomendação e IA da Meta restringiram de forma desproporcional conteúdos relacionados a um dos lados da disputa brasileira.
As manifestações ampliam a pressão para que a companhia explique como suas ferramentas funcionam e demonstre que as regras são aplicadas de maneira consistente.
Entidades também pediram investigação nos EUA
A carta dos 13 parlamentares foi precedida por uma iniciativa de organizações da sociedade civil que pediram ao Congresso estadunidense uma investigação sobre a atuação da Meta nas eleições brasileiras.
Em documento enviado em 20 de outubro, cinco organizações solicitaram esclarecimentos técnicos e a preservação de registros internos relacionados à moderação, à distribuição de publicações e à veiculação de anúncios políticos.
Entre os dados apresentados está um levantamento do NetLab, laboratório da Universidade Federal do Rio de Janeiro (UFRJ), que identificou pelo menos 1.613 anúncios político-eleitorais irregulares pagos em moeda estrangeira nas plataformas da Meta entre julho e setembro de 2026.
Segundo o levantamento, as publicações movimentaram aproximadamente R$ 2 milhões e acumularam 171,1 milhões de impressões. Entre os anúncios cuja origem pôde ser identificada, 98,1% indicavam os Estados Unidos.
As organizações defenderam auditorias independentes e maior transparência sobre os mecanismos usados pela empresa para identificar propaganda eleitoral irregular e aplicar suas políticas.
A Meta nega interferência eleitoral e afirma que trata as candidaturas de forma igualitária. Os questionamentos dos parlamentares estadunidenses, do Conselho de Supervisão e de organizações da sociedade civil, porém, ampliam a cobrança por explicações sobre o funcionamento dos sistemas da empresa em momento decisivo da eleição brasileira.
Rodrigo Mozelli é jornalista formado pela Universidade Metodista de São Paulo (UMESP) e, atualmente, é redator do Olhar Digital.

articles.title: Windows-Taste: Bekommt sie nach 30 Jahren eine neue Funktion?
articles.text:
Öffnet seit Jahrzehnten das Startmenü: Gibt Microsoft der Windows-Taste eine neue Funktion?
Bei der Einführung von Windows 95 im Jahr 1995 stellte Microsoft die Windows-Taste vor. Seitdem sitzt sie auf den meisten Tastaturen zwischen der Strg- und der Alt-Taste und öffnet zuverlässig das Startmenü. Die User:innen können darin ihren Rechner oder das Internet durchforsten.
Doch wie die Microsoft-Expert:innen von Windows Latest schreiben, könnte die Taste mit dem Windows-Symbol bald eine neue Funktion bekommen. Dies könnte laut dem Portal mit der neuen Suchleiste für Windows 11 zusammenhängen, an der Microsoft gerade arbeitet.
Fällt Windows-Taste neuer Suchleiste zum Opfer?
Microsoft kündigte Anfang Oktober dieses Jahres an, Windows Search im großen Stil umzumodeln. Das Desktop-Suchprogramm soll schneller und effizienter werden.
Dieser neu gestalteten Benutzeroberfläche könnte laut Windows Latest die Windows-Taste zum Opfer fallen. Denn laut dem Blog würde Windows Search dann genau dieselbe Funktion erfüllen wie die Suche, die sich nach einem Klick auf die Windows-Taste öffnet. Dass Microsoft zwei identische Features nebeneinander laufen lässt, scheint eher unwahrscheinlich.
Microsoft denkt über neue Funktion für Windows- Taste nach
Wenn Search künftig die Aufgabe der Windows-Taste übernimmt, würde der legendäre Button frei werden. Auf X schlug ein User vor, welche Funktion die Taste erfüllen könnte.
Der Nutzer kommentierte auf X einen Post von Microsoft-Mitarbeiterin Tali Roth, die auf der Plattform die neue Suchleiste feierte. Tali Roth ist bei dem Unternehmen für die Windows Shell Experience verantwortlich. Der User suggerierte, dass man künftig über die Windows-Taste E-Mails schreiben könnte.
„Sobald wir diese Funktion auch in Start integriert haben, werden wir uns mit der richtigen Funktionsweise der Windows-Taste befassen“, antwortete Tali Roth auf die Nachricht des Users.
Die Windows-Taste habe sich laut Roth in das Muskelgedächtnis vieler Nutzer:innen eingegraben. Aufgeben werde man sie also nicht.

articles.title: Uber puts all 30,000 employees on ChatGPT Work | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Uber and OpenAI announced an expansion of their partnership on Thursday, with the ride-share giant telling TechCrunch that its entire global workforce — some 30,000 people — will now be using ChatGPT Work.
ChatGPT Work was introduced in July as an enterprise-focused AI agent that corporate teams could deploy for various workflows.
Uber originally piloted ChatGPT Work with 1,000 employees earlier this year but has now scaled up its usage to the entire company.
That earlier pilot was deployed to workers from across Uber’s various departments, including finance, operations, and product. Indeed, a majority of the early adopters — some 80% — were non-engineers, Sumanth Sukumar, Uber’s VP of engineering, told TechCrunch.
“They used it for a wide range of tasks: analyzing complex data from our operations to identify trends and develop recommendations; localizing training materials for different markets and languages; and building personalized interactive dashboards to manage their daily work,” he said.
Yet while the ride-share giant is now going all in on ChatGPT, it has not settled on exactly how employees will use it. “Our approach is to make powerful AI tools available across Uber while giving teams room to experiment,” Sukumar said. “For example, earlier this year we paired 30 AI engineers with teams across Uber and gave them two weeks to automate key parts of their job. Those ‘AI pods’ showed us how much opportunity there is when you combine technical expertise with a deep understanding of a particular job.”
Uber didn’t disclose how much it’s spending on the new rollout of the chatbot. Instead, Sukumar said the company will track how employees use the tool. “We’ll look at how employees are using the technology, the kinds of workflows they develop and how it helps them work more effectively. We’ll evaluate those outcomes and use what we learn to guide how we deploy AI across the business,” he said. Uber says OpenAI worked closely with the company on integrating the chatbot.
OpenAI has moved quickly to scale up its enterprise business as it competes with its chief competitor, Anthropic. Once known largely as a consumer brand, the ChatGPT creator has swiftly gained a loyal following with business customers, while other AI companies have struggled to keep up.

articles.title: The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
articles.text:
On October 13th, Brendan Carr’s FCC gave itself a new power — it can block gadgets for containing any computer chip made by any company on its list of potential threats to national security. Today, it’s exercising that power for the first time, blocking two gadgets because they contain “foreign surveillance chips,” the FCC claims.
The FCC is beginning to block gadgets with ‘foreign surveillance chips’
The first exercise of a new FCC power.
The first exercise of a new FCC power.
The agency doesn’t say which specific gadgets it blocked, and it didn’t immediately respond to our request for comment, but it does name the “surveillance chip”: it’s a HiVision Hi3516CV610 UHD Smart Vision SoC, a chip that turns a raw camera sensor into a home security camera, a dashcam, or the like. It’s often sold as a package with a Sony camera sensor and sometimes even a lens already on board, according to listings we viewed on AliExpress.
The FCC is calling it a foreign surveillance chip because HiVision advertises it as “designed for the surveillance market” with “[b]uilt in detection algorithms for human faces,” the FCC explains — and because HiVision is a subsidiary of Huawei, one of the first telecom companies the US government decided to call a national security risk.
Huawei is indeed on the FCC’s Covered List, and the FCC’s new power helps it close a loophole where companies could sneak in banned companies’ products inside another company’s gadgets. It did something similar when it gave itself the power to retroactively ban gadgets, and when it gave itself the power to block modular radio transmitters.
As with the router ban and the Roomba ban, he question remains: is the FCC keeping people safer, or just picking winners and losers while making a show of enforcement? We’ve asked the agency many times to chat about its efforts, but it won’t engage.

articles.title: Why Engineers Should Brave Capitol Hill
articles.text:
When San Antonio–based software engineer Nikhil Jathar first went to Washington, D.C., to advocate for federal support for technology education and research funding, he was in awe of the opportunity. It was spring of 2025, not long after Jathar settled in the United States from India, when he got an invitation to join the annual Congressional Visits Day organized by IEEE-USA.
“My first reaction was, ‘Wow, I get to visit Congress,’ ” says Jathar, CTO of AvanSaber, a business software company he cofounded in 2014. At the time, he did not have a specific lobbying position on behalf of the company. But he was intrigued by the invitation—which goes out to all U.S. IEEE members—and as he read more about congressional visits, his motivation deepened. He realized: “I need to try this. I want to see where it goes.”
What’s Your Ask?
Congressional staffers expect clarity from advocates. Be clear on what you plan to ask for when you arrive. Here are some common options:
- Cosponsor (or oppose) an existing bill or amendment.
- Preserve, remove, or modify legislative text in a bill under consideration.
- Add language to an appropriations bill or committee report.
- Ask a federal agency a specific oversight question.
- Request a briefing, hearing, Government Accountability Office review, or stakeholder roundtable.
- Encourage an agency to clarify a technical rule.
Congressional staffers say they welcome the knowledge and perspective that engineers like Jathar and other visitors from beyond Washington, D.C., provide. It’s also important for those visitors to be clear on what they are advocating for. One staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology, who agreed to speak anonymously due to the office’s media policy, says, “Ideas for new policies come from multiple places. It could begin at the [legislator] or staff level, an ask from a constituent, or needs from industry. It’s up to us to figure out what would do the most good,” the staffer said. “For instance, if you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”
For engineers in the United States, speaking with elected representatives is an effective way to shape key policies, but it takes some preparation and the right approach, as Jathar learned over the course of two visits.
Mapping Your Way Into Washington
Congress’s job is to act on behalf of the people, and it has rules for how people can lobby it. It distinguishes between broader advocacy—conversations between constituents and U.S. representatives—and professional lobbying, which involves paid professionals and is governed by the Lobbying Disclosure Act. Many professional groups like IEEE also organize congressional visits for their members. Those visits can be subject to lobbying rules, so the organizers told Jathar that: “You are representing the organization, not your own views.” He would need to stick to the talking points IEEE-USA had prepared for all its participants, regardless of their specialty, to promote across several congressional offices.
On Jathar’s first visit, those organizational talking points included advocating for funding smart grids, authorizing Department of Energy research, and investing in STEM education. That represents one of the trade-offs of access in Washington. IEEE-USA’s priorities didn’t all overlap directly with Jathar’s work, but they were broad enablers of science and technology and, he says, “STEM education funding is close to my heart.”
Anyone can approach their representatives in Washington with their personal priorities, Jathar notes, but given how pressed for time congressional staff are, they are more likely to prioritize a meeting that represents the views of as many of their constituents as possible. “I could have gone outside the IEEE structure,” Jathar says, but congressional staff “are more likely to listen if you are part of a much bigger organization.”
For Jathar’s first congressional visit, organizers assigned him to call on the offices of several representatives from both political parties based on where he lives: Representatives Greg Casar (D-Texas), Lloyd Doggett (D-Texas), and Barry Moore (R-Ala.). “Meeting a staffer or a senior member from their office is good. They tend to relate to these issues more than a representative, because a representative has 10 different high-level things they have to worry about whereas the staffer can be more focused on the policy details,” Jathar says.
A typical visit like this may last anywhere from 15 minutes to an hour, so Jathar kept his talking points simple and short. “First and foremost you’re gonna get a very small window,” he says, “Make sure you’ve got everything ready to present in bullet points and not a lot of jargon. You can always bring that out later if they ask more questions.” Simple visual aids, in the form of one-page handouts, may be helpful for communicating numeric or technical information, too.
“If you leave it to the lobbyists, they’re understandably going to do what’s in their clients’ interests.”–Staffer for the House Committee on Science, Space, and Technology
The House Science Committee staffer agrees: “I prefer meetings where people know what they want and know what we’re doing in Congress.” In addition to having a clear request, the staffer says engineers and other advocates should keep track of where Congress is in its cycle: Is it appropriations season, and when is the next budget being set? How far along is a given piece of legislation in the process, and what is realistic to change at that point?
During Jathar’s 2025 visit to one Capitol Hill office, he learned firsthand the importance of preparation. For one of the three representatives he visited, staff politely pointed out that the legislator they worked for was not on the committee with jurisdiction over the IEEE-USA talking point they were discussing. “They explained that there are only certain things [the legislator] can do on that issue and that there are other people we need to talk to, to achieve more,” Jathar recalls.
Shortcuts to Influence
Earlier this year, Jathar decided to go back to Capitol Hill with his newfound knowledge, again within the framework of an IEEE-USA visit. This time he was able to provide something else legislative staff want from engineers: authoritative technical knowledge.
“When I introduced myself as a software developer to one staffer, his first question was, ‘Do you think AI will replace coders?’ ” Jathar says. The conversation went back and forth, with the staffer asking Jathar and his other engineering companions questions. Jathar went on to explain that his company developed an open-source business-management software it calls ERPClaw, designed to be used with AI agents such as OpenClaw. That led naturally to discussing the role of open source in AI, which plays a role in one of IEEE-USA’s proposals for democratizing AI. This time Jathar was able to align his organization’s advocacy with his expertise and the staffer’s areas of interest.
It’s too soon to know what legislative impact that advocacy might have, but it’s the sort of informed, relevant proposal that legislative staff seek out. “The people who build trust have more cachet with congressional staff because they’ve asked for something that’s reasonably thought out,” the House Science Committee staffer says. In turn, congressional staffers can advocate better within their offices for policies brought to them by people they trust.
And talking about the issues you care the most about can deepen that trust. The House Science Committee staffer once visited Congress as an advocate before switching to the other side of the table. On that visit, as on Jathar’s, the professional society organizing the visit provided a pitch. “I was making a pitch that was given to me without a lot of personal buy-in,” the staffer says. Instead, “you should feel emotionally connected to any issue you’re advocating for.”
Jathar’s support for the open-source movement is like that. Open source gives smaller companies a foundation they can adapt and build upon, while allowing other developers to extend that work. “We can progress a lot faster,” Jathar says. “I’m not doing it only because it’s good for my business, but because I feel it’s good for any technological advancement.”
