Lucas Laursen is the technology policy editor at IEEE Spectrum. He covers how emerging technologies are changing the balance of power between companies, governments, and individuals. The rest of the time, he worries about his own balance on a bicycle, skis, or the side of a mountain.

articles.title: Sauron recruits his future Ringwraiths in Rings of Power S3 trailer
articles.text:
Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power returns next month for its third season. Prime Video unveiled a teaser earlier this year at San Diego Comic-Con, but we haven’t heard much about the new season otherwise. We now have the official full trailer, and it’s jam-packed with a rising Sauron, who is intent on conquering Middle-Earth with his army of Orcs—with the fractured opposition of elves, dwarves, and men scrambling to figure out how best to stop him. We also meet the human men who will become the Ringwraiths; the showrunners have dubbed them the Nazgnagol (“Rings-servant”).
(Some spoilers for the first two seasons below.)
Prime Video made a major investment in The Rings of Power when it acquired the rights to the source material from the Tolkien estate, even committing to multiple seasons upfront. S3 is set seven years after the events of S2 and opens when the war between the elves and Sauron is at its height. Per the official synopsis:
In season three, Middle-earth is at war. Five years have passed since the fall of Eregion. Sauron’s armies have marched across the whole of the world, conquering all in their path. Only a few isolated pockets stand between the Dark Lord and total victory—Khazad-dǔm, where the Dwarves are now sealed deep within their mountain halls, and the elven realms of Lindon and Rivendell, which are protected by their Three Rings.
But deep in the land of Mordor, in his newly completed tower of Barad-dûr, the Dark Lord toils day and night, obsessed with harnessing a power that will bring the last of his enemies to their knees: One ring to rule them all. Now, all the free peoples of Middle-earth—Dwarves, Elves, Men, and Wizards alike—must find a way to come together, in a race against time to prevent Sauron from achieving his goal of utter domination of all life
We’re also getting some new characters this season, most notably Jamie Campbell Bower as Galadriel’s (Morfydd Clark) long-lost husband, Celeborn. Zubin Varla will play Khamul the Easterling of Rhun; Eddie Marsan will play Thrain, older brother to King Durin IV (Owain Arthur); Andrew Richardson will play Anarion, youngest son of Elendil (Lloyd Owen) and brother to Isildur (Maxim Baldry); and Adam Young will play an Orc named Marnukh, who “might not be what he seems.” Oh, and none other than Simon Pegg will voice the fiery Balrog.

articles.title: NVIDIA Cosmos Opens New Tools to Train, Evaluate and Deploy World Models
articles.text:
To help developers rapidly build world models, which help physical AI systems understand and simulate the real world, NVIDIA has expanded the Cosmos platform with new training tools, simulation checkpoints and Cosmos Data Factory blueprints.
Ranking top five on six different open models leaderboards, the NVIDIA Cosmos platform gives world model builders the frontier open models — as well as data, training and optimization tools and recipes — to scale training data, adapt models, test behavior and optimize for performance before deployment.
Build Better Training Data
Building world models begins with multimodal, multisensory data.
NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory brings together the tools and skills for labeling, curating, augmenting and evaluating data at scale for training physical AI. Cosmos Curator, a GPU-accelerated solution for curating video training datasets, has now added support for multimodal multisensory inputs and processing blocks.
Cosmos Data Factory now offers the following five cloud-native blueprints and is available through GitHub, Microsoft Azure, Nebius and CoreWeave:
- Autonomous Vehicle Dataset Generation: Curates and labels driving data, then adds synthetic examples of hard-to-capture scenarios to expand training coverage.
- Image Attribute Augmentation: Varies object appearance to improve image search.
- Event Video Generation: Turns still images into synthetic videos of rare or unsafe events.
- Defect Image Generation: Generates printed circuit board, metal and glass defect images for inspection models.
- Video Data Augmentation: Changes weather and lighting in existing footage while preserving scene structure.
Cosmos Data Factory accelerates data curation, processing and synthetic data generation with agentic skills.
Companies are already putting Cosmos Data Factory blueprints to work to speed their physical AI development workflows.
Porsche is leading the development of a shared AV data flywheel across Volkswagen Group brands, using Cosmos Data Factory through Voxel51 on Microsoft Azure. This is expected to reduce repeated physical test drives by up to 90% and shorten development cycle times by up to 85%.
Porsche searching and augmenting autonomous vehicle data footage in Voxel51, powered by Cosmos Data Factory.
ANYbotics generated over 1,500 synthetic video clips with Cosmos Data Factory blueprints, curating real-world data and validating outputs with Encord’s platform, to train its industrial-inspection robots to recognize liquid spills and other changes between facility visits.
ANYbotics generating anomaly clips with Encord powered by NVIDIA Cosmos Data Factory.
Ultralytics, a computer vision company, retrained its YOLO model with real images and targeted synthetic defects generated using Cosmos Data Factory, improving defect localization and recall.
Train, Adapt and Optimize Models
With training data prepared, developers may train their own architecture or start with a pretrained model.
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA extended Cosmos Framework training, optimization and deployment tools and recipes as agent skills to more open models, along with Cosmos 3, giving world model builders a faster path from experimentation to deployment.
Developers and agents can now adapt open models like GR00T, Alpamayo, QWEN, Pi0.5 and other compatible Hugging Face models through fine-tuning and reinforcement learning, optimize the model with distillation and quantization, and deploy with high-performing inference.
To develop a world model specialized for egocentric manipulation, robotics research lab MicroAGI post-trained Cosmos 3 on videos of humans manipulating objects and distilled its 32-billion-parameter reasoner down to an 8-billion-parameter Nano model with no loss in accuracy.
Developers can label data and post-train Cosmos 3 on Roboflow for their specific environments and tasks, then deploy those models to RoboFlow hosted or on-premises NVIDIA GPUs to bring video reasoning into factories and warehouses.
Test Policies and Run Models Faster
Alongside these tools, NVIDIA continues advancing foundational technology through its work on Cosmos models.
New Cosmos 3 Nano model variants for simulation enable developers to test autonomous policies in repeatable, hard-to-capture, multiview multisensor scenarios. Accompanying code allows developers to adapt the models to train and evaluate their own policies for autonomous vehicles and bimanual robots in interactive simulations before real-world testing.
Developers can deploy core Cosmos models using updated NVIDIA Cosmos 3 NIM microservices, which deliver up to 2x faster inference with no quality loss in validated configurations, while continuous video analysis enables sub-second alerts.
For vision AI developers, the new NVIDIA Metropolis Blueprint for video search and summarization (VSS) 3.3, built on Cosmos NIM microservices, turns one prompt into an efficient video AI application and helps teams monitor 40% more video streams with the same GPU.
ADNOC uses Fogsphere’s MistIQ agentic platform, built with Cosmos and the NVIDIA Metropolis VSS Blueprint, to detect safety hazards in real time across 65 sites. For rare events, Fogsphere also uses the Cosmos Data Factory to generate synthetic training data, improving detection without needing to physically stage dangerous situations.
The Cosmos platform is fully modular and open. Developers can use Cosmos Data Factory to generate training datasets, Cosmos Framework to train and adapt world models, then deploy supported Cosmos models through NIM microservices.

articles.title: How Companies Are Using NVIDIA DSX to Break the Power Bottleneck
articles.text:
Companies around the world are building on the NVIDIA DSX AI Factory Platform to plan, simulate and run the grid and the AI factory as one system, from the substation to the rack. Their adoption of the platform responds to an acute problem.
Power is now the biggest bottleneck in infrastructure. More than $300 billion in equipment is backlogged, and over 200 gigawatts of projects are waiting in U.S. interconnection queues.
One root cause of the bottleneck is siloed systems. The grid, the facility and the compute inside have long been designed independently from one another, creating the conditions for delays, risk and stranded capacity.
To help address this, NVIDIA DSX brings these systems together:
- NVIDIA DSX Sim and SimReady assets from leading energy manufacturers let engineers simulate the grid, substation and AI factory together, validating generators, switchgear, power systems and cooling before breaking ground.
- NVIDIA DSX Flex syncs AI factory demand with grid conditions and onsite generation, turning AI factories from static loads into flexible grid assets.
- NVIDIA DSX MaxLPS and DSX Exchange squeeze more compute from every watt and securely share signals across compute, networking, energy, cooling and operations.
GE Vernova is deploying its grid-to-facility and rack power expertise to complement NVIDIA DSX systems, enabling customers to transform power constraints into competitive advantages while maximizing compute and token output, sustainability and grid reliability.
Hitachi Energy’s battery energy storage system has qualified as NVIDIA DSX Ready, helping customers identify power infrastructure that meets applicable NVIDIA DSX reference architecture design requirements for resilient, reliable and scalable AI factories.
Schneider Electric, together with AVEVA and ETAP, is advancing NVIDIA DSX with validated NVIDIA Vera Rubin power and cooling reference architectures and an NVIDIA Omniverse-powered AI factory digital twin.
Combining AVEVA’s engineering software expertise with NVIDIA SimReady assets, OpenUSD and Omniverse enables connecting simulations, real-time operational data and AI-driven optimization across AVEVA, Schneider Electric and third-party solutions. Together, these capabilities help organizations design, simulate, operate and optimize data centers across their lifecycle, improving energy efficiency and workload performance while accelerating time to token.
Siemens Energy is expanding its collaboration with NVIDIA by developing a reference design for resilient, scalable and grid-aware power infrastructure across power generation, transmission and distribution. This design is aligned with the requirements of the NVIDIA DSX Vera Rubin AI factory design. The company is also exploring usingNVIDIA technologies such as RAPIDS, Metropolis and Isaac Sim for its Noedra digital twin platform, evaluating how the technologies could enhance grid infrastructure monitoring, identify emerging risks and support unplanned outage prevention.
Phaidra integrated DSX Flex, DSX Max-Q and DSX Exchange into its self-learning agents, optimizing cooling and power allocation to maximize tokens per watt, improve grid flexibility and deliver about 10% more compute within the same power envelope.
Emerald AI integrated its Conductor platform into DSX Flex to help utilities tap underused grid capacity, an approach modeled to unlock up to 100 gigawatts on the existing U.S. grid.
Explore the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint and the Vera Rubin DSX AI Factory Reference Design. Learn more from NVIDIA and energy leaders who are accelerating power-flexible AI factories to strengthen the grid at GTC Berlin.
Visit Hitachi Energy (booth 7004, hall 7), Schneider Electric (booth 3041, hall 3) and Siemens Energy (booth 3048, hall 3) and tune into sessions with Schneider Electric on Wednesday, Oct. 21: From Grid to AI: Engineering the Future of AI Factories and Energy Intelligence: Powering the AI Era.

articles.title: Forget "Malaise 2.0," GM says it's still all-in on EVs and autonomy
articles.text:
It’s easy to criticize US automakers and their tepid approach to electric vehicles under the current administration and the expiration of the EV tax credit. It’s also easy to look at the rest of the world’s embrace of EVs and wonder if the US is entering a “Malaise 2.0” era. Which is why GM wants the world to know that it is still focused on its end goals of electrification, autonomy, and improving vehicle quality while reducing development time.
At this year’s GM Forward event, company executives announced that its hands-off, eyes-off Super Cruise technology will expand across the lineup and be available on nearly every vehicle. This will include the pickup trucks and the crossovers, and not just the Escalade IQ that it was announced for last year.
Sterling Anderson, GM’s head of product, said the company is testing this technology to the tune of 1 million miles (1.6 million km) a month in both the virtual and real world. The goal is that not only would the vehicle be able to take you places, but it could go and do things for you.
That sounds rather dystopian. But Anderson told Ars in an interview that once you realize what your vehicle is capable of doing (beyond the paradigm of being a car to go places), it opens up a world of convenience that might be hard to envision right now. He’s not talking about an Optimus-style robot that’ll do your laundry, but a tool that you use every day that expands to do more things.
OnStar is your new PA
GM’s newly announced OnStar AI will play a role. “Imagine you worked late, and you get in your car to go home,” he told us. “Your car might remember that you ordered takeout from a restaurant recently that you frequent and like. The car could prompt you and place a pick-up order for you, which will be ready when you arrive to pick it up.”
Trust is the key here, and Anderson reiterated that several times, suggesting that a car might be a more trusted piece of technology than a mobile phone. “People have a relationship with their cars that they don’t have with other things,” he said. “If your phone randomly suggested your favorite restaurant, it might give you pause, but if your car did so within the appropriate context you might be more willing to accept that.”
OnStar AI will do more than just learn your habits; it will be able to help you better understand and better use your vehicle, we’re told. For example: a driver hears the car beep but doesn’t know what the alert was for. In this case, they could ask OnStar and it would be able to tell them—for example, a speed limit warning. Being a specialized AI trained specifically on the details of the car, it can be integrated in a way that other models, like Google’s Gemini, cannot.
GM’s new central compute module installed in a car.
Credit:
GM
GM’s new central compute module installed in a car.
Credit:
GM
Thanks to new compute on board, announced at last year’s Forward, the car will be able to handle much of that processing locally without requiring a connection to the cloud at all. But a cloud connection could improve the drive or make it safer. For some time now, automakers and suppliers have promised systems that crowdsource data to infer and predict road conditions—if you’re driving through a snowy area, and the cars in front of you have had traction control events, you could receive a warning to be extra careful as you approach.
GM also wants to keep customers within its own ecosystem. Imagine a two-car, two-GM OnStar AI household, and you’re late picking up your child from practice. Here, OnStar AI could look and see your spouse is actually closer, swap roles, and redirect you to the takeout place to pick up dinner. OK, it’s a very specific use case.
Can you trust it?
Trust continues to be the key. Anderson knows that must be earned, and trust is difficult to get back if it’s broken.
His approach is to put that customer trust first in what he does. For example, GM’s new infotainment system will have the ability to record from the cameras as a dash cam and store that video. And it can upload that video to GM’s cloud to access anywhere. But it is end-to-end encrypted, meaning that when it hits GM’s servers, it’s in a format that GM can’t read. If law enforcement wanted to view the video, GM wouldn’t be able to help because it could not decrypt the video.
That is the type of trust that is absolutely needed when dealing with this type of personal data, because there is a convenience to a lot of this. But the opportunity for that data to be misused is also there—it wasn’t too long ago that GM was found to be selling customers’ data, often without their knowledge, to insurance companies.
We’ll want to experience GM’s new attitude in practice, of course, but hearing an automotive executive directly address that concern head-on was refreshing.
Car, take the wheel
GM might have shuttered Cruise and mothballed the robotaxis, but it’s still working on autonomous vehicles.
Credit:
GM
GM might have shuttered Cruise and mothballed the robotaxis, but it’s still working on autonomous vehicles.
Credit:
GM
This all leads into the fully autonomous functionality that GM is working on. Ars also spoke with Rashed Haq, VP of Autonomous Vehicles at GM, about the current state of the level 4 technology, and more importantly, when it’ll be safe enough for customers to use.
“We look at two key factors, safety and roadcraft,” Haq told me.
Safety obviously includes the vehicle’s occupants, but also the general public. And that requires millions of miles of testing in the real world but also digitally. Automakers like GM will never be able to prepare for every scenario, but it will combine training data with an open vocabulary to assess what information is there and make a driving decision based on that. Haq also reiterated the company’s expectation that when the car is driven by the computer, the responsibility falls on GM and the computer if something goes wrong due to a malfunction.
The second key here is roadcraft. That means making sure that the vehicle isn’t creating a hazard or problem for other vehicles on the road. You’ve likely seen videos where Waymo vehicles are all crowded on a street blocking traffic: That’s not something GM wants its cars to do.
Eventually, all of this leads back to the idea of a car working for you for tasks that aren’t just driving places. Your car could go pick up your dry cleaning, or at least drive there and wait while someone comes out and deposits the clothes inside it. You could ride to school with a child, both sitting in the back seat, reclaiming some time together because the car is doing the mundane task of driving.
It’s an interesting idea and will only happen if consumers trust GM and their vehicle enough to do that, something we won’t know until closer to that technology maturing.
LMR batteries
A render of GM’s Gen-4 EV skateboard.
Credit:
GM
A render of GM’s Gen-4 EV skateboard.
Credit:
GM
GM also announced its Gen-4 EV architecture based on LMR battery technology. As we learned last year, the new lithium manganese-rich battery chemistry promises energy densities close to nickel-manganese-cobalt but without that expensive cobalt, making their cost closer to that of lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry cells.
A 30 percent cheaper battery should help GM offer a wide variety of EVs, hopefully including some affordable models, like the now-limited-run Bolt.
If GM can also deliver affordable autonomy, built on a foundation of trust and safety, it’ll be a unique offering from a US automaker and will put the company in a better position to take on the challenges from global competition.
How about this, buddy? I'll come in promptly at 8, take my lunch, work my day, leave at 5, and go home and make my own dinner. Silicon Valleyism must be eradicated, root and branch. Semi-ironically, car companies (for all their other ills) used to be kind of good at understanding this stuff.

articles.title: Foundries And OSATs Increasingly Overlap
articles.text:
Advanced packaging growth and capacity constraints are pushing more onto OSATs.
Key Takeaways:
Foundries and outsourced assembly and test (OSAT) houses have traditionally had distinct lanes, but the lines are blurring as OSATs acquire select foundry capabilities and foundries return some of the jobs they have taken from OSATs.
“We’re at this bridging point where the IDMs and the foundries are doing more of what OSATs can do, and the OSATs are also trying to get much closer to what the foundry does at the back end,” said Raghu Nayak, head of sales at Zeiss.
OSATs will never compete with foundries on advanced nodes and front-end wafer fabrication. But for backend activities, where dimensions aren’t as demanding, OSATs are acquiring capabilities that replicate what foundries can do. The biggest areas of overlap are 2.5D integration and panel assembly, with hybrid bonding likely to move there as well.
The change affects equipment and materials. “We are seeing the migration of lithography-related materials and processes from traditional wafer fabs into advanced packaging environments,” said Poupak Khodabandeh, chief business officer at Brewer Science. “As advanced packaging increasingly relies on fine-pitch redistribution layers (RDLs), OSATs and packaging organizations are using materials and process flows that historically would have been associated with wafer fabrication.”
“The industry has traditionally operated in silos across equipment, front-end fabrication, design, packaging, and test,” said Jack Berg, vice president of business development at Silvaco. “We need to connect those disciplines so teams can use shared, physics-grounded insight to make faster, better-informed design decisions, while also providing greater manufacturing flexibility — especially at the backend.”
It used to be “to each his own”
Foundries and OSATs have taken on complementary duties for many years. Foundries fabricate the silicon chip, while OSATs put the chip into a housing and test the final product. A vast array of EDA tools and fab equipment makes what the foundry does possible, while OSATs have worked more with tools that originated in the printed circuit board (PCB) world.
Two industry trends are challenging this status quo. The first is the development of advanced packaging. It’s no longer enough to put a chip on a substrate, wire it up, and pour molding compound over it. This doesn’t minimize the effort required to do those basics well, but they’re very different from what advanced packaging requires.
“Advanced packaging is becoming more lithography-intensive,” said Khodabandeh. “The industry’s push toward higher interconnect density for AI, HBM, chiplet architectures, and heterogeneous integration is driving the adoption of wafer-fab-style patterning processes within packaging facilities. RDL fabrication is a good example, where increasingly sophisticated lithography is required to create finer features.”
Intel Foundry works both sides of the aisle, with foundry and packaging capabilities. “When you do fine pitch bumps, the bump count goes up quite a bit compared to coarse pitch,” said Ravi Mahajan, fellow at Intel Foundry. “So you have to figure out things like embedding [bridge dies such as EMIB]. You have to figure out alignment and equipment precision.” For them, they can attempt these things on either side of the divide.
Foundries have been heavily involved in 2.5D packaging, but a second industry trend is making that more difficult — a lack of capacity. Foundries can’t make all the chips their clients want, so they’re prioritizing and allocating. That may mean turning away some business they would otherwise entertain, likely in backend and legacy processes, since foundries will focus on newer-node silicon processes they are uniquely capable of.
The OSATs are ready to pick up those processes. These are lower-resolution processes that foundries have historically employed but for which OSATs share capabilities. Legacy-node builds can spill over to assembly houses, especially since advanced packaging requires tooling consistent with those older technologies.
Although this overlap largely affects older processes, as constraints continue, even more aggressive technology, which foundries have often packaged (or done the first packaging steps) themselves, may be offloaded. “With further volume restrictions, both legacy-node and leading-edge products are shifting toward OSAT packaging,” said Thomas Uhrmann, vice president of sales at EV Group.
Three primary tasks
These market dynamics have driven three primary assembly-related processes from foundry to OSAT: 2.5D packaging, panel packaging, and eventually, hybrid bonding.
2.5D packaging in a manner resembling TSMC’s CoWoS (chip on wafer on substrate) involves mounting one die atop another. When the base is an interposer, this is 2.5D. When it’s another active die, it becomes 3D. Typical processes place the top die, already singulated, on a bottom die on a wafer that hasn’t been diced up yet. Once the top die is in place, the bottom wafer can be diced, with the stack-up headed for a package.
One fast-growing area that needs this technology is photonics. “Customers are coming to us asking if we can do electrical die to photonics die or wafer attach,” said Gerard John, senior director in Amkor’s Chiplets/FCBGA Business Unit. “We take this module, dice it out, and then attach it to a substrate. That’s a new trend we are seeing, and we can do that.”
It may, however, bring some tough new requirements. “This is a big challenge because now you have the optic side of the wafer or die,” added John, and this needs active alignment to attach fibers and test them.
Panels, meanwhile, have grown to the 500 mm range per side, but moving to a smaller size actually helped. “Several OSATs had early development lines for panel-level packaging, mainly targeting large panels with 500 mm dimensions,” explained Uhrmann. “TSMC’s decision to move to panel-level packaging with 310 × 310 mm2, which is a format closer to classical 300 mm round process tools, has enabled traditional wafer-based equipment manufacturers to scale up for high-performance materials and resolution, rather than PCB equipment manufacturers to scale down.”
Meanwhile, some assembly houses are doing hybrid bonding. But for high volume, it largely remains a foundry task, owing to the challenges the process presents. As hybrid bonding loses its novelty and becomes standard, it represents another task that foundries could hand off to OSATs.
How are you paying for that?
Whereas foundries typically have the equipment for these processes, OSATs have to invest to match those capabilities. They’re not buying leading-edge stuff (you’re not going to find EUV in an OSAT), but they are equipping themselves with tools they haven’t traditionally used.
The return-on-investment (ROI) outlook for these capital purchases appears to be very good. The first thing one needs for a good ROI is a sizeable, growing market. Advanced packaging is now common enough (while supporting high-revenue markets such as AI in the data center) to promise a reasonable payoff. Fortune Business Insights says advanced packaging grew to over $45B in 2025 and expects it to reach $100B by 2034, with a CAGR (compound annual growth rate) just over 9%.
“If you look at ASE alone, the company has already passed its $3.5 billion target for leading-edge packaging this year, and it is expecting to double that in 2027,” noted Uhrmann.
Backend processes are becoming more important to foundries. Much of the performance advantage being sought comes from innovative packaging technologies rather than smaller transistors.
“This performance race is driven primarily by AI and high-performance computing, where margins are exceptionally high, partly due to constrained supply,” observed Uhrmann. “The margin is shifting from front-end chip manufacturing toward packaging and system integration, because a growing share of system performance now comes from advanced packaging, heterogeneous integration and 3D integration rather than from node scaling alone.”
So fabs would typically want to hang on to that business. Not only is there an ROI, but it is likely to come sooner than the ROI from advanced front-end tools.
OSATs have different economics. “Their business model is based on cost competitiveness and volume, with structurally lower margins than foundries, which makes ROI highly dependent on utilization and long-term customer commitments,” said Uhrmann.
Because foundries are oversubscribed, OSATs are also fully utilized, which favors ROI. “The sector is constrained by equipment lead times and cleanroom space rather than by orders,” said Uhrmann. “In this environment, investments in 2.5D, panel-level and test equipment pay back quickly.”
But if OSATs largely fulfill a spillover role when markets get tight, then foundries are in a position to win under most circumstances, whereas OSATs could be more exposed to economic cycles as the need for overflow comes and goes.
Waiting in the wings
Hybrid bonding is yet another technology that could spill over, but which hasn’t yet in high volume. OSATs are getting into the game, but foundries still dominate, and that could continue as long as advanced packages are managed vertically, with one company sourcing all the chiplets.
“Hybrid bonding is a foundry and IDM-dominated technology,” explained Uhrmann. “As long as the demand can be covered by the incumbent suppliers, there is no logic in investing by the OSATs.”
But when heterogeneous integration starts bringing different dies from different technologies and sources — think memory and photonics — it may make more sense for OSATs to participate in that business as well. That will require more equipment purchases.
“We expect hybrid bonding to follow the same path as CoWoS: adoption begins at the foundries, and once demand exceeds foundry capacity and processes mature, it will expand to OSATs as a second source,” said Uhrmann.
All in all, OSATs are buying equipment at a healthy clip, not just to take on new processes, but to simply to add capacity. Amkor, for instance, is investing in a new Arizona facility. And purchases are increasing. ASE spent $3.4B on equipment and raised its 2026 budget by 27%. And even after that, mid-year it raised its capital spend by another $1.5B, of which $600M is for equipment, according to Seeking Alpha.
Ultimately, having each side work on what the other side used to do can result in new business. “It creates more of an opportunity to understand these new architectures,” said Sanjiv Bhatt, senior director of global marketing and business development for the semiconductor business at Mitsubishi Chemical. “But it requires us to work with all stakeholders, including the tool makers, on how they are going to incorporate these new materials and tools.”

articles.title: Tesla revendique son « carnet de commandes le plus important en quatre ans », mais la production coince - Numerama
articles.text:
Pour Tesla, le problème n’est plus de trouver des acheteurs pour ses véhicules électriques, mais de réussir à les fabriquer et les acheminer rapidement. Entre un carnet de commandes qui explose et des usines poussées à plein régime, la marque doit néanmoins composer avec des goulets d’étranglement sur sa chaîne logistique, à commencer par le nerf de la guerre : les cellules de batterie.
Le mauvais souvenir de la fin de 2024 et du début de 2025 est désormais loin derrière. À l’occasion de sa conférence sur les résultats financiers du troisième trimestre 2026, ce mercredi 21 octobre, Tesla a balayé d’un revers de la main tous les doutes. Derrière l’enthousiasme affiché, la situation est pourtant moins idyllique qu’il n’y paraît.
Des carnets de commandes pleins à craquer, mais des batteries qui freinent le rythme
Face aux analystes financiers, la direction de Tesla n’a pas caché sa satisfaction : l’entreprise boucle son trimestre avec son carnet de réservations le plus garni depuis 2022. « La demande pour nos véhicules croît rapidement et dépasse largement notre production », a indiqué Elon Musk dès l’ouverture de sa prise de parole. Le directeur financier, Vaibhav Taneja, a ensuite confirmé la tendance : « Dans le secteur automobile, nous avons clôturé le trimestre avec notre carnet de commandes le plus important depuis quatre ans, les livraisons étant principalement limitées par la production. »
Tesla peut remercier le marché européen pour ce coup de boost inespéré de la demande. Les résultats en Chine et aux États-Unis sont loin d’être aussi spectaculaires.
Pour absorber cette tendance, Tesla pousse ses lignes de montage à des cadences supérieures. « Nous augmentons donc notre production de manière significative », a affirmé Elon Musk. L’objectif est de produire 5 millions de véhicules par an d’ici à 2030. « Et je pense que nous avons de bonnes chances d’y parvenir », précise le patron de la marque. Mais il y a une différence entre vouloir accélérer les cadences d’assemblage et pouvoir le faire, surtout lorsque la chaîne d’approvisionnement se tend sur l’élément clé des batteries.
Interrogé sur le rythme effectif des usines, Lars Moravy, vice-président de l’ingénierie des véhicules, a rappelé : « Nos usines fonctionnent à des cadences records ce trimestre. Bien entendu, leur capacité de production est directement liée au processus ou au composant le plus fragile. » Tesla indique que la disponibilité des batteries est restée le « facteur limitant » l’augmentation des volumes automobiles, dans un contexte de carnet de commandes le plus élevé depuis quatre ans et de très forte demande pour le stockage stationnaire.
« Ils ne demandent pas une Model Y, ils demandent le FSD »
Tesla n’attribue plus le boom des commandes à la qualité de ses véhicules ou à son tarif compétitif, mais au succès de son logiciel de conduite autonome : Full Self-Driving (FSD) et ses autres déclinaisons selon les marchés. « Le principal moteur de cette demande est la conduite entièrement autonome », a affirmé Elon Musk dans son introduction. Selon lui, « Aujourd’hui, aucun véhicule disponible sur le marché ne propose la conduite entièrement autonome », mais cette affirmation est à prendre avec des pincettes, car la concurrence est bel et bien en embuscade sur le sujet sur certains marchés (juste pas aux États-Unis).
Le directeur financier apporte même un éclairage encore plus précis : « Dans nos concessions aux États-Unis, les clients entrent et demandent : « Peut-on avoir un véhicule avec conduite entièrement autonome ? » Ils ne demandent pas une Model Y ou un Cybertruck. Ils demandent : « Peut-on avoir un véhicule avec conduite entièrement autonome ? » Et c’est devenu le principal argument de vente, car cela offre une bien plus grande flexibilité à différentes catégories de la population qui avaient des difficultés à conduire auparavant. »
La direction de Tesla a apporté quelques exemples chiffrés en ce sens. Au troisième trimestre, plus de 75 % des clients nord-américains ont souscrit un abonnement FSD payant au moment de prendre livraison de leur véhicule, soit près de 20 points de plus qu’au trimestre précédent. La flotte compte désormais plus de 1,7 million d’utilisateurs payants du FSD dans le monde, dont 50 % ont désormais basculé sur la formule d’abonnement mensuel plutôt que sur l’achat comptant.
Ce plébiscite du FSD permet d’ailleurs à Tesla de porter sa marge automobile, hors crédits réglementaires, à 18,1 % (contre 16,3 % au deuxième trimestre). Reste désormais à exporter ce modèle économique lucratif hors d’Amérique du Nord. Alors que Tesla multiplie les tests et les gestes pour préparer le terrain en Europe, Elon Musk espère une homologation paneuropéenne du FSD très prochainement : « C’est difficile à prévoir, mais peut-être d’ici quelques mois. Je serais surpris que cela prenne plus longtemps que le premier trimestre [2027]. »
En affirmant sans ciller que ses carnets de commandes débordent et que le FSD est désormais l’unique moteur d’achat, la direction balaie d’un revers de main le contexte géopolitique qui booste ses ventes en Europe, le vieillissement de sa gamme et la concurrence chinoise qui grignote ses parts de marché sur deux de ses trois principaux marchés. À force de survendre un narratif où le monde entier réclamerait des robotaxis plutôt que des voitures électriques abordables et bien finies, Tesla prend le risque de s’enfermer dans sa propre bulle, déconnectée des vraies attentes du marché. Attention au retour du boomerang.

articles.title: Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
articles.text:
Oh sure, SpaceX’s credit risk is pretty high because it’s about to borrow another $40 billion to spend on Nvidia chips, but who cares about that? SpaceX and Tesla have formed special committees to discuss a merger!
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
Sure, let’s smoosh SpaceX and Tesla together, who cares
Yes, of course there are pay package incentives in play for Musk. But that’s not all.
The degree to which you find this merger compelling likely has to do with the degree to which you believe Elon Musk about wanting to go to Mars, or “spread the light of consciousness,” as he put it in this week’s SpaceX earnings call (and earlier S-1). Now, a reasonably informed person knows that we don’t have the technology — or, frankly, even the raw information to build the technology — in order to support human life in space. So that means robots. But a lag between Earth and the Moon or Mars makes for difficulty in controlling the robots. So having artificially intelligent robots who can make decisions on their own with minimal supervision from Earth is the next sci-fi logic step.
“There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.”
If you believe Musk’s story, the technology we are talking about is being developed through self-driving cars (Tesla), LLMs (SpaceX), and humanoid robots (Tesla), all of which require data centers (SpaceX). Conveniently, we have just had earnings for both companies. On the other hand, if you view Mars as a useful fiction Musk uses to explain his antics in public, well, there’s a lot of money and a lot of control Musk gets from the merger.
Musk said on the recent SpaceX earnings call that “there’s a lot of merit to combining” SpaceX and Tesla. Why? “There’s a lot to be gained from cooperating on developing superintelligence software.” But artificial intelligence — ah, excuse me, super intelligence software isn’t the business SpaceX is really in right now. In its Q3 earnings on Tuesday, SpaceX reported $7.56 billion in revenue from the artificial intelligence — sorry, sorry, super intelligence division. The subcategory “SI solutions & infrastructure revenues” — which I think is Grok, Cursor, and the neocloud business wrapped together — jumped to $7 billion, or more than three times what it was last quarter. Now some of this was getting Cursor stapled on, which added $608 million in revenue. Most of the rest of that $7 billion was likely renting out compute to Anthropic and Google; Grok is probably contributing less, says Gil Luria, an analyst at DA Davidson.
At first blush, this may look comparable to the revenue of a company like Anthropic, whose leaked S-1 shows the company had $16.3 billion in revenue in the first half of this year from its frontier models. But SpaceX’s AI business looks more like CoreWeave than Anthropic. While we are told in the press release there was “increased Grok adoption across enterprise customers and consumers,” that number wasn’t broken out from bare-metal revenue. And if Musk wanted to brag about it, he would.
As for Tesla, which released Q3 results on Wednesday, its earnings sucked — a second consecutive quarter of declining profits. That’s because Musk is apparently not especially interested in normal cars anymore. Instead, Tesla is focusing on robots and, I guess, self-driving taxis. (There was also a Roadster hopping car demo recently, but that’s not going into production for a couple years, it’s very expensive, and Tesla cannot guarantee it will be delivered.) Musk did not elaborate on his comments about the merger on the Tesla call.
Macroharder
SpaceX and Tesla have some tie-ups already; SpaceX, for instance, bought $131 million of the low-selling Cybertrucks from Tesla. It has, in the past, held Tesla bonds. More crucially, the companies have also announced two AI — fuck it, we’re just sticking with AI — projects together: Terafab and Macrohard.
Terafab is the chip-making venture that Musk intends to build in Texas and run to supply himself with chips; Intel is partnered, kinda, with Musk to develop the technology. Macrohard is, uh, an AI project that lets people simulate software already made by Microsoft. At least, I think that’s what it’s supposed to be. Typing the name of the latter makes me pray for the asteroid to hit us all right now, so perhaps it’s fortunate that we haven’t heard much about it since the announcement in March.
“Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement
SpaceX’s S-1 from May said that Terafab and Microhard “are in the very early stages, as a result of which we and Tesla have not finalized a variety of details relating to our collaboration, including, but not limited to, financial terms, intellectual property rights, and the ultimate term of our collaboration.” As of earlier this month, Intel’s CEO said the company remained committed to the partnership, but it’s not obligated to remain part of Terafab and the S-1 says there may never be a definitive agreement. Intel’s Thomas Hannaford didn’t immediately respond to my emails asking if anything had been signed in the interim.
On this week’s call with SpaceX investors, Musk claimed the Terafab will reach volume production in the second half of 2028. He also said the company will have its first test chip from the facility in May or June 2027. “Musk has a history of setting timelines that his companies have missed,” Reuters notes, with a degree of what I can only describe as wry understatement. When an analyst on the call asked if Musk had placed orders for machines needed to make cutting-edge equipment, Musk did not answer.
Companies often are doing more privately than they announce publicly, so I do not view the S-1 filing as fully definitive. But Macrohard isn’t mentioned in the last 10Q. Neither is Terafab.
The Matt Levine case for the SpaceX-Tesla merger
Musk is going to pound the table about the Moon, Mars, “and beyond,” and a significant chunk of his fan base is very into this. But there are maybe some boring financial reasons shareholders may have an interest.
Let’s say you are constitutionally very different from me, and much richer, and for this reason you own a number of shares in Tesla. You’re a big believer in Elon Musk — obviously — but you notice that the man has an attention span of a squirrel on cocaine. He’s on X basically constantly and often racistly. He keeps showing up at the White House to do stuff that pisses off would-be Tesla customers. Then he publicly feuds with the president. Sometimes he’s very excited about rockets, and sometimes he’s very excited about Dogecoin and sometimes he’s really into Grok and sometimes he thinks about cars. But you notice that one way or the other he’s been thinking about cars a lot less lately.
Basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money
Since he seems to be focused — insofar as he can be said to focus — on AI, you notice some pretty big conflicts of interest. Musk’s companies “all need the same scarce Nvidia chips to power their AI, for instance,” notes Matt Levine, a longtime Musk observer. But if you combine the companies, well, maybe you build the best general-purpose AI. And then? “If you build the best general-purpose AI model, maybe it can drive the cars and operate the robots and upload people’s brains and serve right-wing takes on Twitter.”
Also, there’s a massive AI infrastructure buildout happening, and so basically all you have to do is say “Nvidia” and someone will give you a fuckton of money. The merger puts all the AI projects in one pile, plus also some cars and rockets and satellites I guess. “‘Give us $100 billion to build data centers in space, but if for some reason we don’t build data centers in space you can repossess our car factories and data centers on earth’ is a good pitch to credit investors,” Levine writes.
Musk also has a history — not always successful — of building physical infrastructure. This is, at least from my point of view, a better bet when it comes to building data centers than some Bitcoin miners who pivoted. “If Elon builds at the rate he talked about, he will have lots of extra capacity and be able to sell much of it,” says Luria.
From this point of view, obviously SpaceX and Tesla should merge, Levine writes:
It’s crazy that they are separate companies! One guy runs two gigantic physical AI companies with huge overlaps! What a nightmare of conflicts of interest and red tape! Just merge them, so that the one guy can come into the office each day with a simple mandate: Make the choices that maximize overall value for the giant AI complex, and for the shareholders of that complex. If some chips or engineers or drills or whatever should be working on robots, work on the robots; if they should be working on data centers, work on the data centers. The shareholders have come this far; surely they trust Musk to make those decisions. It’s just that right now, working on the robots is good for Tesla and bad for SpaceX; working on the data centers is bad for Tesla and good for SpaceX. Musk can’t put both of their interests first. There’s an easy fix.
It’s not exactly that simple, of course. The details of the deal matter; a lot of people are assuming a stock-for-stock merger. (“I assume the acquirer would be SpaceX, in part because it has a bigger market capitalization but mostly because of Musk’s greater control there,” Levine writes.) So does the regulatory environment. The case that SpaceX and Tesla should combine due to AI is also kind of an antitrust reason they shouldn’t?
The current regulatory environment is, in large part due to Musk’s meddling via his DOGE cronies, let’s say lax. Donald Trump, the current president, has two more years left in his term. Also, the markets have started getting waves of nervousness around AI. Earlier this summer, there was the Situational Awareness thing, and then there was the more recent CoreWeave thing, and, well, investor sentiment may be changing. That means “there’s a push to announce a deal by the first half of 2027 so that it closes during this administration,” Bloomberg writes, attributing this to “people who are familiar with the matter.”
Musk has more control at SpaceX than he does at Tesla. His voting power is above 50 percent, because he owns special supervoting shares. He is the CEO, CTO, and chairman of the board. Shareholders are very limited in how they can legally challenge that power. The filing puts it this way: “This will limit or preclude your ability to influence corporate matters and the election of our directors.”
At Tesla, however, Musk only has about 20 percent of the vote. (“Only!”) So in a stock-for-stock merger, where SpaceX is the acquirer, Musk suddenly has voting control of the whole enchilada. “He gets voting control of Tesla in the only way he can,” says Ann Lipton, a professor at the University of Colorado Boulder’s law school. “He can’t change it to a dual-class entity now that it’s publicly traded. This is the only way to do it.”
If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more for Tesla, Musk gets a payout
Both companies are based in Texas, which makes it very difficult for shareholders to sue, says Lipton. “The chances of a shareholder being able to sue on the Tesla or SpaceX side are vanishingly small because Texas has erected so many barriers to shareholder litigation.” So there’s that risk gone.
Leave aside the more complicated issues of national security (for SpaceX) and antitrust. At a federal level, securities laws are largely “Did you disclose it?” notes Lipton. So the SEC, or what remains of it, will want to see that everything is disclosed to shareholders before the vote. As long as the disclosures are accurate, that’s that. At the state level, there may be some issues — it’s a breach of fiduciary duty to create an unfair transaction as a result of conflicts of interest — but Shari Redstone did merge Paramount and CBS, so it’s not impossible.
What does Musk get from this merger? Well, control, a thing he historically loves most of all. Potentially also, the combination adds $110 billion to his net worth, according to Bloomberg. More interesting, however, is how the merger interacts with Musk’s massive Tesla compensation package. If there’s a legal change of control — for instance, because SpaceX buys Tesla — the operational milestones in Musk’s enormous pay package fall away.
What matters then is Tesla’s valuation. If SpaceX pays $2 trillion or more, Musk gets a payout. At $2 trillion, Musk gets $6 billion of shares. He also gets accelerated vesting of shares from his 2018 pay package — which would otherwise have vested in 2028. The change of control also means he can sell them sooner.
Is that good for SpaceX? Assuming we wind up at or around the $2 trillion figure, we’re looking at basically a merger of equals — which means current SpaceX shareholders get diluted all to hell. Worse, Tesla’s business is stagnating, and its AI ambitions are expensive. “It’s likely that SpaceX and Tesla combined will spend close to a staggering $50 billion on capex in Q4, and their businesses won’t come close to covering that number,” writes Shawn Tully in Fortune.
So on a numbers basis, I kind of think no, not really, not that good for SpaceX. But none of Musk’s businesses are about numbers in the end — they are, to some extent, about how much you believe in Elon Musk. That’s what the Tesla valuation versus regular automakers was about in the first place. So sure, fine, slap them together and see what happens. The people who are buying what Musk’s selling, at this point, surely know what they signed up for.

articles.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations - Microsoft Research
articles.text:
At a glance
- Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions.
- Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators.
- Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations.
- Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another.
AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations.: We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: 
- (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select?
- (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data?
Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face:
- High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time.
- Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them.
These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions.
ACADEMIC CONFERENCE
Flint-interactive
Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications.
How to use
1. Use Flint in your chat
Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation.
2. Build an interactive app with Flint
Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas.
3. Create bespoke interactions
To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks.
How it works
Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level:
- Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates.
- Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states.
This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards.
Try it now!
Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery.
App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab). Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app.
Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab), design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary.

articles.title: Qotom Q51551UT 4x 10GbE and 6x 2.5GbE Mini PC Review
articles.text:
With a sea of performance and efficient cores, an Intel iGPU, NPU, six 2.5GbE ports, two SFP+ 10G ports, and two 10Gbase-T ports, the Qotom Q51551UT does a bit of everything. At first, you might think this is a networking box looking at the rear panel. Then you see multiple display outputs and wonder if it is a desktop. Once you install Proxmox VE, it becomes a virtualization platform. While it can do a lot, several caveats make it interesting enough that we also have a video for it, debuting some of our new graphics look.
Today we are looking at a Qotom design that places heavy emphasis on networking: the Qotom Q51551UT. Part of the company’s larger Q31500UT S18 Series, the Q51551UT features eight RJ45 Ethernet jacks, plus a couple more SFP+ ports for good measure. As a result, the mini-PC is well suited to networking-centric workloads that require multiple high-speed Ethernet connections, whether as a software firewall or a more typical edge computer.
| Qotom Q51551UT Key Specs |  | 
| Processor | Intel Core Ultra 5 125H, 4P + 8E + 2LPE (4.5GHz) | 
| Operating System | Pre-Installed: None (As tested: Ubuntu 26.04 LTS) | 
| Memory | 96GB DDR5-5600 (2x48GB SO-DIMM) | 
| System Storage | 128GB SSD (PCIe Gen3 x4, M.2 2242) | 
| PCIe Slots | 1x Headless PCIe x16 (Gen5 x8 Electrical) | 
| GPU | Intel Arc Graphics (Xe-LPG, 7 cores) | 
| PSU | 120W External PSU | 
| Form Factor | Mini-PC | 
| Dimensions | 200 x 200 x 53 mm (7.9 x 7.9 x 2.1 in) | 
| Weight | 1.75 kg (3.9lbs) | 
| Networking | 6x 2.5GbE (RJ45, Intel I226-V) 2x 10GbE (RJ45, Intel X540-AT2) 2x 10GbE (SFP+, Intel X710-BM2) | 
| Color | Silver (Aluminum) | 
| Ports | Front: 1x USB-A 5Gbps, 4x USB-A 480Mbps, 3.5mm Audio Jack, 1x Serial (RJ45) Rear: 2x USB-A 5Gbps, 1x USB-C 5Gbps, 1x DisplayPort 1.4, 1x HDMI 2.0, 6x 2.5GbE (RJ45), 2x 10GbE (RJ45), 2x 10GbE (SFP+) | 
The Q51551UT is notable because it has no “slow” Ethernet interfaces. Every single port is at least 2.5GbE, while a smaller set of ports (including the SFP+ ports) supports 10GbE. So it is not just a mini-PC with a lot of connectivity. It is a mini-PC with the bandwidth to back it up.
Here is an AliExpress Affiliate link to the unit. Always double-check the options before you buy.
Qotom Q51551UT External Hardware Overview
With this type of system, we typically see two styles: either a fully passive system filled with heatsink fins, or a smaller system that relies on active cooling. Qotom’s Q51551UT falls into the latter category, using a low-profile blower to cool the system. With ventilation on virtually every side except the front, it is a downright airy system.
Starting our brief tour from the front of the system, the Q51551UT looks like a fairly consumer-ish mini-PC at first glance, with a mix of power buttons and I/O ports. Looking a bit more closely, though, we can quickly see the telltale signs that this mini-PC is geared toward the industrial market.
All told, Qotom has equipped the system with five USB-A ports on the front. Only one of these ports supports high-speed (5Gbps) operation. The rest are USB 2.0 ports (480Mbps), designed to hook up a larger-than-normal number of peripherals. As we will see in a bit, part of this design is also pragmatic, since the rear of the system is consumed by Ethernet ports.
Speaking of networking, the system has an RJ45 jack on the front. But this is not an Ethernet jack. Instead, it is an RJ45-form-factor RS-232 serial port. Next to it are the system status LEDs and a ringed power button.
While Qotom’s promotional material shows the system in multiple orientations, in practice it is meant to sit on its side unless you mount it via a VESA bracket. That is because only the left edge (or rather, bottom edge) has any rubber feet, while the bottom lacks any mechanism to elevate the system and keep its bottom air intake cool.
Shifting gears to the rear of the system, here we can see the Q51551UT’s true specialization in action: Ethernet ports. Lots of Ethernet ports.
With 10 ports in total, the Q51551UT is a networking powerhouse in both the number of connections and the bandwidth available.
Starting from the right side, we have a pair of SFP+ ports driven by an Intel X710-BM2 controller. The Fortville controller is over a decade old, but it has proven to be a reliable networking platform, giving the Q51551UT the option of using either 1GbE or 10GbE modules and an easy way to add optical networking to the system.
To the left, we have the first two RJ45 Ethernet jacks, which are a distinctive red. This indicates they are 10GbE jacks, powered by Intel’s X540-AT2 (Twinville) controller. This dual-port 10GbE controller gives the system a pair of ports for copper 10GbE connectivity. Selecting the X540 controller is a bit puzzling, as it is a 16-year-old (and long-discontinued) Intel design that predates the newer NBASE-T standard, meaning these ports don’t support the intermediate 2.5Gbps or 5Gbps speeds. For carefully planned applications, this should not be an issue, but it is an atypically inflexible design for a modern mini-PC.
That said, if you need 2.5Gbps connectivity, Qotom has you covered with the remaining Ethernet ports. To the left of the 10GbE jacks are six additional RJ45 Ethernet jacks, all powered by Intel’s I226-V controller. Using the company’s modern mainstream 2.5GbE controller, these ports can run at up to 2.5Gbps or any speed below that, and they provide most of the mini-PC’s network connectivity.
However, Qotom’s specification sheet indicates that the RJ45 jacks are wired so there is not enough bandwidth to run every NIC at full speed at once. Each of the 2.5GbE ports has a Gen2 x1 connection, and two of the 10G ports share 12Gbps of upstream bandwidth, while the other two 10G ports have sufficient PCIe connectivity. We will get into that later in our review.
Aside from network connectivity, the rest of the rear I/O space on the Q51551UT is for USB and display connectivity. Here is the system’s sole USB-C port, which runs at just 5Gbps. At the far edge are two additional 5Gbps USB-A ports.
Between those are the system’s display outputs: an HDMI 2.0 port and a DisplayPort 1.4 output. Both of these are attached to the Core Ultra 5 125H’s integrated GPU, which can easily drive displays up to 4K. One ancillary market for the Q51551UT is digital signage, and while two display outputs do not particularly stand out, they are enough to get the job done. It also means we have an Intel iGPU for Quick Sync onboard.
Finally, we can quickly see the DC barrel jack for the system’s external power supply. Note that while the case is labeled “12V” the system takes a 19V adapter, with our system shipping with a 120W unit.
Taking a quick look at the top of the system, we can see this side is fairly open, with a large grate that provides plenty of airflow clearance. We can also just barely make out the blower fan driving the system’s active air cooling.
With the external tour complete, let us crack open the Q51551UT and take a look inside.
So no chance of it routing 10Gbs at line speed between any of the 10Gbe or SFP+ ports

articles.title: 333 Tor exit nodes hijacked to intercept SSH traffic and retrieve plaintext email
articles.text:
Unknown hackers hijacked more than 300 Tor exit nodes and reconfigured them to favor unencrypted email traffic and redirect SSH connections through servers they controlled, a researcher reported Tuesday.
The hijacking began in late August, when, according to Tor volunteers, the attacker used a valid password that had been reused to gain access to a Tor management server. The attacker then installed Ebury, a backdoor written for Linux that was discovered 12 years ago.
Mysteries remain
Then the attacker connected from the management server to a second Tor server, called Switzerland2, through SSH, using an RSA key that, for unknown reasons, investigators couldn’t find among Switzerland2’s authorized keys. With administrative control of Switzerland2, the attackers installed Ebury there as well. Finally, the attacker reconfigured settings on two exit nodes that Switzerland2 hosted.
Ultimately, 333 exit relays were involved in the SSH and email interception campaign, although investigators haven’t established how the attackers gained control of all the underlying servers. The attackers then reconfigured the servers. One set of changes redirected SSH traffic traversing Tor to one of 12 attacker-controlled interceptor servers. Tor users who ignored warnings that the SSH host key had changed would then enter their SSH passwords.
A second set of changes caused the exit nodes to block ports 25, 465, 587, 993, and 995—used to accept various forms of encrypted email—while continuing to allow ports for receiving unencrypted email. If email services downgraded the connections, the attackers used their access to the exit nodes to obtain unencrypted messages. It’s unclear whether any such downgrade attempts succeeded. The hijacking occurred from October 2 to October 5.
Tor volunteers partially outlined the initial compromise of the management server and Switzerland2 and the attempt to intercept unencrypted email. Tuesday’s report revealed many new details, including how many exit nodes were compromised and how the attackers used them to redirect SSH traffic.
“If you happen to get a circuit that exits over one of those 333 infected exit nodes, you won’t notice anything at first,” Kaba, the name of the Tor volunteer who authored the post, wrote. “Encrypted web traffic is forwarded as usual, but if you attempt an SSH connection over Port 22, you’re unknowingly redirected to one of 12 SSH interception servers. That’s exactly what happened to me on Friday morning.” Kaba then received the following warning:
https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc3207/#section-2

articles.title: Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
articles.text:
Physicists discover “astonishing” property of light that defies expectations
- Date:
- October 13, 2026
- Source:
- University of East Anglia
- Summary:
- Scientists have uncovered a surprising hidden ability of light that allows it to develop spinning, twisting behavior as it travels through empty space, without special lenses, mirrors, or materials. Researchers discovered that light’s internal geometry can naturally produce left- and right-handed patterns, challenging long-standing assumptions about how light behaves. By carefully arranging a beam’s structure, scientists can control where and how these spinning patterns emerge, unlocking a new way to manipulate light.
- Share:
Scientists have discovered a surprising ability of light that allows it to develop spinning patterns as it moves through empty space, without relying on special lenses, mirrors, or materials. The finding reveals that light possesses a hidden geometric structure that can influence its behavior in ways researchers previously thought were difficult to achieve.
The discovery comes from an international team led by researchers at the University of East Anglia (UEA) in the United Kingdom, working with scientists in South Africa. Their experiments demonstrate that carefully prepared light can be controlled through its own internal geometry, offering a new approach to manipulating how light spins and twists.
The findings challenge long-standing assumptions about how different properties of light interact. They could eventually lead to more sensitive medical tests, faster and more secure communications, and advanced quantum technologies that use light to transmit and protect information.
Why the Direction of Light's Spin Matters
One of the most intriguing aspects of the discovery involves chirality, a scientific term describing the difference between left-handed and right-handed structures.
Human hands provide a familiar example. Although they are mirror images of each other, a left hand cannot be perfectly superimposed on a right hand. Many molecules have a similar property, including compounds used in medicines. Two versions of the same molecule can have nearly identical chemical structures yet produce very different effects in the body.
Scientists can distinguish these molecular forms by studying how they interact with light that has a particular rotational behavior. Traditionally, producing and controlling such light has often involved specialized materials, carefully designed surfaces, or powerful lenses that focus beams extremely tightly.
The research demonstrates that appropriately prepared light can develop this behavior naturally as it travels, without requiring those additional optical components.
"Our work shows that light can naturally develop this handed behavior all on its own," said Dr. Kayn Forbes from UEA's School of Chemistry, Pharmacy and Pharmacology.
"You just have to prepare it in the right way.
"Most people think of light as traveling in straight lines. But scientists can also create structured light -- light whose brightness, shape, and direction are carefully arranged.
"One extreme example is light that twists as it travels, forming a corkscrew shape known as an optical vortex. Each twist can carry information, making this kind of light valuable for high-speed internet, secure communications, and advanced sensors.
"Light can also spin as it travels, depending on how it is polarized. This spin can be left-handed or right-handed -- another form of chirality."
Scientists Discover How Light Develops a Hidden Spin
Light can exhibit different kinds of rotational behavior. An optical vortex, for example, has a wave pattern that twists around its direction of travel, much like a corkscrew. Light also has a property known as polarization, which describes how its electric field oscillates. Certain polarization patterns produce a form of rotation called spin.
Physicists have long studied the relationship between these two properties. However, the interactions responsible for the newly observed effect were generally considered extremely weak and difficult to detect without specialized experimental conditions.
The researchers found that the situation changes when a beam of light is prepared in a particular balanced configuration.
Under those conditions, the beam can initially have no spin, yet distinct regions with spinning behavior emerge as it travels through free space. The effect does not require the light to pass through engineered materials or additional optical devices.
"It starts off with no spin at all," explained MSc student Light Mkhumbuza, who carried out key experiments. "But as the beam travels forward, spinning regions appear and separate out -- almost as if the spin was hiding and then revealed itself."
Rather than creating spin through an external optical component, the researchers demonstrated how the beam's existing internal structure can determine where spinning regions develop during propagation.
The Hidden Geometry That Controls Light
To explain this unexpected behavior, the researchers turned to topology, a mathematical field concerned with properties that remain unchanged when objects are continuously stretched, bent, or reshaped.
Dr. Isaac Nape, from the University of the Witwatersrand in Johannesburg, South Africa, offered a simple way to understand the concept.
"To explain it, imagine a mug and a doughnut," he said. "You can morph one into the other without tearing it, because they both have one hole. That hole is a topological feature."
The researchers found that structured light possesses its own topological characteristics, encoded in the arrangement of its polarization.
This underlying pattern acts like a mathematical fingerprint. Even as the light beam changes shape while traveling, its topological structure remains, influencing how different regions of the beam evolve.
As a result, the arrangement of the light itself can determine where its left-handed and right-handed spinning patterns become visible.
The discovery gives scientists a way to guide this behavior by designing the beam's initial structure, rather than depending on specialized materials to produce the desired effect.
"This gives us a completely new tuning knob for light. By adjusting its topology, we can decide how and where chirality appears," said Dr. Nape.
Potential Breakthroughs in Medicine and Communications
The ability to control light through its geometry could eventually make several important optical technologies simpler, more affordable, and more versatile.
One particularly promising application involves medical diagnostics and pharmaceutical research. Because many biologically important molecules have left-handed and right-handed forms, carefully structured light could help scientists identify these differences with greater sensitivity. Such tools could be valuable for evaluating drug safety and detecting biological markers associated with disease.
The same principles could support smaller optical sensors capable of identifying chemicals or biological substances without requiring large, sophisticated laboratory instruments.
Communications technology could also benefit. By encoding information into different twisting and spinning patterns, researchers may be able to increase the amount of data carried by individual light beams. This could contribute to faster optical communications, improved information security, and future quantum networks.
Other potential uses include manipulating microscopic particles, cells, and molecules with light, as well as developing more resilient quantum systems. Topological properties may help protect delicate quantum information against certain forms of noise and interference.
"The implications are wide-ranging," said Dr. Forbes. "This work could lead to simpler and more sensitive medical tests, especially in drug development.
"It could also be used to pack more information into laser beams -- boosting data capacity for communications, including future quantum networks.
"And because the effect doesn't rely on fragile materials or precision-engineered surfaces, it could be easier and cheaper to use in real-world technologies.
"This research could lay the foundations for a new generation of light-based technologies, by showing that light's behavior can be controlled using its own internal geometry," he added.
These applications remain possibilities for future development, but the underlying discovery provides researchers with another way to design and control the behavior of light.
A Hidden Property of Light Finally Revealed
For decades, scientists have relied on increasingly sophisticated optical equipment to produce and manipulate unusual forms of light. The findings suggest that some of these behaviors can instead arise from carefully designed structures already encoded within a light beam.
By showing how topology governs the emergence of spinning regions during propagation, the team has revealed a previously underappreciated connection between light's geometry and its physical behavior.
The discovery also illustrates how much remains to be learned about something as familiar and extensively studied as light.
"For something so familiar, light is proving to be far richer, stranger and more powerful than anyone imagined," said Dr. Forbes.
"And astonishingly, this new behavior has been there all along -- just waiting to be seen."
The research, 'Topological Control of Chirality and Spin with Structured Light', was published in the journal Light: Science & Applications.
