articles.title: Qué es QFab, la fábrica cuántica de USD 284 millones que Nueva York y NYU abrirán en Manhattan en 2030 y cómo podrán usarla startups y estudiantes
articles.text:
Nueva York y New York University desarrollarán QFab, una instalación de fabricación cuántica en Manhattan que reunirá una inversión de USD 284 millones y prevé abrir en 2030 para fabricar y probar chips, componentes y dispositivos basados en mecánica cuántica. El proyecto busca reducir el costo de acceso a equipamiento especializado para investigadores, estudiantes, startups y empresas, de acuerdo con la Corporación de Desarrollo Económico de la Ciudad de Nueva York (NYCEDC).
La instalación ocupará 2.137 m² (23.000 pies cuadrados) en 770 Broadway, en el área de Greenwich Village/NoHo, cerca de Union Square. Su apertura no será inmediata: el anuncio realizado en octubre de 2026 corresponde al financiamiento y desarrollo de la iniciativa, mientras que las obras, la compra de equipos y los programas académicos se desplegarán durante los próximos años.
El plan combina USD 29,2 millones aportados por la ciudad con otros USD 255 millones de NYU. De esa contribución universitaria, cerca de USD 100 millones se destinarán a la infraestructura y USD 155 millones financiarán la operación durante sus primeros diez años.
La tecnología cuántica estudia y utiliza el comportamiento de la materia y la energía a escalas extremadamente pequeñas. QFab no será una computadora cuántica, sino una planta compartida para construir y evaluar los componentes físicos necesarios para distintas aplicaciones de esa tecnología.
Equipos para transformar prototipos en dispositivos
La instalación contará con salas limpias, ambientes que controlan partículas, contaminación, temperatura y otras condiciones que pueden afectar la fabricación de componentes diminutos. También tendrá sistemas criogénicos, necesarios para tecnologías cuyos dispositivos deben funcionar a temperaturas extremadamente bajas.
El decano ejecutivo de la Escuela de Ingeniería Tandon de NYU, Juan de Pablo, explicó que el centro incluirá un sistema de litografía ultravioleta profunda. Ese equipamiento permite fabricar estructuras muy pequeñas en chips y otros componentes, pero su costo y complejidad dificultan que una startup pueda adquirirlo por cuenta propia.
La universidad conectará el nuevo espacio con sus centros de investigación en ingeniería, ciencias matemáticas, ciencia de datos, química, biología y neurociencia. La intención es que los desarrollos académicos puedan pasar de un experimento de laboratorio a un prototipo, y luego a una instancia de fabricación con potencial comercial.
Las aplicaciones previstas abarcan sensores de alta precisión, sistemas de comunicación con nuevas herramientas de protección de información, materiales avanzados, diagnósticos y diseño de medicamentos. La computación cuántica es una de las áreas involucradas: utiliza qubits, sistemas que aprovechan propiedades cuánticas para realizar ciertos cálculos de una manera diferente de los bits tradicionales, representados por cero o uno.
Estas computadoras no están pensadas para sustituir teléfonos o computadoras personales. Sus posibles ventajas se concentran en problemas de elevada complejidad, mientras que otras tecnologías cuánticas podrían utilizarse para estudiar materiales, detectar cambios ambientales o efectuar mediciones difíciles con herramientas convencionales.
Más de 100 empresas y 35.000 participantes previstos
Durante su primera década, QFab proyecta apoyar a más de 100 empresas: prevé incubar cerca de 50 compañías y prestar servicios especializados a otras 50 startups recientemente creadas. El esquema apunta a que las firmas puedan fabricar y probar prototipos antes de asumir inversiones mucho mayores en instalaciones industriales propias.
Las autoridades estiman que el centro alcanzará a más de 35.000 neoyorquinos entre actividades de investigación, educación y capacitación laboral. Más de 5.000 estudiantes podrían participar de programas de grado y posgrado, cursos, prácticas profesionales y otras oportunidades formativas.
La iniciativa también estará vinculada con la Universidad de la Ciudad de Nueva York (CUNY) y las escuelas públicas de Nueva York. NYU prevé abrir parte de su infraestructura a estudiantes de CUNY mediante programas asociados, certificados para técnicos, pasantías y otras modalidades orientadas a empleos en fabricación avanzada.
Los alumnos de escuelas públicas podrán acceder a campamentos de verano, talleres y propuestas educativas que contemplan herramientas de realidad virtual. El programa no se limita a la formación de investigadores con doctorados: la industria requiere técnicos, especialistas en equipamiento, ingenieros y trabajadores con distintos niveles de preparación.
El potencial económico del sector es otro de los fundamentos de la inversión. Según el anuncio oficial de la ciudad, las tecnologías cuánticas podrían generar hasta USD 2,7 billones —trillion en la escala estadounidense— de valor económico global en 2035, una proyección que comprende múltiples tecnologías y no una previsión de facturación exclusiva para computadoras cuánticas.
Participación municipal en futuras innovaciones
Nueva York tendrá tres lugares en el Consejo Asesor Ejecutivo de QFab, lo que le permitirá intervenir en la orientación estratégica de la instalación. El acuerdo incorpora además un mecanismo financiero poco habitual para una inversión pública de este tipo.
Cuando se genere propiedad intelectual con equipamiento financiado por la ciudad, el gobierno municipal recibirá 15% de los ingresos que correspondan a la administración central de NYU por esa propiedad. La participación puede incluir regalías, licencias de patentes, pagos asociados a determinados hitos y participaciones accionarias.
El modelo busca que la ciudad recupere parte del valor económico si las tecnologías desarrolladas con infraestructura pública alcanzan éxito comercial. También conserva una presencia formal del gobierno municipal en la conducción de un proyecto diseñado para ocupar el espacio entre la investigación universitaria y las grandes plantas comerciales de semiconductores.

articles.title: Panique sur Internet : deux failles PHP critiques touchent des centaines de millions de sites web
articles.text:
C’est l’une des alertes de sécurité les plus sérieuses de ces dernières années. Depuis le mardi 20 octobre 2026, le monde de l’informatique est passé en alerte rouge à cause de PHP2Shell, un duo de failles débusquées dans le cœur de PHP. Pour ceux qui ne connaissent pas, PHP est un langage de programmation omniprésent sur Internet. Il fait tourner les coulisses d’une bonne partie du web, des petits blogs aux boutiques en ligne, en passant par d’importants systèmes de gestion de contenu comme WordPress, Drupal, Joomla ou Magento. Des centaines de millions de sites web reposent en fait sur PHP.
Les deux failles sont jugées « critiques » par les experts en cybersécurité. Pour éviter une explosion des cyberattaques, l’équipe de PHP n’a pas tardé à mettre en ligne des correctifs de toute urgence. Les versions 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36 et 8.2.35 de PHP corrigent le tir et empêchent les pirates d’exploiter les vulnérabilités.
À lire aussi : Ces box Orange et SFR peuvent se faire pirater à distance grâce à une faille Wi-Fi
Deux failles débusquées par l’intelligence artificielle
Ces vulnérabilités ont été dénichées par les chercheurs de Wiz, une société de cybersécurité. Les chercheurs se sont appuyés sur plusieurs intelligences artificielles de pointe, à savoir Gemini 4 Argon de Google et GPT d’OpenAI. « L’équipe de Wiz a montré pourquoi l’IA de pointe change la donne pour la cyberdéfense », résume Raluca Ada Popa, responsable de la sécurité de Gemini chez Google DeepMind.
 Researchers at @wiz_io put Gemini 4 Argon to the test against complex cyber threats.
In real-world testing, it found more than two times more vulnerabilities than baseline models — catching a critical risk that previous frontier models missed.
See how they did it ↓ pic.twitter.com/EeKVi0kwjo
— Google (@Google) October 21, 2026
Les deux failles se cachaient dans le code de PHP depuis plus de dix ans. Il aura fallu attendre l’essor de l’IA générative pour les débusquer. Greg Brockman, président d’OpenAI, souligné que l’un des bugs se nichait même dans PHP « depuis quatorze ans ». « Compte tenu de la gravité de ces failles et de l’usage très répandu de PHP, nous considérons qu’il s’agit de l’un des problèmes de sécurité les plus importants », déclare OpenAI.
 OpenAI models helped researchers—operating as part of our Patch the Planet initiative—discover critical security flaws in PHP, an open-source programming language used to run an estimated 70% of websites.
Over the past two months, we led a coalition of maintainers, researchers,…
— OpenAI (@OpenAI) October 21, 2026
70 % des sites web vulnérables
En exploitant ces deux failles de PHP, un pirate peut exécuter son propre code sur un serveur vulnérable, sans aucun mot de passe ni identifiant. Concrètement, un hacker peut prendre le contrôle total d’un site, voler les données des clients, modifier les pages ou installer une porte dérobée, en vue d’une future cyberattaque, sans jamais avoir besoin de s’authentifier. Pour rappel, PHP fait tourner environ 70 % des sites web de la planète. C’est une grande partie d’Internet qui se retrouve en danger.
« Avec 70 % d’Internet touché, l’impact de PHP2Shell ne peut être sous-estimé », avertissent les chercheurs de Wiz.
Les autorités du monde entier n’ont pas tardé à réagir. En Allemagne, l’agence de cybersécurité (BSI) a classé la menace au niveau « orange », soit « extrêmement élevé ». L’organisme allemand a conseillé aux administrateurs de débrancher leurs serveurs d’Internet s’ils ne peuvent pas les corriger tout de suite. Par précaution, des communes, universités et hôpitaux ont mis tous leurs services en ligne hors ligne. Au Luxembourg, les autorités ont jugé les failles critiques et organisé des réunions de crise pour réagir dans les plus brefs délais.
 Effective Immediately, all organizations using PHP for their systems are advised to be prepared for an update addressing two critical vulnerabilities. PHP is widely used for web applications. These vulnerabilities often provide a direct path to the server’s file system or database. If an immediate update is not feasible, it is recommend that organizations take the system offline until it can be fully mitigated. NSA will follow up shortly with more specific guidance.
— NSA Cyber (@NSACyber) October 21, 2026
Outre-Atlantique, la NSA, l’agence de renseignement américaine, demande à « toutes les organisations qui utilisent PHP de se préparer à une mise à jour corrigeant deux vulnérabilités critiques ». Selon la NSA « ces vulnérabilités offrent souvent un accès direct au système de fichiers ou à la base de données du serveur. Si une mise à jour immédiate n’est pas possible, il est recommandé de mettre le système hors ligne ». Toute la journée d’hier, des administrations et des entreprises ont indiqué que leurs portails étaient temporairement désactivés. Tous les développeurs et les équipes de sécurité étaient sur le pied de guerre.
 #Maintenance 🛠️ A la demande de l'Agence Nationale de la Sécurité des Systèmes d’Information (ANSSI), le ministère de l'Intérieur a procédé à la mise en maintenance préventive de l'ensemble de ses sites Internet exposés à une vulnérabilité de sécurité. Par conséquent le site des… pic.twitter.com/8VqdMIYhwa
— Préfète du Gard (@Prefet30) October 21, 2026
 🔵 À la demande de l’@ANSSI_FR, le ministère de l’Intérieur a procédé à la mise en maintenance préventive de plusieurs de ses sites internet. Cela fait suite à une vulnérabilité critique de sécurité, annoncée quelques heures auparavant par l’éditeur d’un composant logiciel… pic.twitter.com/dHMC22E3AL
— Ministère de l'Intérieur (@Interieur_Gouv) October 21, 2026
À lire aussi : 3,25 millions de sites en danger – cette faille critique d’un plugin WordPress risque de faire des dégâts
Des cyberattaques déjà en cours
Sans surprise, les pirates n’ont pas tardé à exploiter les vulnérabilités. Les premières tentatives d’exploitation ont été repérées avant même que les correctifs soient disponibles. Dane Knecht, directeur technique de Cloudflare, a révélé que « des attaques précoces » avaient été épinglées par ses équipes. Il ajoute que les pare-feux ne sont qu’une « rustine » temporaire. Les experts en sécurité redoutent surtout les scripts automatisés, capables de scanner tout Internet pour repérer et pirater en masse les serveurs non protégés.
« C’est une mine d’or pour les hackers », résume Shahak Shalev, de Malwarebytes.
En tant qu’internaute, vous n’avez rien à faire pour vous protéger. La faille ne se trouve pas sur votre ordinateur ou votre smartphone, mais sur les serveurs à l’origine des sites web. Il n’y a aucune mise à jour à installer pour vous protéger contre les pirates. Les experts recommandent à tous les administrateurs d’installer la mise à jour sans attendre. En attendant, redoublez de vigilance lorsque vous surfez sur Internet. Par prudence, méfiez-vous des contenus inhabituels, des redirections ou des demandes de connexion répétées, même si vous vous trouvez sur un site web de confiance que vous avez l’habitude de consulter. Il est possible que ce site ait été compromis.

Ce défroisseur vapeur présente le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif
Le défroisseur vapeur Calor AeroSteam s'affiche aujourd'hui à 109,99 € chez Amazon. C'est actuellement le meilleur rapport qualité / prix de notre comparatif, selon les 6 modèles testés dans notre laboratoire.
Calor et le soin du linge, c’est une grande histoire. Pour défroisser ses vêtements en quelques secondes, le fabricant français sort le steamer AeroSteam, qui combine vapeur et aspiration du linge, pour de meilleurs résultats.

articles.title: Noté 9/10, le clavier gamer Apex Pro TKL Gen 3 efface son tarif prohibitif grâce à cette offre Amazon — Frandroid
articles.text:
L’Apex Pro, c’est le haut de gamme des claviers SteelSeries, connu depuis plusieurs années pour ses interrupteurs magnétiques ajustables. Cette troisième génération garde le même look. Elle récupère en revanche des fonctions déjà vues chez la concurrence, comme le Rapid Tap. Le modèle en promo est la version TKL filaire, sans pavé numérique. Bref, un clavier pensé d’abord pour le jeu, aujourd’hui disponible à moins de 180 euros.
Les atouts du SteelSeries Apex Pro TKL (Gen 3)
- Des interrupteurs magnétiques OmniPoint 3.0 au point d’activation réglable
- Rapid Trigger, Rapid Tap et double activation au programme
- Mousse acoustique, stabilisateurs retravaillés et interrupteurs lubrifiés en usine
Noté 9/10 dans notre test, l’Apex Pro TKL Gen 3 n’a récolté qu’un seul vrai reproche, son tarif jugé prohibitif. Amazon le fait passer de 249,99 euros à 179,99 euros. 70 euros d’économie qui le rendent bien plus recommandable.
Si, par la suite, l’offre mentionnée dans cet article n’est plus disponible, merci de jeter un coup d’œil ci-dessous afin de dénicher d’autres offres concernant le SteelSeries Apex Pro TKL (Gen 3). Le tableau s’actualise automatiquement.
Protégez votre vie numérique avec Bitdefender, la protection européenne de confiance. Bitdefender vous protège contre les arnaques et les fraudes du web. Profitez de vos activités en ligne en toute tranquillité.
Une frappe peaufinée dans un châssis tout sobre
Visuellement, SteelSeries n’a rien changé avec cette Gen 3. La version TKL reste entièrement noire, avec des lignes plus droites et plus sages que le modèle plein format, qui conserve les courbes de la toute première génération. Franchement, c’est moins original. En contrepartie, il se fond sans problème sur n’importe quel bureau.
Le gros du travail se trouve dans la frappe. SteelSeries a ajouté une mousse acoustique, retravaillé les stabilisateurs et lubrifié les interrupteurs en usine. Ces recettes sont devenues courantes sur les claviers haut de gamme, mais elles font leur effet. Notre testeur a salué une qualité d’assemblage excellente et une expérience de frappe impeccable.
OmniPoint 3.0, des touches qui s’adaptent à votre jeu
Les interrupteurs OmniPoint 3.0 sont magnétiques, et c’est tout l’intérêt de la gamme Apex Pro. Vous réglez vous-même la profondeur à laquelle chaque touche se déclenche, de 0,1 à 4 millimètres. On retrouve le Rapid Trigger et la double activation, désormais classiques sur ce type de clavier. La nouveauté s’appelle Rapid Tap. Elle donne la priorité à la dernière touche pressée, même si une autre est encore enfoncée (pratique pour enchaîner les déplacements gauche-droite dans un jeu de tir). Un mode de protection fait aussi son apparition pour limiter les frappes involontaires sur les touches voisines.
Honnêtement, tout ce paramétrage ne sert que si vous comptez vraiment l’exploiter. Pour taper des mails et coder, un clavier mécanique classique fera le taf pour bien moins cher. Le modèle en promo est aussi filaire, ce qui ne conviendra pas à tout le monde (la version Wireless coûte environ 50 euros de plus). Pour un joueur qui veut régler son clavier touche par touche, en revanche, il coche quasiment toutes les cases.

articles.title: Running Frontier-Class AI Models Across 8 NVIDIA DGX Spark Nodes | NVIDIA Technical Blog
articles.text:
AI developers aren’t just running a single model anymore—they’re orchestrating multiple models in parallel, chaining inference calls, and experimenting with frontier-class architectures that demand hundreds of gigabytes of memory. NVIDIA DGX Spark was built to bring AI development to the desk, and now you’ll be able to link even more Spark nodes together.
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA announced official support for eight-node DGX Spark clusters, scaling unified memory to 1 TB and opening the door to frontier-class models, multi-agent workloads, and near-linear pre-training—all running locally.
NVIDIA Sync makes it easy to cluster. Its Cluster Assistant handles setup and device management. Support for eight-node clusters in NVIDIA Sync is coming by the end of the year.
Read on for benchmark data on how inference, orchestration, and training scale as the cluster grows.
Run larger, newer frontier-class models
The biggest benefit of an eight-node cluster is memory. A single DGX Spark provides 128 GB of unified memory; four nodes reach 512 GB; eight nodes reach 1 TB. That capacity opens the door to a class of models that previously wouldn’t start on a four-node system, including the full GLM 5.3 (753B) model from Z.ai.
Beyond simply fitting these models, the cluster is designed to serve them interactively. As an early example, we ran GLM 5.3 Flash across an eight-node cluster, and measured roughly 80 tokens per second (TPS) in generation, suitable for interactive local development against a frontier-class mixture-of-experts model.
The full GLM 5.3 (753B) checkpoint runs across the 8x 128 GB cluster, making it one of the largest open models you can serve locally.
| Concurrency | Prefill, total tokens per second (TPS) | Prefill, per user (TPS) | Decode, total (TPS) | Decode, per user (TPS) | 
| 1 | 1,600 | 1,600 | 31 | 31 | 
| 4 | 1,600 | 750 | 51 | 21 | 
| 8 | 1,600 | 473 | 67 | 18 | 
Faster collectives with a Spark-optimized backend
Tensor-parallel inference spends a meaningful fraction of its time in collective operations such as all-reduce. On switch-connected clusters, we have been evaluating a Spark-optimized collective backend, RoCEnante, that reduces collective latency for the small-message, low-concurrency, modest-rank-count pattern typical of tensor-parallel decode on local AI hardware.
This backend implements an all-to-all exchange followed by local reduction. Each rank shares its input with every other rank, then adds the inputs locally. A single GPU kernel coordinates the exchange and reduction.
The main benefit is fewer communication steps. Ring all-reduce passes data between neighboring ranks over multiple rounds. This approach exchanges data directly with all peers, avoiding that chain of forwarding. For small messages and a modest number of ranks, this can reduce latency.
The tradeoff is more data movement. Each rank sends its full input to every peer and reduces all the inputs itself. As messages or number of ranks (nodes) grow, that extra traffic becomes more expensive, making ring all-reduce’s bandwidth efficiency increasingly attractive. If you need to support high concurrency, larger clusters, or ring topologies, NVIDIA Collective Communications Library (NCCL) would perform better.
In practice we see roughly 5% higher prefill and 21% higher decode throughput at four nodes (NVFP4), and about 18% higher decode throughput at eight nodes on the non-quantized model, consistent with the latency-versus-bandwidth tradeoff above. The backend is merged into FlashInfer and falls back transparently to NCCL if its startup test fails.
The backend applies only to switch-connected topologies, because it relies on direct point-to-point exchange between every node. It is not a replacement for NCCL, which remains the supported default and the better choice as cluster size and concurrency grow. The original one-shot all-reduce approach was contributed by the community (Jason Cook/el8).
Two, four, eight: Scaling the cluster
Low-latency NVIDIA ConnectX-7 NICs and RDMA on Converged Ethernet (RoCE) communication let DGX Spark nodes exchange tensors efficiently, so you can scale a model across more nodes to fit it in memory and to improve throughput. To isolate cluster scaling behavior and remove context-dependent behavior, we benchmarked a dense Qwen3.8-27B (NVFP4) model without speculative decoding/MTP across one to eight nodes:
| Number of Spark nodes | Topology | Prefill (TPS) | Prefill scaling | Decode (TPS) | Decode scaling | 
| 1 | — | 2,635 | 1.00x | 11.86 | 1.00x | 
| 2 | Direct connect | 3,285 | 1.25x | 21.71 | 1.838x | 
| 4 | Physical ring | 4,446 | 1.69x | 32.82 | 2.77x | 
| 4 | Switch (ROCEnante) | 4,556 | 1.73x | 36.34 | 3.06x | 
| 8 | Physical ring | 4,962 | 1.88x | 40.11 | 3.38x | 
| 8 | Switch (ROCEnante) | 5,105 | 1.94x | 52.58 | 4.43x | 
Two patterns stand out. First, decode throughput scales strongly with node count, from about 12 TPS on one node to 52 TPS on eight nodes.
Second, the best topology depends on the workload: A physical ring delivers excellent decode throughput for a single model spread across all nodes. A switch is needed once you want to split the cluster into independent groups, or run workloads that require direct any-to-any connectivity between nodes.
To try this yourself, this networking guide walks through cluster setup starting from a two-node configuration and scaling up.
Switchless ring topology and setup simplicity
Not every cluster may need a switch. DGX Spark nodes can be wired directly together in a ring, which lowers cost and simplifies setup—an attractive option for enthusiasts and small deployments.
Within a four-node DGX Spark deployment, NCCL defaults to ring-based algorithms for tensor-parallel communication, allowing a switchless ring topology to align perfectly with traffic flows and offer impressive throughput at lower expense. As Table 2 shows, the four-node ring performs well in prefill and decode throughput for this workload.
The picture changes as you scale or specialize:
- Eight nodes or split allocations: If you want to split a cluster into, say, two groups of four, a ring cannot express that topology; you need a switch.
- All-to-all and traditional HPC workloads: Anything that depends on point-to-point patterns (for example, MPI-based clustering) requires a switch; a ring would pay a hop penalty.
- The optimized collective backend: The Spark-optimized backend described above requires direct point-to-point connectivity between every node, so it applies to switched configurations only.
In short: Reach for a switchless ring when you want the simplest, lowest-cost four-node inference box, and choose a switch when you need to scale up to eight nodes, split the cluster, or run communication patterns that a ring cannot serve.
Multi-model orchestration with Switchyard
Not every request needs your largest model. On a shared eight-node cluster, you can get substantially more aggregate throughput by routing easy requests to a small, fast model and reserving a larger model for the hard ones.
NVIDIA NeMo Switchyard makes this practical: A lightweight classifier inspects each request (or session) and routes it to the appropriate model pool, with a load balancer distributing traffic across replicas. Because this layout splits the eight nodes into independent model pools, Switchyard runs on a switch-connected cluster, which provides the any-to-any connectivity needed to route requests across replicas.
In our prototype, we used OpenBMB’s MiniCPM5 2B as the classifier and execution model for simple tasks and Qwen3.8 Flash Next for complex ones. On a standard-plus-hard tool-use benchmark, the routed agent matched the quality of the Qwen-only configuration while freeing capacity on the cluster.
On the 92-case tool-use benchmark (including hard cases), the routed agent scored 91/100, matching the Qwen-only configuration.
Because MiniCPM serves roughly an order of magnitude more requests per second than Qwen per replica, shifting part of the traffic to the smaller model raises the throughput ceiling of the whole cluster. Allocating three Qwen replicas (two Spark nodes each) and two MiniCPM replicas (one Spark each) across the eight nodes, we get:
- ~1.5x aggregate throughput over a Qwen-only baseline when half of requests route to Qwen.
- ~3.0x aggregate throughput when a quarter of requests route to Qwen and the rest to MiniCPM.
A routing policy is a simple YAML file, and NVIDIA provides a sample policy as a starting point; developers can tune the split and classifier to their own workload.
Pre-training from scratch: near-linear scaling with nanochat
Training behaves differently from inference. When each node holds a full copy of the model, the only cross-node communication is gradient synchronization once per step, so clustering scales close to linearly. To demonstrate, we pre-trained a nanochat model from scratch (about 896.5M parameters, 20 transformer layers, hidden dimension 1,280- and 2,048-token sequences) and measured training throughput as we added nodes.
| Nodes | TPS | Speedup | Scaling efficiency | 
| 1 | 8,741 | 1.00x | 100.0% | 
| 2 | 17,202 | 1.97x | 98.4% | 
| 4 | 33,640 | 3.85x | 96.2% | 
| 8 | 68,079 | 7.79x | 97.4% | 
Eight nodes deliver a 7.79x speedup at 97.4% efficiency, the kind of near-linear scaling that makes an eight-node Spark cluster a credible platform for training small models from scratch, not just serving large ones. It is also a natural on-ramp workflow: Prototype and pre-train locally, then scale out as the model grows.
To reproduce the nanochat pre-training experiment or adapt it to your own model, the full code is available on GitHub.
Get started with multi-system DGX Spark
Eight-node DGX Spark clusters give you the memory to load frontier-class models, the flexibility to orchestrate several models at once, and the efficiency to train small models from scratch, all on the desk.

articles.title: Enhanced Games statt Olympia? Kein offizieller Weltrekord – aber eine Werbeshow für Steroide
articles.text:
Enhanced Games statt Olympia? Kein offizieller Weltrekord – aber eine Werbeshow für Steroide
Dutzende Athleten traten im Sommer bei den „Enhanced Games“ an – einer Gegenveranstaltung zur Olympiade, bei der Doping ausdrücklich erlaubt war. Eine Werbeveranstaltung, die einen tiefen Einblick in unsere Gesellschaft erlaubt.
Bevor Megan Romano an den Enhanced-Games teilnahm, hatte sie fast ein Jahrzehnt lang keine Wettkämpfe mehr bestritten. Sie schwamm in Las Vegas die 50 Meter Freistil als 35-jährige schneller als mit 22 Jahren. (Foto: Saeed Rahbaran)
Testosteron. Methenolon. Nandrolon. Somatotropin und EPO. Meldonium, Modafinil und gemischte Amphetaminsalze. Clomifen, Anastrozol, Levothyroxin und Liothyronin. Pflaster und Kapseln, Cremes und Tabletten. Eine ganze Galaxie von Steroiden, Stoffwechselmodulatoren und synthetischen Hormonen strömt durch das Blut von ein paar Dutzend Schwimmern, Sprintern und Gewichthebern. Millionen Dollar sind für diese Athletinnen und Athleten zu gewinnen, die das Zeitalter der Übermenschen einläuten sollen.

articles.title: Android XR llegará a las primeras gafas de Samsung en noviembre
articles.text:
Samsung prepara el lanzamiento de sus primeras gafas con Android XR para noviembre de 2026. Un responsable de la empresa ha confirmado a The Korea Herald que tienen previsto lanzar productos de este tipo a finales de este año (hace unos meses fijaron el lanzamiento en otoño, aunque aún no han concretado el momento exacto, ni el precio, ni si será simultáneo en España).
Las gafas inteligentes sin pantalla, con cámara y micro para leer el entorno y escuchar a Gemini a través de los altavoces, son un formato que Samsung está desarrollando junto con Gentle Monster y Warby Parker.
Las gafas han pasado por la Comisión Federal de Comunicaciones de Estados Unidos (FCC), un trámite habitual antes de que el producto se comercialice, y la información de noviembre proviene de la prensa coreana. La certificación en EE. UU. no facilita conocer el precio ni la disponibilidad en otras naciones.
Samsung entra en un mercado dominado por Meta
Meta sigue siendo el principal competidor en este segmento. La empresa propietaria de Facebook concentra el 94 % de los envíos mundiales de gafas inteligentes con IA sin pantalla del primer semestre de 2026, al tiempo que las gafas inteligentes sin pantalla representan el 96 % de todos los envíos de gafas con IA de ese periodo, según un comunicado de prensa de Counterpoint Research.
Además, contar con una cámara podría resultar molesto para algunas personas. En una entrevista a la dirección de Samsung sobre las nuevas gafas inteligentes, explican que hay indicadores luminosos dentro y fuera de la montura, y que la grabación se desactiva si se bloquea la luz externa o si las gafas se han quitado. La entrevista incluye un resumen (entre otras cosas) de cómo el teléfono se integrará en el proceso.
Si la gente está pensando en comprarlas, debería saber la diferencia entre lo que ha presentado Google con respecto a las gafas con Gemini y lo que ofrece Samsung. El 19 de mayo, Google presentó las funciones de Gemini para las gafas, incluida la conexión con teléfonos Android e iOS, y el objetivo es poder pedir información sobre lo que se ve, recibir instrucciones, responder a llamadas, resumir mensajes de texto, traducir conversaciones o textos y utilizar aplicaciones del teléfono mediante la voz.
Los requisitos para utilizar sus funciones
Esto no significa que todo eso funcione sin más, y en los comentarios finales del comunicado de prensa de Samsung se menciona que algunas funciones pueden requerir una conexión a Internet, un teléfono Galaxy compatible o la aplicación adecuada.
La integración con Samsung Notes puede que necesite servicios y dispositivos compatibles de Samsung. Los controles por gestos deben utilizarse con el Galaxy Watch9, y las traducciones y la navegación pueden variar según el idioma o el país.
Otra restricción en relación con las aplicaciones: hay que dar un permiso específico para acceder a la cámara y al micrófono de las gafas, tal y como se indica en Permisos de Android XR. No es únicamente dar en “Permitir” cuando el teléfono Android pida permiso para acceder a su cámara y a su micrófono; la solicitud debe indicar que ese permiso es para las gafas, y el usuario puede denegarlo.
Además, Google ha indicado que Android XR abarca distintos tipos de gafas inteligentes. Las gafas de asistencia sin pantalla son una categoría propia, y las gafas con pantalla son aquellas que muestran información adicional en las lentes.
Todavía no hay una fecha de disponibilidad confirmada para aquellos interesados en comprarlas en España, pero Google publicó una nota en Alemania en la que indicaba que las gafas de sonido llegarían a Estados Unidos durante el otoño de 2026, e incluso sin conocer el precio, noviembre es una referencia de lanzamiento, no de disponibilidad confirmada en España.

articles.title: NVIDIA Transforms European Retail, From Digital Discovery to Physical Operations
articles.text:
European retailers are using open models and physical intelligence across use cases — from a commerce platform cutting inference costs by 90% to to a fulfillment center where collaboration of different robotic fleets is simulated inside a digital twin.
Frontier Results With Open Models
Retail leaders and technology companies across Europe are using NVIDIA-accelerated open and frontier models to advance agentic commerce, digital product discovery and retail R&D.
Shopify post-trains open models to reach frontier-level accuracy at a fraction of the cost. Its engineers use the NVIDIA Megatron Bridge library for faster fine-tuning and NVIDIA NeMo RL for reinforcement learning. Shopify has post-trained NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Lightning for the GraphQL subagent integrated into Sidekick, Shopify’s AI assistant for merchants. The subagent retrieves store data for several Sidekick features, including Sidekick Pulse, which researches a merchant’s store and recommends ways to improve it.
On Shopify’s internal benchmark, the post-trained model surpasses a leading frontier model in accuracy while cutting serving costs by 90% and delivering responses 7x faster. Beyond Sidekick, NVIDIA CCluster vLLM inference optimization software helped Shopify achieve 4.5x faster performance and up to 12x lower inference cost across five additional use cases: catalog enrichment, merchant assistant, e-commerce shopping simulation, product taxonomy classification, and merchant and buyer recommendations.
Zooplus, Europe’s leading online pet retailer, with Infosys and NVIDIA technologies rebuilt its product discovery stack for the agentic era. A production ready prototype deployed inside Zooplus’ Amazon Web Services (AWS) environment achieved 86% search accuracy using the NVIDIA Nemotron Retriever library for semantic search and the NVIDIA Blueprint for retail catalog enrichment for generated, search-ready product attributes.
Photoroom results from its deployment with Vestiaire Collective, where its Image Editing API now standardizes every primary image, about 40,000 a day across 70 countries, at the point of listing. Listings processed by Photoroom sold at a 5% higher rate of liquidity, with 3% to 7% more unique views per product page. The pipeline runs on NVIDIA GPUs with TensorRT and Triton Inference Server, and NVIDIA Dynamo Snapshot can help users quickly respond to demand spikes.
Omi launched ProductDrop, a workflow that anchors every generated image to an approved digital twin, letting brands scale creative output across entire catalogs without introducing product errors. L’Oréal is using this approach, combining Omi’s digital twins with generated brand environments within its CreAItech program. Omi runs TRELLIS 3D asset generation on NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPUs, speeding up inference by 10x and reducing pipeline latency by 4x.
In addition, L’Oréal is accelerating the discovery of the best ingredient combinations, moving from months of experimentation to hours of computational screening, with the integration of NVIDIA ALCHEMI into its research workflow.
L’Oréal is also testing this approach with CurieOS, Orbital Industries‘ operating system for science and engineering, using OrbMol-v2, its open source molecular simulation model. Integrated with the NVIDIA ALCHEMI Toolkit and powered by NVIDIA accelerated computing, OrbMol-v2 is five times faster than comparable models and delivers 21% lower error than the next-best model of its kind. This AI-based workflow enables researchers to identify the most promising ingredient combinations for solubilizing UV filters and optimizing performance before committing to laboratory testing.
Mirakl, a software company for intelligent commerce, runs open models on NVIDIA GPUs, both on its own infrastructure and through European cloud providers like Scaleway. This keeps its technology sovereign, avoids vendor lock-in and delivers the speed and scale its customers expect. Mirakl’s Catalog Transformer pairs fine-tuned open models with proprietary services and has onboarded more than 70 million products, turning messy vendor data into accurate, well-organized catalogs.
Physical Intelligence Enables Training in Simulation
NVIDIA physical AI, digital twins and open models help simulate retail environments, automate warehouse operations and deliver virtual try-on experiences for European retailers and fashion brands.
Otto Group advanced its autonomous warehouse under human supervision initiative — built with Reply on NVIDIA Omniverse libraries and running on Google Cloud — to the group’s largest fulfillment center in Haldensleben, Germany. New capabilities let logistics teams design, test and optimize warehouse operations entirely in simulation before any physical implementation.
ALLSIDES launched its 3D Digital Twin Factory: an automated pipeline that transforms physical objects into SimReady 3D digital twins in minutes, capturing sub-millimeter geometric accuracy, measured physical properties and fully relightable materials that maintain accuracy under any lighting condition. Those digital twins serve as the foundation for simulating entire store layouts in 3D, as well as for tracking products reliably throughout the shopping journey and at checkout regardless of ambient light. Built on NVIDIA CUDA, OptiX and TensorRT, the platform already serves brands including adidas, Amazon, Nike, Zalando and Zara.
CATCHES achieved production results from its RealFit deployment with AMIRI of conversion up 55%, add-to-cart up 80% and gross sales up 56%, all after seasonal adjustment against like-for-like styles. The company launched PredictiveFit, extending physics-based virtual try-on to retailers, as well as CASI, a personal fashion agent that shops, styles and sizes for customers over WhatsApp, powered by open weight models including NVIDIA Nemotron 3, built on NVIDIA Omniverse and the Newton Physics Engine.
Explore New NVIDIA Retail Blueprints at the Nebius Booth
At GTC Berlin, Nebius is showcasing three NVIDIA Blueprints for retail, all available in early access and running on Nebius infrastructure, accelerated by NVIDIA:
- Agent Harness for Employee Productivity: An agentic assistant that consolidates scheduling, task management, inventory alerts and operational insights for store managers.
- Inventory Simulation and Optimization: A blueprint that can help retailers reduce overstock and stockouts by modeling demand scenarios, testing replenishment strategies and optimizing stock levels before users need to commit in the real world.
- Agentic Finetuning Flywheel: A self-improving loop that uses agentic workflows to continuously generate training data, fine-tune open source models and feed real-world performance back into the next training cycle.
Request early access to the blueprints and learn more about NVIDIA technologies for retail and consumer packaged goods.

articles.title: Tesla is prepping a Cybercab onslaught | TechCrunch
articles.text:
Tesla says it is preparing to launch its shiny gold Cybercab in new markets outside its home of Austin, Texas, in a bid to “literally take over every part of terrestrial transportation.”
“We’re starting with getting people from one place to the other, but we want to basically own transportation of any kind on Earth,” Chief Financial Officer Vaibhav Taneja said on the company’s third-quarter earnings call Wednesday.
Tesla has previously shown a concept version of a multi-passenger vehicle it calls the “Robovan,” but it’s unclear if Taneja’s bombastic comments mean the company is working on other types of transportation.
What was clearer on the call is that Tesla’s Cybercab expansion will begin in Dallas next month and spread to other cities by the end of this year. Tesla already operates robotaxi versions of its Model Y SUV in small fleets in Dallas, Houston, and the Florida cities of Miami, Orlando, and Tampa. The company also said on its earnings call that it will start selling Cybercabs to fleet operators by the end of this year.
Broader expansion of the Cybercab could set up a real fight with Waymo, which is currently the market leader for robotaxis in the United States, with more than 4,000 of them deployed across more than a dozen cities. Tesla has argued that its Cybercab is cheaper and easier to build, which should allow it to undercut Waymo and other robotaxi operators on price. But the company has to reach real scale outside Austin in order to prove that point.
Tesla said it’s ready thanks to a dramatic increase in the number of miles its self-driving cars have traveled in recent weeks. While that may be true, Tesla was mum on Wednesday about how much money the overall robotaxi effort is bringing in. Tesla CEO Elon Musk said the new ride-hailing business won’t be noticeable in the company’s overall financial figures until the second quarter of 2027, “and probably a big deal by Q3 or Q4 of next year.”
Tesla also made a change to its letter to shareholders that further obscures what little visibility there was into its robotaxi business.
In Tesla’s second-quarter letter, the company included a chart for “Cumulative Paid Robotaxi Miles.” A close read of that chart showed a 36% decline from the first quarter of the year. In the new letter released on Wednesday, Tesla changed that chart to show “Cumulative Unsupervised Robotaxi Miles” — an indicator of how far the fleet cars are driving, whether or not they have paying riders on board.
There wasn’t much more clarity on the call, either. When asked about paid robotaxi miles traveled, Taneja said the company is “seeing utilization improving,” but didn’t offer specifics.
Instead, Taneja kept most of his comments generally focused on Tesla’s plans to scale the Cybercab. That included praise for Tesla’s engineering team for creating a vehicle that, according to the manufacturing team, is very easy to build — and build quickly.
“They think this is one of the easiest products for them to scale in terms of manufacturing,” he said. “So scaling would not be that much of a challenge.”
What might be a challenge, Taneja said, is that Tesla needs to make sure it has “all the regulatory approvals” so it can “start deploying the Cybercabs as fast as we can produce them.” That echoes many previous comments from Musk, who has long claimed that “regulatory approval” was the biggest barrier to Tesla’s robotaxi plans, not technical progress.
Musk has always been a bit hazy about what approvals, specifically, he felt were needed. The company has run into a regulatory hurdle this year, though. In September, just hours after Tesla formally launched its Cybercab in Austin, the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) opened an investigation into whether the vehicle complies with current federal motor vehicle safety standards.
All automakers self-certify that their vehicles conform to these standards, and Tesla has claimed that the Cybercab is compliant. But it is missing features that the current standards require, like a brake pedal and side mirrors. The NHTSA has proposed removing some of these requirements, but that rule change is likely still at least a few months away.
Not every Tesla executive agreed on this during Wednesday’s call.
Asked about the remaining bottlenecks for a wider robotaxi rollout, Ashok Elluswamy, Tesla’s vice president overseeing autonomy, said they are “not purely regulatory.”
“It’s technology-driven,” he said. “We had initially had the robotaxi service from 6 a.m. to 9 p.m., and then expanded to 10 p.m. to 11 p.m, now it’s going to be pretty soon, [to] 2 a.m. So we’re slowly expanding the availability of robotaxi, and that is driven by the capability of the AI software.”
That could be why Tesla’s service still doesn’t operate on highways, and in certain conditions, although it has been spotted operating in heavy rain many times in Austin — something Waymo’s robotaxis have largely avoided. Elluswamy said Wednesday that Tesla plans to tackle more of these challenging driving scenarios by the end of this year, before scaling further.
“We just want to make sure that there’s not a single safety incident. That is our operating principle. And even if there’s the slightest possible risk at all, we don’t like to take on that risk,” he said.

articles.title: Localizing compliance at scale: Achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
articles.text:
Localizing compliance at scale: achieving South Korea’s ISMS certification
For ten days, auditors appointed by the Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) sat together with us and worked through 80 controls. That is what it took for a company headquartered in the United States, operating a global network serving Korean users, to be certified in South Korea. Cloudflare has now obtained South Korea's Information Security Management System (ISMS) certification under the ISMS-P framework.
For customers in Korea, this is more than a compliance checkbox. It is evidence that Cloudflare's security and privacy program has been examined not only for whether our controls exist, but for how they operate in the context of Korean law, the Korean language, and the particular expectations of Korean regulators.
What a Korean user sees when they sign up
The most visible result of this work is the Cloudflare account sign-up page. In most parts of the world, the line that sits above the sign-up button reads: "By continuing, I agree to Cloudflare's terms, privacy policy, and cookie policy."
A user signing up from South Korea sees something different. The Korean experience is triggered by the country selected at sign-up and by IP geolocation from within South Korea, and it breaks the same agreement into four separately labeled items, each marked required or optional, each linking to its full text, with an option to agree to all of them at once:
- 모두 동의 (Agree to all)
- [필수] 서비스 약관 ([Required] Terms of Service)
- [필수] 개인정보 수집 및 이용 ([Required] Collection and use of personal information)
- [필수] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 해외 이전 ([Required] Transfer of a limited amount of personal information overseas)
- [선택] 제한된 범위의 개인정보 제3자 제공 ([Optional] Sharing a limited amount of personal information with marketing third parties)
The three required items are hard gates. The sign-up button stays disabled until all three are checked, so there is no path through the form that creates an account without an affirmative action on each one. The optional item governs marketing permission only, and leaving it unchecked has no effect on the account creation (it merely opts the user out of receiving marketing communications).
The hard part: sign-up paths that never show a form
Itemizing consent on a form we control is straightforward. The difficulty was the sign-up paths that skip that form entirely.
Globally, you can create a Cloudflare account with Google, Apple, or GitHub. Those flows hand the user to an identity provider and return with an authenticated identity, and they never render our own sign-up form, which is precisely where the four consent items live. There is no step in that handoff where we can present three required items, link each to its full Korean text, and require an affirmative action on each before the account exists. The identity provider's screen is not ours to change.
We could either build a separate post-authentication consent gate for one country, or remove the paths that bypass the gate we already had. We chose the second. Social sign-up is not offered in South Korea, so every account created there goes through Cloudflare’s sign-up form, which enforces the required consents.
The country signal is the same one available to any Cloudflare customer. Cloudflare derives a two-letter country code from the client IP address and exposes it on the request, as the CF-IPCountry header at the origin and as request.cf.country inside a Worker. Reduced to its essentials, the branch is a string comparison:
// Illustrative: the shape of the check, not Cloudflare's own dashboard code.
export default {
  async fetch(request) {
    // Two-letter country code derived from the client IP.
    // Same value as the CF-IPCountry request header.
    // Cloudflare's network populates this on the incoming request, so there is
    // no geolocation database, lookup service, or extra round trip of our own.
    const country = request.cf?.country;
    if (country === "KR") {
      return renderSignUp({
        locale: "ko-KR",
        consent: "itemized",  // four separate items, three of them required
        socialLogin: false,   // no path that skips the consent form
      });
    }
    return renderSignUp({ locale: "en-US", consent: "combined", socialLogin: true });
  },
};
What that does not show is why the country code is not the whole trigger. We document the limits of IP geolocation: it is an estimate rather than an exact science, addresses rotate and change ownership, and it should not be the only signal where the use case is critical to meeting the objectives of a local requirement. A Korean resident traveling abroad, or behind a VPN or a mobile carrier's NAT, may not arrive with a Korean address. So IP-based geolocation decides which form appears by default, but the country a user selects at sign-up overrides that and carries the decision from there. The IP address tells us where a request came from; only the user can tell us where they reside. Keeping those two apart is what makes the consent meaningful rather than presumed.
It is a small feature. It took a country-level product decision, and a change to the account creation path.
What ISMS is and why it matters
ISMS is a detailed, localized certification standard. It covers security policy, access control, authentication and permission management, encryption, incident response, risk management, and disaster recovery, all assessed against how personal data actually moves through an organization's systems, and against Korea's Personal Information Protection Act and its associated regulatory guidelines.
Certification requires an independent audit by an auditor appointed by KISA, a governmental institution affiliated with the Ministry of Science and ICT (MSIT), followed by review from a special committee. It is valid for three years, with an annual audit required to maintain it.
The ISMS certification is primarily established under Article 47 of Korea's Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection, etc., with the certification criteria and procedure set out in its Enforcement Decree and in the public notification on ISMS certification issued by MSIT.
What the audit examined
Cloudflare is already certified against ISO/IEC 27001, ISO/IEC 27701, ISO/IEC 27017, ISO/IEC 27018 and many other globally recognized frameworks. ISMS does not replace any of them. It is a localization of the same principles, layered with Korean regulatory requirements, and that changes what auditors look for and how they look for it.
The controls in scope started with the review of data flows. We presented detailed data flow diagrams showing every path by which employees could access personal information that Cloudflare collects, processes, and stores. The flows themselves are not Korea-specific. What was different was the form the evidence had to take: the auditors were not willing to work from a narrative description of how data moves, they wanted diagrams they could read and interrogate. For each one, they examined every access control layer and tested its effectiveness, across our internal systems, our public-facing websites, event pages, and the Cloudflare dashboard, covering the full lifecycle of a user's data from first interaction through to destruction. Those diagrams are not published here due to confidentiality.
The audit also scrutinized the language and terminology of our consent collection: the exact wording at sign-up, the structure of each notification, and whether the items were presented separately and clearly. That is the kind of detail the ISMS framework is designed to surface.
Why the timeline ran to a year and a half
Part of the answer is how audit cycles work. An ISMS audit covers a single annual period, and all evidence, documentation, and systems must reflect that period. Our preparation ran past one audit year and into the next, which meant retranslating updated policies for the new audit year, re-collecting and reassessing evidence, republishing an updated privacy policy, and absorbing formatting and design changes our marketing and website teams had introduced in the meantime.
What the certificate covers
KISA defines the certified scope as a service boundary rather than as an enumerated list of in-scope products. The Statement of Scope submitted to KISA describes that boundary in three parts:
- the organizational and operational perimeter: the Cloudflare entities, teams, and processes that operate the service;
- the infrastructure perimeter: the network and platform the certified service runs on;
- the information assets and personal information flows that fall inside the boundary under the ISMS control set.
If a customer-consumed Cloudflare product is delivered through that certified service boundary, meaning it runs on the same certified platform, is operated by the same certified teams, and is governed by the same ISMS, it is covered by the certificate. The certificate is held by Cloudflare, Inc.
That is a different shape from the reports most procurement teams work with. A SOC 2 report or an ISO 27001 certificate describes the system it covers and names the services included, so coverage is confirmed by finding the product in that list. The ISMS certificate carries no such list. Coverage follows the delivery path instead, whether or not a product is named anywhere.
What this means for customers
For organizations operating in Korea, this gives legal, security, and procurement teams a local assurance benchmark alongside Cloudflare's broader compliance portfolio. ISO/IEC 27001 and SOC 2 demonstrate a general security posture. ISMS reflects Korea-specific legal and regulatory expectations. That distinction matters in third-party risk reviews and in preparing for a team’s own compliance assessments.
Cloudflare’s entry can be found on KISA's public register of certified organizations, which is the independent, verifiable confirmation to cite in a risk review. Broader privacy and data protection material sits on the Cloudflare Trust Hub.
The question that usually stalls a vendor review of Cloudflare is whether a particular product in use is in scope. The certificate does not answer that by name, because it lists no products. It answers by boundary, meaning that the product is in scope if it is delivered through the certified service.
For multinational teams managing security across regions, the certification confirms that Cloudflare's program has been reviewed against local requirements in one of Asia's most important digital markets, not just designed for global scale.
Building a better Internet, for everyone
ISMS is not a harder certification than the other assurance audits we go through. It is a more nuanced one. It is built around the regulatory needs of one specific region, and it asks for genuine investment in understanding and embedding those needs, rather than mapping them onto a common control framework.
Going through it made Cloudflare more global, not less. It pushed us to think carefully about what it means to serve users in a specific local context, with local language, local consent expectations, and local data protection requirements, and to put that into how the product behaves rather than only into a document.
That is consistent with what we are working toward: helping build a better Internet for everyone, not just in the regions where regulatory requirements are straightforward, but everywhere.
To learn more about Cloudflare's compliance and assurance programs, visit our Trust Hub.

articles.title: How bug bounty sharpens one researcher’s security skills
articles.text:
As Cybersecurity Awareness Month continues, the GitHub Bug Bounty team is excited to spotlight another top-performing security researcher from the GitHub Security Bug Bounty Program: @r31n!
As home to the world’s developers, GitHub is dedicated to the security and reliability of the code behind millions of projects, and our Bug Bounty Program remains a cornerstone of that commitment. Collaboration with external researchers is one of the most effective ways to improve security, and every year, the community helps us identify and fix vulnerabilities that make the platform safer for everyone.
The security research landscape is changing rapidly. AI has lowered the barrier to entry and become a genuine force multiplier. We use it across our own internal security programs, and we welcome researchers who do the same. However, what separates great research has not changed: validation, a working proof of concept, and a clear demonstration of real security impact. The tools do not matter; the quality of the work does. The researchers we spotlight this month exemplify exactly that standard through findings that are verified, reproducible, and demonstrate that a security boundary has been crossed rather than simply theorizing that one exists.
Researchers who consistently work at that level can earn an invitation to our permanent VIP program, which offers higher payouts, faster response times, and early previews of beta products and features. Learn more about how to qualify on our public bounty site.
As we wrap up our Cybersecurity Awareness Month celebration, we interview @r31n, a researcher renowned for their work on GitHub Enterprise Server, where they have repeatedly uncovered high-impact issues. Their reports consistently include working proofs of concept and clear reproduction steps, helping our engineering teams move from triage to remediation more quickly.
How did you get started in security and bug bounty, and what keeps you coming back to GitHub’s program?
I got into bug bounty because I wanted a way to keep developing my security skills outside the environments I work with every day. It exposes me to different products, technologies, and architectures I probably wouldn’t run into otherwise. GitHub is one of those programs I keep coming back to because there’s just so much surface area. It’s large, complex, and constantly changing. New features ship all the time, so it never really feels like a finished target. They also work closely with researchers, the bounty structure is competitive, and the swag is a nice bonus. It’s simply a program I enjoy spending time on.
What are your favorite classes of bugs to research and why?
I don’t really have one favorite bug class. What interests me more are exploit chains, especially cases where a few things that seem relatively harmless on their own come together and create something much more serious. An open redirect is a simple example. By itself, the impact might be limited. But if you find an allowlisted-domain SSRF that follows redirects, suddenly that open redirect can become a useful part of a much bigger chain. That’s probably the part of vulnerability research I enjoy most: finding those connections, looking at two or three separate bugs and realizing they can be combined in a way that wasn’t intended. It takes some technical knowledge, but also quite a bit of creativity.
How do you keep your skills sharp and stay on top of new vulnerability trends?
It’s actually a mix of different things. Security blogs, vulnerability write-ups, conference talks, proof of concepts, research papers, courses. I try to learn from wherever useful work is being shared. But most of it only really sticks once I try it myself. I can read a vulnerability write-up, but working through it myself gives me a much deeper understanding. If I actually reproduce the technique, play around with it, break it, and figure out why it behaves the way it does, that’s when it really stays with me. And later, when I see a similar pattern on a real target, it’s much easier to recognize.
What tools or workflows have been gamechangers for your research? Any lesser-known utilities you’d recommend?
I tend to prefer manual investigation and small, purpose-built scripts over large automated toolchains. If I notice I’m repeating the same task during research, I’ll usually automate that specific part. AI has probably impacted my way of working more than any individual security tool.
Even then, I think mindset matters more than tooling. You can become extremely good with a particular tool and still miss interesting bugs because you’re only looking at the target through the lens that tool gives you. Sometimes relying too heavily on tooling actually narrows the way you think. Tools change. Techniques change. Curiosity and persistence tend to age much better. So, I don’t really have one tool I’d recommend to everyone. The most useful tool is usually the one that helps answer the specific question I’m investigating.
Walk us through your general approach. How do you pick a target area, and how do you go from “interesting feature” to a confirmed finding?
I usually start by mapping out the application and getting a feel for how its different parts fit together. I tend to spend more time on complex functionality, integrations, trust boundaries, and anything that behaves a little differently from the rest. Experience and intuition matter too. Some areas simply look more likely to expose interesting security behavior. From there, I often think in terms of sources and sinks rather than starting with a specific vulnerability class. A source is a point where attacker-controlled data enters the application.
Think of a request parameter, uploaded file, API input, or data coming from another service. A sink can be a security-sensitive operation that consumes this data, for example, a network request, file access, process execution, database query, or authorization decision. The interesting part is tracing the path between the two. I look at how the data is transformed, validated, or passed across trust boundaries, and whether those controls are sufficient before it reaches the sink.
I like this approach because it lets me reason about attack paths without forcing my investigation into a predefined bug class. Sometimes the vulnerability only becomes obvious once you understand how a particular source can influence a security-sensitive operation. I consider a finding confirmed once I understand the attack path, can produce a working PoC, and can explain the impact.
Do you use AI in your research? Where does it genuinely help and where does it fall short?
Yes. Quite a lot, actually, but mostly as an accelerator. I use it for navigating unfamiliar code, finding call sites, tracing data through the codebase, and understanding how a system is structured and how its components interact. I also find it helpful for writing PoC scripts once I’ve identified the vulnerability.
Where it works best is when the question is specific. “Is this application vulnerable?” usually isn’t a very useful prompt. Give it the right context, explain what you already know, and ask a narrow question, and the quality goes up dramatically. There’s a bit of a paradox there. AI becomes more useful as you understand the problem better yourself. And I never treat its conclusions as facts. Hallucinations, false positives, bad assumptions, and confidently wrong answers are all common. Everything should still be manually verified. AI makes my work faster. However, it doesn’t replace understanding the application, developing intuition, or proving that something actually works.
What’s your guidance on using AI responsibly in bug bounty?
Use it to improve your research, not to outsource responsibility for it. If AI tells you it found a vulnerability, that doesn’t mean you found a real vulnerability. You still need to reproduce it yourself. You should understand exactly what’s happening, which security boundary or control is being violated, and what the real impact is. Ideally, you should understand the issue well enough that you could write the report without AI at all. Build a clear PoC. Make sure the security team can follow it. Know why every step matters.
AI has lowered the barrier to doing security research, which is great in a lot of ways. But you can also see the downside in the number of unverified reports teams now have to deal with. AI should make research better. Not just make more reports.
As the industry ships more AI-powered features, does testing them require a different mindset than traditional web bugs?
Yes. Conventional vulnerabilities still matter, but attackers may also be able to influence a probabilistic decision-making component through the data, instructions, or context it receives. But getting a model to say or do something unexpected isn’t necessarily the interesting part. The more important question is what that influence allows an attacker to achieve. Can they access something they should not or cause the system to act with privileges the attacker does not have? That’s why I don’t think model-level guardrails should ever be treated as the only or primary security boundary. You still need deterministic controls around the model. This includes proper authorization, least-privilege access, isolation, and validation. The surrounding systems matter just as much as the model itself. And traditional application security doesn’t disappear just because AI is involved. Model output should still be treated as untrusted input. If that output ends up in a browser, database query, shell command, web request, or another downstream system without the right controls, you can still end up with very familiar vulnerabilities: XSS, SQL injection, command injection, SSRF, and so on. I think the model is new. A lot of the dangerous sinks aren’t.
What’s one thing you wish you’d known when you first started?
Learn systems, not checklists. When I started, I was tempted to collect huge lists of techniques, payloads, tools, and bypasses and then work through them one by one. Those lists can be useful.
I still use them. But understanding how a system works has been far more valuable. Its internal logic. The data flows. Trust relationships. Assumptions. Why one component is allowed to talk to another. Why a particular restriction exists in the first place. I also learned not to assume something is secure because it looks secure, or because plenty of researchers have already tested it.
A lot of interesting research begins with: “Why does this work this way?” rather than “Which payload should I try next?” There’s some luck involved too. Sometimes you spend days following something that goes absolutely nowhere. Then you notice one tiny detail almost by accident and it turns into a high-impact finding. You can’t control that part. You can control whether you keep questioning things long enough to notice it.
What advice or resources would you recommend to researchers trying to land their first valid report?
Get comfortable with the fundamentals, then pick one program and one target and stick with them for a while. Constantly jumping between targets makes it difficult to build a real mental model of any of them. Use the application. Explore weird flows. Test different roles and permission levels. Read the documentation. Watch the requests and responses. Look at the APIs. Labs, courses, public write-ups, disclosed bug bounty reports, and intentionally vulnerable applications are all useful too. They teach you where bugs tend to hide and, over time, help build the intuition to recognize similar situations elsewhere.
One mistake I see a lot is relying on tools too early. Another is giving up because the obvious tests didn’t find anything. Tools help. They don’t build the mental model for you. And when you finally do find something, spend the extra time validating it properly. Create a working PoC. Make reproduction easy for the security team. Understanding one target deeply will usually get you further than trying to find a bug as quickly as possible.
What do you enjoy doing when you aren’t hacking?
Endurance sports, mainly road cycling, especially in the mountains. I enjoy the physical challenge of a long climb and pushing myself over longer distances. It’s also a great way to get away from screens for a while and spend some time outside. There’s actually something about climbing that feels pretty similar to vulnerability research. You can put in a lot of effort without seeing much progress. Sometimes you have no idea whether what you’re doing is going to lead anywhere. You just keep going. And every now and then, it pays off.
Any social media profiles you’d like to share with our readers?
You can find me on HackerOne.
Thank you, @r31n, for participating in GitHub’s bug bounty researcher spotlight! Each submission to our bug bounty program is a chance to make GitHub, our products, and our customers more secure, and we continue to welcome and appreciate collaboration with the security research community. So, if this inspired you to go hunting for bugs, feel free to report your findings through HackerOne.

Written by
