articles.title: Big Tech’s thirst for water is sparking a global resistance
articles.text:
After ChatGPT was released in November 2022, the tech industry was quick to herald the chatbot as the marker of a new wave of technological progress. As companies pushed to create more powerful AI models, the water demand of their ambitions took a while to become clear. In April 2023, a research paper out of the University of California estimated that training the large language model behind the initial version of ChatGPT had required 185,000 gallons of water. For every extended conversation someone had with the chatbot or every time they asked it to write an email, they were effectively pouring a bottle of water down the drain.
That statistic got a lot of play when it was released. It became an early warning sign of what was coming as companies pushed chatbots as a universal technology that could replace psychologists, educators, lawyers, and even people’s friends or partners.
As public concern grew, Google and OpenAI came out with their own figures. The companies suggested that querying one of their chatbots used mere drops of water. Independent researchers were not impressed, arguing the companies were taking a narrow view of the water use necessary to power and cool increasingly monstrous data centers. Those water demands can be quite significant too.
A hyperscale data center can suck up between 1 and 5 million gallons of water a day, comparable to the amount used by a city of 10,000 to 50,000 people — depending on the part of the world we’re talking about. Consider how these companies often cluster data centers together and it becomes obvious what a challenge it can be to supply them.
The water demands of individual data centers are also continuing to grow. It’s not just that they need more water for cooling as they become larger and contain more servers. The graphics processing units (GPUs) that power generative AI are much more resource-intensive than the chips and storage devices that traditionally filled data center racks. GPUs run harder and throw off more heat, meaning they also need more energy or water to keep them cool.
Data centers cannot just use any kind of water either; it has to be clean enough to ensure the equipment and pipes are not damaged. Tapping into public drinking water is both easier and cheaper than paying the cost of treatment themselves. That means data centers end up competing with communities over their potable water supply.
If we want to look at a part of the world where the issue of data center water use has taken center stage, there are few better countries to turn to than Chile. In October 2019, mass social demonstrations broke out across the country. One of the movement’s driving slogans was about water. It was poor timing for Google as it was fighting for approval and public support of its latest data center project, a $200 million data center project in Cerrillos, on the southwest side of Santiago.
The company made a pitch similar to the one residents in communities the world over have heard whenever a data center is proposed: that the facility would bring jobs and prosperity, and give the area a leg up on further tech investments. The reality was not so straightforward. Google’s new data center would bring a lot of short-term construction jobs but not much long-term employment. And it would need a lot of water — something Cerrillos did not have much of to spare.
Local residents were not as passive as the company had hoped. A group of concerned citizens established an organization called MOSACAT, which stands for Community Socio-Environmental Movement for Water and Land, and started poring over whatever information they could get their hands on to try to understand what the project would mean for them. “Usually these reports use quite technical language, and this is a working- class community where not many people are lawyers, for example, or experts on ecology,” explains Sebastián Lehuedé, a researcher at King’s College London who is from Chile and spent time in Cerrillos.
According to its own projections, the data center Google wanted to build in Cerrillos was poised to use 169 liters of water every single second. In just one day, the data center would consume as much water as all 80,000 residents of Cerrillos use for drinking in a year. To make matters worse, it wanted to draw that water from an underground aquifer that had been under a decree that restricted how much water could be removed since 2005. Just weeks before the project was rubber-stamped by the environmental authority, that decree had been upgraded to a complete prohibition on new extraction.
The water use estimates set off alarm bells for the residents. Chile had already been in an unprecedented drought since 2010. By 2021, more than half the country’s 19 million residents lived in areas experiencing severe water scarcity, forcing hundreds of rural communities to rely on tankers to deliver drinking water.
The local activists ultimately built the case against one of the largest companies on the planet. After months of meetings and advocacy to spread awareness, they were able to put a referendum question to the residents of Cerrillos about the project in December 2019. The results were damning: 49% of voters chose to reject the project, while 38% wanted it to go forward.
After both the municipality and community members filed claims against Google in 2020, the company returned with a new proposal in February 2022. It offered to cool the data center exclusively with air-conditioning rather than with water.
Across the city in Quilicura, opposition was building too. Microsoft announced its intention to build a data center in the community in 2022, the same year strict water-rationing rules had come into effect in Santiago. As in Cerrillos, residents were worried that another large data center would threaten their access to water and provide little in return.
Vicente Bardales, a member of the Quilicura Socio Environmental Resistance group, told Rest of World that the companies touch down in places like Quilicura only to “use water, [and] dry up the territory, but don’t give anything back to the population.”
Similar scenarios to that of Chile played out across Latin America. The following year, the Uruguayan capital of Montevideo found itself under a state of emergency as the country was hit by its worst drought in 70 years. As residents demonstrated against the misuse of water by industry, they found out Google was planning a data center in Canelones, a little less than an hour north of Montevideo.
“Only a tiny proportion of water in Uruguay is used for human consumption,” explained Daniel Pena, a researcher at University of the Republic. “The majority is used for big agro industries, such as soya, rice, and wood pulping. Now we have Google planning to use enormous quantities of water.” Pena had to go to court to get details of its planned water use from the Ministry of Environment, ultimately finding Google’s 72-acre site was planning to use 2 million gallons of water each day to power its cooling systems.
Uruguayans had fought for fresh drinking water to be considered a basic right in the national constitution two decades earlier, and as companies like Google moved in, they feared its realization was slipping from their grasp.
Uruguayans suspected Google had shifted its focus to their country because it had run into such opposition in Chile. Neighboring Brazil already has over 180 data centers, even as many regions regularly experience drought conditions. On the outskirts of Fortaleza, Brazil’s fourth-largest city, at least four major data centers were looking to set up shop to take advantage of a free-trade zone in the municipality of Caucaia. One in particular would be the size of 12 football fields, costing an estimated $10 billion, and though it will technically be owned by a local wind energy company, it is actually being developed to serve TikTok. This is in a region that experienced emergency drought conditions for 16 of the 21 years between 2003 and 2024.
What Cerillos, Canelones, and Caucaia are experiencing is increasingly a global phenomenon. Around the world, data center companies claim they will be respectful and considerate neighbors, but too often they hide the extent of the damage that follows from the scale of their demands on local resources. This is particularly acute in parts of the Global South, but the effects are now also being felt across the United States and Europe.
Adapted from “Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech’s Data Empires” by Paris Marx published by Riverhead Books, an imprint of Penguin Random House © 2026 by Paris Marx, and reprinted with permission.

articles.title: UN says we're going to blow past 1.5º warming, offers a "now what?" answer
articles.text:
In 2015, all but two countries agreed to make an effort to keep global temperatures from reaching 1.5° C above pre-industrial readings. Since then, most of the world has largely treated what they signed on to as aspirational, and one of the largest emitters (the US) has alternately withdrawn and recommitted to the agreement. Meanwhile, the planet has responded as expected to steadily rising carbon emissions and appears to be practically at the 1.5° limit.
On Wednesday, for the first time, the United Nations Environmental Programme (UNEP) acknowledged that reality and conceded that the goal of keeping warming below 1.5° was no longer a viable one. Instead, its new goalposts focus on keeping both how long we exceed that limit and how much we exceed it by, at a minimum. Doing that will require both dramatic emissions cuts now and the removal of hundreds of gigatonnes of carbon dioxide from the atmosphere before the century is out.
Bowing to the inevitable
Depending on which baseline you use to establish pre-industrial temperatures, as well as which reconstruction of global temperatures you rely on, the world has either gotten very close to, or already exceeded, the 1.5° milestone. The current El Niño event, which appears exceptionally strong, will almost certainly mean that we’ve gone over it no matter which records you choose.
The UN relies on temperatures averaged over a few decades to determine where we are, which means we have technically not gone above the limit yet. But, as temperatures seem stubbornly disinterested in dropping much even after extremely hot years, we’re likely at the start of the period where the 1.5° goal is passed. So, while it’s not technically too late to get on a pathway that keeps us below this, practically it’s already too late.

articles.title: Pioneers Across Europe Deploy NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models to Power Real-World Weather and Climate Prediction
articles.text:
Weather forecasts shape more than daily plans; timely weather information is crucial for energy producers, insurers and transport operators to plan around changing conditions. A global forecast can show a storm taking shape, but decisions about solar farms, shipping routes or insured property depend on what happens locally.
NVIDIA Earth-2 gives developers and researchers a family of open AI models and tools they can customize with their own data. Running on NVIDIA computing, these technologies support global weather prediction, detailed regional forecasts and environmental research.
StormScope EU is the latest model to join Earth-2 — a regional version of the StormScope model for short-term forecasting, trained over Europe weather and climate data. It uses EUMETSAT satellite observations to predict evolving cloud conditions across 16 Meteosat channels at 10-minute intervals.
At GTC Berlin, NVIDIA is showcasing a live StormScope EU pipeline in an interactive weather demo built in partnership with Earthmover. The demo uses Earth2Studio to run forecasts and Earthmover’s data platform to manage and serve the real-time results, which are updated as soon as new satellite observations come in, every 10 minutes. Earthmover serves these results as map tiles, letting visitors explore predictions across Europe without downloading entire datasets.
Developers can combine Earth-2 models in workflows tailored to regional needs, using StormScope for short-term forecasting and CorrDiff to add local detail to coarser weather data. Developers can also pick up these model architectures and train them for new environmental applications such as air-quality modeling. The open source NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo framework provides training and customization tools so teams can build applications that incorporate proprietary data and domain expertise to meet regional needs.
Organizations building on Earth-2 capabilities include:
AXA is using NVIDIA Earth-2’s FourCastNet 3 to study regional cyclone risk beyond the historical record across more than 1,000 simulated seasons, generating insights that can inform risk assessments and help customers target prevention efforts.
Vaisala Xweather is combining Earth-2 with its proprietary observations, lightning data and forecasting expertise to enhance its weather intelligence platforms for government, energy, maritime, transportation and insurance customers. Its work includes adapting StormScope with lightning data to advance short-term forecasting lead time and make these warnings accessible through Vaisala Xweather’s software-as-a-service offerings and AI-assistant integrations.
Video courtesy of Vaisala Xweather.
University of Manchester researchers adapted the Earth-2 CorrDiff model for U.K. air-quality modeling. It trained the model on the NVIDIA-powered Isambard-AI supercomputer and ran it locally on NVIDIA DGX Spark systems, bringing environmental modeling from a national supercomputer to the desktop.
TotalEnergies is exploring NVIDIA Earth-2 for solar-energy forecasting, evaluating StormScope-based solar-radiation nowcasts at two photovoltaic sites and developing models to provide weather information at subhourly intervals. The work explores how more detailed forecasts could help anticipate changes in solar-power generation.
Space42 developed SARDiff4Height using CorrDiff and NVIDIA PhysicsNeMo. The research estimates surface heights from a single radar image and produces uncertainty maps, helping analysts understand where estimates need closer scrutiny.
Explore NVIDIA Earth-2 open models and tools, and explore with Earth2Studio’s forecasting examples. Read AXA’s hurricane-risk case study and Manchester’s air-quality story to learn how teams are adapting weather AI to specialized challenges.

articles.title: NVIDIA Open Models Power a New Wave of European Public Sector Projects
articles.text:
Governments need modern solutions to serve the public while keeping sensitive information under their control.
Open models provide a path forward, letting governments evaluate them, adapt them to local languages and public services, run them on infrastructure they control, apply their own safeguards and keep sensitive data within controlled environments. Some open models go further, with the datasets they were trained on published so governments can verify if training data was licensed, biased or compliant.
NVIDIA partners and European governments are teaming to bring advanced models to boost the efficiency of public administration while retaining control of data and infrastructure.
Several are also building editions of the NVIDIA Nemotron-Personas collection, the partner-grounded datasets behind NeMo User Sim, NVIDIA’s open source library for population-scale user simulation that dynamically evaluates and trains models and agents in local languages.
European Commission: Scaling Governed AI Applications
Berlin-based software company deepset is expanding its Haystack Enterprise Platform, the foundation of AI@EC, the European Commission’s shared platform for building and running AI applications on commission-managed infrastructure.
The update connects agent development, execution, optimization and governance for all customers, adding capabilities to compare operating costs, evaluate answer quality and trace problems.
NVIDIA Triton Inference Server supports the shared services used to find and rank relevant information. The expansion builds on operating requirements demonstrated by deployments such as AI@EC, where reusable components, role-based access, audit trails and guardrails support applications including document summarization, knowledge management and multilingual policy analysis.
Poland: Advanced Computing for Healthcare and Employment
Deloitte is helping Poland build agentic systems for healthcare and employment services using open models.
Poland’s eHealth Centre is building its Intelligent Services Platform for medical imaging with NVIDIA DGX BasePOD and the MONAI framework. The tool will help physicians analyze X-rays, CT scans and MRI images, detect abnormalities and prioritize urgent cases, reducing the time patients wait for results.
With Deloitte’s support, Poland’s Ministry of Family, Labour and Social Policy is developing an agentic factory on NVIDIA accelerated computing infrastructure. Designed to support more than 400 labor offices, it will run models including PLLuM, GPT OSS and Inkling for document search, summarization and digital assistants, helping staff more efficiently assist job seekers.
NVIDIA is also working with SpeakLeash in Poland and the University of Ljubljana in Slovenia on country-specific additions to its synthetic personas program, with localized datasets planned to follow.
UK: Data for Locally Relevant Advanced Modeling
London-based Locai Labs released Nemotron-Personas-UK, a dataset of 1 million synthetic personas reflecting the U.K.’s demographic and geographic diversity while reducing privacy risk. Potential uses include healthcare evaluation and bias testing across age groups, education levels and rural and urban populations. For developers building public-service models, it offers a way to test whether models work consistently across different communities.
Germany: Digital Assistants and AI for Classified Work
In Germany, Materna is introducing Sinfonie, an on-premises platform combining generative AI, voice interaction and 3D avatars, with NVIDIA Audio2Face available for animation. Built on a project for a German state administration, it helps employees access institutional knowledge through spoken questions while keeping data on their organization’s infrastructure.
For organizations handling classified information, secunet, NVIDIA, Red Hat and deepset are going a step further. The four companies are developing a sovereign cloud offering built on secunet’s proven SINA Cloud foundation, which includes security components that have been authorized for use with classified information. The planned offering combines four components: NVIDIA accelerated computing and NVIDIA Nemotron open models; Red Hat OpenShift AI for deploying and managing AI workloads; deepset’s Haystack AI agent orchestration; and infrastructure operated by secunet in German data centers.
To support local development, the Sovereign Open Source Foundation Models research initiative (Soofi) is developing a family of AI models for German industry and the public sector. That includes Nemotron-Personas-Germany, an open dataset of 1 million records, each with six synthetic personas, grounded in the 2022 census across all 16 federal states and 400 districts. Created with NVIDIA NeMo Data Designer without real people’s private data, the dataset helps developers test whether public-service models work consistently across regions, age groups and communities. Like the U.K. edition, it can be used with NeMo User Sim so developers can evaluate and train models against simulated users based on synthetic German personas.
France: Advanced Open Models in the Public Sector Workspace
CANUT, France’s public purchasing body for digital services, selected LINAGORA and Docaposte to provide a sovereign collaborative workspace built on Twake.ai.
More than 2,500 eligible organizations, including municipalities, schools and healthcare institutions, can access the framework without running their own tender. The workspace offers public employees email, document sharing and collaboration tools, with NVIDIA technology supporting speech transcription and infrastructure hosted in France. Région Occitanie is the preferred partner for scaling deployment.
Greece: A Local Agentic Ecosystem
Greek AI and energy company KIEFER is developing an agentic factory built on NVIDIA DGX SuperPOD with DGX GB200 alongside Sophea open weight models and Greek-language tools for knowledge retrieval, speech and digital assistants. These capabilities stand to make institutional information easier to find and use for Greek-speaking public sector teams, while giving organizations control over where agents run and how data is handled.
Codefest: Building the Next Applications
In an effort to support public sector organizations in integrating agentic AI in Europe and beyond, NVIDIA Open Models Codefest brings together startups, software providers and labs across the region to turn open models into locally controlled solutions for public sector challenges, including medical reasoning, AI tutoring and model governance. The top five teams are Pleias, Zehnlab.ai, Disseqt, Algoritmica GmbH and ABA Technology. Deutsche Telekom and T-Systems have provided the compute infrastructure for teams to train and deploy large language models.
Learn how NVIDIA helps governments and communities accelerate secure advanced modeling and agent creation.
